title: Ukraine - Russia delays  forex  and repo trading and postpones stock market opening until late afternoon
text:
MADRID, 28 (EUROPA PRESS)

The Bank of Russia, as financial market supervisor, has decided to intervene in the country's capital markets following the package of economic sanctions announced by Western powers over the weekend, including the expulsion of certain Russian banks from the Swift system and the freezing of central bank assets.

Specifically, the bank has decided to delay the opening of the money markets, foreign exchange (forex) and repurchase transactions (repos) until 10:00 local time (08:00 Spanish peninsular time), three hours later than expected.

Likewise, stock trading (buying and selling of shares) is suspended indefinitely. The Bank plans to announce at 1:00 p.m. local time (11:00 a.m. Spanish time) whether the market will be opened. If so, trading will not begin until two hours later.

In any case, the regulator has ordered brokers operating in Russia to halt any sales of securities belonging to non-residents of the country, thus preventing foreign investors from exiting the Russian financial market.

These sanctions - which also include the exclusion of some Russian banks from the Swift financial mechanism - paralyze a large part of the monetary authority's 600 billion euros in gold and foreign currencies.

title: Kazakhstan cenbank to protect tenge from rouble volatility
text:
MOSCOW, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Kazakhstan's central bank said on Sunday it expects the Russian rouble to be highly volatile in coming days due to Western sanctions against Russia and stands ready to intervene and support the local tenge currency.

The bank said it would stick to a flexible exchange rate policy and only use interventions in order to "curb the unwarranted impact of excessive rouble fluctuations on the tenge". (Reporting by Olzhas Auyezov; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

title: Global Central Banks Likely to Review Policy Outlooks After Russia Attacks Ukraine -- Market Talk
text:
1941 ET - Russia's invasion of Ukraine will likely have global central banks recalibrating their policy outlooks, says Franklin Templeton . Markets are entering uncharted territory in terms of the implications of a war on Europe's borders, it says. The conflict between Ukraine and Russia could draw in other countries and NATO , or the war could be short, but the occupation long, it adds. In the coming days and weeks, investors will be weighing a range of topics, including the implications for hard and soft commodities, and whether the current global inflationary wave will give way to deflation, as global demand weakens in a prolonged conflict scenario, FT adds. (james.glynn@wsj.com ; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1806 ET - Strong Australian wages growth will continue even after the RBA raises official interest rates multiple times, says ANZ. The experience from the pre-GFC period is that high wages growth can be persistent, even in the face of aggressive RBA rate hikes. ANZ adds that current policy settings are on track to generate a material acceleration in wages growth. After a decade of weak wages growth, restrictive policy settings will eventually be required to bring wages growth down to a level consistent with achieving the 2%-3% inflation target over time, it says. This is likely to be a cash rate of 3% or more. The official cash rate now stands at 0.10%. (james.glynn@wsj.com; @JamesGlynnWSJ)

1749 ET - Municipal bond prices reversed weeks of decline Thursday as investors flocked to haven assets following the Russian attack on Ukraine. Benchmark ten-year triple-A general obligation muni bonds yields fell to 1.57% Thursday from 1.65% Wednesday, according to Refinitiv MMD, declining alongside Treasurys. Yields on more speculative triple-B munis also dropped to 2.28% from 2.36%. Yields fall as prices rise. (heather.gillers@wsj.com)

1649 ET - One Bank of Mexico board member considered the Feb. 10 interest-rate decision to be a dilemma between a 50bp and a 75bp hike, although minutes to the meeting give no indication the larger increase was seriously considered as the board voted 4-1 to lift the overnight rate target by 50bp to 6%, with a dissenting member favoring 25bps. The hawkish member noted that other central banks have raised rates in triple digits and intend to maintain such a tightening pace. The dissenting member said the bank shouldn't get too far ahead of the Fed in raising rates. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1648 ET - Mexican stocks recover opening losses prompted by Russia's invasion of Ukraine and close up 0.2% at 51454 points. Mining shares gain with Grupo Mexico up 4.1% and Peñoles shares rising 2.2%. Cemex shares close down 1.1%, adding to yesterday's losses. Cemex said it activated its $500M share buyback program yesterday purchasing around 10M CPO shares for about $5.2M. The peso slid to 20.56 against the US dollar from 20.24 yesterday. In local economic data, core inflation rose to a more than 20-year high 6.52% in mid-February from 6.21% in January, and December retail sales were down 0.4% from November but 5.2% above year-earlier levels. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1607 ET - The Ukraine-driven dollar rally stabilizes, with the WSJ US Dollar index rising nearly 1% to 90.36, off its intraday high of 90.90. The greenback gains around 1% versus the euro and the pound and 0.5% versus the yen. Elliot Wave's Murray Gunn tells WSJ the geopolitical tension favors the USD. "Given that the vast majority of global debt is denominated in US dollars, periods of 'risk-off' like this generally result in a scramble for dollars." He adds the Japanese currency is also a potential save haven "given Japan's domestic macroeconomic bias." Gunn expects the yen to strengthen for the time being. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1547 ET - The 10-year Treasury yield closes little changed, at 1.969%, after sliding in the morning on news that Russia attacked Ukraine, while the 30-year manages to rise 0.017 percentage point to 2.291%. Investors wonder how the conflict might alter US monetary policy. "With the Fed already being perceived as 'behind the curve,' we doubt these events will stay the Fed's hand next month," BMO says. But given the economic risks and volatility, the war "will at the very least, likely temper some of the most aggressive calls on the Fed," such as a 50 basis point rate increase, according to BMO . (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1351 ET - The number of newly listed homes for sale during the four weeks ending Feb. 20 was down just 2% year over year, says Redfin , for the smallest decline since mid-November. Pending sales rose 1%, the first increase since mid-January. The market again set new record highs for home sale prices, asking prices, buyers' mortgage payments and the share of homes selling within days of hitting the market. There was also a new all-time low for the total number of homes for sale. The good news, Redfin says, is that each week more homes are being listed for sale.(chris.wack@wsj.com)

1330 ET - Gildan Activewear 's "blowout" 4Q, according to CIBC , was driven by strong consumer demand and the benefits from its Back To Basics strategy. Net income totaled $173.9 million, or 89 cents per share, up from $67.4 million, or 34 cents per share, last year. The company's new three-year growth strategy outlines the next phase of growth "as it looks to deliver organic sales growth off an improved cost profile," says CIBC . With strong demand in North America, the company reported an EBIT margin of 20.2%, surpassing its aspiration of 18%. CIBC says that Gildan is built on strong fundamentals and is well-positioned to grow its share across end-markets . CIBC increases its target price on the stock to $49 from $47.(adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

1220 ET - The Russian ruble's depreciation in reaction to the Ukraine crisis is likely to fuel expectations that Russia's central bank could raise interest rates aggressively in coming months, Rabobank says. "USD/RUB may be trading below its early morning highs just below the 90.00 area, but the RUB is the worst performing currency in the world this year," Rabobank says. USD/RUB rises 7.4% to 87.3706, having earlier reached a record high of 89.9900, according to FactSet . The ruble has pared some of its earlier losses after Russia's central bank said it would intervene in the currency market and market participants are likely betting on further rate rises to bolster the ruble, Foley says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1218 ET - The Swedish krona is the worst performing G10 currency on Thursday due to Sweden's sensitivity to Russia's military invasion of Ukraine, Rabobank says. "Neither Sweden nor Finland are members of NATO and their geographical position around the Baltic sea ensures that whether or not they should be in NATO is a topical and sensitive discussion," Rabobank says. "The SEK could remain under pressure as long as Russia remains on the offensive." EUR/SEK rises 0.5% to 10.6737 after hitting a 21-month high of 10.7570 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1201 ET - The Ukraine conflict adds to the tailwind already boosting the US dollar, says Nancy Lazar, from Piper Sandler. "Prior to the invasion, we were expecting a stronger dollar on the back of the [global] slowdown we've been expecting," she says, adding that now the "Russia/Ukraine war will put even more upward pressure on the dollar." The greenback strengthens against all major currencies, especially the euro and the pound, and the WSJ US Dollar Index rises 1.1%. Longer term, the USD/EUR is up 9% in 12 months. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Volatility grips markets: stock markets rise and oil stabilizes amid Russian troops' advance into Kiev
text:
Volatility is taking markets that seem to have gone on a roller coaster ride in the wake of the Russian attack in Ukraine. Yesterday the stock markets collapsed with the announcement of the military offensive, but towards the end of the day they recovered while oil prices fell back sharply after having surpassed the US$ 100 barrier.

This change in trend was influenced by the speech of US President Joe Biden, who, although he reaffirmed tough sanctions against Moscow by the West, gave no indication of sending troops to Ukraine, alleviating an escalation of the conflict.

This boosted Wall Street and relieved investors.

Europe's stock markets are up more than 1% at the moment, but have shown several oscillations amid the advance of Russian troops into Ukrainian territory, reaching as far as the capital, Kiev.

In this context, the Moscow Stock Exchange is up more than 22% after the collapse of more than 33% it suffered the day before, which forced it to close its operations.

Biden threatened with limitations on the importation of technology, blockades to large banks and punishments to oligarchs close to Putin. However, he was not entirely clear on the energy issue, nor did he remove Russia from the SWIFT system, which allows transfers in dollars and euros to the country.

The Russian currency, the ruble, soared 2.3% against the dollar to 83.30 units, after touching an all-time low of 89.60. The currency was supported by the Russian central bank's first monetary interventions since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine, reported CincoDías The market expects more action from the central bank, which has to address inflationary risks.

What will happen to equities in the immediate?

"We lowered our conviction on the recommendation and moved from an overweight in equities to neutral. There was a change and the current status quo, with Western countries decreeing sanctions and Russia being in Ukraine, can be maintained for a while and generate additional volatility," Cristóbal Doberti, Sura Asset Management's Regional Manager of Savings and Investment Strategies, told Pulso.

Oil prices, on the other hand, stabilized and registered practically no variations in relation to the previous day. Brent is quoted at US$ 99.12 while WTI is quoted at US$ 92.68. In any case, both benchmarks are at their highest levels since 2014.

Crude oil prices are sensitive for Chile as it imports more than 90% of what it consumes and high hydrocarbon prices have become the engine of inflation in several economies around the world. It should be recalled that in the country, gasoline and gas prices are at historic highs.

"War conflicts are difficult to forecast. Historically, when there are rumors of this type of conflicts, the worst day for the markets is the moment when it starts, but then the markets recover, it has happened with Vietnam and the annexation of Crimea by Russia, and in the months following these conflicts the markets have a positive performance. here is the inflation issue. Although here it is not exactly the same, because the issue of rates and inflation is hanging around," Francisco Errandonea, partner of Focus Capital, told Pulso.

Russian invasion: daily updates of cyber actions to track

Feb 25, 2022

Editor's Note: This blog will be updated by the IronNet threat research team daily and on weekends.

Since November 2021, Russian troops have been building up at the Ukrainian border, worrying many of an imminent invasion as the conflict escalated. Last night, our worries became reality.

In a national address, which coincided with a UN Security Council meeting last night, Russian President Putin announced  that Russia will carry out "a special military operation" in Ukraine in order to "demilitarize and de-Nazify" the country. Shortly after the announcement, Russian forces began to move into Ukrainian territory in a move not seen in Europe since WWII. Russia is now launching a full-scale invasion  of Ukraine by land, air, sea.

What we know about the Russian invasion:

Political

* Russia states that it is ready to negotiate with Ukraine if they surrender.

* EU is considering a third round of sanctions targeting Russia's energy and financial sectors ( link ), including freezing Putin's and PM Lavrov's assets ( link ).

* Russian tank in Kherson flies a USSR flag ( link ).

* During the national address last night where Putin announced the military operation in Ukraine, he called on Ukrainian soldiers to put down their weapons. He also warned against outside interference, saying: "A couple of words for those who would be tempted to intervene. Russia will respond immediately and you will have consequences that you never have had before in your history." * Access a full English transcript of the speech here. 

* NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenbergstates NATO has no troops inside Ukraine, and there are no plans to send troops into the country.

* Western countries including the U.S. and U.K. are expected  to announce additional sanctions against Russia and those involved in the invasion later today (02/24).

Economic

* Russian gas exports through Ukraine rose 38% on Thursday (2/24) and are expected to increase another 24% on Friday (2/25) ( link ).

* Russia's billionaires have lost $39 billion in the last 24 hours (2/24) ( link ).

* Oil prices have surged  over $100 a barrel for first time since 2014.

* Russian stocks  fall the most on record, losing more than $250 billion (~45%).

* The market cap of Russia's largest bank cut almost in half.

* The Russian central bankhas purchased  billions of roubles to prevent Moscow stock exchange collapse and to prop up the currency after it plunged to an all-time low of 89.60 against the dollar.

Kinetic

* Kyiv has entered a defensive phase ( link ).

* Russian military claims it has taken the Hostomel airport just outside Kyiv and that Kyiv is blocked from the West.

* Unconfirmed reports that Russian forces are massing at the Ukrainian-Polish border ( link , link ).

* The initial wave of strikes appears to involves cruise missiles, artillery, and airstrikes targeting border guards and military infrastructure, including airbases.

* There are various reports of bombings and explosions in multiple Ukrainian cities, including Mariupol, Kramatorsk, Kharkiv, Kyiv, and more.

* Russia launched an air assault  against Antonov International Airport (~15 minutes west of Kyiv). Some reports state that they have seized control.

* Russian troops are moving on three main axes : Crimea toward Kherson, Belarus toward Kyiv, and from the northeast toward Kharkiv.

* Ukrainian President Zelenskyy states  Russian forces are trying to seize the Chernobyl nuclear plant.

Cyber actions the IronNet threat analyst team is currently tracking

Cyber Warfare

* Threat actor leaks International Monetary Fund (IMF) emails and hashed passwords ( link ).

title: Operation  kill the ruble: new record in its exchange rate against the dollar
text:
The Russian currency has depreciated 16% against the U.S. dollar since its 2021 peak and set a record low of 0.0118 dollars on Thursday. That is, one dollar was exchanged for 89.60 rubles: something unprecedented.

On December 15, 2014, with the first international sanctions in force for the annexation of Crimea, the ruble plummeted in its cross against the dollar and broke a record: one dollar was exchanged for 60 rubles. A figure that was considered "a psychological barrier" for the Russian currency, as Steve Rosenberg, the BBC's Moscow correspondent, wrote at the time.

This Thursday, that record was buried. The Russian currency hit a new all-time low, exchanging one dollar for 89.60 rubles, prompting Russia's Central Bank to say it would "intervene in the foreign exchange market and provide additional liquidity to the banking sector," CNN Business reported. By Friday afternoon, one dollar was worth 83 rubles; in other words, one ruble exchanged for 0.012 dollars and 0.010 euros.

Stemming the depreciation Destroying the ruble seems to be the goal of international sanctions, imposing restrictions on trade and financial transactions. "Should the ruble relatively quickly reach and exceed 100 against the dollar, the possibility of a rate hike could come into play," Piotr Matys, a senior currency strategist at London-based InTouch Capital Markets, said in remarks picked up by Bloomberg this week.

"Currency options see a greater than 50% chance of the ruble reaching 100 to the dollar in the second quarter," according to data compiled by the economic information agency.

Matys assured that "monetary intervention is the first line of defense and the central bank has accumulated significant foreign exchange reserves that allow it to intervene to slow the pace of ruble depreciation."

As for sanctions, another flank that could be targeted is Russian exports of gas, oil, wheat and other raw materials, such as nickel: Russia is one of the largest exporters of this mineral, with a global market share of 49%, KPMG's Metals & Mining in Russia report revealed in 2016. Palladium's market share was 42% then; diamonds, 33%; aluminum, 26%; platinum, 13%; and steel, 7%.

Some of those metals are going to Germany, a country to which Russia exported $18.9 billion in 2019 and from which it imported $30 billion, according to the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC), a project that emerged from MIT. Russia's main trading partners that year were China, the Netherlands, Belarus, Germany and Italy.

The link between Moscow and Beijing cannot be overlooked. Last year, Russia communicated that it was going to reduce the dollar assets of its sovereign wealth fund and instead invest in euro, yuan and gold assets. At the same time and for the first time, more than three quarters of Russia's trade with China was settled in euros. And also in 2021, Vasily Zablotsky, chairman of the Russian banks lobby confirmed to Reuters that Russia could issue OFZ government bonds denominated in Chinese yuan in two years.

title: UPDATE 3-Rouble climbs off record low, Russian stocks soar but sanctions bite
text:
* Rouble recovers from all-time lows

* Russian stocks jump after massive plunge

* Russian missiles pound Kyiv

* Investors eyeing c.bank's every move (Updates prices, adds bullets, JP Morgan)

By Andrey Ostroukh and Alexander Marrow

MOSCOW, Feb 25 (Reuters) - The rouble firmed on Friday after hitting all-time lows the previous day when Russia began invading Ukraine, while stock indexes rose sharply after their biggest one-day fall on record and the central bank stepped up support for sanctioned banks.

No Russian assets were left unscathed in heavy selling on Thursday. The fighting in Ukraine continued on Friday, with Russian missiles pounding Kyiv, families cowering in shelters and authorities telling residents to prepare Molotov cocktails to defend Ukraine's capital.

By 1600 GMT, the rouble had gained 2.6% against the dollar to 83.03 after hitting a record low of 89.60 in highly volatile trading on Thursday.

Against the euro, the rouble firmed 2% to trade at 93.27 , having hit an all-time low of 101.03 on the interbank market on Thursday.

The currency was supported by the first Russian central bankcurrency interventions since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

SANCTIONS BITE

The market was also digesting new harsh Western sanctions against Russia.

The measures stopped short of disconnecting Russia from the SWIFT global interbank payments system or targeting its oil and gas exports, and Russia has spent the past seven years building up formidable financial defences.

"However, the possibility (of disconnection from SWIFT)remains and uncertainty hurts the market more than the worst sanctions – focus will be on developments in Ukraine, the potential for negotiations, and any further sanctions," BCS Brokerage said in a note.

But analysts said Russia's economy is unlikely to withstand the onslaught of coordinated sanctions from the West in the long run.

Clients of some Russian banks under Western sanctions will no longer be able to use their cards abroad or with mobile payment systems from Apple and Google, the central bank said, as it stepped up support for banks.

Russian stock indexes pared heavy losses after Thursday's record one-day fall.

The dollar-denominated RTS index soared 26.1% to 936.9 points. The rouble-based MOEX Russian index gained 20% to 2,470.5 points, heading away from its weakest level since early 2016 of 1,681.55 that it hit on Thursday.

JP Morgan said it was interested to see what would happen to dividend payments, with the top five listed companies in Russia forecast to dish out $18 billion in dividends.

"Will a sanctioned Russian financial system be happy to pay away that much money to largely foreign shareholders when they are excluded from the financial system?"

VTB Bank on Friday said it may still pay dividends for 2021, Russian news agencies reported, but would analyse all possibilities between now and April.

INFLATION

The market expects more action from the central bank, which has to address inflationary risks. The weakening in the rouble after the invasion of Ukraine is expected to dent living standards in Russia and to stoke inflation that is already close to 9%.

The central bank may now carry out an unplanned interest rate hike as it did in late 2014, when it raised the key rate to 17% from 10.5% late at night as the rouble plummeted, analysts say.

"We think a prompt out-of-schedule 400bp or bigger hike by the CBR is likely with the key rate exceeding 13%," Morgan Stanley said in a note.

Alor Brokerage said the central bank could hike the rate by 2-3 percentage points in the near future, aiming at keeping the rouble near 80 to the dollar and 90 to the euro.

The central bank, which targets inflation at 4%, is next due to consider raising rates at its board meeting on March 18.

(Reporting by Andrey Ostroukh and Alexander Marrow; additional reporting by Elena Fabrichnaya in Moscow and Marc Jones in London; Editing by Kim Coghill, Gareth Jones and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

title: Dollar opens sharply lower in Chile and returns to $810 levels on further calm after Ukraine invasion
text:
The dollar in Chile opened sharply lower on Friday, in a market that followed closely -although somewhat more calmly than yesterday- the second day of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, which led the United States and other Western countries to decree a series of sanctions that investors were evaluating how they will impact the global scene.

The dollar opened down $5.10 to settle at $815.00, after yesterday's jump of almost $30.00, and then deepened its decline by $8.78 to trade at $810.63 before 9am.

Despite the initial sharp decline, however, the view from the market is that the unfolding news in Europe will continue to have an impact in the days ahead.

"Although today we could see a natural correction after such a strong advance on Thursday, any indication of further attacks by Russia on Ukrainian soil and/or war intervention by other world powers could support a strong advance of the greenback in our country, considering that the dollar has been used as a safe haven currency (for economic support), while emerging currencies would continue to show weakness," says Capitaria's head of Trading studies, Ricardo Bustamante.

For midday this Friday, the Ministry of Finance convened an emergency session of the Financial Stability Council (FSB) to address the economic and market implications of the war situation involving Russia and Ukraine.

The instance is chaired by the Treasury and has the participation of the Central Bank, the Superintendence of Pensions and the Financial Market Commission (CMF).

title: VIDEO. Russian all-out offensive in Ukraine: intensified attacks and went for the capital
text:
KIEV and MOSCOW

Ukraine decreed this morning a general mobilization to try to stop a total Russian offensive, which in less than 24 hours approached Kiev - explosions had already been heard in the capital -, leaving more than dozens of people dead -many of them civilians- and some 100,000 displaced. Meanwhile, Volodomir Zelenski's government claimed to have killed some 50 Russian soldiers and downed at least 7 planes and helicopters.

The invasion provoked in response a reinforcement of Western economic sanctions against Russia, judged insufficient by the Ukrainian president, who regretted that his country has been left "alone" to face the Russian troops.

Last night, most of the population in Kiev was taking refuge, while the Government was distributing weapons to resist the Russian advance.

U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said he was "convinced" that Russia will try to overthrow the Ukrainian government and did not rule out that Moscow may try to go further in its attempt to regain influence in neighboring countries.

The attacks were air and ground attacks. Russian troops entered from the north, south and east of the country and seized a strategic air base near Kiev, as well as the area of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, still contaminated by radioactivity from the 1986 nuclear accident, when Ukraine was part of the now dismembered Soviet Union.

A STONE'S THROW FROM KIEV

The Gostomel air base fell after an attack carried out by soldiers flown in by helicopter from Belarus, a country allied with Russia, witnesses reported.

"The helicopters arrived and the fighting started. They were firing with machine guns and grenade launchers," said one of the witnesses, Serguiy Storojouk. That airfield was to be the outpost for launching an offensive on Kiev, which was expected in the early hours of the morning.

The Russian Ministry of Defense stated that all missions on the first day of operations "were successfully completed".

President Vladimir Putin announced the offensive during the early hours of Thursday morning, as reported in yesterday's edition of this newspaper.

The Russian military claimed that it destroyed 74 military installations, including 11 airfields, and that separatists in eastern Ukraine are advancing and taking control of territories.

Putin, who demands that NATO close its doors to Ukraine, assured that he does not seek the "occupation" of this former Soviet republic, but "a demilitarization and denazification" of the country and to defend the pro-Russian rebels, whose independence he recognized on Monday.

About 100,000 people fled their homes and thousands sought refuge abroad, the UN said.

Olena Kurilo was injured by glass shattering in her home caused by shelling in Chuguev, near Kharkov. "I will never, under any conditions, surrender to Putin. Better to die," said the 52-year-old teacher, her face covered with bandages.

U.S. President Joe Biden announced restrictions on exports to Russia and technology imports from Russia, as well as sanctions against Russian banks and tycoons. The European Union (EU) also decided to adopt sanctions with "massive and severe" consequences against Russia. French President Emmanuel Macron called Putin to "call for an immediate end" to the offensive, the French Presidency said.

The invasion has hit international markets. Brent crude oil surpassed $100 per barrel for the first time in seven years and European stock markets plunged yesterday, although Wall Street closed in the green.

The Russian currency, the ruble, hit an all-time low against the dollar before Russia's central bankintervened.

FALL OF CHERNOBYL

The Ukrainian government announced the seizure by Russian troops of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant. "After a fierce battle we lost control of the Chernobyl site," said Mikhail Podoliak, chief advisor to President Zelenski's office.

Following the loss of control of this area still heavily contaminated by the worst nuclear accident in history, the condition of the plant's facilities, the cover insulating the accident reactor and a repository for nuclear fuel is unknown, the senior official said.

"This is one of the biggest threats to Europe today," he said, estimating that the Russians could organize "provocative" activities at the site to blame Ukraine.

Separately, Russian police detained about 1,400 people in several cities for participating in anti-war demonstrations in Ukraine, according to human rights NGO OVD-info.

The UN Security Council is expected to vote today for a resolution condemning Russia in the strongest possible terms for attacking Ukraine and demanding the immediate withdrawal of all its forces, according to US sources.

title: Russian troops intensify attacks against Kiev
text:
Russian military forces are trying to advance towards Kiev, the target of missiles on Friday at dawn, according to the Ukrainian government, which denounced attacks against civilians on the second day of this invasion, which has already left more than 100 dead and some 100,000 displaced.

The Russian invasion provoked an increase in Western economic sanctions against Russia, judged insufficient by the Ukrainian president, Volodomir Zelenski, who decreed a general mobilization to stop the Russian advance and regretted that his country was "alone" in the face of this offensive.

Kiev dawned Friday with two loud explosions in the center of the capital, as AFP journalists could verify. "Horrible shots from Russian missiles over Kiev," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba denounced on Twitter.

The Ukrainian military confirmed that it was Russian "missile fire" on the capital and that two of them had been able to be intercepted in mid-flight. The mayor of Kiev, Vitali Klichko, indicated that three people were wounded, one of them in critical condition, in a residential neighborhood.

According to Western military sources, Kiev is Russian President Vladimir Putin's main target to "decapitate the government" of Ukraine and install a pro-Moscow executive.

On Thursday, Russian troops entered through northern, southern and eastern Ukraine in an offensive that Zelenski said claimed 137 civilian lives and wounded more than 300 people.

"They said civilians were not targeted, but it's another one of their lies (...) Tonight, they started shelling civilian neighborhoods. This reminds us of (the Nazi offensive of) 1941," the Ukrainian president denounced Friday in a video posted on social networks.

Zelenski praised Ukrainians for their "heroism" and assured that his troops "do everything possible" to defend the country.

"Russia will have to talk to us sooner or later. The way we will be able to stop the fighting and stop the invasion. The sooner this conversation takes place, the smaller the losses will be, including for Russia," he estimated.

On Thursday, the Russian army took control of the Chernobyl power plant area, still contaminated by radioactivity from the 1986 nuclear accident, and the Gostomel air base, a strategic point at the gates of Kiev.

According to Zelenski, Russian "sabotage groups" have already gained access to the capital, where a curfew is in force. Also, according to the governor of Sumy (northeast), all the municipalities of that region bordering Russia "are surrounded" and "many" Russian armored vehicles were sent towards Kiev.

- Refugees fleeing

After weeks of increasing tension, with more than 150,000 troops on the borders with Ukraine, Putin decided to begin the invasion of its pro-western neighbor, which immediately came under Russian fire in a large part of its territory.

The Russian army assured that it destroyed 74 military installations, including 11 airfields, and that separatists in eastern Ukraine are advancing and taking control of territories.

For their part, the Ukrainian armed forces estimated that more than 30 tanks, up to 130 combat vehicles, 7 aircraft and 6 Russian helicopters were neutralized by their forces.

Putin, who demands that NATO closes its doors to Ukraine, assured that he does not seek the "occupation" of this former Soviet republic, but "a demilitarization and denazification" of the country, as well as to defend the pro-Russian rebels, whose independence he recognized on Monday.

About 100,000 people fled their homes and thousands sought refuge abroad, the UN said. Just hours after the start of the invasion, the first Ukrainian refugees were beginning to arrive in Hungary, Romania or Poland.

"My life has completely changed in half a day. But it is very good to know that we have somewhere to go," explained Iryna, a 42-year-old woman, who spent the night together with dozens of compatriots at the Przemysl train station in Poland, near the Ukrainian border.

In eastern Ukraine, heavy fighting filled civilians with fear and anger.

"I will never, under any conditions, surrender to Putin. Better to die," said Olena Kurilo, a 52-year-old teacher, her face covered with bandages, in Chugnev, a town in eastern Ukraine that was shelled.

- Sanctions

As they had warned for months, the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and other allies such as Japan and Canada decreed sanctions against Moscow.

U.S. President Joe Biden announced restrictions on exports to and technology imports from Russia, as well as sanctions against Russian banks and tycoons.

After a summit of its leaders, the EU announced measures against the financial sector, energy, transport, exports and visa restrictions.

The sanctions package "will increase inflation, accelerate capital outflows and progressively affect the industrial base" of Russia, said the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.

French President Emmanuel Macron stressed the importance of the sanctions, but also of "leaving the way open" for an eventual dialogue with the Russian leader, when "the conditions are met".

The invasion also hit the international markets: Brent oil surpassed $100 per barrel for the first time in seven years and there were significant setbacks on the stock markets on Thursday.

The Russian currency, the ruble, hit an all-time low against the dollar before the intervention of Russia's central bank.

The Russian invasion also triggered demonstrations around the world, with thousands of people criticizing Putin's decision. There were even protests in Russia, where police detained more than 1,700 people, according to human rights NGO OVD-info.

This Friday, Zelenski called on Russians to continue protesting this crackdown. "You heard us and believe us. Fight for us, fight against the war," he said.

title: Invasion Presents Big Risks For Putin -- WSJ
text:
Russian president has sought for decades to recapture the Soviet Union's lost status 


By Ann M. Simmons and Matthew Luxmoore 

MOSCOW -- Russia's invasion of Ukraine is President Vladimir Putin's most aggressive move yet in his two-decade-long campaign to reassert Russia's place in the world and redeem the humiliation of the fall of the Soviet Union.

It is an extraordinary gamble.

In invading his smaller neighbor, Mr. Putin now faces a breakdown in Moscow's ties with the West, which will slap sanctions on Russia aimed at inflicting deep pain on its economy.

Members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which have already sent fresh military equipment and forces to its eastern members in recent weeks, have found new unity in deterring Russia.

"He's gave priority to his own obsession over Russia's interests," said Kadri Liik, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations. "But he risks Russia's economic development, Russia's global position and also Russia's internal stability in order to get hold of Ukraine."

Mr. Putin, in power since 1999, now runs the risk of a prolonged conflict in Ukraine that could be akin to the Soviet Union's disastrous 1980s war in Afghanistan -- something that could ultimately stir dissent at home.

The "risk of getting stuck for a long time" wouldn't sit well with most Russians, said Pavel Salin, an independent political analyst based in Moscow. "The situation inside the country could turn against him."

The invasion quickly reverberated inside Russia on Thursday. Russian banks experienced a run on deposits, while the Russian stock market plummeted. The Russian central bank had to intervene to prop up the ruble.

But Mr. Putin has laid the groundwork for his decision for years, with demands for a wholesale revision to the trans-Atlantic security arrangements that emerged from Russia's defeat in the Cold War.

"Judging by [his] actions, he considers the risk justified," Mr. Salin said. Mr. Putin likely believes that "this quick action will force the West to accept a new reality. These are his calculations. How much they correspond to reality, how they will be justified, time will tell."

The military campaign marks the continuation of a policy that has seen Mr. Putin steadily expanding Russia's sphere of influence, reasserting Moscow's dominion over former Soviet republics such as Belarus, Georgia and Moldova.

But in doing so, he is sacrificing his relations with the West and risks making Russia a pariah. That could in turn leave Moscow more reliant on China, a more powerful neighbor with whom Russia already has an unequal relationship.

"Russia will upend its old relationship with the West, it'll now turn openly confrontational," Ms. Liik said. "And that will leave Moscow both politically and economically much more firmly in China's orbit. And I wonder if that is something that Moscow actually wants."

On Thursday, the U.S. and Europe were preparing far-reaching sanctions that follow a first round of penalties leveled this week for Mr. Putin's recognition of two separatist, Russian-controlled regions in Ukraine's east. The earlier sanctions targeted Russian sovereign debt, banks and wealthy Russians linked to Mr. Putin's inner circle.

Mr. Putin told a meeting Thursday with heads of Russia's leading businesses that the military campaign was "a necessary measure" and said "we were simply left with no chance to act otherwise."

He projected calm as he told the gathering that "Russia remains a part of the world economy and, in this regard, as much as it remains a part of it, we are not planning to damage the system in which we ourselves feel ourselves a part," he said. "It seems to me that our partners should understand this and not set themselves the task of pushing us out of this system."

The Kremlin has sought to protect its economy against sanctions, building a buffer against economic retaliation by the U.S. and its allies. After the West imposed sanctions on Russian individuals and entities following Moscow's 2014 annexation of Crimea and its incursion into eastern Ukraine soon after, Russia began building a cushion of reserves.

Russia's central bank has $630 billion in reserves of foreign exchange and gold, having grown from $368 billion in 2015, when billions of dollars were spent supporting the ruble after the West imposed sanctions in response to Crimea.

Still, jitters over the events rippled Thursday in Russia.

The Russian central bank had to intervene Thursday to prop up the ruble after it plunged to a record low in the hours after troops invaded Ukraine.

Following an early morning address by Mr. Putin announcing the start of a "special military operation" in Ukraine, Russians lined up at ATMs to withdraw cash amid fears the government would restrict hard currency withdrawals.

Mr. Putin has steadily tightened his grip over Russian society, which could help him withstand any domestic opposition to the Ukraine invasion.

He enjoyed a burst of popular support when Russia annexed Crimea. And while his popularity had slipped somewhat in recent years on concerns over the economy, a poll taken before the invasion by the independent Levada Center pollster found Mr. Putin's approval rating at 69%.

On Thursday, crowds of Russians demonstrated at rallies across the country. Authorities detained more than 850 people, according to protest monitor OVD-Info. On Moscow's Pushkin Square, several hundred people gathered with signs reading "No to War!" In St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, some 200 people chanted antiwar slogans.

But room for dissent has generally been squeezed in Russia after authorities over the past year dismantled the opposition, closed top rights groups and forced several independent media to close.

"The elites are under control, the disaffected part of the population, which right now could oppose the military scenario, don't have the infrastructure with which they can mobilize. And the majority is under the influence of propaganda," Mr. Salin said.

Leading opposition politician Alexei Navalny, who in recent years had organized the largest street protests against Mr. Putin, was jailed in February 2021.

A popular opposition blogger, Arseny Bobrovsky, said in an interview before the Ukraine invasion that he warned his fellow Russians about the steady buildup of Russian troops around Ukraine over the past few months to little avail. "It's like you're watching a guy put on diving equipment but instead of thinking he's now going to go diving, you say, 'Oh, he's just going to go for a walk,'" the 38-year-old said.

Meanwhile, Russian state media has offered a full-throated defense of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine, claiming that Russia was goaded into pursuing the military campaign.

On Thursday, the country's communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, threatened heavy fines and blocking websites of media that published information about the campaign not citing official Russian sources

"There will be difficulties," said Andrey Veselov, a supporter of Mr. Putin who owns a store selling European-made gardening equipment, speaking before the Ukraine invasion. "But we won't fall apart."

Mr. Veselov's store imports German-made Stihl chain saws and landscaping equipment, and he said that if EU businesses sever ties he can switch to buying Japanese and Chinese-made equipment.

He praises the import substitution campaign Russia launched following sanctions imposed over its annexation of Crimea in 2014, and said Mr. Putin is right to defend Russia's interests in the face of Western pressure. "We have to stand our ground," he said.

title: Russia's all-out offensive in Ukraine, decreeing general mobilization
text:
Ukraine decreed this Friday a general mobilization to try to stop an all-out Russian offensive that in less than 24 hours approached Kiev, leaving more than 100 dead and some 100,000 displaced.

The invasion provoked in response a reinforcement of Western economic sanctions against Russia, judged insufficient by the Ukrainian president, Volodomir Zelenski, who regretted that his country has been left "alone" to confront Russian troops.

The general mobilization will affect persons subject to "compulsory military service and reservists" and will be in force for 90 days, said the decree issued by Zelenski.

At least 137 people were killed, both civilians and soldiers, and 316 were wounded as a result of the air and ground attacks, he said.

Russian troops entered from the north, south and east of the country and seized a strategic air base near Kiev, as well as the area of the Chernobyl power plant, still contaminated by radioactivity from the 1986 nuclear accident, when Ukraine was part of the now dismembered Soviet Union.

The Gostomel air base fell after an attack carried by soldiers flown in by helicopter from Belarus, a country allied with Russia, witnesses reported.

"The helicopters arrived and the fighting started. They were firing with machine guns and grenade launchers," said one of the witnesses, Serguiy Storojouk.

That airfield could serve as an outpost for launching an offensive on Kiev where, according to President Zelenski, Russian "sabotage groups" have already entered.

Early Friday morning, the capital woke up again to loud explosions. "Attacks on Kiev with cruise or ballistic missiles resumed," said Ukrainian Deputy Interior Minister Anton Herashchenko.

And in the Sumy region (northeast), bordering Russia and not far from Kiev, all municipalities "are surrounded" and "many" Russian armored vehicles marched toward Kiev, its governor Serhiy Zhyvytskiy told the UNIAN agency.

- Russia celebrates "success" -

The Russian Defense Ministry stated that all missions on the first day of operations "were successfully completed."

President Vladimir Putin announced the offensive during the early hours of Thursday morning.

The Russian military claimed that it destroyed 74 military installations, including 11 airfields, and that separatists in eastern Ukraine are advancing and taking control of territories.

For its part, the Ukrainian armed forces estimated the damage inflicted on the Russian army at more than 30 tanks, up to 130 combat vehicles, 7 airplanes and 6 helicopters.

Putin, who demands that NATO close its doors to Ukraine, assured that he is not seeking the "occupation" of this former Soviet republic, but "a demilitarization and denazification" of the country and to defend the pro-Russian rebels, whose independence he recognized on Monday.

About 100,000 people fled their homes and thousands sought refuge abroad, the UN said.

Olena Kurilo was injured by glass shattering in her home caused by shelling in Chuguev, near Kharkov.

"I will never, under any conditions, surrender to Putin. Better to die," said the 52-year-old teacher, her face covered with bandages.

- Sanctions -

U.S. President Joe Biden announced restrictions on exports to and technology imports from Russia, as well as sanctions against Russian banks and tycoons. Japan and Canada enacted similar measures against Moscow.

The European Union (EU) also decided to adopt sanctions with "massive and severe" consequences against Russia that will focus on the financial sector, energy, transport, export control and visa restrictions.

The sanctions package "will increase inflation, accelerate capital outflows and progressively affect the industrial base" of Russia, said the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen.

French President Emmanuel Macron, who spoke with Putin during the day to "call for an immediate end" to the offensive, stressed the importance of sanctions, but also of "leaving the way open" for an eventual dialogue with the Russian leader, when "the conditions are met".

The invasion has hit the international markets. Brent crude oil surpassed $100 per barrel for the first time in seven years and European stock markets plummeted on Thursday, although Wall Street closed in the green.

The Russian currency, the ruble, hit an all-time low against the dollar before Russia's central bankintervened.

- The fall of Chernobyl -

The Ukrainian government announced the seizure by Russian troops of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant.

"After a fierce battle we lost control of the Chernobyl site," said Mikhail Podoliak, chief advisor to the office of President Volodomir Zelenski.

Following the loss of control of this area still heavily contaminated by the worst nuclear accident in history, the state of the plant's facilities, the cover insulating the accident reactor and a nuclear fuel storage tank is unknown, the senior official said.

"This is one of the biggest threats to Europe today," he said, estimating that the Russians could organize "provocative" activities at the site to blame Ukraine.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for "the utmost restraint to avoid any action that would endanger the country's nuclear sites."

- Protesters detained in Russia -

Russian police detained more than 1,700 people in several cities for participating in anti-war demonstrations in Ukraine, according to human rights NGO OVD-info.

On the streets of Moscow, there were residents expressing their concern and others their support for Putin.

"I'm not happy, I'm very nervous," said Nikita Grushin, a 34-year-old businessman, saying he had no idea who "is right" in this crisis.

"I am not going to criticize an order of the supreme commander. If he thinks this is necessary, it must be done," said Ivan, a 32-year-old engineer.

title: Russian Ruble Seen Facing Further Sharp Falls -- Market Talk
text:
0935 GMT - The Russian ruble faces further significant losses even as Russia's central bankintervenes in the currency market to stabilize market conditions, MUFG Bank says. The central bank on Thursday said it would start foreign exchange interventions as the ruble hit a record low after Russia launched an invasion of Ukraine. Market participants already expected the bank would need to raise interest rates aggressively before the conflict, MUFGcurrency analyst Lee Hardman says in a note. "It is likely that ruble volatility will remain at more extreme levels with the ruble at risk of further sharp sell offs in the days and weeks ahead." USD/RUB rises 5.5% to 85.1960 after hitting a record high of 89.9900 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0925 GMT - The European economy could suffer a significant setback from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Berenberg says. Negative shocks to business and consumer confidence as well as even higher energy prices and thus inflation would dampen growth near-term, economists at Berenberg say. The rebound in eurozone economic growth following Omicron's setback could be delayed by up to two months, but a eurozone recession--two consecutive quarterly GDP contractions-- seems unlikely to Berenberg. In the medium term, economic growth in the eurozone should be back on track for a strong post-Omicron rebound amid easing supply shortages, the German bank says. But inflation could stay slightly more elevated, around 0.3 percentage points up, due to somewhat higher energy prices, Berenberg says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

0917 GMT - The Swedish krona is vulnerable if a full-scale war breaks out in Ukraine, and SEB says it can't rule out EUR/SEK rising above 11.00. Rapidly rising energy prices provide additional fuel for inflation, while equity market falls have a negative effect on growth and confidence barometers, SEB says. "The Riksbank 's reaction to what is happening should, if anything, become dovish, which in [the] short term will cement the krona's handicap as a low-interest rate currency and as sensitive to geopolitical risk." EUR/SEK trades 0.9% higher on the day at 10.7148, having earlier hit its highest since May 2020 at 10.7440, according to FactSet . (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0913 GMT - EUR/CHF hit a record low of 1.0292 in early trade Thursday, according to FactSet , as Russia's attack on Ukraine prompts investors to scramble for safe-haven assets, and ING analysts say the possibility a drop towards 1.0 can't be ruled out. "Investors could speculate that Russian money will be heading to Switzerland and out of dollars, ahead of likely more aggressive sanctions," they say in a research note. "Until [the] Ukraine tension is resolved, expect EUR/CHF to stay offered and we cannot rule out a test of 1.00 if the situation deteriorates further." (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

0906 GMT - Taken at face value, the main takeaways from Sweden's Labor Force Survey is that employment has recovered well, says Nordea . The number of employed increased by 3.4% year-on-year in January while the employment rate reached new highs, it says. Unemployment stood at 8.1%, still much higher than the registered-based Swedish Public Employment Services unemployment at 7.3% in January, due to a large inflow of workers into the labor force, Nordea says. "Indicators point to a remarkable strong labor market ahead with new vacancies at all-time highs, incredibly high employment plans and labor shortages at record levels." (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0849 GMT - Rate-setters at the Bank of England and the European Central Bank are likely to sound a more cautious tone at their respective upcoming meetings in March as war grips Europe, says Berenberg. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is likely to soften the communication surrounding these central banks' decisions. Both central banks are likely to "tread more cautiously at their March meetings" providing "even stronger emphasis on keeping options open upon charting the course of stimulus removal," it says. Yields on U.K. government debt fall as investors seek haven assets. Yields move inversely to bond prices. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

0841 GMT - The currencies most vulnerable after Russia's attack on Ukraine, aside from the ruble itself, are those geographically closest to the crisis and exposed to the imported energy story, ING analysts say in a note. The Czech koruna, Hungarian forint and Polish zloty drop sharply, while the Swedish krona also "looks exposed," ING says. The Swedish krona earlier fell to its lowest against the euro since May 2020, according to FactSet . EUR/CZK is last up 1.4% at 24.9198, while EUR/PLN rises 0.9% and EUR/HUF is up by 0.6%. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

0834 GMT - Investors shed risk assets and rotate into perceived safe-haven securities, including U.K. government debt, as Russia begins a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Gilts gain as the yield on the 10-year U.K. benchmark government bond, which moves inversely to the price of the bond, falls four basis points to 1.426%, according to Tradeweb . The move follows a similar flight to safety in other government bonds, including U.S. Treasurys and German sovereign debt. "It's panic in the markets," says Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

0826 GMT - The dollar, Swiss franc and yen rise as investors seek safe-haven assets after news that Russia has launched a military attack on Ukraine, with missiles and air strikes hitting the capital. "Dollar liquidity will be in demand at very uncertain times like this," ING analysts say in a note, adding that they expect the DXY dollar index to rise to 97.00. The DXY is last up 0.4% at 96.6130, having earlier hit a three-and-a-half week high of 96.7650. The Swiss franc rose to a record high against the euro overnight, with EUR/CHF falling to 1.0292, according to FactSet , while a drop in the Russian ruble to record lows prompted the Russian central bank to say it would start intervening to prop up the currency. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

0823 GMT - Russia's attack on Ukraine is likely to cause a sharp rise in energy prices, increasing average headline inflation in the eurozone by 1.5% this year, Capital Economics says. The economic-research firm forecasts that oil prices could settle between $120 and $140 a barrel, while gas prices could return to the all-time high of EUR180 a megawatt hour. However, the impact of higher prices could be mitigated by fiscal measures or alternative solutions to increase supply, CE says. "Eventually, oil trade flows would be re-routed which should bring prices back down. It might take longer for gas prices to fall, but we wouldn't expect them to stay at EUR180 indefinitely unless there were an irrevocable breakdown in EU-Russian economic relations," it says. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

0751 GMT - USD/SGD has spiked higher and is approaching key resistance at 1.3540, which represents the top of what seems to be a "falling wedge" formation on the daily technical chart, UOB says. A break of 1.3540 could possibly lead to a swift rise to subsequent resistance at 1.3581 followed by the top of the daily Ichimoku cloud, which is currently at 1.3600, UOB says. On the downside, the currency pair's support is at 1.3485, UOB adds. USD/SGD is up 0.5% at 1.3532 after earlier touching 1.3541, highest intraday level since Jan. 31, according to FactSet . (ronnie.harui@wsj.com)

0751 GMT - Flight to safety is dominating markets as Russia attacks Ukraine, with eurozone government bond yields falling sharply across the board, led by the safe-haven German Bund. "Market expectations regarding [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's next steps will determine the way forward," Commerzbank 's rates strategists say. "Given the high uncertainty in that regard as well as regarding the NATO response, fears of Russian troops crossing further Rubicons should loom large." Commerzbank 's rates strategists expect flight to safety to intensify as markets are facing the prospect of a "very long, headline prone week-end," they add. The 10-year German Bund yield is trading 8.6 basis points lower at 0.139%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Russian Ruble's Sell-Off Seen Fuelling Rate Rise Bets -- Market Talk
text:

"USD/RUB may be trading below its early morning highs just below the 90.00 area, but the RUB is the worst performing currency in the world this year," Rabobank says. USD/RUB rises 7.4% to 87.3706, having earlier reached a record high of 89.9900, according to FactSet . The ruble has pared some of its earlier losses after Russia's central bank said it would intervene in the currency market and market participants are likely betting on further rate rises to bolster the ruble, Foley says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1218 ET - The Swedish krona is the worst performing G10 currency on Thursday due to Sweden's sensitivity to Russia's military invasion of Ukraine, Rabobank says. "Neither Sweden nor Finland are members of NATO and their geographical position around the Baltic sea ensures that whether or not they should be in NATO is a topical and sensitive discussion," Rabobank says. "The SEK could remain under pressure as long as Russia remains on the offensive." EUR/SEK rises 0.5% to 10.6737 after hitting a 21-month high of 10.7570 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1201 ET - The Ukraine conflict adds to the tailwind already boosting the US dollar, says Nancy Lazar, from Piper Sandler. "Prior to the invasion, we were expecting a stronger dollar on the back of the [global] slowdown we've been expecting," she says, adding that now the "Russia/Ukraine war will put even more upward pressure on the dollar." The greenback strengthens against all major currencies, especially the euro and the pound, and the WSJ US Dollar Index rises 1.1%. Longer term, the USD/EUR is up 9% in 12 months. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1153 ET - It is unlikely that Brussels will intervene to help curb the price of carbon, Jefferies says. Carbon prices in the EU 's Emissions Trading Scheme have surged over the last few weeks to more than EUR90 a metric ton, data from Intercontinental Exchange shows. This presents challenges for industrial companies and consumers at a time of rising energy costs, Jefferies says, noting that some diplomats met on Monday to discuss measures to curb prices. The likelihood of intervention remains low, as the bloc won't take steps that could be perceived as watering down its climate ambitions, Jefferies says. The measures could lead to much higher prices in the late 2020s when deeper emissions reductions are necessary to meet the bloc's goals, it adds. (maitane.sardon@wsj.com)

1152 ET - Large, late inventory orders are increasingly weighing on corporate balance sheets. Logistics and finance experts say extended shipping delays are tying up importers' cash as they rush to restock depleted inventories, pushing businesses to borrow money and seek other forms of financing. Commercial banking services provider US Bancorp says its supply-chain finance business balances doubled YoY. Freight forwarder Flexport says its inventory-financing loans more than doubled from 3Q to 4Q last year, and COO Sanne Manders says companies' liquidity needs "are going through the roof" as ocean shipping delays mount. (lydia.oneal@wsj.com)

1136 ET - Due to the latest events in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Oxford Economics expects higher European gas, oil and food prices over the medium term. The economic research firm also expects more financial market disruption and tougher European Union and U.S. sanctions on Russia. "Higher inflation is the main transmission channel for a weaker economic outlook," Oxford Economics says. The conflict and all its spillover effects leads Oxford Economics to cut its global GDP growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points in 2022 and 0.1 percentage point in 2023, reducing its global GDP growth estimates to 3.8% this year and 3.4% in 2023. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1135 ET - The conflict in Ukraine is expected to bring sanctions that may limit the amount of grain exports out of both Ukraine and Russia -- but that isn't likely to filter all the way down to US consumers, says US agriculture secretary Tom Vilsack. "We in the US are fortunate, we have tremendous production capacity," Vilsack says. He adds that US domestic farming is likely to mitigate any of the price increases that may occur for grains overseas, while European consumers are more at risk for higher prices. "I don't forsee a circumstance where US consumers will feel the uptick," Vilsack says. CBOT grain futures are higher in trading Thursday. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com; @kirkmaltais)

1130 ET - Treasury yields bounce back from early lows as Russia attacks Ukraine and global leaders threaten with sanctions. The 10-year now trades at 1.939%, up from an intraday low of 1.847%. But the conflict is expected to keep weighing on yields, as spooked investors seek safety in US government debt, potentially giving some pause to monetary authorities. "No one will be surprised if the Fed eases their approach if the situation hasn't improved by the time of their next Open Market Committee meeting on March 15-16," says asset manager Louis Navellier . "It would seem likely that before then the ECB will make easing maneuvers, paving the way for the Fed." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com)

1119 ET - A measure of expected price swings for the euro versus the dollar in the options market, or implied volatility, rises after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. EUR/USD one-week implied volatility is last around 8.5%, the highest level since November 2020, according to Refinitiv. "The bearish skew of the options demand is also telling, as one-week risk reversals plumb lows last seen in April 2020," Monex Europe analysts say, noting that risk reversals show a skew in favor of options that bet on EUR/USD falling. Uncertainty over the Ukraine-Russia conflict means "risks are tilted to the downside" for the euro, particularly given Europe's reliance on gas supplies from Russia, they say. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1103 ET - Cryptocurrencies could become a safe haven as authorities involved in the Russia-Ukraine conflict tighten cash withdraw rules, says Nigel Green , CEO of consulting firm deVere Group. Bitcoin has lost 9% since yesterday's intraday high and 22% from this month's intraday high on February 10. But Green says it could be bound to strengthen. "I think we might see [crypto] revert to being regarded as a safe haven asset as the situation in Ukraine develops because it is unconfiscatable - which could become extremely important as centralised authorities take drastic steps." Bitcoin is down 4% today. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1048 ET - Investors' reaction to the invasion of Ukraine shows that "markets had not fully priced in the likelihood of deeper conflict," UBS says. "Against a backdrop of heightened concerns about Ukraine, inflation, and interest rates, it is important to remember that global economic growth remains above trend and Covid-19-related restrictions are being lifted." UBS says value and cyclical sectors stand to gain, "including energy, financials" and even the Eurozone. "Despite their proximity to the crisis in Ukraine...the forces of economic recovery remain powerful and are potentially still a more important driver of global markets than events in Eastern Europe." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1044 ET - The conflict between Russia and Ukraine is a headwind for U.S. economic growth, but likely a modest one, Comerica Bank says. Higher energy prices mean less consumer spending on other goods and services, while a drop in U.S. exports to the eurozone is likely to occur, the financial services company says. "U.S. growth this year should be supported by less drag from the pandemic and consumers dipping into the $2 trillion in savings they accumulated since the start of the pandemic. These factors will likely matter more for the U.S. economy than the Russia-Ukraine conflict," Comerica Bank says. The U.S. economy is expected to grow over 3% in 2022, it says. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Mexican Stocks Close Higher; Peso Weakens Against Dollar -- Market Talk
text:

(anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1607 ET - The Ukraine-driven dollar rally stabilizes, with the WSJ US Dollar index rising nearly 1% to 90.36, off its intraday high of 90.90. The greenback gains around 1% versus the euro and the pound and 0.5% versus the yen. Elliot Wave's Murray Gunn tells WSJ the geopolitical tension favors the USD. "Given that the vast majority of global debt is denominated in US dollars, periods of 'risk-off' like this generally result in a scramble for dollars." He adds the Japanese currency is also a potential save haven "given Japan's domestic macroeconomic bias." Gunn expects the yen to strengthen for the time being. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1547 ET - The 10-year Treasury yield closes little changed, at 1.969%, after sliding in the morning on news that Russia attacked Ukraine, while the 30-year manages to rise 0.017 percentage point to 2.291%. Investors wonder how the conflict might alter US monetary policy. "With the Fed already being perceived as 'behind the curve,' we doubt these events will stay the Fed's hand next month," BMO says. But given the economic risks and volatility, the war "will at the very least, likely temper some of the most aggressive calls on the Fed," such as a 50 basis point rate increase, according to BMO . (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1351 ET - The number of newly listed homes for sale during the four weeks ending Feb. 20 was down just 2% year over year, says Redfin , for the smallest decline since mid-November. Pending sales rose 1%, the first increase since mid-January. The market again set new record highs for home sale prices, asking prices, buyers' mortgage payments and the share of homes selling within days of hitting the market. There was also a new all-time low for the total number of homes for sale. The good news, Redfin says, is that each week more homes are being listed for sale.(chris.wack@wsj.com)

1330 ET - Gildan Activewear 's "blowout" 4Q, according to CIBC , was driven by strong consumer demand and the benefits from its Back To Basics strategy. Net income totaled $173.9 million, or 89 cents per share, up from $67.4 million, or 34 cents per share, last year. The company's new three-year growth strategy outlines the next phase of growth "as it looks to deliver organic sales growth off an improved cost profile," says CIBC . With strong demand in North America, the company reported an EBIT margin of 20.2%, surpassing its aspiration of 18%. CIBC says that Gildan is built on strong fundamentals and is well-positioned to grow its share across end-markets . CIBC increases its target price on the stock to $49 from $47.(adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

USD/RUB rises 7.4% to 87.3706, having earlier reached a record high of 89.9900, according to FactSet . The ruble has pared some of its earlier losses after Russia's central bank said it would intervene in the currency market and market participants are likely betting on further rate rises to bolster the ruble, Foley says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1218 ET - The Swedish krona is the worst performing G10 currency on Thursday due to Sweden's sensitivity to Russia's military invasion of Ukraine, Rabobank says. "Neither Sweden nor Finland are members of NATO and their geographical position around the Baltic sea ensures that whether or not they should be in NATO is a topical and sensitive discussion," Rabobank says. "The SEK could remain under pressure as long as Russia remains on the offensive." EUR/SEK rises 0.5% to 10.6737 after hitting a 21-month high of 10.7570 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1201 ET - The Ukraine conflict adds to the tailwind already boosting the US dollar, says Nancy Lazar, from Piper Sandler. "Prior to the invasion, we were expecting a stronger dollar on the back of the [global] slowdown we've been expecting," she says, adding that now the "Russia/Ukraine war will put even more upward pressure on the dollar." The greenback strengthens against all major currencies, especially the euro and the pound, and the WSJ US Dollar Index rises 1.1%. Longer term, the USD/EUR is up 9% in 12 months. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1153 ET - It is unlikely that Brussels will intervene to help curb the price of carbon, Jefferies says. Carbon prices in the EU 's Emissions Trading Scheme have surged over the last few weeks to more than EUR90 a metric ton, data from Intercontinental Exchange shows. This presents challenges for industrial companies and consumers at a time of rising energy costs, Jefferies says, noting that some diplomats met on Monday to discuss measures to curb prices. The likelihood of intervention remains low, as the bloc won't take steps that could be perceived as watering down its climate ambitions, Jefferies says. The measures could lead to much higher prices in the late 2020s when deeper emissions reductions are necessary to meet the bloc's goals, it adds. (maitane.sardon@wsj.com)

1152 ET - Large, late inventory orders are increasingly weighing on corporate balance sheets. Logistics and finance experts say extended shipping delays are tying up importers' cash as they rush to restock depleted inventories, pushing businesses to borrow money and seek other forms of financing. Commercial banking services provider US Bancorp says its supply-chain finance business balances doubled YoY. Freight forwarder Flexport says its inventory-financing loans more than doubled from 3Q to 4Q last year, and COO Sanne Manders says companies' liquidity needs "are going through the roof" as ocean shipping delays mount. (lydia.oneal@wsj.com)

1136 ET - Due to the latest events in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Oxford Economics expects higher European gas, oil and food prices over the medium term. "Higher inflation is the main transmission channel for a weaker economic outlook," Oxford Economics says. The conflict and all its spillover effects leads Oxford Economics to cut its global GDP growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points in 2022 and 0.1 percentage point in 2023, reducing its global GDP growth estimates to 3.8% this year and 3.4% in 2023. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1135 ET - The conflict in Ukraine is expected to bring sanctions that may limit the amount of grain exports out of both Ukraine and Russia -- but that isn't likely to filter all the way down to US consumers, says US agriculture secretary Tom Vilsack. "We in the US are fortunate, we have tremendous production capacity," Vilsack says. He adds that US domestic farming is likely to mitigate any of the price increases that may occur for grains overseas, while European consumers are more at risk for higher prices. "I don't forsee a circumstance where US consumers will feel the uptick," Vilsack says. CBOT grain futures are higher in trading Thursday. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com; @kirkmaltais)

title: Pound Likely to Extend Losses Vs Dollar on Russia-Ukraine Crisis -- Market Talk
text:
1028 GMT - Sterling should weaken further versus the dollar after Russia launched an unprecedented invasion of Ukraine, MUFG Bank says. The market had already lowered its U.K. interest rate rise bets in recent days after comments from Bank of England officials and could further rein in those expectations in response to the conflict, MUFGcurrency analyst Lee Hardman says in a note. "The scaling back of more aggressive BOE rate hike expectations in the near-term combined with more risk-off trading conditions should see cable [GBP/USD] correct lower and test year to date lows at 1.3358 in the coming weeks," he says, noting the dollar's safe haven status. GBP/USD falls 0.9% to a three-and-a-half-week low of 1.3419, according to FactSet .

The firm is expected to sell around $840 million in 10-year senior notes non callable on the first five years Thursday, as it is looking to finance its spin-off from Post Holding. "Demand for this issuance will be key to understand whether appetite for junk remains intact despite the escalation in Ukraine, and a spike in inflationary expectations," it says. Russia's attack on Ukraine Thursday has prompted investors to flight to safety, as they sell risk assets such as stocks and buy perceived haven government bonds. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

1012 GMT - European stocks lose ground as Russia's military assault on Ukraine spooks investors. The Stoxx Europe 600, DAX and CAC 40 fall more than 3% and the FTSE 100 is down 2.7%. Brent crude surges 7% to $100.77 a barrel and gold and silver prices rise 2% and 3%, respectively as traders flock to safe havens. "Shares continued to tumble globally Thursday, with all European sectors down as investors fled riskier assets amid worsening military conflict in Ukraine," ActivTrades says. "It's now harder and harder for investors to predict where markets are going to go next as many expect the U.S. and its allies to proceed with strong retaliation measures in the shape of deeper economic sanctions." (philip.waller@wsj.com)

1011 GMT - Safe-haven assets such as German Bunds, the U.S. dollar and gold are likely to remain in demand until there's more clarity regarding the escalating situation in Ukraine, Donner & Reuschel says. "The decisive factors now are how long the military operation will last, how far Russian troops will advance into Ukraine and what the reactions will be from the West and China," Carsten Mumm, chief economist of the bank, says. The situation is still too unclear to take a new position, he says, adding that in the past, armed conflicts have usually only resulted in short-term setbacks on stock markets. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

"We think that market expectations of six or seven U.S. interest rate hikes are likely to support the US dollar in the months ahead. As such, we see the U.S. dollar as an attractive tactical currency position at present," UBS says. (mauro.orru@wsj.com; @MauroOrru94)
