title: Number of Newly Listed Homes Down Slightly, Pending Sales Rise -- Market Talk
text:
1351 ET - The number of newly listed homes for sale during the four weeks ending Feb. 20 was down just 2% year over year, says Redfin , for the smallest decline since mid-November. Pending sales rose 1%, the first increase since mid-January. The market again set new record highs for home sale prices, asking prices, buyers' mortgage payments and the share of homes selling within days of hitting the market. There was also a new all-time low for the total number of homes for sale. The good news, Redfin says, is that each week more homes are being listed for sale.(chris.wack@wsj.com)

1330 ET - Gildan Activewear 's "blowout" 4Q, according to CIBC , was driven by strong consumer demand and the benefits from its Back To Basics strategy. Net income totaled $173.9 million, or 89 cents per share, up from $67.4 million, or 34 cents per share, last year. The company's new three-year growth strategy outlines the next phase of growth "as it looks to deliver organic sales growth off an improved cost profile," says CIBC . With strong demand in North America, the company reported an EBIT margin of 20.2%, surpassing its aspiration of 18%. CIBC says that Gildan is built on strong fundamentals and is well-positioned to grow its share across end-markets . CIBC increases its target price on the stock to $49 from $47.(adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

1220 ET - The Russian ruble's depreciation in reaction to the Ukraine crisis is likely to fuel expectations that Russia's central bank could raise interest rates aggressively in coming months, Rabobank says. "USD/RUB may be trading below its early morning highs just below the 90.00 area, but the RUB is the worst performing currency in the world this year," Rabobank says. USD/RUB rises 7.4% to 87.3706, having earlier reached a record high of 89.9900, according to FactSet . The ruble has pared some of its earlier losses after Russia's central bank said it would intervene in the currency market and market participants are likely betting on further rate rises to bolster the ruble, Foley says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1218 ET - The Swedish krona is the worst performing G10 currency on Thursday due to Sweden's sensitivity to Russia's military invasion of Ukraine, Rabobank says. "Neither Sweden nor Finland are members of NATO and their geographical position around the Baltic sea ensures that whether or not they should be in NATO is a topical and sensitive discussion," Rabobank says. "The SEK could remain under pressure as long as Russia remains on the offensive." EUR/SEK rises 0.5% to 10.6737 after hitting a 21-month high of 10.7570 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1201 ET - The Ukraine conflict adds to the tailwind already boosting the US dollar, says Nancy Lazar, from Piper Sandler. "Prior to the invasion, we were expecting a stronger dollar on the back of the [global] slowdown we've been expecting," she says, adding that now the "Russia/Ukraine war will put even more upward pressure on the dollar." The greenback strengthens against all major currencies, especially the euro and the pound, and the WSJ US Dollar Index rises 1.1%. Longer term, the USD/EUR is up 9% in 12 months. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1153 ET - It is unlikely that Brussels will intervene to help curb the price of carbon, Jefferies says. Carbon prices in the EU 's Emissions Trading Scheme have surged over the last few weeks to more than EUR90 a metric ton, data from Intercontinental Exchange shows. This presents challenges for industrial companies and consumers at a time of rising energy costs, Jefferies says, noting that some diplomats met on Monday to discuss measures to curb prices. The likelihood of intervention remains low, as the bloc won't take steps that could be perceived as watering down its climate ambitions, Jefferies says. The measures could lead to much higher prices in the late 2020s when deeper emissions reductions are necessary to meet the bloc's goals, it adds. (maitane.sardon@wsj.com)

1152 ET - Large, late inventory orders are increasingly weighing on corporate balance sheets. Logistics and finance experts say extended shipping delays are tying up importers' cash as they rush to restock depleted inventories, pushing businesses to borrow money and seek other forms of financing. Commercial banking services provider US Bancorp says its supply-chain finance business balances doubled YoY. Freight forwarder Flexport says its inventory-financing loans more than doubled from 3Q to 4Q last year, and COO Sanne Manders says companies' liquidity needs "are going through the roof" as ocean shipping delays mount. (lydia.oneal@wsj.com)

1136 ET - Due to the latest events in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, Oxford Economics expects higher European gas, oil and food prices over the medium term. The economic research firm also expects more financial market disruption and tougher European Union and U.S. sanctions on Russia. "Higher inflation is the main transmission channel for a weaker economic outlook," Oxford Economics says. The conflict and all its spillover effects leads Oxford Economics to cut its global GDP growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points in 2022 and 0.1 percentage point in 2023, reducing its global GDP growth estimates to 3.8% this year and 3.4% in 2023. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

1135 ET - The conflict in Ukraine is expected to bring sanctions that may limit the amount of grain exports out of both Ukraine and Russia -- but that isn't likely to filter all the way down to US consumers, says US agriculture secretary Tom Vilsack. "We in the US are fortunate, we have tremendous production capacity," Vilsack says. He adds that US domestic farming is likely to mitigate any of the price increases that may occur for grains overseas, while European consumers are more at risk for higher prices. "I don't forsee a circumstance where US consumers will feel the uptick," Vilsack says. CBOT grain futures are higher in trading Thursday. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com; @kirkmaltais)

1130 ET - Treasury yields bounce back from early lows as Russia attacks Ukraine and global leaders threaten with sanctions. The 10-year now trades at 1.939%, up from an intraday low of 1.847%. But the conflict is expected to keep weighing on yields, as spooked investors seek safety in US government debt, potentially giving some pause to monetary authorities. "No one will be surprised if the Fed eases their approach if the situation hasn't improved by the time of their next Open Market Committee meeting on March 15-16," says asset manager Louis Navellier . "It would seem likely that before then the ECB will make easing maneuvers, paving the way for the Fed." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com)

1119 ET - A measure of expected price swings for the euro versus the dollar in the options market, or implied volatility, rises after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. EUR/USD one-week implied volatility is last around 8.5%, the highest level since November 2020, according to Refinitiv. "The bearish skew of the options demand is also telling, as one-week risk reversals plumb lows last seen in April 2020," Monex Europe analysts say, noting that risk reversals show a skew in favor of options that bet on EUR/USD falling. Uncertainty over the Ukraine-Russia conflict means "risks are tilted to the downside" for the euro, particularly given Europe's reliance on gas supplies from Russia, they say. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1103 ET - Cryptocurrencies could become a safe haven as authorities involved in the Russia-Ukraine conflict tighten cash withdraw rules, says Nigel Green , CEO of consulting firm deVere Group. Bitcoin has lost 9% since yesterday's intraday high and 22% from this month's intraday high on February 10. But Green says it could be bound to strengthen. "I think we might see [crypto] revert to being regarded as a safe haven asset as the situation in Ukraine develops because it is unconfiscatable - which could become extremely important as centralised authorities take drastic steps." Bitcoin is down 4% today. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Investors Should Build Robust Portfolios to Navigate Ukraine Crisis -- Market Talk
text:
0951 GMT - Investors should keep calm and build a robust portfolio to navigate the Ukraine crisis and rising U.S. interest rates, UBS says, after Russian missiles and airstrikes hit Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, and more than a dozen other cities across the country. Investors should diversify their portfolios across regions, sectors, and asset classes, use commodities as a geopolitical hedge and brace for strength in the U.S. dollar, UBS notes. "While it is impossible to judge the precise magnitude of geopolitical effects on markets, such events have generally not prevented equities from moving higher over a medium-term horizon, and drawdowns driven by geopolitical stress events are typically short-lived for well-diversified portfolios," UBS says. (mauro.orru@wsj.com; @MauroOrru94)

0951 GMT - Malaysia's inflation risks seem to remain tilted to the upside despite the consumer-price index moderating for the second straight month to 2.3% in January, UOB says. Among key upside risks include global supply-chain disruptions, escalating commodity prices, higher wages due to post-pandemic labor shortages and a revised national minimum wage, UOB says. The moderation in CPI for January was purely a result of high base effects, partially cushioned by higher prices in most goods and services, particularly food and beverages, the bank adds. UOB maintains its 2022 full-year inflation forecast at 3.0%. (chester.tay@wsj.com)

0948 GMT - The possibility that the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict sends inflation to new heights adds to the case for additional protection and a prudent approach to risk assets, Amundi says. The asset manager prefers European equities with a value tilt and is cautious on the highest growth areas of the market. Amundi has reduced its exposure to credit risk, in particular, to euro-denominated investment-grade bonds, and added hedges, it says. "The idea that the local crisis could morph into a global situation suggests that we should add protection regarding U.S. equity markets as well as U.S. credit high yield," Amundi says. (maitane.sardon@wsj.com)

0941 GMT - Investors should reconsider credit risk, says Saxo Bank . While high-yield corporate bonds have outperformed investment-grade bonds since the beginning of the year, there are signs that credit risk might start to crumble, the Copenhagen-based bank says, adding that no junk bond has been issued since Feb. 10 on heightened market volatility. Also, leverage loan indexes are falling on both sides of the Atlantic and real rates rising, it says. Risk assets come under renewed pressure Thursday as Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the pan-continental Stoxx Europe 600 down 2.8%. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

0936 GMT - European bank stocks trade sharply lower after Russia attacks Ukraine, prompting Western countries to prepare broad sanctions against Moscow. Raiffeisen Bank International leads the decline with a 14% drop. The Vienna-listed bank made 33% of its pretax profit in Russia last year and is by far the most exposed out of large listed European banks. Its shares have lost 30% of their value in the past week amid escalating conflict in the region. Societe Generale and UniCredit , which made about 6% and 4% of their pretax profit in Russia according to JPMorgan analysts, fall 6.8% and 7.1%, respectively. Major European banks also trade deep in the red, with BNP Paribas falling 6%, Deutsche Bank 6.4% lower and UBS down 5.8%. (cristina.roca@wsj.com; @_cristinaroca)

0935 GMT - The Russian ruble faces further significant losses even as Russia's central bankintervenes in the currency market to stabilize market conditions, MUFG Bank says. The central bank on Thursday said it would start foreign exchange interventions as the ruble hit a record low after Russia launched an invasion of Ukraine. Market participants already expected the bank would need to raise interest rates aggressively before the conflict, MUFGcurrency analyst Lee Hardman says in a note. "It is likely that ruble volatility will remain at more extreme levels with the ruble at risk of further sharp sell offs in the days and weeks ahead." USD/RUB rises 5.5% to 85.1960 after hitting a record high of 89.9900 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0925 GMT - The European economy could suffer a significant setback from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Berenberg says. Negative shocks to business and consumer confidence as well as even higher energy prices and thus inflation would dampen growth near-term, economists at Berenberg say. The rebound in eurozone economic growth following Omicron's setback could be delayed by up to two months, but a eurozone recession--two consecutive quarterly GDP contractions-- seems unlikely to Berenberg. In the medium term, economic growth in the eurozone should be back on track for a strong post-Omicron rebound amid easing supply shortages, the German bank says. But inflation could stay slightly more elevated, around 0.3 percentage points up, due to somewhat higher energy prices, Berenberg says. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

0917 GMT - The Swedish krona is vulnerable if a full-scale war breaks out in Ukraine, and SEB says it can't rule out EUR/SEK rising above 11.00. Rapidly rising energy prices provide additional fuel for inflation, while equity market falls have a negative effect on growth and confidence barometers, SEB says. "The Riksbank 's reaction to what is happening should, if anything, become dovish, which in [the] short term will cement the krona's handicap as a low-interest rate currency and as sensitive to geopolitical risk." EUR/SEK trades 0.9% higher on the day at 10.7148, having earlier hit its highest since May 2020 at 10.7440, according to FactSet . (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0913 GMT - EUR/CHF hit a record low of 1.0292 in early trade Thursday, according to FactSet , as Russia's attack on Ukraine prompts investors to scramble for safe-haven assets, and ING analysts say the possibility a drop towards 1.0 can't be ruled out. "Investors could speculate that Russian money will be heading to Switzerland and out of dollars, ahead of likely more aggressive sanctions," they say in a research note. "Until [the] Ukraine tension is resolved, expect EUR/CHF to stay offered and we cannot rule out a test of 1.00 if the situation deteriorates further." (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

0906 GMT - Taken at face value, the main takeaways from Sweden's Labor Force Survey is that employment has recovered well, says Nordea . The number of employed increased by 3.4% year-on-year in January while the employment rate reached new highs, it says. Unemployment stood at 8.1%, still much higher than the registered-based Swedish Public Employment Services unemployment at 7.3% in January, due to a large inflow of workers into the labor force, Nordea says. "Indicators point to a remarkable strong labor market ahead with new vacancies at all-time highs, incredibly high employment plans and labor shortages at record levels." (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

0849 GMT - Rate-setters at the Bank of England and the European Central Bank are likely to sound a more cautious tone at their respective upcoming meetings in March as war grips Europe, says Berenberg. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is likely to soften the communication surrounding these central banks' decisions. Both central banks are likely to "tread more cautiously at their March meetings" providing "even stronger emphasis on keeping options open upon charting the course of stimulus removal," it says. Yields on U.K. government debt fall as investors seek haven assets. Yields move inversely to bond prices. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

0841 GMT - The currencies most vulnerable after Russia's attack on Ukraine, aside from the ruble itself, are those geographically closest to the crisis and exposed to the imported energy story, ING analysts say in a note. The Czech koruna, Hungarian forint and Polish zloty drop sharply, while the Swedish krona also "looks exposed," ING says. The Swedish krona earlier fell to its lowest against the euro since May 2020, according to FactSet . EUR/CZK is last up 1.4% at 24.9198, while EUR/PLN rises 0.9% and EUR/HUF is up by 0.6%. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

Swedish Krona Vulnerable if Full-Scale War Breaks Out in Ukraine

0917 GMT - The Swedish krona is vulnerable if a full-scale war breaks out in Ukraine, and SEB says it can't rule out EUR/SEK rising above 11.00. Rapidly rising energy prices provide additional fuel for inflation, while equity market falls have a negative effect on growth and confidence barometers, SEB says. "The Riksbank 's reaction to what is happening should, if anything, become dovish, which in [the] short term will cement the krona's handicap as a low-interest rate currency and as sensitive to geopolitical risk." EUR/SEK trades 0.9% higher on the day at 10.7148, having earlier hit its highest since May 2020 at 10.7440, according to FactSet . (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

FTSE 100 Drops as Ukraine Conflict Hits Stocks

0915 GMT - The FTSE 100 Index slumps 2.7%, or 206 points, to 7292 as the outbreak of hostilities in Ukraine broadly weighs on stocks. Russia-focused miner Polymetal International falls 43%, Russian steel maker Evraz is down 30% and a range of financial and travel-related stocks also fall after Moscow began attacking its eastern European neighbor. Shares in WPP drop 6% even as the advertising, marketing and public-relations firm reported a swing to pretax profit for 2021. Lloyds Banking Group retreats 8% after the U.K. bank's fourth-quarter profit missed expectations. Still, BAE Systems rises 3% after the arms group said pretax profit rose in 2021 on higher sales. (philip.waller@wsj.com)

EUR/CHF Risks Fall Toward 1.0 as Russian Money Could Head to Switzerland

0913 GMT - EUR/CHF hit a record low of 1.0292 in early trade Thursday, according to FactSet , as Russia's attack on Ukraine prompts investors to scramble for safe-haven assets, and ING analysts say the possibility a drop towards 1.0 can't be ruled out. "Investors could speculate that Russian money will be heading to Switzerland and out of dollars, ahead of likely more aggressive sanctions," they say in a research note. "Until [the] Ukraine tension is resolved, expect EUR/CHF to stay offered and we cannot rule out a test of 1.00 if the situation deteriorates further." (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

Ukraine War Expected to Soften BOE, ECB Tone at March Meetings

0849 GMT - Rate-setters at the Bank of England and the European Central Bank are likely to sound a more cautious tone at their respective upcoming meetings in March as war grips Europe, says Berenberg. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is likely to soften the communication surrounding these central banks' decisions. Both central banks are likely to "tread more cautiously at their March meetings" providing "even stronger emphasis on keeping options open upon charting the course of stimulus removal," it says. Yields on U.K. government debt fall as investors seek haven assets. Yields move inversely to bond prices. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

Central European Currencies Drop Due to Geographical Proximity to Ukraine

0841 GMT - The currencies most vulnerable after Russia's attack on Ukraine, aside from the ruble itself, are those geographically closest to the crisis and exposed to the imported energy story, ING analysts say in a note. The Czech koruna, Hungarian forint and Polish zloty drop sharply, while the Swedish krona also "looks exposed," ING says. The Swedish krona earlier fell to its lowest against the euro since May 2020, according to FactSet . EUR/CZK is last up 1.4% at 24.9198, while EUR/PLN rises 0.9% and EUR/HUF is up by 0.6%. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

UK Gilts Gain as Investors Turn to Safe-Haven Assets

0834 GMT - Investors shed risk assets and rotate into perceived safe-haven securities, including U.K. government debt, as Russia begins a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Gilts gain as the yield on the 10-year U.K. benchmark government bond, which moves inversely to the price of the bond, falls four basis points to 1.426%, according to Tradeweb . The move follows a similar flight to safety in other government bonds, including U.S. Treasurys and German sovereign debt. "It's panic in the markets," says Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

Dollar, Safe-Haven Currencies Rise as Russia Attacks Ukraine

0826 GMT - The dollar, Swiss franc and yen rise as investors seek safe-haven assets after news that Russia has launched a military attack on Ukraine, with missiles and air strikes hitting the capital. "Dollar liquidity will be in demand at very uncertain times like this," ING analysts say in a note, adding that they expect the DXY dollar index to rise to 97.00. The DXY is last up 0.4% at 96.6130, having earlier hit a three-and-a-half week high of 96.7650. The Swiss franc rose to a record high against the euro overnight, with EUR/CHF falling to 1.0292, according to FactSet , while a drop in the Russian ruble to record lows prompted the Russian central bank to say it would start intervening to prop up the currency. (jessica.fleetham@wsj.com)

Ukraine Conflict Could Add Up to 1.5% to Eurozone's Inflation This Year

0823 GMT - Russia's attack on Ukraine is likely to cause a sharp rise in energy prices, increasing average headline inflation in the eurozone by 1.5% this year, Capital Economics says. The economic-research firm forecasts that oil prices could settle between $120 and $140 a barrel, while gas prices could return to the all-time high of EUR180 a megawatt hour. However, the impact of higher prices could be mitigated by fiscal measures or alternative solutions to increase supply, CE says. "Eventually, oil trade flows would be re-routed which should bring prices back down. It might take longer for gas prices to fall, but we wouldn't expect them to stay at EUR180 indefinitely unless there were an irrevocable breakdown in EU-Russian economic relations," it says. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

Gold, Safe Havens Rally as Russian Invasion Hits Risk Appetite

0813 GMT - Gold prices rise as investors flock to safe havens after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Comex gold futures rose 1.8% to $1,944 a troy ounce, their highest level in over a year. Global stock markets dropped and gold, the dollar, and bonds--assets considered safe havens in times of turmoil--all rose. "The Russian invasion of Ukraine puts the markets in panic mode," German refiner Heraeus Precious Metals says. "Investors are throwing shares out of their portfolios and fleeing to safe havens." (william.horner@wsj.com)

Flight to Safety Dominates Bond Markets

0751 GMT - Flight to safety is dominating markets as Russia attacks Ukraine, with eurozone government bond yields falling sharply across the board, led by the safe-haven German Bund. "Market expectations regarding [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's next steps will determine the way forward," Commerzbank 's rates strategists say. "Given the high uncertainty in that regard as well as regarding the NATO response, fears of Russian troops crossing further Rubicons should loom large." Commerzbank 's rates strategists expect flight to safety to intensify as markets are facing the prospect of a "very long, headline prone week-end," they add. The 10-year German Bund yield is trading 8.6 basis points lower at 0.139%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

Uncertainty, Risk-Off Dominate Markets

0751 GMT - Uncertainty and risk-off is the name of the game for Thursday, KBC Bank 's analysts say, after Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a special military operation to target military facilities across Ukraine. KBC 's analysts say that while the market impact could eventually fade, they recommend investors to err on the side of caution. "Although the market impact of geopolitical events tends to fade after a short period of time, we'd advise not to row against the current tide," they say. Eurozone government bond yields--which move inversely to prices--trade sharply lower in a sign of investors' flight-to-safety. The 10-year German Bund yield trades 7 basis points lower at 0.155%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

Eurozone Government Bond Yields Drop as Russia Targets Ukraine's Military Infrastructure

0717 GMT - Eurozone government bond yields slide in early trade in risk-off mode after Russia conducts attacks on Ukrainian military infrastructure. The 10-year German Bund yield trades 7 basis points lower at 0.155% and 10-year bond yields of peer eurozone countries also drop, according to Tradeweb . The 10-year French OAT yield trades 5 bps lower at 0.681%, and the 10-year Italian BTP yield is down 2.5 bps at 1.907%, according to Tradeweb . (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0637 GMT - Oil prices surge but fall short of hitting the keenly watched $100 a barrel level after Russia launches an invasion of Ukraine. Brent crude oil continuous futures jump 5% to $98.66 a barrel, their highest level since 2014. Front-month Brent futures which expire in April jumped as high as $102.07 a barrel. U.S. benchmark WTI futures rose over 5% to $96.89 a barrel. Russian missiles and airstrikes hit dozens of cities throughout Ukraine early on Thursday, immediately after President Putin said he would launch an operation against Ukraine. Investors fear Russia's plentiful oil supplies could get snarled in a conflict or in the ensuing sanctions that are expected to target the Kremlin at a time when energy markets are already tight. The asset manager prefers European equities with a value tilt and is cautious on the highest growth areas of the market. Amundi has reduced its exposure to credit risk, in particular, to euro-denominated investment-grade bonds, and added hedges, it says. "The idea that the local crisis could morph into a global situation suggests that we should add protection regarding U.S. equity markets as well as U.S. credit high yield," Amundi says. Also, leverage loan indexes are falling on both sides of the Atlantic and real rates rising, it says. 1339 ET - The US agricultural economy is expected to have another strong year in 2022, but there are significant factors that could add pressure, says Nathan Kauffman of the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City . "There are reasons to be optimistic, but there are notable risks," says Kauffman, speaking at the USDA Ag Forum today. Kauffman points out that government payments during the Covid-19 pandemic helped prop up farm incomes, and that support has likely faded as government payments have slowed. Inflationary pressures are also expected to impact farmer incomes, amid higher costs for inputs such as fertilizer. "These costs likely will weigh on profit margins and incomes," says Kauffman. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com; @kirkmaltais)

1330 ET - Gildan Activewear 's "blowout" 4Q, according to CIBC , was driven by strong consumer demand and the benefits from its Back To Basics strategy. Net income totaled $173.9 million, or 89 cents per share, up from $67.4 million, or 34 cents per share, last year. The company's new three-year growth strategy outlines the next phase of growth "as it looks to deliver organic sales growth off an improved cost profile," says CIBC . With strong demand in North America, the company reported an EBIT margin of 20.2%, surpassing its aspiration of 18%. CIBC says that Gildan is built on strong fundamentals and is well-positioned to grow its share across end-markets . CIBC increases its target price on the stock to $49 from $47.(adriano.marchese@wsj.com)

1300 ET - Dish Network says it's agreed to live with T-Mobile 's planned shutoff of its 3G network on March 31 through a truce now at the desks of DoJ and FCC regulators. T-Mobile 's planned decommissioning could affect many of Dish 's Boost Mobile customers who still rely on T-Mobile infrastructure and haven't yet upgraded to a 4G-capable phone. The two companies had tangled over the timing of the shutdown and Dish secured a three-month reprieve but wasn't able to win further delays. Dish Chairman Charlie Ergen says both carriers now share a "good spirit of cooperation," on network issues, though Dish will keep using AT&T capacity under an earlier network access agreement. (andrew.fitzgerald@wsj.com; @drewfitzgerald)

1254 ET - Moderna says it has signed advance purchase agreements totaling $19B to supply Covid-19 vaccine doses this year to countries outside the US. But that figure includes no new supply agreements with the US government . The company is close to fulfilling an older supply agreement with the federal government, CEO Stephane Bancel tells WSJ. But it's not clear what will happen after that--whether the government will want to sign a new agreement to stockpile more doses for a fall booster campaign, or leave it to private distribution channels and insurers to cover boosters, he says. (peter.loftus@wsj.com; @Loftus)

1220 ET - The Russian ruble's depreciation in reaction to the Ukraine crisis is likely to fuel expectations that Russia's central bank could raise interest rates aggressively in coming months, Rabobank says. "USD/RUB may be trading below its early morning highs just below the 90.00 area, but the RUB is the worst performing currency in the world this year," Rabobank says. USD/RUB rises 7.4% to 87.3706, having earlier reached a record high of 89.9900, according to FactSet . The ruble has pared some of its earlier losses after Russia's central bank said it would intervene in the currency market and market participants are likely betting on further rate rises to bolster the ruble, Foley says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1220 ET - European stocks slump in closing trade as Russia's full-scale military invasion of Ukraine dents market sentiment. The Stoxx Europe 600 falls 3.3%, the FTSE 100 drops 3.9%, the DAX declines 3.9% and the CAC slips 3.8%. Anglo-Russian precious metals mining company Polymetal International is biggest faller on the Stoxx with its shares plunging 37.8%. European bank stocks also tumble. Energy stocks rise as oil prices jump. "The escalation of tensions arising from the Russian action has pulled the rug from markets, adding to an already brittle environment in the face of rising inflation and interest rate concerns," Interactive Investor says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1219 ET - The Federal Trade Commission 's complaint counsel has filed a notice of appeal in the agency's antitrust case against Altria Group and Juul Labs . The FTC sued two years ago to unwind Altria 's 2018 investment in the e-cigarette startup. An administrative law judge last week made a preliminary ruling that the tobacco giant didn't break antitrust laws when Altria shuttered its own e-cigarette business and took a 35% stake in Juul . Chief Administrative Law Judge D. Michael Chappell 's decision in the case was made public Thursday. The matter will next go to a vote by the FTC's commissioners. (jennifer.maloney@wsj.com; @maloneyfiles)

1153 ET - It is unlikely that Brussels will intervene to help curb the price of carbon, Jefferies says. Carbon prices in the EU 's Emissions Trading Scheme have surged over the last few weeks to more than EUR90 a metric ton, data from Intercontinental Exchange shows. This presents challenges for industrial companies and consumers at a time of rising energy costs, Jefferies says, noting that some diplomats met on Monday to discuss measures to curb prices. The likelihood of intervention remains low, as the bloc won't take steps that could be perceived as watering down its climate ambitions, Jefferies says. The measures could lead to much higher prices in the late 2020s when deeper emissions reductions are necessary to meet the bloc's goals, it adds. (maitane.sardon@wsj.com)

1152 ET - Large, late inventory orders are increasingly weighing on corporate balance sheets. Logistics and finance experts say extended shipping delays are tying up importers' cash as they rush to restock depleted inventories, pushing businesses to borrow money and seek other forms of financing. Commercial banking services provider US Bancorp says its supply-chain finance business balances doubled YoY. Freight forwarder Flexport says its inventory-financing loans more than doubled from 3Q to 4Q last year, and COO Sanne Manders says companies' liquidity needs "are going through the roof" as ocean shipping delays mount. (lydia.oneal@wsj.com)

1146 ET - Coke bottler Coca-Cola HBC is halting production in Ukraine after Russia launched a military attack on the country. The bottler also does business in Russia. "The safety of our people is our number one priority and we have enacted our contingency plans that include stopping production in the Ukraine, closing our plant and asking colleagues in the country to remain at home and follow local guidance," the bottling company said. "We will keep this under review over the coming days." (jennifer.maloney@wsj.com; @maloneyfiles)

1144 ET - International Consolidated Airlines Group looks likely to report an upturn in fourth-quarter traffic at full-year results Friday Feb. 25, UBS says. While 3Q traffic was about 43% of the same period in 2019, UBS says it expects an improvement in the final quarter of the year. It also forecasts 4Q revenues of about EUR3.5 billion, versus the previous year's EUR1.2B and 3Q's total of EUR2.7B, and a pretax loss before interest of EUR306 million against a loss of EUR4.2B a year ago. Still, the shares already reflect market expectations that 2022 is likely to be better than last year, UBS says.(philip.waller@wsj.com)

1143 ET - The DOJ's move the block UnitedHealth Group 's $7.8B acquisition of Change Healthcare gets a muted reaction from investors, who were already expecting the antitrust challenge. Change shares, which have recently been changing hands at prices more than 20% below the $25.75 takeover price, edge up 0.8% to $20.40, while UnitedHealth slips 1.5% amid a lower overall market. The DOJ claims the deal that was unveiled in January 2021 would unlawfully reduce competition. (colin.kellaher@wsj.com)

The greenback strengthens against all major currencies, especially the euro and the pound, and the WSJ US Dollar Index rises 1.1%. Longer term, the USD/EUR is up 9% in 12 months. The measures could lead to much higher prices in the late 2020s when deeper emissions reductions are necessary to meet the bloc's goals, it adds. (maitane.sardon@wsj.com)

title: Market Talk Roundup: Volatility Rules The Day As Russia Attacks Ukraine
text:
Markets remain turbulent after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, with US stocks finishing higher after selling off earlier in the day. The following is a selection of market reaction and comments from analysts and asset managers.

Dollar Rally Weakens as Markets Digest Attack on Ukraine

16:07 ET - The Ukraine-driven dollar rally stabilizes, with the WSJ US Dollar index rising nearly 1% to 90.36, off its intraday high of 90.90. The greenback gains around 1% versus the euro and the pound and 0.5% versus the yen. Elliot Wave's Murray Gunn tells WSJ the geopolitical tension favors the USD. "Given that the vast majority of global debt is denominated in US dollars, periods of 'risk-off' like this generally result in a scramble for dollars." He adds the Japanese currency is also a potential save haven "given Japan's domestic macroeconomic bias." Gunn expects the yen to strengthen for the time being. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

US Stocks Erase Big Losses as Investors Weigh Russia Fallout

16:05 ET - US stocks rebound from sharp early losses that briefly pushed the Nasdaq Composite into bear market territory and the Dow Industrials into correction region as the US announces sanctions on Russia that are not as deep as some had feared. Oil trims early gains that lifted prices temporarily over $100 after Russia invaded Ukraine, while gold turns lower and Treasury yields recover much of their early declines. Information technology and communications services are the best performing sectors, while, consumer staples, energy and financials fall sharply. DJIA gains 92 points to 33223, the S&P 500 gains 1.5% to 4288 and the Nasdaq jumps 3.3% to 13473. (patrick.sullivan@wsj.com)

Sanctions Seen as Hurting Russians, Driving Negative Growth

15:52 ET - Sanctions announced by the US and its allies "will have a significant impact [on] Russia's overall economy, and average Russians will feel the cost," says the IIF, the global association of the financial industry. "These sanctions target Russia's domestic financial system, causing bank runs and forcing Russia's central bank to continue hiking rates. As a result, we are likely to see negative growth in an economy that has already been hindered by increasing isolationism." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

Treasury Yields Bounce Back From Ukraine-Driven Losses

15:47 ET - The 10-year Treasury yield closes little changed, at 1.969%, after sliding in the morning on news that Russia attacked Ukraine, while the 30-year manages to rise 0.017 percentage point to 2.291%. Investors wonder how the conflict might alter US monetary policy. "With the Fed already being perceived as 'behind the curve,' we doubt these events will stay the Fed's hand next month," BMO says. But given the economic risks and volatility, the war "will at the very least, likely temper some of the most aggressive calls on the Fed," such as a 50 basis point rate increase, according to BMO. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

Chips, Defense and Uranium ETFs Could See Upswing From Russia Invasion

14:56 ET - The war in Ukraine could boost some ETFs, Emles' Louis Ricci tells WSJ. An example is semiconductor ETF SMH, which is "a good play if you think attention turns to Taiwan after Ukraine," Ricci says. ETFs holding defense contractors, such as ITA, XAR and Emles' FEDX tend to "benefit from escalated tensions or from general defensive positioning in a down market." Ricci also points to China-focused KWEB and Russia-focused RSX as "places to go bottom fishing." Uranium-mining ETF URNM "is an interesting play if you think Europe...will greenlight more nuclear energy on the back of the shortages we are seeing now."(paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

Russia-Ukraine Fighting Sends Livestock Lower

14:56 ET - Russia's attack on Ukraine sent CME livestock futures toppling today, going in the opposite direction of grains futures. Live cattle futures fell 1.7% today to $1.423 per pound, while lean hog futures dropped 2.3% to $1.05525 per pound. "Impact from restrictions on Russian protein purchases in the world market are likely to have no impact on global trade," says Steiner Consulting Group. "However, Russia and Ukraine are major contributors to global grain and oil trade and they are also major suppliers of fertilizers. High feed and energy costs are negative for US livestock producers and they will negatively impact their ability to bring more product to market." President Biden said Thursday that a new wave of sanctions will be imposed on Russia, but did not release details. (kirk.maltais@wsj.com; @kirkmaltais)

Natural Gas Prices End Session Lower

14:50 ET - Natural gas prices finish the session 1.2% lower at $4.568/mmBtu after President Biden indicated in a press conference that despite Russia's invasion of Ukraine there were no immediate plans to sanction Russia in a way that would prevent it from exporting natural gas or crude oil. Gas prices had rallied more than 5% higher earlier in the trading day on the potential for Europe seeing its gas supplies from Russia suddenly halted, which may have meant US producers would have to fill the void. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

Oil Ends Below $100 After Historic Surge on Russia-Ukraine

14:45 ET - US benchmark oil prices finish 0.8% higher at $92.81 a barrel, a somewhat anticlimactic finish for a session in which prices surged by more than 9% at one point to $100.54, which marked the first $100-plus price since 2014. The initial spike in prices was sparked by Russia's pre-dawn invasion of Ukraine. But a Biden press conference late in the trading session in which he indicated oil export sanctions against Russia weren't part of any immediate plan caused prices to reverse sharply. Brent crude, which hit a seven-year intraday high of $105.79, ended its session below $100 also. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

Europe's Gas Woes Highlight Struggle with Energy Transition

14:03 ET - Europe's natural gas market, still licking its wounds from earlier this winter when prices soared amid weak wind production and the phasing out of coal, is in crisis mode again as gas supplier Russia invades Ukraine. "European natural gas prices are up 56% on the day to over $45/MCF which is over ten times the price in the U.S. at around $4.49/MCF," says Infracap founder and CEO Jay Hatfield, who says consumers can't afford that rise so it'll have to be absorbed by governments. "In addition, it graphically demonstrates that Europe has failed in its efforts to rapidly transition away from all hydrocarbons instead of just focusing on coal as COP26 recommended." (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

Russian Ruble's Sell-Off Seen Fuelling Rate Rise Bets

12:20 GMT - The Russian ruble's depreciation in reaction to the Ukraine crisis is likely to fuel expectations that Russia's central bank could raise interest rates aggressively in coming months, Rabobank says. "USD/RUB may be trading below its early morning highs just below the 90.00 area, but the RUB is the worst performing currency in the world this year," Rabobank says. USD/RUB rises 7.4% to 87.3706, having earlier reached a record high of 89.9900, according to FactSet . The ruble has pared some of its earlier losses after Russia's central bank said it would intervene in the currency market and market participants are likely betting on further rate rises to bolster the ruble, Foley says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

European Stocks Slide as Russia-Ukraine Conflict Weighs

12:20 ET - European stocks slump in closing trade as Russia's full-scale military invasion of Ukraine dents market sentiment. The Stoxx Europe 600 falls 3.3%, the FTSE 100 drops 3.9%, the DAX declines 3.9% and the CAC slips 3.8%. Anglo-Russian precious metals mining company Polymetal International is biggest faller on the Stoxx with its shares plunging 37.8%. European bank stocks also tumble. Energy stocks rise as oil prices jump. "The escalation of tensions arising from the Russian action has pulled the rug from markets, adding to an already brittle environment in the face of rising inflation and interest rate concerns," Interactive Investor says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

Swedish Krona Is Likely to Remain Under Pressure

12:18 ET - The Swedish krona is the worst performing G10 currency on Thursday due to Sweden's sensitivity to Russia's military invasion of Ukraine, Rabobank says. "Neither Sweden nor Finland are members of NATO and their geographical position around the Baltic sea ensures that whether or not they should be in NATO is a topical and sensitive discussion," Rabobank says. "The SEK could remain under pressure as long as Russia remains on the offensive." EUR/SEK rises 0.5% to 10.6737 after hitting a 21-month high of 10.7570 earlier, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

12:01 ET - The Ukraine conflict adds to the tailwind already boosting the US dollar, says Nancy Lazar, from Piper Sandler. The greenback strengthens against all major currencies, especially the euro and the pound, and the WSJ US Dollar Index rises 1.1%. Longer term, the USD/EUR is up 9% in 12 months. Coke Bottler Halts Production in Ukraine

11:46 ET - Coke bottler Coca-Cola HBC is halting production in Ukraine after Russia launched a military attack on the country. The bottler also does business in Russia. "The safety of our people is our number one priority and we have enacted our contingency plans that include stopping production in the Ukraine, closing our plant and asking colleagues in the country to remain at home and follow local guidance," the bottling company said. title: Summary: What is going on between Russia and Ukraine?
text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin began the invasion of Ukraine early Thursday morning with shelling and ground incursions by Russian troops in several parts of the country, including near the capital Kiev, which have already caused dozens of deaths. The start of the invasion has generated a barrage of international condemnations and reactions. Some 27 members of the European Union will meet this Thursday and announce new sanctions to pressure and isolate Moscow. For its part, NATO is planning a meeting by videoconference this Friday. For its part, the United States will submit this Thursday a draft resolution to the UN Security Council to condemn Russia for this "war".

 Putin, who for weeks had deployed more than 150,000 military personnel on the borders with Ukraine, crossed a point of no return on Thursday at dawn.

"I have taken the decision for a military operation", declared the President, three days after having recognized the independence of the separatist regions of eastern Ukraine and having obtained the legal framework from the Parliament for a military intervention. Putin assured that he was not seeking "occupation", but "demilitarization and denazification" of Ukraine and to defend pro-Russian rebels in the east of the country. Shortly after his speech explosions began to be heard in several Ukrainian cities, from Kiev to Kharkov, its second city on the border with Russia, but also in Odessa or Mariupol, on the shores of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. The Russian army assured that it destroyed 74 Ukrainian military installations, including 11 airfields, and the separatists in eastern Ukraine are advancing and taking control of territories.In Moscow, the Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri Peskov, affirmed that the offensive will last as long as necessary, depending on its "results" and considered that the majority of Russians will support it.

Why did the operation take place? After decades of tensions between the neighboring countries, which increased in the last weeks due to the presence of troops near the Ukrainian border and the practice of missiles inside Russia, the President of this country, Vladimir Putin, ordered a special military operation on Ukrainian territory. The reason is that the Ukrainian territories of Donetsk and Lugansk have declared that they want their independence from the country and consider themselves pro-Russian, so Putin, the President of Russia, recognized them as independent republics and sent troops to their territory on a peaceful mission. Because of this, the Russian Army now has the green light to be in these two regions of the Donbas, where these rebel republics of Ukraine are located, however, the arrival of the troops has been seen as an invasion, which has already caused deaths and structural damage to the territory. Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelenski on Wednesday called for security guarantees from Western countries and Moscow."Ukraine needs clear and concrete security guarantees, immediately," from both Western countries and Russia, Zelenski told a press conference. "I think Russia should be among the countries that give us those guarantees," he insisted, recalling that he had proposed on several occasions to meet with his counterpart Vladimir Putin to seek solutions to this crisis.The Ukrainian president thanked his Polish and Lithuanian counterparts for their support and for deliveries of weapons and military equipment."We are united in the conviction that the future of European security is decided at this moment at our home, in Ukraine," Zelenski said.

First casualties In Ukraine, the authorities broke off diplomatic relations with Moscow, compared Putin's Russia to Nazi Germany and vowed to defend themselves, while calling for international help to force Moscow to respect the peace.The government announced that more than 40 Ukrainian soldiers and a dozen Ukrainian civilians were killed. In addition, 18 people were killed in a shelling of a military base in a town near the Ukrainian port of Odessa, local authorities reported.Ukrainian border guards also admitted that Russian troops penetrated from Belarus, in a region 150 kilometers north of Kiev, to carry out a Grad missile attack on military targets.There were also other ground incursions from the south in the Crimean peninsula, annexed by Moscow in 2014. Belarus, a Kremlin ally, assured it was not participating in the offensive.Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelenski announced martial law throughout the country, but asked the population not to panic.The president also raised the specter of World War II by comparing the invasion suffered by his country with the 1941 Nazi offensive against Ukraine, then part of the Soviet Union."The Ukrainian forces are fighting fierce battles. The enemy has suffered heavy losses which will be even heavier," he guaranteed, promising to "inflict maximum casualties" on the aggressor.The Ukrainian army claimed to have killed 50 Russian occupants and shot down five planes and a helicopter in the east of the country. All these casualty reports are so far impossible to verify with independent sources.The Ukrainian authorities also closed the airspace to civil aviation for security reasons, while Russia shut down shipping in the Sea of Azov, which connects the two countries.

The global economy The situation on the Ukrainian border worsened last week, with violence escalating in the east of the country, the scene of a war since 2014 between the Ukrainian army and pro-Russian separatists that has left more than 14,000 dead.On Monday, after recognizing the independence of the separatist "republics" of Donetsk and Lugansk, Putin questioned the very legitimacy of Ukraine's existence. A day later, the Russian Parliament gave the green light for the deployment of Russian forces in Ukraine.The invasion has hit international markets. Brent crude oil topped $100 per barrel for the first time in seven years and stock markets around the world plummeted on Thursday. The Moscow Stock Exchange, which halted trading for a few hours, suffered losses of more than 30% and the Russian currency, the ruble, hit an all-time low against the dollar before Russia's central bankintervened.

Fleeing the war Russia assured that civilians in Ukraine "have nothing to fear", however, in Kiev hundreds of people rushed to the subway to seek shelter or a way out of the city."I woke up to the sound of bombs, packed my bags and fled," said Maria Kashkoska, 29, in a state of shock in the subway.In the middle of the night, traffic in the capital was typical of rush hour. Vehicles full of families were seeking to get out of the city, westward, as far as possible from the Russian border 400 km away.On the roads of eastern Ukraine, the army was omnipresent. A spokesman for the Civil Defense indicated that civilians were being evacuated, but that these operations were disrupted by gunfire and poor communications.Colombians in Ukraine have reported that mobility is reduced, as many inhabitants of the city look for ways to leave to take shelter from the impending conflict.

title: More than 100 killed, 300 injured, 10,000 displaced in first 24 hours of terror in Ukraine
text:
Ukraine decreed this Friday a general mobilization to try to stop an all-out Russian offensive that in less than 24 hours approached Kiev, leaving more than 100 dead and some 100,000 displaced.The invasion provoked in response a reinforcement of Western economic sanctions against Russia, judged insufficient by the Ukrainian president, Volodomir Zelenski, who regretted that his country has been left "alone" to face the Russian troops. The general mobilization will affect people subject to "compulsory military service and reservists" and will be in force for 90 days, said the decree issued by Zelenski.At least 137 people were killed, both civilians and soldiers, and 316 were wounded as a result of the air and ground attacks, said the president.

Read also: European Union leaders agree on sanctions package against RussiaRussian troops entered the north, south and east of the country and seized a strategic air base near Kiev, as well as the area of the Chernobyl power plant, still contaminated by radioactivity from the 1986 nuclear accident, when Ukraine was part of the now dismembered Soviet Union. The Gostomel air base fell after an attack carried out by soldiers transported by helicopter from Belarus, a country allied with Russia, witnesses reported."The helicopters arrived and the fighting started. They were firing with machine guns and grenade launchers," said one of the witnesses, Serguiy Storojouk.That airfield could serve as an outpost to launch an offensive on Kiev where, according to President Zelenski, Russian "sabotage groups" have already entered. Early Friday morning, the capital woke up again to loud explosions, AFP reported. And in the Sumy region (northeast), bordering Russia and not far from Kiev, all municipalities "are surrounded" and "many" Russian armored vehicles marched towards Kiev, its governor Serhiy Zhyvytskiy told the UNIAN agency.

Ukrainians flee the war About 100,000 people fled their homes in Ukraine and thousands sought refuge abroad following the Russian invasion, the UN said Thursday. "We cannot yet confirm exact figures, but it is clear that there was significant displacement inside the country and some movement across borders," a spokeswoman for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), Shabia Mantoo, told AFP."We think that about 100,000 people have already fled their homes and may have moved inside the country and that several thousand crossed international borders," she said. Filippo Grandi, UN High Commissioner for Refugees, announced during the day the reinforcement of UNHCRoperations and capacity in Ukraine and neighboring countries.He also called on the governments of those countries to "leave borders open for people seeking safety and protection" coming from Ukraine."We stand ready to support everyone's efforts to respond to any situation of forced displacement," he wrote in a statement.

Russia welcomes "success" The Russian Defense Ministry said all missions on the first day of operations "were successfully completed." President Vladimir Putin announced the offensive during the early hours of Thursday morning. The Russian army claimed that it destroyed 74 military installations, including 11 airfields, and that separatists in eastern Ukraine are advancing and taking control of territories.For its part, the Ukrainian armed forces estimated the damage inflicted on the Russian army at more than 30 tanks, up to 130 combat vehicles, 7 airplanes and 6 helicopters. Putin, who demands that NATO closes its doors to Ukraine, assured that he does not seek the "occupation" of this former Soviet republic, but "a demilitarization and denazification" of the country and to defend the pro-Russian rebels, whose independence he recognized on Monday.Nearly 100,000 people fled their homes and thousands sought refuge abroad, according to the UN. Olena Kurilo was injured by shattered glass in her home caused by shelling in Chuguev, near Kharkov."I will never, under any conditions, surrender to Putin. Better to die," said the 52-year-old teacher, her face covered with bandages.

Sanctions U.S. President Joe Biden announced restrictions on exports to and technology imports from Russia, as well as sanctions against Russian banks and tycoons. Japan and Canada decreed similar measures against Moscow.The European Union (EU) also decided to adopt sanctions with "massive and severe" consequences against Russia that will focus on the financial sector, energy, transport, export control and visa restrictions.The sanctions package "will increase inflation, accelerate capital outflows and progressively affect the industrial base" of Russia, said the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen. French President Emmanuel Macron, who spoke to Putin during the day to "call for an immediate end" to the offensive, stressed the importance of sanctions, but also of "leaving the way open" for an eventual dialogue with the Russian leader, when "the conditions are met". The invasion has hit the international markets. Brent crude oil topped $100 per barrel for the first time in seven years and European stock markets plummeted on Thursday, although Wall Street closed in the green and Asian bourses followed suit at their open on Friday. The Russian currency, the ruble, hit an all-time low against the dollar before Russia's central bankintervened.

The fall of Chernobyl The Ukrainian government announced the seizure by Russian troops of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant."After a fierce battle we lost control of the Chernobyl site," said Mikhail Podoliak, chief advisor to the office of President Volodomir Zelensky. After the loss of control of this area still heavily contaminated by the worst nuclear accident in history, the state of the plant's facilities, of the casing that isolates the accident reactor and of a nuclear fuel storage tank is unknown, said the senior official.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for "maximum restraint to avoid any action that would endanger the country's nuclear sites."

Protesters detained in Russia Russian police detained more than 1,700 people in several cities for participating in demonstrations against the war in Ukraine, according to human rights NGO OVD-info. On the streets of Moscow, there were residents expressing their concern and others their support for Putin. "I'm not happy, I'm very nervous," said Nikita Grushin, a 34-year-old businessman, saying he had no idea who "is right" in this crisis."I'm not going to criticize an order of the supreme commander. If he thinks this is necessary, it must be done," said Ivan, a 32-year-old engineer.

title: Currencies : Dollar advances against rivals after Russian invasion of Ukraine
text:
The dollar traded higher against rival currencies, as the market digested the developments of the Russian invasion of Ukraine and responses from Western leaders. The U.S. currency is considered a security asset, so it appreciates in the face of geopolitical conflicts with global impacts. The Russian ruble, on the other hand, has reached the lowest level in history against the dollar.

At the end of the afternoon in New York, the euro retreated to US$ 1.1205 and the pound fell to US$ 1.3397, giving traction to the DXY index, which advanced 0.98%, at 97.137 points. The US currency was still up at 115.62 Yen at the same time.

The DXY index even slowed to a trough this afternoon after US President Joe Biden said he authorized additional sanctions against Russia. According to UBS, in addition to the support provided by the geopolitical crisis, the US dollar will be favored by expectations of six or seven US interest rate hikes. According to the CME Group, the market estimates at 86.7% the chances of a 25 basis point interest rate hike in the US at the March monetary policy meeting.

For Western Union, the invasion of Ukraine triggered a slide in risk aversion, causing investors to run for safety in the dollar. "Safe havens like the dollar appear to be in a better position to weather global uncertainty," it said in a report sent to clients.

In the early morning hours, in the face of the first news about the attack, the dollar surpassed a historic high against the ruble, reaching 90.0165 rubles. Russia's central bank announced that it will begin intervention in the foreign exchange market, as the country has more than $600 billion in foreign exchange reserves and gold, an alternative that can be used in the foreign exchange markets to prop up the ruble. According to Edward Moya of Oanda, the Russian CB has clearly not been successful. "Foreign exchange interventions often fuel excessive movements against what a central bank is trying to achieve and that is exactly what happened with Russia," he pointed out. By late afternoon in New York, the dollar was bouncing at 85.567 rubles.

title: Russia's military offensive against Ukraine causes uncertainty among Ecuadorian banana exporters and flower growers
text:
The start of a 'military operation' in Ukraine by Russia, announced by President Vladimir Putin early Thursday morning and which Kiev claims to be a "full-scale invasion", comes at a time when governments around the world are struggling to contain inflation, fueled by the growing demand for inputs due to the global economic reopening after the COVID-19 closures. This situation is already having an impact on the world economy and may soon begin to be felt in the Ecuadorian economy.

Russia is the fourth destination of Ecuador's exports, with bananas, shrimp, flowers, fresh fish and coffee being the main products that reach that country.

There have been closures and paralyzations of ports and customs in Ukraine in the last hours. One of them is the port of Odessa, which is inoperative, which will complicate the distribution of products, says Richard Salazar, executive director of the Association of Banana Exporters (Acorbanec), who mentions that different shipping companies have announced that they will no longer transport bananas to Ukraine; however, he says that the real effects will begin to be seen from next week.

In the case of the flower sector, Ines Ortiz, CEO of Inorflowers, also mentions that the current situation for this export product is complicated.

"What is to Ukraine shipments have stopped, what was scheduled to be shipped this weekend and next week, are canceled, even shipments that had already been sent and arrived between Wednesday and Thursday to Holland with which customers are trying to refuse them because of the situation," she says and adds that, along with the tension, there has been a rise in the cost of transport in that region which further darkens the picture.

Ortiz says that the atmosphere is one of uncertainty and that it is necessary to wait to see if the markets can be stabilized and that it must also be taken into account that flowers are not a staple product at this time, which can complicate this guild and generate an imbalance.

According to figures from the National Association of Producers and Exporters of Flowers of Ecuador (Expoflores) during the months of February and May, for festivities such as Valentine's Day, Women's Day (March 8) and Victory Day (May 9), on average the flower sector allocates $ 70 million to Eurasian countries, equivalent to 40% of its annual sales in these markets.

Products for export to Russia 2021The Ecuadorian Federation of Exporters (Fedexpor) issued a statement on the situation in which it mentions that there is a possibility that, if Ukraine receives greater support from Turkey, the passage of the Dardanelles and Bosphorus straits to Russian vessels will be closed, which would return to the most open way to trade with Russia the port of St. Petersburg.

The Ecuadorian flower sector allocates $ 70 million to Eurasian countries, equivalent to 40% of its annual sales in these markets, which could be affected by the situation in Ukraine.In the event of a total closure of trade with Ukraine, the sector will stop exporting $ 2.4 million per week, according to the union.

However, Salazar says that the situation is not new and that the same could happen as when Russia made the annexation of the Crimean peninsula in 2014 and economic sanctions were established.

Among the effects that are going to be registered, Salazar comments that the currency devaluation can already be evidenced and that it will generate an increase in the price of bananas that will cause a decrease in the purchase volume, at the same time controls the outflow of foreign currency from Russia and therefore payment problems.

The Russian ruble reached its historical low against the dollar (up to 9 %), before the intervention of the Central Bank of Russia.

"As we already experienced at the time, we are going to have collection problems, in 2014 there were between 30 to 35 days of delay", says Salazar and stresses that they also experienced cancellation of contracts due to the low demand that Ecuadorian bananas began to have.

Export products to Ukraine 2021Fausto Ortiz, economic expert and former Minister of Finance, agrees that it is necessary to wait and see the size of the conflict and its duration.

"As the size grows and more actors become involved, this will take on other dimensions," he says.

The expert states that the situation between both countries and the escalation of tension has also been reflected in the prices of commodities such as oil, gold, copper and other raw materials that Ecuador is also exporting, which could lead to an increase in the import of derivatives.

The price of a barrel of oil surpassed $ 100 for the first time in more than seven years on Thursday and world stock markets plunged after the launching of the military offensive and gold rose 2.43% to $ 1,955.47 per ounce.

Meanwhile, Acorbanec issued a statement and says that "it is urgent and important that the National Government implements compensatory measures to the banana sector that at the close of 2021 reduced its exports by about 4% in monetary terms and 3% in MT according to figures from the Central Bank of Ecuador". Among these measures they suggest the implementation of the unified simplified refund of taxes for the banana sector, contemplated in article 43 of the Organic Law of Simplification and Tax Progressivity, which awaits its regulation.

Salazar also says that other alternative measures could be to pay the producer at the price of the bunch for the fruit that does not come out.

The Corporación de Gremios Exportadores del Ecuador (CORDEX) said it has sent a letter to Foreign Minister Juan Carlos Holguín, requesting the creation of a public-private working commission to operate as an early warning system.

This commission, through coordination between CORDEX and the diplomatic missions to the European Union, the United States, Russia and China, would allow timely knowledge of the measures taken in the different countries in order to anticipate any inconvenience that may affect the usual performance of exports.

Currently, Ecuador exports to Russia an average of 83 products from 504 companies engaged in the agricultural, agro-industrial, aquaculture, fishing and manufacturing sectors. To this destination between 2020 and 2021 about one billion dollars were exported and export growth went from 7% to 9%, according to figures from Fedexpor.

Impact at international levelIn

its first package of sanctions against Russia, the United States included "total blockades" to two large Russian financial institutions, the Russian military bank and the VEB, the state bank in charge of supporting the development of the economy, managing state debt and pension funds and announced complementary sanctions to hit Russia's sovereign debtAt

the same time, the threat of a war unleashed in the last weeks fears about the supply of basic products, such as wheat and metals, in the middle of the reopening of the economies

.This Thursday, grain prices broke a record for trading in Europe and wheat rose to a high of 344 euros per ton on the Euronext platform.

The price of wheat and corn - of which Ukraine is the world's fourth largest producer - climbed sharply at the opening, a few hours after the offensive.

"Russian-Ukrainian tensions lead to a potential demand shock [in Europe] and a larger one in supply for the rest of the world, given the importance of Russia and Ukraine in energy," noted Tamas Strickland of National Australia Bank.

For a Swissquote analyst, "rising energy prices are a big headache for Europe, because 40% of its natural gas and 30% of its oil come from Russia."

As for natural gas, the benchmark market in Europe was 50% higher than the day before. (I)

title: Markets tremble after Russia's offensive on Ukraine: Wall Street and European stock markets plunge up to 4%.
text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a military operation in Ukraine to fend off separatists in the east of the country. "I have made a decision on a military operation," Putin declared in an unexpected TV message shortly before 03H00 GMT. In the message he called on the Ukrainian military to "lay down their arms." As expected, markets react in the worst way. Oil skyrocketed to u$s100, gas became 30% more expensive. Stock markets fall up to 4%.

Wall Street

U.S. stock indexes sink more than 1% on Thursday, led by losses in banking stocks, as a Russian invasion of Ukraine triggered a widespread sell-off in global markets.

In the S&P 500, all 11 major sectors traded with losses, with financial stocks plunging 2.9%, while technology and consumer discretionary shares were down more than 1%.

Most large lenders, including Bank of America Corp, Citigroup Inc, Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs Group Inc, plunge more than 4%. Tesla Inc fall 2.5% to lead losses among mega-cap papers. Apple and Amazon.com Inc give up more than 2%. The CBOE Volatility Index, also known as Wall Street's fear gauge, was trading at 36.81, its highest level since Jan. 24.

"While the invasion is not a total surprise, the stock market continues to take a sell first, ask questions later approach," said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at LPL Financial.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average sank 1.92% to 32,495 units, the S&P 500 was down 1.42% to 4,165.23 units, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.88% to 12,922 units. The Dow Jones was on track to confirm a correction from its all-time closing high on January 4, settling 12% below its record closing level.

Oil

The price of a barrel of crude oil surpassed the US$100 mark on Thursday for the first time in more than seven years. Brent North Sea crude oil in its May contract reached u$s101.84 with a jump of almost 9%, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil traded in the New York futures market in its April contract surpassed u$s100 a barrel with a rise of 8%. Brent crude oil after the escalation of the conflict reached u$s103, its highest level since August 2014. During operations, it managed to moderate increases until trading slightly below u$s100 but maintaining the upward trend.

Since the tension between both countries began, the cost of the barrel has increased 25%. It must be taken into account that Russia is the second largest oil exporter in the world and this may threaten the world recovery.

The level of harshness of the new economic sanctions that are being prepared to stifle the Kremlin economically will be key to gauge how far the rise in energy commodity prices can go. Although Vladimir Putin pledged not to turn off the gas or crude oil tap - a decision that could change overnight - his credibility is at rock bottom after the attack on Russia.

Gas

Even more relevant is the rise in gas, with which Russia covers approximately 25% of EU consumption, a share that in the case of oil exceeds 40%. The Dutch market benchmark TTF soared more than 30% compared to Wednesday's close and exceeded 118 euros per megawatt hour (MWh), after touching the 120 euros/MWh barrier in the first minutes of trading.

This is a level that gas has not reached since the eve of last Christmas. In just three days, and since Russia recognized the independence of the Ukrainian provinces of Donetsk and Lugansk, the TTF has risen by more than 60%. The Russian attack on Ukraine comes after Germany decided to indefinitely suspend the Nord Stream 2 pipeline license and comes at a time when gas reserves in Europe are at a historically low level of just over 30%.

The exponential rise in gas prices over the last year is, together with the increase in the price of CO2 emission rights, mainly responsible for the record electricity prices of the last few months. Each euro increase in the price of this raw material is equivalent to an increase of around two euros in the wholesale electricity market price.

Metals

Gold prices hit a more than one-and-a-half year high on Thursday and palladium was up 6%, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine raised fears of war in Europe, generating flows into safe-haven assets. Spot gold climbed 0.6% to u$s1,919.30 an ounce after reaching u$s1,973.96, its highest since September 2020. U.S. gold futures gained 0.6% to u$s1,921.

"Obviously there is safe haven demand in the (gold) price, but this crisis is very inflationary because it is adding upward pressure on commodity prices (...) it is recessionary also in terms of the growth outlook," said Ole Hansen, an analyst at Saxo Bank.

Meanwhile, palladium was up 6% to u$s2,631.95 an ounce after reaching its highest level since July at u$s2,711.18. Palladium's advance is a natural reaction because Russia is a major supplier of the metal, Hansen said. "The only thing that could counteract it is the risk of a recession, especially in Europe and Germany, which is a big auto producer."

Oil prices were soaring and stock markets were falling Thursday as the situation deteriorated. Gold has risen sharply so far in February as the crisis between Russia and Ukraine hit appetite for risk assets. The metal is heading for its best monthly performance since July 2020. Russia is the world's third-largest gold producer, while Moscow-based Nornickel is also a major producer of palladium and platinum.

Among other precious metals, silver gained 0.5% to u$s24.65 an ounce and platinum fell 1.2% to u$s1,079 after climbing to u$s1,126.18.

Asian stock markets

Major stock market indexes in Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan plunged after Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a military operation in Ukraine.

The Hong Kong Stock Exchange benchmark, the Hang Seng, fell by up to 3%. The index that measures the performance of mainland Chinese stocks listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, the Hang Seng China Enterprises, touched 4.14%. For their part, the two main mainland Chinese stock exchanges, Shanghai and Shenzhen, fell by up to 2%.

Russian stock market

The Moscow Stock Exchange Index fell more than 50% on Thursday and the Russian currency, the ruble, reached an all-time low against the dollar after Russia launched a military offensive against Ukraine.

The start of the military operation was followed by the suspension of trading on the Moscow Stock Exchange and the St. Petersburg Stock Exchange due to strong volatility in the markets. At 10:00 Moscow time, trading was reopened on the Moscow Stock Exchange. Losses were as high as 50%.

The currency and bonds also plunged, prompting the central bank to announce its first foreign exchange intervention designed to shore up financial stability since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine. "In the coming days, the Russian market will be extremely volatile. Given the high risks of tightening sanctions against Russia, we are revising our target benchmarks for Russian equities," Evgeny Loktyukhov, Head of Economic and Industrial Analysis at PSB, told Russian media outlet Quote.

"There has never been such a significant drop in the recent history of the Russian stock market. The main reason for what is happening is the flight from risks amid the escalating geopolitical aspect," added Vladislav Silaev, a senior trader at Alfa Capital. In his opinion, until diplomats and politicians sit down at the negotiating table, the market will remain in the red.

The ruble slid to a record low of u$s89.60 against the dollar and approached a crucial threshold of 100 against the euro. It was around 70 to the dollar and 81 to the euro before the recent round of geopolitical tensions between Moscow and the West began to escalate in October.

"To stabilize the situation on the financial market, the Bank of Russia decided to initiate interventions on the foreign exchange market," the bank said Thursday. The move helped the ruble cut losses slightly.

The Moscow and St. Petersburg stock exchanges were forced to halt trading after their main indexes plunged by more than 30%. "Trading on all markets was suspended. The restart will be announced at a later date," the Moscow Stock Exchange said in a statement, reports Efe. The St. Petersburg Stock Exchange, the country's second largest, also announced a "ban on bids and contracts for all trading modes and all types of securities.

European stock exchanges

At the middle of the session, falls of 4.41% were recorded for Paris, 4.26% for Milan, 2.91% for London and 2.85% for Frankfurt. The Euro Stoxx 50, which groups together the largest capitalization European companies, fell by 3.60%. In addition, the euro fell against the dollar and exchanged at 1.1177 units.
