title: Russia attacks Ukraine: Minute by minute after Russian invasion
text:
Russia today launched a military operation against Ukraine, with the alleged aim of pacifying the armed conflict that has been taking place in eastern Ukraine since 2014. This is the minute by minute of everything that has happened in the country. All updates in Central European Time (CET).

13:41 Russia nips anti-war demonstration attempts in the bud.

"I was detained when I was leaving home," activist Marina Litvinovich, who had called for a protest after learning about the Russian military operation in Ukraine, wrote on Telegram. She confirmed her detention by police in a message to Reuters. Litvinovich had called on Russians to gather in protest in several Russian cities tonight.

13:31 UNHCR calls for keeping borders open for refugees.

UN High Commissioner for RefugeesFilippo Grandi called on countries neighboring Ukraine to "keep their borders open to those seeking safety and protection," after Ukrainian citizens have already sought refuge in territories such as Romania, Hungary or Slovakia.

"There are no winners in a war, but countless lives will be shattered," the head of the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) said in a statement and called for respect for both civilian lives and non-military infrastructure.

13:18 "It is an attack on democracy and freedom in the world".

British Prime Minister Boris Johnson said that the Russian offensive "is not just an attack on Ukraine, but on democracy and freedom in Eastern Europe and around the world." In a message to the nation, Johnson promised a "huge package of sanctions" and added that "diplomatically, politically, economically and militarily, this horrific and barbaric action by Putin must end in failure."

13:09 Russian troops cross the border in the Kiev region.

Russian troops crossed the Vilcha border point in the Kiev region, 50 kilometers from the border with Belarus, the Ukrainian Border Service reported. "Russian troops violated the state border. The enemy's war equipment crossed through the Vilcha border point," the entity reported, according to which the Ukrainian Army put up a battle with the Russian Army.

12:40 NATO activates its "defense plans".

Europe is facing a new security reality after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said as he confirmed the alliance's decision to activate defense plans aimed at strengthening the defense of member countries in Eastern Europe. "It will be a new Europe after the invasion we saw today," Stoltenberg told a news conference after an emergency meeting of NATO ministers in Brussels.

Stoltenberg said Russia had been planning a "cold-blooded" invasion while NATO sought a diplomatic solution to the Ukraine crisis and warned that Russia's attack on Ukraine will affect Moscow's relationship with the alliance. "We have no plans to send NATO troops to Ukraine," the official confirmed in Brussels.

12:38 Turkey condemns Russian attack as "a threat to the world."

The Turkish government has condemned the Russian invasion of Ukraine as an "unacceptable violation of international law" and a threat to the security of the world. After concluding a session of the Turkish security council, chaired by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, the presidency issued a statement calling the attack "unacceptable" and assuring that Turkey will maintain its support for Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and political unity.

A Foreign Ministry statement also called the invasion "a violation of international law," a "serious threat to the security of the region and the world" and urged Russia to "put an end to this illegal and unjust act as soon as possible."

12:35 Ukrainian President compares Russia to "Nazi Germany".

Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelensky compared the Russian invasion against his country to the actions of "Nazi Germany" during World War II in an appearance broadcast via social networks. "Russia attacked Ukraine in a cowardly and suicidal way, just like Nazi Germany did during World War II," he stated. He also urged Russian citizens to "go out" on the streets to "protest against the war." The Russian president had accused the Kiev government of neo-Nazism in the speech in which he announced the attack.

12:22 Moscow: military operation will last as long as it takes

The Kremlin affirmed that the military operation launched against Ukraine will last as long as necessary, depending on its "results" and "relevance", estimating that the Russians will support such an offensive. Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists that Moscow's goal is to impose a "neutral status" in Ukraine, a demilitarization and the elimination of "Nazis" in the country.

12:19 Costa: NATO will not intervene, but will have "deterrent" role.

"NATO will not intervene or act in Ukraine," but will act with a "deterrent" role in neighboring coalition partner countries, said Portuguese Prime Minister António Costa in his first public speech after meeting with the foreign and defense ministers. Costa "vehemently" condemned the Russian offensive and recalled that Portugal is a member of NATO's rapid reaction group this year and affirmed that Portuguese forces are prepared to place themselves under NATO's orders in "these deterrence missions".

In addition, Costa opened Portugal's doors to Ukrainian citizens leaving the country and announced that instructions have been given to the Portuguese embassies in Ukraine and neighboring countries to speed up the issuance of visas and expedite evacuation processes.

12:13 NATO to hold virtual summit on Friday

The leaders of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) will hold a summit via videoconference tomorrow, Friday, to discuss the military actions initiated by Russia in Ukraine, diplomatic sources said Thursday (24.02.2022).

Meanwhile, NATO announced today in a statement that its member states had decided to take "additional steps" to strengthen "defense across the alliance." "Our measures are preventive, proportionate, and not scalable," the text notes.

12:01 Olaf Scholz: "This is Putin's war."

"There is no justification. This is Putin's war," German Chancellor Olaf Scholz said at an appearance in Berlin in which he again stressed that the Russian president is "flagrantly violating international law." Scholz joined London and Paris in calling for a NATO summit.

The chancellor advanced that "as a next step" NATO and European Union (EU) partners will decide on a package of "tougher" sanctions with which to make it clear to Moscow that it will pay "a bitter price" for the aggression.

11:55 Macron calls for NATO meeting.

French President Emmanuel Macron called for a NATO summit "as soon as possible" in the wake of the Russian offensive in Ukraine, his office said. The president "wishes the holding of a NATO summit as soon as possible, in concert with our partners and allies," the Elysée said, following a similar request from British Prime Minister Boris Johnson.

11:45 Lithuania to impose state of emergency after Russian invasion of Ukraine

Lithuania, an EU and NATO member country, declared that it is going to impose a state of emergency on its territory. "Today I am going to sign a decree to impose a state of emergency," declared Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda after a meeting of the National Defense Council.

He also indicated that the country will request the activation of "NATO Article IV", which allows for emergency consultations if a member of the military alliance is under threat, as other countries have already announced. The ambassadors of NATO's 30 member countries are scheduled to hold an emergency meeting on Thursday, a spokesman for the military alliance announced, although more and more voices are calling for a summit of leaders.

11:26 Germany offers to help with refugees from Ukraine

German Interior Minister Nancy Faeser offered support to Eastern European countries, especially Poland, in the face of the expected wave of Ukrainian refugees. The German press estimates that between two hundred thousand and one million people could arrive in the European Union from Ukraine. "We will offer massive help to the affected countries, especially to our neighbor Poland, if there are strong movements of refugees," he said in a statement.

Also the governor of Berlin, Franziska Giffey, told local television that the city is preparing for the arrival of refugees. "For the next week, we have set ourselves the goal to discuss concrete implications, what preparations we can make, especially in case people flee this situation," Giffey told rbb.

11:22 Ukrainian refugees cross the border to Moldova

About two thousand Ukrainian refugees already crossed the border with Moldova after the beginning of the Russian military operation, Moldovan Interior Minister Anda Revenko reported. "So far we have registered about 1,900 Ukrainian citizens who have crossed the Moldovan border. There are even whole families. Five people applied for asylum," he informed at a press conference, quoted by the Russian agency TASS.

For her part, Moldovan President Maia Sandu assured that her country "will take care" of the refugees and noted an increase in the migration flow at the border crossing points with Ukraine. "We will help people who need our help. At the moment we are ready to receive tens of thousands of people," he added.

11:18 United Kingdom calls for emergency NATO meeting.

British Prime Minister Boris Johnson on Thursday called for an urgent meeting of leaders of NATO member countries in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which he called a "catastrophe" for Europe. "I call for an urgent meeting of all NATO leaders as soon as possible," Johnson tweeted, adding that he will address a speech to Britons during the day.

11:18 Ukrainian casualty toll rises: 40 soldiers, 10 civilians

More than 40 Ukrainian soldiers and a dozen civilians were killed in the first hours of the invasion launched by Russia against the neighboring country, an adviser to the Ukrainian presidency said. "I know that more than 40 servicemen were killed and several dozens were wounded. There are also about ten civilians killed," Oleksiy Arestovich told reporters.

Read: Russia defends its attack in Ukraine, says it is not seeking occupation

11:05 Moscow says pro-Russian separatists are gaining territory.

The Russian Army announced that the pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine it supports are making territorial gains against the Ukrainian army. General Igor Konashenkov, spokesman for the Russian Defense Ministry, said in statements to television that the rebels advanced three kilometers in the Donetsk region and one and a half kilometers in Lugansk, and assured that civilians had "nothing to fear" because Russia has only military objectives.

10:43 Ukraine breaks off diplomatic relations with Russia

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his country breaks diplomatic relations with Russia after the military aggression against Ukrainian territory ordered by the head of the Kremlin, Vladimir Putin.

10:34 Navalni says he is "against this war".

Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalni, who is imprisoned and faces new charges, expressed his opposition to the attack launched by Moscow, which "will cause a large number of casualties, ruin lives and continue the policy of impoverishment of Russian citizens."

"I am against this war. I believe that this war between Russia and Ukraine is being waged to cover up the robbery of Russian citizens and divert their attention from the problems inside the country, from the deterioration of the economy," he said at a hearing of the retrial opened against him last week, according to a video posted by the opposition Dojd channel.

10:23 Slovakia will also ask NATO to activate its Article 4.

Slovakia, which shares a 97-kilometer border with Ukraine, will ask today at the urgent meeting of the North Atlantic Council to open consultations on Article 4 of the treaty, which applies when one of the alliance countries feels threatened. "The situation demands it," said Foreign Minister Ivan Korcok.

In addition to Slovakia, the governments of Poland and the Baltic countries Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia also appealed to NATO's Article 4, which provides for immediate consultations among allies, while warning against the "foreseeable" Russian disinformation campaign and cyberattacks.

10:23 Berlin calls for a strong reaction from the G7, Europe and NATO.

"We will coordinate, within the EU, NATO and the G7, to implement the toughest sanctions package," German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock said, warning that these punitive measures will hit the German economy.

This war in our neighborhood will have repercussions for us, such as rising prices or falls in the stock markets," she admitted. "But if we do not react with fortitude, the price will be even higher," he added in a formal statement without questions.

Baerbock today chaired a virtual conference of G7 foreign ministers - which Germany chairs this year - at which, according to a ministry press release, all members condemned the Russian attack. A meeting of the group's leaders is scheduled for this afternoon.

Read: Biden accuses Putin of unjustified attack on Ukraine

10:19 Ukraine calls volunteer reservists to arms.

Kiev has issued a call to arms to volunteers of the Territorial Defense Units. "Ukraine has entered full defense mode. Anyone who is ready and able to hold a weapon can join the Territorial Defense Units in their region," this military formation announced on its Facebook page, while giving a list of addresses of all recruitment centers in the country.

10:17 Council of Europe condemns attack and announces measures

The Secretary General of the Council of Europe, Marija Pejcinovic Buric, condemned the Russian attack on Ukraine, "a flagrant violation of the Statute" of that body, while announcing a meeting of its bodies to "respond to the current situation".

"This is a dark hour for Europe and everything it stands for," Pejcinovic said in a statement, in which he pointed out that the armed action is also a violation of the European Convention on Human Rights.

10:06 Hundreds of Ukrainians cross the border to take refuge in Romania.

"Several hundreds" of Ukrainian citizens crossed in the early hours of Thursday the border separating their country from Romania (over 600 km long) to seek refuge in homes of friends and relatives in the face of the large-scale military invasion activated by Russia, Romanian authorities reported.

"The first data from the Border Police show an increase of several hundred people, although many of them have Romanian nationality, relatives or friends and even their own homes in Suceava," the prefect of this Romanian province bordering Ukraine told G4Media.

According to some estimates, the Romanian minority in Ukraine numbers about 400,000 people. Romania's Defense Minister Vasile Dincu told the media this week that his government is ready to take in more than half a million refugees from Ukraine.

09:57 Russian stock market opens with a 45.2% drop

The Russian stock market resumed trading after a temporary halt following the announcement about the start of a Russian military operation in Ukraine with the MOEX index currently down 45.2%. This morning, the Russian MOEX stock index suspended all trading on the trading floor until further notice. European stock exchanges also opened with declines of around 4%.

09:49 Belarus does not take part in the Russian military operation

Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko said that his country's troops are not taking part in the "special military operation" launched by Russia in Ukraine. "Today I read: 'About 05.00 a.m. the Ukrainian border in sector of Russia and Belarus was attacked by Russian troops, supported by Belarus.' You scoundrels! Our troops have no participation in this operation," the head of state said at a meeting with military personnel, quoted by the official BELTA agency.

09:39 Ukraine denounces entry of Russian tank columns into Lugansk

The Ukrainian Interior Ministry denounced the entry of several columns of Russian tanks into the area of the Kiev-controlled Lugansk region in the east of the country. "Russian tank columns entered the Lugansk region near the villages of Krasna Talivka, Milove, Horodysche," the Ministry states on its Facebook page.

09:32 Russia assures that it does not attack Ukrainian cities.

"The Russian Armed Forces do not attack Ukrainian cities. There is no threat to the peaceful population," the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement. The Russian military indicated that high-precision weapons are used against Ukrainian military infrastructure, anti-aircraft batteries and air bases.

"According to intelligence data, units and servicemen of the Ukrainian Armed Forces leavemassively their positions indicated Defense, which stressed that the places where the Ukrainian forces have laid down their arms are not subjected to attacks. He added that the statements of the Ukrainian side about the losses of aircraft and armored vehicles by the Russian army are a "complete lie".

09:28 Ukrainian order to inflict "maximum casualties" on Russian forces.

"The supreme commander of the armed forces [President Volodimir Zelensky] has ordered to inflict maximum casualties on the aggressor," said Ukrainian armed forces commanding general Valery Zaluzhni, assuring that the army was "countering with dignity" the enemy's attacks.

09:20 Ukraine claims to have recaptured town in Lugansk and killed 50 Russian troops

The Ukrainian Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security assured that the Ukrainian Army recaptured the town of Shchastia in the Lugansk region, and annihilated 50 Russian troops. "Shchastia is in our power!" the entity announced on its Facebook account.

09:17 Von der leyen condemns the "barbaric" attack and announces further sanctions.

European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen condemned Russia's "barbaric attack" on Ukraine, announced new European sanctions against Russian "strategic sectors," including blocking its banks from the European market, and warned Moscow that the European Union will not allow it to "tear down the security architecture" on the continent.

"Once again, in the heart of Europe innocent women and men are suffering. We condemn this barbaric attack and the cynical argument to justify it," Von der Leyen said in a statement to the press alongside the European Union's high representative for foreign policy, Josep Borrell.

"We are in Europe's darkest hours since World War II," said Borrell, for whom the sanctions package they are preparing will be the "most massive and toughest we have ever adopted" and warned Russian President Vladimir Putin that if he does not back down Russia will be "subjected to unprecedented isolation."

09:14 Poland asks to activate NATO Article 4

The government in Warsaw called for activating Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which provides for consultations between members "when, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties would be threatened."

"A moment ago, the (Polish) ambassador (ndlr) in Brussels submitted this request to the NATO secretary general, with a group of allies," Polish government spokesman Piotr Müller said. The ambassadors of the 30 member countries of the military alliance are due to meet urgently on Thursday in Brussels, a NATO spokesman announced.

08:50 Moscow closes sea transport between Ukraine and Russia

Russia decreed the closure of maritime traffic in the Sea of Azov, which stretches between Russia and Ukraine, following Vladimir Putin's announcement of an attack on the neighboring country, Russian agencies said. "In connection with the development of anti-terrorist activities, transportation in the Sea of Azov is suspended from 04:00 (02:00 CET) on February 24 until further notice," a representative of the federal maritime traffic agency Rosmorrechflot told Russian press agencies.

Read: Attention: Putin announces Russian military operation in Ukraine

08:48 Beijing insists on "keeping calm" despite attack.

"China is closely following the latest developments in Ukraine. We call on all parties involved to remain calm to prevent the situation from getting out of control," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying told a press conference.

Hours earlier, the Chinese ambassador to the United Nations, Zhang Jun, commented before the last meeting of the Security Council that the Asian country believes that "the door to a peaceful solution of the Ukrainian crisis has not yet been completely closed". The ambassador said China's position on "safeguarding the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states" has always been "consistent," but avoided explicitly condemning the Russian attack on Ukraine.

08:46 Germany can maintain its supply without Russian gas

German Vice Chancellor and Economics Minister Robert Habeck said that Germany is in a position to secure energy supplies without Russian gas and that one cannot be energetically dependent on a country that violates international law.

"We had hoped that it would come to this situation but we knew it could happen and had taken precautions. We cannot be so dependent on a country that violates international law. We are in a position to maintain supply," Habeck told German television.

Habeck also referred to the status of the Nord Stream II pipeline - which should transport gas from Russia to Germany via the Baltic - and said he did not see it being able to start operating in the short or medium term. However, he added that in the long term, work must be done to bring Germany back to normal relations with Russia.

08:39 France "strongly" condemns war in Ukraine.

"France strongly condemns Russia's decision to wage war on Ukraine," French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday, calling on Moscow to "immediately end its military operations." "France stands in solidarity with Ukraine. It stands by the Ukrainians and acts with its partners and allies to stop the war," the head of state added in two tweets.

Macron spoke by telephone with the Ukrainian president, Volodimir Zelenski, who asked him for "unity" of the Europeans in the face of the Russian attack. The French president, who also spoke with the head of the European Council Charles Michel, expressed "all the support and solidarity of France," the Elysee added.

08:48 Ukraine reports at least eight dead and a dozen wounded.

"A woman and a child were injured in the Konopot region, where a car burned. In the city of Podolsk of the Odessa region, seven dead, seven wounded and 19 missing as a result of shelling. In the city of Mariupol, Donetsk region, one dead and two wounded," Interior Ministry advisor Anton Geraschenko reported on his Telegram channel.

08:39 UK orders its airlines to avoid Ukrainian airspace

The UK ordered its airlines to avoid Ukrainian airspace "to keep passengers and crew safe," Transport Minister Grant Shapps announced. The minister assured that his government "stands with the Ukrainian people and is working with our international partners to respond to this act of aggression".

British Prime Minister Boris Johnson is chairing from 08:30 CET a meeting of his emergency cabinet (COBRA) at which new sanctions against Russia and other measures are expected to be adopted.

08:32 Russia's central bankintervenes to halt the ruble's slide

Russia's central bank on Thursday announced "interventions" in the foreign exchange market to "stabilize the situation" following the start of a Russian military offensive in Ukraine, which triggered falls of up to 10% in the ruble against the dollar. In early morning trading, the ruble was already at an all-time low of 90 rubles to the dollar, down 9.02% from the previous day's close.

"The Bank of Russia will ensure the maintenance of financial stability and the continuity of operations of financial institutions, using all necessary tools," the institution said, assuring that it had "clear action plans for any scenario."

08:30 Russian troops enter Ukraine through Crimea

Russian troops entered Ukraine's Kherson region bordering the Crimean peninsula, illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, the Ukrainian Border Guard reported Thursday (24.02.2022). "Currently, movement of military equipment across the peninsula from the administrative border is observed," the Ukrainian entity assured in a statement.

The Border Guard Service published a video in which the crossing of armored vehicles, tanks and military trucks through the border crossing point can be seen. The entity noted that Russian forces use artillery and heavy weapons against the border units of the Ukrainian provinces of Lugansk, Sumi, Kharkov, Chernigov and Zhitomir.

title: Russian stock market plummets almost 30% and the price of a barrel of oil rises above US$ 100 for the first time in seven years
text:
The Russian Moex stock index returned to trading after its suspension with a 40% plunge, now shrinking its sharp fall and losing almost 30%. For its part, the Russian currency, the ruble, reached its historic low against the dollar -before the intervention of Russia's central bank-, after the launching of a military offensive by Russia against Ukraine.

Before the opening, the Moscow Stock Exchange announced in a brief statement that it was suspending "trading in all its markets until further notice".

Meanwhile, the price of a barrel of oil exceeds US$ 100 for the first time in more than seven years and world stock markets fall after the launching of a military offensive by Russia against Ukraine.

The European stock exchanges have fallen sharply since the first exchanges. Thus, the Frankfurt stock exchange lost 3.73%, followed by Paris (3.15%), Milan (3.10%), Madrid around 3% and London (2.45%).

In Asia, Hong Kong lost 3.24%. Tokyo closed with a fall of 1.81% and Shanghai, with a decline of 1.70%.

Russian President, Vladimir Putin, announced early Thursday morning the start of a "military operation" in Ukraine. Kiev claims it is a "far-reaching invasion".

"At the moment it is impossible to bet on any scenario," points out Ipek Ozkardeskaya, an analyst at investment company SwissQuote, for whom "it's panic on the markets."

"We can only follow the latest developments closely and be prepared for more volatility," he added.

The threat of war sparked fears over the supply of commodities such as wheat and metals in recent weeks as economies reopened after shutdowns due to the coronavirus pandemic.

Other assets considered safe havens, such as gold, the dollar and the Japanese yen, also rose in value.

World authorities have tried unsuccessfully to contain the conflict and Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelenski said he tried to communicate with Putin but was not answered.

U.S. President Joe Biden deplored Russia's "unwarranted attack" and warned that it "will bring catastrophic loss of life and human suffering."

"Russian-Ukrainian tensions lead to a potential demand shock [in Europe] and a larger supply shock for the rest of the world, given the importance of Russia and Ukraine in energy," noted Tamas Strickland of National Australia Bank.

Regarding natural gas, the reference market in Europe, the Dutch TTF, was trading this Thursday at 107.615 euros (about 121 dollars) per megawatt hour (MWh), 21% more than the day before.

The crisis comes at a time when governments around the world are struggling to contain inflation, fueled by rising demand due to the global economic reopening.

Much of the attention is focused on the U.S. Federal Reserve (Fed), whose authorities are preparing to raise interest rates in March to contain rising prices.

title: Reaction in the markets after Russia's offensive: commodities rise and stock markets fall by up to 4%.
text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a military operation in Ukraine to fend off separatists in the east of the country. "I have made a decision on a military operation," Putin declared in an unexpected TV message shortly before 03H00 GMT. In the message he called on the Ukrainian military to "lay down their arms." As expected, markets react in the worst way. Oil skyrocketed to u$s100, gas became 30% more expensive. Stock markets fall up to 3%.

Oil

The price of a barrel of oil surpassed 100 dollars on Thursday for the first time in more than seven years. Brent North Sea crude oil in its May contract settled at u$s101.84 with a jump of almost 9%, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil traded in the New York futures market in its April contract surpassed u$s100 a barrel with a rise of 8%. Brent crude oil after the escalation of the conflict reached u$s103, its highest level since August 2014.

Since the tension between the two countries began, the cost of a barrel has increased by 25%. It should be taken into account that Russia is the second largest oil exporter in the world and this may threaten the global recovery.

The level of harshness of the new economic sanctions that are being prepared to stifle the Kremlin economically will be key to gauge how far the rise in energy commodity prices can go. Although Vladimir Putin pledged not to turn off the gas or crude oil tap - a decision that could change overnight - his credibility is at rock bottom after the attack on Russia.

Gas

Even more relevant is the rise in gas, with which Russia covers approximately 25% of EU consumption, a share that in the case of oil exceeds 40%. The reference of the Dutch market TTF has already shot up about 33% compared to Wednesday's close and exceeded 118 euros per megawatt hour (MWh), after touching the barrier of 120 euros/MWh in the first minutes of trading.

This is a level that gas has not reached since the eve of last Christmas. In just three days, and since Russia recognized the independence of the Ukrainian provinces of Donetsk and Lugansk, the TTF has risen by more than 60%. The Russian attack on Ukraine comes after Germany decided to indefinitely suspend the Nord Stream 2 pipeline license and comes at a time when gas reserves in Europe are at a historically low level of just over 30%.

The exponential rise in gas prices over the last year is, together with the increase in the price of CO2 emission allowances, mainly responsible for the record electricity prices of the last few months. Each euro increase in the price of this raw material is equivalent to an increase of around two euros in the wholesale electricity market price.

Metals

The price of gold, the quintessential safe-haven asset, soared 6% this month to over 1,907 dollars per ounce. Following news of the Russian offensive, gold is trading at a record high, soaring 3% to trade at u$s1,969.90, triggering a strong stampede in equities and taking refuge in metals. If tensions continue to rise, analysts believe that the price of the metal is likely to approach record highs when it reached u$s2055.70 due to the fear caused by the coronavirus pandemic.

Next, another of the metals rising this morning is silver (+4%), whose price is already above u$s25 per ounce, leaving behind the psychological level of u$s23.80, which it could not break in previous weeks. Therefore, the flight of investors to the metal could trigger the approach to $ 30, a level that it did not visit since last May 2021.

On the other hand, Palladium (+9%) is another metal that is bouncing strongly, trading at a high of u$s2,667.00 and practically approaching levels of August 2021, so we do not rule out a test of u$s2800, the highs of July.

Asian stock markets

The mainstock market indexes of Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan plunged after Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered a military operation in Ukraine.

The Hong Kong Stock Exchange benchmark, the Hang Seng, fell 3% . The index that measures the performance of mainland Chinese stocks listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, the Hang Seng China Enterprises, fell as much as 4.14%. For their part, the two main mainland Chinese stock exchanges, Shanghai and Shenzhen, fell by up to 2%.

Russian stock market

The Moscow Stock Exchange Index fell more than 50% on Thursday and the Russian currency, the ruble, reached an all-time low against the dollar after Russia launched a military offensive against Ukraine.

The start of the military operation was followed by the suspension of trading on the Moscow Stock Exchange and the St. Petersburg Stock Exchange due to strong volatility in the markets. At 10:00 Moscow time, trading was reopened on the Moscow Stock Exchange. Losses were as high as 50%.

The currency and bonds also plunged, prompting the central bank to announce its first foreign exchange intervention designed to shore up financial stability since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine. "In the coming days, the Russian market will be extremely volatile. Given the high risks of tightening sanctions against Russia, we are revising our target benchmarks for Russian stocks," Evgeny Loktyukhov, Head of Economic and Industrial Analysis at PSB, told Russian media outlet Quote.

"There has never been such a significant drop in the recent history of the Russian stock market. The main reason for what is happening is the flight from risks amid the escalating geopolitical aspect," added Vladislav Silaev, a senior trader at Alfa Capital. In his opinion, until diplomats and politicians sit down at the negotiating table, the market will remain in the red.

The ruble slid to a record low of u$s89.60 against the dollar and approached a crucial threshold of 100 against the euro. It was around 70 to the dollar and 81 to the euro before the recent round of geopolitical tensions between Moscow and the West began to escalate in October.

"To stabilize the situation on the financial market, the Bank of Russia decided to initiate interventions on the foreign exchange market," the bank said Thursday. The move helped the ruble cut losses slightly.

The Moscow and St. Petersburg stock exchanges were forced to halt trading after their main indexes plunged by more than 30%. "Trading on all markets was suspended. The restart will be announced at a later date," the Moscow Stock Exchange said in a statement, reports Efe. The St. Petersburg Stock Exchange, the country's second largest, also announced a "ban on bids and contracts for all trading modes and all types of securities.

European stock exchanges

The main European stock exchanges opened with massive sell-offs by investors. Frankfurt lost 4.9%, Milan 4.3%, Paris 4% and London 2.7%. The Euro Stoxx 50 also opened in the red by more than 3.5%. The Ibex fell back to close to 8,000 points. The fall is a far cry from the 14.06% of March 12, 2020, when the markets panicked due to the pandemic and the mass confinements that were being decreed halfway around the world. Even so, the tensions unleashed by Putin with major Western powers, including the US and the EU, has dealt a blow to markets that had been heading into negative territory for weeks.

"Emerging market equities could fall as much as 10% in the near term unless they can be offset by a mediating policy response, mainly due to investor confidence and growth prospects," said Leonardo Pellandini, an analyst at Julius Baer.

title: Real Time Economics: Russia Attacks Ukraine, Oil Prices Jump, Globalization in Retreat
text:
Russia Attacks Ukraine

Russia's invasion of Ukraine heaped fresh risks on a global economy struggling with soaring inflation, supply-chain snarls and a rocky recovery from the pandemic. The economic impact will depend on the scale of the fighting and the new sanctions that the U.S. and its allies have promised. Financial markets reacted swiftly to the invasion, with stock markets in Europe dropping sharply and commodity prices soaring, Paul Hannon reports.

A global oil benchmark surged above $100 a barrel for the first time since 2014. While Ukraine isn't a big oil producer, Russia is one of the world's biggest and most influential crude-market players , Joe Wallace and Jenny Strasburg report.

Russia is also the single biggest exporter of natural gas, and the country's military push poses another threat to Europe's already tenuous supply . Fresh military action ratchets up risks to Ukraine's gas-transport infrastructure. It also poses the threat that Russia will shut off its gas in response to Western sanctions. More broadly, if European gas prices stay high, that can affect markets further afield, by diverting supplies and driving up prices elsewhere, Joe Wallace reports.

Russia's central bank said Thursday that it would start interventions in the foreign-exchange market after the ruble plunged to a record low . Russia holds a formidable war chest of over $600 billion in foreign exchange reserves and gold that it can use in currency markets to prop up the ruble, Caitlin Ostroff reports.

The U.S. and its allies are poised to unveil further sanctions against Russia . WSJ podcast: How Putin has planned for sanctions. Ann Simmons and Georgi Kantchev describe the sanctions that could be coming, and how Russia has prepared for this moment . Western companies with operations in Russia and Ukraine are girding for disruptions . With Nord Stream 2 freeze, Germany takes first step to cut Russian gas reliance . Crisis kicks off new superpower struggle. Beijing and Moscow now hold a stronger hand in confronting the West than during the Cold War . Live coverage: The latest news on the Russia-Ukraine crisis . What to Watch Today

Bank of England Gov. Andrew Bailey gives opening remarks at a BOE conference on the monetary toolkit at 8:15 a.m. ET.

U.S. jobless claims are expected to fall to 235,000 in the week ended Feb. 19 from 248,000 one week earlier. (8:30 a.m. ET)

U.S. gross domestic product for the fourth quarter is expected to advance at an annual pace of 7% from the prior quarter, revised from a previous estimate of 6.9% growth. (8:30 a.m. ET)

U.S. new-home sales are expected to fall to an annual pace of 803,000 in January from 811,000 one month earlier. (10 a.m. ET)

The Kansas City Fed's manufacturing survey is expected to tick up to 25 in February from 24 one month earlier. (11 a.m. ET)

Federal Reserve speakers: Richmond's Thomas Barkin to the Maryland Chamber of Commerce at 9 a.m. ET, San Francisco's Mary Daly at a Bank of England panel on unwinding quantitative easing at 11 a.m. ET, Atlanta's Raphael Bostic at a banking outlook conference at 11:10 a.m. ET, Cleveland's Loretta Mester on the economic outlook and monetary policy at 12 p.m. ET, and governor Christopher Waller on the economic outlook at 8:25 p.m. ET ( webcast ).

Live Q&A: What happens next in Ukraine? Join WSJ's Executive Washington Editor Jerry Seib, in conversation with reporters, as they discuss the latest developments in Ukraine and what might lie ahead . (1 p.m. ET)

Enjoying this newsletter? Get more from WSJ and support our work with a special subscription offer .

Top Stories Clash Over Ukraine Drives a Dagger Into Globalization

The global economic order is unraveling. After the Cold War, globalization was triumphant in Western capitals. Market forces and global rules determined where goods, services, capital and knowledge would flow, not governments, ideology or spheres of influence. Russian president Vladimir Putin rejected that vision. To him, economic integration ought to reflect geographic, cultural and strategic ties. Ukraine's 2013 bid to integrate with the European Union, and Russia's response-blocking Ukrainian imports and threatening to charge more for natural gas-shows that the growing schism between Russia and the West is as much a fight about the rules that govern the global economy as it is about military alliances and missile installations. To Mr. Putin, the EU is a threat just like NATO, Greg Ip writes.

Working on the Highway

Rising prices and snarled supply chains are poised to blunt the impact of the $1 trillion infrastructure law Congress passed with bipartisan support last year. How many roads, bridges, railways, fiber optic lines and other types of infrastructure the U.S. can build or fix under the law will largely hinge on the extent of increases in everything from the cost of diesel fuel to workers' wages. Elevated costs for materials and labor are already pushing contractors to charge more for construction projects, government data show, increases that economists and industry officials say could reduce the number of infrastructure projects the new federal money can finance. State and local officials facing higher prices may give priority to easier, less ambitious projects, and some worry that a rush of government spending could exacerbate inflation in the industry, Andrew Duehren reports.

With spring and summer travel season comes a familiar pandemic reality: Car rentals will be expensive . Rental-car companies and analysts say they expect shortages to continue in the coming months due to the global chip shortage and other supply-chain constraints. With demand for rental cars expected to be high, plan to book early and brace for high prices in popular leisure destinations, Allison Pohle reports.

A more infectious type of the Omicron variant has surged to account for more than a third of global Covid-19 cases sequenced recently, adding to the debate about whether countries are ready for full reopening. Health authorities are examining whether the subvariant of Omicron, known as BA.2, could extend the length of Covid-19 waves that have peaked recently in Europe, Japan and some other places, Peter Landers and Miho Inada report.

Tweet of the Day What Else We're Reading

More than half of unemployed men in their 30s have a criminal record. "We estimate 64% of unemployed men have been arrested, and 46% have been convicted. Unexpectedly, these rates vary only slightly by race and ethnicity. Further investigation of other outcomes such as marriage, education, household net worth, and earnings shows large differences between unemployed men who have a criminal history record and those who do not. One major implication of these findings is that employment services should focus more on the special challenges facing unemployed men with criminal history records," the RAND Corporation's Shawn Bushway and co-authors write in a new study .

title: Stock markets plunge and oil prices rise above $100 after Putin's attack in Ukraine
text:
Russia's attack in Ukraine early this morning is causing the markets to tremble. After the generalized collapses in Asia, the main European stock exchanges opened Thursday with declines that in cases such as Germany and Spain have reached more than 4% in the first minutes of trading, while the Russian stock market plunged more than 40% and dragged the ruble down by more than 10%.

The fall of the Ibex 35 is close to 2.8% after the initial plunge of 4.5%, with almost all the stocks in the red and falls that are especially significant in the banking sector. Santander (-4.8%), BBVA (-4.1%), Sabadell (-4%) and CaixaBank (-3.7%) lead the losses that place the selective in the fight to maintain the level of 8,200 points. The situation is similar in the rest of Europe, where the Dax in Frankfurt and the Cac 30 in Paris dropped 3%, while the Ftse Mib in Milan fell by almost 3.5%.

In recent days, the stock markets had avoided the increased tension in Ukraine, which led analysts to believe that investors had discounted a large part of the geopolitical risk in the area. However, Russia's step forward has put panic back into investor sentiment and triggered volatility.

"Based on the movement seen at the European open, Ukraine risk was not discounted. Uncertainty will remain in the short term," notes Javier Molina, spokesman for the multi-asset investment platform eToro in Spain.

It was after 4:00 a.m. when Russian President Vladimir Putin announced "a military operation" in the Donbas region following a request for military aid from the self-proclaimed republics of Donetsk and Lugansk and in the middle of the emergency Security Council being held in New York.

Then, several explosions shook several Ukrainian cities, Russian troops landed in Odessa and artillery shelling took place on the border following the announcement by the Russian president.

In this scenario, Russia has blamed Ukraine for the escalation of the conflict and has defended its decision to launch a military operation in the Donbas region before the United Nations Security Council, which met on Thursday night on an emergency basis.

For its part, the European Union has announced that it will respond with "massive" sanctions to Russia's military aggression against Ukraine, assuring that Russian President Vladimir Putin will "pay" for an "unprecedented" attack.

"We expect a sharp drop in equities from current levels. Developed market equities could lose up to 10% in the short term, mainly due to a loss of investor confidence and growth prospects," notes Leonardo Pellandini, equity strategist at Julius Baer.

Falling rubleThe fear is most evident in the Russian markets, where both the major indices and the ruble are being hit hard. MOSCOW, Feb 22 (Reuters) - The Russian central bank on Tuesday said it was ready to take all necessary measures to support financial stability, as Russian assets were hammered after Moscow sent what it called "peacekeeping" forces into eastern Ukraine.

The rouble hit a near two-year low after President Vladimir Putin ordered the deployment of troops to two breakaway regions in eastern Ukraine after recognising them as independent.

The sharp drop in the rouble from levels around 70 to the greenback seen just four months ago is expected to fuel already high inflation, one of the main concerns among Russians, which would dent the country's already falling living standards.

"The Bank of Russia is keeping the development of the situation on the financial market under control and is ready to take all necessary measures to support financial stability," the bank said in a statement.

It also announced some easing of requirements for banks, saying lenders would be permitted to use the market value of stocks and bonds in their portfolios as of Feb. 18 in earnings reports until October.

But the central bank, which does not target a particular exchange rate for the free-floating rouble, fell short of saying what other measures it could take as Russia braced for a new round of Western sanctions that could target Russian banks and state debt.

"Volatility would obviously increase in this situation (of new sanctions), and it would be worth the Bank of Russia considering entering the market with interventions at some points," said Egor Susin, managing director at Gazprombank Private Banking.

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Deepening Ukraine crisis jolts stocks, sends oil surging
text:
* European and U.S. futures tumble

* Asia stocks set for worst day in February

* Russian rouble hits 15-month low

* Most currencies more muted

* Brent crude races to 7-year high, gold jumps

By Xie Yu and Alun John

HONG KONG, Feb 22 (Reuters) - Global stocks tumbled while safe-havens rallied and oil surged on Tuesday as Europe's eastern flank stood on the brink of war after Russian President Vladimir Putin ordered troops into breakaway regions of eastern Ukraine.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia Pacific shares outside Japan was on course for its worst day for this month, off 1.66%, weighed by markets in Hong Kong and mainland China. Japan's Nikkei shed 1.7%.

U.S. and European markets were also braced for sharp losses at the opening bell, with S&P 500 futures down 1.4%, Nasdaq futures off 1.9%, the pan-region Euro Stoxx 50 futures 1.1% lower, and FTSE futures down 0.6%.

Both Asian shares and U.S. and European futures had fallen more earlier in the session.

In contrast, Brent crude futures rose 2.1% to $97.44, a new seven-year high, on worries Russia's energy exports could be disrupted. Spot gold added 0.1% to $1,908.10, having earlier hit a new six-month top of $1,913.89.

Putin on Monday recognised two breakaway regions in eastern Ukraine as independent and ordered the Russian army to launch what Moscow called a peacekeeping operation into the area, upping the ante in a crisis that could unleash a major war.

A Reuters witness saw columns of military vehicles including tanks early Tuesday on the outskirts of Donetsk, the capital of one of two breakaway regions, and Putin signed treaties with leaders of the two breakaway regions giving Russia the right to build military bases.

Washington and European capitals condemned the move, vowing new sanctions. Ukraine's foreign minister said he had been assured of a "resolute and united" response from the European Union.

Following Russia's latest move "we are much closer to military intervention, which of course is going to drive a lot of the risk off sentiment in the markets,” said Carlos Casanova, senior Asia economist at UBP, adding the short term volatility in markets caused by both geopolitical factors and the U.S. Federal Reserve was 'relentless'.

Casanova said the consequences would be higher oil prices, an equity sell off, and people flocking to safe haven assets like the Japanese yen.

In Hong Kong, shares of Russian aluminium producer OK Rusal plunged as much as 22.1% to HK$6.18, their biggest daily percentage decline since April 2018.

Away from Russia, and not helping the Hong Kong market, Hong Kong-listed Chinese tech stocks fell 2.3%, with heavyweights Tencent and Alibaba both hit by speculation about a new wave of regulatory scrutiny.

CURRENCIES QUIETER

In currency markets, moves were more muted, barring the Russian rouble which hit an 15-month low early in Asian trading, before steadying.

The Japanese yen walked back early gains which had taken it to a near three-week high of 114.48 per dollar, fellow safe-haven the Swiss franc was holding steady near the previous day's one-month high, and the euro recovered to trade flat after earlier falling to a one-week low of $1.1286.

"Currency markets are not really showing the same level of caution as equity markets," said Matt Simpson, senior market analyst at City Index.

"When you read the headlines .. you'd expect to see some follow-through in the markets. We are in equities but we're not in currencies," he said.

"Interestingly, overnight the Swiss franc was the safe haven, not the Japanese yen."

The nerves also drove U.S. Treasury yields lower, with benchmark 10-year Treasury yields diving as much as 7 basis points to 1.846%. Bets on Federal Reserve rate hikes also eased and the chance of a 50 basis point hike next month fell below 1-in-5.

U.S. policy makers have been sparring publicly about how aggressively to begin tightening.

Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman said on Monday that she will assess incoming economic data over the next three weeks in deciding whether a half percentage point interest rate rise is needed at the central bank's next meeting in March.

title: European Stocks Drop on Fear of War in Ukraine -- WSJ
text:
Stock futures and bond yields whipsawed, pointing to another volatile day on Wall Street, as investors tried to assess the possibility of a war in Europe.

Futures for the S&P 500 rose 0.1% after sliding early Monday. Contracts for the technology-focused Nasdaq-100 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average also ticked up 0.1%, recouping earlier losses. Stocks fell Friday after U.S. warnings that Moscow could invade Ukraine at any moment.

Yields on government bonds also bounced back, after falling as investors reached for the safety of U.S. Treasurys. The yield on 10-year Treasury notes ticked up to 1.968% from 1.951% Friday. Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions.

Overseas stock markets dropped, catching up with Wall Street's late-week tumble. The Stoxx Europe 600 lost 1.9%, led lower by banks and travel and leisure companies. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.2% and China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1%.

Oil prices edged down, after jumping on concern a war would curtail supplies of Russian crude amid a lack significant spare supplies. Brent, the benchmark in energy markets, fell 0.8% to $93.72 a barrel, holding near its highest level since 2014.

Prices for natural gas -- of which Russia is the single biggest exporter globally -- rose on both sides of the Atlantic. In the U.S., gas prices rose 3.1% to $4.06 per million British thermal units. Prices in Europe, which depends on Russia for much of its gas, a chunk of it flowing through Ukraine, jumped 5%. Prices for palladium -- a metal widely used in the auto industry and heavily produced in Russia -- added 3.5%.

Stocks have been buffeted this year by the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates. The central bank is gearing up to increase borrowing costs to combat the highest rate of inflation in four decades, winding down the easy-money policies that have pushed riskier assets higher for much of the past two years.

The possibility of a ground war in Europe has loomed as an additional source of uncertainty for investors. Moscow has denied intending to invade Ukraine, but Russia's military buildup has quickened, with forces positioned on three sides of the country.

In recent weeks, investors had wagered that war would be averted, piling into the ruble and hryvnia, as well as Russian and Ukrainian government bonds. Those assets were volatile Monday, initially selling off before clawing back some ground.

Russia's benchmark stock index, the Moex Russia, fell 1%. Ukraine's hryvnia weakened 1.7% to 28.55 a dollar. The yield on a dollar-denominated Russian government bond maturing in 2026 rose to 4.441% from 3.926% Friday, according to Tradeweb. Investors say the standoff over Ukraine is difficult to trade. If Moscow were to attack and the U.S. and its allies responded with sanctions, the hostilities could affect the world economy and markets in unpredictable ways.

Prices in Europe, which depends on Russia for much of its gas, a chunk of it flowing through Ukraine, jumped 8.8%.

Investors reached for assets they perceive to be havens at times of uncertainty. The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes fell to 1.924% from 1.951% Friday, having reached a two-year high of 2.028% Thursday. Yields and bond prices move in the opposite direction. Gold futures rose 0.8% to $1,857.40 a troy ounce.

Stocks have been buffeted this year by the prospect of an increase in interest rates by the Federal Reserve. The central bank is gearing up to raise borrowing costs to combat the highest rate of inflation in four decades, winding down the easy-money policies that have pushed riskier assets higher for much of the past two years.

The possibility of a ground war in Europe has loomed large as an additional source of uncertainty for investors. Moscow has denied intending to invade Ukraine, but Russia's military buildup has quickened, with forces positioned on three sides of the country. They include some of Russia's best-trained battalions and missiles that could strike targets throughout Ukraine.

The U.S. and its allies are withdrawing diplomatic staff from Kyiv in a sign Western capitals see diplomatic options narrowing. Companies are also taking precautions. Dutch airline KLM has stopped flying in Ukrainian airspace. Shares of Air France KLM, the Paris-listed holding company, dropped 5%.

In recent weeks, investors had wagered that war would be averted, piling into the ruble and hryvnia currencies as well as Russian and Ukrainian government bonds. On Monday, those trades started to reverse.

Russia's benchmark stock index, the Moex Russia, fell 3.1%. Ukraine's hryvnia weakened 1.7% to trade at 28.55 a dollar. The yield on a dollar-denominated Russian government bond maturing in 2026 rose to 4.574% from 3.919% Friday, according to Tradeweb. A Ukrainian government bond maturing in 2033 traded at a yield of 11.286%, up from 10.222%.

Catching some investors off guard, the ruble strengthened 0.7% to trade at 76.93 a dollar. Timothy Ash, a strategist at BlueBay Asset Management, said the move suggested Russia's central bank had intervened in foreign-exchange markets. "On the geopolitical risk, the ruble should be weaker," he added.

Russia's central bank has ample reserves of foreign currency with which to support the ruble. The bank didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Investors say the standoff over Ukraine is difficult to trade because they have no particular insight into the possibility of an invasion and the nature and severity of the West's response. If Moscow were to attack and the U.S. and its allies responded with sanctions, the hostilities could affect the world economy and markets in unpredictable ways.

One likely consequence, given Russia's position as a commodities superpower, would be higher energy prices, which could keep up the pressure on central banks to raise interest rates. At least in the short term, stocks and bond yields would likely decline as investors sought safe assets, investors say.

"We have the inflation story and then we have the Russian story," said Lars Skovgaard Andersen, senior investment strategist at Danske Bank Wealth Management. In the event of an invasion, "there will be some negative effect on markets, but I also think investors are incorporating this," he added.

Airline stocks were hammered in Europe after reports that several were avoiding Ukraine's airspace. Budget carrier Wizz Air dropped 9.2%, British Airways owner International Consolidated Airlines Group lost 6.1% and Deutsche Lufthansa fell 4.7%.

Among individual U.S. stocks, Splunk rose 8.2% in premarket trading after The Wall Street Journal reported that Cisco Systems had made a takeover offer worth more than $20 billion for the software maker. Blackstone slipped 2.6% ahead of the bell after the private-equity company agreed to buy Australian casino operator Crown Resorts for $6.3 billion.

London-listed energy company BP, which owns almost 20% of Russia's state-backed Rosneft Oil and invests in several joint ventures in Russia, fell 2.3%.

title: Ilya Ponomariov: 'With the Ukrainian crisis Putin's aim is to control Belarus'.
text:
In 2014, when Vladimir Putin asked for the formal approval of the Duma (the Russian Parliament) to complete the annexation of Crimea only one deputy voted against. It was Ilya Ponomariov (Moscow, 1975), who years later had to leave Russia. Today he lives in Kiev, where he combines business and public activity. In his opinion, the Kremlin's goal is not Ukraine, but to control Belarus and to be accepted by the West.

Will it be possible to solve the current confrontation through diplomacy or should Ukraine really prepare for a Russian attack?

I am convinced that now there is not going to be any new attack from Russia, and that it has not planned it. I think it is a game between the United States and Russia. Each side has its goals and they demand from the other that they be met at the expense of Ukraine. The Biden administration needs a brilliant victory after what happened in Afghanistan and on the eve of this year's Congressional elections. It is in their interest to have maximum tension here and then heroically defend Ukraine. On the other hand, the Kremlin has everything ready to de facto control Belarus. Not in the form of annexation, as with Crimea, but with a state union between the two countries. And it is in Russia's interest for this to happen without sanctions. For that it needs to make a trade-off: we will not attack Ukraine, but do not pay attention to Belarus.

Ukraine has regained the Western support front again, but its economy is suffering." Are you saying that Ukraine is a kind of victim of this game?

Ukraine also gains benefits, because the support front that was formed in 2014 and 2015 had virtually ceased to exist last year, and now it has been restored. But it also suffers great harm, because rumors of attacks have greatly weakened business activity in the country. A large number of businessmen have stopped investing, the national currency has weakened. That is why Zelensky and his team are trying to calm things down and say that there will be no attack.

Why is the Kremlin now putting pressure on the West and Ukraine?

A year ago now Russia already put large numbers of troops near the Ukrainian border, and then in the West there was no fuss like there is now. It was quieter, although there was a large Russian military deployment. And all that ended with a personal meeting between Putin and Biden (in June 2021 in Geneva) that the Kremlin had long been looking for. And from that experience they learned that you have to tense the situation, because the method works. So they have now repeated something that worked for them a year ago.

Putin wants to show the threat of an attack, but not execute it." The Kremlin provides no clue as to what it will do if the West does not agree to its demands. Why is Putin so cryptic?

He is a Chekist, his profession is to create intrigue. That is why one should not expect direct confrontation from Putin. He conducts special operations, secret, under the carpet, as he did in the Donbass, when he was declaring that they were not there. And that he is openly showing his troops near the Ukrainian border shows that what he wants is to show a threat, but not to execute it.

Putin has convinced himself that with the West there are no clear agreements and then it is difficult to keep them. Could Putin simply be seeking respect from the West, a return to international forums like the G-8?

He doesn't believe in that. He has convinced himself that with the West there are no clear agreements and then it is difficult to keep them. So he needs a tactical victory to be implemented here and now. That short-term goal, in my view, is Belarus.

Can Western sanctions change Russia's strategy?

No. But that doesn't mean they won't suffer from them. But they are not enough because they were made inconsistently and belatedly. A simple example: the story of excluding Russia from the SWIFT system. If this measure had been implemented in 2014 then for Russian business it would have had the effect of a bomb. But if such a measure is taken now, it will most likely have a boomerang effect, because during these seven years the Russian Central Bank has thoroughly prepared itself against such measures.

Is there a chance that Ukraine will regain Crimea in the future, or has Putin left it securely tied to Russia?

As long as Putin is in power the status of Crimea will not change. After that it will depend on how the political scenario in Russia transforms. Events may unfold in a variety of ways. Including the division of Russia. I hope this will not happen, but anything can happen. Putin has built a system that now stands on his person. And no doubt the Crimea issue will return that day to the agenda. But as long as Putin is in power, for him this is a fundamental, immovable issue.

If the conflict in the Donbass were somehow resolved, could Ukraine recognize that Crimea is already part of Russia?

It is not possible. I think that if it were put to the people of Ukraine to recognize Crimea as Russian in exchange for peace in the Donbass, I would say no. Ukrainian society is ready to make many and varied compromises to achieve peace in Donbass, even more than its politicians. But not at the cost of Crimea.

In Crimea it is necessary to respond with something to the fake referendum organized by the Kremlin." When you voted against Russia's annexation of Crimea, your argument was that the desire to become independent or not from Ukraine was an internal issue and that Russia did not have to intervene. Is it possible to hold a referendum in Crimea in the future to put an end to the issue?

At some point we will have to go through some referendum in Crimea, because it is necessary to respond with something to the fake referendum that the Kremlin organized. And that can only be done with a real referendum. Now this idea is not popular in Ukraine. But I think that at some point you will be able to come to an agreement. To do this, it is necessary for the Russian army to leave, to vote only the people who then lived in Crimea, and not the people who have come from Russia, mostly military. It would be necessary to conduct a free election campaign, as in Scotland, where each force set out its position and as a result take in the end an objective and fair decision.

How do you see the Russian extra-parliamentary opposition after the events of last year, after the imprisonment of Navalny?

The so-called Russian non-systemic opposition is defeated, there is no place for it at the moment. I am not saying that there are no concrete opponents, who are increasingly appearing in the West, but there is no organized political force. From my point of view, with his return from Germany, Navalni unintentionally helped the power to achieve an excuse to defeat it.

title: Fitch Rtgs: Severe Russia Sanctions Could Pressure Sovereign, Bank Ratings
text:
Fitch Ratings-London-08 February 2022: This commentary was originally published at 6:19 AM ET today and is being republished for technical reasons.

Severe sanctions on Russia could have negative rating implications for the sovereign and banks, Fitch Ratings says. For the sovereign, this would depend on their capacity to undermine macroeconomic and financial stability, or impede sovereign debt service payments, in line with Fitch’s rating sensitivities. For banks, sanctions that impede the ability to execute foreign-currency (FC) payments could be ratings negative.

Our base case is that new sanctions would not be sufficiently severe to warrant negative rating actions, but the risk of this scenario has become more significant in recent weeks.

Russia’s ‘BBB’/Stable rating is constrained by existing sanctions and the prospect of additional sanctions weighing further on GDP growth, financing flexibility and prospects for structural improvements, which are credit weaknesses relative to peers. The probability of some form of new sanctions was high when we affirmed the rating in December.

Tensions over Ukraine have increased the risk of conflict and more far-reaching sanctions, although our base case remains there is no full-scale invasion. Sanctions would likely be calibrated according to the extent of any Russian operations, which is highly uncertain.

Triggers could include contained military operations, or cyber-attacks. In the absence of conflict, more likely sanctions include preventing US investors transacting in secondary market sovereign debt, and additional sanctions on senior officials, government institutions and Vladimir Putin’s supporters’ wealth. Alone, these would be unlikely to cause ratings pressure.

Russia’s strengthened macro-policy framework since 2015, the build-up of large external and fiscal buffers and reduced external exposures have enhanced resilience to shocks.

FW Russian Improved Resilience Feb 2022

US secondary market sovereign debt sanctions would further constrain Russia’s fiscal financing flexibility and foreign investment, while capital outflows and a weaker Russian rouble could precipitate tighter policy. However, this would not significantly affect macro-stability or buffers, which include a Federal Treasury cash reserve and National Wealth Fund assets totaling 16.5% of GDP, and the ‘BBB’ category’s highest international reserves (17 months of CXP).

Non-resident OFZ holdings have fallen to 20.5% of the total (below 3% of GDP); we forecast general government surpluses (average 1.3% of GDP in 2022-2023) and the banking sector can absorb more debt. The Central Bank of Russia could provide additional liquidity and address market volatility through FX interventions.

FW  Russia Reserves, NWF Assets Feb 2022

Nevertheless, heightened risks around Ukraine and the US draft Menendez Bill underline the potential in a downside scenario for measures with a larger sovereign credit impact, such as preventing systemic banks and corporates from transacting in US dollars or accessing the international payments system, or broad-based energy market sanctions disrupting exports.

The biggest impact on banking sector creditworthiness would be if sanctions impaired large state-owned banks’ ability to execute FC payments, particularly through banning dollar transactions. Exclusion from SWIFT’s messaging system would also cause sizeable near-term disruption, given alternative systems have limited international participation. We do not expect such measures in our base case, partly because they would impede repayment of foreign creditors, and consider sanctions on less systemically important banks more likely.

The rating impact on banks of such severe sanctions would depend on their formulation, especially how far payments to creditors could be channelled through alternative payment systems and other Russian banks, and exposures switched to other currencies or settled with Asian and European counterparties. Bank ratings would likely be placed on Rating Watch Negative if such sanctions were imposed, and could be downgraded if greater uncertainty over the ability and willingness to service debt persisted. If sanctions resulted in freezing banks' FC assets, Viability Ratings would also come under pressure.

The impact on financial metrics is unlikely to result in downgrades given banks have generally large liquidity buffers to offset deposit outflows, foreign payment schedules are not onerous (reflecting adjustment to earlier sanctions) and potential regulatory forbearance, if needed.

FW Russian Bank FC Exposure Feb 2022

Rated Russian corporates are generally well positioned to cope with sanctions. Balance sheets are strong, including FC positions, and corporates with FC external debt typically benefit from export receipts. The biggest impact would be if sanctions restricted corporates’ ability to access FC cash or draw credit lines, and depends on whether Russian banks could still transact in dollars and international banks could service export cash flow and facilitate FC cash accumulation. Lower-rated Eurobond corporate issuers with short-term maturities are most sensitive to such measures.

By Natalia Zinets

KYIV, Feb 8 (Reuters) - Ukraine inflation slowed down only slightly to 9.9% in January as worries about a Russian military attack dragged down the hryvnia and weighed on prices despite another interest rate increase, a Reuters poll showed on Tuesday.

Russia, which seized Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 and backs separatists in the east of the country, has massed more than 100,000 troops near the Ukrainian border in recent weeks. Moscow denies planning a further invasion.

Ukrainian analysts from banks and brokerages estimated January inflation at 9.9%, according to the median figure in the poll, compared with 10% in December.

"We expect it to decline slightly in January," said Serhii Kolodii from the Ukrainian subsidiary of Raiffeisen Bank.

"A particular risk for inflation is represented by the devaluation of the hryvnia in the second half of January, mainly caused by geopolitical tension," Kolodii said.

The hryvnia currency lost about 5% against U.S. dollar in January by slipping to 29/$1 for the first time since February 2015. This reduced the impact of the central bank's efforts to restrain price rises.

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) raised its key interest rate by a further one percentage point to 10% in January following five increases in 2021 to fight inflation, which peaked at a three-year-high of 11% in September.

Nevertheless, analysts expect no further weakening of the hryvnia, which regained some strength in early February and returned to the level of around 28/$1. The median forecast in the poll shows the hryvnia at 27.8/$1 at the end of February.

"Russia's less aggressive rhetoric and significant NBU interventions played in favour of the local currency," analysts from the ICU brokerage said in a report. (Editing by Matthias Williams and Jane Merriman)
