title: UPDATE 2-Russia to increase daily  forex  sales in coming month
text:
(Updates, adds detail in paragraphs 6, 9-10)

By Alexander Marrow and Darya Korsunskaya

June 5 (Reuters) - Russia's finance ministry will increase daily foreign currency sales to the equivalent of 3.6 billion roubles ($44.3 million) a day between June 7 and July 6, it said on Monday, far exceeding analyst forecasts as it compensates for reduced fuel revenues.

After a hiatus of several months, Russia resumed foreign currency interventions in January, selling yuan rather than what it terms "unfriendly" Western currencies, underscoring the growing importance of China's currency as Moscow seeks to ensure economic stability in the face of Western sanctions.

The finance ministry said its regular FX sales on the market would total 74.6 billion roubles over the coming month. Analysts surveyed by Reuters had predicted sales would total 20 billion roubles.

In the previous period, between May 10 and June 6, the ministry had planned to sell foreign currency worth 40.4 billion roubles to compensate for lower oil and gas revenues.

The government carries out forex interventions to cover shortfalls - or build up reserves in the event of a surplus - in earnings from Russia's vital oil and gas exports, revenues from which have shrunk this year due to Western sanctions.

The central bank sold almost 450 billion roubles' worth of yuan and gold from the National Wealth Fund (NWF) on the finance ministry's behalf between January and May.

The finance ministry said May's oil and gas revenues were 30.6 billion roubles below plan. It said it expected a 44-billion-rouble shortfall from federal energy revenues in June.

Reduced revenues and soaring spending pushed Russia's Jan-April budget deficit to almost $44 billion, already 17% higher than the target for all of 2023, creating fiscal pressure as Moscow continues its military offensive in Ukraine.

The ministry had been reducing its monthly forex sales, and analysts had been waiting for it to begin buying rather than selling. Forecasting volumes is complicated by a lack of information on oil production dynamics.

"A regime switch from selling yuan to (large-scale) FX purchases would be significant," Rosbank analysts said. The ministry's foreign exchange operations help Russian banks maintain yuan liquidity, Rosbank said. ($1 = 81.2075 roubles) (Reporting by Darya Korsunskaya and Alexander Marrow; Editing by Toby Chopra, Sharon Singleton and Barbara Lewis)

title: UPDATE 1-Russian to sell 2 bln roubles of  forex  daily in coming month
text:
(Adds detail on energy revenues, deficit, NWF, analyst)

May 4 (Reuters) - Russia's finance ministry said on Thursday it would sell 2 billion roubles' ($25 million) worth of foreign currency a day between May 10 and June 6, a decrease in the volume of daily operations from the previous month.

After a hiatus of several months, Russia resumed foreign currency interventions in January, selling yuan rather than what it terms "unfriendly" Western currencies, underscoring the growing importance of China's currency in Moscow's efforts to ensure economic stability amid Western sanctions.

The finance ministry said its regular FX sales on the market would total 40.4 billion roubles ($513 million) over the coming month. A Reuters survey of analysts had predicted sales would total 27.5 billion roubles.

In the previous period, between April 7 and May 5, the ministry had planned to sell 74.6 billion roubles' worth of foreign currency to compensate for lower oil and gas revenues.

Russia halted forex interventions last year as Western nations imposed sweeping sanctions against Moscow, including the freezing of about $300 billion in foreign exchange reserves, after it sent its armed forces into Ukraine.

The government carries out forex interventions to cover shortfalls - or build up reserves in the event of a surplus - in earnings from Russia's vital oil and gas exports.

The ministry forecast the shortfall in oil and gas revenues to the budget in May at 8.1 billion roubles. In April, those revenues were 32.4 billion roubles less than expected.

Russia's federal budget balance sank to a deficit of 2.4 trillion roubles ($31 billion) in the first quarter of the year as Moscow spent heavily and energy revenues fell.

The central bank sold 409.1 billion roubles' worth of yuan from the National Wealth Fund (NWF) on the finance ministry's behalf between January and April.

Extra commodity income from June onwards may lead to small foreign currency purchases, said Dmitry Polevoy, head of investment at Locko-Invest.

title: Russian  central bank  rules out  foreign exchange  market  intervention  to support ruble
text:
The governor of the Central Bank of Russia (BCR) ruled out on Wednesday intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the ruble, which has depreciated since early March by nearly 10 percent against the dollar and by nearly 23 percent against the euro. "We know from experience that attempts to manage the exchange rate do indeed lead to sharp devaluations, to financial crises," BCR Governor Elvira Nabiulina told a joint session of several Duma economic committees. The head of the Bank of Russia noted that the monetary regulator is in favor of a more stable foreign exchange market, but is against the administrative determination of the exchange rate in order not to distort economic realities and to maintain a balance between the interests of exporters and importers. Dear shareholders,

For the year ended 31 December 2022, ENR Russia Invest SA and its subsidiaries produced a consolidated net profit of CHF 0.18 million (2021: consolidated net profit of CHF 3.34 million).

During 2022 our profitability was impacted by ruble strength or weakness. In early 2022, the ruble depreciated sharply against the Swiss Franc on the back of events in Ukraine. After Central Bank of Russia ("CBR") intervention, stability returned. The ruble then strengthened strongly against major currencies for most of the year due to rising export revenues, ruble based gas payments by customers and falling Russian imports (at half-year 2022, ruble strength resulted in an uplift in profits at that time). The ruble remained strong until December 2022, but then depreciated sharply against major currencies during the last few weeks of the year. Year-on-year, it appreciated by 3.72% against the Swiss Franc.

Our flower production facility is the largest Rus- sian domestic flower producer and benefits from its locally produced flowers to substitute imported flowers. The flowers are high-quality and last longer compared to imported flowers and the business provides regular and reliable supply to customers. Greenhouses are at full capacity utilisation with 25.1 hectares in productive use. 15 hectares are planted with more than 40 rose varieties; 2 hectares are planted with more than 20 germini and gerbera varieties; 5

hectares are used for a large annual tulip program and a range of seasonal flower programs; 3 hectares are used for chrysanthemums and 0.1 hectares for flower plant propagation. Flower growing, cutting and sales increased in 2022 as rose, gerbera and germini plants mature and yields improve. Clients include retail and wholesale groups and the smaller regional client base continues to grow.

At the Petrovsky Fort business centre in Saint- Petersburg the business continues to perform solidly. A new supermarket store now brings convenience grocery shopping to our tenants. As part of the optimisation program on the retail floors, a 1'000 square meter area is under refurbishment to create a new value added coworking rentable space. Regular ongoing improvements and capex programs continue.

At the Turgenevskaya parking garage in Mos- cow, daily parking income is stable and the new card payment system makes it easier for customer payments. The rental of longer-term parking bays to corporates and individuals are also improving.

Due to the sanctions against Russia, Russian en- tities, and individuals, the operating environment in Russia was impacted by import and export restrictions, import substitution, new regional and international sourcing and distribution routes, capital controls, and a lower growth environment.

Notwithstanding, our operational businesses, which are all focused on the domestic economy, continue operating at levels comparable to 2021. However, there are challenges as our listed equities and bonds have been blocked (we are restricted from trading or repatriating sales proceeds abroad) and the CBR tightened available channels to repatriate cash distributions from our operational businesses. We have taken the necessary actions to optimise available channels for cash repatriations. In addition, we renegotiated terms with our service providers and applied a range of measures within our group to cut costs.

On the economic front, the CBR initially increased the key rate in February to 20% to stabilise financial markets, but within a few months reduced this rate via number of cuts. At year- end 2022 the rate was 7,5%, below the 9.5% one year earlier. Notwithstanding the impact of sanctions and higher inflation in 2022, economic growth contracted by 2.9% in 2022, much lower than initial forecasts.

ENR continues to monitor geopolitical developments and the economic environment to evaluate how the situation is evolving, and to assess what actions to take.

text:

March 15 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble weakened on lower oil prices on Wednesday, as the finance ministry held debt auctions and investors looked ahead to this week's interest rate decision by the Bank of Russia.

By 1241 GMT, the rouble was 0.9% weaker against the dollar at 75.98 and had gained 0.3% to trade at 80.39 against the euro. It had shed 0.5% against the yuan to 10.99.

Brent crude, a global benchmark for Russia's main export, was down 2% at $75.9 a barrel, its lowest mark since mid-December.

The rouble hit its strongest level against the dollar since the start of March early on Tuesday, before easing. The U.S. currency has come under pressure from fears of a broader banking crisis following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank.

Currency interventions are providing some support to the rouble, as Russia is selling 5.4 billion roubles ($71.7 million) worth of Chinese yuan per day between March 7 and April 6 to compensate for lower oil and gas revenues.

Domestic attention is focused on Russia's central bank, which will set interest rates on Friday and has signalled it will weigh up hiking rates in the coming months.

Analysts polled by Reuters widely expect the bank to hold its key interest rate at 7.5% before possibly raising the cost of borrowing later this year.

Russia's finance ministry sold 74.7 billion roubles in OFZ treasury bonds at auctions on Wednesday, with one still to come, after a pause in debt issuance last week.

"Investors will continue to be cautious in the debt market ahead of this Friday's central bank meeting," said Promsvyazbank analysts. "With expectations that the key rate will be held, the regulator's signal will likely remain quite hawkish."

Russian stock indexes were lower.

title: *S&PGR Revises Kazakhstan Outlook To Stable From Negative
text:
3 Mar 2023 16:13 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Kazakhstan Outlook To Stable From Negative


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Government borrowing costs are increasing, given rising interest rates 
and the reliance on domestic debt issuance. 
     -- Kazakhstan relies on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium for about 80% of 
its oil exports, a prolonged disruption of which could negatively affect its 
external and fiscal metrics. 
     -- In our view, however, Kazakhstan's strong fiscal and external balance 
sheets make risks related to temporary disruptions to the pipeline manageable. 
     -- We therefore revised our outlook on Kazakhstan to stable from negative 
and affirmed our 'BBB-/A-3' ratings on the sovereign. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On March 3, 2023, S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on the Republic of 
Kazakhstan to stable from negative. At the same time, we affirmed our 
'BBB-/A-3' long- and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit 
ratings on the sovereign. We also affirmed our 'kzAAA' national scale rating 
on Kazakhstan. The transfer and convertibility assessment remains 'BBB'. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our view that Kazakhstan's government and external 
balance sheets will remain strong, providing sufficient buffers to absorb 
temporary disruptions to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) pipeline. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower the ratings if Kazakhstan's oil exports declined significantly 
for a prolonged period, weakening the economy's external position and 
increasing fiscal deficits. This could be the case, for instance, if the CPC 
pipeline were incapacitated for an extended period. We could also lower the 
ratings if rising borrowing costs continued to increase the government's 
debt-servicing burden. Other disruptions, such as deteriorating domestic 
stability with severe civil unrest, could also lead to a downgrade. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could raise the ratings if the medium-term fiscal trajectory improves more 
than we expect, reducing the pace of debt accumulation and debt-servicing 
requirements; and monetary policy effectiveness improves, as shown by more 
modest inflation, continued commitment to exchange rate flexibility, and a 
less dollarized economy. 
 
RATIONALE 
We base the outlook revision on our assessment that, although risks to 
Kazakhstan's oil exports through the CPC pipeline remain, absent a prolonged 
closure, the country's fiscal and external positions should be able to absorb 
temporary disruptions. 
 
In 2022, at least four incidents affected the CPC pipeline. In our view, 
geopolitical tensions from the Russia-Ukraine conflict could cause further 
disruptions (see "Kazakhstan Remains Vulnerable To Russian Intervention Over 
CPC Pipeline," published July 13, 2022, on RatingsDirect). About 90% of oil 
flowing through the CPC pipeline originates from Kazakhstan, while the 
remaining 10% is Russian. The U.S. government explicitly excluded 
Kazakh-origin crude oil from the pipeline from its sanctions related to the 
prohibition of dealing in Russian oil. 
 
We also account for the government's efforts to develop alternative export 
routes to the CPC pipeline, a significant portion of which is in Russia. 
Still, it seems likely that the CPC pipeline, which accounted for about 52 
million tons, 1.04 million barrels per day (bbl/d), or 81% of Kazakh oil 
exports over the first nine months of 2022, will remain the dominant export 
route for the foreseeable future. The most significant effort to diversify 
export routes is the government's aim to eventually export 6.0 million-6.5 
million tons, or 120,000-130,000 bbl/d, of oil through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan 
(BTC) pipeline. The government expects to begin exporting about 1.5 million 
tons, or 30,000 bbl/d, through BTC in 2023. The BTC pipeline runs through the 
"Middle Corridor," meaning the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey. 
Earthquake damage in the Turkish port of Ceyhan has delayed progress. 
 
Against the backdrop of the uncertain geopolitical environment, we think 
Russia could disrupt flows through the pipeline to gain leverage against 
Kazakhstan or the oil's consumers, namely countries in Europe that support 
Ukraine; or to hurt Western interests in the Kazakh oil sector (shareholders 
of the pipeline and oil fields include Chevron, ExxonMobil, Shell, and 
TotalEnergies). In such an event, disruptions at the pipeline might not be 
directed at causing economic pain in Kazakhstan. We think the country's fiscal 
and external buffers are sufficiently strong to absorb a temporary reduction 
in oil exports, similar to the incidents of 2022. But if the pipeline's 
closure were to be prolonged, this could be more damaging. 
 
Oil is the key economic sector in Kazakhstan, directly accounting for about 
15% of GDP, more than 30% of general government revenue, and over half of 
exports. We expect Brent oil prices will average $90 per barrel (/bbl) in 
2023, $80/bbl in 2024, and $55/bbl from 2025 and beyond (see "S&P Global 
Ratings Cuts 2023 European, U.S., And Canadian Gas Price Assumptions On Lower 
Demand," published Feb. 23, 2023). 
 
We expect the government's fiscal deficit to narrow sharply in 2023. However, 
government borrowing costs are increasing, given rising interest rates and 
reliance on domestic debt issuance. We project that interest will average 
close to 10% of revenue over 2023-2026. 
 
The ratings on Kazakhstan are supported by the country's strong fiscal and 
external balance sheets. These were built primarily with budgetary surpluses 
from the period of high commodity prices that ended in late 2014. The related 
assets were accumulated in the National Fund of the Republic of Kazakhstan 
(NFRK) and largely invested abroad. We forecast that the economy's liquid 
external assets will exceed external debt through 2026. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: GDP growth averaging close to 4% over 
2023-2026 will be supported by both the oil and non-oil sectors 
     -- Relations with Russia appear to be relatively strong for now. 
     -- President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was reelected at snap elections in 
2022. Constitutional changes extended the president's term of office to seven 
years from five. 
     -- Diversifying the economy, developing the private sector, and 
increasing the population's wealth levels will remain policy priorities. 
 
The impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict on Kazakhstan has thus far been 
moderate for the country's economic growth and banking sector. Russia is 
Kazakhstan's largest trading partner and a key source of imports. However, 
trading patterns are changing and Russian imports now make up about 30% of 
Kazakhstan's total imports, down from over 40% before the conflict, while 
exports to Russia make up about 10% of the total. Export bans imposed by 
Russia on sugar and grains and the depreciation of the Kazakhstan tenge (KZT) 
against the Russian ruble in 2022 contributed to rising food prices in 
Kazakhstan, driving annual average inflation to 15%. The secondary hit from 
sanctions imposed on Russia likely also made it more difficult for local 
companies to trade in some sectors, although we understand that informal trade 
has likely increased given the free flow of goods and people between the two 
countries. Kazakhstan mostly exports iron ore and uranium to Russia while 
importing cars, semi-finished goods, coal, and refined petroleum. 
 
The CPC pipeline connects Kazakhstan's Tengiz, Kashagan, and Karachaganak oil 
fields to the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in Russia. The incidents that led 
to the pipeline's disruption in 2022 included storm-related damage in March 
that reduced exports for almost a month; safety inspections for World War 
II-era deep-sea mines in June; a Russian court ruling in July to stop loading 
for 30 days due to alleged violations of the pipeline's oil spill plan, which 
was overturned a few days later and replaced with a minor fine; and subsea 
cracks discovered on buoyancy tanks that limited loading on two of three CPC 
single-point moorings. As a result, we estimate Kazakh oil production at 84 
million tons per year (equivalent to about 1.7 million bbl/d), down from 90 
million tons in 2021. 
 
Kazakhstan--along with Armenia, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, and Russia--is a member 
of the Eurasian Economic Union, a customs union that provides tariff-free 
trade and uniform custom tariffs for trade with nonmember states. The Eurasian 
Economic Union ensures the free movement of goods, services, labor, and 
capital between the states, and since mid-March it announced the ruble's use 
for reimbursement of customs fees with Russia and Belarus. 
 
Russia is also a key source of investment, accounting directly for about 8% of 
Kazakhstan's total external liabilities, although this could be larger since 
investment in its oil, gas, and mining sectors is often recorded through the 
Netherlands and the U.K. On the other hand, for Kazakhstan, unlike other 
Central Asian sovereigns, remittances from Russia are not an important source 
of income. 
 
Although Kazakhstan is a member of the Collective Security Treaty Organization 
(CSTO), a mutual defense organization with members from ex-Soviet states, we 
think it is unlikely to be directly involved in the Russia-Ukraine war. The 
government has affirmed its policy of neutrality, similar to when Russia 
annexed Crimea in 2014; stating its commitment to the territorial integrity of 
all nations, including Ukraine; and abstaining on U.N. votes to condemn the 
invasion. In response to the civil unrest in January 2022, the government 
requested assistance from the CSTO, and peacekeeping troops, mostly from 
Russia, arrived quickly to help restore order. In our view, should a similar 
situation occur, it is unclear whether Russia would have the resources or 
willingness to intervene to the same extent, without some reciprocation in 
terms of Kazakhstan indicating more support for Russia's foreign policy. 
 
The January 2022 protests quickly spread throughout Kazakhstan. They were 

3 Mar 2023 16:13 ET 
Press Release: S&PGR Revises Kazakhstan Outlook -2-


ignited by an increase in the price of liquified petroleum gas (LPG) but 
expanded to encompass broader grievances, including persistent inequality, low 
wages and living standards, aging infrastructure, constraints on political 
representation, and the perceived high level of corruption. Almaty--the 
largest city--saw the most unrest, damage, and loss of life. 
 
In response to the protests, President Tokayev announced a series of economic 
and governance reforms. The government reinstituted caps on gasoline, LPG, and 
utility prices for six months. The price controls for lower quality gasoline 
were then extended until the end of the year, while tariff increases will be 
tiered based on consumption. The president also announced institutional 
changes to reduce the influence of former President Nursultan Nazarbayev and 
his family on politics and business; increase plurality; decentralize power 
away from the president somewhat; and improve the competitiveness and social 
role of the large state-owned enterprises, such as Samruk-Kazyna. 
 
We expect political reforms will be gradual and modest. In our view, 
decision-making will stay centralized, while government checks and balances 
are limited, and there is no credible political opposition party. Moreover, 
limitations on independent media outlets are significant and perceived 
corruption is high, with Kazakhstan ranking 101 of 180 countries in 
Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index. 
 
President Tokayev held snap elections in November 2022, winning a second term 
in office with 81.3% of the vote. The win gave him a longer second term after 
a recent constitutional reform changed the presidential term to a single, 
seven-year term, from the previous system that was a maximum of two 
consecutive five-year terms. Mr. Tokayev started his new term on Nov. 26, 
2022. 
 
Government policy aims to diversify the economy through capital investment 
programs, including infrastructure and housing projects. The pool of 
investment projects under consideration amount to an estimated KZT30 trillion 
(26% of 2023 GDP). The government also focuses on cultivating the investment 
climate, reducing state participation in the economy, increasing 
private-sector competition, improving tax policy, reforming public 
procurement, and reducing administrative barriers for businesses. Although we 
believe the government's prudent and generally effective economic policymaking 
will continue, we do not anticipate that the broad scope of reforms will bring 
about significant economic changes. 
 
The economy expanded an estimated 3.2% year on year in 2022, supported by 
growth in construction, information and communications, trade, transport, and 
manufacturing. Government stimulus measures have continued since 2019, 
including higher spending on development projects, defense, wages, social 
security, and education. 
 
Over the next three years, we expect growth will average just under 4% 
annually. A key factor will be the expansion of the Tengiz oil field, which 
should significantly increase oil production. Absent disruptions to 
Kazakhstan's oil exports, we expect oil production could exceed 100 million 
tons per year by 2025, from 85.9 million in 2021. Ongoing investment and 
efforts to attract foreign investment should also support strong non-oil 
sector growth. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Although government debt remains modest, 
the interest bill is rising 
     -- We expect rising oil production and reduced spending of the oil fund 
will support fiscal consolidation in 2023. 
     -- We expect Kazakhstan's external asset position will remain strong, 
with liquid external assets exceeding external debt by 33% of current account 
payments by 2026. 
     -- Inflation averaged 15% year on year in 2022, above the National Bank 
of Kazakhstan's (NBK's) target range of 4%-6%, amid expansionary fiscal policy 
and higher imported prices. 
 
We expect the consolidated general government deficit will narrow to about 2% 
of GDP in 2023 from 3% in 2022. We expect higher rising oil production and 
reduced spending of the oil fund to support fiscal consolidation. We expect 
the government deficit to remain at about 2% of GDP annually through to 2026, 
supported by efforts to broaden the revenue base and moderate spending growth. 
 
The government will implement fiscal rules from 2023 to limit growth in 
spending and transfers from the NFRK to the budget. Still, spending will 
likely stay elevated as social priorities and reliance on government spending 
to boost economic growth will continue to steer fiscal policy in an uncertain 
external environment. Despite strong growth in non-oil revenue after the new 
tax code's introduction in 2017, a large share (30%) of fiscal revenue will 
continue depending on the oil sector over our forecast period to 2026. 
 
The government's strong balance sheet relies on a relatively large stock of 
liquid assets. We estimate net debt at about 0.5% of GDP in 2023-2026, with 
government liquid assets averaging about 26% of GDP, slightly below our 
estimate of gross government debt at 27% of GDP. We expect the implementation 
of a fiscal rule limiting transfers from the NFRK to the budget, and expanding 
oil production volumes, to help maintain government liquid assets near current 
levels as a percentage of GDP. 
 
Based on our forecast of relatively modest government deficits alongside 
strong nominal GDP growth, we expect the level of gross government debt to 
remain largely unchanged through 2026. Tenge depreciation will put some upward 
pressure on the debt burden because 36% of government debt is external and 
denominated in foreign currency--of this, about 60% is commercial and the rest 
is mostly from multilateral lenders. In the past two years, the government has 
increased borrowing from multilateral lenders and issued in the ruble market. 
 
Despite relatively low government debt levels, interest expenditure is rising 
partly because of the growing proportion of domestic debt. We expect interest 
costs will remain high given past monetary tightening, with average yields on 
short-term local currency government debt having risen to about 16% in 
November 2022 from about 10% on average in 2021. Nevertheless, since August 
2022, the Ministry of Finance has been issuing floating-rate bonds linked to 
the tenge overnight index. This can ease the interest expenditure burden when 
inflation recedes. We expect the government's interest-to-revenue ratio will 
average about 10% over 2023-2026, compared with 5% in 2019. 
 
In 2022, high oil prices led to the first current account surplus since 2014. 
The strong trade balance was partly offset by net outflows in the primary 
income account, spurred by profit repatriation on foreign direct investment 
related to oil production. We expect that falling oil prices and rising 
imports will bring the current account broadly into balance over 2025-2026. 
 
Kazakhstan's external asset position is strong, and we expect gross external 
financing needs will stay below 100% of current account receipts and foreign 
exchange reserves. Reserve assets at the NBK increased slightly, to about $35 
billion in 2022 from $34 billion in 2021. About 55% of reserves are gold. The 
NBK purchases gold with domestic currency, providing the government a way to 
increase reserves despite past current account deficits. We forecast reserves 
will remain broadly stable with the revaluation effect of lower gold prices 
being mitigated by the NBK's decision to decrease the share of gold. S&P 
Global Ratings forecasts gold prices of $1,600 per ounce (/oz) in 2023 and 
$1,400/oz over 2024-2025, compared with $1,829/oz in 2021 (see "S&P Global 
Ratings' Metal Price Assumptions: Lower Prices And Higher Costs Start 
Squeezing Profits," published Nov. 1, 2022). 
 
In our view, the more freely floating exchange rate, following the tenge's 
sharp devaluation in 2015, has helped the economy adjust to external pressure. 
The expected decrease in the current account surplus, to near balance in 
2024-2025, and the government's plan to reduce transfers from the NFRK, a key 
tenge purchaser in the market, will weigh on the currency over the forecast 
period to 2026. 
 
Annual average inflation soared to 15% in 2022, leading the NBK to raise the 
base rate 700 basis points (bps) to 16.75%. In its most recent monetary policy 
meeting of January 2023, the NBK kept the policy rate unchanged and has 
indicated its intention to stay at current levels for an extended period. We 
expect inflation will average 12% in 2023, slowing to 5% by 2025 because of 
improvements to inflation targeting, the higher base rate, and expected slower 
tenge depreciation. 
 
To increase independence and effectiveness of its monetary policy framework, 
the NBK announced it will not take part in new economic lending and support 
programs. It remains a shareholder of oil and gas company KazMunayGas NC JSC, 
with ownership of 9.8%. 
 
The NBK is also working with the Ministry of Finance to build out a yield 
curve for local currency debt to improve liquidity in the domestic secondary 
market. To increase transparency in the tenge market, the NBK began publishing 
all sales of U.S. dollars from the NFRK. While the central bank continued to 
focus on price stability, in 2019, it was reorganized by spinning off 
financial sector regulation to the new Agency for Regulation and Development 
of Financial Markets. The agency is in charge of financial market regulation 
and supervision while the ?entral bank focuses on macroprudential policy. 
 
Financial stability risks from the Russia-Ukraine conflict have been 
manageable so far, in our view. The three Russian banks that made up about 14% 
of systemwide deposits--Sberbank, VTB Bank, and Alfa Bank--have rapidly 
downsized their operations in Kazakhstan(see "Financial Stability Risks 
Stemming From Sanctioned Russian Bank Subsidiaries In Kazakhstan Have Been 
Limited," published July 7, 2022). This came through acquisitions and the

partial sale of the loan portfolio to other banks. Currently, only one bank 
with Russian participation (VTB Kazakhstan) operates in the country, with less 
than 0.5% share in systemwide customers funds. 
 
Despite significant exchange rate volatility, dollarization levels remained 
relatively stable in 2022, at 32% for deposits and 7% for loans. Individuals 
were encouraged to keep their deposits in local currency, due to rising 
deposit interest rates and a one-time premium of 10% on some types of 
tenge-denominated deposit accounts, the costs of which were shared by the NBK 
and Ministry of Finance. The scheme ended in February 2023, and given the more

We believe Kazakhstan remains in a prolonged correction cycle after previously

title: This is Russia living the Kremlin's alternate reality
text:
"We have to erase those symbols, the V and the Z, and whoever sticks them on our vehicles should be put in jail. A totalitarian regime is never as firm as it was before it collapsed." Over the past year Russian citizens have suffered the consequences of the Kremlin's intervention in Ukraine. Hundreds of thousands fled Russia to avoid being mobilized. Those who stayed behind live in a bearable parallel reality following government measures that have so far prevented economic collapse. And those who protest are repressed. In Russia, allegations like the above against the Kremlin can only be heard in court, during trials against activists, opponents or simple citizens accused of discrediting the armed forces.

The above words were uttered by journalist Maria Ponomarenko last week in her last word before judges in Barnaul (Altai krai) who sentenced her to six years in prison for a post she published on Telegram on March 17, 2022 saying that Russian forces had shelled the Mariupol theater, where hundreds of civilians had taken refuge. The Russian Defense Ministry had denied having anything to do with it and blamed the shelling on Ukrainian "nationalists."

The law against "fake news" about the army and the crackdown has reduced opposition to almost zero.Vladimir Putin signed the law against spreading "false news" about the army shortly after sending troops to Ukraine. Since then that rule, which can punish the offender with up to 15 years in prison, has conditioned Russian opposition to the Kremlin's plans in Ukraine and reduced it to almost zero.

Pavel Chikov, head of the Agora NGO, counted 180 criminal charges brought in this case as of December. This week, Alexander Bastrikin, head of the Russian Investigative Committee under the Kremlin, told the Tass news agency that to date "152 criminal cases have been opened, in which 136 people were prosecuted. Fifty-three criminal cases have been brought to court, 16 sentences have already been handed down."

It has affected both prominent political opposition figures (Ilya Yashin, sentenced to 8.5 years in prison) and activists (artist Sasha Skochilenko may spend 10 years in prison if convicted for changing supermarket price tags in St. Petersburg to peace messages) or simple citizens (in Arkhangelsk, university student Olesia Krivtsova is under house arrest for a message on Instagram about the explosion of the Crimean bridge in October). To citizens who have stayed in Russia and others who have left the country: recently well-known journalists Alexander Nevzarov and Veronika Belotserkhovskaya have been sentenced in absentia to 9 years in prison.

All these cases are an unmistakable message to those who in the first months of the special military operation , the euphemism used officially in Russia, were ready to show their faces and demonstrate. "From the very beginning we carried out protests against the war as an organization. In accordance with the new laws that reduce freedom, we were forced to stop carrying them out," explained Oleg Orlov, of the historical outlawed NGO Memorial, winner of the Nobel Peace Prize 2022, to La Vanguardia a few months ago.

Today only a vague memory remains of protests that the enormous police repression ended up blurring. From time to time, one can still see in Moscow a green ribbon that someone forgot to hang in a window or on a tree branch. Few know that for a few days it was used as a symbol of a resistance that today is totally silent.

Silent are also the few spontaneous signs of rejection, as when anonymous citizens left flowers next to a statue of the Ukrainian poet Lesya Ukrainka after a Russian attack on the city of Dnipro this January. And the police continue to arrest anyone who still dares to step forward. According to the NGO OVD-Info, more than 19,500 people have been arrested since February 24, 2022 for demonstrating against the war and military mobilization.

The IMF forecasts that Russia will grow by 0.3% in 2023 and the government believes it will emerge from recession this year.Every once in a while little glimmers of hope appear. Grigory Yavlinsky, founder of the liberal Yabloko, the only opposition party still active, wrote a few weeks ago an article in the magazine Novaya Rasskaz-Gazeta , one of the many banned or blocked media in Russia. In it, he insisted on achieving peace, the goal set by his party.

Peace "in practice can only be implemented if at least Putin, Zelenski, Biden and the leaders of the EU and NATO want to do it." But he regrets that "to date all parties intend to continue hostilities on a large scale, wrongly counting on a military victory, which in modern conditions is unattainable for anyone," wrote the veteran politician. And he ended with an emotional "Reflect! Stop!".

During the first Cold War, crossing the Iron Curtain was accompanied by a strange sensation of having arrived in a parallel world, where many things were familiar but totally different. Something similar is gradually happening in today's Russia. Except for the regions close to the Ukrainian border (Belgorod, Kursk, Bryansk), Russian cities give the impression that life goes on as if thousands of people were not dying a thousand kilometers away.

But there are disturbing signs that everything is changing. On their way to work, many Muscovites still stop by Starbucks to pick up their morning coffee or a Dunkin Donuts coffee shop to complete a quick breakfast. The problem is that they are now called Stars Coffee and Donutto. You look up and on the office building where there used to be a billboard advertising Ikea or Decathlon, now a huge Z and other patriotic messages are drawn.

After February 24, 2022, the Moscow we knew is turning into a parallel Moscow, as the authorities try not to make the changes too noticeable. It is part of the process of adapting to the sanctions and the departure of more than a thousand Western companies.

In the grocery stores there is no more Coca-Cola, Pepsi or Sprite, to name the best known. The factories of these and other brands have been sold to Russian entrepreneurs who continue to produce the same products under different names. The McDonald's chain was bought by a Russian entrepreneur and renamed Sabroso y Punto. Ikea has just announced the sale of its four factories.

Despite the war earthquake, the population that was not affected by the military mobilization in October has hardly felt a tremor. Why?

The explanation may lie in the fact that the catastrophic forecasts that many analysts and observers made about the Russian economy under the pressure of sanctions have not come true. Last March, Russian Central Bank experts expected an 8% drop in GDP, annual inflation of over 20% and an average annual rate of 110 rubles to the dollar. But none of these things happened. There was no banking crisis, because the Kremlin and the Central Bank took drastic measures to plug any holes and prevent the outflow of foreign currency from the country.

At the end of the year, Putin announced a 2.5% drop in GDP, much lower than the best forecasts of months earlier.Russia has also been helped by its main economic resource: hydrocarbon exports. Together they allowed the ruble to recover from the March slump and inflation to be contained. In the first six months of the intervention in Ukraine, Russia made a piggy bank of $158 billion from the sale of energy products, according to the Energy and Clean Air Research Center, Finland. Moscow found in Asian markets, especially China and India, an alternative to the loss of customers in Europe.

In the first months of the conflict, the sanctions hardly affected hydrocarbon exports, explained Oleg Itzhoki, a professor at the University of California in Los Angeles, in Meduza. Only the US imposed an embargo on Russian oil, but supplies there were small, while the European Union continued to buy oil and gas.

At the end of the year, Putin announced a 2.5% drop in GDP. Much lower than the best forecasts months earlier. Moreover, the IMF has predicted that this year Russia may even have growth. In January it stated that the Russian economy will grow by 0.3%, when its previous forecasts indicated a fall of 2.3%. By 2024 he forecasts growth of 2.1%. Deduction in Moscow: Russia has resisted.

With these figures Andrei Belousov, Russian deputy prime minister, said two weeks ago that Russia can emerge from recession this year 2023. And the Ministry of Economic Development said in a statement that "the Russian economy is confidently overcoming the barriers of sanctions from hostile countries."

Another reason why many Russians have not noticed the change too much is that many Western products, in theory affected by sanctions, are still coming into the country. This is due to the so-called "parallel imports" allowed by the government.

In the context of the fight against intellectual piracy, in 2002 Russia banned products from entering the country without a license or permission from the manufacturer or rights owner. That ended last year, when Moscow decided that it was no longer illegal to import through third countries - such as Kazakhstan - a long list of products, including iPhones, cars or furs.

Will Russia continue to resist and will many Russians continue to live in this sort of alternative limbo?

The situation may start to change. On December 5, the EU implemented the full embargo on Russian oil, and since this February 5, on petroleum products. Also on December 5, the G-7 "price ceiling" began to operate, which set at $60 per barrel the maximum price at which ships and insurers can transport Russian oil. As a result, the Kremlin's coffers began to feel the pressure. In January, the fiscal deficit soared and state revenues from energy sales fell by 46%.

More than 19,500 people have been arrested for protesting against the war, according to the NGO OVD-Info.Another challenge Russia will have to face is the fall in consumption, exacerbated by uncertainty. In a December report Natalia Orlova, chief economist at Alfa Bank, predicted that the economy will shrink by 6.5% in 2023 due to a slowdown in consumption, lower investment and the loss of export potential.

But forecasts are just that, forecasts sometimes influenced by our own desires. With or without them, this year Russia has definitely moved away from the West and, as in the first cold war, is already walking in parallel.

title: Russian  central bank  forecasts 2.4% year-on-year economic contraction in first quarter
text:
MOSCOW, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Monday it expects the country's gross domestic product (GDP) to fall 2.4 percent year-on-year in the first quarter of 2023, with annual inflation at 3.6 percent.

The bank warned this month that any increase in Russia's budget deficit could force it to raise interest rates, sending a hard-line signal after it kept borrowing costs unchanged but adjusted forecasts for next year.

It maintained its hawkish tone on Monday, expanding those forecasts in a monetary policy report in which it reiterated that a rate hike was more likely than a cut this year, given inflationary and disinflationary risks.

According to the central bank, annual inflation is expected to slow in April to its slowest pace this year, reflecting last year's high base effect, before accelerating again.

"In the following quarters, the impact of pro-inflationary factors will gradually increase, while that of disinflationary factors will decrease," the bank said in its monetary policy report.

Russian households' inflation expectations will continue to significantly influence the Central Bank's monetary policy decisions.

Expectations would have to return to levels seen when inflation was approaching the central bank's 4% target before the policy rate could return to the neutral 5%-6% band.

The bank said it expected the banking sector's structural liquidity surplus to be between RUB2.8 trillion and RUB3.4 trillion ($37.5 billion to $45.5 billion) by the end of 2023.

The 2022 liquidity surplus stood at 2.8 trillion rubles. The bank said its new forecast took into account the resumption of interventions in the foreign exchange market. Russia is selling Chinese yuan to cover its growing budget deficit.

(1 dollar = 74.7455 rubles)

title: UPDATE 2-Russian c.bank sees economy contracting by 2.4% y/y in Q1
text:

MOSCOW, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Monday it expects the country's gross domestic product (GDP) to fall by 2.4% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2023, with annual inflation standing at 3.6%.

The bank this month warned that any further widening of Russia's budget deficit might compel it to raise interest rates, sending a hawkish signal as it kept the cost of borrowing unchanged but adjusted forecasts for the year ahead.

On Monday, it retained its hawkish tone as it expanded on those forecasts in a monetary policy report, reiterating that a rate hike was more likely than a rate cut this year when taking into account conflicting pro-inflationary and disinflationary risks.

Annual inflation is expected to ease to its slowest pace this year in April, the central bank said, on the back of last year's high base effect, before accelerating again.

"In the subsequent quarters the impact of pro-inflationary factors will gradually increase, while the effect of disinflationary factors will decrease" the bank said in its monetary policy report.

It said the inflation expectations of Russian households would continue to significantly influence the central bank's decisions on monetary policy.

It said inflation expectations would need to return to levels seen when inflation was near the central bank's 4% target before the key rate could return to the neutral range of 5%-6%.

The bank said it expected the banking sector's structural liquidity surplus to be between 2.8 and 3.4 trillion roubles ($37.5-$45.5 billion) by the end of 2023.

The 2022 liquidity surplus stood at 2.8 trillion roubles. The bank said its new forecast took into account the resumption of foreign exchange market interventions.
