title: Ukraine finally in NATO? The US 'theory of victory
text:
In his 2015 book, Conflict in Ukraine: The Unwinding of the Post-Cold War Order, co-written with fellow international relations specialist Eugene Rumer, Rajan Menon discussed one of the possible future scenarios of the Donbas war, which began in 2014: the ceasefire, he wrote, "breaks down and the conflict in eastern Ukraine escalates again and leads to direct Russian military intervention beyond the Donetsk and Lugansk regions; Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and occupies significant parts along the right bank of the Dnieper River, possibly including Kiev, leaving a truncated independent Ukrainian state."

Despite explicitly contemplating this scenario eight years ago, Rajan Menon, professor emeritus of international relations at City College of New York, senior fellow at the Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies, Columbia University, and director of the Grand Strategy program at the Defense Priorities think tank, acknowledges that last year's full-scale invasion surprised him. By the scale of the gamble and by the scale of the response, as if we had been catapulted into one of those epic conflagrations you only read about in history books.

We spoke with Menon, who has just returned from his second visit to war-torn Ukraine, about the prospects for the conflict and the role played by the United States - the main material and diplomatic driver of the Ukrainian war effort. We asked him about Biden's plans, European defense, the roots of the Russian invasion and the role of China. From a, as he says, "realistic" and "measured" perspective. The interview has been slightly edited for clarity.

QUESTION. First of all, I'd like to clarify something about the think tank you work for, whose mission, expressed on the front page of its website, is to promote a U.S. foreign policy based on diplomacy and temperance. What is the philosophy of international relations that underlies Defense Priorities?

ANSWER. It is a center that accommodates realism and restraint. That is, a policy that understands what the vital national security interests of the United States are, but without necessarily having to intervene elsewhere in the world, stretching our capabilities too far and reducing our ability to solve our domestic problems. Part of this philosophy was born as a result of the disastrous wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. But also to solve the problems that accumulate at home. You live in New York and you see what's going on in the streets.

At the same time, if you look at places like Europe, and you add up their GDP, their technology and their population, the idea that they can't organize their own defense against Russia is simply impossible to believe. People say that's a lot of countries and how are you going to organize them. But look at what the European Union has done. Who would have thought, 20 years ago, that there would be a central bank and a common currency for most countries, or the abolition of travel restrictions. So it can be done. Only Europe doesn't have the incentive to do it, as long as the US remains its protector. And the US, even though it wants to be the protector, complains. But part of the US position in the world is because it provides security for Europe, Japan, South Korea and Australia. In other words: all the great economic power centers of the world, except China and perhaps India.

P. It's a paradoxical relationship. Presidents as different as Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden have been asking European partners for years to raise their defense spending, since only 10 of the 30 NATO members reach the agreed 2% of GDP. The United States wants Europe to defend itself so that it can devote its resources to China, to the Pacific. However, the Americans are also pressuring European nations not to do business with the Chinese, and there is a perception, especially on the left, that Washington is using the war in Ukraine to secure its political and military influence in Europe.

A. That's very interesting. The complaints about Europe date back even to the time of John F. Kennedy in the 1960s. That the Europeans were not doing enough to defend themselves and that they had to be made to do so. But at the moment when, in Europe, someone like Emmanuel Macron is talking about strategic autonomy, that's not allowed. So we want them to spend more money on defense within NATO, but we're not comfortable with them going beyond that. And we're tolerating a lot of underspending on defense. If you look at the richest country in Europe, Germany, the reports of the parliamentary committee on the armed forces paint a picture of the German military that is shocking. I have a hard time understanding it. So the U.S. complains, but then sends its secretary of state, almost as if he were a Roman proconsul visiting the provinces of the empire, and I think we like that. We like going to Japan, we like going to Korea.

Regarding competition with China, the interesting thing is to look at new industrial policies. We've always talked, in general, about how much the U.S. likes the free trade system and dislikes protectionism. But if you look at agriculture, for example, it is heavily subsidized. Not as much as the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, at least for now. But essentially, we're making adjustments to produce in the U.S. as much as possible. Joe Biden's latest law, the Inflation Reduction Act, and others, give a lot of incentives to produce here, also for foreign companies. So Europe and Japan see this and worry about job losses. In this initiative there is also the need to prevent the leakage of sensitive technologies to China. So Europe is in a difficult situation: on the one hand, the Europeans understand that these leaks have to be prevented; on the other hand, it is a protectionist policy that causes tensions. It is important to remember that the U.S. has been committed to free trade since 1945. But throughout the 19th century it was an enormously protectionist country.

P. I wanted to ask you about the reasons behind the Russian decision to invade. The realist school tends to place part of the responsibility on the US, which would have overreached itself and behaved arrogantly, getting involved in Ukraine with promises and military investments, knowing, as the former ambassador to Moscow, William Burns, now director of the CIA, said, that Ukraine for the Russians was the "most vivid of red lines". The other side, which we can call idealistic, explains the aggression as a consequence merely of Russian traumas, of their revanchism and their apocryphal understanding of Ukraine. What is your position?

A. It is a mixture. I don't quite fit into either camp. Let me briefly present the landscape of the debate. On the one hand, you have people like John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago who say that the invasion is entirely due to NATO expansion. The idea is that because the 2008 NATO summit in Bucharest opened the door to Ukraine, Russia concluded that Ukraine was going to be a NATO member. And this is a special country for Russia. They are geographically tied. Putin faced, as John says, an existential threat. On the other hand, to mention two names, you have Michael McFaul and Anne Applebaum, who say that the invasion has absolutely nothing to do with NATO expansion. That Putin wants to control as many ex-Soviet countries as possible, in particular Ukraine, whose independence he cannot accept. These two extremes end up nullifying the possibility of standing in the middle.

My position is this: from the moment NATO expansion was shuffled around in the 1990s, and then made a reality, I always thought it was a terrible idea. Because, if you put yourself in Russia's position, whether you're a leftist, liberal or conservative, and you see a Cold War alliance parading to your borders, even if the United States tells you that the Cold War is over and Russia is democratizing, and so on, the question remains: why are you moving the alliance to our borders? And the idea that this enlargement was harmless is absurd. Imagine for a moment that the U.S. loses the Cold War and the USSR places Mexico in the Warsaw Pact. We would not accept it either way. This is where I differ with Applebaum and company. I think telling the story of the invasion of Ukraine without mentioning NATO expansion makes no sense.

But I also differ with John Mearsheimer. In 2008 NATO opened the door to Ukraine, but in order to accept it, the first thing to do is to draw up a Membership Action Plan. 14 years later, Ukraine had not been given such a plan. So it was clear that, for whatever reason, the unanimity required to accept this new member did not exist. I don't buy the argument that Putin invaded a country larger than Spain because of its imminent NATO membership.

Another thing to keep in mind is that the expansion of NATO has shifted, little by little, the balance of power within the organization away from countries like Spain, France and Germany, towards countries like Poland and the Baltics, which have a very different, very complicated history with Russia, with many conflicts. So I think the harder line towards Russia, in a way, is a consequence of NATO's expansion into these countries. There is also the argument that these countries wanted to join NATO, that they kept asking for it and that's why we had to accept them. But a military alliance is not a book club. A military alliance is serious, because it involves going to war to protect the other members.

P. Be that as it may, the damage has already been done. What do you think of the Biden Administration's policy towards Ukraine after the invasion began?

A. For me, especially after going to Ukraine and seeing the incredible damage, which I don't mind having seen on television or in the newspapers before, because it is shocking, I am not opposed to providing Ukraine with the means to defend itself. But I think that difficult decisions will have to be made. For example, let's say the war evolves and the Ukrainian Army is in a position to enter Crimea, will the West be united in its support for Ukraine, or will it be considered too dangerous? Because, if Putin is left with nothing, the war could spiral out of control. We would need a deal that would leave him something, so the Crimea issue would have to be fine-tuned as a problem that would be solved by future generations. Ukraine has not been given a blank check, because it has not been given certain weapons, such as ATACMS tactical missiles or fighter jets. It is being supported, but without allowing the war to escalate. The rule is to give weapons, but not to reach Russian territory.

P. The United States was absolutely right with the prediction of invasion, and with months to spare. But it also made a mistake. It thought that Ukraine would be quickly defeated by Russia. Washington was preparing to arm a Ukrainian resistance, not to support a full-fledged war effort, as turned out to be the case. Interestingly, it was the same mistake Russia made: the notion that the Ukrainians didn't stand a chance against the Russian tank roll.

A. The Russians have made many mistakes. When Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in World War II, the Russians demonstrated an impressive capacity for sacrifice to defend their country. What did they expect would happen when they invaded Ukraine? That the Ukrainians would not defend themselves? Ukrainian soldiers told me the same thing many times: for us this is no ordinary war. If we lose this war, we lose a country. Are there any Russian soldiers who believe that, if they lose this war, they would lose Russia? No. There is an asymmetry in combat morale. That was one mistake. Another mistake has to do with the training provided by NATO to the Ukrainian Army since 2014. 60,000 Ukrainian soldiers received training and the Ukrainian armed forces have been adopting NATO military practices. In addition, they have been fighting in two separatist provinces. So the Ukrainian Army had changed a lot. I don't think Putin took it seriously. But neither did we. The CIA thought the Ukrainian resistance would collapse immediately. Honestly, I thought so too, because, if you look at any measure of power, like population, tanks, aircraft or artillery, Russia had a huge advantage. But it's not just that the Ukrainians have higher morale, it's that the Russian Army didn't turn out to be what was expected.

Ukrainian soldiers told me the same thing many times: this is no ordinary war. If we lose this war, we lose a country

. P. You have mentioned in your articles that peace negotiations, for now, are impossible, because neither Ukraine, nor Russia, have incentives to sit down and negotiate. Both believe that they can improve their position in the spring or summer, that is why neither country seriously offers to mediate between them, because they know it would fail. On the other hand, we are getting curious signals, like that anonymous White House source who told The Washington Post that, essentially, Ukraine had this spring to carry out its counter-offensives, but then American support would probably cease and they would have to sit down and talk. What do you think the United States will do? What is its next step?

A. The Washington Post article came up at an event we hosted at Defense Priorities. In my view, it has received a lot of attention precisely because it is an exception. If you read most of the statements from the Biden Administration, they don't say they will give all the aid to Ukraine all at once, but they do say they will help Ukraine get the territories back, although without mentioning to what extent [Menon is referring to the possibility of Ukraine getting the entire territory back, up to the 1991 borders, including Crimea, or the territory from before February 24, 2022]. So I wouldn't read too much into it. It's not consistent with what the administration has been saying. And, if you compare it to other articles, you'll see that those articles say the opposite. I think what it suggests, probably, is that there's a debate within the Biden administration about how far they're willing to go.

P. Certainly, but it's also true that while the Biden Administration presents a consistent message, sometimes it leaks to the media what looks like a knock on the Ukrainians. For example, when it was leaked that Biden had raised his voice to the president, Volodymir Zelensky, during a telephone conversation, and told him to show a little gratitude for the aid. A way, perhaps, to remind the Ukrainians that American aid is not unconditional.

A. It's the oldest game in Washington and I'm sure in Madrid as well. To have in the government someone with a different opinion who wants it publicized. I don't know what exactly is going on. What we have to do is look at concrete actions, and what we see is $27 billion in U.S. military assistance. And, if you add in European, it's $7 billion or $8 billion. We're talking about 40% of the Russian defense budget last year. If we had sat down to talk a year and a half ago, and asked ourselves whether there was any chance of an all-out war between Ukraine and Russia, we probably would have said no. And, if there was such a war, and we had wondered whether the US and NATO would act in unison and send some $40 billion in military aid, we would have thought it was highly unlikely because of the risk of escalation. This has been a war of surprises for me. So much so that I am very reluctant to make predictions, because I have seen things that I thought would never happen.

Now people say Putin is an expansionist and an imperialist. He is an expansionist, but he has never done anything like this. A full-scale invasion of a large country. Georgia in 2008 was very different. In Syria, it was mostly the air force. In 2014, in Donbas and Crimea, it was provinces very close to Russia. What is happening now is an extraordinary step. How do you explain it? There is a theory going around that, during the covid, Putin was reading a lot about the conquests of Peter the Great and Catherine the Great, and all these nationalist philosophers like Ivan Ilyin. Some kind of Russian fascist. Who knows. But I didn't expect Putin to do something like this, even when he was amassing his troops on the border. I thought it was a bullying tactic to force the US to stall NATO involvement in Ukraine. That was my view.

P. A year after the start of the full-scale war, there is a possibility that is sounding more and more in military and geopolitical circles: that of ending up with a territorially diminished Ukraine, but integrated, at last and as a reward for what it has suffered, into NATO. Or with some other security guarantee. It would also be the only way to make possible its reconstruction, which promises to be very costly, without the risk of Russia attacking again in the future. Figures of more than $300 billion are being bandied about. That is 50% more than the Ukrainian GDP in 2021.

A. Now there is even talk of a trillion [trillion] dollars. A gigantic amount.

Q. How do you see the option of a Ukraine in NATO as an outcome of this war or as a kind of compensation for the loss of territories?

A. I can certainly imagine a peace, even though Zelensky says he wants everything back, including Crimea, in which Ukraine is territorially diminished: perhaps preserving 85% of its territory [that is currently under its control], but not all of it. NATO expansion is a complicated issue, because the alliance would possibly be divided. The eastern flank, plus the United Kingdom and the United States, would say yes, after all that Russia has done, and Russia has shown its true colors, Ukraine should be admitted to NATO. The question is: would Hungary, France and Germany think the same? I am not so sure. Look at what has happened with the Turks regarding the admission of Finland and Sweden. So it is not clear that Ukraine can join.

If you are in Ukraine and you say this, they get angry, because.There it is almost a religious question. They believe that, after all that has happened, joining NATO and the European Union is a birthright. But even the EU has been very careful in its statements. Also, if Ukraine joins the EU, the EU would have to bear most of the cost of reconstruction. We are talking about an awful lot of money.

"For every artillery shell Ukraine fires, the Russians fire ten. But they can't take it, because they are too badly commanded"

Now, there is a second possibility, although the

Ukrainians refuse to mention it because they don't want anyone to think that there are better options than NATO, and that is a different security guarantee. But a security guarantee would be worthless if it doesn't include the United States. So, if you have the UK, the Baltics and the US, maybe they'll be happy with second prize. It would be interesting to see what happens. The other possibility is a neutral Ukraine, which is what the Russians will demand, and I think the Ukrainians will put up a lot of resistance.

There are many things we cannot predict. Some will depend on what happens in the next year. And I also don't exclude the possibility that the war will continue. If the Ukrainians regain a lot of territory, they will be in a position of strength, vis-à-vis Russia and vis-à-vis the West. One thing to watch in the next three months is the Russian offensive. From what we can see they are attacking all along the front, from north of Lugansk to the south, but they are not doing well. They have not been able to take Bakhmut. They have been trying to take Bathmut since the end of August. A town that before the war had 70,000 inhabitants and now has 7,000, and they can't, despite having many advantages. For every artillery shell Ukraine fires, the Russians fire ten. But they can't take it, because they are too badly commanded.

P. As you watch this war, don't you worry that we might be missing something? Ukraine has a lot of activists, young, English-speaking, charismatic, social media-savvy people who are often the fixers who guide foreign reporters and who are active on Twitter. Zelensky's government has many such profiles and has led an iron grip on content. There is no doubt that pro-Russian views have greatly diminished since 2014, and it would not be correct to speak of a divided country, especially now. But, according to the director of the Kiev Sociological Institute, Anton Hrushevsky, there were around 30% of pro-Russian voters in Ukraine at the beginning of 2022. Probably many of them changed their minds soon after, but it is still a significant number.

A. That's an excellent question. As you said, the Ukraine narrative has been very well coordinated and orchestrated by Zelensky. And I'm not saying it's propaganda, but they have a point of view. And they've been very efficient promoting it in Western countries. They use social media and they do an excellent job. So in the West there is huge support for this narrative, which is backed by the U.S. foreign policy establishment, and by major newspapers. Even the British Guardian, a reference of the left, supports it.

It is true that there have been divisions in the country. Before 2014, it was not clear that there was broad support for joining NATO. The country was divided. The west and the center were more inclined to join NATO and the EU than the east and the south. But I think the war has changed a lot of things. All this talk by Putin that the war is to protect Russian speakers from genocide is absurd. The Russian-speaking parts of Ukraine have suffered the most destruction. Look at Mariupol, for example. The war has changed a lot of things. More and more Ukrainians, even if they are Russian speakers or ethnic Russians, identify themselves as Ukrainian citizens. There is a sense of a consolidating national identity. The Ukrainian language is increasingly used in cities like Kiev. It is encouraged by the government. And resistance to joining NATO is now much lower. The problem is not in Ukraine, the problem is to see to what extent NATO is ready to open its doors.

P. Speaking of narratives, a question about the tone of the debate. I'm going to read you this that realist thinker Stephen Walt, professor of international relations at Harvard University, wrote recently in Foreign Policy: "The public debate over Ukraine has been extraordinarily vituperative, with warmongering commentators competing with each other to see who expressed the most support for Kiev, while dismissing alternative perspectives as naïve, immoral, pro-Russian, or worse." As a realist, do you recognize this sentiment?

A. Personally, I find no difficulty in expressing my views, but there is no doubt that people critical of mainstream narratives, say, John Mearsheimer or the late Stephen Cohen of Princeton, have been vilified. They've been called all sorts of things, almost treated as Putin sympathizers. And I think that's a very unfortunate thing, because you can debate someone on the assumption that, if that person disagrees with what you think, it's because they work for a foreign government. I find it in very bad taste and social media has exacerbated the problem. All you have to do is sit in front of your computer, type something without caring, and make it go viral. But people with alternative views to those of the establishment, like John Mearsheimer, have not been quiet. Is it harder for them to be heard in the mainstream media? Absolutely. When was the last time you read a piece by John in The New York Times or The Washington Post

? P. The New Yorker did two interviews with him and in both cases he got a good one.

Right, right. And the guy who did the interviews, Isaac Chotiner, is known to be a suck-up. But John is a different guy. He almost likes controversy, he loves to be in the middle of it. But yes, I think the debate has degenerated because there are so many passionate beliefs. The NATO expansion people believe that the invasion justifies their position. So when John Mearsheimer comes along and reminds us that NATO expansion would lead to war and that Ukraine would be destroyed by Putin, the insults get very harsh. And the more nuanced part of the debate is drowned out between these two extremes. Yes, I think Steve Walt is right.

P. We can't end without asking you about Taiwan. Despite the many differences, the case of Russia and Ukraine, in which a revanchist power wants to annex by force a neighboring country that it does not recognize and considers a province, has led many analysts to draw parallels with the case of China and Taiwan. To what extent do you think it is useful to conflate the two disputes?

A. Some people who show almost unconditional support for Ukraine make exactly that argument: that the current war goes beyond Ukraine because, depending on how we act, the Chinese will gauge our resolve and conclude that they may or may not attack Taiwan. I hear the same thing all the time. The credibility argument. You have to do something in this conflict because your credibility is at stake. My sense is that the Chinese are much smarter than this. They are not going to think about invading Taiwan based on what the Americans have done in Ukraine. They are going to look at the local circumstances. What capacity do we have to defeat Taiwan? What could the Americans do? Can we defeat them? If not, can we raise the cost so high as to deter them from defending Taiwan? What will be the effect on the global economy? Because this is no longer Mao's China. China is deeply connected to the global economy. An attack on Taiwan would make the markets go crazy. I think they will look at local circumstances. I don't think Ukraine is the element that will make them make a decision. But, of course, if you're someone who considers Ukraine a sacred cause, you'll conflate it with Taiwan and China. I'm not persuaded by that argument.

In his book published in 2015, Conflict in Ukraine: The Unwinding of the Post-Cold War Order, written four-handed with fellow international relations specialist Eugene Rumer, Rajan Menon shuffled through one of the possible future scenarios of the Donbas war that began in 2014: the ceasefire, he wrote, "breaks down and the conflict in eastern Ukraine escalates again and leads to direct Russian military intervention beyond the Donetsk and Lugansk regions; Russia launches a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and occupies significant parts along the right bank of the Dnieper River, possibly including Kiev, leaving a truncated independent Ukrainian state."

title: Western banks struggle to exit  Russia  after Putin's  intervention
text:
Advisors to Western banks trying to leave Russia say a law introduced by Vladimir Putin is disrupting sales and allowing businessmen close to the Kremlin to grab business.

Nearly a year after the invasion of Ukraine, only a handful of Western banks have managed to leave Russia, albeit at a high cost, while others have opted to keep their businesses in the country.

However, for most of those trying to sell their Russian assets, hopes of a quick exit were dashed when Putin declared last year that foreign owners in "enemy" countries could not close deals without his approval. The list of companies involved includes 45 banks with subsidiaries in Russia.

Advisors working on deals expect the Russian president's intervention to scuttle some sales already under discussion, while fundamentally altering the terms of others.

In addition, they expect sale prices already agreed to be cut by as much as half as the Kremlin exerts more influence over the deals. And they claim that potential buyers, who were initially beaten to the punch, have obtained presidential approval and are attempting to hijack sales from rivals who do not have the Kremlin's favor.

"There are some very powerful Russians with close ties to the Kremlin who are trying to use their influence to snatch these entities from fleeing foreigners," said a person involved in the negotiations, one of several who spoke to the Financial Times on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the talks with the Russian government.

"We are working on these kinds of deals every day, but it's getting harder and harder," said Laura Brank, a partner at law firm Dechert, which is advising Western banks on the sale of their Russian subsidiaries; adding that the situation is very fluid and the rules are not really clear.

Putin says Russian military operation in Ukraine is going Well.

Challenges from foreign banks

Within days of the invasion, Western banks that had spent decades slowly building up their Russian branches faced a stark choice: sell the business quickly and take a heavy loss, or hold on and scale back gradually.

Western sanctions and Moscow's counter-sanctions made it virtually impossible for foreign banks to do business in the country.

Austria's Raiffeisen Bank International, the Western lender with the largest presence in Russia and Ukraine, increased its currency coverage and cash reserves in anticipation of customers withdrawing their savings as troops massed on the border early last year.

But the Feb. 24 invasion took bank executives, like most Western bankers, by surprise. "It was one of the most shocking days of my life," said Hannes Mösenbacher, Raiffeisen's chief risk officer.

Raiffeisen's subsidiary is the largest on the Kremlin's list, with 4.2 million customers and 9,400 employees in Russia on the eve of the invasion, and the bank has yet to figure out how it will be evicted from the country.

Of its €22.9 billion of assets in Russia at the beginning of 2022, only €354 million were exposed to financial institutions subject to Western sanctions and €119 million to other companies affected by sanctions.

In late July, HSBC agreed to sell its Russian subsidiary to local lender Expobank in a deal that would allow it to exit a country that had become politically toxic since Moscow's invasion of Ukraine earlier this year.

But that sale has now been delayed. HSBC said it was still working to try to complete the transaction, but a person with knowledge of its plans said Expobank, as the acquirer, had to get Putin's approval.

"For us, there is no change since the deal was signed," the HSBC executive said. "It just needs to go through these machinations."

One bank that managed to change its Russian subsidiary before the presidential decree was France's Societe Generale, which agreed in April to sell its Rosbank business, as well as its Russian insurance operations, to an investment firm founded by billionaire Vladimir Potanin .

Along with Raiffeisen and Italy's UniCredit, SocGen had one of the largest exposures to Russia of any Western bank, with €18.6 billion of assets at the beginning of 2022. Rosbank employed 12,000 people.

SocGen was able to strike a quick deal because it sold to Potanin, one of Russia's richest men with close ties to the Kremlin, who was sanctioned by the U.S. last month. The French bank had also bought the business from Potanin in 2008.

"We did it very, very quickly; it helped that we sold it to someone who knew the bank well," said a SocGen executive. "We even got congratulatory calls from rivals saying how efficiently and neatly we were able to get rid of it."

However, by arriving at such a hasty sale, SocGen was forced to take a €3.3 billion hit .

Other banks looking for a quick exit did not have a ready buyer waiting in the wings, nor were they prepared to absorb a financial hit like the one SocGen suffered.

UniCredit's Russian operations include 2 million customers and 3,500 employees. CEO Andrea Orcel even considered increasing his exposure by buying Russian bank Otkritie just weeks before the invasion. As of mid-October, its total exposure to Russia was still €7 billion.

The Italian bank's failure to cut ties with Russia has caused friction with the European Central Bank, the FT reported, after Orcel said over the summer that liquidating the business or selling it at a discount was "not morally right."

More recently, however, the bank has said it is "committed to withdrawing from Russia in an orderly and decisive manner," which Orcel said is different from the "get rid of everything" strategies pursued by other banks, without naming them.

"You're throwing it at the very people you're trying to fight," he told a Bank of America conference in September. "We're trying to make sure there's an orderly containment of what we have and ultimately get out, but in a way that's not a giveaway."

He did, however, agree to sell RN Bank, his Russian joint venture with Renault and Nissan, to Lada maker Avtovaz. Putin gave the deal the green light in late November.

Citigroup, whose local subsidiary is subject to the decree, has taken a different approach to dealing with its exposure, which stood at $7.75 billion at the end of December.

After failing to find a buyer for its Russian business for more than a year, the U.S. lender decided to liquidate the business. Last month, the bank sold a portfolio of Russian consumer loans to Uralsib, a local commercial lender.

It also plans to close most of its institutional banking services in Russia by the end of the first quarter of 2023, although its custody operations are likely to prove more difficult to unwind, according to people with knowledge of the business.

Intesa Sanpaolo Chief Executive Carlo Messina has outlined his intention to turn Italy's biggest lender by assets into a "zero exposure bank to Russia" by winding down cross-border lending between Italian and Russian companies, which makes up the majority of its business in the country.

But like the other Western banks trapped in the country, the fate of its Russian subsidiary is in Putin's hands.

"It's an extremely difficult situation for us as it is for most banks," said the executive of a bank with a subsidiary on the restricted list.

"Not being able to sell initially to sanctioned entities and now holding all these banks hostage plays into what the Russian government wants. There is no incentive to facilitate the exit of banks."

He added: "We are in limbo, but it is not for lack of wanting to solve it. It is very difficult to see what is the way out of this."

title: UPDATE 2-With a sale of Chinese yuan,  Russia  kicks off 2023  forex intervention
text:
*

Russia to resume forex intervention

*

Russia to sell yuan amid lower oil and gas revenue

*

Use of yuan underscores greater role of China

(Recasts headline and lead, adds quotes)

By Guy Faulconbridge and Darya Korsunskaya

MOSCOW, Jan 11 (Reuters) -

Russia said it would resume foreign currency interventions with the sale of yuan from Friday, underscoring the growing importance of China's currency in Moscow's efforts to ensure economic stability amid Western sanctions.

After the West imposed the most severe sanctions in modern history over the war in Ukraine, Russia's economy has shown remarkable resilience but the world's biggest producer of natural resources is now turning increasingly towards China.

Chinese students have flocked to Russian universities, Mandarin graces signs in Moscow tourist spots alongside English and Russian, and President Vladimir Putin has touted a "no limits" partnership with President Xi Jinping.

Russia's finance ministry, which along with the central bank led Moscow's economic response to the sanctions, said it would sell 54.5 billion roubles ($798 million) in foreign currency from Jan. 13 amid lower oil and gas revenues.

"In order to increase the stability and predictability of domestic economic conditions, as well as to reduce the impact of volatile energy market conditions on the Russian economy and public finances, the Finance Ministry will resume operations for the purchase/sale of liquid assets," the ministry said.

Russia's 2023 budget is based on a Urals blend price of around $70.1 a barrel, though Russia's main blend is currently trading at below $50 a barrel. Russian nominal GDP is likely to be $2.14 trillion this year, the highest level since 2013, according to the International Monetary Fund.

In Russia, where the U.S. dollar was king for years following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, China's yuan, or renminbi, has become a major player in Moscow since the imposition of Western sanctions.

Its share of the currency market reached 48% in November, MOEX Group said last month, up from less than 1% at the start of 2022.

The Russian central bank said it would carry out forex transactions on the yuan market of the Moscow Exchange - the yuan-rouble for settlement tomorrow (CNYRUB_TOM).

"To minimize the impact of these operations on the dynamics of the exchange rate, the Bank of Russia will buy (sell) foreign currency on the market evenly during each trading day of the month," the bank said.

($1 = 68.6875 roubles) (Reporting by Reuters Writing by Guy Faulconbridge Editing by Gareth Jones)

title: EXCLUSIVE-Russia likely to buy yuan on  FX  market in 2023 - sources
text:
*

This content was produced in Russia where the law restricts coverage of Russian military operations in Ukraine

By Elena Fabrichnaya

MOSCOW, Dec 22 (Reuters) - Russia will start buying yuan on the currency market next year if oil and gas revenues meet expectations, two sources said, opening a new front in an accelerating dedollarisation drive designed to reduce its dependency on Western finance.

Western sanctions on Moscow over its actions in Ukraine have curbed its use of and access to dollars and euros, and the Chinese currency's role in Russia's economy is growing fast.

Daily yuan-rouble trading volumes on the Moscow Exchange are already exceeding dollar-rouble trades on some days, according to Refinitiv data, a trend set be to accentuated in 2023 as an oil embargo and price cap squeeze Russia's traditional export routes.

Russia stopped intervening on the FX market in February due to restrictions imposed on its use of foreign exchange reserves after it sent tens of thousands of troops into Ukraine.

Interventions will resume next year in yuan, the two sources told Reuters, provided that revenues from oil and gas exports exceed 8 trillion roubles as set out in budget plans.

"The central bank can currently now buy yuan," a banking source close to monetary authorities told Reuters. But the bank would not do so while the government continued, as now, to spend its oil and gas revenues.

"(However), if next year budget revenues from the export of oil and gas exceed 8 trillion roubles, then the central bank will buy yuan," that source added.

Under the budget rule, designed to replenish state reserves, oil and gas revenues above that figure are currently directed to the National Wealth Fund (NWF), which Finance Minister Anton Siluanov has said is equivalent to oil prices of $62-63 a barrel.

The central bank and finance ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Russia has for years adopted conservative fiscal policies and sought to run budget surpluses, but is on course for a deficit of 2% of GDP this year as Moscow ramps up spending to finance its military campaign in Ukraine.

Siluanov's ministry expects 900 billion roubles in additional hydrocarbon revenues next year, though analysts, wary of the impact of export restrictions, are sceptical.

'FRIENDLY' CURRENCY

A senior government source confirmed that FX interventions next year would be in yuan.

"We have a lot of friendly currencies. On the exchange, the Chinese yuan is the most traded currency, it is the friendliest currency so far," the source said.

Russia considers countries that have not joined in with Western sanctions as "friendly".

The banking source said the central bank's operations with yuan would be protected from sanctions and freezing. Russian government assets worth around $300 billion have been frozen since the conflict in Ukraine began.

The government source said a decision about interventions within the framework of the budget rule was needed in order to start accumulating reserves, and as soon as authorities adopted the plan, it would be announced.

At the start of this year, the yuan accounted for 17.1% of Russia's FX and gold reserves, the most recent available data. Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina last week said Russia has sufficient funds in yuan and gold.

The yuan, or renminbi, has already enjoyed a dramatic acceleration into Russia's markets and trade flows, with its share of the currency market reaching 48% in November, MOEX Group said last week, up from less than 1% at the start of the year.

Moscow Exchange, Russia's largest bourse, will expand the range of yuan instruments it offers next year, changes the exchange's head Yuri Denisov said would enable traders to hedge currency risk and increase yuan liquidity.

(Reporting by Elena Fabrichnaya; additional reporting and writing by Alexander Marrow; editing by John Stonestreet)

title: Without imports, Russia relies on smuggling to sustain economy in war
text:
The suitcases were full of equipment bought in Austria. The products were not particularly original -professional electronic equipment for use in schools-, but they were manufactured by a Western brand that had decided to boycott Russia over the invasion of Ukraine.

"It was made to look like it was just for personal use. As if I had bought it all for myself," says Stanislav, who met the men at a hotel in Istanbul, took them to dinner, and then flew to Moscow with the bags.

"Of course it was smuggling, pure and simple," he says, speaking on the condition of anonymity due to the illegal nature of the activity.

It was an unusual order for Stanislav. He normally specializes in using trucks to smuggle out of Europe the much bulkier and more delicate items that are under sanctions in Russia, such as materials for the construction sector and parts and machinery for heavy industry.

Stanislav is part of a growing number of so-called Russian import-export specialists -professionals at finding loopholes and getting goods through customs- who have emerged in response to Western sanctions on the country.

Interviews with participants in this underground market reveal a lucrative but highly unpredictable and unstable trade that Russia's beleaguered economy will have difficulty relying on.

Increasingly, however, it needs to trust. The severe sanctions applied since the beginning of the war have disrupted Russian supply chains and left many companies struggling to source crucial foreign brand products and parts.

When the heaviest sanctions were adopted in March, some economists predicted a rapid collapse of the Russian economy, perhaps as much as 30 percent. But that didn't happen: oil and gas revenues continued to flow and the currency soon recovered.

What is emerging is something different - not a dramatic decline, but a steady degradation of its productive capacity that economists in Russia and the West argue is setting the country back decades. Russia is trying to operate a modern economy without the ability to import many components, raw materials, and technologies on which it depends.

The impact is felt throughout the economy - from banks that need servers to process payments to the country's poultry industry, which relied on the Netherlands as a supplier of the chicks from which chickens are grown for mass production of eggs.

Agricultural companies are struggling to get tractor tires, while airlines can't get foreign components to fix their planes.

The blow has already been significant. Data from Russia's trading partners show that Russian imports have fallen by 20 to 25 percent since the start of the war -a blow to a country embedded for decades in the global economy.

"If you look at the pharmaceutical industry, chemical production, machine building, metals and mining.... It's hard to find a sector in Russia that doesn't rely on imports for at least 50% [of inputs]," says Elina Ribakova, an economist at the IFI (Institute of International Finance).

In the medium term, the sanctions will likely set Russia's economy back by years. Consumers will be forced to adapt to a more limited choice of low-quality goods and products that may be reminiscent of the deprivations at the end of the Soviet era.

"Life will be simpler and there will be less money. People will make do with less. There will be more paper in the sausage," says a Russian oligarch who is under sanctions.

"It will be like that for 15 to 20 years, unless [President Vladimir Putin] dies. Fundamentally, nothing will change."

Ultimately, Russia's long-term economic future depends on whether Moscow can quickly produce domestic alternatives to the foreign goods it can no longer access, or obtain analogues from "friendly" countries such as China. When these two options fail, it is left to rely on imports from smugglers like Stanislav.

For him, the new restrictions have created a land of opportunity. Previously, foreign goods were shipped to Russia by official importers, and there were few ways for a new player to sneak in. Trying to import brands illegally was no use either, as there was little demand.

"I could have put the goods in a double bass box and brought them in, but nobody would have bought them, because I couldn't give the buyer an official warranty, etc.," Stanislav says.

"Now I can import this, I can import that, like everybody else. So for me, of course, it's interesting," he adds. "The doors have opened."

'Everything is being imported anyway' Several smuggling routes have already become popular.

Stanislav buys most items through front companies established in Europe, with no visible connection to Russia. The products are then shipped on trucks from the European Union to one of the former Soviet Union countries that share a customs union with Russia, such as Kazakhstan and Armenia.

"Any brand that came out of Russia, no matter what it is -aspirators, clothes, alcohol- is being imported anyway," says another Russian citizen living in Europe who works in the import-export trade.

But the process is irregular at best. Take the example of clinker brick -a material used, among other things, in decorative facades.

"The last deliveries were in June and that's it. No one knows how to bring it in," explains the person. Some builders involved in high-end construction have already clad half of their buildings, he says. "What to do with the other half? It's not clear."

Over time, routes will be found to get the material to Russia, but, as with many other imported products, it will be expensive and therefore available only to special customers, the person adds.

Russia put its import data under wraps early in the war, but economists are building a picture using information on exports to Russia from its major trading partners.

Exports from the United States to Russia fell 85 percent in May compared with the same month a year earlier, according to research by the European Central Bank. The World Bank, IMF, and other institutions predict that Russian imports this year will fall 25 percent from a year earlier. From June to August this year, Russia imported $4.5 billion less per month than it did in 2021, according to the Kiel Institute for World Economics.

Demand for imports also fell as the economy went into recession and inflation began to squeeze household incomes, while a growing number of Western companies that had branches in Russia pulled out.

Given the shortage of imported parts, automobile production has been one of the hardest hit sectors, with a drop of nearly 80 percent in September compared to the same month in 2021, according to state statistics service Rosstat. The drop has prompted authorities to loosen some safety requirements over the summer for anti-skid brakes and airbags.

So many Western automakers and dealers sold their business in Russia that only 14 automakers remained in the market for Russian buyers, according to an industry analysis published in December. All but three of the brands were Chinese, including the iconic Soviet Lada.

A billionaire close to the Kremlin says that the potential profit from smuggled goods is so high that luxury goods will always arrive in the country, regardless of sanctions. He tells how over the summer he bought two Maybachs instead of the Mercedes he wanted, but couldn't get. If the first one breaks, he can use the second one to get parts out, he adds.

Others have already glimpsed new opportunities. "It's going to be hard for two, three, four years. Then we will adapt," says another oligarch under sanctions. "Look at Iran. They do everything themselves [...] they have their own supply chains, and if they don't have a spare part, they get it on the black market. They will do anything. We are learning our lessons now, and in the future we will be the same."

Collapse delayed So far, the economy has avoided the worst predictions. Economists estimate a drop in gross domestic product of between 3.5 percent and 5.5 percent this year.

In part, this is because export revenues have remained strong and Russia is increasingly finding alternative buyers for its oil.

There has, for example, been an increase in exports to Russia among the countries through which some companies are redirecting trade. Exports to Russia from countries such as Turkey and Kazakhstan are on the rise. While the European Union exported 43 percent fewer goods to Russia from June to August, China exported 23 percent more, according to the Kiel Institute.

While there has not been a disintegration of the economy, analysts believe that long-term growth will be substantially reduced as import restrictions destroy the potential for technological upgrades. Local industries that end up replacing production are usually less efficient, they say, while parallel market import flows are volatile.

"If you go back to the Soviet Union and how they got the technology, it was through the FSB, spies and fronts, buying things in other countries undercover," says economist Jacob Nell, a member of a sanctions expert working group headed by former U.S. Ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul and Andriy Yermak, chief of staff to Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelensky. "But it's very difficult to build supply chains when you have these kinds of comprehensive sanctions."

Nell adds, "Even if you can steal the designs, it's very difficult to replicate -in an economically and commercially sustainable way, without subsidy- the production of these things."

Stanislav agrees. Shipments are volatile, and intermediary countries are adopting new rules designed to eliminate this kind of trade. Earlier this month, the EU proposed making sanctions evasion a criminal offense, and he immediately felt a massive drop-off from suppliers. One of his deliveries got stuck in Kazakhstan customs.

"A loophole was found, and thanks to connections and a small bribe, we found a way to move things along," he says. Still, "it's getting more difficult every day."

In general, companies and state agencies are looking for ways to respond to the import crackdown.

In July, Putin appointed former Trade Minister Denis Manturov to a senior government post with a mandate to restore supply chains. Manturov promised to defend Russia's "technological sovereignty" and make import substitution "a matter of national security."

Although Manturov later insisted that this would not mean "completely abandoning the principles of the market economy," the push to increase domestic production will inevitably lead to much heavier state intervention that limits competition, according to another Russian oligarch under sanctions.

"If you have ten companies making plates, it won't work. You have oversupply and insufficient quality. Nobody needs that," says the oligarch.

"Instead, you need to be sure of just a few producers. They need to continue to compete with each other and produce a quality material, but you want to avoid overproduction. You have to be sensitive to the size and power of the market."

Some solutions have already been found. A central bank survey of Russian companies found in April that two-thirds were struggling with disrupted supply chains. By the summer, that number had dropped to 50 percent.

"So for companies looking for alternative suppliers, there is a marginal improvement," says IFI's Ribakova, referring to the survey. "But on the other hand...these are aggregate numbers. They don't reveal the bottlenecks."

The critical list In a new underground complex known as a "bunker" near the Ukraina hotel in Moscow, Russia's cabinet meets regularly to discuss presentations dissecting the country's dire economic prospects on a huge 180-degree screen.

One such presentation, prepared by a major state-owned bank since August this year and also seen by the Financial Times, lists some of these critical areas.

In five columns, it grouped the industries by degree of risk, with the last one colored in red and labeled "supercritical." Industries listed in this category include aircraft construction, pharmaceuticals and medical technology, microchip production and high-end IT equipment, and spacecraft-building technology.

The cabinet claims that it has already successfully replaced imports in some of the industries. "They wanted to ground our air fleet. Take the sky from us," Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in November, at a time when there were several reports in the local media about how airlines were struggling to get spare parts. "But we have maintained our planes and are expanding the deployment of domestic technology."

One way Russia's government intervened to support importers, especially of consumer technology goods, was by legalizing what it calls "parallel imports."

The law made it legal to pass a long list of Western branded products through customs into Russia without the consent of the brand itself. Previously, this would have been considered piracy, but now it is Stanislav's semi-official trade.

The government has estimated that $20 billion worth of goods have been imported into Russia this year, including the new iPhone 14, which was released in September and not officially on sale in the Russian market. "If consumers want to buy these phones, they are welcome," Manturov said in September.

Kirill, another Moscow import specialist, opened a parallel import business focusing on furniture and appliances soon after the war began. He says that one of the most common schemes for parallel imports is to work with a company, for example from Kazakhstan, that already has a relationship with a Western brand.

This company then places its usual orders, but in significantly larger volumes. The Russian partner pays discreetly to import the surplus into Russia, which is easy when the goods are safe in Kazakhstan, since there is no customs border.

But the gray market route is less effective for harder-sourced imports, mainly microchips and servers, says an executive at a Russian technology company.

"You can't make it a mass [business] because banks also need servers" and will pay more than smaller buyers, the executive says. "That makes it much more expensive and unsustainable."

Producers have become much more wary of the increased volume of microchip orders by Armenia and Kazakhstan, which have become home to large communities of Russian IT specialists exiled since the war, but are also centers of customs-free parallel imports.

"Some American companies have stopped shipping to Armenia. They say, 'We had one license a year before. Now you are asking for a hundred licenses?'," says the executive.

A senior executive at a major Russian technology company warns of the long-term impact of the microchip shortage.

If the sanctions last for two to four years, it will still be worth paying for the most sought-after chips at twice the market price, the executive says. However, if they last longer, the executive believes Russia will be forced to switch to inferior Chinese chips. Expanding Russia's own microprocessor production capacity to the level of China -now struggling under U.S. export restrictions- would likely cost $50 billion a year for ten years, and even then would not be guaranteed to work, the executive adds.

To get through the complex compliance procedures required to demonstrate that customers are not circumventing sanctions, some manufacturers require their customers to prove that they are not physically in Russia when placing an order, the executive adds.

"Do you want ten mainframe servers for Gyumri?" the executive explains, referring to a city in Armenia, another parallel import hub. To prove it, "go to Zoom with a purchasing officer to show him that you are in Armenia and have people in the office."

Even Russian government organizations are turning to parallel imports as a result of the sanctions. Stanislav says he has been approached by two different regional Russian chambers of commerce, one located in Siberia and the other in central Russia, asking him for help in obtaining foreign products that are under sanctions or embargo.

"They turn to us businessmen and say, 'Guys, can you bring this to us? Can you import this?'"

The 'do-it-yourself' economy Soon after the first sanctions packages were introduced, Grigory Bolotin, head of the Cheboksary Energy Machinery Factory, gathered his team around a large blank sheet of paper and started drawing.

He drew a huge map of the company -a vast factory on the banks of the Volga River east of Moscow that produces forklifts, tractors, and other heavy machinery- and outlined all the supply chains on which it depended.

The team quickly identified the areas that were heavily dependent on the western parts. These product lines had to be discontinued.

In other areas, they got creative. Where they used to import microchips to operate their tractors, they decided to try making their own. They bought basic transistors and other chip parts in Asia and learned to solder them themselves. "They come out pretty simple, but they get the job done," says Bolotin.

For other key components, they found domestic substitutes. The Japanese motors used in their forklifts were replaced with alternatives produced in Minsk, the capital of Russian ally Belarus.

"Sure, the Minsk engine is noisier, less economical, less reliable. ButIt's there, it's available. And everybody kind of got used to it," says Bolotin.

In general, they've managed to get by. But Bolotin could see the broad effect of the import restrictions on quality and the level of technology.

Cheboksary's products were once considered of average quality. But since the sanctions were imposed they have "moved to the higher end of the market."

"We probably won't be able to produce equipment with the same technological level as products supplied by Western countries," says Bolotin. But now Russian customers don't mind, he says.

Economist Branko Milanovic has labeled this process "technologically regressive import substitution," exchanging imported goods for "inferior and outdated domestic substitutes."

Economies of scale from importing raw materials and components are being lost.

Ribakova of the IFI explains, "You will be able to produce it, but it will be much more expensive, because it is inefficient." She adds, "If you are a factory in Russia producing buttons for half the world, your unit cost of production is completely different from having to produce a limited number of buttons for a specific production."

For example, Finland was a major exporter to Russia of chemicals used in paper bleaching. After their shipments stopped, several Russian pulp mills had to learn to do without or started producing the bleaching chemicals themselves. The Soviet Union was also self-sufficient in these products.

But one result of using non-existent or substandard chemicals is that some of the paper used in Russian offices has a grayish-brown tint.

A deputy industry minister insisted earlier this year that there is a silver lining, citing new findings showing that excessively white paper can damage the eyes. "Very bright white office paper is really bad for health," he said.

title: Russia holds up much better than expected and forces IMF to revise upwards its growth by more than 5 points since April
text:
What was going to be an economic debacle a few months ago could end up as a simple, run-of-the-mill recession. Russia is weathering Western sanctions much more boldly and skillfully than expected. It is true that the central bank (and the government) had been accumulating gold and foreign exchange reserves for years to survive such a scenario, but it is also true that the Russian economy is holding up better than expected, with the invaluable help of rising commodity prices, which have boosted its export revenues and generated a historic current account surplus for the Russian economy.

Such is the surprise of Russia's economic resilience that the International Monetary Fund has been forced to revise upwards its growth forecast for the economy by 5.1 points from the April WEO and by 2.6 points from the July update.

Thus, the IMF now forecasts a contraction in the economy of 3.4%, compared to 8.5% in April. At the beginning of the war, several analysts and organizations predicted GDP falls of up to double digits for the Russian economy, figures which are now a dead letter.

When the first sanctions were imposed, the ruble plummeted violently. Analysts and Western governments predicted the apocalypse for the Russian economy, with inflation running out of control (the depreciation of the ruble partly supported this argument). Today, however, Russian inflation is 13.7% (admittedly very high), not far from the 10% of the Eurozone and even lower than the Baltic countries, which despite being in the euro have an inflation rate of 20%.

The rapid intervention of the Bank of Russia, with drastic interest rate hikes and capital controls, at the beginning of the war in Ukraine, the search for new customers (China and India, above all) to place a much more expensive oil, together with an economy that had been equipped for years to resist a scenario of Western isolation, are allowing Russia to keep the rate. Meanwhile, Ukraine's (war-torn) economy will sink 35% this year, according to IMF forecasts.

A resilient labor market The international body's paper stresses that Russia's economy suffered an intense blow at the start of the war, but soon after began to revive as export revenues rose, the ruble regained all the ground lost against the dollar and the economy adapted to the new normal under sanctions. "Russian domestic demand is showing some stability, thanks to the containment of the effect of sanctions on domestic financial sector policy support and a resilient labor market," the IMF report admits.

Against all odds, Russia's unemployment rate has fallen to 3.8%, when in January 2022 (before the war and sanctions), unemployment stood at 4.4%. The Bank of Russia revealed in a recent document that some sectors such as mining or energy were growing strongly, which could explain this trend.

Thus, the IMF projects growth of -3.4% and -2.3% in Russia in 2022 and 2023, compared to the expected 35% contraction in Ukraine in 2022, as a result of the war. On the price side, inflation will be just over 13% in Russia (versus over 20% estimated by several agencies at the start of the war), while it will fall to 5% in 2023.

The strength of the ruble The IMF admits in the report that "the contraction in Russia's economy is less severe than previously projected, reflecting resilience in crude oil exports and domestic demand with stronger fiscal and monetary policy support and a restoration of confidence in the financial system."

A good summary of all of the above is the performance of the ruble/euro cross. Theory and logic would say that the currency of a country immersed in a war and under sanctions from the almighty West should be suffering a debacle. The reality is that the Russian ruble is up more than 30% against the euro so far this year.

title: Russia  sets new budget rule, may resume  FX interventions  this year -FinMin
text:
*

This content was produced in Russia where the law restricts coverage of Russian military operations in Ukraine

By Darya Korsunskaya

MOSCOW, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Russia estimates the new cut-off price for its budget rule that diverts excess oil revenues into its wealth fund at $62-$63 per barrel and may resume foreign currency purchases as early as this year, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said on Wednesday.

The rule, designed to replenish state reserves by buying foreign currency when oil prices are high, was fully suspended amid harsh Western sanctions imposed after Moscow launched what it calls a "special military operation" in Ukraine on Feb. 24.

Siluanov, whose ministry published spending plans from its National Wealth Fund (NWF) earlier on Wednesday, said domestic borrowing would be ramped up to the tune of around $43 billion next year, with extra borrowing to reduce NWF spending also possible.

"We are planning on big volumes on the borrowing market - 2.5 trillion roubles ($43 billion) next year on a gross basis," Siluanov said.

"Plus, the government will be given the right to carry out additional borrowing of up to 1 trillion roubles to replace the use of NWF funds under favourable market conditions. That's a total of 3.5 trillion roubles."

Russia's finance ministry has held just one successful OFZ treasury bond auction since sending thousands of troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24, a 10 billion rouble placement on Sept. 14.

Market volatility has forced it to cancel weekly auctions since then.

"For us it is important that the budget is not a bottomless barrel in which to take decisions on spending," Siluanov said. "We need to live within our means. We have defined these means as 8 trillion roubles in base oil and gas revenues over three years."

Siluanov said that corresponded to a cut-off price of $62-$63 per barrel. Anything above that should be sent to the NWF.

"If in foreign currency, then naturally only in a friendly currency, there are no other alternatives. In which foreign currency? Obviously, right now it is the yuan."

Russia considers those countries that have imposed sanctions on it as "unfriendly".

FX INTERVENTIONS

Siluanov also did not rule out a return to the FX market this year with currency interventions. The central bank stopped such interventions earlier this year as sanctions targeted Russia's state reserves.

"We can also save in roubles, but then there will be no impact on exchange rate rations," Siluanov said. "We of course as exporters do not want a strong exchange rate, but we don't want sharp fluctuations either."

Siluanov said any FX purchases made this year would be based on the current budget rule and its cut-off price of $44.2 per barrel.

It would be up to the central bank to decide whether to enter the market or not and whether to make all purchases in yuan or leave some in roubles, Siluanov added. ($1 = 58.2930 roubles) (Reporting by Darya Korsunskaya; Writing by Alexander Marrow; Editing by Hugh Lawson)

title: The suspicious resilience of the Russian economy
text:
When the first economic sanctions against Putin were announced, politicians and analysts expected a destructive effect on the Russian economy. Six months into the conflict, the exact impact of these measures is still unknown. In fact, headlines about the country's economic performance in the Western media defy expectations, raising suspicions about the veracity of the data.

Even during seemingly peaceful years, the transparency of the Russian economy could be compared to a blizzard in Siberia, but since the invasion, national agencies have stopped publishing various time series. For example, the Kremlin no longer publishes monthly data on international trade, the Central Bank of Russia hides data on the monetary base and origin of liabilities, and even the Federal Air Transport Agency stopped providing information on the evolution of passengers.

Moreover, since May of this year, the Russian national statistics institute, Rosstat, has been under the direction of Sergei Galkin, who previously worked for Maxim Oreshkin, Putin's economic advisor during the Western financial siege.

Based on the available data, it seems reasonable to argue that sanctions have damaged the Russian economy, but not annihilated it. One of the undoubted reasons is the escalation of hydrocarbon prices, which in 2021 accounted for half of exports and 40% of tax revenues.

According to Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), Russia has earned almost 160 billion euros (of which 88 billion from the EU) from fossil energy exports since February 24. In the first 100 days since the start of the attacks on Ukraine it has cornered 20% more revenue from this item than in the same period of 2021. Russian military expenditures are estimated at 100 billion euros since the beginning of the conflict.

Additionally, the Russian ruble has strengthened considerably due to the authorities' intervention. The Central Bank of Russia announced on February 28 to raise interest rates from 9.5 % to 20 % in order to curb consumption and encourage savings. In addition, the authorities imposed strong capital controls to prevent investment flight. This combination of economic policies, together with the hydrocarbon bonanza, has stabilized the currency and tripled the country's current account balance.

A stronger ruble makes imports cheaper and the abundance of energy sources avoids the inflationary pressures found in the Western European energy market. As a result, inflation fell from 18% to 15% between April and July.

As for unemployment, it is suspiciously low since the invasion, as many international companies have gone on lay-offs by temporarily halting their activities in the country. However, there has not been an explosion of unemployed people. In fact, employability and lower inflation have allowed Russians to continue to consume.

However, the real damage from the sanctions is expected in the longer term. According to The Economist, the most potent sanction lies in limiting Western exports to Russia. These exports include goods such as software, semiconductors and other intermediate products, which are key to the Russian mechanical and military industries.

In fact, Russian military equipment is already suffering from a shortage of semiconductors, connectors, transistors and components that used to be imported from the US, Germany, the Netherlands, Taiwan or Japan, and they are forced to dust off old Soviet-era equipment. They cannot even replace them with Chinese components, since the Asian giant does not produce the most sophisticated microchips either and has to import them from Taiwan or South Korea.

In the absence of official data on the evolution of GDP, the International Monetary Fund predicts a fall in Russian GDP of 6% in 2022 and 3.5% in 2023. The World Bank expects a contraction of 8.9% in 2022 and 2.2% in 2023. Even the Central Bank of Russia warned that the second half of the year will be tougher and forecasts a recession of 4-6% in 2022 and 1-4% in 2023.

In short, Russia will suffer a recession but it will not be a calamity, compared to the turbulent evolution of its economy since the fall of the USSR. And nothing, compared to the expected fall of 35-45% of the Ukrainian economy.

Eszter Wirth, Professor of International Economics (ICADE), Comillas Pontifical University
