title: *S&PGR Revises Kazakhstan Outlook To Negative; Affirms Ratings
text:
2 Sep 2022 16:09 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Kazakhstan Outlook To Negative; Affirms Ratings


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- In our view, Kazakhstan remains vulnerable to potential disruptions to 
the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC)  pipeline, which the country relies on 
for about 80% of its oil exports. 
     -- If Kazakhstan's oil export capacity reduced for a prolonged period, 
this could negatively affect external and fiscal metrics. 
     -- An increasing reliance on domestic funding and rising borrowing costs 
could further increase the government's debt-servicing burden and weigh on its 
fiscal accounts. 
     -- We therefore revised our outlook on Kazakhstan to negative from 
stable, and affirmed our 'BBB-/A-3' sovereign credit ratings. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On Sept. 2, 2022, S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on Kazakhstan to 
negative from stable. At the same time, we affirmed the 'BBB-/A-3' long- and 
short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings. 
 
We also affirmed our 'kzAAA' long-term national scale rating on Kazakhstan. 
 
The transfer and convertibility (T&C) assessment remains 'BBB'. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The negative outlook reflects risks to Kazakhstan's oil exports through the 
CPC pipeline, as well as rising debt financing costs. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower the ratings over the next two years if Kazakhstan's oil exports 
declined significantly for a prolonged period, weakening the economy's 
external position and increasing fiscal deficits. This could be the case, for 
instance, if the CPC pipeline's loading capacity were incapacitated for an 
extended period. We could also lower the ratings if inflationary pressures and 
rising borrowing costs continued to increase the government's debt-servicing 
burden. 
 
Further disruptive factors, such as a deterioration in domestic stability, 
evidenced by incidents of severe civil unrest, could also lead to a downgrade. 
Upside scenario 
We could revise the outlook to stable if the medium-term fiscal trajectory 
improves more than we expect, reducing the pace of debt accumulation and 
debt-servicing requirements. This could be the case, for example, if the 
government materially increases its non-oil revenue base or lowers spending. 
 
RATIONALE 
The rating action reflects risks to Kazakhstan's oil exports through the CPC 
pipeline, as well as rising government debt financing costs. 
 
There have been at least four incidents this year affecting the country's main 
oil export artery, the CPC pipeline, through which Kazakhstan exports about 
80% of its oil production. The pipeline connects Kazakhstan's Tengiz, 
Kashagan, and Karachaganak oil fields to the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk in 
Russia. These incidents include storm-related damage in March that reduced 
exports for almost a month; safety inspections for World War II-era deep-sea 
mines in June; a Russian court ruling in July to stop loading for 30 days due 
to alleged violations of the pipeline's oil spill plan, which was overturned a 
few days later and replaced with a minor fine; and most recently, subsea 
cracks discovered on buoyancy tanks that could limit loading on two out of 
three CPC single-point moorings for around a month. As a result, we expect 
Kazakh oil production of 85.6 million tons per year (equivalent to about 1.8 
million barrels per day [bbl/day]); this is lower than our previous estimate 
of 87.5 million tons for 2022. 
 
In our view, geopolitical tensions caused by the Russia-Ukraine conflict could 
be the source of potential disruptions at the CPC pipeline (see "Kazakhstan 
Remains Vulnerable To Russian Intervention Over CPC Pipeline," published on 
July 13, 2022, on RatingsDirect). About 90% of oil flowing through the CPC 
pipeline originates from Kazakhstan (representing 54 million tons or about 1 
million bbl/day), while the remaining 10% is Russian. Alternative export 
routes to the CPC pipeline can replace less than a third of its capacity and 
are more logistically challenging and expensive. Against the backdrop of the 
uncertain geopolitical environment, in our view, Russia could disrupt flows 
through the pipeline to gain leverage against Kazakhstan or the consumers of 
the oil, namely countries in Europe that support Ukraine, or to hurt Western 
interests in the Kazakh oil sector (shareholders of the pipeline and oil 
fields include Chevron , ExxonMobil , Shell , and TotalEnergies ). In such an 
event, disruptions at the pipeline could be unrelated to Russia's relationship 
with Kazakhstan, but damaging nonetheless. 
 
Oil is the key economic sector in Kazakhstan, directly accounting for about 
15% of GDP, more than 30% of general government revenue, and over half of 
exports. We expect Brent oil prices will average about $100 per barrel (/bbl) 
in 2022, $85/bbl in 2023, and $55/bbl from 2024 (see "S&P Global Ratings 
Raises Oil And Natural Gas Price Assumptions On Further Market Price 
Step-Ups," published June 8, 2022). Despite high oil prices in the near term, 
upside to the external and fiscal accounts could be limited due to stagnant 
oil production. 
 
In addition, the government's fiscal response this year to the civil unrest in 
early January could make it more challenging to curb spending growth from 
2023. Meanwhile, we expect lower oil prices from 2024 will likely weigh on 
revenue. We anticipate the government's net asset position will turn into a 
small debtor position from 2022, largely due to rising debt. At the same time, 
government borrowing costs are increasing, given the rising interest rates and 
reliance on domestic debt issuances. We project that interest as a proportion 
of revenue will average 9.8% over 2022-2025. 
 
The ratings on Kazakhstan are supported by the country's strong fiscal and 
external balance sheets. These were built primarily with budgetary surpluses 
generated during the period of high commodity prices that ended in late 2014. 
The related assets were accumulated in the National Fund of the Republic of 
Kazakhstan (NFRK) and largely invested abroad. We forecast that the economy's 
liquid external assets will exceed external debt through 2025. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: GDP growth averaging 3.6% over 2022-2025 
will be supported by both the oil and non-oil sectors 
     -- We expect spillovers from the Russia-Ukraine war will keep inflation 
elevated and could slow the pace of fiscal consolidation. 
     -- We expect President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev  will likely maintain his 
position following elections and any political reforms to be modest. 
     -- Diversification of the economy, developing the private sector, and 
increasing the population's wealth levels will remain policy priorities. 
 
In our view, the impact of the Russia-Ukraine conflict has thus far been 
moderate for the country's economic growth and banking sector. However, Russia 
is Kazakhstan's largest trading partner and a key source of imports. Russian 
imports made up about 35% of total Kazakhstan's imports during the first 
quarter of 2022, while exports to Russia make up about 9% of the total. Export 
bans imposed by Russia on sugar and grains and depreciation of the Kazakhstan 
tenge (KZT) against the Russian ruble have contributed to rising food prices 
in Kazakhstan, driving inflation to 15% year on year in July. The secondary 
hit from sanctions imposed on Russia could also make it more difficult for 
local companies to trade in certain sectors, although we understand that 
informal trade has likely increased given the free flow of goods and people 
between the two countries. Kazakhstan mostly exports iron ore and uranium to 
Russia while importing cars, semi-finished goods, coal, and refined petroleum. 
The U.S. government  explicitly excluded Kazakh-origin crude oil from the CPC 
pipeline from its sanctions related to the prohibition of dealing in oil of 
Russian origin. 
 
Kazakhstan--along with Armenia, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, and Russia--is a member 
of the Eurasian Economic Union , a customs union that provides tariff-free 
trade and uniform custom tariffs for trade with non-member states. The 
Eurasian Economic Union  ensures the free movement of goods, services, labor, 
and capital between the states, and since mid-March it announced the use of 
the ruble for reimbursement of customs fees with Russia and Belarus. 
 
Russia is also a key source of investment, accounting directly for about 8% of 
Kazakhstan's total external liabilities, although this figure could be larger 
since investment in its oil, gas, and mining sectors is often recorded through 
the Netherlands and the U.K. For Kazakhstan, unlike other Central Asian 
sovereigns, remittances from Russia are not an important source of income. 
 
Although Kazakhstan is a member of the Collective Security Treaty Organization  
(CSTO ), a mutual defense organization with members from ex-Soviet states, we 
view it as unlikely that it will be directly involved in the Russia-Ukraine 
war. The government has not recognized the breakaway Luhansk People's Republic 
or the Donetsk People's Republic, and it has abstained on the U.N . vote to 
condemn the invasion of Ukraine, affirming its policy of neutrality, similar 
to when Russia annexed Crimea. In response to the civil unrest in January, the 
government requested assistance from the CSTO , and peacekeeping troops, mostly 
from Russia, arrived quickly to help restore order. Should a similar situation 
occur in the future, we think it is unclear whether Russia would have the 
resources or willingness to intervene in Kazakhstan again, without some 
reciprocation in terms of Kazakhstan indicating more support for Russia's 
foreign policy. 
 
In early January, protests quickly spread throughout Kazakhstan. They were 
ignited by an increase in the price of liquified petroleum gas (LPG) but 
expanded to encompass broader grievances, including persistent inequality, low 
wages and living standards, aging infrastructure, constraints on political 
representation, and the perceived high level of corruption. Almaty--the 
largest city--saw the most unrest and damage.

In response to the protests, President Tokayev announced a series of economic 
and governance reforms. The government reinstituted caps on gasoline, LPG, and 
utilities prices for six months. The price controls for lower quality gasoline 
were then extended until the end of the year, while tariff increases will be 
tiered based on consumption. The president also announced institutional 
changes to reduce the influence of former President Nazarbayev and his family 
on politics and business, increase plurality and decentralize power away from 
the president to some extent, and improve the competitiveness and social role 
of the large state-owned enterprises, such as Samruk Kazyna . 
 
We expect political reforms will be gradual and modest in nature. In our view, 
decision-making will stay centralized, while government checks and balances 
are limited, and there is no credible political opposition party. Moreover, 
limitations on independent media outlets are significant and perceived 
corruption is high, with Kazakhstan ranking 102nd in Transparency 
International 's Corruption Perceptions Index. 
 
Economic reforms in response to the unrest largely continue prior efforts. The 
government aims to diversify the economy through capital investment programs, 
including infrastructure and housing projects. The pool of investment projects 
under consideration amount to an estimated KZT30 trillion (33% of 2022 GDP). 
The government is also focusing on cultivating the investment climate, 
reducing state participation in the economy, increasing private-sector 
competition, improving tax policy, reforming public procurement, and reducing 
administrative barriers for businesses. Although we believe the government's 
prudent and generally effective macroeconomic policymaking will continue, we 
do not anticipate that the broad scope of reforms will bring about significant 
changes to the macroeconomic environment. 
 
We expect economic growth will slow to 3.0% this year, from 4.1% in 2021, 
largely due to stagnant oil production and the impact of high inflation on 
consumption. The economy expanded an estimated 3.3% year on year over 
January-July 2022, supported by growth in construction, information and 
communications, trade, transport, and manufacturing. Government stimulus 
measures have continued since 2019, including higher spending on development 
projects, defense, wages, social security, and education. 
 
Over the next three years, we expect growth will average just under 4% 
annually. A key driver will be the expansion of the Tengiz oil field that 
should significantly increase oil production. In the absence of disruptions to 
Kazakhstan's oil exports, we expect oil production could exceed 100 million 
tons per year by 2025, from 85.8 million in 2021. Ongoing investment projects 
and efforts to attract foreign investment should also support strong non-oil 
sector growth. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Although government debt remains modest, 
the interest bill is rising 
     -- High oil prices will support strong revenue outcomes in 2022-2023, but 
higher spending this year could be difficult to reverse. 
     -- We expect Kazakhstan's external asset position will remain strong, 
with liquid external assets exceeding external debt by 28% of current account 
payments by 2025. 
     -- Inflation averaged 12% year on year over January-July, above the 
National Bank of Kazakhstan 's (NBK 's) target range of 4%-6%, amid expansionary 
fiscal policy and higher imported prices. 
 
We expect the consolidated general government balance will reach a deficit of 
3.8% of GDP in 2022, down from 4.6% in 2021. We project that revenue will 
increase by nearly 17% this year, backed by higher oil and other commodity 
prices driving corporate income taxes. At the same time, we expect government 
spending to rise by 11%. To address public grievances from the recent protests 
and mitigate the effects of inflation, the government is prioritizing the use 
of the revenue windfall to increase current and capital spending. 
 
We expect deficits will decline to 1.3% of GDP on average over 2023-2025 on 
the back of efforts to broaden the revenue base and moderate spending growth. 
The government will implement certain fiscal rules from 2023 to limit growth 
in spending and transfers from the NFRK to the budget based on oil prices. 
That said, spending will likely stay elevated as social priorities and 
reliance on government spending to boost economic growth could continue to 
steer fiscal policy in an uncertain external environment. Despite strong 
growth in non-oil revenue after the introduction of a new tax code in 2017, a 
large share (30%) of fiscal revenue will remain dependent on the oil sector 
over our forecast period to 2025. 
 
The government's strong balance sheet underpins the rating, with relatively 
large liquid assets. We estimate net debt at 0.4% of GDP in 2022. This has 
deteriorated from a net asset position of nearly 40% of GDP in 2015. The value 
of total NFRK assets declined to about $53 billion (27% of GDP) in July from 
$73 billion at year-end 2014, as oil prices came down from historical highs 
and transfers from the fund to the government were elevated over this period. 
Implementation of a fiscal rule limiting transfers from the NFRK to the budget 
and expanding oil production volumes should help increase assets to about $71 
billion by year-end 2025, as per our forecasts. However, we project that net 
government debt will continue on an upward trend, reaching 2.8% of GDP by 
2025. 
 
We expect gross government debt will rise to 33% of GDP at year-end 2022 from 
25% at year-end 2019, because of increased funding needs and tenge 
depreciation. About 40% of debt is external and denominated in foreign 
currency--of this, about 60% is commercial and the rest is mostly from 
multilateral lenders. In the past two years, the government has increased 
borrowing from multilateral lenders and issued in the ruble market, because of 
what had been a natural currency hedge between the tenge and ruble, in our 
opinion. 
 
Despite the relatively low debt, interest expenditure is rising partly because 
of the growing proportion of domestic debt issuances. We expect interest costs 
will rise further given monetary tightening; average yields on short-term 
local currency government debt had risen to 14% in July from about 10% on 
average in 2021. We expect the interest-to-revenue ratio will increase to 
11.0% by 2025, relative to 5.4% in 2019. 
 
Higher oil prices should lead to the first current account surplus since 2014. 
The strong trade balance will partly be offset by net outflows in the primary 
income account, spurred by profit repatriation on foreign direct investment 
related to oil production. We expect that falling oil prices and rising 
imports will revert the current account to deficits averaging just under 2% of 
GDP over 2023-2025. 
 
Kazakhstan's external asset position is strong, and we expect gross external 
financing needs will stay below 100% of current account receipts and foreign 
exchange reserves. Reserve assets at the NBK  decreased slightly to about $33 
billion in July from $34 billion at year-end 2021. About two-thirds of 
reserves are gold. The NBK  purchases gold with domestic currency, providing 
the government a way to increase reserves despite current account deficits. We 
forecast reserves will remain broadly stable despite foreign direct investment 
inflows, partly because of the revaluation effect of lower gold prices. S&P 
Global Ratings forecasts gold prices of $1,600 per ounce (/oz) in 2022 and 
$1,400/oz over 2023-2025, compared with $1,829/oz in 2021 (see "S&P Global 
Ratings' Metal Price Assumptions: Prices Settle Lower As Slowdown Fears Grow," 
published Aug. 8, 2022). 
 
In our view, the more freely floating exchange rate, following the sharp 
devaluation of the tenge in 2015, has helped the economy adjust to external 
pressures. The currency depreciated by nearly 18% at its peak in mid-March 
compared to end-2021, driven by the risk-off sentiment following Russia's 
invasion of Ukraine. The tenge had recovered a significant part of its losses 
by end-March, and we expect it will depreciate by 9% on average over 2022. 
Ongoing current account deficits and the government's plan to reduce transfers 
from the NFRK, a key tenge purchaser in the market, will weigh on the currency 
over the forecast period to 2025. 
 
Soaring inflation in 2022 has led the NBK  to raise the base rate by a total of 
475 basis points (bps) thus far to 14.5%. We expect inflation will average 13% 
this year, owing to the government's accommodative fiscal stance, higher 
import prices (especially on food), and early withdrawals of savings from the 
government pension scheme by eligible citizens for use in housing, medical 
services, or transfers to private asset managers. We expect inflation will 
slow to about 5% by 2025 because of improvements to inflation targeting, the 
higher base rate, and expected slower tenge depreciation. 
 
To increase independence and effectiveness of its monetary policy framework, 
the NBK  announced that it will not take part in new economic lending and 
support programs and will exit from all such programs by 2023. Out of the 
seven initial programs, only two are still running and will be phased out by 
next year: a mortgage program and financing to the Economy of Simple Things 
program. The NBK  remains a shareholder of oil and gas company KazMunayGas NC 
JSC, with ownership of 9.8%. 
 
The NBK  is also working with the Ministry of Finance to build out a yield 
curve for local currency debt to improve liquidity in the domestic secondary 
market. To increase transparency in the tenge market, the NBK  began publishing 
all sales of U.S. dollars from the NFRK. The central bank also improved its 
focus on macroeconomic stability in 2019 by spinning off financial sector 
regulation to the newly created Agency for Regulation and Development of 
Financial Markets, which focuses on financial system stability.

Financial stability risks from the Russia-Ukraine conflict have been 
manageable thus far, in our view. The three Russian banks that made up about 
14% of systemwide deposits, Sberbank , VTB Bank , and Alfa Bank , have rapidly 
downsized their operations in Kazakhstan to about 2% of the deposit base (see 
"Financial Stability Risks Stemming From Sanctioned Russian Bank Subsidiaries 
In Kazakhstan Have Been Limited," published July 7, 2022). This has been 
accomplished through acquisitions and the partial sale of the loan portfolio 
to other banks. 
 
We expect that banks' asset-quality indicators may be temporarily constrained, 
partly due to the spillover effects from a recession that we expect in Russia 
this year. We also think that the changing operating environment, due to a 
reshuffling of the political class, could affect the competitive landscape, 
since many banks remain reliant on their owners' business and political 
connections. We currently classify Kazakhstan in group '9' under our Banking 
Industry Country Risk Assessment, on a 1-10 scale with '10' being the weakest 
score (see "Ratings On Eight Kazakhstani Banks Affirmed Under Revised Criteria 
Despite Elevated Uncertainties; Outlooks Unchanged," published Jan. 26, 2022). 
The local banking sector is relatively small with the overall loan portfolio 
accounting for only 26% of GDP in 2021, reducing the efficiency of financial 
intermediation on the economy. We consider contingent liability risks to the 
government from the banking system as limited.

title: UPDATE 3-Russian rouble sinks past 60 vs dollar to over 2-week lows
text:
* Rouble falls past 60 vs dollar for first time since July 11

* Russian currency crosses 61 threshold vs euro

* Market alert to news on FX interventions, budget rule

* This content was produced in Russia where the law restricts coverage of Russian military operations in Ukraine (Updates prices)

MOSCOW, July 26 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble fell sharply to its lowest in two weeks against the dollar and euro in volatile trade on Tuesday, as the market remained alert to any news on possible currency interventions or tweaks to Russia's fiscal rule.

By 1520 GMT, the rouble was 3.6% weaker against the dollar at 60.20, its weakest mark since July 11. It had lost 3.2% to trade at 61.10 versus the euro, also a more than two-week low.

Jittery trade has characterised the rouble's last few sessions. On Friday, Russia's central bank cut its key interest rate by a bigger-than-expected 1.5 percentage points to 8.0% and said it would study the need for more cuts as inflation slowed and an economic contraction continued for longer than previously expected.

"As well as expectations related to the new budget rule, the increased demand for foreign currency could be due to continued repayment of foreign currency loans," SberCIB Investment Research said.

ROUBLE STRENGTH

The rouble failed to capitalise on the peak of a favourable tax period on Monday as it extended its losses, but remains relatively close to the near seven-year highs it hit in late June.

The currency's strength has concerned officials, because it dents Russia's income from exports of commodities and other goods priced in dollars and euros.

The rouble is still the world's strongest-performing currencyhere("https://emea1.apps.cp.thomsonreuters.com/Apps/NewsServices/mediaProxy?apiKey=6d416f26-7b24-4f31-beb6-1b5aa0f3fafb&url=http%3A%2F%2Ffingfx.thomsonreuters.com%2Fgfx%2Frngs%2FGLOBAL-CURRENCIES-PERFORMANCE%2F0100301V041%2Findex.html") so far this year, boosted by measures to shield Russia's financial system from Western sanctions imposed after Moscow sent troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24. These include restrictions on Russian households withdrawing foreign currency savings.

Before Feb. 24, the rouble traded near 80 per dollar and 85 per euro.

Alfa Capital analyst Alexander Dzhioev said Russia's trade surplus and restrictions on the movement of capital were continuing to support the rouble.

"The supply of foreign currency on the domestic market from exporting companies is still hefty, while demand for this foreign currency is limited due to weak activity from importing companies," Dzhioev said.

Russian stock indexes were mixed. The dollar-denominated RTS index was down 1.3% to 1,140.7 points. The rouble-based MOEX Russian index was 2.5% higher at 2,182.5 points.

Moscow-listed shares in internet giant Yandex were up 8.2% after the company reported higher revenue and profit for the second quarter. (Reporting by Reuters; Editing by Alison Williams and Mark Potter)

title: At least three killed in 13-missile attack in central Ukraine
text:
KeymomentsKey moments4h agoAt least 358 minors killed in Ukraine since start of conflict17h agoWhat happened in the last hours EL PAÍS offers free of charge the latest news on the conflict in Ukraine as a public service. If you want to support our journalism, subscribe.

At least three people have been killed in a Russian attack with 13 missiles on a military airfield and railroad network in Kirovograd province in central Ukraine, local governor Andriy Raikovich said Saturday. In a televised interview, Raikovich detailed that at least nine Ukrainian soldiers have been injured and that the provincial capital, Kropivnitsky, is currently without electricity due to infrastructure damage. Ukrainian authorities have also denounced a Russian missile attack on the Black Sea port of Odessa, a day after Kiev and Moscow signed two separate agreements with Turkey - with UN mediation and supervision - to resume grain exports from Ukraine. "The enemy has attacked the port of Odessa with cruise missiles. The air defense forces fired two missiles that hit the port infrastructure," the Southern Ukrainian Military Command has warned in a message on the Telegram network.

Latest videos of the invasionKey dates of the conflict: when and how it started. New publications Expansion | Ukraine asks UN to hold Russia to agreement to unblock grainTheUkrainian Foreign Ministry on Saturday asked the United Nations and Turkey to hold Russia to its commitments made yesterday with the signing of an agreement to unblock grain stored in Ukrainian ports. Kiev has denounced this Saturday a missile attack on the port of Odessa, in the south of the country.

The spokesman for the Ukrainian administration in Odessa, Serhi Bratchuk, has assured the portal New Voice of Ukraine that two other missiles were intercepted by the Ukrainian Army's air defense systems. All the projectiles were Kalibr model, used by the Russian forces, the administrator detailed. Earlier, MP Oleksiy Goncharenko had reported that there had been six explosions in the city, as well as the start of a fire in the port.

The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry has condemned the attack. "Russia has taken less than 24 hours to launch a missile attack on the port of Odessa, reneging on its promises and undermining its commitments to the UN and Turkey under the Istanbul agreement," ministry spokesman Oleg Nikolenko lamented on his Twitter account. "In case of non-compliance, Russia will bear the full responsibility for the global food crisis," he lamented. (Agencies)

Kiev denounces Russian missile attack on Odessa port, a day after signing deal to unblock Ukrainian grainUkrainehas denounced on Saturday that Russia has attacked the Black Sea port of Odessa with missiles, a day after Kiev and Moscow signed two separate agreements with Turkey - with UN mediation and supervision - to resume grain exports from Ukraine

."The enemy has attacked the port of Odessa with cruise missiles. The air defense forces fired two missiles, which hit the port's infrastructure," the Military Command of Southern Ukraine has warned in a message on the Telegram network.(Reuters)

Orbán calls for new European war strategy after 'failure' ofsanctionsHungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán said on Saturday that the European Union needs a new strategy to react to the war in Ukraine, as the sanctions adopted against Moscow "have not worked," he said in a speech in Romania. (Reuters)

Borrell: "Spain is in a very good position to help supply gas to the EU "The European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs, Josep Borrell, advocates that the European Union should prepare "as soon as possible" for a possible cut-off of Russian gas, with savings in consumption, and considers that Spain is in a "very good" position to help supply that energy from other suppliers

."We can't suddenly say, 'Oh, they've cut off our gas!' We have to take measures and those measures are savings measures, but there are measures to increase supply and Spain is in a very good position to help Europe have more gas that is not Russian gas," Borrell said in a telephone interview with Efe. The also Vice President of the European Commission responded in this way when asked about the opposition of Spain and other countries of the community club to the proposal to cut 15% of gas consumption until next spring, which was presented on Wednesday by the President of the Community Executive, Ursula von der Leyen, and which will be discussed by the countries in the extraordinary Energy Council next Tuesday in Brussels.

Borrell pointed out that 37% of the natural gas liquefaction capacities and 40% of the storage of this gas in the EU are in Spain, which long ago began to import from Algeria as opposed to other countries that "relied solely and exclusively on Russian gas".

At least three people were killed in aRussian

missile attack in central UkraineAtleast three people were killed Saturday in a Russian attack with 13 missiles in Kirovograd province in central Ukraine, local governor Andriy Raikovich said. They were two security guards at a power substation and a Ukrainian soldier, Raikovich said in a televised interview. Nine other servicemen were wounded, he added.

The provincial capital, Kropivnitsky, is currently without electricity, according to the governor. Initial reports of the attack suggest that the missiles hit a military airfield and the railroad network. (Reuters)

At least 358 minors killed in Ukraine since start of conflict, says country's prosecutor's officeTheUkrainian prosecutor's office for minors said Saturday that at least 358 children have been killed and around 683 injured in attacks by Russia since the invasion of Ukraine began in late February

.Most of the child casualties, counting killed and wounded, have been recorded in Donetsk region with 361, Kharkov with 194, the capital Kiev region with 116, Chernihiv (68), Lugansk region (54), Kherson (54), Mikolaiv (48), Zaporiyia (40), Sumy (17), and Yitomir (15).

Some 5,110 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and nearly 6,800 injured as a result of the Russian invasion, according to the latest updated balance sheet of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, published last Monday. The UN has recorded, in the same balance sheet, 346 children killed and 547 wounded since the beginning of the war.

However,both the United Nations and the Ukrainian Prosecutor's Office fear that these data are actually lower than the real figures given the difficulty of collecting information during the conflict. (EP)

Erdogan, the balancing act between Kiev and Moscow, achieves a diplomatic victory with the Ukrainian grain agreementTheagreement to unblock the export of grain from Ukraine, signed this Friday in Istanbul, has allowed the Turkish President, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, to insist that the diplomatic route is the best way to stop the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. But beyond the negotiating table, the Turkish leader is scoring a victory on the international stage as a mediator. After the Russian invasion last February, and while bombs were falling on Ukrainian cities, Turkey postulated itself as mediator between the two actors: Kiev's friend and Moscow's partner. Both turn out to be, for Turkey, of paramount importance. And the conflict between the two has shown that Ankara does not want to tip the balance in favor of either. In fact, while the international community was closing in on Russia and supporting sanctions packages against the Kremlin, Turkey remained neutral and did not follow any guidelines for punishing Moscow. But neither did it forget Ukraine, to which the Turkish arms industry has sold the Bayraktar drones, of utmost importance for Kiev's military objectives and Ankara's diplomatic weapon.

Immersed in a galloping economic crisis, with the lira vanishing day by day and inflation continuing to escalate, Turkey continues to seek friends abroad and wants to assert itself on the international scene. António Guterres, UN Secretary General, has highlighted and thanked Turkey for its role in the achievement of the agreement - in the signing of which he participated - which will allow the distribution of basic foodstuffs to millions of people all over the world. Erdogan, on the other hand, has boasted about hosting the event and recalled that after four months of work -since the first meeting promoted by Ankara- the negotiations are beginning to yield positive results.

By Albert NayaIn

the image, by Umit Bektas

for Reuters, Erdogan, on Friday, during the signing ceremony in Istanbul of the agreement to resume the export of grain through the Black Sea.Read the full story here

Russian troops' supply lines west of the Dnieper River are in danger, says UKInthe last 48 hours, heavy fighting has been raging in the Kherson province of southern Ukraine, where Ukrainian forces are continuing their offensive against Russian occupation, the UK Ministry of Defense highlights Saturday. Supply routes for Kremlin troops west of the Dnieper River are increasingly at risk, adds the latest British intelligence report.

Difficulties in fulfilling deal releasing Ukrainian grain: sailing around mines and distrust of RussiaTwoseparate but symmetrical agreements with Turkey - one signed by Russia and the other by Ukraine, mediated and monitored by the UN - are the hope for unlocking millions of tons of Ukrainian grain, trapped since the Russian invasion last February by the blockade of Ukrainian ports. After weeks of diplomatic negotiations, the pact signed Friday in Istanbul, which envisages an almost cinematic deployment to get the wheat out, provides for the arrival of cargo ships to Ukrainian ports through "safe channels" identified by the Kiev authorities to avoid mines in their territorial waters, guided by Ukrainian pilots, without military escort, but supervised beforehand by Turkish and UN teams to ensure they are not carrying weapons into Ukraine. Moscow has sought to downplay the role of the agreement in alleviating the food crisis aggravated by Russian aggression and its export policies. The Kremlin insists that the problem, which could escalate into a severe famine, has been caused by Western sanctions against Russia over the invasion.

The aim of the deal, which would open a path for significant volumes of commercial food exports from three key Ukrainian ports - Odessa, Chernomorsk and Yuzhny - is to enable Ukraine to export around five million tons of grain per month, a volume similar to that before the full-scale war launched by Russia five months ago, which blocked Ukrainian ports leaving tens of millions of tons of grain in silos and clogged the global supply chain. In addition, Ukrainian authorities have accused Moscow of stealing grain in the territories it has occupied - as an investigation by EL PAÍS showed - and of deliberately bombing Ukrainian fields to set them on fire and thus fuel the global crisis, with great destabilizing potential.

By María R. Sahuquillo and Javier G. CuestaIn

the picture, by Luis de Vega

, an engineer next to one of the conveyor belts of the Mlybor granary, in Chernihiv, northern Ukraine, last month.Read the full story here

Ukraine denounces 13-missile attack in central UkraineAtleast 13 Russian missiles hit a military airfield and railroad network in Kirovograd province in central Ukraine on Saturday, local governor Andriy Raikovich said in a message posted on the Telegram network. Raikovich claims that the attack has caused dead and wounded, without detailing how many.(Reuters)

Putin awakens identity sentiment in UkraineUkraineis a young state that, since it gained its independence 30 years ago, coexists with a neighbor that denies its existence. This neighbor, Russia, has wanted to militarily subdue the former Soviet republic since 2014. Ukrainian national sentiment has been growing exponentially since Vladimir Putin ordered that year the annexation of Crimea and promoted the uprising of the Donbas separatists (in the east). The invasion that began last February has further boosted the population's affinity for a Ukrainian identity, both in the western provinces and in those closest to Russian culture, those in the east.

Andrew Wilson, professor of Ukrainian Studies at University College London, wrote in the latest edition of his acclaimed The ukrainians, unexpected nation (2015, Yale University Press) that Ukrainian national identity is still in the process of construction after centuries of subjection to outside powers-Poland, the Austro-Hungarian Empire, tsarist Russia and the Soviet Union. "Nations are formed by circumstances and opportunities," Wilson wrote. "Ukrainians like to talk about a 'national idea.' Concepts like 'nation' belong to the realm of political and cultural imagination," this scholar reflected. Putin, according to his thesis, has been the determining circumstance in building the new Ukrainian citizen.

By Cristian Segura

(Special Envoy)In the image, by Luis de Vega

, a boy with a Ukrainian flag in the center of Lviv, in March.Read the full story here

Macron and Al Sisi discuss Ukraine, Middle East and IranThePresidents of France and Egypt, Emmanuel Macron and Abdelfatah al Sisi, today discussed the threat to food security created by the war in Ukraine, the situation in the Middle East and the Iranian nuclear program. The two leaders met today at the Elysee, without making statements, in their first meeting after Macron's re-election last April. The consequences of the war in Ukraine, especially the threat to international food security, were among the main issues they discussed, the Elysee said in a statement. Egypt is a grain-importing country, so it has been hit hard by the international price increases of recent months.

After Macron has recently received in Paris the Israeli prime minister and the Palestinian National Authority, the situation in the Middle East was another topic discussed. The two presidents also discussed the Iranian nuclear program, about which the director general of the UN atomic agency, Rafael Grossi, was "alarmed" this week by Tehran's recent claims about its progress towards the possibility of building nuclear weapons. Cooperation in the fight against terrorism and the situation in Libya were other topics discussed. On Libya, Macron and Al Sisi agreed to continue working to restore the unity and sovereignty of that country, neighboring Egypt, after the long period of instability and civil war it has suffered.

EFE agency reports.

Zelenski, on the agreement to export grain: "It is possible to avoid a global catastrophe, a famine that could lead to political chaos "The Ukrainian President, Volodymir Zelenski, expressed his satisfaction for the agreement reached this Friday in Istanbul, since it could unblock the export of grain from the country, stranded in the ports due to the war. "It is possible to avoid a global catastrophe, a famine that could lead to political chaos in many countries of the world, particularly in the countries that help us," he said. In his address via social networks tonight, Zelenski indicated that about 20 million tons from last year's harvest and also from this fiscal year's harvest could be exported. "These are revenues for farmers, for the entire agricultural sector and for the national budget. These are jobs," he said. "There is a possibility to reduce the severity of the food crisis caused by Russia," Zelenski stressed.

The agreement reached today will allow exporting from three Ukrainian ports - Odessa, Pivdennyi and Chornomorsk - about 22 million tons of wheat, corn and other grain stored in silos, which could not be sold due to the Russian naval blockade. Russia and Ukraine are world grain exporters and together, they sell a third of the world's wheat supply. This is the first major agreement between the two warring countries since the Russian invasion of Ukraine on February 24 and is expected to ease a crisis forged by the Russian naval blockade of Ukraine and Western sanctions on Russia, which have also driven up fertilizer and energy prices.

EFE agency reports.

Ensuring pricestabilityInflation is too high. Russia's war in Ukraine has pushed up the cost of energy and agricultural products. Shortages of materials, equipment and labor resulting from the pandemic are also contributing to higher prices, which is hurting citizens and businesses across the euro zone, especially those with low incomes.

Much of this inflation is due to factors that central banks cannot control, but what we can do is ensure that inflation does not become persistent. This is what could happen if price increases spread throughout the economy and people start to expect higher inflation in the future. In such a case, wage and price spirals of the kind that have historically led to inflation spiraling out of control could be generated.

An opinion of Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank.

You can read the full article here.

Lithuania reintroduces rail transit of goodsa KaliningradLithuaniaon Friday resumed allowing unrestricted transit of non-military goods by rail between Russia and its Kaliningrad enclave bordering Poland and the Baltic country. Vilnius thus complies with the protocol agreed by the European Commission, which states that sanctions only apply for goods transported by road.

Vilnius had been preventing the transit of several sanctioned goods between Russia and its enclave since June, which aroused the ire of Moscow, which accused Lithuania of breaching the treaties signed between the two countries regulating transit to and from Kaliningrad. Moscow can now return to transporting cement, timber and alcohol to its territory. According to Russia's TASS news agency, the Kaliningrad regional government has 60 concrete wagons ready to be transported.

However, yesterday, Thursday, Lithuanian Transport Minister Marius Skuodis claimed that "transit will not be the same as it was before." "We have certain limits on how much cargo can be transported, and clearly we can say what cannot be transported in general. The change is obvious, no matter what anyone says." (Reuters)

Zelenski says Ukraine has $10 billion worth of grain instorageUkrainian President Volodymir Zelenski said Friday that Ukraine has $10 billion worth of grain in storage and will also be able to sell this summer's harvest after signing an agreement in Istanbul with the UN and Turkey (and, indirectly, with Russia) to be able to export grain to the rest of the world through its ports

.In his usual daily televised address, Zelenski has indicated that Russia may try to discredit international and Ukrainian efforts through "provocations" but that the improved export capacity is "another demonstration that Ukraine can resist war." "It is important that we control our territorial waters," he has considered. (Reuters)

Russia opens 25 files a day for criticizing UkraineinvasionRussian police have opened more than 3,300 files for "discrediting" the military since the start of the invasion of Ukraine, 25 a day on average, according to Russian NGO Setevye Svobody (Freedom Network). The organization, which legally assists victims of political repression in Russia, said it had calculated the figure between March 4 and July 14, based on Russian Interior Ministry data. "On average, Russian police issue 35 files for discrediting the army every working day," the NGO said via its Telegram account.

The offense, which came into force in March to silence criticism of the offensive in Ukraine, carries fines of up to 100,000 rubles (€1,700) for an individual and up to 1 million rubles for a legal entity. According to the specialized NGO OVD-Info, about 200 people who have denounced the intervention in Ukraine were prosecuted in Russia in criminal cases, which carry very harsh prison sentences. On July 8, a Moscow city councilor, Alexei Gorinov, was sentenced to seven years in prison for "spreading false information" about the Russian military after publicly condemning the attack on Ukraine.

US announces new $270 million military package to UkraineThePentagon on Friday announced a new $270 million military aid package to Ukraine. Of that figure, $100 million will be earmarked for the purchase of an additional 580 Phoenix Ghost drones. This class of unmanned vehicles can fly for six hours and is designed for ground targets with unreinforced armor. More than a hundred Phoenix Ghost drones were sent to Ukraine last April for use in the battle for the Donbas region. In addition, four more HIMARS multiple missile launcher systems will be sent, bringing the total delivered to Ukraine to 20.

Pentagon spokesman John Kirby said that the U.S. Defense Department is conducting "preliminary explorations" into the possibility of delivering fighter jets to Ukraine, an option so far ruled out by Washington in view of the possibility of an escalation of the direct conflict by Russia. However, he has indicated, if it were to happen, "it would not be executed in the short term."

(Reuters)

What has happened in the last few hours On the 149th day of the war launched by Russia against Ukraine, these are the key facts as of 20.05 this Friday, July 22:

Ukraine and Russia agree to unblock Ukrainian grain exports

. Ukraine and Russia have taken a step on Friday that may mean the end of the blockade on Ukrainian grain exports. The two have agreed to create a Black Sea corridor, now guarded by Russian frigates, to get grain trapped in ports to global markets without being attacked by Russian frigates. The pact, partially reached last week, was signed Friday in Istanbul with the mediation of Turkey and the UN. Its text establishes that Ukraine will be able to recover the departure of its ships to the sea under the protection of its frigates and thus unblock up to 22 million tons of grain.The IAEA considers the situation at the Zaporiyia nuclear power plant to be "increasingly alarming"

. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said in a statement released Friday that the latest available information on the situation at the Zaporiyia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine is "increasingly alarming" and has again called for a mission by its international organization to verify the situation at the plant. Zaporiyia is the largest nuclear power plant in Europe, with six nuclear reactors totaling 5,700 megawatts of power.Zelenski compares Putin to "a python": "He thought we were just another bunny rabbit.But we are not and he can't swallow us."

Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski has reiterated that his country seeks first to recover the territories occupied by Russia since 2014 and which it considers as its own before opening any peace negotiations with the Kremlin because, in his view, a ceasefire now "would only prolong the war." Zelenski has compared Russian President Vladimir Putin as "a python," gobbling up territories in Georgia and Moldova and Ukraine itself before setting his sights on conquering the country in February. "They thought we were just another bunny rabbit," he has claimed. "But we're not a bunny and it turns out they can't swallow us - and, in fact, they run the risk of us tearing them apart."Gazprom warns that the turbine that would restore gas flow through NordStream is still in Germany

. Russian gas company Gazprom said Friday that the turbine at the Portovaya compressor station, whose repair has become a diplomatic crisis between Moscow, Berlin and Ottawa, is still in Germany in the absence of permits to allow its return to Russia. The gas company, which in principle requires the turbine to fully restore the flow of hydrocarbon through the NordStream 1 pipeline, has stated that the contract it has with the German company Siemens Energy makes the latter responsible for obtaining all the appropriate permits.Russian Central Bank extends veto on circulation of dollars and euros beyond September

. The central bank will extend beyond September 9 its veto on the cash delivery of foreign currencies, especially dollars and euros. At the beginning of the offensive, the regulator had banned the sale of other currencies to individuals and had limited to $10,000 the maximum amount that could be withdrawn from accounts that had been deposited before March 9. The rest, including what was deposited later, would be converted to rubles. "There is no reason now to expect that the flow of foreign currency in cash to our country will improve," the governor of the Central Bank of Russia (BCR), Elvira Nabiulina, explained at a press conference. "So in September we will be forced to extend the restrictions."In the photo by Dmytro Smolienko for Reuters, the Zaporiyia nuclear power plant as seen from Nikopol, on the other side of the Dnieper River.

"Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski has reiterated that his country first seeks to regain the territories occupied by Russia since 2014 and which it considers as its own before opening any peace negotiations with the Kremlin because, in his view, a ceasefire now "would only prolong the war." "Our society believes that all territories should be liberated first, and only then should we negotiate what to do," he said in an interview published Friday by the Wall Street Journal. "Freezing the conflict with Russia means a pause that will give Russia a pause to rest."

Zelenski has likened Russian President Vladimir Putin as "a python," gobbling up territories in Georgia and Moldova and Ukraine itself before setting his sights on conquering the country in February. "They thought we were just another bunny rabbit," Zelenski has claimed. "But we are not a bunny and it turns out that you can't swallow us - and, in fact, you run the risk of us tearing you apart."

title: Russian rouble hits near 2-week high vs dollar
text:
* This content was produced in Russia where the law restricts coverage of Russian military operations in Ukraine

MOSCOW, July 18 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble strengthened to a near two-week high against the dollar on Monday, heading towards the 56 mark, boosted by a favourable tax payment period and capital controls as market players looked ahead to a central bank rate decision this week.

The rouble is set to see extra support towards the end this month as export-focused companies usually step up conversion of their forex revenues to meet local liabilities. Tax payments began last week and the bulk are due in the last week of July.

At 0752 GMT, the rouble was 1.2% stronger against the dollar at 56.48, earlier touching 56.3425, its strongest mark since July 5.

It had gained 1.5% to trade at 57.12 versus the euro , earlier hitting a two-week high of 56.97.

"There is still potential for the rouble to strengthen," said Promsvyazbank in a note, suggesting the rouble could move to the lower end of the 56-58 range against the greenback, supported by approaching tax and dividend payments.

The rouble is the world's best-performing currencyhere("https://emea1.apps.cp.thomsonreuters.com/Apps/NewsServices/mediaProxy?apiKey=6d416f26-7b24-4f31-beb6-1b5aa0f3fafb&url=http%3A%2F%2Ffingfx.thomsonreuters.com%2Fgfx%2Frngs%2FGLOBAL-CURRENCIES-PERFORMANCE%2F0100301V041%2Findex.html") so far this year, boosted by measures - including restrictions on Russian households withdrawing foreign currency savings - taken to shield Russia's financial system from Western sanctions imposed after Moscow sent troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24.

The rouble's strength has concerned officials as it dents Russia's income from exporting commodities and other goods priced in dollars and euros. Finance Minister Anton Siluanov has said Russia could turn to currency intervention.

"Currency appreciation can be restrained either by currency interventions or by increasing import opportunities," German Gref, CEO of dominant lender Sberbank, was quoted as saying by news agencies on Sunday.

The rouble may see weaker upside pressure from interest rates at home this week as the central bank is widely expected to cut its key rate from 9.5% at the July 22 board meeting after Russia posted a drop in consumer prices in June.

Veles Capital analysts said an interest rate cut on Friday was likely.

Russian stock indexes were mixed.

The dollar-denominated RTS index was up 0.9% to 1,172.3 points, at its highest since July 5. The rouble-based MOEX Russian index was 0.2% lower at 2,105.4 points. (Reporting by Reuters)

title: Euro traded below the dollar for the first time in two decades
text:
? The EU currency fell to its worst level due to fears of economic recession in Europe and uncertainty in the supply of Russian gas.Photo Ap Clara Zepeda Periódico La JornadaThursday, July 14, 2022, p. 17Theeuro broke the one dollar level for the first time in two decades, falling to 0.9998 dollars, before recovering to trade at 1.0061. This is the worst level for the continent's currency since December 2002. The situation could worsen if the energy price shock triggered by the conflict in Ukraine pushes the bloc into a protracted economic crisis.

This comes as fears of an economic recession in Europe are growing in the markets, against a backdrop of high inflation and increasing uncertainty about the continuity of Russian gas supplies.

Gone are the years when the euro was so strong (1.6 times the dollar during the 2008 global financial crisis) that many Europeans went on vacation to the United States because of the low prices in hotels and food, and returned home with suitcases full of electronics and clothes. But now the situation is completely different, with Europe suffering the economic consequences of the war in Ukraine and the decision of the European Central Bank (ECB) to maintain interest rates.

Thus, there is concern that this crisis could cause a recession with unsuspected consequences, a shadow that intensified on Monday with the reduction of Russian gas supplies and the concern that inflation will continue to rise.

According to analysts, the EU currency has lost ground against the U.S. currency since 2021, but this was accentuated after Russia's intervention in Ukraine, taking into account the low economic growth in the euro zone and a less restrictive central bank, which has also caused distrust in the euro.

title: Russians rush to buy Chinese yuan, Otkritie bank says
text:
July 7 (Reuters) - Russians have rushed to buy Chinese yuan to diversify their holdings away from U.S. dollars and euros, the state bank Otkritie said, as the finance ministry aims to re-start foreign exchange interventions using 'friendly' nations' currencies.

Demand for the yuan has increased eightfold since May 20 when the central bank lifted the restrictions on forex-buying that it introduced to limit the impact of western sanctions on the financial sector, Otkritie, under sanctions itself, said in a note.

At the same time, purchases of the British pound and Swiss francs by Russians have increased 2.5 times, while other once popular currencies, such as the U.S. dollar and the euro, were less in demand, Otkritie added.

"The Chinese yuan has shown stability and relatively low volatility over the past years, and it can become the main tool for diversifying forex savings," Aliya Zubkova, deputy head of the financial markets department at Otkritie, told Reuters.

Rouble-yuan trading volumes hit a record high of 44.3 billion roubles ($703 million) this week, the Moscow Exchange said, as the finance ministry seeks to re-start forex buying using what Russia terms 'friendly' currencies to curb the rouble's growth.

The Moscow Exchange launched rouble-yuan trading in 2013 and in April, its daily trading volumes reached 25 billion roubles.

Authorities in Russia stopped buying foreign currency via market interventions in early 2022, under a budget rule designed to shield the rouble from external shocks and ease pressure on the currency that was falling sharply.

It has recovered strongly, climbing to seven-year highs just over a week ago.

The rouble remains the world's best performing currency this year even though it has shed about 20% against the dollar since last month's peaks as officials voiced concerns about its strength, which dents Russia's income from exporting commodities and other goods priced in dollars and euros.

The finance ministry has yet to announce how it plans to conduct forex buying.

Economists say the comfortable level for the rouble would be around 70-80 per U.S. dollar.

($1 = 63.0500 roubles) (Reporting by Reuters; editing by Barbara Lewis)

title: Currency  Trading: Strong Ruble Hurts Oil-and-Gas Revenue -- WSJ
text:
The Russian currency has risen 41% against the dollar this year, weakening the value of the country's oil-and-gas revenues 


By Caitlin McCabe and Kate Vtorygina 

After its first default on international debt in a century amid a grinding war with Ukraine, one might expect Russia's currency to be suffering. But Russia has the opposite problem.

The Russian ruble has soared to a roughly seven-year high against the U.S. dollar -- an astounding turnaround for a currency that earlier this year was in free fall after Russia invaded Ukraine. The ruble on Wednesday had risen 42% against the dollar this year, making it the best performer against the greenback, according to a Dow Jones Market Data analysis of 56 currencies.

That strength has come with a cost. A strong ruble threatens to hit Russia's budget by reducing the value of oil-and-gas tax revenues that are denominated in dollars.

The ruble "really is too strong for Russia right now," said Liam Peach, an emerging markets economist at Capital Economics, who said that with the ruble nearly twice as strong as it was three months ago, Russia is now receiving roughly half as much in oil-and-gas tax revenue in ruble terms. "The damage that this is likely to continue doing to the public finances has probably made policy makers quite concerned."

On Wednesday, Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov unveiled a new proposal to counter the ruble's gains: buying the currency of so-called friendly countries to help influence the exchange rate of the ruble and against the dollar and euro.

With Western sanctions against Russia blocking the central bank's ability to intervene traditionally in the foreign-exchange market, Mr. Siluanov's proposal marks the latest attempt to stabilize the ruble as the country grapples with the effects from its war in Ukraine.

"The issue is that Russia can't simply sell rubles and purchase dollars -- there are sanctions on the holdings and transactions from the Russian central bank," Mr. Peach said. "I think that's why they're now trying to do this with friendly currencies."

Four months ago, Russia was facing a far different problem: Its currency was too weak. In late February, the ruble cratered in the immediate aftermath of the country's invasion of Ukraine. Russian officials were forced to scramble to implement capital controls to prop the currency up.

Throughout February and March, Moscow took drastic measures. Russia's central bank limited the amount of dollars that Russians could withdraw from foreign-currency bank accounts. Moscow initially required companies to change 80% of their foreign-currency revenues into rubles. And the country doubled its key interest rate to 20%, essentially rewarding people for holding rubles.

The capital controls worked and pushed the ruble higher. Meanwhile, Russia's commodity exports, which were boosted by high prices, gave the currency further upward momentum. At its worst during the war, the ruble in early March reached a record intraday low of about 158 rubles to the dollar, according to data from Tullett Prebon. On Wednesday, it finished at nearly 53 rubles to the dollar.

But Russia in recent months has been taking steps to weaken the ruble, including loosening capital controls and cutting the country's key interest rate -- efforts that have yet to pay off.

Now, Russia is considering deploying excess oil-and-gas revenues to purchase "friendly" country currencies to try to influence the exchange rate of the ruble against the dollar and euro. Speaking during a meeting of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, a Russian lobby group, Mr. Siluanov said the Ministry of Finance would discuss the idea with the government's economic bloc.

Mr. Siluanov didn't specify which currencies Russia could buy. Earlier in the day, the ruble pared its gains and then turned lower in offshore trading Wednesday after Mr. Siluanov's comments. The Russian currency recovered to finish 2.4% higher for the day.

title: UPDATE 2-Russia may buy 'friendly' countries'  currencies  to weaken rouble -Siluanov
text:
* This content was produced in Russia where the law restricts coverage of Russian military operations in Ukraine (Adds detail, officials' comments)

MOSCOW, June 29 (Reuters) - Russia may start buying the currencies of "friendly" countries and use those holdings to try to influence the exchange rate of the dollar and euro, as a means of countering sharp gains in the rouble, its finance minister said on Wednesday.

The rouble has soared to seven-year highs, boosted by capital controls that include curbs on Russians withdrawing foreign currency savings, thereby eating into Russia's export income by denting the value of dollar and euro proceeds from sales abroad of commodities and other goods.

Authorities in Russia stopped buying foreign currency via market interventions in early 2022, under a budget rule designed to shield it from external shocks, to ease pressure on the rouble at a time when it was falling sharply.

Those declines were triggered by fears of tough Western sanctions in the run-up to what Moscow calls the "special military operation" in Ukraine that began on Feb. 24.

Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said that, under a "modified" budget rule, his ministry was ready to step in and accumulate other currencies in its reserves.

"Through the currencies of friendly countries, through cross-rates with the dollar and the euro it will be possible to regulate the cost of the euro and the dollar to the rouble," he told a conference organised by a Russian business lobby group.

"...We will discuss this with the economic bloc in the government. The central bank has agreed."

Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina, who was speaking at the same conference, said the bank - which maintains a floating rouble policy - was ready to take part in the trade to increase liquidity in other nations' currencies.

Exporters were ready to switch to other currencies while importers preferred dollars and euros, she said.

Siluanov gave no other details of how the scheme might work, though the rouble pared gains after his and Nabiullina's comments, heading away from levels around 50 against the dollar that it had neared for the first time since May 2015.

With Russia looking for ways to soften the sanctions blow on its financial sector, Siluanov said his ministry would also suggest allowing export-focused companies to receive proceeds from non-residents in cash.

The Moscow currency exchange this week started trading the South African rand and the Armenian dram, and is preparing to launch trading in the Uzbek sum and the United Arab Emirates dirham. It has been trading the Chinese yuan for years.

title: The ruble strengthens today against the dollar to values not seen since 2015
text:
With information from EFE

The ruble continues to strengthen against the dollar and the euro, and today was trading at its strongest value since June and May 2015, respectively, on the Moscow Stock Exchange.

At 11:10 a.m. Peruvian time (15:10 GMT) the Russian currency was trading at 53.91 rubles to the dollar unit, the first price below 54 rubles since June 24, 2015, according to business daily RBK.

The currency was also being bought at 56.65 rubles per euro, a value not seen since May 2015. Thus, the Central Bank of Russia has set the official exchange rate for tomorrow at 54.70 rubles per dollar and 57.45 rubles per euro.

Thus, the ruble has more than doubled in almost four months since the currency plummeted at the start of the Russian military campaign in Ukraine last February 24.

The ruble then fell to levels not seen since 1994 and 1994 against the dollar and the euro, but the intervention of Russia's Central Bank and currency controls allowed the bleeding to be reversed.

The strengthening of the ruble comes against the backdrop of the approaching tax payment period and high prices on commodity markets, according to Otrkitie Investments analyst Andrei Kochetkov.

The current demand for the currency does not cover the oversupply in the market by exporters, which puts pressure on the dollar and the euro, he said. The day before, the number two in the Russian government, Andrei Belousov, told the Interfax agency that the authorities are considering returning the ruble to its "optimal quotation."

"As for the ruble's optimal rate there is a more or less consensus opinion that it is in the range of 70-80 rubles to the dollar," the Russian deputy prime minister said. Asked about the time frame in which the Russian currency should reach its optimal rate, Belousov replied, "As soon as possible."

title: Putin hikes Russian pensions, plays down Ukraine impact on economy
text:
LONDON (Reuters) -President Vladimir Putin ordered 10% rises on Wednesday in pensions and the minimum wage to cushion Russians from inflation, but denied the country's economic problems were all linked to the war in Ukraine.

With annual inflation near 18% last month, the Kremlin leader acknowledged that 2022 would be a "difficult" year for the Russian economy.

"When I say 'difficult', it doesn't mean all these difficulties are connected to the special military operation," Putin told a televised meeting of the State Council in Moscow.

"Because in countries that aren't conducting any operations - say, overseas, in North America, in Europe - inflation is comparable and, if you look at the structure of their economies, even more than ours."

His comments ignored the fact that rising inflation in Western economies is in part a direct consequence of Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven up prices for energy and food around the world.

The pension increase comes into effect from June 1, while the minimum wage hike kicks in on July 1. Analysts said the steps would not prevent a sharp fall in real incomes.

Putin -- whose approval rating has jumped more than 10 points since the start of the Ukraine campaign to 82%, according to the independent Levada Centre's April poll -- pledged in March to reduce poverty and inequality this year despite crippling Western sanctions and high inflation.

The Russian economy has been rocked by an unprecedented barrage of Western sanctions imposed over his decision to send troops into Ukraine on Feb. 24, with consumer prices soaring and foreign companies quitting Russia en masse as trade becomes near-impossible.

The Research and Expert Review Institute of the bank VEB said the increase in social payments would slow but not prevent a decline in Russians' real incomes, wages and pensions - after inflation is taken into account.

Even with a 10% increase in the minimum wage and retirement pensions, VEB expects Russians' real disposable incomes to fall by 7.5% and real wages to drop nearly 6% this year. VEB also expects poverty to rise to 12.6% this year from 11% in 2021.

Russia's minimum wage currently stands at 13,890 roubles ($250) a month, while the average retirement pension amounts to 18,521 roubles per month.

The increase in wages and pensions may add to the inflation pressures that the central bank tried to cap with an emergency rate hike to 20% in late February, as the rouble's foreign exchange value plunged. It has cut its rate twice since then as the rouble has recovered. [RU/RUB]

Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said the measures would cost the federal budget around 600 billion roubles ($10.5 billion) this year and about 1 trillion roubles in 2023.

On Thursday, the central bank is set to hold an out-of-schedule policy meeting, where analysts expect it to slash the benchmark interest rate from 14% back towards the 9.5% where it stood before the intervention in Ukraine.
