07:13 Expulsion of French and Italian diplomats As well as the 27 diplomats expelled from the Spanish Embassy in Moscow and the Consulate General in St. Petersburg, Russia has also taken a similar decision with French and Italians. Thus 34 French diplomats were expelled in response to the same measure taken by Paris in April against 41 Russian diplomats stationed in France. Moscow also announced today the expulsion of another 24 Italian diplomats.

07:00 Baltic MPs call for prompt and determined action against Russia The chairmen of the foreign affairs committees in the parliaments of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia have raised the importance of acting together "promptly and with determination" against Russia to curb its expansionist ambitions and prevent its disinformation campaigns from succeeding. The Estonian parliamentarian, Marlo Minkelson, stated that 70 percent of the Ukrainian population is asking to join NATO and "we must give them the category of candidate country because they deserve to be admitted because they are fighting for their freedom, if not for everyone's freedom". For her part, the representative of the Lithuanian Parliament, Liucija Laima Andrikiene, assured that the next NATO summit in Madrid should serve for the organization to rethink its policy of deterrence and defense, since the territories claimed by Russia "must be defended and also recovered".

06:51 First Russian soldier on trial in Ukraine pleads guilty to killing civilian Ukraine on Wednesday began the first trial of a Russian soldier for allegedly committing war crimes since the Russian invasion on February 24. In this the first session of the trial, the defendant, Vadim Shishimarin, pleaded guilty to killing an unarmed civilian. The 21-year-old sergeant Shishimarin faces 10 to 15 years in prison or life imprisonment if convicted on the charges against him: violation of the laws of war in combination with premeditated murder.

06:42 Kremlin continues to fail to disclose whether it will agree to prisoner exchange Following the withdrawal of nearly 1,000 Ukrainian defenders who have left the Azovstal plant in Mariupol, the Kremlin continues to fail to disclose whether it will agree to prisoner exchange as proposed by Kyiv in the face of growing rejection among the political elite at home and pro-Russian leaders in the Donbass. Russia claimed yesterday that another 694 Ukrainian defenders of the metallurgy "had surrendered", including 29 wounded. Russia has not disclosed whether it will agree to a swap, but within the country there have already been harsh voices in the lower house, the Prosecutor's Office and in the pro-Russian Donbass strongly rejecting this possibility.

06:30 Russia calls on the southern Ukrainian town of Melitopol to join "the Russian family " Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Jusnulin has called on the southern Ukrainian town of Melitopol to join "the Russian family" during a visit to areas controlled by Russian forces. "The future of this city is to work within the framework of the Russian family. That is why I have come here, to offer maximum support, the possibility of integration," he said. The Russian politician visited the city of about 160,000 people that was seized two days after the start of the Russian military campaign in Ukraine.

06:19 Turkey blocks Sweden and Finland's accession to NATO Turkey is not in favor of Sweden and Finland's accession to NATO. Moments after the accession application was submitted, the Ottoman country has officially made it known that it was not prepared to accept the entry of the Nordic countries if its concerns are not "listened to". It is not the first time that Istanbul has spoken of conditions for accepting Sweden and Finland into the Alliance, in particular its request that they end their policy of tolerance towards members of the Kurdish political exile, in particular the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers' Party). Esther Herrera reports from Brussels.

06:10 Finland and Sweden formalize their NATO membership application The Swedish and Finnish ambassadors to NATO handed in their NATO membership application on Wednesday at NATO headquarters, where they met with NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg, who said "this is a good day at a critical moment for our security". Stoltenberg said that NATO allies "are determined to resolve all issues and reach rapid conclusions". NATO is relying on a rapid entry process given the threat from Russia, although the process usually takes between eight and 12 months.

06:01 Russia expels 27 Spanish diplomats Last April 5, the Spanish Executive expelled 27 people from the Russian embassy in Madrid among diplomats and other staff. This Wednesday, therefore, Russia has responded with the expulsion of 27 diplomats from Spain The Spanish Foreign Ministry rejects the measure taken by the Russian Government but will not take any decision in response, at least for the time being.

05:56 Russia digs in and prepares for a long war Ukrainian Defense Minister Oleksiy Reznikov has assured that "Russia is preparing for a long military campaign. In the Kherson and Zaporiyia regions the Russian occupants are building fortifications to go on the defensive in case of necessity". In the same speech, the Defense Minister called "not to allow Russia to prolong this conflict" as a prolonged campaign "carries the risk of a global food crisis and a new migration crisis".

05:50 Ukrainian surrender at Azovstal steel mill (Mariupol) After many days of defense, Ukraine has finally surrendered at the Azovstal steel mill in an attempt to maintain its control. In a first step, 265 men, 51 of them seriously wounded, were evacuated since Monday night in buses identified with the letter Z, as hated in Ukraine as praised by many in Russia, where there is talk of surrender. To know more: The last fighters of Azovstal, in Mariupol, surrender to the Russian forces. Catalina Gomez Angel reports from Dnipro, Ukraine.

05:45 Russia-Ukraine war | Latest news on the conflict and Putin, live Good morning and welcome to a new day in which we will inform you of all the latest news on the conflict and Putin.current events concerning the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

title: European unity breaks down: Italy's ENI opens ruble account to pay for gas
text:
The Italian hydrocarbons company ENI, 30% controlled by the Italian Treasury, has begun the formalities for opening a ruble account at Gazprombank, as a "precautionary measure" and "in view of the imminent expiration of the deadline for payment expected in the next few days", the company announced. In this way, the European unity in the face of the sanctions is broken by one of the most important countries.

ENI has initiated the opening "of the two current accounts named K, one in euros and the other in rubles, indicated by Gazprom Export, in accordance with a unilateral claim to modify the existing contracts, in line with the new gas payment procedure ordered by the Russian Federation", it said in a statement.

However, the Italian group clarifies that "it has long rejected these changes" and that , "therefore, the opening of the accounts is on a temporary basis and without prejudice to the contractual rights of the company, which provide for the fulfillment of the obligation to pay in euros."

"This express reservation will also accompany the execution of the corresponding payments," the company adds. Close sources told Efe a few days ago that ENI intended to open an account in rubles to fulfill the Russian gas payment commitment and that it was waiting to see if the European authorities would make it clear with a regulation that paying in rubles, as demanded by Russian President Vladimir Putin, is not allowed.

"The decision, shared with Italian institutions, was taken in compliance with the framework of international sanctions and in the context of ongoing discussions with Gazprom Export to expressly confirm the allocation to Gazprom Export itself of any possible costs or risks associated with the different way of executing the payment," ENI explained in its note.

Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi said last week in the United States - where he traveled for talks with President Joe Biden on the situation in Ukraine - that "most of the European importers" of Russian gas have already "opened their accounts in rubles" and assured that ENI would pay on time, although he did not specify whether it would do so in euros or rubles, and reiterated that the European Union (EU) has not officially indicated what to do about this situation.

"On the one hand, to date, Gazprom Export and the competent Russian federal authorities have confirmed that the invoicing (effectively received by ENI in recent days in the contractually correct currency) and the corresponding payment by ENI will continue to be executed in euros, as foreseen in the contract."

Also "that the operational activities of conversion from euros to rubles will be performed by a special clearing agent operating on the Moscow Stock Exchange within 48 hours from the credit and without intervention of the Central Bank of Russia" and that, "in case of delays or technical impossibility to complete the conversion within the foreseen deadlines, it will not have any impact on the supplies".

"On the other hand, the execution of payments in this way does not find for now any European regulatory provision that foresees prohibitions directly affecting the possibility of executing these operations," adds the Italian company.

ENI stresses that the new procedure "is not incompatible with the existing sanctioning framework and its compliance occurs at the time of the transfer of the euros."

"A failure to pay would expose ENI both to the risk of non-compliance with the obligation to fulfill in good faith any contractual request from Gazprom Export imposed by its own authority, and to the risk posed to Eni of non-compliance with sales commitments to downstream customers in the event of supply disruption," it adds.

However, ENI "in the absence of future full, comprehensive and contractually substantiated responses by Gazprom Export, will initiate international arbitration on the basis of Swedish law (as provided for in existing contracts) to resolve doubts regarding the contractual changes required by the new payment procedure and the correct allocation of costs and risks."

title: Italian oil company Eni to open ruble account to pay for Russian gas
text:
Italian oil company Eni announced Tuesday night the forthcoming opening of an account in euros and another in rubles at the Russian bank Gazprombank to pay for gas supplies arriving from that country, thus bowing to Moscow's demands and opening a crack within the European Union, opposed to that mechanism. "The payment obligation can be fulfilled by transferring euros" and that procedure "should not be incompatible with the sanctions" imposed by the European Union (EU) against Russia in response to the invasion of Ukraine, the company said in a statement.

Read moreFollow the latest on the war in UkraineTheItalian group's decision has consequences at the European level and would grant a small victory to Russian President Vladimir Putin in his strategy of division. The energy company, 30.3% controlled by the Italian state, goes against the recommendations of the European Commission, which considers that opening an account in rubles violates sanctions and could lead to infringement proceedings by Brussels. "Anything that goes beyond the guidelines" given by the Commission to member states "would be a violation of sanctions," Eric Mamer, spokesman for the European Commission, said hours before Eni's announcement. "Member states have taken a collective decision to impose a certain number of sanctions, so it is quite normal that member states have an obligation to enforce this decision that has the force of law in the European Union. And if the Member States fail to do so, the general framework of infringement procedures that can be applied by the European Commission applies," Mamer threatened.

Italy is heavily dependent on Russian gas - 43% of that energy source comes from that country - and, at present, could not afford a supply cut-off, as Putin has already threatened could happen (Poland and Bulgaria have already suffered). Prime Minister Mario Draghi has been working hard to secure new suppliers. But the situation is still very complicated. The government, consulted by this newspaper, does not want to comment on the decision and leaves the communication of this matter in Eni's hands. But some sources recall that Draghi, who had referred to this problem as "the grey area of sanctions", has asked the European Commission on several occasions to clarify this matter without receiving a clear answer.

The Italian company further claims that the Russian authorities have confirmed that "invoicing and payment will continue to be made in euros", which is the currency stated in the contracts. Subsequently, they have been told, "an operator of the Moscow Stock Exchange will carry out the conversion into rubles within 48 hours without the intervention of the Central Bank of Russia". An element that Eni wields as mitigating the European guidelines when a Kremlin decree introduced the new two-stage payment procedure: with a payment into a Gazprombank account in euros or dollars and then conversion into rubles in a second account at the same institution.

Initially, this conversion mechanism involved a transaction with the Russian Central Bank, which the EU sanctions regime prohibits. Although Brussels said several times that this ruble conversion mechanism is a way to circumvent EU sanctions, several member states that want to maintain supplies asked the European Commission for clarification. Italy was one of them and, sources close to the Executive insist, there was no clear answer. Draghi, as an alternative, had proposed setting a ceiling on the price of methane.

title: Ukraine - Russia war, live: breaking news on the invasion
text:
???? Keys of the day:

- Russia begins cutting off gas to Europe by suspending shipments to Bulgaria and Poland.

- Fighting continues with heavy shelling in Kherson and nearby Izium area

- The UN assures to be "preparing" the evacuation of Mariupol

- Shelling continues in the city of Kharkiv and the blockade and shelling of the Azovstal plant near the port of Mariupol

- Guterres arrived in Kyiv on peace mission to meet with Zelenski after seeing Putin

21:00 Ukraine goes a step further and launches several attacks inside Russian territory, two small towns in Donbass will decide the fate of the Russian offensive.

20:46 Ukraine calls shelling on Kyiv a "barbaric act" Ukraine has called the Russian shelling on Kyiv a "heinous act of barbarism", amid the visit of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres to the Ukrainian capital. "With this heinous act of barbarism, Russia once again demonstrates its attitude towards Ukraine, Europe and the world," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba wrote on Twitter.

20:35 Biden launches $33 billion package for "continued aid" to Ukraine in arms and money The U.S. president has proposed to Congress to approve a $33 billion package to arm Ukraine "without interruption" and help its citizens and government weather the Russian invasion. La Vanguardia's Washington correspondent, Fernando García, details Biden's proposal and its possible political consequences.

20:22 ENLARGEMENT | Two missiles hit Kyiv during Guterres' visit Two projectiles fired by Russia have hit Kyiv during the visit of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, as reported by the capital's own mayor, Vitali Klitchko. "Tonight, the enemy fired on Kyiv. There have been two hits in the Shevchenkivski district. All emergency services are on the spot. Information about possible casualties is being clarified," the ex-boxer wrote on his Telegram channel. For his part, President Volodimir Zelenski's advisor Mikhail Podoliak remarked that the shelling took place during Guterres' visit: "The day before he was sitting at a long table in the Kremlin and today there are explosions over his head. A postcard from Moscow?" he wrote on his Twitter account.

20:08 Shelling continues in Kyiv Despite the apparent withdrawal of Russian troops, two explosions have rocked a central district of the city of Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko has claimed. The attack comes on the same day that UN Secretary General António Guterres visited the Ukrainian capital.

19:53 Zelenski confident of "successful outcome" in attempt to unblock Azovstal Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski has assured that he is confident of a "successful outcome" in the attempt to unblock the besieged Azovstal metallurgical plant in the port city of Mariupol, where some 1,000 civilians and 2,000 Ukrainian soldiers are sheltering. "I believe that a successful outcome is possible in the unblocking" of Azovstal in which Ukraine is working together with the United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross, Zelenski said at a press conference after meeting with UN Secretary General António Guterres.

19:40 Guterres says UN is doing "everything possible" to evacuate Mariupol UN Secretary General António Guterres has assured that the UN is doing "everything possible" to evacuate civilians from the Azovstal metallurgical plant in the Ukrainian city of Mariupol, where about 1,000 people still remain refugees together with about 2,000 Ukrainian soldiers. "We are doing everything possible to make it a reality. My first and only priority is the people who are suffering and have to be rescued," said the UN Secretary General at a press conference after meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelenski.

19:29 Russia calls the US initiative to include the country on the list of sponsors of terrorism "idiotic" Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has called the US government's initiative to include the country on the list of sponsors of terrorism "idiotic". In her own words, it is a measure "of an idiotic nature" which will bring, moreover, its "consequences" and against which Russia will take measures, TASS news agency noted. "All the measures they take, even if they are idiotic, will be analyzed and monitored. They will be followed up and, of course, will not go unanswered, this must be understood," she has said. Zakharova has warned that the international community has not yet addressed the legal issues of U.S. actions in countries such as Syria, Libya or Irakh, so she has assured that if Washington continues to take measures against Moscow because the alleged crimes committed against Ukrainians could have repercussions in the United States.

19:14 Bulgaria will repair damaged Ukrainian military equipment Bulgaria has announced that it will take over the repair of Ukrainian military equipment damaged in combat in the war against Russia. This was made public by Bulgarian Prime Minister Kiril Petkov after a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky in Kyiv. "Specialized companies of works in the military sphere will repair heavy Ukrainian military equipment. I will submit to the Cabinet of Ministers such a request and I think it will be approved by the Parliament next week as military technical assistance to Ukraine," Petkov said. In addition to repairing an unspecified amount of military equipment, the Balkan country will offer Ukraine the Black Sea port of Varna for export of agricultural products. During his visit, the Bulgarian prime minister thanked Zelensky for the leadership shown by Zelensky during the Russian invasion. "Ukraine will win this war and all democracies are behind you, there is no doubt that this is the only way out," Petkov has declared to the Ukrainian president. The announcement comes hours after Russia cut off gas supplies to Bulgaria for non-payment of amounts in rubles.

19:00 UN confirms the death of some 2,830 civilians in Ukraine The UN Office for Human Rights has already counted 2,829 civilians killed in Ukraine as a result of Russia's military offensive. Within this figure, 205 children stand out, although it assumes that the real figure would be "considerably higher". The UN has also recorded 3,180 wounded, including 303 minors, according to a count which places most of the victims in territories controlled by forces loyal to the Ukrainian government. Moreover, the High Commissioner for Human Rights has assured that it still lacks more information on some areas where there is still "intense" fighting and includes in this group the area of Mariupol.

18:46 Peace talks stall for almost a month It has been almost a month since the last face-to-face meeting between Russian and Ukrainian negotiators. Although talks between experts from both countries continued telematically after the meeting in Istanbul last March 29, the sides still have not brought their positions closer and today Moscow assured that it has not yet received Ukraine's response on its latest proposals to reach a possible peace agreement. "This morning, at the time of preparing the press conference, the Russian side had not received a reply," said Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. Zakharova was referring to Russian counter-proposals sent to Kyiv after studying its version of a possible agreement between the parties. Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky has repeatedly insisted on the need for a direct meeting with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, because contacts through mediators and third countries will not produce the "desired result".

18:34 Ukrainian justice says it has identified "more than 8,000 cases" of alleged war crimes Ukrainian investigators say they have identified "more than 8,000 cases" of alleged war crimes since the beginning of the Russian invasion, Ukrainian Prosecutor General Iryna Venediktova has said. "We have more than 8,000 cases," she said in an interview with German media outlet Deutsche Welle. "We are actually talking about 8,600 cases that only concern war crimes and more than 4,000 cases that are related to war crimes," Venediktova said. These alleged war crimes include "killings of civilians, shelling of civilian infrastructure, torture" and "sexual crimes" reported in the "occupied territory of Ukraine", according to the judge.

18:24 Russia continues to advance into the Donbass Russian troops continue their advance into the Donbass from Kharkiv, a region considered key to being able to outflank Ukrainian positions in northern Donetsk, while consolidating their control over the south of the country, bordering the annexed Crimean peninsula. According to the Ukrainian General Staff, the Russian army has spent the last hours concentrating troops and weapons around Izium, while intensifying attacks to definitively control that area. In addition, Moscow has reportedly moved airborne units and up to 500 military equipment to Izium, which is located 70 kilometers from Kramatorsk, a Ukrainian military stronghold in the Donbass.

18:12 War in Ukraine fuels right-wing extremists in the Netherlands Dutch intelligence services have warned that Russia's war in Ukraine is fueling "the narrative of right-wing and anti-government extremists" in the Netherlands. Director of the General Intelligence and Security Service, Erik Akerboom, has said that the war in Ukraine is being seen "becoming part of the narrative of right-wing extremists and anti-government extremists," which is also fueling polarization in the Netherlands. Russian President Vladimir Putin's narrative about the war he launched in Ukraine at the end of February "fits" with the ideas already held by some radical groups and "that inspires to be against the government, in this against the institutions," he said.

18:00 OSCE announces the closure of its special mission in Ukraine The OSCE Chairman-in-Office, the Pole, Zbigniew Rau, has announced the end of the Special Monitoring Mission in eastern Ukraine, which had been in operation since 2014. The decision follows the lack of consensus at the OSCE Permanent Council on March 31, 2022 to extend the mission's mandate. All decisions of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, which has 57 partner states from Europe, Central Asia and North America, must be made with full consensus among its members. "It is not an easy decision to make. We have explored all possible options through political dialogue with the participating states to achieve the renewal of the SMM's mandate, but Russia's position left us no choice but to take steps to close the mission," Rau said. In a statement, the Pole assured that the SMM has played a "crucial role" in providing objective information on the ground, facilitating the ceasefire and working to alleviate the effects of the conflict on the civilian population."

17:44 Biden proposes $33 billion more in aid to Ukraine U.S. President Joe Biden has asked the U.S. Congress for $33 billion in additional aid to Ukraine, of which more than $20 billion will go to militarily support Kyiv's fight against the Russian invasion. "As long as the assaults and atrocities continue, we will continue to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian aggression," Biden said in a speech from the White House.

17:34 Gas cut-off to Poland and Bulgaria complicate Western sanctions Russian gas company Gazprom's decision to cut off supplies to Poland and Bulgaria for not paying for deliveries in rubles has tangled up the complex framework of EU sanctions, which are intended to punish Moscow economically but also leave open a way for the EU to buy hydrocarbons from Russia. "The Commission is, as a matter of principle, always in contact with the authorities of the Member States" to "ensure that gas deliveries to Europe continue," said the EU executive's chief spokesman, Eric Mamer. The supply cuts to Warsaw and Sofia are the first practical application of the decree approved at the end of March by the Kremlin, according to which European gas importers must open two accounts in the Russian bank Gazprombank before May 20, one in euros and the other in rubles, to make their purchases of the hydrocarbon. According to this mechanism designed by Vladimir Putin's regime, the purchase does not formally end until the euro deposit has been converted into rubles, but this process, which is "entirely in the hands of the Russian authorities, involves the Central Bank of Russia, whose transactions are prohibited under European sanctions.

17:17 Sanchez expresses his support to Bulgaria in the face of Russia's "unacceptable blackmail" with the gas cut The President of the Government, Pedro Sanchez, has expressed Spain's support to the President of Bulgaria, Rumen Radev, in the face of Russia's "unacceptable blackmail" against his country, whose gas supply was cut off yesterday. Sánchez met with Radev at the Moncloa Palace. As indicated by the President of the Government on his Twitter, he took the opportunity to convey to the Bulgarian leader "Spain's support in the face of the unacceptable Russian blackmail of suspending gas supplies". In Sánchez's opinion, "the effects of Putin's attack on Ukraine redouble the importance of the already excellent Spanish-Bulgarian relations".

17:02 Kyiv still not safe Kyiv authorities have reported that they still cannot guarantee the safety of the residents waiting to return, even after Russian forces withdrew from the area. There are more than 200 buildings in the city damaged by shelling, with reconstruction potentially costing around $100 million. "We don't know how long the war will last and how much it will cost in the coming weeks, maybe months, maybe years," former boxer and Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko has maintained. Since Russian forces withdrew from northern Ukraine, many residents have begun to return to Kyiv, even as the city continues to be the target of sporadic missile attacks. The capital remains barricaded, some bridges remain impassable, and the metro runs only until 8 p.m., so its stations can serve as air-raid shelters during regular attack alerts.

16:47 Why Transnistria may be relevant in the Russia-Ukraine war. Ukraine has recently accused Moscow of trying to drag the border region of Transnistria, a self-proclaimed breakaway republic of Moldova, into the war against Kyiv. La Vanguardia's journalist explains why this region may be key in the Ukrainian war.

16:35 Transnistria could prove key in Ukraine war Recent infrastructure explosions in the pro-Russian region of Transnistria, officially still part of Moldova, have triggered rumors that the Kremlin could launch a new offensive here. However, Moldova has not increased security measures in the area. Transnistrian authorities have accused Ukraine of perpetrating "terrorist attacks," something the Kyiv government denounces as an excuse to justify entering the war. An offensive from Transnistria, where Moscow has had troops deployed for decades, would facilitate the seizure of the strategic Ukrainian city of Odessa and the connection of the already occupied territories in southern Ukraine with the regions already controlled by Russia in the east of the country.

16:23 Germany and Japan to strengthen security and energy collaboration vis-à-vis Russia The leaders of Germany and Japan, Olaf Scholz and Fumio Kishida, have pledged to strengthen their security collaboration vis-à-vis Russia, as well as to reduce their energy dependence on Moscow. Scholz and Kishida met in Tokyo during the German Chancellor's two-day visit. In doing so, the two leaders wanted to send "a signal of their political commitment" and "shared democratic values". The two leaders pledged to work hand in hand to "take firm steps" in response to Russia, which willincludes the implementation of the successive rounds of sanctions coordinated with the G7, as well as "additional measures," Scholz said at a joint press conference.

16:11 Chernobyl has elevated, but not "dangerous" levels of radioactivity One month after the Russian occupation of the Chernobyl nuclear plant, the UN nuclear agency (IAEA) has analyzed samples in the "exclusion zone" revealing that radiation levels are not "dangerous" despite being elevated. The fear of an accident that could release nuclear material due to the beginning of the war in Ukraine that led the Russian army to occupy Chernobyl finally did not go further, as nuclear experts have confirmed. The agency has also denounced the excavations in the area carried out by Russian troops, something that "they would never recommend to anyone".

16:03 EU warns that buying Russian gas in rubles violates sanctions against Russia European Union authorities have called on governments and companies in the bloc on Thursday not to buy Russian gas supplies in rubles, as Moscow is now demanding, as they would be in violation of sanctions against Russia. From Brussels they defend that if the purchase is made with the Russian national currency, this would favor the weakened Russian central bank, which is one of the big targets of international sanctions due to the war in Ukraine. Energy companies such as Italy's Eni SpA have already given in to pressure from Vladimir Putin to purchase in rubles directly from the supplier Gazprombank JSC .

15:54 Mariupol port could be back in operation in May The plans of pro-Russian Donetsk separatists in Mariupol envisage the return to operation of the Ukrainian city's port in May to support the Russian effort in the Ukrainian war. This has been advanced by the governor of the separatist republic of Donetsk, Denis Pushilin, who explains that they plan that "already in May the first cargo will be shipped from the port of Mariupol". On the other hand, Puhilin has made known that the Russian forces that have stormed the city are at "inventory stage, cleaning of the territory, preparation of regulations so that the port can fully function"

15:46 Margarita Robles promises that Russia "will not win this cruel war " The Spanish Minister of Defense, Margarita Robles, on Thursday attended a meeting with the Spanish military stationed at the Adazi base in Latvia, where she promised that Vladimir Putin "will not win this cruel war" in Ukraine. This is how forceful Robles has been with the 500 Spanish soldiers who are on the eastern flank of NATO in the face of the Russian threat led by a Putin whom they will not let "get away with it," according to the head of defense. "It is important that in such difficult times we tell the world that Spain is committed to peace, wants peace, is not going to leave Ukraine and the Ukrainian people alone," Robles remarked

15:37 Russia insists again with another offensive in the Donbass The Russian Armed Forces have increased the pressure on Ukrainian defenders in the Donbass region, the main battlefront of the Ukrainian war, which continues to keep both armies in contention. The latest report from the Ukrainian General Staff has also made it known that the country's western border with Moldova is being reinforced, as the threat of an entry into the Transnistrian war is growing. From Kyiv they describe that "Russian invaders are increasing the pace of the offensive operation. In almost all directions, Russian troops are intensifying their war activity."

15:29 Pedro Sanchez warns that "doing nothing" for Ukraine would be "the end of Europe " The Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sanchez, has called on the international community to continue supporting Ukraine, because otherwise it would be "the end of Europe". "Doing nothing and letting Putin sweep Ukraine, would be the end of Europe", has considered Sanchez, who has stressed the need to invest in military equipment because security "does not come for free". For the president, the war in Ukraine is "Putin's war" and he points out this stage as a key moment in which it is necessary to "make the right decisions because they will shape the future".

15:20 German Chancellor announces preparations for possible Russian gas cut-off The threat of gas supply disruption from Russia has been hovering over Germany since the beginning of the Ukrainian war, and on Thursday Chancellor Olaf Scholz announced that preparations have begun in case such a cut-off happens. Scholz acknowledged from Tokyo, where he met with Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida, that it will be difficult for Germany to eliminate gas imports from Russia. "Any disruption has an impact on the economy, the government is very clear about that," warned the chancellor, who has justified that "that's why it is one of the things that was not immediately included in the sanctions."

15:12 Spain sends the ship Ysabel to Poland with the largest shipment of military supplies for Ukraine 200 tons of ammunition, military equipment and weapons and 40 combat-ready trucks have arrived this Thursday in Poland by the Spanish ship Ysabel, sent to Eastern Europe to support Ukraine in the war. The Ministry of Defense has informed of the massive shipment that the Ukrainian army will receive in the coming hours to reinforce itself in the face of persistent Russian attacks throughout the country. The supplies were a personal promise by Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to his counterpart Volodimir Zelenski, whom he visited in Kyiv last week

15:03 ???? 100,000 inhabitants are "in danger of death" in Mariupol The razed city of Mariupol is still hosting 100,000 inhabitants who are "in danger of death" from the war, the city council of the stricken Ukrainian town warned Thursday. The mayor of Mariupol, Vadim Boichenko, has denounced the "unhealthy" conditions in which the residents who still resist in the city live and who must face diseases such as "cholera, dysentery and Escherichia coli". On the other hand, Boichenko has regretted that the Russian army does not try to help the civilians who still remain in the locality and assures that "the occupants cannot provide food, water and medicines, or they are simply not interested".

14:54 Russian economy stagnates growing by 1.6% due to Ukraine war sanctions The Ministry of Economic Development today released data confirming that the Russian economy is suffering from the numerous international sanctions in the wake of the Ukraine war and that they have already blocked its growth to only 1.6% compared to last year. According to the figures, the noticeable drop in Russian economic growth is a far cry from the high rates of January this 2022, with a 5.8% rise and even February, when 4.3% year-on-year GDP was recorded. The manufacturing, food, chemical and steel industries have been particularly hard hit by the rain of international punishments in the wake of the war in Ukraine

14:45 Biden to compensate Ukraine with confiscated Russian oligarchs' funds U.S. President Joe Biden has launched an initiative in the U.S. Congress to have the seized assets of Russian oligarchs sympathetic to Vladimir Putin used as aid to Ukraine. The measure will be accompanied by actions to facilitate the application of sanctions against Russian elites resident or with bank accounts in the United States for the war in Ukraine. On the other hand, the U.S. government's confiscatory capacity against oligarchs will also be expanded, adding more assets within the list of possible assets to be seized

14:36 NATO pledges to support Ukraine in war, even if it lasts for years Kyiv on Thursday received indefinite support from NATO in its war against Russia after the alliance's secretary general, Jens Stoltenberg, guaranteed that they will stand by Ukraine. A National Security Council spokeswoman said no decision has been made. A Commerce Department spokeswoman did not respond to a request for comment.

07:30 Ukraine puts Russian damage at $90 billion Russia has caused Ukraine infrastructure damage valued at about $90 billion (more than 85 billion euros) since the March 24 invasion, the Kiev government said Wednesday.Ukrainian Infrastructure Minister Oleksandr Kubrakov told the meeting of the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities, which was attended by President Volodymir Zelensky, that the damage to infrastructure as a result of the war launched by Russia amounted to almost $90 billion.

07:22 Robles visits today the 500 Spanish military deployed in Latvia to deter Russian threat on the border Defense Minister Margarita Robles travels this Thursday to Latvia to visit the 500 Spanish military deployed on NATO's eastern border to deter any threat from Russia. Spain has been participating since 2017 in this Atlantic Alliance operation that was designed with the objective of maintaining a permanent presence in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland as a deterrence and defense measure. The objective, as defined by NATO, is to "prevent potential conflicts, protect allies and preserve peace and stability beyond the Alliance's borders." However, the mission has become particularly relevant following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, after which the Alliance decided to strengthen protection and deterrence in the countries on its eastern flank.

07:15 Transnistria opens a new hotbed of tension on Ukraine's borders, reports La Vanguardia Moldovan President Maia Sandu warned yesterday that attacks in the self-proclaimed republic of Transnistria, bordering southwestern Ukraine and backed by Russia, are an attempt to increase tension on the part of "pro-war factions". The Security Council of the separatist region yesterday denounced several "terrorist attacks" in less than 24 hours against government facilities and telecommunication antennas. "There were three terrorist attacks in Transnistria. They fired grenade launchers at the building of the Ministry of State Security, there were two explosions at the broadcasting center in the village of Maiak and they also attacked a military unit in Parcani," the press service of the region's president , Vadim Krasnoselski, said on his Telegram channel.

07:07 Borrell asks EU to bet on green energies after new Russian "aggression" The European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, Josep Borrell, on Wednesday described as "aggression" Russia's decision to cut gas supplies to Poland and Bulgaria and asked the EU bloc to move towards green energies. Borrell, who is on an official visit to Chile, said that European dependence on Russian gas and oil "has gone too far" and that Moscow's announcement "will only accelerate Europe's conversion to green energies that do not create dependencies and do not harm the climate". "What Russia is doing today is turning a dependency into an act of aggression. We have the means to confront it and we will confront this new act of aggression jointly and in solidarity. Europeans can be sure of them," he added. Russia's state-owned Gazprom announced on Wednesday the total interruption of its exports to Poland and Bulgaria because of their refusal to pay in rubles, a demand from Moscow rejected by most of the countries of the European bloc.

07:00 UK calls for providing fighter jets to Ukraine The UK and other Western powers should provide weapons, tanks and fighter jets to Ukraine as part of long-term military support, British Foreign Secretary Liz Truss said Wednesday. In a speech at Mansion House, the mayor's residence in the City of London (financial center), Truss said the West "must be prepared for the long term and redouble our support" for the country so that Russian President Vladimir Putin cannot find a place to fund this "terrible war." "Heavy weapons, tanks, aircraft: deepen our inventories, increase production. We need to do all this," said the minister, who considered that "the war in Ukraine is our war, it is everyone's war, because the victory of Ukraine is a strategic imperative for all of us." Western sanctions, she stressed, have already caused Russia to face its first debt default in a century.

06:52 World discusses how to ensure justice for atrocities in Ukraine Countries, international organizations and human rights bodies discussed at the UN on Wednesday how to ensure accountability for the grave atrocities being committed in Ukraine, a war that will be a litmus test for international justice, they warned. Meeting in an informal session, the UN Security Council heard from, among others, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Michelle Bachelet, International Criminal Court (ICC) Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan, Ukrainian Prosecutor General Iryna Venediktova, and organizations such as Human Rights Watch (HRW). They all insisted that the crimes being witnessed in Ukraine cannot go unpunished if the world is to maintain a glimmer of justice for the future.

06:45 Europe prepares for the shutdown of the Russian gas tap, reports Esther Herrera from Brussels Russia has taken the step that so many in Europe feared. Gazprom has cut off gas supplies to Poland and Bulgaria after these two countries refused to pay in rubles. Reactions have been swift, in the midst of the debate about a future embargo on Russian-origin fossil fuels. "Gazprom's announcement that it will unilaterally suspend gas deliveries to customers in Europe is another attempt by Russia to use gas as an instrument of blackmail," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. "This is another provocation by the Kremlin, but it is not a surprise," she added.

06:37 Russian journalist detained for reporting attack on Mariupol theater Journalist Maria Ponomarenko of the RusNews news portal was detained for reporting the "alleged Russian airstrike" on March against the Drama Theater in the Ukrainian city of Mariupol where hundreds of civilians were hiding, Sputnik agency reported Wednesday. A statement released by the joint press service of the St. Petersburg courts, quoted by the Russian agency, adds that "the Oktyabrsky district court ruled on the imposition of the preventive measure in the form of detention on Maria Ponomarenko." The arrested woman is accused of publicly spreading false information about the use of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, adds the note published by Sputnik. Ponomarenko, according to the statement, posted the information on her Telegram channel, was arrested last April 24 and will remain under arrest until next June 22.

06:30 Putin promises to respond "ultra-rapidly" to anyone who tries to intervene in the Ukrainian conflict Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday promised to respond "ultra-rapidly" to anyone who tries to intervene in the Ukrainian conflict from outside and creates "a threat" against the Eurasian country. "If someone intends to interfere in the ongoing events (the invasion) from outside and create a nature of strategic threats, they should know that our response to counterattacks will be ultra-fast," Putin has said at a meeting with lawmakers, Russian news agency Interfax has reported. Putin has added that Russia has "all the tools" to respond. "Those that no one can now boast about. And we are not going to boast. We will use them if necessary and I want everyone to know them," he has emphasized.

06:22 Turkey confident of a meeting between Putin and Zelenski in the "coming days" Turkey's Defense Minister Hulusi Akar on Wednesday expressed confidence in holding a meeting between the presidents of Russia Vladimir Putin and Ukraine Volodimir Zelenski in the "coming days." "We hope that, despite some difficulties, the two leaders will be able to meet in the coming days," Akar moved, after participating in the meeting held at the German Ramstein air base, and hosted by the United States, in which Western defense ministers have participated to discuss military assistance to Kyiv. "Turkey continues to contribute, doing everything necessary, including playing a mediating role, so that the humanitarian situation in Ukraine does not deteriorate and a ceasefire is reached as soon as possible," the Turkish minister stressed, Russian TASS news agency reported.

06:15 This is how Ukrainian artillerymen are resisting Russian attacks on the Kharkiv front, reports Xavier Xas de Xaxàs from Kharkiv Dimitri lives on the eastern front of Kharkiv, where the asphalt and the chimneys of the industrial estates give way to the wide, unpopulated plain, sown with wheat that is now beginning to sprout. His house is simple, one-story with a gable roof. It has a beautiful garden with almond trees in bloom and tulips that grow from bulbs planted many years ago. The chickens roam freely, as crazy as ever. The fence that guarded them was blown up at the beginning of the invasion and it is useless to repair it.

06:07 Zelenski insists to Von der Leyen that the new package of sanctions on Russia should include the oil embargo Ukrainian President Volodimir Zelenski on Wednesday again asked the President of the European CommissionUrsula von der Leyen that the new package of sanctions on Russia should include the oil embargo. In a message via his Twitter profile, Zelenski told that he had a conversation with the president of the European Commission, whom he thanked for Brussels' decision to abolish tariffs on imports of Ukrainian products. "We are grateful to the European Commission for deciding to abolish tariffs and quotas on Ukrainian industrial goods and foodstuffs," Zelenski wrote, who also let it be known that other issues of support and collaboration have been addressed through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

"We estimate that a large-scale reconstruction will cost around $600 billion," Shmigal said in an article for The Economist in which he not only mentioned damage to infrastructure, but also to industry and the environment. "The Ukrainian government has already set up a long-term recovery fund. In our opinion, it can be a universal solution that will ensure reconstruction. It will reduce logistical and administrative costs, and we encourage our international partners to direct all resources through this fund," he encouraged.

After meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, Guterres was received by Putin in the Kremlin. The meeting lasted an hour and only the first parts were made public, through images on the Russiya 24 television channel.

05:48 Guterres arrives in Ukraine to meet with Zelenski after visiting Putin in Moscow UN Secretary General António Guterres arrived Wednesday afternoon in Ukraine to meet with its president, Volodimir Zelenski, after visiting Vladimir Putin in Moscow, in the context of the Russian invasion of its neighboring country. As Guterres has moved through his account on the social network Twitter, he seeks to expand humanitarian support to Ukraine and ensure the evacuation of civilians from conflict zones. "The sooner this war ends, the better for Ukraine, Russia and the world," he added. As reported by Guterres' spokesman Stephane Dujarric on Friday, the UN secretary general will meet with Zelenski and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dimitro Kuleba on Thursday. The Ukrainian president openly criticized Russia as the first leg of Guterres' trip in the midst of the armed conflict.

05:45 Russia-Ukraine war | Latest news from the conflict and Putin, live. Good morning and welcome to La Vanguardia for a new day of coverage of all the information related to the war in Ukraine, which is now in its 64th day. Russian President Vladimir Putin warned Wednesday that Moscow will respond with "lightning strikes" in case of strategic interference in Ukraine, as the Russian Army destroyed a large consignment of Western-supplied weaponry in the south of the country. "If someone, I insist, sets out to interfere in the ongoing events and creates inadmissible strategic threats to Russia, they should know that our response strikes will be lightning, swift," the Russian leader assured during an address to the Council of Parliamentarians in St. Petersburg.

title: UK GDP Growth Expected to Slow -- Market Talk
text:
1758 ET - S&P Global Ratings said it expects U.K. GDP growth of 3.5% this year, below its previous forecast of 4.6% made in December of last year. "Upward price pressures, aggravated by the fallout from Russia's military intervention against Ukraine, are driving real incomes lower," S&P said. The U.K. is a net energy importer, and exposed to the conflict's impact on oil and gas prices, according to S&P. Inflation in March hit a 30-year high for the U.K., coming in at 7% year-on-year, S&P said. The agency also said it affirmed its 'AA/A-1+'sovereign credit ratings on the U.K with a stable outlook. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1731 ET - S&P Global Ratings said it revised down Italy's GDP growth projection for 2022 to 3.1% from 4.4%. The downward revision is a consequence of the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, S&P said. "The Russia-Ukraine conflict poses a risk to Italy's open industrialized economy via trade, supply chains, oil and gas prices, and confidence effects," S&P said. Even as inflation hit 30-year highs in Italy, S&P said it believes "the government's ongoing delivery of key structural and fiscal reforms will boost long-term potential growth and, ultimately, benefit Italy's public finances." S&P affirmed its unsolicited 'BBB' long-term and 'A-2' short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on Italy, with a positive outlook. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1654 ET - S&P Global Ratings upgraded its long-term sovereign credit rating on Greece to BB+ from BB with a stable outlook. S&P said the upgrade reflects it expectation of continuous improvement in Greece's policy effectiveness. Fallout from the war in Ukraine appears manageable, S&P said, but it also said the war is the key driver of its projection Greek GDP growth will slow to 3.4% in 2022, from 8.3% last year. Inflation was 8% in March, a 27-year high, but there is no evidence so far of upward pressure on wages, according to S&P. The agency also affirmed Greece's short-term rating at B. (stephen.nakrosis@wsj.com)

1645 ET - The IPC stock index closes down 0.1% at 53191 points with conglomerate Femsa shares off 1.1%. Grupo Financiero Banorte jumps 8.2% after the group reports a 26% rise in 1Q net profit. Performing loans grew 4.2% on the year, including a 6.3% rise in consumer loans, but 2022 loan-growth guidance is cut to 5%-7% from 7%-9%. Kimberly-Clark de Mexico shares rise 2.4%. The consumer products company had record 1Q sales, up 4% on the year, while higher raw materials costs contributed to a 22% decline in Ebitda. "Margins still a ways from prepandemic levels," analysts with Barclays say in a note, although "the company did produce quarter-on-quarter improvement." The peso weakens to 20.24 against the US dollar from 20.17 yesterday as prospects of more aggressive Fed tightening fuel dollar gains. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

1635 ET - Canadian stocks sink, with financials, industrials and materials posting some of the largest sector declines. The benchmark S&P/TSX Composite Index drops 2.1% to 21186.38, ending the week down 3.1%, according to FactSet . The blue-chip S&P TSX 60 Index slides 2.2% to 1281.87, ending the week down 3%. (maria.armental@wsj.com)

1626 ET - The WSJ Dollar Index is on track to gain 1.1% this week and accumulate a 2.7% increase in three weeks, which would be the largest three-week gain since March 2020. Capital Economics' Jonathan Petersen says in a research note that the equities selloff is behind the recent appreciation this time around. "The dollar is in a 'heads I win, tails you lose' situation," he says. "Either US yields rise further and widening yield gaps help the dollar, or risk appetite worsens on worries about the economic outlook and that drives dollar strength." The USD gains 2% versus the Australian dollar and 1.5% to the pound sterling. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1555 ET - The selloff on US government debt continued this week, sending the 10-year yield up 0.097 percentage point to 2.905%, its fourth consecutive weekly rise, despite falling 0.012 p.p. today. Investors are increasingly confident that the Fed will raise rates by a steep 50-basis point next month. Piper Sandler 's Roberto Perli tells WSJ the rise in yields signal that inflation expectations could get out of control and become a headache for the Fed. "History has shown that every time the Fed has to raise rates aggressively, growth suffers,' he says. "The risk of recession five to six quarters ahead is high." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1509 ET - The chorus of analysts who expect the Bank of Canada to deliver another mammoth interest rate increase grew after data on Wednesday showed Canada's annual inflation hit a fresh three-decade high, at 6.7%. Bank of Canada Gov. Tiff Macklem told reporters the following day that he was ready to be "as forceful as needed," in normalizing monetary policy. While many analysts now expect another half-percentage point increase in June, Desjardins Securities said Macklem's comments, coupled with this week's inflation report, suggest the BoC could go even further and raise rates by three-quarters of a percentage point during its next meeting. (kim.mackrael@wsj.com; @kimmackrael)

1256 ET - Diverging interest rates will keep the Japanese yen weak and drive the USD/JPY to 140 by the end of this year, "before dropping back as the Fed takes its foot off the gas in 2023," Capital Economics' Jonas Goltermann says in a research note. Goltermann says the yen has depreciated around 10% against the dollar since early March, mainly because the BoJ "has stuck to its ultra-loose policy stance," while the Fed is aggressively tightening. Japan's terms of trade "have also worsened significantly on account of the surge in commodity prices," Goltermann says, warning that the BoJ is under pressure to change its policy, which could support the yen. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1127 ET - The People's Bank of China may welcome a potential further depreciation of the Chinese renminbi, Capital Economics economist Mark Williams says in a research note. The recent rise in USD/CNY has further to go as yield differentials move against the renminbi, consumer demand weakens in key export markets and inventory restocking in many sectors potentially runs its course, he says. The PBOC has good reason to embrace a gradual depreciation of the renminbi, Williams says. "In an environment of weaker global demand, the renminbi's current strength would increasingly hold exporters back." Capital Economics raises its year-end USD/CNY forecast to 7.00 from 6.70. USD/CNY rises 0.7% to 6.4971 after earlier hitting a near nine-month high of 6.5067.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1114 ET - The euro could rise toward $1.15 from $1.0805 currently if the European Central Bank raises interest rates by more than market expectations to tame inflation, Unicredit Research says. The ECB could raise its deposit facility rate 100 basis points above the 1.5% peak that is priced in by markets over a two-year horizon, Unicreditforex strategist Roberto Mialich says in a research note. That could prompt the forex market to favor more pronounced EUR/USD long positioning, or bets on the pair price rising, he says. "The intensity of the EUR rally would also depend on the extent to which high inflation also affects the U.S. economy, possibly forcing the Federal Reserve to deliver even more tightening than that already priced in," Mialich says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1108 ET - The rise in Mexican inflation to a new 21-year high in early April, coupled with worsening inflation expectations and hawkish signals from the Federal Reserve support another 50bp rise in the Bank of Mexico 's policy interest rate to 7% at the May 12 meeting, Goldman Sachs chief Latin America economist Alberto Ramos says in a report. Annual CPI stood at 7.72% mid-month, with core CPI up 7.16%. Ramos notes that supercore inflation -- which tracks prices most sensitive to demand conditions -- rose to 5.81% from 5.38% in the second half of March. "This is likely to keep the central bank conservative in the calibration of monetary policy despite the weak real activity backdrop," he says. (anthony.harrup@wsj.com)

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: Ukraine - Russia war, live | Latest news from Mariupol
text:
The key points of the day

- Ukrainian President Volodymir Zelensky claims that Russia has started "the great battle" for Donbass.

- Pedro Sanchez will travel to Kyiv in the coming days and will meet with Zelenski

-The Ukrainian army in Mariupol asks the Pope for help to evacuate civilians.

- A total of 2,072 civilians, 169 of them children, have died since February 24 due to the war in Ukraine.

- Ukraine has already filled out the form to join the European Union.

- A Russian town near the Ukrainian border has been attacked by Ukrainian forces, according to the governor of Belgorod.

- Russia gives another ultimatum to Ukrainian forces in Mariupol to surrender.

14:12 Brussels working on sanctions on Russian oil as part of its sixth package against MoscowThe

European Commission explained Tuesday that it is working on an embargo on Russian oil imports as part of the EU's sixth package of sanctions against Russia and in response to the announcement of Moscow's offensive in Donbas. 14:06 Ukraine says it has so far located 420 bodies of civilians in Bucha

Ukrainian authorities said Tuesday that they have already located a total of 420 bodies of citizens of Bucha, a locality in Kyiv region where Russian troops perpetrated a massacre of civilians before withdrawing, according to the Ukrainian government. "The police in Kyiv region continue to work. As of Saturday night, more than 420 bodies were found, only in Bucha," regional police chief Andriy Nebytov has said, his press service reports on its Facebook page. 13:59 China says it will "strengthen" its "coordination" with Russia The Chinese government has said it will "strengthen" its "strategic coordination" with Russia regardless of "the international situation", with a view to "safeguarding the common interests of both sides". Chinese Deputy Foreign Minister Le Yucheng met with Russian Ambassador to China Andrey Denisov on Monday, according to a Chinese Foreign Ministry statement released Monday, which specified that the aim was to "exchange views on Beijing-Moscow relations and the international and regional situation."

13:51 Russia affirms that the Army has started "the next phase" of the "special operation" against Ukraine Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov affirmed on Tuesday that the Russian Army has started "the next phase" of the "operation" launched on February 24 against Ukraine, before stressing that the objective is "the total liberation of the Donetsk and Luhansk republics". Lavrov further pointed out that the war "is rooted in the desire of the United States and the West to lead the world." "They want to show the world that there will be no multipolarity and created a launching pad against us on our border," he has argued, referring to Ukraine. "They sent weapons to Ukraine," he has trenched.

13:43 About 70,000 people remain trapped in Luhansk, local authorities say

The head of the Luhansk regional military administration, Serhii Haidai, claims that about 70,000 people remain trapped in the eastern Ukrainian region, where the major Russian offensive has begun, President Volodymir Zelensky confirmed on Monday. Before the conflict, which started on February 24, the region had about 350,000 inhabitants. 13:35 Morawiecki calls from Lviv to intensify aid to Ukraine Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki visited the Ukrainian city of Lviv on Tuesday, where he urged the international community to "put calculators aside" and intensify its aid to Ukraine. Morawiecki warned that the evidence of Russian "barbarism" in Ukraine is also "a call to action" for Western governments, from which Poland has been calling for stronger measures against Russia in recent weeks.

13:28 WHO brings attacks on health facilities in Ukraine to 147

title: Bank of Russia admits sanctions hit real economy
text:
Beyond the political rhetoric, Western sanctions are starting to hurt the Russian economy. The governor of the central bank, Elvira Nabiullina, noted that they first hit the financial sector, but now they will have "a bigger impact on the economy in general". In her opinion, "the main problems will be associated with import restrictions, foreign trade logistics and, in the future, possible restrictions on the export of Russian products," she warned.

"The imposition of sanctions caused strong volatility in the market and this was coupled with the nervousness of the population, so that at the beginning of March, the outflow of citizens' funds amounted to 2.4 trillion rubles(27.357 billion euros)," the governor admitted.

"The period in which we can live on reserves is finite," Governor Elvira Nabiullina acknowledged.In her speech, Nabiullina sent another message: Russia's ability to save is limited. "The period when the economy can live on reserves is finite. And already in the second and third quarter we will enter a period of structural transformation and search for new business models," she acknowledged.

Long before the Ukrainian invasion, the central bank began to reduce its exposure to the dollar, bringing its share over the last decade to just under 11% of its total reserves at the end of last year. This would have allowed it, as planned by the Kremlin, to have a large volume of foreign currency with which to sustain the military onslaught. But more than a third of the total was in euros, plus additional investments in currencies such as sterling and the yen.

And this made it possible for international governments to seize about half of the reserves in retaliation for President Vladimir Putin's attack. Restrictions imposed on the Bank of Russia prevented the entity from intervening in the market to defend the ruble, forcing it to impose capital controls and raise the emergency interest rate to calm the markets.

Its reserves peaked at $643.2 billion on February 18 and then declined sharply, before stabilizing. Moscow wants to go on the counterattack: as half of them cannot be used, it plans to take legal action by blocking gold, foreign currency and assets belonging to Russian citizens, although, as Elvira Nabiullina said, "the measure would have to be carefully thought out and legally justified."

title: Russia without clear alternatives for investing reserves after sanctions
text:
The governor of Russia's central bank, Elvira Nabiullina, admitted Monday that the country has yet to find "clear alternatives" for investing beyond the world's major currencies following sanctions. title: Economic sanctions: an overused but effective weapon?
text:
In recent weeks, international sanctions have shone as one of the weapons most resorted to by the West to confront Russia and try to persuade Moscow to end its invasion of Ukraine, which began on February 24. But the invasion continues, raising questions about the effectiveness of this strategy. "We have never talked so much about sanctions, it has become a common theme," lawyer Olivier Dorgans of the Ashurst law firm, whose job is to advise Western companies involved in the Russian market in the face of the tangle of sanctions, tells AFP.

Russia, the country with the most sanctions Sanctions have been piling up as Russian tanks advanced in Ukraine: exclusion of several banks from the Swift interbank system, freezing of central bank assets and oligarchs, export restrictions and embargo on coal. The first rounds of sanctions began on February 22, the day after Putin announced that Russia would recognize the independence of the rebel regions of Donetsk and Lugansk in eastern Ukraine. Russia then had 2,754 sanctions, making it already the second most sanctioned country in the world, behind only Iran, according to data from Castellum.ai, a sanctions monitoring website. Since that day, Russia has accumulated 6,445 sanctions from G7 members, the European Union, Switzerland and Australia. This brings the total to 9,199 sanctions, nearly triple the 3,616 sanctions on Iran. The EU is preparing a sixth round of penalties, almost seven weeks after the start of the war. Russian President Vladimir Putin indicated Tuesday that the Russian economy is still standing despite Western sanctions. "The 'blitzkrieg' (blitzkrieg) our enemies were counting on has not worked," Putin said referring to the financial sanctions at his first press conference in several weeks.

An increasingly used tool However, some data show that the Russian economy is not as unperturbed as Putin claims: car production plunged, the risk of a debt default worsens and inflation threatens to skyrocket, as data released a week ago show. The Russian Finance Ministry announced that it paid in rubles a $650 million debt after a foreign bank refused to make the payment in dollars, exposing it to a risk of default at the end of a 30-day grace period, starting on April 4. For several weeks, Russia dodged the risk of default, as the U.S. Treasury allowed the use of foreign currencies held by Moscow to pay foreign debts. But last week Washington tightened sanctions, and no longer accepts dollars held by Moscow in U.S. banks. "It is difficult for Russia to avoid a sovereign default," assures Timothy Ash, analyst at Blue Bay Asset, however. "A default might not immediately bring down the markets and the Russian economy, but it will have longer-term consequences," says the analyst, who foresees "an impact on investment, growth, living standards," among others. What do apartheid in South Africa, Libya under Muammar Gaddafi or the Russian invasion of Ukraine have in common? Sanctions, a tool that Western states have been using for 30 years, but whose effectiveness has yet to be proven.

Long-term impact "This tool boomed when military responses were no longer popular," says Dorgans. And they have been increasingly used in inter-state conflicts since 1950, up to about 30 occasions per year until 1990, then clearly increasing. Between 1950 and 2019, 1,101 conflicts between statesinvolved sanctions, according to the Global Sanctions Data Base (GSDB), which keeps detailed records. The multiplication of regional economic agreements meant an increase in sanctions with third countries, Erdal Yalcin, professor of international economics at the University of Konstanz in Germany, and founding member of the GSDB, explains to AFP. Another reason for their recurrent use is the development of international financial integration since the end of the 20th century. "Most countries were integrated into an international financial system, and there is a great temptation to punish countries with economic instruments," he says. The recourse to sanctions was mostly decided in cases of human rights, restoration of democracy and wars, describes the GSDB. Some cases have gone down in the annals of history, such as the struggle against apartheid in South Africa, the US embargo against Cuba, or sanctions against the Iranian nuclear program. But despite their growing use, their effectiveness is in question.

In a recent interview with AFP, researcher Gary Hufbauer, a fellow at the Peterson Institute think tank (PIIE) in Washington, recalled that penalties were effective in less than a third of conflicts, generally when imposed against small countries. "These sanctions are very effective in the economic damage they entail. At the political level, the level of effectiveness is in the order of 30 to 40%," says Erdal Yalcin. According to him, it can take years for these punitive measures to produce real effects. For this specialist, their effectiveness is also difficult to measure because many of them are accompanied by other measures, such as the US sanctions against Iraq during the invasion of Kuwait in 1990, in addition to Washington's military intervention. In Russia, the economic effectiveness of the sanctions is already being felt: the World Bank forecasts a recession of 11.2% this year and the S&P Global Ratings agency declared that the country was in "selective default" after it paid a dollar debt in rubles. The Russian currency nevertheless remains at a high level after initially falling sharply. On the political level, "sanctions cannot make the tanks turn around, at least not immediately," Juan Zarate, a consultant at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), told AFP. According to this former U.S. counter-terrorism strategy advisor under President George W. Bush, "the full effect of the sanctions will not be felt for weeks, months or perhaps years." With information from AFP

"The United States wants to have a monopoly on the dissemination of information. We cannot allow it," the lawmaker said on his Telegram account. According to Google, the channel was shut down due to recent sanctions enacted by the US government.

Ukraine evacuates Kramatorsk by road after attack on railway stationResidents of Kramatorsk board a minibus to leave the city. Photo: AFP/Fadel Senna.

The evacuation of civilians from Kramatorsk continued Saturday with buses and minibuses, following the attack on the local train station that left at least 50 dead and nearly 100 wounded.

A day after the bombing, civilian evacuations were continuing by highway, including dozens of survivors who spent the night in a church in the city center, not far from the attacked station.

Kramatorsk is in an area of Donetsk province not controlled by the self-proclaimed republic of the same name, a Russian-speaking region of Ukraine that took up arms against the national government eight years ago.

09:06

Standard & Poor's downgrades Russian debt to "selective default".Russia paid off dollar-denominated sovereign debt with rubles. Photo: EFE/Yuri Kochetkov.

Ratings agency S&P Global Ratings on Saturday cut Russia's foreign currency debt rating to "selective default" after Moscow settled a dollar-denominated item with rubles earlier this week.

The agency downgraded the note on foreign currency debt, such as the dollar, to the "SD" category and left ruble payments at the "CC" step, the rating agency said. The "SD" rating is almost the lowest on the ladder, one level above "D" which indicates a "defaut" or debt default.

"We do not believe that investors will be able to convert these payments into dollar ruble equivalents of the amounts originally due, nor that the government can convert the payments within the 30-day grace period," S&P estimated.
