title: Canada March Jobs Data Points to 5.1% 1Q Growth -- Market Talk
text:
1143 ET - The big headline from Canada's jobs report in March was that the unemployment rate fell to a record low 5.3%. The report also indicated hours worked jumped 1.3% in March, after a 3.6% rise in the previous month. Bank of Nova Scotia 's economics team, based on an hours-worked figure, now suggests 1Q GDP in Canada rose 5.1% at annual rate, well above the Bank of Canada initial forecast of 2%. The March and February employment reports, coupled with high and rising inflation, "make the task of withdrawing monetary stimulus more and more urgent," Scotiabank says. The firm forecasts a half-point increase from the Bank of Canada Wednesday. (paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

1126 ET - The euro could rise against the dollar this year and early next year as the European Central Bank raises interest rates but this appreciation won't last, Commerzbank says. The ECB is likely to start raising rates in the third quarter of 2022 and take its deposit rate to positive territory in early 2023, Commerzbank 's Ulrich Leuchtmann says in a research note. However, later in 2023 the ECB could pause its rate hike cycle due to falling inflation while the Federal Reserve could raise rates further than expected, which may weaken EUR/USD, he says. Commerzbank expects EUR/USD to rise to 1.15 by March 2023 from 1.0878 currently, before falling to 1.12 by December 2023. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1058 ET - Some economists and analysts are skeptical that a White House push to boost domestic manufacturing will help tame inflation, as Biden administration officials have contended. The White House is rolling out several policies aimed at increasing domestic manufacturing, and officials have said the aim is to insulate the US from the kinds of global supply disruptions that occurred during the Covid-19 pandemic and helped fuel inflation, which is at a 40-year high of near 8%. But some economists noted that offshore production contributed to the moderate price increases Americans broadly saw for decades prior to the pandemic. From 1990 to 2019, average annual inflation was 2.4%, according to the Labor Department's consumer-price index. (amara.omeokwe@wsj.com, @TheAmaraReport)

1053 ET - Supply chain conditions in the U.S. deteriorated in March for the second consecutive month, according to an indicator compiled by Oxford Economics. Pressures increased particularly on the price and transportation fronts as the war in Ukraine pushed commodity prices higher and aggravated logistics logjams, the economic-research firm says. Inventory dynamics and worker shortages improved over the month, but the economy's productive capacity was under more stress as demand remained resilient, Oxford Economics says. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

1045 ET - Inventories of U.S. merchant wholesalers rose 2.5% in February compared with the previous month, more than doubling the 1.2% increase registered in January, according to data from the Commerce Department. Economists polled by The Wall Street Journal expected wholesale inventories to advance 2.1% on month. The ratio of inventories to sales was 1.21 in February, up from 1.20 in January but below the 1.27 the same month a year earlier, the data showed. (xavier.fontdegloria@wsj.com)

1041 ET - The recovery of the Russian ruble to pre-Ukraine war levels isn't a reliable indicator of offshore activity, TD Securities says. The ruble's levels in offshore trading don't reflect normal transactions or indicate any real capability for international investors to trade the currency as they used to before the war, TD analyst Cristian Maggio says in a research note. "The final hint that the currency market is mostly unreliable, and levels should not be taken as proof of success of the [Central Bank of Russia 's] attempt to regain control of the RUB, is the extreme volatility recorded in [foreign exchange] forwards," Maggio says. Such fluctuations suggest that signs of stress remain, he says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1023 ET - The euro credit market rally of the past few weeks has lost steam and a repeat looks unlikely, Societe Generale says. There are ongoing concerns over high levels of inflation and central banks becoming increasingly more aggressive to tame prices, as the Fed is now anticipated to raise rates by 50 basis points in May, analysts at the French bank say." The worry is that the faster central banks have to tighten monetary policy, the greater the risks of a policy misstep as the economy slows," they say. While euro credit spreads correctly reflect the threats ahead, Societe Generale no longer expects a strong rally. Instead, "spreads will move in a range with a very small tightening bias," it says. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

1019 ET - A recent easing in used-car prices might be short-lived, JPMorgan says. Used prices dropped 3.4% in March from February, the second straight decline after hitting a record in January, according to data released yesterday by Manheim. JPMorgan says in a note today that the price decline was likely driven by rebuilding of new-vehicle inventories, which in March hit their highest level since June. But the bank expects used-car prices could go back up, because rising commodity costs and continued supply-chain disruption will squeeze new-car inventories and keep new and used prices elevated. That could benefit shares of Avis and Hertz but hurt parts suppliers' stocks, it says. (mike.colias@wsj.com; @MikeColias)

1010 ET - Brazil's consumer prices rose more than expected in March and the 12-month inflation rate is likely to remain above 10% through August of this year, according to Alberto Ramos, an economist at Goldman Sachs . Brazil's statistics agency says its headline measure of inflation, the IPCA, rose 1.62% in March from February and rose 11.30% from a year earlier. The consensus was for an increase of 1.35% in the month, Ramos says in a research note. Price pressures are now highly disseminated throughout the economy, and the recent increase of commodities prices is expected to sustain those pressures in the medium term, he said. There's a growing risk that wage and price indexing could add continued pressure, according to Ramos. (jeffrey.lewis@wsj.com)

1003 ET - The Russian ruble's recovery has accelerated since Russia's government last month announced plans to seek ruble payments for gas sold to "unfriendly" countries,TD Securities says. "Strength of the ruble would suggest ongoing hoarding of the currency to allow for these and other payments, which we do not have evidence of, however," TD analyst Cristian Maggio says in a research note. It could also suggest the Central Bank of Russia has found ways around sanctions and has managed to intervene in offshore markets, he says. The CBR may have sold part of its foreign exchange reserves denominated in currencies that aren't subject to restrictions, he says. USD/RUB falls to a six-and-a-half-week low of 76.2600, according to FactSet . (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0954 ET - Euro high-yield corporate bonds are set to underperform investment-grade debt, says Societe Generale . The high-yield market has so far proved very resilient compared to the investment-grade market since the beginning of the year, reflecting market expectations of a poor investment-grade performance as the European Central Bank ends its quantitative easing programs, the French bank says. While the corporate sector purchase programme, or CSPP, remains active, current spread levels are already pricing in a market without ECB distortion, it says. Societe Generale expects high yield paper to bear the brunt of slower growth, with "HY in both cash and synthetics... set to underperform its IG counterpart," it adds. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

0945 ET - Fed communication, including FOMC meetings and minutes, is responsible for 69 basis points of a 109bp increase in 10-year Treasury yields this year, Bank of America analysts estimate. This is the highest impact based on data going back to 2004, BofA says. "The news flow - likely related to inflation - was also a large contributor at 23bp this year, and we find the sensitivity of rates to news this year has been at the top of the historical range as was 2021 with the pandemic," BofA says. "The hawkish pivot of the Fed may be mostly priced by now." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

The economic research firm highlights the upward pressure on prices due to increased demand after the easing of pandemic restrictions. Additionally, the supply disruption was also a component and has been increasing since the end of 2020 and is now well above previous peaks. The increase in core inflation is unlikely to be entirely due to temporary supply problems, as stronger demand has also played a role, CE economists say. (maria.martinez@wsj.com)

Even if default rates are likely to rise slightly, they will continue to stay low in historical terms, it says. The bloc's 27 member states has banned coal imports but further proposals to restrict oil and gas imports from Russia are finding resistance from some member states. Russian gas accounted for 40% of the bloc's gas imports last year, according to the European Commission . "Further escalation of the war and any resulting ban on gas delivery from Russia remain the main risk factor for the capital markets," the German bank says. The U.S. has already declared a complete ban on Russian oil, gas and coal imports. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

"The rise in yields for the 'risk-free' rate of return left its mark on the overall fixed-income segment and also affected EUR corporate bonds," the German bank says, adding that the total return on investment-grade corporate bonds is currently hovering around the same level as that of German government debt, also known as Bunds. Total returns, which include capital gains and interest, stood at minus 5.8% in the first quarter of 2022, the second weakest quarter ever, it says. On a quarter on quarter basis, the slump was only greater in the first quarter of 2021, during the outbreak of the pandemic, it says. (lorena.ruibal@wsj.com)

0931 ET - European equities could fall on Monday if incumbent French President Emmanuel Macron 's challengers secure more votes than expected in the first round of the country's presidential election on Sunday, Barclays says. "If the two far right candidates, [Marine] Le Pen and [Eric] Zemmour, and/or the far left candidate, [Jean-Luc] Melenchon, score better than expected, market reaction could be pretty negative on Monday," Barclays 's head of European equity strategy Emmanuel Cau says in a note. Utilities, telecoms, real estate and financial shares would be hit by a Le Pen win while exporters, healthcare, technology and materials stocks could fare relatively better and be helped by a potentially weaker euro, he says. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0917 ET - A recently-announced US-EU deal to send more US LNG to Europe is important for US gas markets long-term but not short-term since US export capacity is already maxed-out, says Goldman Sachs in a research note. "As we've discussed, we expect that any incremental volumes from the US to Europe this year will be the result of reallocated volumes [away from Asia and elsewhere] rather than additional exports," it says. "What we believe is more relevant to US gas markets is the longer term impact of Europe's efforts to reduce its dependency on Russia. Specifically, we estimate that US liquefaction capacity can increase by 3-5 Bcf/d beyond what we already basecase." (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

0843 ET - Natural gas prices are up 2% at $6.485/mmBtu as they continue to hit fresh highs not seen in more than 13 years. Yesterday's closing price of $6.359/mmBtu was the highest since Dec. 2, 2008. "Last week's 33bcf [EIA storage] draw was tighter than estimates in the 27-29bcf range, our forecasted 30bcf draw, and well ahead of the 5-year average 8bcf build," says Tudor Pickering in a research note. "With Residential/Commercial increasingly a lesser factor as we shift into shoulder season, power generation remains the story outside of the ebb and flow of LNG exports, with a combination of factors keeping natural gas power burn robust vs. historical levels." (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

0829 ET - US benchmark oil prices climb 1% to $97.03 a barrel, but are on course for a $2 weekly decline that would mark a second straight weekly decline and the fourth weekly retreat in the past five. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in late February caused WTI prices to skyrocket to a 13-year-high $123.70 on March 8, the day the US announced a ban on Russian crude-oil imports. But the market has fallen 22% since then as investors realized Russian oil was just 3%, or 200k bpd, or US imports, and major oil-importers China, India, Europe and others have continued to buy Russian crude. Soaring gasoline prices have weakened demand, which is also pushing down crude prices. (dan.molinski@wsj.com)

0805 ET - The war in Ukraine has completely changed the outlook for the European chemical industry, according to Baader Helvea. The equity-research firm says it views the sector more negatively as the chemical cycle--in which demand has recently risen as economies exit the Covid-19 pandemic period--will end earlier than previously expected due to the effects of the invasion. Order-book visibility will likely get more volatile, and demand is likely to deteriorate in 2Q, Baader says. There is also the risk of supply-chain effects increasing, which, while increasing sale prices, will also lead to volume declines later on, it says. Baader downgrades six companies to add from buy--BASF , Covestro , Fuchs Petrolub , K+S , Lanxess, and Sika . (edward.frankl@dowjones.com)

0704 ET - Pent-up demand should work as a cushion for the European industrial machinery sector through 2022, but all eyes are now on growth prospects into 2023, with risks of U.S. industrial production growth turning negative and a European manufacturing recession in the second half of 2022, says Citi . title: "The resurrection of the ruble": despite the risk of default and sanctions, it is back to its pre-war level
text:
Despite the sanctions imposed by the West, the Russian currency is recovering against the US dollar and is trading at levels close to those seen before the Russian invasion, a sign that the initial impact of the sanctions - one of the harshest in history - may be fading.

The ruble trades at 75.9500 per dollar, a record not seen since February 16, eight days before Russia' s first offensive into Ukraine. It is worth recalling that the Russian currency fell to historic lows against the US dollar, a large part of the foreign currency reserves held by the Central Bank were frozen and rating agencies downgraded Russia's credit rating to "junk bond" status. In early March, the ruble suffered its steepest decline of more than 33% against the dollar. Despite all this, the ruble managed to recover.

What measures were taken to make this happen? The Central Bank of Russia took drastic measures to intervene in the market, applying capital controls preventing investors and companies from selling the currency. These measures allowed Russia to maintain demand for its own currency. The problem lies in the fact that when the restrictions are lifted, it is not guaranteed that investors will decide to buy the currency of their own free will.

Another factor fueling demand is an increase in gas export earnings, as well as a significant drop in imports. According to Bloomberg Economics, Russia is expected to earn about $321 billion (about €292 billion) from its energy exports in 2022, a third more than it earned in 2021, if its big customers, including the European Union, continue to buy Russian oil and gas.

"Russian currency swings do not reflect the fundamentals of the Russian economy. Most of the time, those fundamentals are reflected in the currency. But as soon as capital controls are implemented, that picture is dulled," Craig Erlam, senior market analyst at OANDA, told DW.

"There is no way of knowing whether the Russian economy is now facing the same picture as it was in mid-February, before the invasion of Ukraine, even if the ruble seems to suggest so," he told DW.

Although the International Monetary Fund (IMF) predicted in January that Russia's economy would grow by 2.8% this year, it is now forecast to fall by 10-15%.

As the ruble plunged in the wake of the invasion and the ensuing Western sanctions, Russia's Central Bank stepped in to play the role of fire extinguisher to rescue the currency, which was falling further and further. In an attempt to save it, the financial institution doubled the benchmark interest rate to 20%, restricted domestic companies' access to foreign currency and set limits on foreign currency withdrawals. It also took measures to prevent dollar flight, including a ban on investors dumping Russian stocks and bonds.

"Effectively, he's just artificially propping up the ruble, while appearing to be forcing buyers in hostile countries to use that currency," Erlam explained. "That's similar to the measures that have already been imposed on Gazprom bank, and other Russian banks, in terms of forcing them to convert 80% of their foreign currency payments into rubles. This further supports those kinds of desperate measures."

Despite this rally,the outlook for the ruble looks less positive in the long term. The Russian currency - which has weakened markedly against the dollar over the past two decades - is expected to continue to struggle to re-emerge as the West looks to move swiftly away from Russian oil and gas, the lifelines of Moscow's economy.

title: Why the ruble is soaring as Russia faces historic recession and massive sanctions
text:
Russia's economy is facing the worst economic recession since the breakup of the Soviet Union. In addition, Moscow is dealing with a battery of sanctions imposed by the West that are hitting the country's investment and consumption. To all of the above must be added the uncertainty generated by a war in which Russia is the major player. In theory, all this should have driven the ruble to hell, and initially it did. However, after a violent and rapid fall, the ruble has started a comeback that has allowed it to regain pre-war levels. What is behind this miraculous recovery?

Since the ruble hit a low of $0.0073 per unit on March 4, the ruble has rallied more than 70% to over $0.0131 per unit. This rally, which continues this Thursday, has taken place despite the fact that the war is not going well for Russia and, above all, despite the fact that the economic expectations for the country are getting worse and worse and international sanctions keep on coming. Everything suggests that the strength of the ruble is a mirage caused by an intervened exchange rate that does not even remotely reflect the fundamentals of the Russian economy and the sharp rise in the price of raw materials.

In a scenario without direct intervention by the Bank of Russia (drastic capital controls) and with total freedom of trade, the Russian ruble should have depreciated much more. The fundamentals of the economy are very negative: GDP is expected to sink 10% this year (a crisis worse than that of 1998), inflation is expected to soar above 15%, while foreign investment has already frozen and is not expected to return, which will weigh on growth, innovation and productivity in the medium term.

Deloitte economists summarily outline the keys to this surprising resurrection of the ruble: "In part it is because the Russian government imposed severe capital controls, thus limiting the ability of Russians to take money out of the country. It is also evidence that foreign investors are restricted in disposing of their assets in Russia. In addition, the sharp rise in the central bank's benchmark interest rate provided savers with an incentive to retain their Russian bank deposits. On the other hand, higher prices for oil and other commodities have allowed Russia to continue to generate foreign exchange earnings, despite the obstacles."

A dead-end maze for money Russia has become a sort of dead-end maze for the money already inside the country, so the massive capital flight has been stopped by the tight controls of the Russian central bank and authorities. This move has prevented billions from leaving the country (through the sale of rubles for foreign currencies) putting further selling pressure on the ruble, which has created a solid short-term 'floor' for the Russian currency exchange rate.

The International Institute of Finance (IIF) commented in a note that "the Bank of Russia reacted quickly to the sanctions by more than doubling its interest rates on February 28 from 9.5% to 20%, providing targeted liquidity support to the banking sector and introducing severe capital controls. In the early days of the crisis, the Bank of Russia intervened in the market to stabilize the ruble, whose fall was halted after the asset freeze, as Governor Nabiullina acknowledged."

Nevertheless, the central bank lost $38.8 billion in reserves between February 18 and March 25 (defending the ruble exchange rate), which has reduced total reserves to $600 billion (including the frozen assets). In addition, the Russian authorities also shut down the domestic stock market for a month and reduced the number of ruble trading sessions, any restrictive measure was good to prevent any leakage through which rubles could escape.

All of the above has prevented the ruble from sinking further, but there are also other factors that have given 'wings' to the Russian currency in recent weeks, such as international trade. Sanctions and the repulsion of multinational companies against the invasion of Ukraine have left Russia without a large part of its imports (almost nobody in the West continues to do business with Russia), while Moscow continues to export large quantities of oil and gas, which have also become much more expensive during the last few months. Sharp falls in imports coupled with exports that have held up better have generated very large current account surpluses for Russia.

Current account surpluses These surpluses mean direct inflows of foreign currency that have helped to contain the exchange rate of the ruble, which in turn has also benefited from Vladimir Putin's pressure on Europe and other countries to buy gas and oil in rubles (a way of increasing demand for rubles on international markets), although Europe has later managed to partially avoid using the ruble to continue buying gas and crude oil.

All of the above, according to IIF data, has generated historically high current account surpluses: $39 billion in January-February and probably an additional $40 billion in March, and possibly more than $250 billion for the whole year (in the absence of an energy embargo). This being the case, "Russia should be able to recover the 'lost' reserves in a relatively short period of time," the IIF assures.

In addition, Russian exporters are obliged to convert 80% of their revenues into rubles, which contributes to the inflow of foreign currency on the local market. At the same time, families cannot exchange more than $10,000 (rubles to dollars) until September and there is enough evidence that even this amount is difficult to obtain in banks.

On the other hand, Russian financial intermediaries must receive explicit approval for debt payments to non-residents (payments in hard currency such as dollars or euros, usually). All these controls have artificially strengthened the ruble. "Therefore, the recent strengthening of the ruble is not surprising and could be reversed once again if sanctions were to be tightened in the coming weeks. It is unlikely that this position can be maintained for much longer if more evidence of Russian war crimes emerges," they warn from the IIF.

title: *S&PGR Cuts Turkey LC Rtg To 'B+', Affrms 'B+' FC Rtg; Otlk Neg
text:
1 Apr 2022 16:12 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Cuts Turkey LC Rtg To 'B+', Affrms 'B+' FC Rtg; Otlk Neg


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- The fallout of the Russia-Ukraine military conflict, including rising 
food and energy prices, will further weaken Turkey's already tenuous balance 
of payments and exacerbate inflation. The latter is on course to average 55% 
in 2022, the highest level of all the sovereigns we rate. 
     -- While we expect Turkey's net general government debt to amount to 34% 
of GDP by the end of 2022, preserving some fiscal space, the government's 
foreign and domestic borrowing costs have increased, and the key fiscal risk 
remains the underlying health of Turkey's recently recapitalized state banks. 
     -- The government's balance sheet and the broader economy have become 
increasingly dollarized, with over 50% of resident deposits now denominated in 
foreign currency. 
     -- We lowered our unsolicited long-term local currency (LC) rating on 
Turkey to 'B+' from 'BB -' and affirmed our unsolicited long-term foreign 
currency (FC) rating at 'B+'. The outlook remains negative. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On April 1, 2022, S&P Global Ratings lowered its unsolicited long-term local 
currency sovereign credit rating on Turkey to 'B+' from 'BB -'. At the same 
time, we affirmed the unsolicited long-term foreign currency rating at 'B+' 
and the unsolicited foreign and local currency short-term ratings at 'B'. The 
outlook remains negative. 
 
We also lowered Turkey's transfer and convertibility assessment to 'B+' from 
'BB -' and the unsolicited national scale ratings to 'trAA-/trA-1+' from 
'trAA+/trA-1+'. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The negative outlook reflects what we view to be rising balance-of-payments 
and financial stability risks over the next 12 months amid the economic 
fallout from Russia's military intervention in Ukraine, global monetary 
tightening, and possible policy missteps in the run-up to Turkey's 
parliamentary and presidential elections in mid-2023. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower the ratings if the adverse economic spillover from either the 
Russia-Ukraine conflict or global monetary tightening became more significant 
for Turkey, weakening its already vulnerable balance of payments and 
complicating the task of controlling inflation. We could also lower the 
ratings if policy missteps, for example, ahead of the elections next year, 
further undermined exchange-rate stability and worsened the inflation outlook. 
This would heighten the risk of banking system distress and thereby imply 
potential contingent liabilities for the government. Weakened asset quality 
following several rounds of large-scale credit stimulus in recent years could 
also weigh on the banking system in such a scenario, particularly state-owned 
banks that have seen their balance sheets expand more rapidly in recent years. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could revise the outlook to stable if we observed sustained and enhanced 
predictability of public policy and effectiveness of monetary policy while 
Turkey's balance-of-payments position strengthened, particularly the central 
bank's net foreign-exchange (FX) reserves. 
 
RATIONALE 
The lowering of the local currency rating reflects what we now view as similar 
credit risks characterizing Turkey's foreign- and local-currency debt. A 
differentiation between foreign and local currency ratings is a comparatively 
rare phenomenon, with only 12 sovereigns benefiting from uplift for the local 
currency rating among all 137 sovereigns we rate. In our view, the conditions 
for such uplift are no longer present in Turkey's case. 
 
We typically differentiate between the local and foreign currency ratings for 
sovereigns that can set interest rates and manage their local currency 
independently, that is, without reference to its external value. In our view, 
this is not the case in Turkey at present, as the multiple tools that it 
deployed previously effectively aimed at influencing the exchange rate, 
including foreign-currency interventions and the introduction of the 
FX-protected deposit scheme late last year. We also note that Turkey's 
interest expenditure on local-currency government debt constitutes about 70% 
of total interest expenditure. We consider that, in a downside case, this 
could reduce the government's flexibility to accord a higher priority to 
servicing its local-currency obligations, thus eroding the credit-risk 
distinction between the two types of debt. 
 
In parallel, Turkey's economy has been persistently dollarizing in recent 
years. Resident deposits in foreign currency amounted to 55% of the total at 
the end of 2021, up from 39% at end-2017. If precious-metal deposits are 
included, this rises to about 60%. Meanwhile, the currency composition of 
government debt has also been shifting in favor of foreign currency, with 
foreign-currency debt at 66% at the end of 2021, up from under 40% at 
end-2017. 
 
Our affirmation of the foreign currency rating primarily reflects our view 
that Turkey has some fiscal headroom in case of need. At 36% of GDP at 
end-2021, net general government debt looks favorable vis-a-vis other emerging 
markets such as Brazil or South Africa. We expect Turkey's net general 
government debt to stabilize at close to 32% of GDP over the medium term. 
Balance-of-payments risks, however, remain elevated, and public debt could 
increase further in the event of a more significant depreciation of the 
Turkish lira, or if the government provided more extensive support to the 
banking sector in a downside scenario. We consider that the global economic 
effects of Russia's military intervention in Ukraine in February 2022, as well 
as the tightening monetary policy of central banks in developed markets, 
present additional balance-of-payments risks. 
 
Overall, our ratings on Turkey remain supported by the country's diversified 
economy and resilient and adaptive private sector, which, in the past, has 
weathered external shocks, currency volatility, and frequent changes in 
economic policy. Contained net general government debt, which we forecast will 
amount to 34% of GDP by the end of 2022, also supports the ratings. 
 
The ratings on Turkey are constrained by its vulnerable balance-of-payments 
position and the limited effectiveness of its monetary policy. The ratings are 
also restricted by what we view as weak institutional arrangements. We see 
limited checks and balances between government bodies, with power concentrated 
in the hands of the executive branch, which renders policy responses difficult 
to predict. 
 
Institutional and economic profile: Turkey's growth prospects have weakened in 
the aftermath of Russia's military intervention in Ukraine 
     -- We project economic growth in Turkey of 2.4% in 2022, less than our 
3.7% forecast at the end of 2021. 
     -- Turkey's institutional arrangements are weak, with limited checks and 
balances in place. 
     -- We think that economic policy uncertainty will remain elevated in the 
run-up to the 2023 general election, with possible additional stimulus 
measures at the expense of longer-term economic stability. 
In our view, Russia's intervention in Ukraine in February 2022 presents 
downside risks to global growth and we now expect weaker economic performance 
for European emerging markets, including Turkey. Last year, Turkey's growth 
outcome exceeded our previous forecasts, reaching 11%. Around half of this 
growth is attributable to a carryover effect due to a lower base stemming from 
the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and the quick recovery in the latter part 
of 2020. However, quarterly growth was still very strong, with consumption and 
exports performing particularly well. In contrast, we expect a sharp slowdown 
to follow in 2022. 
 
Turkey remains exposed to the fallout from the Russia-Ukraine conflict across 
several dimensions. Specifically: 
     -- Turkey's important tourism sector, which generates earnings in foreign 
currency, has in the past depended significantly on arrivals from Russia and 
to a lesser degree Ukraine. In 2021, arrivals from Russia constituted 19% of 
all foreign visitors to Turkey (16% pre-pandemic in 2019), while Ukraine had a 
share of 8% (3% in 2019). There is likely to be a significant reduction in 
these tourism flows in 2022 due to the direct impact of the military conflict 
in the case of Ukraine, and the large economic impact of sanctions, as well as 
disruption to transport and payment systems in Russia. In the case of tourists 
from Russia, this could be partially mitigated by the fact that Turkey is 
currently one of few destinations with direct flights from Russia still in 
place, as well as visa-free travel. Stronger European tourism thanks to an 
improved pandemic situation and a competitive lira could also provide support, 
but we consider the overall risks to be on the downside. 
     -- Russia and Ukraine's share of Turkish goods exports is more modest, at 
a combined 4% in 2020. However, given the scale of recessions (we expect a 
real GDP contraction of 8.5% in Russia and 22% in Ukraine this year), 
logistical challenges, and supply chain disruptions, this could still 
materially dampen Turkish exports, particularly taking into account 
second-round effects on European economies. 
     -- Turkey remains an energy importer and therefore significantly higher 
global prices for oil and gas will complicate the task of bringing inflation 
under control, with a likely adverse effect on domestic demand dynamics. 
Inflation rose to 54% year on year in February 2022, the highest level in 20 
years. 
Consequently, we now forecast real growth of 2.4% in 2022, compared with our 
previous forecast of 3.7%. We expect a significant slowdown in exports and 
consumption growth, while we project that real investment will contract by 
3.5% owing to high uncertainty and dwindling global growth momentum. 
 
The future direction of government policy also remains highly uncertain. The 
political pressure on the central bank continues after it made a series of

interest rate reductions in the latter half of 2021 against a background of 
soaring inflation. We also think that policy missteps could occur in the 
run-up to the 2023 general elections. Recent opinion polls suggest declining 
popular support for the ruling Justice and Development Party (Adalet ve 
Kalkinma Partisi; AKP), with the pandemic, high inflation in food prices, and 
a hit to real incomes likely to be contributing factors. In that context, 
additional policy-stimulus measures--for example, to boost the availability or 
reduce the price of credit--cannot be ruled out in 2022, even though Turkey 
still faces lingering imbalances from previous such measures, including lower 
useable FX reserves and higher inflation. 
 
We consider that Turkey's broader institutional arrangements remain weak and 
continue to constrain the sovereign credit ratings. In the June 2018 
presidential and parliamentary elections, the president and the AKP-led 
alliance secured a victory that marked the final chapter in Turkey's 
transition to an executive presidential system. We see limited checks and 
balances between government bodies. 
 
Flexibility and performance profile: Economic imbalances persist, with high 
inflation and weak balance of payments 
     -- We forecast that Turkey's inflation will average 55% in 2022, the 
highest level of all the sovereigns we rate. 
     -- Net general government debt should remain about 32% of GDP through 
2025, still leaving some fiscal policy space. 
     -- Turkey's balance-of-payments position is weak, while its monetary 
policy flexibility is limited, underpinning the risk of a disorderly external 
adjustment. 
In our view, over the past year, Turkey's economic policy has become 
increasingly unpredictable and less conventional, presenting economic and 
balance-of-payments risks. Over the second half of 2021, and under political 
pressure, the central bank persistently lowered the policy rate (one-week repo 
rate) to 14% from 19%, even with inflation hitting multi-year highs and 
reaching 54% in February 2022, the highest rate of all the sovereigns we rate. 
In turn, this contributed to a significant disorderly depreciation of the 
exchange rate toward the end of 2021, similar in magnitude to that during the 
August 2018 currency crisis in Turkey. 
 
Although the authorities managed to arrest the slide in the lira through sales 
of FX reserves and the introduction of the so-called FX-protected deposit 
scheme, we consider that Turkey's balance-of-payments position remains 
fundamentally weak and is a key constraint for the sovereign ratings. The 
country has consistently run a current account deficit in the past, except in 
2019, when imports contracted following the impact of the currency crisis in 
2018. Following a reduction in the current account deficit to 1.8% of GDP in 
2021 from almost 5.0% of GDP in 2020, the current account appears to be 
deteriorating again. In January 2022, the current account deficit totaled $7 
billion, which in nominal U.S. dollar terms is almost half the entire deficit 
for 2021. 
 
We consider that Turkey's longstanding structural external vulnerabilities are 
aggravated by what we view as an end to a period of ultra-loose monetary 
policy by developed-market central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve . 
Additionally, the likely loss of tourist inflows from Russia and Ukraine and 
higher oil and gas prices following the onset of conflict in Ukraine could 
weaken Turkey's balance of payments as the country remains a net energy 
importer. 
 
In parallel, the amount of external debt maturing over the next 12 months 
remains significant as of January 2022, at $174 billion, or 25% of GDP, around 
half of which pertains to the banking sector. At the same time, the central 
bank's FX reserves are weak. As of mid-March 2022, they amounted to $109 
billion (16% of GDP). However, excluding the institution's foreign-currency 
obligations to domestic residents, useable reserves--which represent the 
central bank's effective capacity to intervene--remained much lower, at $22 
billion (3% of GDP) at the end of 2021. 
 
We forecast that Turkey's current account deficit will widen to 3.6% of GDP in 
2022 as oil prices are significantly higher, while tourism inflows will suffer 
from the impact of Russia's intervention against Ukraine, and goods exports 
might take a hit if there is a more pronounced slowdown of the global economy. 
There are downside risks to our forecasts, but the key reason for not 
projecting an even higher current account deficit is that we expect the 
availability of and appetite for external funding for a more sizable shortfall 
to be more limited in the future, including because of global monetary 
tightening. Given the central bank's limited capacity to intervene, we expect 
the lira to correct itself further in such a scenario, in turn putting a lid 
on import growth, rather than the current account deficit continuing to expand 
unchecked. 
 
Positively, available data so far suggest that confidence in Turkey's 
externally leveraged banking sector endures, with households choosing to keep 
their savings in the banks rather than withdraw them. Additionally, Turkish 
banks managed to roll over their sizable foreign debt coming due during 
previous episodes of financial market stress. 
 
Nevertheless, financial stability risks are elevated, in our view. These 
could, in turn, present a contingent liability risk to the government if the 
government had to rescue a bank in a downside case, either because of a loss 
of confidence among domestic depositors, or if foreign creditors' appetite for 
rolling over Turkish banks' foreign debt were to reduce. The government has 
already contributed capital to public banks several times, with the latest 
capitalization worth 0.5% of GDP taking place in March 2022. We think that in 
a hypothetical scenario of a loss in banking sector confidence, the government 
may be called upon to contribute significantly higher amounts of equity and 
loans to the banks. 
 
Banks' asset quality could also face further pressure, since about 38% of 
loans were denominated in foreign currency as of December 2021, effectively 
making this debt more expensive to service as the lira depreciates. Risks to 
loan-book quality are particularly pertinent for public banks, in our view, 
since they have been heavily involved in episodes of rapid credit expansion at 
low rates in the past, raising questions about the borrowers' subsequent 
ability to repay these lines of credit. The other risk to Turkey's banks stems 
from rising global interest rates and a worsening of market conditions for the 
refinancing of external debt. We estimate the financial sector's short-term 
external debt by remaining maturity at about $83 billion or 12% of GDP as of 
end-January 2022. 
 
The rapid depreciation of the lira also contributes directly to a rise in net 
general government debt. At the moment, about 66% of government debt is 
denominated in foreign currency, a marked shift from under 40% before 2018. An 
additional source of vulnerability for the government's balance sheet stems 
from the FX-protected lira deposits under a scheme that the authorities 
introduced at the end of 2021 as a measure to stabilize the currency. Under 
this scheme, the government has committed to compensate deposit holders for 
the difference between the rate of exchange-rate depreciation and the interest 
earned on the Turkish lira deposits. Essentially, on top of its own FX risk 
stemming from the debt denominated in foreign currency, the government has now 
assumed contingent liability risks to compensate private-sector depositors. We 
expect the government to account for the compensation directly in the budget. 
The total amount of such deposits currently stands at about $38 billion (5.5% 
of GDP), with around half of that amount being sponsored by the Treasury (that 
is, the Treasury is liable for compensation payments on that half) and the 
rest by the central bank. 
 
That said, we consider that Turkey still has some fiscal headroom. At 34% of 
GDP, net general government debt looks favorable vis-a-vis some other emerging 
markets such as Brazil or South Africa. In our base case, we forecast that the 
general government deficit will widen to 4.2% of GDP in 2022 from an estimated 
3.1% in 2021, driven by additional expenditure to offset the impact of higher 
energy and food prices, as well as potential additional spending ahead of the 
elections in 2023. 
 
Positively, Turkey maintains a liquidity buffer that could help cover upcoming 
debt maturities. We estimate that liquidity buffer at about 6% of GDP at the 
end of 2021. The authorities also aim to reduce the foreign-currency portion 
of domestic borrowing, while the average maturity of new domestic borrowing 
has increased from 37 months in 2020 to 55 months in 2021. 
 
In our view, inflation will accelerate in the coming months, and we have 
revised our annual average inflation forecast for 2022 up to 55%. In monthly 
year-on-year terms, reported consumer price inflation could peak at over 60% 
in the coming months. Producer price inflation is even higher, reaching 105% 
year on year in February 2022.

title: As Oil Briefly Dips Below $100, Russia and Europe Play a Game of Chicken -- Barrons.com
text:
U.S. oil prices briefly dipped below $100 barrel Friday, as President Joe Biden's plan to release one million barrels a day of reserves began to have the desired effect.

But it's premature to start thinking it's the beginning of the end of higher prices, or even volatility.

Biden intervened where the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and Russia didn't, as the group of major oil producers stuck to its modest oil output increase for May on Thursday. If OPEC didn't help at $110 a barrel last month, it's safe to assume it isn't going to help at all.

The group said, perhaps significantly, that "current volatility is not caused by fundamentals, but by ongoing geopolitical developments."

That implies that the impact of Biden's massive release of oil reserves could be overshadowed in a heartbeat.

The warning signs are certainly there. Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday Russia will cut off gas supplies to "unfriendly" countries unless they start paying in rubles. That would spell trouble for Europe, as Russian natural gas accounted for close to 40% of the European Union's total gas consumption last year.

European natural-gas prices rose as a result, although gas still flowed into Europe early Friday, according to reports. It's a reminder of the delicate nature of energy markets and raises the prospect of Russia retaliating to sanctions.

While the U.S. isn't directly affected by Russia's threat, the nature of global commodities markets means one country's issue is everyone's issue. At a time of heightened inflation, the standoff is just one more worry.

-- Callum Keown

Biden Prods Oil Companies in Fight to Cut Fuel Prices

Biden criticized U.S. oil-and-gas companies for prioritizing shareholders over consumers, pointing to the industry's nearly $80 billion in profit last year. He announced a "use-it-or-lose-it" policy that will make oil producers pay for sitting on unused wells. 


   -- There are 9,000 approved-but-unused drilling permits on 12 million acres 
      of federal lands, though some oil companies have announced plans to raise 
      production. Charging for unused leases would increase costs on top of 
      inflation, said Tyler Glover, CEO of Texas Pacific Land Corp. 
 
   -- Biden confirmed he will release 180 million barrels of oil from the 
      Strategic Petroleum Reserve -- one million barrels a day for the next six 
      months, starting in May. The U.S. is waiting to see how much oil other 
      countries release. 
 
   -- The price of regular unleaded gasoline averages $4.22 a gallon. Biden 
      said prices could drop 10 cents to 35 cents a gallon in coming days. 
      Andrew Lipow, president of Houston consulting firm Lipow Oil Associates, 
      told MarketWatch the savings might be between 5 and 10 cents a gallon. 
 
   -- The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies 
      including Russia approved prior plans to increase oil output by 432,000 
      barrels a day in May. Biden has called on OPEC members to increase 
      production, while banning Russian oil imports. 

What's Next: RBC Capital Markets found fuel demand isn't waning, despite higher prices. California Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed $400 payments to all vehicle owners, regardless of income, for up to two cars, and Mayor Lori Lightfoot said Chicago will distribute $150 prepaid gas cards.

-- Janet H. Cho

***

What to Watch on Jobs Friday

Economists expect the U.S. economy to have added 477,500 jobs in March, as the labor market continued to tighten and employers competed for talent, bringing more workers in from the sidelines as the Covid-19 pandemic ebbs. 


   -- The unemployment rate is expected to fall to 3.7%, down from 3.8% in 
      February, and would leave the jobless rate only slightly above its 
      prepandemic low of 3.5%, where it stood in February 2020. 
 
   -- Hourly wages are expected to rise 0.4% in March from February, marking a 
      sizable increase from the sluggish 0.03% growth the month before. That 
      would put wage growth at a 5.5% annual pace, as employers hike pay to 
      lure in workers and more employees demand raises to keep up with rising 
      inflation. 
 
   -- The jobs report will be closely monitored by the Federal Reserve, which 
      is expected to boost interest rates many times in 2022 and 2023 to curb 
      the steep increase in consumer prices. 

What's Next: The central bank will be keeping a close eye on the strength of the labor market as it prepares this monetary policy shift. A strong jobs report could strengthen the case for higher interest rates.

-- Joe Woelfel and Megan Cassella

***

Metaverse Could Become a $13 Trillion Market by 2030

The metaverse economy, encompassing virtual worlds such as gaming and virtual reality as well as smart manufacturing, online events, and digital currency, could become an $8 trillion to $13 trillion total market by 2030, Citi said in a research report. That would make it 1% of the $128 trillion global economy. 


   -- Even though investments tied to the metaverse have been underperforming, 
      Citi said the metaverse could see five billion unique internet visitors 
      by the end of the decade, driving trillions of dollars in revenue. 
 
   -- Metaverse gaming companies include Fortnite maker Epic Games, Roblox, 
      Ubisoft Entertainment, and Microsoft, which owns Minecraft. 
 
   -- Citi is the latest banking giant to call the metaverse and web 3.0 a 
      multi-trillion-dollar opportunity. Goldman Sachs in December valued the 
      metaverse at $12.5 trillion, an outlook that assumes one-third of the 
      digital economy becomes virtual and then expands another 25%.

      applications and artificial-intelligence innovations, remains a key part 
      of analysts' optimism for its stock, which jumped 103% over the past 
      year. Shares of Roblox, a platform for building and experiencing virtual 
      worlds, have plummeted 31% over the past year.

title: Markets: Companies Put M&A on Hold Amid Russian War on Ukraine
text:
Futures and bond yields are up to start the second quarter, as investors await employment data to gauge the health of the labor market. I'm James Willhite, and here's what we're watching in Friday's trading.

Economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal estimate that employers added 490,000 jobs in March. That would mark 11 straight monthly gains above 400,000, the longest such stretch of growth in records dating back to 1939. Robust job growth is one of the factors pressuring the Federal Reserve to pick up the pace of interest-rate rises. Read our full market wrap here .

Meanwhile, our Kristin Broughton reports that the conflict in Ukraine is pushing some companies to abandon planned deals or take more time to analyze them.

Companies Put M&A on Hold Amid Russian War on Ukraine

By Kristin Broughton

Companies are scrapping planned mergers in Europe or taking more time to analyze potential deals as the Russian war on Ukraine puts a damper on what is otherwise expected to be a robust year for acquisitions.

A handful of European companies, including U.K.-based Spectris, a measurement-device company, and Gett, a corporate-transportation company, called off prospective deals following the Russian invasion in late February, citing market uncertainty.

The conflict also is affecting deals in earlier stages, prompting some acquirers to stay on the sidelines, at least temporarily, as they assess the impact of rising energy prices, or conduct additional fact-finding about a target's operations, mergers and acquisitions executives said.

Global deal making hit record levels in 2021 as companies took advantage of low interest rates and a surge in private-equity fundraising to expand their businesses through M&A. While the conflict in Ukraine hasn't affected global M&A on a large scale, it has prompted some acquirers, particularly those looking at targets in Europe, to conduct additional due diligence or question whether transactions are worth the legal or financial risk.

Companies through March 29 withdrew European M&A transactions worth $147.1 billion, or 31% more compared with the prior-year period, according to Dealogic, a financial data provider. The increase was driven by large withdrawals before the Russian invasion, including Unilever's decision in January not to raise its $68 billion offer for GlaxoSmithKline's consumer healthcare business, effectively walking away from the potential deal, as well as Nvidia and SoftBank's decision to terminate their planned $40 billion deal for the U.S. semiconductor company to acquire buy chip-design firm Arm.

title: *S&PGR Revises Outlook On Estonia To Stable; Ratings Affirmed
text:
31 Mar 2022 16:06 ET  Press Release: S&PGR Revises Outlook On Estonia To Stable; Ratings Affirmed


 
 
The following is a press release from S&P Global Ratings: 
 
OVERVIEW 
     -- Russia's military action against Ukraine will weigh on the Estonian 
economy. We estimate real GDP growth at 1.8% for 2022 versus 8.3% in 2021, and 
equivalent to average quarterly growth this year of negative 0.15%. 
     -- Although Estonia still has significant fiscal policy space, we believe 
the conflict will put upward pressure on refugee and defense spending, slowing 
the budgetary consolidation path. 
     -- The uncertainty regarding the conflict's duration means that the 
potential for an upgrade has decreased in the near term. 
     -- We revised our outlook to stable from positive and affirmed our 
'AA-/A-1+' long- and short-term sovereign credit ratings on Estonia. 
 
RATING ACTION 
On March 31, 2022, S&P Global Ratings revised its outlook on Estonia to stable 
from positive. At the same time, we affirmed our 'AA-/A-1+' long- and short 
term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings on Estonia. 
 
As a "sovereign rating" (as defined in EU CRA Regulation 1060/2009 "EU CRA 
Regulation"), the ratings on Estonia are subject to certain publication 
restrictions set out in Art 8a of the EU CRA Regulation, including publication 
in accordance with a pre-established calendar (see "Calendar Of 2022 EMEA 
Sovereign, Regional, And Local Government Rating Publication Dates," published 
Dec. 16, 2021, on RatingsDirect). Under the EU CRA Regulation, deviations from 
the announced calendar are allowed only in limited circumstances and must be 
accompanied by a detailed explanation of the reasons for the deviation. In 
this case, the reason for the deviation is the risk of macroeconomic fallout 
due to Russia's military intervention against Ukraine. The next scheduled 
publication on the sovereign ratings on Estonia will be on Aug. 19, 2022. 
 
OUTLOOK 
The stable outlook reflects our expectations that the Estonian economy can 
weather temporarily reduced growth and higher spending pressures without any 
significant deterioration of its credit metrics over the next two years. The 
conflict in Ukraine will lead to a recession and potentially higher inflation 
for the Estonian economy, in our view. However, the fallout on public finances 
should prove manageable; we project that gross government debt should remain 
below 18% of GDP over the next three years. Beyond then, EU  transfers and 
Estonia's strong macroeconomic fundamentals will support a return to solid 
growth. 
 
Downside scenario 
We could lower the ratings if the impact on Estonia from the conflict were 
more significant than we expect, or if the conflict escalated beyond Russia 
and Ukraine. This would imply economic growth and external accounts falling 
significantly short of our projections, and potentially leading to protracted 
fiscal support measures that weaken public finances much more than we 
anticipate. 
 
Upside scenario 
We could raise the ratings if Estonia's economy returns to its pre-conflict 
path. Under this scenario, Estonia's high-value-added services sector would 
post renewed productivity gains over the next few years, boosting incomes, and 
leading to an improved economic assessment. We could also raise the ratings if 
external position metrics exceeded our expectations; for example, if there 
were persistently high current account surpluses leading to a net external 
asset position for Estonia (excluding foreign direct investment [FDI] 
liabilities). 
 
RATIONALE 
We expect that the indirect effects of Russia's military intervention against 
Ukraine will push Estonia's small open economy into recession, while 
redoubling inflationary pressure, already notable throughout second-half 2021. 
As a result, we have revised down our real GDP growth rate projections for 
Estonia to 1.8% in 2022 from an estimate of 3.5% before the conflict (and 
versus GDP growth of 8.3% in 2021). This projection is equivalent to an 
average decline of negative 0.15% quarter over quarter for 2022. At the same 
time, the conflict is driving up hydrocarbon and other commodity prices, with 
evidence of a renewed broadening of inflationary pressure. Inflation touched 
11.6% year over year in February 2022 (with wage increases averaging just 
under 7%), and is likely to remain elevated throughout 2022, weighing on 
households' disposable incomes and business confidence in what continues to be 
a very tight labor market. 
 
Given the significant uncertainty and risk that the conflict entails, we 
believe upside potential on the rating has decreased in the near term, leading 
us to revise our outlook to stable from positive. 
 
In our view, the conflict's effects on Estonia's economy will stem from 
worsening supply chain bottlenecks, leading to trade disruptions; rising 
commodity and energy prices pushing up inflation and eroding household and 
business spending capacity; and weakening external demand. At the same time, 
although Estonia's direct exposure to Russia has decreased significantly over 
the past decade, it remains relatively sizable. Exports to Russia, Ukraine, 
and Belarus combined represent about 5% (about half of national origin) of 
total exports, while imports represent close to 15%. More than half of imports 
of petroleum-related products come from Russia, making some sectors--for 
example, transportation--particularly vulnerable to trade disruptions. 
 
Estonia is one of the few producers globally of oil shale, which covers 70% of 
domestic energy requirements. This enables Estonia to be largely 
self-sufficient in energy, albeit at the cost of rising carbon dioxide 
emissions and significant levels of hazardous waste connected to oil shale 
combustion and refining. Close to one-tenth of the EUR969 million in Next 
Generation EU grants for Estonia are targeted at reducing the economy's 
reliance on oil shale in electricity generation. Investments in green 
transition, digitalization, and real estate will support growth in 2022-2025, 
largely funded by inflows of EU funds. The slowdown in global demand and 
economic activity among Estonia's key trading will hurt the country's small 
and open economy and reduce exports. However, we consider overall risks to 
Estonia's external position low. The country has a solid external position, 
thanks to small surpluses, which have aided consecutive net external 
deleveraging over the past few years. 
 
We believe spending pressure will rise as a consequence of the Russia-Ukraine 
conflict via, for example, already announced defense spending of EUR600 
million until 2025; compensation to households for rising energy bills; and 
costs to cater for the large inflow of refugees. This could delay Estonia's 
consolidation efforts post pandemic, in our view. Nevertheless, Estonia's 
public finances remain robust, despite the temporary increase in spending 
induced by the COVID-19 pandemic and the ongoing conflict. We predict that net 
debt will rise slowly over the next few years, but stay below 10% of GDP, 
which is exceptionally low by global standards. 
 
In our view, external security risks for Estonia, which borders Russia, have 
risen since the conflict's outbreak. However, Estonia has been a member of 
NATO  since 2004 and we believe this reduces the risk of the conflict 
escalating beyond Ukraine's borders. NATO  has repeatedly confirmed its 
commitment to Article 5, stating that if one member was subject to an armed 
attack, the other members would provide support. Since the start of the 
military conflict, NATO  troops in Estonia have doubled. That said, other 
security risks, including to cyber security, are on the rise. 
 
The ratings remain supported by the established institutional set-up and a 
track record of strong fiscal and economic policies. Further strengths are 
Estonia's history of modest fiscal deficits and low public debt. As a eurozone 
member, Estonia benefits from access to the monetary union's deep capital 
markets and monetary policy support from the European Central Bank . The 
ratings are constrained by Estonia's moderate income levels compared with 
those of similarly rated peers.

title: Top News Today: Stocks Move Lower; Biden to Tap Oil Reserves in Bid to Tame High Fuel Prices
text:
MARKET WRAPS

STOCKS: U.S. stocks fell to cap a quarter in which Federal Reserve monetary tightening and the Russian invasion of Ukraine have weighed on sentiment. The S&P 500 posted its first quarterly loss in two years.

TREASURYS: Treasury prices rose, pulling down yields, even after data showed the Fed's preferred inflation gauge jumping again.

FOREX: The dollar strengthened against the euro but weakened against the yen.

COMMODITIES: Oil prices settled sharply lower with the U.S. announcing its largest-ever release from the nation's crude reserves and the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies sticking to a previously agreed plan to raise output in May.

HEADLINES

U.S. Inflation Rises to 40-Year Peak in February by Fed's Preferred Measure

Inflation reached a new 40-year peak in February, according to the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge, buoyed by supply problems and strong U.S. consumer demand.

The Commerce Department said Thursday that its personal-consumption-expenditures price index climbed 6.4% in February from a year ago, faster than the 6% increase for the year that ended in January. The February rise was the fastest since 1982.

Biden to Draw Down Oil Reserves in Bid to Ease Gas Prices

WASHINGTON-President Biden will tap up to 180 million barrels of government oil reserves to help tamp down near-record high fuel prices, an unprecedented government intervention into oil markets following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

In remarks from the White House Thursday, Mr. Biden framed high energy prices as a wartime issue that requires a robust and wide-ranging response. The oil release-about 1 million barrels a day for six months, starting in May-would be the biggest-ever drawdown from the country's emergency stockpile of roughly 568 million barrels.

Mr. Biden said he would also invoke the Defense Production Act, a Korean War-era national security mobilization law, to boost domestic output of minerals used in batteries for electric vehicles and other clean-energy technology.

U.S. Probes Meeting Between Activision CEO and Option Buyer

Authorities investigating timely trading in Activision Blizzard Inc. securities are looking at at least one meeting between the videogame firm's chief executive and one of three traders days before they placed a large bet on Activision shares, according to people familiar with the matter.

Activision CEO Bobby Kotick met with Alexander von Furstenberg in the week before Mr. von Furstenberg and media moguls Barry Diller and David Geffen bought options to purchase Activision shares at $40 each on Jan. 14. The options trade, which has generated an unrealized profit of about $59 million, was arranged days before Activision agreed to be acquired for $95 a share by Microsoft Corp., The Wall Street Journal has reported.

The Justice Department is investigating whether the options trade violated insider-trading laws, the people familiar with the matter said. The Securities and Exchange Commission is separately conducting a civil insider-trading investigation, the people said.

Following Fed's Lead, Banks Shift Forecasts to Big Rate Increases

After key Federal Reserve officials opened the door to raising interest rates by more than the customary quarter-percentage point, several of Wall Street's biggest banks now believe the increases will come in jumbo increments.

Major banks in recent days have predicted some combination of half-percentage point rate rises by the Fed throughout the year. The Fed usually moves its federal-funds rate target by quarter-percentage point increments, but faced with surging inflation bringing the worst price pressures in 40 years, economists believe aggressive action by the central bank is now likely.

The Fed lifted the federal-funds rate earlier this month for the first time since 2018, to a range of between 0.25% and 0.50%. The Fed's next meeting is scheduled for May 3-4, and it is likely to result in a half-percentage point increase, with more such increases later in the year, in the view of many large banks.

Walgreens Posts Higher Sales, Powered by Covid-19 Vaccine, Testing Demand

Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc. posted higher sales for the most recent quarter as demand for Covid-19 tests and vaccines continued to drive growth.

Executives said Thursday they are strategizing how the company's drugstores can continue playing a key role in providing diagnostic and other health services beyond the current pandemic.

"Our pharmacists and our technicians are more than capable, as we've shown during the pandemic, of delivering these kinds of services," said Walgreens President John Standley. "That's a pretty big game changer if we can gain access to that market and in terms of how we grow our business and in terms of the value we can provide in the communities we serve."

Bain Capital Looks at Possible Takeover Bid for Toshiba

TOKYO-Bain Capital said it was examining a possible bid for Toshiba Corp., and Toshiba's top shareholder pledged its support to Bain, making initial steps toward fulfilling foreign shareholders' desire to take the Japanese conglomerate private.

Bain, a U.S.-based private-equity firm, said it wanted to hold "careful and sincere" discussions with Toshiba's management, the Japanese government and banks over the possible deal. It cautioned that no decisions have been made.

"There are many issues that need to be addressed before delisting Toshiba," Bain said in a statement.

Mortgage Rates Surge to Highest Since 2018

The average rate for a 30-year fixed-rate home loan jumped to 4.67%, mortgage-finance giant Freddie Mac said Thursday, marking the weekly figure's highest reading since December 2018.

The 30-year fixed rate rose from 4.42% a week ago, continuing a steady rise that has pushed home-loan rates within sight of 5% for the first time in four years. This year's surge in mortgage rates was hardly unforeseen, given the record lows reached in the pandemic period and concerns about high U.S. inflation readings, but it has unfolded faster than expected. At the beginning of the year, the average rate on America's most popular home loan was 3.22%.

Inflation Weighed on Consumer Spending Growth in February

Consumer spending growth, a key engine of the economy, slowed sharply in February, as the Omicron surge of Covid-19 eased and inflation accelerated amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

U.S. households boosted their sending at a seasonally adjusted 0.2% pace in February from the month before, down from a revised 2.7% rate in January, when spending rebounded from an Omicron-related dip in December, the Commerce Department said Thursday.

SEC Tells Exchanges to Treat Customer Crypto Holdings as Liabilities

WASHINGTON-Publicly traded cryptocurrency exchanges would have to report their customers' digital tokens as liabilities on their balance sheets under guidance released Thursday by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The guidelines are designed to introduce consistency to the way crypto-trading platforms account for their holdings of assets like bitcoin on behalf of customers, SEC officials said.

WWE Expands Reach to Traditional TV Shows-and Yes, They're About Wrestling

World Wrestling Entertainment Inc. is starting to produce fictionalized TV shows, part of an effort to generate more revenue outside of the wrestling ring and capitalize on streaming services' growing hunger for fresh content.

The company, which runs the world's most famous wrestling league, said it has two scripted TV series in the works: a Spanish-language comedy about an aspiring female wrestler in Mexico and a drama about a fictional family that runs a wrestling company.

Colin Campbell, WWE's vice president of development, said the company expects the shows to help it reach new audiences and expand its relationships with media companies. 



TALKING POINTS CFOs Find It Harder to Land Board Seats as Companies Seek Change By Nina Trentmann

As company boards start to put the chaos of Covid-19 behind them, directors are focusing on new sets of issues, such as those related to environmental, social and governance matters or cybersecurity.

That is spurring companies to fill their boardrooms with a wider range of experiences and skills, making it difficult for some CFOs to find a seat at the table with financial expertise alone. Slightly less than a quarter of chief financial officers-23%-at companies in the Fortune 500 hold board positions, down from a high of 32% in 2009, according to recruitment firm Spencer Stuart. This includes CFOs who sit on their companies' own boards.

"Financial experts increasingly are competing with other skill sets like technology or human-capital expertise," said Joel von Ranson, who leads Spencer Stuart's global functional practices, adding that finance chiefs remain sought after to chair audit, compensation or governance committees.

With many boards undergoing a refreshment cycle, their size is growing, resulting in boards at S&P 500 companies having an average of 11.2 board members now, up from 11.1 in 2021 and 11.0 in 2020, according to ISS Corporate Solutions, a data and analytics provider. Meanwhile, the average tenure on a board has fallen to 7.7 years in 2021 from 8.7 years in 2011, Spencer Stuart said.

"We are seeing a rise in demand for people with different backgrounds: racially diverse directors, people with cybersecurity experience, experience in how to deal with climate change, or in human-capital management," said Brianna Castro, a senior director of governance research at proxy advisory services company Glass, Lewis & Co. A recent SEC proposal on new cyber disclosure could boost the demand for such experts further, Ms. Castro said.

Marija Kramer, head of ISS Corporate Solutions, said that given the increase in sustainable investing and the rise of ESG corporate ratings, "it's no surprise we're seeing demand for prospective corporate directors with ESG credentials."

These shifts mean CFOs have to communicate clearly to boards about what they can bring to the table. "It's about positioning yourself as a two-for: You bring the financial expertise, and you bring something else, " said Spencer Stuart's Mr. von Ranson.

Amy Butte, a former CFO of the New York Stock Exchange, said she is positioning herself as an audit chair for boards and an expert for initial public offerings. "This has helped with differentiating from others," she said, adding that "if you are a generalist, it is hard" to do that.

Ms. Butte sits on several boards, including those of DigitalOcean Inc., a cloud infrastructure company; Bain Capital Specialty Finance, a business development firm; and BNP Paribas USA, the U.S. arm of the French bank. "It is really about the experience" that one brings to the company, Ms. Butte said.

Ukrainians Who Sheltered in the Mariupol Theater Made It a Thriving Village By Brett Forrest in Odessa, Ukraine and Isabel Coles in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine

As Russia laid siege to the Ukrainian port city of Mariupol, battering apartment blocks and killing civilians, more than 1,000 people took shelter inside the local performing-arts theater.

Evgeniya, a theater lighting technician, and her husband, Sergey, arrived on Feb. 25 and welcomed the first few dozen people. "Someone had to go and help," she said.

A barrage from air, land and sea terrorized Mariupol's 450,000 residents, destroying most of the city's habitable buildings. The theater became a last-chance refuge, including for many who had once gone to see plays there and those left homeless. By then, the theater had no electricity, no food, no running water and just six bathrooms.

Evgeniya and her husband, an actor, had worked at the theater for two decades and knew its offices and passageways, its strong walls and false ones. For nearly three weeks, their knowledge and gut instincts directed the daily lives of those crowding in the building.

"We clutched at our heads," Evgeniya said. "This is madness. I panicked because I didn't know how to organize all these people."

The chaos would transform into a mini-society created from scratch, according to interviews with more than a dozen people who stayed at or visited the Mariupol theater after the Russian invasion.

At first, Evgeniya and Sergey admitted only women and children. The couple had brought their own kids thinking they might be there for some time. They soon opened the doors to everyone.

Severed Internet services plunged Mariupol into an information blackout. People who emerged from the darkness of basements in the daylight hours, when the Russian shelling subsided, followed others to the theater, hoping for news about an organized exit from the city.

Nadya Navka lived on the left bank of the Kalmius River, on the other side of town. She caught a ride to the city center with her husband and mother after shelling shattered the windows and doors of their home. She saw people streaming toward the theater and joined them. "If people gather there," she said, "then if there is any evacuation, it's going to be from there."

WEALTH MANAGEMENT How Much More Will You Spend in Retirement Than Expected? My Rule: $400 a Month

You should tell readers about your "$400 rule." Maybe they have some rules of their own.

That's my brother Stephen speaking. Yes, I have a "rule" about retirement and nest eggs. I don't pretend that it's anything as consequential as, say, the "4% rule." (That's the one tied to annual withdrawals from savings.) And my research, admittedly, involves a small sample. (Just me.)

Still, I think it's interesting how this "guideline" (a better word) has worked in my retirement. What follows, then, is a brief explanation-and a request.

Actually, my guideline is borrowed. Several years ago, as I was approaching retirement from full-time work, a person-and I'm afraid I can't recall who it was, but I'm happy to give credit if you're reading this-told me: "You will spend about $400 each month in retirement above and beyond what you think you'll spend."

I remember thinking: This sounds silly. Surely, I can craft an annual budget for retirement that doesn't miss the mark by almost $5,000.

And yet...more months than not, my wife and I find ourselves with a bill, or combination of bills, that total about $400.

--Glenn Ruffenach
