title: European Morning Briefing: Markets on Pause Before Fed's Verdict
text:
SNAPSHOT:

========

European bourses, bunds and gilts seen mixed; euro, oil lower, spot gold higher

-Japan's Trade Gap Narrows

-Speedy Traders Face U.S. Scrutiny

-BOE's Carney: Welcome Move By China to Widen Yuan Trading Band

-BOE's Carney: U.K. Economy to be Buffeted by Global Forces

-White House Spokesman's Advice: Don't Invest in Russian Stocks

-MPS Foundation Launches Sale of Monte dei Paschi Stake

-Insurer Allianz Pays Compensation to Malaysia Airlines

-Oracle Profit Rises, but Disappoints Wall Street

WATCH FOR: U.K. unemployment data, Bank of England meeting minutes, Chancellor Osborne's budget statement; U.S. oil data, Federal Reserve decisions

EUROPEAN OUTLOOK & U.S./ASIAN SUMMARIES:

========

European stock markets, along with bunds and gilts, may start mixed as attention shifts to the U.S. Federal Reserve's meeting announcements, followed by a press conference by Fed Chairwoman Janet Yellen.

The Fed is expected to announce a further cut of 10 billion dollars per month in its bond-buying program. But despite jitters in stock markets last week and some weather-affected economic data, investors doubt the Fed will shift from that path.

Investors will also continue to keep an eye on Ukraine and on Russia's reactions to sanctions imposed by the U.S. and the EU. Although investors were relieved after President Vladimir Putin addressed the Russian parliament Tuesday and indicated he had no further designs on Ukraine territories, any signs that tensions are escalating will put a damper on risk appetite.

Chinese stocks moved lower, as property developers continued to weigh on the market, while the rest of Asia was softer ahead of the conclusion of Federal Reserve's policy meeting.

Wall Street futures were lower, with Treasurys nudging higher, as the euro and oil trader slightly lower, and spot gold higher.

STOCKS:

======

Investors will see a mixed European opening with the focus on the Federal Reserve after Russian President Vladimir Putin turned down the volume a bit.

Ahead of the opening, IG has called the FTSE down 5 at 6600, the DAX flat at 9242, and the CAC off 8 at 4305.

"Putin's speech didn't indicate he is looking for an escalation of the crisis. All the focus was on Crimea rather than any further areas of Ukraine," said Guillaume Tresca, emerging-market strategist at Crédit Agricole.

With Mr. Putin largely steering clear of inflammatory rhetoric in response to the sanctions, markets are likely to turn their immediate focus to other issues, including the U.S. Federal Reserve meeting, Mr. Tresca said.

Even so, investors remain nervous.

"I don't really see this as a de-escalation. The situation is still a very tense one," said François Savary, who helps oversee roughly $10 billion of assets as chief investment officer at Swiss bank Reyl.

Mr. Savary thinks European stocks have the potential to rise further as the economy improves, but avoids buying while the Ukraine situation remains so uncertain. Reyl reduced its exposure to stocks last week, he said.

U.S. stock futures were lower Wednesday after markets rallied for a second straight session Tuesday, bringing the S&P 500 within a fraction of another record.

Traders said concerns over Russia's intervention in Ukraine remain in the background.

Jim Russell, senior equity strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management, which oversees about $115 billion, said he has seem some flows into domestic equity mutual funds. Those flows may not be heavy, but given the light volumes and a lack of selling, it may be having an "outsize impact on the market," Mr. Russell said.

FOREX:

======

The euro was lower in Asia as traders wait to compare the Federal Reserve's stance against that of the European Central Bank.

The resilience of the euro is impressive, noted Brian Martin, senior European strategist at ANZ. The ability to engineer a "permanent" depreciation in the euro is difficult at present, Martin said. "We feel that current statements on the exchange rate are aimed more at trying to slow the euro's rise rather than reverse it," Martin said.

The dollar fell against the yen amid soft sentiment toward the U.S. currency.

"In general, markets are content to wait for the FOMC before making a move," said Brad Bechtel, managing director at Faros Trading.

The Federal Open Market Committee is expected to keep interest rates unchanged and to announce an additional $10 billion monthly reduction to its bond purchases. Investors also expect confirmation that the recent soft patch in the U.S. economy has been a temporary setback caused by extreme winter weather.

"All of that would be positive for the dollar," said Omer Esiner, chief market analyst at Commonwealth Foreign Exchange Inc.

BONDS:

=====

Bunds may start mixed with a lack of focal points in the euro zone, leaving investors to spotlight the Federal Reserve's meeting in the presumed absence of a flare-up in the Ukraine situation.

In the U.K., gilts may also start mixed with unemployment data on tap. The unemployment rate is expected to remain steady at 7.2% while another sharp fall in monthly jobless claims is expected of 25,000, noted Michael Hewson, chief market analyst at CMC Markets UK.

The U.K. will also issue its budget statement. Chancellor George Osborne has said it will keep a strong focus on austerity but will also include measures to support business investment and exports, long-term soft-spots in the economy.

Treasury prices were slightly higher Wednesday, after markets traded slightly higher as investors awaited the Fed's monetary-policy decision.

Prices eased from prior highs after Mr. Putin said Moscow has no intentions to partition Ukraine.

On Wednesday, the Fed will announce its policy decision and Ms. Yellen will hold a news conference.

"The market is put in a range now as they are waiting for the decision Yellen will make at the FOMC," said Millan L. Mulraine, deputy head of U.S. research and strategy at TD Securities. "This is a new Fed with a new slate of players. As an investor, you wouldn't want necessarily to prejudge that until you have more clarity on where Yellen wants to take the Fed."

The Fed's decision could add pressure on short-term yields by pushing the market's expectation for the firs rate increase further out. Therefore, the Treasury yield curve will steepen.

Some investors said there is a possibility that Ms. Yellen takes a more pro-growth approach at the meeting, for example, by reducing the pace of tapering.

"Just looking from the domestic perspective, I wouldn't rule that out," said Robert Tipp, chief investment strategist at Prudential Fixed Income, referring to the recent softness in economic data.

In Japan Wednesday, government bonds edged higher ahead of the Fed.

ENERGY:

=======

Crude-oil futures drifted lower in Asia after settling higher Tuesday on reports of the Seaway pipeline expanding capacity by May-June. "U.S. inflation figures, which were broadly in line with expectations and positive housing data, helped WTI close the Brent discount to $7/bbl," ANZ said. "Putin's signing of a treaty to annex Crimea also supported oil markets a little. However, the general consensus is that neither Russia nor Europe can afford to cut energy ties," the bank noted. The closely watched survey from the U.S. EIA is due later Wednesday. U.S. oil inventories are projected to have increased by 2.3 million barrels, on average, in the week ended March 14, according to a Wall Street Journal survey. The API said late Tuesday that its own data for last week showed crude stocks rose by 5.9 million barrels.

Nymex crude was down 28 cents at $99.42/bbl, and Brent crude was down 19 cents at $106.60/bbl.

METALS:

======

Gold edged higher in Asia with attention remaining fixed on the outcome of the Fed's meeting. With the geopolitical issue in Ukraine returning to a "high simmer from last Friday's boil" the temperature has lowered enough to take the edge off the fear, Peter Hug, global trading director at Kitco Metals, said in a report. "Metals tend to be an advance trigger trade against upcoming events, but many times after the perception becomes reality, the hedge wanes because the event can be quantified," he said.

Spot gold was at $1,357.90/oz, up $2.40.

Copper looks set to remain rangebound as traders reassess risks in China after news Chinese property developer Zhejiang Xingrun was unable to repay almost $600 million in loans. "The knock-on impact stemming from China, allowing various small privately held companies to default, is hard to gauge, but will likely see a re-appraisal of risk by Chinese investors and banks," Leon Westgate, an analyst with Standard Bank, said in a report.

LME 3-month copper was little changed at $6,483/ton.

U.S. STOCKS 

U.S. stocks rallied for a second straight session, bringing the S&P 500 within a fraction of another record high.

Traders say there was no single piece of news driving the market higher. They say concerns over Russia's intervention in Ukraine remain in the background, but investors believe over the long term, it will end up as a nonevent for the market. If recent upbeat economic data were providing the boost, investors would expect a rise in bond yields, but yields fell on Tuesday.

And with volumes light, they aren't seeing a big increase in buying.

Clark Yingst, chief market analyst at New York brokerage firm Joseph Gunnar, said he couldn't find a fundamental reason for the magnitude of this week's gains. "It just looks like it is another quiet day," Mr. Yingst said.

In corporate news, Hertz Global Holdings slipped as the company's plan to spin off its equipment-rental business was offset by fourth-quarter earnings and revenue that missed expectations. 


 
 
ASIAN STOCKS 

Chinese stocks moved lower, as property developers continued to weigh on the market, while the rest of Asia was softer ahead of the conclusion of Federal Reserve's policy meeting.

The largest movements were in China, where the Shanghai Composite lost 0.7% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 0.1%. Local sentiment continued to be weighed by concerns over the property sector--a key driver of the Chinese economy that accounts for 16% of gross domestic product. So far this week, data showed that growth continued to moderate in property developers, while a real-estate firm in eastern China was unable to pay almost $600 million in debt.

"There is too much negative news in the property industry," said Amy Lin, an analyst at Capital Securities. "Reports that housing prices are diving in major cities are spreading through the Internet, which has severely weighed down sentiment."

Shares in developers fell for a second day, with China Vanke Co. down 3.8% in Shenzhen and China Resources Land 2.3% lower in Hong Kong.

More broadly, the region was cautious ahead of the conclusion of the Federal Reserve's policy meeting later Wednesday. The central bank is expected to reduce its bond-buying program by another $10 billion and change its 6.5% unemployment threshold to keep its fund rate near zero into 2015.

Japan's Nikkei fell 0.3%, giving up its earlier gains as the yen strengthened against the dollar.

Elsewhere, Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was flat and South Korea's Kospi was up less than 0.1%.

The region failed to take a positive lead from the U.S., where the S&P 500 ended the day close to a record as fears of escalating tensions over Crimea abated. Russian President Vladimir Putin Tuesday signed a treaty to formally annex Ukraine's Crimea region and said that while Crimea must be under Russian sovereignty, "we don't want a partition of Ukraine." Over the weekend, Crimeans taking part in a referendum voted overwhelmingly in favor of joining Russia.

In corporate news, shares in Japan Display Inc. slumped 15% on debut trading in Tokyo. The world's largest manufacturer of screen for smartphones and tablets raised as much as $3.2 billion earlier this month in a deal that was priced at the bottom of the proposed range.

Japan Display's poor start came just one day after shares in Hitachi Maxell Ltd. sank 5% below its IPO price on its debut trading Tuesday. The performance for these companies suggests that demand for new listings in Japan might not be strong, and that could bode badly for railway and hotel operator Seibu Holdings Inc., which has a listing next month that could raise as much as $4.9 billion. 

FOREX

The yen strengthened against the dollar. The dollar was last at Y101.32 compared with Y101.43 late Tuesday in New York. 


METALS 

Nickel closed at is highest price in almost a year on the London Metal Exchange Tuesday, after moving into a bull market amid persistent concerns over supply of the metal to the market. 


OIL SUMMARY 

Oil futures strengthened Tuesday after a pipeline company said it would double the capacity of a pipeline connecting Oklahoma storage with Gulf Coast refineries sooner than previously expected.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian stocks, rouble rise after Putin says no need for further Ukraine split
text:
* Russian stock index up 1.5-2 pct, react positively to Putin speech

* Putin says Crimea to unite with Russia, but no need for further division of Ukraine

* Rouble reverses earlier losses after Putin speech (Adds reaction to Putin speech, comments)

By Jason Bush

MOSCOW, March 18 (Reuters) - Russian shares extended gains on Tuesday and the rouble rallied after President Vladimir Putin said Russia had no need for any further division of Ukraine and investors doubted the likelihood of tough western sanctions.

At 1315 GMT, the rouble-denominated MICEX index was up 1.9 percent to 1,308 points. The dollar-denominated RTS had risen 1.6 percent to 1,133 points.

In a pugnacious address to the Russian parliament, Putin lashed out at the West for its policies in Ukraine and other countries, and defended Russia's plan to absorb Crimea.

But investors appeared most interested in signals about Russia's intentions towards the rest of Ukraine. Stock indexes gained 0.5-1 percent after Putin said Russia had no need for further division in Ukraine.

Unrest in eastern cities has heightened fears that Russia could intervene further, which would in turn provoke tougher western sanctions.

Vladimir Osakovskiy, chief Russia economist at Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch, said most investors did not believe that the annexation of Crimea was enough to provoke tough western sanctions that would damage the Russian economy.

"Some people are actually starting to position for a fading of political risks," he said.

"The whole issue boils down to what kind of sanctions we are going to face. Given that the general perception is that the sanctions will be rather limited, why worry?"

However, some are concerned that Russia's annexation of Crimea, in defiance of western warnings, could be enough to provoke much more serious sanctions that would harm Russian companies and the economy.

"The market has got all bulled up on the back of Putin's speech which in effect gives the green light for the Russian annexation of Crimea," said Standard Bank strategist Tim Ash in an emailed comment.

"I am still minded to think that this crisis is far from over yet, and that the U.S., if not the Europeans, will respond more effectively over the next few days/weeks with additional measures which might grate with the Russian administration and markets."

Oleg Dushin, chief analyst at Zerich Capital, said the rise in Russian stocks may also reflect patriotic sentiment among Russian investors fired up by Putin's speech.

"In general I think the market was positive about Putin's speech - it wasn't just the declaration that we don't intend to further divide Ukraine," he said.

"The market is celebrating the victory in the post-Soviet space: Russia can defend its interests."

"We of course are seeing some sales, but I still don't see any mass demand," said Alexander Zalko, head of institutional sales at Finam. "You have the impression that the most interesting is still ahead."

ROUBLE RALLY

The rouble also rallied after Putin's comments, reversing sizeable falls earlier in the day.

At 1315 GMT it was up 0.1 percent to 36.30 against the dollar and 0.1 percent to 50.47 against the rouble. It was up 0.1 percent to 42.76 against a dollar-euro basket.

The central bank announced that on March 14 it had spent $4.4 billion in forex market interventions, an indication of the heavy selling pressure on the rouble. It has spent $22.1 billion to defend the rouble since the beginning of March.

Russian oil company Rosneft denied a report in the newspaper Kommersant that the company was planning to raise $66 billion in rouble bonds to refinance its foreign debts, in response to threats of western sanctions.

"The publication is using unverified information and treats non-existent decisions as fact," Rosneft said.

Refinancing of foreign debts by Russian companies through rouble bond issues would further depress the rouble and domestic bond prices. Analysts were doubtful that such plans could be implemented quickly.

"I'm not sure all those plans would be realised - they would be subject to market conditions - so I would refrain from drawing any implications for the FX market for now," said Maxim Korovin, forex analyst at VTB Capital.

title: EXCLUSIVE- Central bank  says Russia will not impose capital controls
text:
* Central bank says policies provide financial stability

* Finance ministry would oppose capital controls

* Capital fight expected at $50-$70 billion in first quarter

By Oksana Kobzeva and Lidia Kelly

MOSCOW, March 18 (Reuters) - Russia will not impose capital controls, the central bank said on Tuesday, easing concerns that restrictions could be introduced to stem capital flight that has accelerated since the Ukrainian region of Crimea was seized by Russian forces.

President Vladimir Putin's assertions of Russia's rights to intervene in Ukraine and make Crimea part of Russia are expected to cause net capital outflows in the first quarter to $50-$70 billion, compared with $63 billion in the whole of last year.

Limiting money flows, once considered a damaging constraint on open markets, has been more accepted in the aftermath of the 2008-2009 financial crisis as a tool sometimes needed to manage financial stability.

But the Russian central bank said its current monetary policy is strong enough to provide financial stability and the issue of capital controls is not on the table.

"The Bank of Russia is not considering at this time the possibility of introducing measures that would restrict the movement of the capital," the bank told Reuters in an emailed statement.

"Actions taken by the Bank of Russia in the framework of exchange rate policy help contain excessive exchange rate fluctuations, and as such prevent the emergence of risks to financial stability."

The central bank, which has been gradually allowing the rouble to float more freely, had to halt the process earlier this month and start defending the currency, which has lost more than a tenth of its value this year.

Introducing restrictions on money flows would reduce Russians' demand for foreign currency, but it would also raise borrowing costs for the state and corporations alike.

The finance ministry has spent the past few years building up the country's debt by successfully raising billions in foreign borrowing. This year's plans envisage another $7 billion worth of Eurobonds.

"If such an idea (capital controls) were to be discussed, the finance ministry would be against it," Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Moiseev, responsible for financial markets, told Reuters on Tuesday.

POLITICAL DECISION

The Russian rouble has been weakening since the start of the year, along with the Turkish lira and other emerging market currencies. But Russia's declaration in early March of its right to intervene in Ukraine has accelerated the rouble's fall, costing the central bank more than $20 billion in interventions to defend it.

"When any central bank intervenes heavily in the forex market, selling its reserves, one wonders how long it is going to continue its policy. One of the alternatives to not spending reserves is capital controls," said Alexander Morozov, chief Russia economist at HSBC in Moscow.

Russia's gold and foreign currency reserves, the world's fifth-largest, stand at $494 billion, giving the central bank some room to manoeuvre.

But Morozov, who also said there is no need for now for any capital restrictions, reckons there is also a political reason behind the stance of monetary officials.

Russia introduced capital account liberalisation only in 2006, spending years to repair the damage caused by the financial chaos after the fall of the Soviet Union in the 1990s.

"It was done to make the Russian economy open as an OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) economy and it's still one of the more paramount political objectives of the Russian political leadership," Morozov said.

"Any stepping back would be like an admission of failure, so it's a political issue."

MONETARY POLICY

Morozov and other economists in Russia also believe that there is no economic reason to introduce capital controls.

In the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis, the central bank went through $200 billion of its reserves, but without having to introduce capital controls.

On March 3, after Russia's parliament backed possible military action in Ukraine, the central bank was forced abruptly to raise its key lending rate by 150 basis points to stem capital flight. It also said it would make daily decisions on regulating the rouble's exchange rate, increasing its scope to make forex market interventions.

The central bank believes these moves are sufficient for now.

The policy, based on "an assessment of the current situation on the currency market, allows (the bank) to respond quickly to sudden changes in the situation," the bank said in its statement.

Analysts say that central bank will keep employing more conventional monetary policy for the time being.

"Unless capital outflows stabilise, further rate hikes are possible," said Neil Shearing, chief emerging market economist at Capital Economics in London. (Additional reporting by Darya Korsunskaya; Writing by Lidia Kelly; Editing by Jason Bush and Giles Elgood)

US STOCKS: 

U.S. stocks rallied for a second-straight session Tuesday, bringing the S&P 500 within a fraction of another record high.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 102 points, or 0.6%, to 16349. Microsoft and Pfizer paced gains in 26 of the Dow's 30 components.

The S&P 500 index advanced 13 points, or 0.7%, to 1872 and the Nasdaq Composite Index gained 50 points, or 1.2%, to 4330.

The technology, health care and energy sectors led the advance.

The S&P 500 has gained 1.7% in two sessions, and is just 0.3% away from its March 7 record closing high of 1878.04, which was the sixth record close of the year. Meanwhile, the Dow has gained 283 points, or 1.8%, this week, to trade 1.4% below its Dec. 31 record close 16576.77.

Traders say there was no single piece of news driving the market higher. They say concerns over Russia's intervention in Ukraine remain in the background, but investors believe over the long term, it will end up as a nonevent. If recent upbeat economic data were providing the boost, they would expect a rise in bond yields, but yields are down.

And with volumes light, they aren't seeing a big increase in buying, even by those who may have been selling as the market fell last week.

Jim Russell, senior equity strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management, which oversees about $115 billion, said he has seem some flows into domestic equity mutual funds. Those flows may not be heavy, but given the light volumes and a lack of selling, it may be having an "outsize impact on the market," Mr. Russell said.

On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a treaty formally annexing Ukraine's Crimea region after Crimeans voted overwhelmingly over the weekend to join Russia, as expected. But fears of escalating tensions were soothed after Mr. Putin said that while Crimea must be under Russian sovereignty, "we don't want a partition of Ukraine," and would defend Russia's interests by "diplomatic and legal means."

On the economic front, housing starts for February slipped 0.2% to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 907,000, just above expectations of 905,000. Building permits grew 7.7%, exceeding forecasts of a 1.1% increase. The consumer-price index for February rose 0.1% on the month, and by 0.1% if food and energy are excluded, with both measures matching expectations.

In corporate news, Hertz Global Holdings rose 0.2%, erasing earlier losses, as the company's plan to spin off its equipment-rental business overshadowed fourth-quarter earnings and revenue that missed expectations.

Apple advanced 0.9% after the company updated its low-price iPad offering, adding a handful of new capabilities but keeping the price at $399.

Dow component American Express tacked on 0.4% after saying late Monday it will sell half its corporate-travel business for $900 million to a group of investors including Certares and funds managed by BlackRock and Qatar Holdings. 


 
WORLD FOREX: 

The dollar fell against the ruble after a further advance by Russia into Ukraine seemed unlikely, while the Australian dollar strengthened after its central bank suggested rates would remain steady for some time.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday signed a treaty to annex Ukraine's Crimea region, where voters had chosen to rejoin Russia in a Sunday referendum, but indicated there were no plans for a further push into Ukraine. The West has objected to the annexation and has imposed sanctions on senior officials.

The dollar fell to 36.2344 rubles from 36.2865 rubles late Monday.

The sanctions imposed by the U.S. and European Union, including asset freezes and travel bans on officials from Russia and Ukraine, were "relatively weak," said RBC Capital Markets senior currency strategist Sue Trinh in a note.

Meanwhile, the Australian dollar rose to 91.27 U.S. cents from 90.89 U.S. cents. The Reserve Bank of Australia released minutes of its March meeting, which showed expectations for interest rates to remain steady for a while.

Concerns about the pace of growth in China, which is Australia's largest trading partner, had led to expectations that the RBA could cut rates further, said Chris Tevere, a senior currency strategist at Forex.com. "The most recent employment data out of Australia...coupled with the RBA's minutes have led to the realization that maybe the rate cuts that were priced in should be priced out," he said.

U.S. data released Tuesday showed a dip in housing starts in February, a rise in building permits to the highest rate since October, and a 0.1% increase in consumer prices last month.

The ICE dollar index, a gauge of the currency's strength, rose to 79.38 from 79.363. The WSJ Dollar Index, an alternate measure that pits the dollar against more rivals, edged down to 73.01 from 73.07.

Investors are looking ahead to Wednesday's conclusion of the first Federal Reserve meeting led by Chairwoman Janet Yellen. The central bank's guidance on the future path of interest rates should be in focus, with some expecting a reduced emphasis on the unemployment rate. The Fed is widely expected to continue reducing its monetary stimulus at the meeting and will issue new economic projections.

The euro was at $1.3931 from late Monday's $1.3927. The shared currency earlier Tuesday fell below $1.39 after a survey on German sentiment missed expectations. The ZEW indicator of economic sentiment dropped 9.1 points to 46.6, lower than expectations of a 52 reading.

The greenback fell against the Japanese yen, buying Y101.42 versus Y101.71 late Monday. The British pound was at $1.6591 from $1.6593. 


 
US TREASURYS: 

Treasury prices traded slightly higher on Tuesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve's monetary-policy decision.

Prices eased from overnight highs after Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow has no intentions to partition Ukraine.

The benchmark 10-year note added 5/32 in price to yield 2.679%, according to Tradeweb. The 30-year bond was up 2/32 in price to yield 3.625%. Bond prices rise when yields fall.

The Federal Open Market Committee kicked off its two-day meeting Tuesday, the first one under Chairwoman Janet Yellen. On Wednesday, the Fed will announce its policy decision and Ms. Yellen will hold a news conference.

"The market is put in a range now as they are waiting for the decision Yellen will make at the FOMC," said Millan L. Mulraine, deputy head of U.S. research and strategy at TD Securities. "This is a new Fed with a new slate of players. As an investor, you wouldn't want necessarily to prejudge that until you have more clarity on where Yellen wants to take the Fed."

The Fed is expected to announce another $10 billion cut to its bond-buying program and officially step away from the 6.5% jobless threshold for raising the federal funds target rate. The decision could add pressure on short-term yields by pushing the market's expectation for the first rate increase further out. Therefore, the Treasury yield curve will steepen.

Some investors said there is a possibility that Ms. Yellen takes a more pro-growth approach at the meeting, for example, by reducing the pace of tapering.

"Just looking from the domestic perspective, I wouldn't rule that out," said Robert Tipp, chief investment strategist at Prudential Fixed Income, referring to the recent softness in economic data.

In Russia, Mr. Putin signed a treaty formally annexing the breakaway Ukrainian region of Crimea, but sought to reassure Ukrainians by signaling that Moscow isn't planning to send its troops further into Ukraine. The latest move by Mr. Putin eased some fears and sapped demand for safe-haven Treasurys.

On the economic front, U.S. consumer prices rose 0.1% in February from a month earlier, the Labor Department said Tuesday. But on a year-over-year basis, prices were up 1.1% from a year earlier, the weakest 12-month gain since October and far below the Fed's 2% target for annual inflation.

"We expected subdued data, but this is more subdued than we expected," said Kathy Jones, a fixed-income strategist with Charles Schwab. "It is telling us there is still a long way to reach the 2% target." 


 
EUROPEAN STOCKS: 

European stocks extended their rally into a second day Tuesday, with investors interpreting a speech by Russian President Vladimir Putin as a step back from further confrontation with Ukraine.

Mr. Putin signed a treaty to annex the breakaway Ukrainian region of Crimea, but otherwise sounded a more conciliatory tone than many investors had expected. He said Russia isn't seeking "a partition of Ukraine" and would defend the interests of Russian speakers in the country by "diplomatic and legal means."

European shares, which had fallen as investors awaited the speech, rallied sharply, and were followed higher by U.S. markets. The Stoxx Europe 600 index closed 0.6% higher.

In Russia, the RTS index climbed 4.2%, while the ruble bounced back from steep losses earlier in the day.

"Putin's speech didn't indicate he is looking for an escalation of the crisis. All the focus was on Crimea rather than any further areas of Ukraine," said Guillaume Tresca, emerging-market strategist at Crédit Agricole.

With Mr. Putin largely steering clear of inflammatory rhetoric in response to the sanctions, markets are likely to turn their immediate focus to other issues, including the U.S. Federal Reserve meeting, Mr. Tresca said.

Even so, investors remain nervous.

"I don't really see this as a de-escalation. The situation is still a very tense one," said François Savary, who helps oversee roughly $10 billion of assets as chief investment officer at Swiss bank Reyl.

Mr. Savary thinks European stocks have the potential to rise further as the economy improves, but isn't buying while the Ukraine situation remains so uncertain. Reyl reduced its exposure to stocks last week, he said.

All major European indexes picked up from early losses, with Germany's DAX up 0.7% and London's FTSE 100 gaining 0.6%.

Among individual stocks, shares of Intesa Sanpaolo SpA rose 3.2% in Milan, BNP Paribas SA was up 1.8% in Paris and Banco Santander SA added 1.3% in Madrid.

Shares of Metro AG picked up 3.8% after the German retailer said it has pushed back plans for an initial public offering of its Russian Cash & Carry business due to the political uncertainty in Russia and Ukraine. 


 
ASIAN STOCKS: 

Asian stocks rose Tuesday, with Japan supported by a softer yen, while declining Chinese property companies were the focus in Hong Kong and Shanghai.

The region took its lead from the U.S., where stocks finished higher on Monday, after Wall Street shrugged off a referendum in Ukraine's Crimea region showing that the vast majority of voters wanted to secede and join Russia.

"The conflict is far from over. But markets don't regard the situation as critical," said Kengo Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Mizuho Securities.

The improved sentiment was most evident in Japan. Early weakness in the yen had a knock-on effect on Japanese stocks, with the Nikkei up 0.9% at 14411.27--putting the market on a recovery track from its 6.2% slump last week, its worst weekly performance since June last year.

In China, the Shanghai Composite rose less than 0.1% to 2025.20, as declines in developers weighed on the market. Data showed that gains in property prices in 70 Chinese cities continued to moderate in February after slowing in January for the first time in a year. News that a property developer in a small city in eastern China was unable to pay almost $400 million in debt also weighed on the sector.

China Vanke Co. fell 2.1% in Shenzhen, while China Overseas Land & Investment fell 1.3%.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index however gained 0.5% to 21583.50 due to a strong showing by one of its largest constituents. Tencent Holdings jumped 5.2% after the internet giant cashed out of its investment in ChinaVision Media for a total of 1 billion Hong Kong dollars ($129 million).

South Korea's Kospi was up 0.7% at 1940.21, and Singapore's Straits Times Index was up 0.05% at 3093.84. 


 
NEW ZEALAND STOCKS: 

The NZX-50 closed 0.9%, or 47.6 points, higher at 5135.66 as the market benefited from global strength, with risk sentiment improving during the U.S. trading session, Craig Investment Partners broker Belinda Stanley said.

"Asian and Australian markets have been really strong and we've really been dragged along by them," she said.

Xero rallied 3.7% as investors positioned themselves ahead of the stock's inclusion in the S&P/ASX's all ordinaries index.

LONDON METAL EXCHANGE: 

Nickel closed at its highest price in almost a year on the London Metal Exchange Tuesday, after moving into a bull market amid persistent concerns over supply of the metal to the market.

The LME's three-month nickel contract was up 2% at $16,190 a metric ton at the PM kerb close, its highest settlement since April 11 last year. The metal hit an intraday peak at $16,235 a ton, representing a gain of more than 20% since its Jan. 9 low of $13,334 a ton, the definition of a bull market.

Nickel prices have been driven by restricted supply from Indonesia, which has banned exports of ore. Concerns that Crimea-related sanctions on Russia could disrupt exports of its metal have also propped up prices.

While the U.S. and Europe have so far imposed sanctions only on individuals, "players on the nickel market still appear to assume that the Crimean crisis will escalate and that further-reaching sanctions will be imposed," analysts at Commerzbank said.

Nickel's break above $16,000 a ton Tuesday sparked technically driven buying, as stop-loss orders--automatic orders to buy at a certain level--were triggered, Standard Bank analyst Leon Westgate said.

"Nickel's break above $16,000 today should therefore see prices run higher; however, prices have moved a long way and it may need further fresh buying interest to give it a necessary shove," he said.

LME three-month copper closed 0.04% higher at $6,482 a ton Tuesday. 


 
US COMMODITIES: 

Oil futures strengthened Tuesday after a pipeline company said it would double the capacity of a pipeline connecting Oklahoma storage with Gulf Coast refineries sooner than previously expected. Light, sweet crude for April delivery settled up $1.62, or 1.7%, at $99.70 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange. Brent crude on the ICE futures exchange rose 55 cents, or 0.5%, to $106.79 a barrel.

Gold and other precious-metals prices fell sharply after Russia's president said he doesn't want a partition of Ukraine, easing worries that Russia may move further into the country after its annexation of Crimea. Gold for April delivery, the most active contract, fell $13.90, or just over 1%, to settle at $1,359 a troy ounce on the Comex division of the New York Mercantile Exchange. Silver dropped nearly 2% to $20.862.

Wheat futures jumped as the condition of the hard-red winter wheat crop in the U.S. declined amid dry, windy weather. Wheat futures for May delivery gained 18 cents, or 2.7%, to $6.92 1/2 a bushel.

Cotton prices climbed to a seven-month high as traders continued to worry that robust demand for the U.S.-grown fiber would lead to tighter domestic stocks. Cotton for delivery in May on the ICE Futures U.S. exchange ended 1% higher Tuesday at 92.93 cents a pound, the highest since Aug. 16.

Raw sugar for May delivery ended up 0.5% at 17.14 cents a pound. 


 
TOP STORIES OF THE DAY: 
PUTIN SIGNS TREATY TO ANNEX CRIMEA 

Russian President Vladimir Putin moved to annex the breakaway Ukrainian region of Crimea but sought to reassure Ukrainians by saying Moscow has no further designs on its southern neighbour's territories. 


NYSE SAID TO BE FRONT-RUNNER FOR ALIBABA LISTING 

The New York Stock Exchange is the front-runner to win the high-profile listing for the shares of Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., according to people familiar with the matter. 


U.S. HOUSING STARTS FALL SLIGHTLY 

Unseasonably cold weather appears to have chilled new-home construction in February, but underlying figures suggest building could be poised for a spring rebound. 


U.S. CONSUMER PRICES REMAIN NEARLY FLAT IN FEBRUARY 

The consumer-price index increased at a seasonally adjusted 0.1% in February from a month earlier, a sign that inflationary pressures remain tame in the economy. 


GM CEO APOLOGIZES FOR RECALL DELAY, VOWS CHANGES 

General Motors CEO Mary Barra intensified her campaign to show how the auto maker has changed, saying a newly appointed global safety chief will meet with her once a month to discuss issues. 

GOOGLE, VIACOM RESOLVE YOUTUBE COPYRIGHT LAWSUIT 

Google and Viacom said they have resolved copyright litigation between the two companies. Viacom, in a $1 billion lawsuit, had claimed YouTube allowed users to post copyrighted content without permission. 


APPLE UPDATES LOW-PRICE IPAD 

Apple updated its low-price iPad model, adding a handful of new capabilities and a more powerful processor, but keeping the price at $399. 


UKRAINE CRISIS WEIGHS ON GERMANY'S OUTLOOK 

German economic expectations fell sharply in March as a result of the continued uncertainty regarding Russia and Ukraine, a key sentiment indicator showed. 


EURO ZONE REPORTS TRADE SURPLUS 

The 18 countries that share the euro had a surplus in their trade of goods with the rest of the world in January, an indication that the currency area's continued economic recovery.

title: WSJ.com What's News - Worldwide News Briefs For Mar 18
text:
U.S. SUSPENDS SYRIAN EMBASSY OPERATIONS

The U.S. on Tuesday suspended operations at Syria's embassy in Washington and told Syrian diplomats working there and at other consulate locations to leave the country. 


 
IRAN, WORLD POWERS RESUME TALKS 
 

Iran and six major powers resumed high-level nuclear talks in Vienna as Western officials insisted the crisis in Ukraine wouldn't complicate negotiations. 


 
KARZAI NOMINATES MEMBER OF OPPOSITION AS VICE PRESIDENT 
 

Afghan President Hamid Karzai nominated an opposition Tajik politician as a replacement vice president, a choice that could help bridge differences with the opposition as crucial elections approach. 


 
FRANCE POSTPONES PLANS TO ATTEND TALKS IN MOSCOW 
 

France postponed plans for a senior delegation to attend talks in Moscow as the West pushed to deepen the Kremlin's isolation on the world stage in the wake of Russia's military intervention in Ukraine. 


 
JAPAN SUSPENDS RUSSIAN VISA TALKS 
 

Calling Crimea's referendum for independence "unconstitutional" under Ukrainian law, Japan announced Tuesday that it will suspend ongoing talks with Russia on relaxing visas and investment, space cooperation and defense accords. 


 
GREECE REACHES DEAL TO UNLOCK AID 
 

Greece reached an agreement with a troika of international debt inspectors on the reforms the country must take to receive billions of euros in frozen aid payments dating from the middle of last year. 


 
OECD WARNS AGAINST MORE CUTS 
 

Governments seeking to further narrow their budget deficits should ensure spending cuts don't reduce support for vulnerable groups and further increase poverty and income inequality, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development says. 


 
BANK OF ENGLAND SHAKES UP TOP TEAM 
 

The U.K. treasury made three appointments to the Bank of England's top team and shuffled seats on its two policy committees as part of an unprecedented overhaul of the 320-year-old central bank to be unveiled later by Gov. Mark Carney. 

AIR CANADA HALTS VENEZUELA FLIGHTS 
 

Air Canada said it has suspended flights to Venezuela, citing security concerns in the wake of antigovernment protests. 


 
INDIA TO APPEAL ITALIAN RULING ON HELICOPTER DEPOSIT 
 

India said it would appeal an Italian court order that rejected its attempts to recover the 278 million euros it had put down for a scrapped helicopter deal with Finmeccanica. 


 
FRANCE ARRESTS GREENPEACE PROTESTERS 
 

Several Greenpeace activists were arrested after they broke into the Fessenheim nuclear power plant in eastern France and put up a giant banner demanding the closure of nuclear reactors in Europe. 


 
SWISS TRIM 2014 GROWTH FORECAST 
 

The Swiss government trimmed its economic growth forecast slightly for this year but still expects the global economic recovery to boost its exports. 


 
U.S. FORCES TAKE CONTROL OF LIBYAN TANKER 
 

U.S. Navy commandos seized a tanker loaded with Libyan crude near Cyprus early Monday, thwarting an attempted sale by rebels who defied the weak central government and tried to grab a share of the North African nation's oil wealth. 


 
SERBIA'S VUČIĆ PLANS 'PAINFUL' MEASURES 
 

Serbia's likely new prime minister said he plans "several painful" steps to narrow the nation's budget deficit after his party won parliamentary elections on Sunday. 


 
QE NOT THE ONLY OPTION FOR ECB ON INFLATION 
 

Europe File: The solution is a thorough cleanup of the banking system of the sort that the ECB is currently orchestrating. 


 
U.K. CONDEMNS RUSSIA'S ACTIONS ON UKRAINE IN STRONGEST TERMS 
 

Britain condemned "in the strongest terms" Russia's actions in Ukraine after President Vladimir Putin defied international pressure and recognized Crimea as an independent state on Monday. 


 
PERU'S CONGRESS RATIFIES CABINET 
 

Peru's Congress voted to ratify President Ollanta Humala's new cabinet after initially refusing to do so, averting a crisis that could have hurt investor confidence and despite the opposition's complaints about the first lady. 


 
CANADA IMPOSES TRAVEL BAN ON RUSSIAN OFFICIALS 
 

Canada joined its Western allies Monday in unveiling additional sanctions against Russia in an effort to isolate the country for its role in "undermining" Ukraine's sovereignty. 


 
IRAN TALKS RESUME AMID UKRAINE CRISIS 
 

Iran and six major powers begin on Tuesday a fresh round of high-level nuclear talks, the first since tensions erupted within the six-power group over Ukraine. 


 
VENEZUELAN SECURITY FORCES TAKE OVER ALTAMIRA PLAZA 
 

The Government said hundreds of National Guard and police were deployed before dawn to take control of the key site of antigovernment protests. 


 
U.S. WANTS TO BAR TRIAL TESTIMONY BY 9/11 SUSPECT 
 

Prosecutors in the terror trial of Osama bin Laden's son-in-law asked a judge to block supporting testimony by alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheik Mohammed. 


 
MAJOR BRAZIL AIRPORTS BEHIND SCHEDULE FOR WORLD CUP 
 

Three major airports under renovations were behind schedule, according to a report released by Brazil's airport authority, but it isn't worried just yet as it continues to work to help them meet the deadline in time for the World Cup. 


 
WEAK PESO WATERS COLOMBIA'S GARDEN 
 

A 12% drop in the value of Colombia's currency against the dollar in the last year has been a boon to its exports. 


 
RENZI SAYS ITALY WON'T BREACH MAASTRICHT LIMITS 
 

Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi insisted Monday that Rome has no intention of asking to breach the fiscal rules set down for the euro area in Maastricht more than 20 years ago. 


 
IRAN CONSIDERING EXPORTING LNG VIA PLANT IN OMAN 
 

The move would allow the country greater access to gas-hungry Far-Eastern markets.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average slid 3.3% Friday, the biggest one-day loss since Feb. 4, while China's Shanghai Composite fell 0.7%.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-China fears weigh on emerging stocks; Russia, Turkey hit
text:
LONDON, March 12 (Reuters) - Emerging stocks hit a one-month low on Wednesday after fears about China's economy dragged down copper and other commodities, while worries about western sanctions on Russia weighed on the rouble, forcing the central bank to intervene.

The Turkish lira hit a five-week low against the dollar after protests broke out across the country at the death of a 15-year-old boy injured in anti-government protests.

Shanghai shares hit their lowest in nearly eight weeks as worries grew that economic data due on Thursday would confirm a slowdown in the world's second-biggest economy.

Concerns also lingered about China's credit sector following its first domestic bond default last week.

Shanghai copper fell by its 5 percent daily limit, while London copper touched a 44-month low as investors grew worried that tighter credit conditions would weigh on financing deals that use the metal as collateral, which could lead to more selling.

"There are concerns over the health of the Chinese economy, with signs that export growth is slowing sharply," said Neil Shearing, head of emerging market research at Capital Economics.

"And there are signs that the tensions over Crimea are continuing and showing no signs of abating... All these issues are from the emerging world, not to do with the Federal Reserve."

The benchmark MSCI emerging equity index fell more than 1 percent. Emerging markets have been under pressure since mid-2013 when the Fed first suggested it would scale back the pace of monetary stimulus.

Selling snowballed this year as China's economic slowdown and growing political turmoil in countries like Turkey and Ukraine triggered capital flight, forcing many central banks to raise interest rates to support their currencies.

Russian shares lost more than 1 percent as investors grew worried that western sanctions on Russia over Crimea could hit the country's already flagging economy.

Russia's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that Moscow plans to respect the results of a March 16 referendum in Crimea that is expected to back the region's reunification with Russia.

The rouble was steady to lower after the central bank intervened to keep the currency inside the floating corridor.

The country's five-year credit default swap rate rose 11 basis points from Tuesday's close to 248 bps, the highest since June 2012, according to Markit.

Russia's 2043 dollar bond fell 1.4 points to 94.255, the lowest since the bond was launched in September. The bond has lost more than 6 percent this month alone.

The lira fell as low as 2.2582 per dollar while the country's equity index fell around 1 percent. The prospect of renewed protests in Turkey has unsettled investors in the run-up to local elections on March 30.

"Returns from... Turkey remain negative in dollar terms over the year to date, which largely reflects the political conflict within the ruling AKP party in the case of Turkey," Deutsche Bank said in a note to clients.

South Africa's rand dropped more than 1 percent as concerns about China outweighed improvements in the country's own current account deficit, which narrowed more than expected in the final quarter of 2013 as exports outpaced imports.

Hungary's forint fell 0.1 percent to 314.01 per euro after Tuesday's weaker-than-expected inflation data reinforced expectations the central bank would cut interest rates again.

title: Macro Horizons: China Drives Yuan Lower by Largest Amount in 18 Months -- WSJ Blog
text:
By Michael J. Casey, Alen Mattich and Colin Ng

Macro Horizons covers the main macroeconomic and policy news events affecting foreign-exchange, fixed income and equity markets around the world, as selected by editors in New York, London and Hong Kong.

WRAP: While the world is distracted by other events -- Russia and Ukraine sparring, the hunt for a missing airplane, the mysteries of bitcoin -- China has been quietly engineering a major realignment in the currency of the world's most important exporter of merchandise.

The significance of this shift can't be underestimated for global trade. It's not that the 1.6% devaluation of the yuan over the past two months materially alter China's competitiveness -- although the fact that it is happening at a time when some emerging-market currencies have rebounded gives it more significance. It's that it means a markedly more aggressive level of intervention by the Chinese authorities. The conventional wisdom is that they are -- ironically -- being more interventionist now so as to set up a less interventionist regime in the future. They are thought to be bringing the currency to a level they are comfortable with before allowing it to float more freely. Either way, the changes will affect the price paid for goods made in China--and that means all of us. (MC)

CHINA: The yuan slumped against the dollar Monday after the People's Bank of China dropped the value of its daily fixing by the most in a year and a half, continuing a pattern of erratic movements that many observers think is a prelude to widening the currency's trading band. This came after data over the weekend showed Chinese exports fell by 18.1% on-year in February, while inflation came in below expectations, adding fuel to claims that the world's second-largest economy is heading for a hard landing.

The data may have exacerbated the yuan's decline, but analysts noted that the trade figure likely reflected rampant over-invoicing a year ago as well as the effect of the Lunar New Year holiday that fell in early February this year. Mostly, then, this slippage for the currency is seen as a deliberate attempt by the authorities to shift its trajectory and make way for an expected change in the currency down the road. Meanwhile, benign inflation gives the central bank room to ease interest rates later this year if the economy seems unlikely to reach the government's 7.5% growth target. (MA)

UKRAINE: Russian President Vladimir Putin formally endorsed a Crimean push for independence from Ukraine in a referendum set for later this month while U.S. President Barack Obama said he would meet with his Ukrainian counterpart in Washington on Wednesday.

The Crimean impasse could still trigger a serious regional crisis, but for now it seems to have stabilized temporarily. With neither the U.S. nor the European Union looking to intervene forcefully, Russia seems set to get its way. (AM)

JAPAN: The government revised down its fourth-quarter GDP to 0.7% from the initial reading of 1%. Meanwhile, the country posted a current-account deficit of Y1.59 trillion ($15.4 billion) in January, its largest ever.

Weak capex and consumer spending were behind the GDP revision, which will likely intensify the debate about whether the government should go forward with a sales-tax hike in April as planned. For the current account, it was the fourth straight month of deficits, the longest spell on record, and reflects both tepid exports and a surge in import costs due to the weak yen and higher imported fuel volumes. (MA)

FRANCE: January industrial production fell 0.2% on the month against expectations of no change and following a 0.3% decline in December.

The French economy is struggling for growth. The January industrial-production data are particularly worrisome. Forecasters had expected it to level off following December's decline, but, instead, it fell further. The French central bank continues to look for a 0.2% GDP expansion during the first quarter, but with this sort of data coming through, and disappointing business surveys -- sentiment in the services sector has also been glum -- it's hard to see where the growth is coming from. (AM)

ITALY: January Industrial production rose 1.0% on the month and 1.4% on the year against expectations of a 0.4% monthly rise and 1.1% annual fall.

Italian industry started the year strongly. Undoubtedly, demand for Italy's high end manufactured goods is lending support -- the rich seem to be the world's only robust consumers. Emerging market wobbles, however, raise questions over how long this boom might be sustained. (AM)

COMING UP:

CANADA: 8:15 a.m. EDT. February Housing Starts. [Expected 190,000 annualized, up from 180,248 in January.]

A pickup in February would help spur keep construction jobs in check against the impact of a slowdown in what had been a booming Canadian housing market. (MC)

U.S.: 12:40 p.m. EDT Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Charles Evans speaks at Columbus State University.

Mr. Evans is considered a dove, clearly in favor of a measured approach to tapering the bond-buying program. He is not currently a voter on the FOMC. (MC)

U.K.: 8:01 p.m. EDT (12:01 a.m. Tuesday, London) February BRC same store sales [From up 3.9% year on year in January]

The U.K. economy is booming, not least thanks to strong consumer demand. But with real earnings still contracting and credit growth still relatively subdued, one or both will need to pick up for consumption growth to be sustained. (AM)

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Asian stocks slump on disappointing China trade data, Ukraine crisis
text:
* European shares seen moving mostly flat at open

* Weak China data released on weekend offsets upbeat U.S jobs report

* Ukrainian uncertainty add to geopolitical concerns

By Shinichi Saoshiro

TOKYO, March 10 (Reuters) - Asian stocks fell sharply on Monday and the dollar stepped back from its recent highs as surprisingly weak Chinese trade data rattled investors already on edge over the crisis in Ukraine.

European shares were seen opening largely flat with the poor Chinese data tempering optimism from a robust U.S. nonfarm payrolls report.

Financial spreadbetters predicted Britain's FTSE 100 would open as much as 0.06 percent higher, Germany's DAX up 0.13 percent and France's CAC 40 add as much as 0.18 percent.

Investors greeted the new week in Asia on a cautious note after data issued on Saturday showed China's exports unexpectedly tumbled in February, swinging the trade balance into deficit and adding to fears of a slowdown in the world's second-largest economy.

The soft Chinese data put a damper on risk sentiment, which had been temporarily boosted by stronger-than-expected U.S. nonfarm payrolls out on Friday showing employers had added 175,000 jobs to their payrolls last month, up from 129,000 new positions in January.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 1.4 percent, and Tokyo's Nikkei stock average shed 1.0 percent, retreating from Friday's six-week high.

China's CSI300 index slid to its lowest in nearly nine months, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index shed 1.8 percent.

U.S. stock futures fell 0.4 percent from their record closing high on Friday.

"Fundamentally speaking, data out of the U.S. has a bigger underlying market impact, but the psychological effect from Chinese economic indicators cannot be overlooked. The Nikkei's attempt to chase further highs being derailed is a prime example," said Koji Fukaya, president at FPG Securities in Tokyo.

"The rise in yields after the upbeat U.S. data supports the dollar, but latest indicators out of China dampens risk appetite and may foil the currency's advances against the yen," Fukaya said.

Russian forces tightened their grip on Crimea, seizing another border post and a military airfield, fanning tensions ahead of a planned Moscow-backed referendum on Sunday on whether the Black Sea peninsula should join Russia.

Diplomatic efforts to cool the crisis in Ukraine calmed markets toward the end of last week, but rising tensions over Russia's intervention in Crimea have kept investors on edge.

Adding to the sombre mood, a Malaysia Airlines flight with 239 people on board vanished en route to Beijing from Kuala Lumpur in the early hours of Saturday, with questions mounting over possible security lapses and whether a bomb or hijacking could have brought down the plane.

The U.S. dollar index, a composite of six currency pairs dipped 0.1 percent to 79.683 after touching a high of 79.847 on Friday after the U.S. jobs data.

Against the safe haven yen the dollar stood at 103.12, pulling away from a six-week high of 103.77 hit on Friday.

The euro remained near recent highs, with bulls still heartened by the European Central Bank's reluctance last week to take further policy action.

The single currency traded at $1.3879, within striking distance of a 2-1/2 year peak of $1.3915 reached on Friday.

China's yuan opened trade at 6.1554 per dollar on Monday, down 0.5 percent from Friday's close of 6.1260, before moving to 6.1451. The yuan as well as Chinese short-term rates fell amid expectations Beijing is quietly easing monetary policy to buttress wobbly economic growth.

Gold edged lower for a second straight session on Monday after the strong U.S. jobs data eased fears of an economic slowdown and dimmed the metal's safe-haven appeal.

But underlining the fact that the crisis in the Ukraine was likely to remain a key theme for the precious metal, data from the Commodity Futures Trading showed that hedge funds and money managers raised their bullish bets in gold futures and options for a fourth consecutive week as geopolitical tensions boosted speculative interest to its highest in more than a year.

In wake of disappointing Chinese data, Brent crude declined 55 cents to $108.45 a barrel, ending two straight days of gains. Geopolitical tensions in Ukraine and Libya limited the falls.

"Oil pulled back because of the latest data from China despite continuing tensions over Ukraine," said Victor Shum, vice-president of energy consultancy IHS Energy Insight. "The ongoing situation in Ukraine will put a high floor on oil prices and lead to more volatility."

The weak data also fanned concerns over China's metals industry. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange dropped 1.6 percent to $6,674.75 a tonne. It earlier slid as far as $6,608 a tonne, its weakest since June 25, when it stopped at $6,602, the lowest since July 2010.

US STOCKS: 

U.S. stocks closed mostly higher Friday after data showed more jobs were created in February than economists expected.

The latest employment report showed that the economic recovery, while still relatively slow, remained on track. It supported investors' belief that recent disappointing economic data was a temporary stumble because of cold winter weather, but it didn't give them enough of a reason to make further big moves into stocks. Traders also expect the U.S. central bank to continue to scale back its economic-stimulus measures.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 30.83 points, or 0.2%, to end at 16452.72. It had been up as many as 84 points earlier in the session.

The S&P 500 rose 1.01 points, or 0.1%, to 1878.04, closing at a record high but off an intraday peak of 1883.57. The S&P 500 posted a second-straight weekly gain, and has climbed 7.7% since it closed at a 3 1/2-month low on Feb. 3.

The Nasdaq Composite Index fell 15.90 points, or 0.4%, to 4336.22.

Nonfarm payrolls increased by 175,000 in February, exceeding expectations of 152,000. Meanwhile, the unemployment rate ticked up to 6.7% from January's 6.6%, versus expectations of a decline to 6.5%. January payroll growth was revised up to 129,000 from an original estimate of 113,000.

The better-than-expected jobs data came on the eve of the bull market's five-year anniversary. The S&P 500 has nearly tripled since bottoming out at 676.53 on March 9, 2009.

Traders attributed the midday swoon that pulled the market off its highs to investors cashing in on some gains in light volume ahead of the weekend, given the uncertainty surrounding Ukraine.

John Stoltzfus, chief market strategist at Oppenheimer Asset Management, which oversees about $86 billion, said the jobs report is "highly supportive" of the way the market has rallied over the last month in the face of disappointing data, but it is reasonable to "take some money off the table ahead of the weekend."

"It is comfortable to be investing in stocks now, but it is never safe," Mr. Stoltzfus said. "That said, it is a market in which the overall trend outweighs other considerations."

Although fears over the situation in Ukraine have faded over the last week, it was still a source of some concern for investors. Russia's upper house of parliament pledged Friday to support Crimea if it seeks to join the Russian Federation, should its people vote to become part of Russia in a referendum on the issue scheduled for March 16.

In corporate news, Big Lots jumped 22% after the closeout retailer reported fiscal fourth-quarter earnings that were within the range of its forecast, while revenue exceeded analyst estimates.

Public Service Enterprise Group fell 0.4% after the power company unveiled a $12 billion five-year capital spending plan in an effort to boost earnings growth for its utility business.

Coupons.com soared on its debut as a public company, with the stock trading 92% above its initial public offering price of $16. 


 
WORLD FOREX: 

The dollar strengthened against most major currencies Friday after the February U.S. jobs report came in above expectations.

The Labor Department reported that the U.S. economy added 175,000 jobs in February, above expectations of 152,000. The unemployment rate ticked higher to 6.7% from 6.6% in January, as more people joined the workforce.

Friday's strong jobs report reversed the trend of soft employment and other disappointing economic data over the past few of months. It suggested the Federal Reserve will likely continue to reduce its monthly bond purchases, which have weighed on the value of the dollar.

"This isn't necessarily a sign that the economy is beginning to strengthen, but it is a confirmation that the recent weakness we've seen is more related to the weather and less indicative of a broader economic slowdown," said Brian Daingerfield, currency strategist at RBS Securities in Stamford, Conn. "The follow-through of this jobs report will be continued strength in the dollar."

The dollar rose to a six-week high against the yen, at Y103.52, before settling at Y103.29, up 0.2%.

The greenback pared losses against the euro, trading at $1.3870, from $1.3891 before the data, down 0.1%. Earlier Friday, the euro had surpassed $1.39 for the first time since Oct. 31, 2011, rising to as high as $1.3915. 


 
US TREASURYS: 

Treasury bond prices fell Friday and capped the biggest weekly selloff in three months as an upbeat reading of the U.S. labor market sapped demand for haven assets.

Sellers piled in after the Labor Department showed a bigger-than-forecast 175,000 non-farm jobs added last month, sending the 10-year yield to a six-week high. When bond prices fall, their yields rise.

The 10-year note was 14/32 lower in price, yielding 2.790%, according to Tradeweb.

The 10-year note's yield rose by about 0.13 percentage points for the week. The yield, a key benchmark for setting borrowing costs for consumers and businesses in the global arena, remains at historic lows.

"The U.S. economy has underlined strength despite the adverse weather in January and February" and the Fed will continue to scale back monetary stimulus, said Gary Pollack, who helps oversee $12 billion in assets as head of fixed-income trading in New York at Deutsche Bank AG's private wealth management unit.

Still, some investors and analysts don't expect the yield to reach 3% any time soon, a level it last traded in early January.

Factors keeping the rise in check include signs of uneven growth in the U.S. and abroad, ongoing geopolitical concerns in Ukraine and the Fed's pledge to keep short-term interest rates near zero until the economy shows a more robust pace of recovery.

"The rise in bond yields in 2014 is not likely to be as disorderly as it was during the turbulent period last summer mainly because investors are more prepared now for rates to rise, having altered their fixed-income allocations accordingly," said Tony Crescenzi, senior market strategist and portfolio manager at Pacific Investment Management Co. in Newport Beach, California, which has $1.91 trillion in assets under management.

Thomas Roth, executive director in the U.S. government bond trading group at Mitsubishi UFJ Securities USA Inc. in New York, said there have been buyers taking advantage of Friday's selling in bonds which sent the 10-year yield up to 2.821%, the highest level since Jan. 23.

The 10-year yield around 2.8% is still attractive to some investors, because "we still have a lot of work do to get the economy back on track," he said. 


 
EUROPEAN STOCKS: 

European stock markets slid into the close Friday, as investors sold off ahead of the weekend on fears the crisis in Ukraine could escalate. Indexes had earlier pared losses after the highly anticipated U.S. nonfarm-payrolls report beat expectations.

The Stoxx Europe 600 index slumped 1.3% to close at 333.06, losing 1.5% on the week and marking the first weekly slide since January. Germany's DAX declined 2.0%, while France's CAC-40 was 1.2% lower. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 shed 1.1%.

Leading the decliners Friday, shares of Getinge AB tumbled 21% after the medical-technology company said its profit trend for the first quarter will be weak due to a lower level of invoicing.

Shares of Fugro NV fell 2.1% after the oil-field-services firm posted 2013 earnings that missed expectations.

Banks were lower across most of Europe, with shares of Deutsche Bank AG down 2.7% in Frankfurt, Credit Agricole SA off 2.8% in Paris and heavyweight HSBC Holdings PLC 1% lower in London.

In the opposite direction, shares of Air France-KLM SA jumped 4.4% after the airline said passenger traffic rose 1.4% in February, boosted by a rise in both long and medium-haul flights.

More broadly, most European stock markets closed in the red, ending a week that was marked by increased tensions between Russia and Ukraine. The crisis intensified Friday afternoon after part state-owned Gazprom said it might halt gas deliveries to Ukraine as it did in 2009, because the country hasn't paid for its February supply. Gazprom also said Ukraine owes it $1.89 billion for gas, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The U.S. and the European Union has condemned Russia's occupation of Ukraine's Crimea region and earlier in the week unveiled a set of sanctions to punish Russia for the intervention. France's foreign minister, Laurent Fabius, reportedly said Friday that a second round of sanctions could be on the cards if the first round doesn't work.

Chatter that big U.S. pension funds were rebalancing their asset portfolios by dumping equities and instead moving into bonds, also appeared to weigh on the European stock markets.

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Stocks drop on rising Ukraine tensions, oil gains
text:
* European shares fall sharply, German index down 2 percent

* Strong U.S. jobs growth at first lifts equity markets

* Dollar rises from four-month low, bond prices fall

* Oil prices rise on heightened Ukraine concerns

By Herbert Lash

NEW YORK, March 7 (Reuters) - A surprisingly strong U.S. jobs report on Friday sent bond and gold prices sharply lower and initially lifted equity markets, but mounting tensions over Ukraine led stocks in Europe and elsewhere to retreat, while U.S. shares ended little changed.

Diplomatic efforts to cool the crisis in Ukraine calmed markets earlier in the week, but as tensions rose over Russia's intervention in Crimea, investors tried to shield themselves before the weekend from any potential confrontation.

European blue chips exposed to Russia and Ukraine came under renewed pressure as Germany's DAX index, considered the most vulnerable to any fallout, fell 2.0 percent, the biggest drop among major regional indices.

The Euro STOXX Volatility Index, a sign of investor apprehension, jumped 14.9 percent. But its U.S. counterpart, the CBOE Volatility Index, rose less than 1 percent.

President Vladimir Putin rebuffed a warning from U.S. President Barack Obama over Moscow's military intervention in Crimea, saying on Friday that Russia could not ignore calls for help from Russian speakers in Ukraine.

Putin said in a statement after an hour-long telephone call that Moscow and Washington remain far apart, giving investors a reason to take money off the table before the weekend.

"People are a little bit nervous to go into the weekend with fully loaded long positions, given the ongoing Ukraine crisis," said Zeg Choudhry, head of trading at Northland Capital Partners in Ilford, Britain.

The FTSEurofirst 300 index of top European shares extended losses into the close, finishing down 1.3 percent at 1,326.70.

MSCI's all-country world equity index retreated to trade 0.3 percent lower after trading just off peaks last seen at the end of 2007.

Wall Street was mostly flat, with the better-than-expected U.S. nonfarm payrolls report pushing the benchmark S&P 500 index to a fresh intra-day record high before paring gains. The index closed slightly higher, setting a new record close.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed up 30.83 points, or 0.19 percent, at 16,452.72. The S&P 500 gained 1.01 points, or 0.05 percent, to 1,878.04 while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 15.903 points, or 0.37 percent, to 4,336.223.

For the week, the Dow rose 0.8 percent, the S&P 1.0 percent and the Nasdaq 0.7 percent.

U.S. Treasuries yields rose to their highest in six weeks after the February jobs report eased fears of an abrupt slowdown in economic growth and kept the Federal Reserve on track in reducing its monetary stimulus.

U.S. employers added 175,000 jobs to payrolls after creating 129,000 positions in January, the U.S. Labor Department said. However, even as job growth accelerated sharply, the unemployment rate rose to 6.7 percent from a five-year low of 6.6 percent.

Benchmark 10-year Treasury notes dropped 18/32 in price, the yield rising to 2.82 percent, the highest since Jan. 23. It was last down almost 15/32 in price to yield 2.7915 percent.

German Bund futures rose 6 ticks to settle at 142.24, clawing back some ground after suffering their biggest one-day fall since late December on Thursday after the European Central Bank refrained from new stimulus measures.

The dollar rose from a four-month low. The dollar index , a composite of six currency pairs, traded 0.07 percent higher at 79.717. It earlier hit a bottom of 79.433 last seen on Oct. 29.

The dollar was up 0.24 percent against the yen at 103.31 yen, while the euro rose 0.1 percent to $1.3872.

U.S. COMEX gold futures for April delivery fell $13.60 to settle at $1,338.20 an ounce,

Crude oil rose on the U.S. jobs report and Ukraine, offsetting a seasonal slowdown in demand, and analysts expected more traders to take net long positions.

"It is definitely a good idea to have some length ahead of a weekend's worth of rhetoric about Ukraine," said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital LLC in New York. "Any deterioration in the prospect for a reasonable outcome gets rapidly priced into the market."

Global benchmark Brent crude oil settled up 90 cents at $109.00 a barrel. U.S. crude rose $1.02 to settle at $102.58.

title: Russian assets marked down for Moscow's actions in Ukraine
text:
MOSCOW, March 7 (Reuters) - Russian assets declined across markets on Friday, marked down compared to other emerging markets for Russian actions in Ukraine.

At 0630 GMT, the rouble was down 0.4 percent against the dollar at 36.28 after losing 0.4 percent in the previous session, while other emerging market currencies such as the Turkish lira and the South African rand saw gains.

Investors were somewhat reassured by the European Union taking only minor steps in condemning Russian actions in Ukraine, but unnerved by the Crimean parliament's vote in favour of annexing the peninsula to Russia and a decision to bring forward a referendum on the issue.

"While for now, the sanctions mean only visa restrictions (by the U.S.), the decisive position of the Crimean authorities could destabilise the situation, because the volume of accusations against Russia can increase," Oleg Dushin, an analyst at the Zerich investment house, said in a morning note.

The rouble was on a path to end the week more than 1 percent weaker against the dollar. It was trading 0.4 percent down on the day against the euro at 50.30.

This has left the rouble 0.4 percent weaker at 42.53 against the dollar-euro basket that the central bank uses as a guide for the rouble's nominal exchange rate.

The rouble remains the "underdog in the emerging markets space", analysts at VTB Capital wrote in a note.

Analysts expect the central bank, which since Monday has increased its interventions in the foreign exchange market, to keep intervening to prop up the currency.

"As political risks remain elevated, we believe the central bank will be reluctant to unwind its emergency actions (including higher intervention volumes and higher rates) until the risk premium in Russia-related assets diminishes," VTB Capital analysts said.

Both Moscow indexes, the rouble-traded MICEX index and the dollar-denominated RTS, traded 0.1 percent lower, at 1,264.1 and 1,337.2 points respectively, underperforming the broader MSCIEF index, which was up 0.2 percent.

"It's all very sad, the broader emerging markets index MSCI Emerging Markets is near the maximums this year and our MICEX on Monday tested four-year minimums," Zerich's analysts wrote.

Absent any further dramatic developments in Ukraine, analysts expected equities to trade largely flat in Moscow, and the rouble to remain under pressure.

title: *Fitch: Crisis to Weigh on Russia Economy; Credit Profile Robust
text:
6 Mar 2014 06:21 EDT  Press Release: Fitch: Crisis to Weigh on Russia Economy; Credit Profile Robust


 
 
The following is a press release from Fitch Ratings: 
 

Fitch Ratings-London-06 March 2014: The crisis in the Ukraine has increased the risks to Russia's already weakening economy presented by currency depreciation and capital flight, Fitch Ratings says. The situation is still highly unpredictable but Russia's sovereign credit profile is robust and events so far do not have implications for the country's 'BBB' rating.

Market reaction to Russia's intervention in Crimea saw the rouble fall 2.2% to an all-time low against the US dollar on Monday, while the MICEX index of Russian shares fell 10.8% and yields on rouble sovereign debt rose sharply. The Central Bank of Russia (CBR) raised its key interest rate by 150bp to 7%, and intervened to support the rouble, selling USD11bn. Losses were partly recovered on Tuesday as tensions appeared to ease.

The rouble has now fallen around 9% against the dollar this year, partly driven by fears across emerging markets about the impact of US tapering, but also on Russia-specific concerns about low growth and the weakening current account surplus, and in anticipation of further liberalisation of the exchange rate regime.

Higher energy prices and a weaker rouble should provide a fillip to sovereign finances by boosting the local-currency value of oil and gas exports, which contribute around half of federal government revenue and current external receipts. This will keep the fiscal deficit within the target of 0.6% of GDP in the budget, making up for a shortfall in non-oil revenue.

Russia's already strong sovereign balance sheet is characterised by low sovereign debt levels and high international reserves (around USD490bn in late February). Sovereign net foreign assets equivalent to 23% of GDP provide an ample buffer against external shocks, supporting the rating. These are sufficient to cover gross external financing needs more than three times over. The Reserve Fund, the government's main fiscal buffer, contains USD87bn (4.5% of GDP), giving Russia a cushion against a drop in demand for its sovereign debt.

However, the broader economy stands to gain less from a weaker rouble. A lower cost base for commodity exporters may promote some current account adjustment but competitiveness gains for the relatively small non-hydrocarbons export sector will have a limited impact on GDP. We think the economic drag through lower business and consumer confidence and a loss of purchasing power will be more significant.

Russian economic growth has already slipped below the 'BBB' category median, with real GDP growth falling to 1.3% in 2013 due to a decline in investment and the inventory cycle. We recently revised our growth forecasts for 2014 and 2015 to 1.5% and 2%, respectively (from 2% and 2.5%), as economic data in January and February showed little sign of improvement. Rising inflation, higher interest rates and potential capital flight all increase the risks to the downside. Foreign lenders may also seek to scale back their lending to the Russian private sector, with adverse economic consequences.

- Private capital outflows exceeded 5% of GDP in 2013 and remain a persistent problem. The Ministry of Economy estimated year-to-date private sector capital outflows had already reached USD17bn - around half their forecast for 2014 as a whole - prior to the crisis.

Capital flight could accelerate, particularly if the threat of economic and financial sanctions increased. While not our base case, were such sanctions to materialise, the potential impact on growth and investment could lead us to review our sovereign rating on Russia. However, it is not clear whether Russia's European trading partners in particular are prepared to risk the potential disruption to their own economies, and possible Russian retaliation, that sanctions would entail.
