title: Up & Down Wall Street: "Hopeless, But Not Serious" -- Barron's
text:
(FROM BARRON'S 3/3/14) 
   By Randall W. Forsyth 

Can it really be less than four years since markets got all in a tizzy because of violent demonstrations in Athens? Pictures of protestors setting fires were enough to touch off selling that led to the infamous Flash Crash of May 6, 2010. That afternoon, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 1,000 points, only to recoup most of those losses nearly as quickly.

Since then, the markets have developed a sort of immunity to televised sights of mass demonstrations, even violent ones, after witnessing a seemingly unending parade of them. At the risk of sounding like Spiro Agnew, Richard Nixon's vice president until he resigned over corruption charges, when you've seen one political riot with burning cars, you've seen them all. They're all in some square with a bunch of kids recording the events for posterity on YouTube.

The riots have played out in the Arab Spring, which ended up bringing neither democracy nor prosperity to the region. Syria's civil war continues with deaths well into six figures. After that, we're on overload when it comes to political upheavals abroad.

So, it shouldn't be too surprising that the U.S. stock market hit records last week against the backdrop of the crisis in Ukraine, which followed on the heels of protests in Venezuela and Thailand, and yet another currency crisis in Argentina.

Elsewhere, Nigeria and Turkey -- the last two letters of the trendy MINT emerging markets, following Mexico and Indonesia -- saw their currencies under pressure as the result of alleged high-level corruption. The head of the African nation's central bank was suspended recently for blowing the whistle on a massive oil fraud, allegedly involving top officials. Meanwhile, revelations that Turkey's prime minister, Recep Tayyip Edrogan, was caught on tape -- allegedly advising his son on how to get rid of millions of euros stashed in his home -- have renewed pressure on the lira, despite sharp interest-rate hikes in late January to stabilize the currency amid the nation's ongoing economic crisis.

Who can keep track of all these upheavals? And why should you? We Americans almost take pride in not giving a rodent's rectum about what happens beyond our shores. Especially if the Standard & Poor's 500 index notches a record amid our blissful ignorance. And just as we did in the late 1990s amid the civil war that split the former Yugoslavia, and resulted in the deaths of some 140,000 people.

The averages closed at a record on Friday, after retreating from their peaks amid reports of masked men taking over the two airports in Crimea, the pro-Russian southern region of Ukraine that has a major Russian naval base. The action was disavowed by Russian officials. After the close, President Obama warned Russia against military intervention in Ukraine.

While much more is at stake politically for Vladimir Putin, the situation is "hopeless, but not serious," at least in economic terms, quips David P. Goldman, head of Americas strategy at Hong Kong-based Reorient. To put Ukraine's economy in perspective, he noted in a CNBC interview that its entire stock-market capitalization is roughly that of Walt Disney (ticker: DIS), its gross domestic product is one-fifth of Turkey's, and its per capita income is a bit higher than Egypt's. Per capita income of Ukrainians is estimated at well less than half of Russians' and even less than that of Poles.

The smiley face put on all of these conflicts is that they only serve to make the U.S. stock market all the more attractive to investors. Ditto Europe, where those three immortal words uttered in mid-2012 by European Central Bank President Mario Draghi -- "whatever it takes" -- seem to have produced stability and confidence, if not exactly real prosperity.

That's best reflected in the plunge in yields of sovereign bonds of the erstwhile PIIGS -- Portugal, Italy, Ireland, Greece, and Spain. Ten-year yields are about 3.5% in Italy and Spain, and 3.1% in Ireland, while Portugal is under 5% and even Greece is under 7%. Lower borrowing costs for these countries effectively loosens a noose that previously had threatened to asphyxiate their economies. All of which is vastly more important than what happens to the former Soviet republics, provided, of course, that their conflicts don't escalate. But it's hard to envision blunders like those made in 1914 being repeated in 2014.

If U.S. investors look abroad, it should be in the other direction. In China last week, the central bank fostered a sharp decline in its currency, the yuan or renminbi, including a steep 1.5% drop for the week ending Friday, the biggest downward movement since it stopped pegging it to the dollar in 2005.

At week's end, the renminbi traded at 6.1450 to the dollar, its lowest value in 10 months, and much weaker than its peak in January, when a buck bought only RMB6.0406.

That may not sound like much, but a move of "10 big figures," in forex parlance, to 6.14 to the buck from 6.04, is a big deal, especially given that the currency is tightly controlled by the People's Bank of China. But, according to many observers, wagering on the continual appreciation of the renminbi had become too much of a one-way bet for Chinese officials.

Indeed, according to JPMorgan economists, much of the capital outflow from other emerging markets -- some $100 billion from last May to December -- found its way to China, considered a haven, particularly after taking into account the dollar's 2% decline over that span. Subtracting $20 billion of fixed direct investment, the remaining $80 billion came from "hot-money" inflows.

JPM figures that much of that movement reflected greater use of the renminbi for the purposes of trades that previously had been settled in dollars, and borrowing in foreign currencies. On the latter point, if you were a Chinese business that could borrow in a currency that probably would decline, such as the Japanese yen, and use the proceeds to fund assets in appreciating renminbi, it's better than free money.

By some estimates, China's currency no longer is undervalued (although you'll get arguments on that point from many in the U.S. Congress). In response to lagging export growth and a weakening in its purchasing managers index, Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch economists suggest that China could benefit from some currency weakness.

"The risk," they continue, "is that PBoC actions worsen fears of a financial event in China." Signs of increased stress showed up in higher interbank interest rates, relative to risk-free interest rates.

In addition, Gavan Nolan, director of credit research at Markit, noted a sharp rise in the notional amount of credit-default swaps on China's sovereign credit, to $11.1 billion last week. "Leading indicators, such as the HSBC/Markit PMI, will continue to move markets, though the condition of China's shadow banking system is arguably more crucial," which has been noted here previously ("Risk-Off Redux," Jan. 27).

But the continued ascent of U.S. stocks, with the S&P 500 ending the week at another record and the Nasdaq Composite hitting a 13 1/2-year high, is inspiring a sense of deja vu for BCA Research managing editor Chen Zhao. "The broad economic and financial environment today is very similar to that of the second half of the 1990s, when the equity bull market turned parabolic," he writes.

He points to the shift in leadership to growth and cyclical sectors and away from dividend-paying and defensive stocks. "More interestingly," he says, "at the far end of the 'growth' spectrum are the 'social network' stocks, whose prices have been exploding upwards in recent months."

These high fliers trading at 12 to 13 times sales, while the Nasdaq Internet exchange-traded fund (PNQI) trades at 52 times earnings, which recalls the 1990's dot-com bubble. Zhao adds that analysts' assertions that social-network stocks are still cheap, based on their future profit potential, reminded him of the talk of that era.

Still, he adds, "There are increasing odds that the U.S. stock market will march to a much bubblier environment."

In particular, bull markets don't usually end until the yield curve inverts -- that is, short-term interest rates rise above longer-term bond yields. That's not likely to happen anytime soon.

Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen reiterated in testimony to the Senate Banking Committee last week that the central bank remains on course to reduce its purchases of Treasury and agency mortgage-backed securities. But no hike in its key federal-funds rate target from the current level near zero is likely until well into 2015, even as the unemployment rate nears 6.5%. Yellen emphasized that the headline jobless rate didn't fully reflect the slack in the labor market.

This week should provide further clues to the economy's health, with the beginning of the slate of February indicators, especially the jobs report due out on Friday. The impact of the severe winter weather is uncertain, Yellen admitted, and economists in and out of government will be trying to weed out its effects.

In the meantime, the Fed will remain on its accommodative course, continuing to buoy asset prices. So, party like it's 1999, and don't worry what's happening in the rest of the world, except for China.

    SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Most emerging Asian currencies
eased on Thursday as the dollar gained on rising geopolitical
tensions over the Ukraine, but losses were limited as the yuan
steadied after recent losses.
    The Indonesian rupiah fell as local companies
bought the dollar for month-end payments. The Malaysian ringgit
 eased on selling from hedge funds.
    Thailand's baht slipped on dollar demand from some
gold investors and sustained political unrest.
    The dollar held near a two-week high against a basket of
major currencies as Ukraine's protest leaders named ministers
they want to form a new government following the overthrow of
President Viktor Yanukovich.
    Russia's President Vladimir Putin ordered 150,000 troops to
be ready for war games near Ukraine, prompting the United States
to warn Russia that it would be a "grave mistake" to intervene
militarily. 
    A wider conflagration in the Ukraine could spark a rush to
safety and damage vulnerable emerging market assets. 
    The dollar also found support after data showed sales of new
U.S. single-family homes surged to a 5-1/2-year high in January.
 
    Emerging Asian currencies, however, recovered some of their
initial losses as spot yuan turned firmer.
    "Ukraine may have indirect impact on Asian currencies as it
will hurt sentiment on overall emerging markets. What is more
important to Asia is the yuan," said Yuna Park, a currency and
bond analyst at Dongbu Securities in Seoul.
    "It's hard to say the yuan is stabilising for now. The yuan
will see more volatility even though its long-term appreciation
trend remains intact," said Park, adding that regional units may
fluctuate on the Chinese currency.
    Earlier, the yuan or renminbi briefly fell and remained
below the official midpoint fixing, which the central bank set
lower, a trend that is likely to continue as Beijing prepares
for market reforms. 
    
    RINGGIT
    The ringgit eased to the U.S. dollar on selling from
leveraged funds and it fell versus the Singapore dollar
.
    The Malaysian currency pared some of its earlier losses,
tracking a rebound in its non-deliverable forwards.
    Traders also expected oil importers to buy it for
settlements.
    "I am not sure if the dollar demand will persist. The game
is to stay long a bit in Asian currencies," said a senior
Malaysian bank trader, adding that the ringgit has room to
strengthen to 3.2600 per dollar.
    
    RUPIAH
    The rupiah eased on month-end dollar demand from local
companies, while foreign and local banks bought the currency on
dips.
    Traders looked for chances to add long positions on the
Indonesian currency, expecting further capital inflows.
    "Sentiment is still bullish on the rupiah with funds still
coming in," said a Jakarta-based currency trader.
    
    BAHT
    The baht edged weaker on dollar demand from some gold
investors for the precious metal, which fell almost 1 percent on
Wednesday in New York, traders said.
    The precious metal is popular among Thai investors, and
slides in gold prices often prompt some to buy physical gold or
futures. Investors might need the dollar to purchase the
precious metal.
    Investors were keeping an eye on Thailand's anti-corruption
agency. It is to bring charges of negligence against Prime
Minister Yingluck Shinawatra later in the day as anti-government
protesters demand her ouster.

title: FOREX -Dollar near 2-week high as geopolitical tensions heat up
text:
* U.S. dollar stays near 2-week highs hit the previous day               

* U.S. warns Russia it would be 'grave mistake' to intervene militarily in Ukraine               

* Aussie dollar slips on weak domestic capital spending data               

By Ian Chua and Masayuki Kitano               

SYDNEY/SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar held near a two-week high against a basket of major currencies on Thursday, as heightening tensions in Ukraine helped support safe-haven demand for the greenback.               

The dollar index was steady at 80.405, not very far from Wednesday's peak of 80.524, its highest since Feb. 13.               

The dollar was underpinned after emerging market currencies  came under renewed pressure on Wednesday, led by a fall in Ukraine's hryvnia after the central bank abandoned a managed exchange rate policy in favour of a flexible currency.               

Raising tensions in the region, President Vladimir Putin ordered 150,000 Russian troops to be ready for war games near Ukraine, prompting the United States to warn Russia that it would be a "grave mistake" to intervene militarily.               

Protest leaders in Ukraine, a former Soviet republic that Putin has called a "brother nation", want to form a new government following the overthrow of pro-Russia President Viktor Yanukovich.               

Against the dollar, the euro held steady at $1.3687. On Wednesday, the euro had touched a low of about $1.3662, its lowest level in about two weeks.               

The heightened tensions in Ukraine could keep the euro on the defensive, analysts said.               

"Clearly it's all very sensitive at the moment and very, very tenuous I guess in terms of the situation," said Mitul Kotecha, head of global foreign exchange strategy for Credit Agricole in Hong Kong.               

"I think that's probably what could provoke a bigger impact, because obviously you could end up seeing a big escalation of tensions between Russia and the West," he added.               

The euro could prove particularly vulnerable versus the yen if tensions grow and risk aversion increases, Kotecha added.               

The euro's moves versus the yen in Asia on Thursday were subdued, however, with the single currency holding steady at 140.12 yen.               

The dollar edged up 0.1 percent versus the yen to 102.41 yen .               

To be sure, there was no widespread panic in markets despite the heightened geopolitical risk. Asian equities were little changed on Thursday, while Wall Street ended nearly flat on Wednesday.               

The Australian dollar fell 0.4 percent to $0.8935, coming under pressure after data showed a surprise 5.2 percent fall in Australian capital spending in the fourth quarter, the biggest drop in more than four years.               

Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen's weather-delayed testimony before the Senate Banking Committee will be closely watched by the market later on Thursday.               

"It would be a huge surprise if she amended the prepared testimony, but there should be plenty of interest in the lengthy Q&A session in front of the Senate Banking Committee," said Sean Callow, a currency strategist at Westpac in Sydney.

(rebecca.howard@wsj.com; @FarroHoward)

16:47 EST - As new Fed chief, Janet Yellen's near six-hour long Congressional testimony on Feb. 11 led bonds up and down, trying to interpret her outlook on the economy and if that means changes in the pace of tapering. title: UPDATE 1-Russian Finance Ministry to buy $6 billion in foreign  currency
text:
(Adds detail, quotes)

By Lidia Kelly

MOSCOW, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Russia's Finance Ministry said on Tuesday it would buy 212.2 billion roubles ($6 billion) in foreign currency via the central bank through open market operations between Feb. 20 and May 31.

It said the move would not impact the Russian currency.

The ministry said the purchases would be fixed at 3.5 billion roubles a day. The funds are earmarked for the budget's $87 billion Reserve Fund, one of two sovereign funds financed from oil taxes.

Plans by the ministry to purchase foreign currency for the Reserve Fund have been a major factor weighing on the rouble in recent weeks. Earlier this month the rouble temporarily rallied when the finance ministry said that it would delay its purchases in order to ease the downward pressure on the Russian currency.

At that time it said it planned to complete the purchases by April 1, a tighter deadline than envisaged in the final version of the plan announced on Tuesday.

The central bank's purchases on the open market will be factored into the bank's daily interventions.

"I think that this won't have a serious impact on the rouble," Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Moiseev told journalists, announcing the plan.

"The main goal of our actions is to ensure banking liquidity. This mechanism allows us not to decrease the amount of liquidity."

The central bank said that the volume of its daily forex market interventions would be adjusted to compensate for the increased purchases of foreign currency by the finance ministry, as would the amount of foreign currency interventions required to provoke a shift in the rouble's floating corridor.

The central bank spends $400 million a day to support the rouble when it is within 95 kopecks of the edge of a floating corridor against a dollar-euro basket, presently set at 34.70-41.70 rouble per basket.

When an intervention allotment of $350 million is spent, the central bank automatically shifts the corridor by five kopecks.

These amounts would be adjusted by $100 million per day as long as the finance ministry purchases are taking place, the central bank said.

"The indicated corrections in volumes of the Bank of Russia's interventions won't have a significant influence on the dynamics of the national currency," the central bank statement said.

The rouble fell in after-hours trade after the finance ministry and central bank statements. At 1325 GMT it was trading at a record low of 41.45 against the dollar-euro basket , down 0.9 percent on the day.

title: Russia's freeze on grain restocking may be premature - SovEcon
text:
MOSCOW, Feb 14 (Reuters) - Russia's decision to freeze a programme to replenish state stocks next week may be premature if Kazakhstan takes advantage of its weak currency to boost exports to Russia, SovEcon agriculture analysts said on Friday.

One of the world's key wheat exporters, Russia has about 1.8 million tonnes of grain in "intervention stocks", which are used to boost domestic supply in years of poor harvests and to support prices in years of large crops.

The government planned to replenish the stocks during the 2013/14 marketing year, which started on July 1, but is far from its target as the prices it offers are below market rates.

"It's more lucrative for farmers to sell (grain) at the market price than to intervention stocks now," SovEcon said in a note. The government has bought 0.6 million tonnes of grain on the market in Siberia so far in 2013/14 out of plans to buy up to 6 million tonnes.

It will hold the last intervention tender on Feb. 18 after which the programme will be frozen, the Agriculture ministry said on Friday. It bought 270 tonnes of grain - feed barley - for the stock on Feb. 12.

"This decision will be premature," SovEcon said.

Bigger imports from Kazakhstan may depress prices giving farmers in Siberia and Urals region reason to sell their grain to state stocks this spring, it added.

The maximum government price for the third class wheat has been 6,250 roubles ($180) per tonne on intervention tenders compared with an up to 6,600 roubles market price in Siberia last week.

Kazakhstan's central bank devalued the national currency by 19 percent on Feb. 11 to about 185 per dollar to prevent large-scale foreign exchange speculation and adjust to a freer rouble float in Russia, Kazakhstan's main trading partner.

Central Asia's largest grain producer, Kazakhstan still has up to 4.5 million tonnes of grains available for export until the end of 2013/14 marketing year, according to official data.

Russian Agriculture ministry was not able to comment immediately on whether intervention tenders would be resumed later this year.

($1 = 35.2125 Russian roubles) (Reporting by Polina Devitt, editing by David Evans)

title: Bank of Russia Moves Ruble Band Higher For 15th Time in 2014
text:
By Lukas I. Alpert 
 

MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia said Tuesday it has shifted the ruble's trading band higher for the fifteenth time so far in 2014, as continued selling pressure amid a broader emerging market slide has dropped the Russian currency to its lowest point in five years.

The central bank said on its website that it moved the ruble's floating trading band 5 kopecks higher to RUB34.30-RUB41.30 against the euro-dollar basket, which is the central bank's main gauge of the currency market.

The ruble was trading at 41.14 against the basket early Tuesday. Downward pressure on the ruble has intensified after the U.S. Federal Reserve said it would draw back from its bond-buying approach, signalling an exit from its easy-money policies.

At the upper end, the Russian central bank sells dollars and euros to ease downside pressure on the ruble -- as has been the case in the past few months. The bank buys foreign currencies when the ruble strengthens toward the lower boundary of the band. Once an intervention allotment of $350 million is exhausted, it automatically shifts the corridor.

The Bank of Russia isn't planning to stop its interventions on the forex market, the head of the central bank, Elvira Nabiullina, said Friday. The central bank, however, will stick to its policy of reducing interventions and permit a more flexible ruble exchange rate starting in 2015, she said.

title: MORNING BID: EUROPE-A daily note from our Economics/Politics Editor
text:
LONDON, Feb 3 (Reuters) - The European Central Bank meets on Thursday with emerging market tumult bang at the top of its agenda.

It's probably too early to force a policy move this week - particularly since the next set of ECB economic and inflation forecasts are due in March - but it's an unwelcome development at a time when inflation is already uncomfortably low, dropping further to just 0.7 percent in January.

If the market turbulence persists and a by-product is to drive the euro higher, which is quite possible, the downward pressure on prices could threaten a deflationary spiral which ECB policymakers have so far insisted will not come to pass.

Euro zone and UK PMI surveys for January will give the latest on the state of Europe's economic recovery this morning. The Markit/HSBC manufacturing PMI for China has fallen to a six-month low.

The ECB will reveal more detail today on how it plans to go about checking that top euro zone banks have the risks on their balance sheets under control, laying out how it will define when a loan has turned bad and what the next steps will be.

Watch out for signs of coordinated international discussions ahead of the G20 finance ministers in Sydney later in February. Indian central bank governor Raghuram Rajan, a former IMF chief economist, has slammed what he said was a breakdown in global monetary coordination.

Some central banks have already been thrown out of kilter. Turkey whacked up its key rate by more than 4 percentage points last week without doing much good for the lira. South Africa tightened with the same lack of success. Neither move would have been considered remotely likely a month ago.

A failed debt auction in Hungary, Romania being forced to intervene to bolster its leu currency and Russia's central bank declaring it was ready to provide unlimited intervention to support the rouble all showed how contagion can quickly take hold.

Turkey remains the most vulnerable on our patch with Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan's aggressive response to a corruption inquiry unnerving investors already struggling with the impact of the Fed's taper.

Erdogan has promised an "out of the ordinary" economic package without giving any detail and the government has ruled out capital controls. He is determined to maintain growth with elections looming and has railed against what he describes as an "interest rate lobby" of speculators seeking to undermine his country.

Turkey's PMI and latest inflation data are due shortly. Erdogan is due in Berlin.

Ukraine is an equally extraordinary story. President Viktor Yanukovich is due back at work having gone to ground on "sick leave" and appears increasingly isolated having offered a string of concessions to his political opponents but failed to co-opt them.

Kiev bowed to intense Western pressure on Sunday to let an opposition activist fly abroad for treatment after his abduction, torture and then attempted arrest.

Intriguingly, the EU appears not to have given up on luring Ukraine into its fold. It was Yanukovich's decision to shun that offer and turn back to Russia that sparked this whole crisis.

EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton said she was working with the United States on a "Ukrainian Plan" to help support the economy through a period of political transition - an idea that may be designed to help Ukraine cope with any backlash from Moscow, on which it relies for trade and energy.

Moscow is bailing out Ukraine to the tune of $15 billion. President Vladimir Putin said last week Moscow would wait until a new government was formed before fully implementing the bailout deal.

South Africa also bears watching. President Jacob Zuma, SARB Governor Gill Marcus and Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan speak at a Bloomberg Africa Summit on Monday. Ongoing strikes in the platinum sector and the emerging turmoil must be focusing minds with elections approaching.

One of the by-products of the markets' sell-off has been a push up in yields for the euro zone's sicklier members, particularly Greece. Athens will post a sizeable primary budget surplus this year and hopes this will unlock the key to further help from its partners in getting its mammoth debts under control.

Der Spiegel reported that Germany's finance ministry is preparing the ground for a third aid package for Greece before European elections in May. The possibilities outlined include a further debt haircut that would mainly hit public creditors or a "limited additional programme" in which Greece could receive 10-20 billion euros from the European rescue fund. (Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: UPDATE 1-EMERGING MARKETS-Fresh turbulence drives down  currencies , bonds again
text:
LONDON, Jan 31 (Reuters) - Fresh waves of turbulence engulfed emerging markets on Friday, with a renewed slide in the Russian rouble and a sharp rise in bond yields across the board despite policymakers' efforts to staunch the bleeding.

Signs grew that stress is increasingly spreading to central European countries such as Poland and Hungary, which fared relatively well in the first sell-off phase earlier this month.

Poland delayed publication of its monthly debt supply plan until next week due to market turbulence and an overhaul of its pension scheme, a day after Hungary was forced to cut a T-bill action because of a 67 bps jump in yields.

"We are in a negative feedback loop of weak currencies, higher interest rates, weak growth and capital outflows. This feedback loop needs to play out and that means at the end of the day EM assets need to become much cheaper," said David Hauner, head of EEMEA fixed income strategy and economics at Bank of AmericaMerrill Lynch.

"Only then will people come back to buy," he added.

Hungary's central bank was the latest to wade in with assurances that it would act to soothe markets if needed, adding to earlier verbal intervention from India and Russia, as well as big rate rises in Turkey and South Africa.

But the Hungarian forint fell 1.5 percent to the euro , hitting two-year lows, while bond yields jumped 20 basis points across the curve.

"Fears are growing that if the central bank cannot stop the forint's fall in any other way, this will lead to an interest rate hike in the end," a bond trader in Budapest said.

In neighbouring Poland, 10-year bond yields rose 10 basis points to a 4-1/2 month high after the government delayed its debt supply plan and the zloty lost 0.5 percent.

The spotlight remains on the rouble. A rally that started late on Thursday proved short-lived, taking the Russian currency down more than 1 percent, back towards five-year lows against the dollar.

Analysts said the central bank's plans for "unlimited interventions" should the rouble stray outside a target band, had squeezed out short rouble positions on Thursday but the broad trend for flight was very much intact.

The lira and the rand fell almost 1 percent and South African domestic bond yields hit the highest since mid-2011, as markets priced in more rate rises in coming months.

In equity markets, MSCI's main emerging markets index traded just off 4-1/2 month lows and are on track for their biggest monthly loss since mid-2012.

Domestic emerging bond yields have risen around 40 basis points since the start of January and sovereign dollar bond yields have jumped about 50 bps this month on JPMorgan indices.

Pressure is mounting on other emerging central banks to defend their currencies, with Mexico likely to warn later on Friday that it is ready to raise interest rates if needed. The peso is trading just off 18-month lows.

CHINA, FED, CENTRAL BANKS

BofA/ML's Hauner said the moves were being exacerbated by thinner liquidity, caused by the lunar New Year holidays across much of Asia including China where weaker-than-expected growth data was at least partly behind the latest sell-off of emerging market assets.

That added to jitters regarding the U.S. Federal Reserve, which confirmed on Wednesday it would shave another $10 billion from its monthly money printing.

"What's driving this is the fear of a Chinese slowdown and what I want to see is some kind of policy action from the People's bank of China (PBOC)," said Lars Christensen, chief emerging markets analyst at Danske Bank.

India's central bank governor Raghuram Rajan has slammed what he called a breakdown in global monetary coordination, saying developed countries could not "wash their hands" of the turmoil caused in emerging economies by their actions.

Christensen said that in the absence of PBOC input, emerging central bank action, interventions or policy tightening, was unlikely to be effective.

"Russia has indicated they will defend the rouble vigorously (but) my fear is a repeat of 2008 when they spent $200 billion to defend an artifical rouble peg," he said.

Russian 5- and 10-year bond yields rose to 16-month highs, pricing in the likelihood of an interest rate rise in February.

Russian weakness is partly behind the 2.5 percent tumble in the Ukrainian hryvnia, analysts said, referring to the currency's biggest one-day loss since 2009.

But respite from the Fed or China is unlikely, analysts say, noting China wants to engineer a slowdown in its economy while the United States has flagged its plans well in advance.

Hauner expect more pain ahead for emerging markets.

"What's going on now is not the fault of the Fed," he said. "The turmoil is down to China but also the fact that EM currencies and interest rates were misaligned," he said. "We are now around fair value but as history shows us, any selloff in these has a tendency to overshoot."

title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Dollar, stocks advance after strong U.S. GDP
text:
* Emerging markets turmoil eases, Russia pledges on ruble

* Gold, U.S. Treasuries fall after U.S. GDP report

* U.S., European stocks rebound

* Emerging markets equities pare losses

By Herbert Lash

NEW YORK, Jan 30 (Reuters) - The dollar strengthened and global equity markets rebounded on Thursday after data showed the U.S. economy grew strongly in the last quarter of 2013, a rate that suggests solid corporate earnings and continued solid growth into the new year.

Turmoil in emerging markets eased, as the hard-hit Turkish lira and South African rand rebounded. Russia's central bank pledged unlimited foreign exchange interventions if the ruble strays outside its target band.

"There was a general rebound in risk sentiment," said Jeffrey Young, U.S. interest rate strategist at Nomura Securities International in New York. "Some confidence grew back with the emerging markets story no longer developing."

The ruble hit record lows against the euro early in the session, while the rand slid to multi-year troughs before rebounding. Moves earlier in the week by Turkey, South Africa and India to staunch capital flight had failed.

Emerging market currencies have felt the heat since the U.S. Federal Reserve said it would begin to trim its stimulus, a program that has injected more than $3 trillion into the U.S. economy and world markets since the onset of the financial crisis.

The U.S. Commerce Department reported that gross domestic product grew at a 3.2 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter, which combined with the 4.1 percent pace in the third quarter resulted in the biggest half-year increase since 2003.

The GDP growth, which was in line with economists' expectations, drove a turnaround in equity markets in Europe and a broad rise in Wall Street stocks. The S&P 500 scored its biggest gain in more than a month, and the Nasdaq composite index gained more than 2 percent at one point, helped by strong quarterly revenue growth at Facebook Inc.

Facebook shares rose 14.1 percent to finish at a record closing high of $61.08.

The dollar was up 0.7 percent against a basket of six major currencies, at 81.069, and the appeal of the greenback revived against the safe-haven yen and Swiss franc.

"There's a lot of concern over what's happening overseas but in the domestic (U.S.) market GDP was pretty strong," said Cam Albright, director of asset allocation at Wilmington Trust Investment Advisors in Wilmington, Delaware. "If you see growth in the economy pointing to higher earnings growth, that will give markets more confidence in the United States."

The Fed, as expected, said on Wednesday it will cut its monthly bond purchases by another $10 billion in February, to $65 billion, as policymakers see less need for stimulus.

"The end of QE is an indication the economy is getting better, though I'm not sure the market has entirely transitioned to that idea yet," Albright said.

The euro fell 0.81 percent against the dollar at $1.3552, while against the yen the greenback was up 0.38 percent at 102.67 yen.

A measure of global equity markets, MSCI's all-country world index, rebounded, rising 0.19 percent. MSCI's emerging markets index, however, was slightly lower, down 0.22 percent.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones industrial average rose 109.82 points, or 0.7 percent, to 15,848.61. The S&P 500 gained 19.99 points, or 1.13 percent, to 1,794.19, and the Nasdaq Composite added 71.691 points, or 1.77 percent, to 4,123.125.

In after-hours trade, shares of Google Inc jumped 4.4 percent to $1,186, after closing up 2.6 percent in regular Nasdaq trade. Google reported quarterly revenue that beat Wall Street targets after the market close.

In Europe the pan-regional FTSEurofirst 300 index of leading companies closed up 0.3 percent at 1,294.26.

Gold fell more than 2 percent, on track for its biggest one-day drop in more than a month, as the U.S. GDP data and the Fed's decision to keep trimming its stimulus boosted the dollar and led traders to cash in gains in the metal.

U.S. COMEX gold futures for February delivery settled down $20 an ounce at $1,242.20.

Brent oil rose to just over $108 per barrel, and U.S. crude reached its highest level in a month on bitter cold weather in the United States, which has boosted heating oil demand.

Brent crude rose 10 cents to settle at $107.95 a barrel. U.S. crude settled up 87 cents at $98.23.

The U.S. bond market retreated following Wednesday's rally, but some of the money leaving equities found its way into the developed world's government bond market.

German Bund futures rose 33 ticks to settle at 143.23, while German 10-year yields fell to their lowest level in nearly six months before ending at 1.712 percent.

Benchmark 10-year Treasury notes were last down 5/32 in price to yield 2.6949 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian  central bank  sticks to plans for free float - Nabiullina
text:
(Adds quotes)

MOSCOW, Jan 30 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank will stick to its plans to get the rouble floating freely by next year, Governor Elvira Nabiullina said on Thursday, but did not rule out occasional currency market intervention.

A heavy selloff of emerging markets currencies, driven by a flight to the dollar as the U.S. Federal Reserve scales back its monetary stimulus, has put the Bank of Russia's complex intervention mechanism to the test this month.

Nabiullina said Russia's central bank will pursue its strategic shift towards a policy of inflation targeting, but this would not rule out the possibility of central bank intervention on the foreign exchange market.

"We intend to observe these deadlines, as declared previously, of increasing the (flexibility) of the exchange rate this year," she told reporters.

"In our monetary and credit policy we do not intend to forsake interventions completely. We do intend to continue them to support financial stability," she told reporters, adding: "We will of course scale back interventions - this is a declared policy goal and we will stick to it."

The central bank now runs a "dirty" float of the rouble, conducting limited interventions as its exchange rate nears the edge of a flexible corridor. It made clear earlier that rouble interventions could be unlimited if it strays outside the band.

In its statements, the regulator has sought to clarify, but not change, a mechanism that foresees a shift of 5 kopecks in the rouble's trading band against a dollar-euro basket when an intervention allotment of $350 million is exhausted.

Maximum daily interventions inside the seven-rouble corridor are $400 million. The central bank announced on Thursday that it had shifted the corridor by 25 kopecks the day before, implying that its dollar sales reached at least $1.75 billion. title: Why Can Ruble Continue To Fall Even As  Russia  Successfully  Intervenes ? -- Barron's Blog
text:
Russia's ruble has come under fire in this year's emerging markets currency sell-off. Year-to-date, ruble lost about 7% against the dollar and, earlier this week, dropped to its lowest value against the dollar since March, 2009.

Ruble is not a currency associated with current account deficits, so why has there been a sell-off? Michael Shaoul at Marketfield Asset Management explains:

What is important about the RUB is that it is not a currency associated with current account deficits and has also been largely out of the headlines in recent weeks. On the other hand Russia does share very close trade and financial ties with Turkey (much of which takes place in the gray economy) and it is therefore unsurprising that the collapse of the TRY has spilled across the Black Sea to its larger neighbor. We would advise readers to watch the RUB and local equity and bond markets closely in the days ahead.

So far, Russia's central bank has been intervening in the currency markets to prop up the ruble. Given the size of Russia's foreign reserves, the central bank has plenty of room to maneuver. Here is Capital Economics:

For now, the scale of intervention has been relatively small. The Bank has so far sold $5bn this month (to give some perspective, during the 2008/09 ruble devaluation the CBR was selling over $40bn a month). With some $500bn in FX reserves, it can stomach intervention on this scale for some time.

But it would do us well to understand how Russia's central bank operates. It is possible that the ruble will keep on falling even as the central bank successfully intervenes, because the exchange rate corridor that Russia operates on is not fixed but a moving target. Here is Capital Economics again:

The CBR allows the ruble to float freely against its dollar-euro basket (0.55*US$+0.45*Euro) when it is within a "neutral" corridor, currently 35.9-38.9/basket. If the exchange rate is up to one ruble outside this, the CBR intervenes in the FX market, but this is limited to $200mn per day (and limited to $400mn per day if the exchange rate is between one and two rubles outside the neutral corridor). If the exchange rate is more than two rubles higher or lower than the neutral corridor, then the CBR will intervene in the FX market in unlimited quantities.

however, for every $350mn of the CBR's intervention, it moves the corridor by five kopeks towards the current exchange rate. As such, even if the CBR is selling unlimited quantities of FX, it isn't defending a specific peg. In other words, as the CBR steps up FX intervention, the ruble can continue to weaken

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies  Claw Back Some Ground -- Update
text:
Emerging-market currencies recovered from earlier losses on Thursday, as U.S. markets opened to some upbeat economic data and corporate earnings.

But broad risk sentiment recovered later in the session, after data confirmed the U.S. economy grew 3.2% in the fourth quarter of 2013. U.S. stocks opened higher, recovering some of Wednesday's losses, while European indexes bounced back from early declines.

The recent pullback from emerging-market currencies had continued earlier Thursday, after the U.S. Federal Reserve confirmed expectations that it would scale back its bond-buying program by a further $10 billion a month.

The Hungarian forint bore the brunt of the early selling pressure, mimicking large declines in the Turkish lira and South African rand earlier in the week--drops that surprise rate rises from central banks have been powerless to reverse in the short term.

But the forint recovered its early losses against the euro, as some analysts said the broad weakness in emerging markets looked exaggerated.

"The market appears to be treating tapering as actual tightening, which is an overreaction. Tactically, emerging markets look oversold," said George Iwanicki, global emerging markets strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

"As painful as it may be in the short term, it is actually very positive that the brunt of the pain from tapering is being felt through currency adjustments; this is making emerging markets more competitive as a whole. Encouragingly, we are seeing central banks responding with orthodox moves like rate hikes."

Turkey and South Africa--among a group of emerging markets that have struggled to defend their currencies as investors adjust to more restrictive monetary policy in big economies--also benefited from the more optimistic tone.

The Turkish lira bounced from earlier lows to strengthen 0.8% to 224.34 lira to the dollar. Despite the recovery, it remains at a similar level to where it traded before the Turkish central bank raised rates.

The South African rand added 1.6% against the buck, having earlier traded close to a five-year low.

The Russian ruble, which hit a near-five-year low earlier Thursday, clawed back 0.5% against the dollar. The currency was given an added boost after the head of Russia's central bank said there were no plans to stop foreign-exchange interventions after 2014.

Hungary and Russia have moved into the market's cross hairs as the recent spate of emerging-market rate increases-- India also bumped up rates earlier this week--ramped up the pressure on countries that haven't followed suit.

"When Turkey got bullied into hiking rates by the market, there were two next: South Africa and Russia, neither of which had hiked and had become low yielders. The Hungarian forint is next," said Bartosz Pawlowski, global head of emerging-market strategy at BNP Paribas.

Hungary's central bank still has room to continue cutting interest rates, its governor said Wednesday, despite the recent weakness in the forint. The central bank has been trimming rates in small increments for several months.

But Hungary's large reserves of foreign exchange give it greater room for a fightback than many emerging-market nations.

"If officials get uncomfortable with the slide in the forint, I think they will intervene. They have the artillery to do that," Mr. Pawlowski said.

European equities picked up after the U.S. data, having earlier been dragged down by the tension surrounding emerging markets. The Stoxx Europe 600 index was 0.3% higher, while Germany's DAX added 0.4%. London's FTSE 100 lagged behind, paring losses to trade at 0.1% down.

In the U.S., the S&P 500 was up 0.7% in early trade.

Overnight, the Nikkei had dived 2.5%, wiping out most of Wednesday's gains, which came before the positive effects of the Turkish rate rise melted away.

In a further knock to global confidence, purchasing managers' data for January brought more evidence that manufacturing in China is slowing.

Elsewhere in currency markets, the New Zealand dollar remained lower after the country's central bank left interest rates on hold. Citigroup reported widespread selling of the New Zealand dollar against its Australian counterpart, with funds, companies and banks all joining the fray.

title: Russia could consider delaying rouble float -econ minister
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 28 (Reuters) - Russia could delay plans to move to a floating rouble and instead consider limits on the exchange rate, Economy Minister Alexei Ulyukayev said on Tuesday after a sharp sell-off in the currency in recent weeks.

"Under the current conditions, there are other possible approaches to the concept of a floating rouble and to the pace of their implementation," Ulyukayev told journalists at a briefing.

"Ï would have discussed the possibility of introducing certain limits on the degree of freedom of the exchange rate depending on several factors related to financial stability."

Russia's central bank has announced plans to cease targeted interventions on the currency market and shift to a free float of the rouble by 2015, allowing the currency to absorb the shocks of the country's weakening economy.

"Ï might have discussed timing and maybe moving it," Ulyukayev said.

The central bank's plan to target inflation rather than the exchange rate has been seen as potentially helping the economy, but it has also exacerbated a weakening in the rouble.

Worries about China's economy and expectations of the United States easing its monetary stimulus have pushed the rouble to all-time lows against the euro and 4.5 percent down versus the dollar amid a rout in emerging markets, although the currency broke its fall on Tuesday.

Ulyukayev said he sees inflation in 2014 below 5 percent. The annual increase in consumer prices stood at 6.5 percent in December, above the bank's 5-6 percent target range for this year.

"The risk for economic growth is more salient and acute than the risk of inflation ... Formally there is no stagflation. There is a risk (of it) but I believe that we have a pretty clear perspective on inflation. It will decrease and the risk to growth is much greater."

Ulyukayev also said that state companies should pay only 25 percent of their profits in dividends, rather than a 35 percent figure proposed by the Finance Ministry under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).

In the long-running debate, Russia has been considering whether to make state companies pay higher dividends to replenish government coffers and reassure foreign investors worried by a slowing economy.

The government told state companies in November 2012 that they must pay at least 25 percent of their income in dividends, an increase from 15 percent. A later proposal pushed it to 35 percent.

"We do not think it relevant for state companies to raise dividends to 35 percent in the medium term. We are no longer discussing 35 percent, 25 percent IFRS is reasonable," Ulyukayev said. He said it was important to have a clear dividend policy and move gradually to 25 percent.

title: Russia Economy Minister Says Slow Growth Is Higher Risk
text:
MOSCOW--Russia faces more risks of slow growth than of high inflation, even despite a sharp weakening of the ruble, the country's economy minister said Tuesday.

Speaking to reporters, Alexei Ulyukayev said, "Risks for the growth are more acute and present, than the risks of high inflation," adding that Russia isn't in stagflation--a combination of slow growth and high inflation.

Russia's deputy head of the Central bank Ksenia Yudayeva said Jan. 15 that Russia is facing stagflation. Russia's economic growth slowed to 1.4% in 2013, a far cry from an average of about 7% before the financial crisis of 2008, or 5% a year set by President Vladimir Putin as a midterm goal. Inflation stood at 6.5% in 2013 above the Central Bank's target.

However Mr. Ulyukayev was adamant Russia's inflation will stay below 5% in 2014 even amid the ruble's weakening. The ruble is trading at its 5-year's low against the dollar, off more than 3% since the start of the year after shedding 10% in 2013.

The bank of Russia is gradually withdrawing from foreign exchange market interventions, setting 2015 as a target for a fully free-floating ruble and inflation-targeting policy.

Mr. Ulyukayev, who until mid-2013 was the Russian Central Bank's first deputy, said he'd discuss a possibility of postponing the introduction of these measures and a broader approach no a nonintervention policy.

"I'd probably put to a discussion a possibility to introduce some limitations to the free floating regime depending on financial stability, and, possibly discuss the timing of the introduction [of the regime]," he said.

The minister sees investment as the key to regaining the economy's momentum. To this end he supports consolidation in the banking sector, stronger loan guaranties and measures to decrease lenders' liabilities, notably their deposit rates, to permit lenders' credit business and households at lower rates.

The minister added "it's highly probable Russia's current account will remain positive, albeit declining in midterm."

title: Ruble Weakens to New Low Versus euro
text:
MOSCOW--The Russian ruble hit a new low against the euro Monday, but the selloff in emerging markets was not entirely to blame.

Some analysts say the Bank of Russia's determination to let the ruble float freely from 2015 is also dragging the currency down.

U.S. Federal Reserve's plans to reel in stimulus and weak economic data from China have prompted investors to pull back from riskier bets in recent days. On Friday, what began as localized selloffs in emerging markets morphed into a broad flight to safety--a pattern that persisted Monday.

The Russian unit hit its weakest level ever of 47.72 rubles against the euro. It firmed 0.2% to 47.30 by the end of the day. Versus the dollar, the ruble eased 0.2% to 34.60 after briefly hitting 34.86, its weakest level since March 2009.

The Russian currency also shed 0.4% to 40.48 against the euro-dollar basket, a level last seen in early 2009.

The Bank of Russia recently reduced its daily interventions on behalf of the ruble. It now shifts the ruble's trading band five kopecks higher against the basket once the amount of accumulated interventions reaches $350 million. The central bank discloses the boundaries daily.

Fewer interventions would mean a faster but shorter depreciation of the ruble, said Maria Pomelnikova, an analyst at Raiffeisen Bank in Moscow. To defend the upper boundary of the ruble's trading band, the central bank sells unlimited amount of dollars and euros.

Ms. Pomelnikova said she suspects the band was moved four times today and is now located at RUB33.70-RUB40.70. The band stood at 33.50-40.50 rubles early Monday.

Russia's sluggish economic performance is also weighing on the ruble. Bruised by diminished investment, the economy grew just 1.4% in 2013, the slowest pace since the crisis. Capital investment fell 0.3% on the year, official data showed Monday.

Russia was one of the worst performing emerging markets last year compared with precrisis dynamics, Alfa Bank said in a note.

"Combined with overall global investor dissatisfaction with emerging market growth prospects, we take this news as cause for additional nervousness on the local forex market," the bank said.

The trend could reverse this week as companies face tax payments at the end of the month that prompt exporters to convert foreign currencies into rubles.

"As soon as the ruble stops falling and shows stability for around a week, it is quite possible that there will be a rebound of more than one ruble," Ms. Pomelnikova said.

title: EMERGING MARKETS-Rand hits 5-year low on PMI, rouble edges off lows
text:
LONDON, Jan 15 (Reuters) - South Africa's rand hit a five-year low against the dollar on Wednesday after data indicated contraction in the manufacturing sector, while the rouble recovered slightly from 4-1/2 year lows hit this week on a cut in forex interventions.

South Africa's purchasing managers' index ended 2013 at 49.9, below the 50 level that denotes expansion and its weakest level in eight months.

South Africa is one of the "Fragile Five" deficit economies hit hard by expectations of a reduction in the U.S. bond-buying programme that had fuelled demand for higher-yielding assets.

"The key story is that nothing changed over Christmas to alter investors' framework, they are still worried about the Fragile Five," said Charles Robertson, chief economist at Renaissance Capital.

"For investors to change their view ... you would need to see a better current account outlook and/or improved GDP figures."

The rand fell more than 1 percent to five-year lows close to 11 per dollar. South African stocks rallied more than 1 percent, however, with Massmart climbing 5 percent following a positive trading statement.

The MSCI emerging equities index edged up 0.2 percent after the World Bank raised its growth forecasts for the global economy for the first time in three years.

But the World Bank cut its 2014 growth forecast for emerging markets to 5.3 from 5.6 percent seen in June and warned of the risk of sudden changes in interest rates.

"Abrupt changes in market expectations, resulting in global bond yields increasing by 100 to 200 basis points within a couple of quarters, could lead to a sharp reduction in capital inflows to developing countries by between 50 and 80 percent for several months," it said.

(http://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/global-economic-prospects)

The rouble hit four-month lows against the dollar for a second day but recovered slightly from 4-1/2 year lows hit against its dollar-euro basket after the central bank said this week it would scale back forex interventions.

Russia's central bank has no exchange rate target and is shifting towards a free float of the rouble to insulate the economy from volatility on global markets, First Deputy Chairwoman Ksenia Yudayeva said on Wednesday.

The currencies of Russia's neighbours were also weak - the Ukrainian hryvnia tested four-year lows and the Kazakh tenge hit its lowest in 11 years.

Emerging sovereign debt spreads inched in by 1 basis point to 345 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

Emerging European sovereign borrowers have been dashing to raise money in international markets this month.

Following 10- and 30-year dollar bonds from Romania this week, Serbia said on Tuesday it will issue a 600 million euro bond this year.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian  central bank  halts 'targeted'  FX interventions
text:
(Adds context, analyst, refinancing auction)

MOSCOW, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Monday it was ceasing 'targeted' interventions on the currency market as part of a strategic shift towards letting the rouble float completely freely.

The reduction to zero of targeted interventions, which had been set at $60 million per day, will increase the flexibility of the exchange rate corridor used by the central bank and reduce its presence on the market.

This will allow the currency to serve as an external shock absorber for Russia's weakening economy, while reinforcing the role of interest rate policy.

"This adjustment was carried out with the goal of increasing the flexibility of determining the exchange rate, as part of making the gradual shift to a free float of the rouble by 2015," it said in a statement.

The Bank of Russia traditionally conducts targeted interventions to offset the impact of expected imbalances on the current account that are largely the result of changes in the price of oil, the country's main export.

In addition, the central bank targets the rouble's exchange rate against a euro-dollar basket, raising interventions if the currency approaches the edge of an exchange-rate corridor and shifting the range once a $350 million allotment is exhausted.

The central bank last week again adjusted the corridor, allowing the rouble to weaken by 5 kopecks and setting its new range at 33.15 to 40.15 roubles to the forex basket.

The rouble eased slightly after Monday's announcement, trading at 38.67 to the basket compared to 38.55 previously.

Dmitry Polevoy, ING's chief economist in Russia, said in a note that the move confirmed his forecast of rouble weakening.

Under Governor Elvira Nabiullina, appointed last June, the central bank has surprised the market with its hawkish stance, holding its policy rate at 5.5 percent as inflation has strayed above target.

The regulator has, however, sought to keep the banking system liquid: in a separate announcement, the central bank said it had auctioned 480 billion roubles ($14.5 billion) in three-month funds at a cut-off rate of 5.76 percent. title: Bank of  Russia  Scraps 'Targeted'  Forex Interventions --Update
text:
MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia said it would cut interventions to support the Russian ruble in a step toward floating the national currency by 2015, a move that will likely accelerate its weakening.

The central bank will eliminate daily sales totaling $60 million Monday, preparing the market for when it ceases to support the exchange rate, the bank said. It will, however, continue larger sales of dollars and euros if the ruble rises toward the edge of a trading band.

The ruble slipped after the announcement, ending 0.7% lower at 38.7 against the euro-dollar basket.

"The ruble's volatility will increase and will be similar to that on other emerging markets. If funds leave emerging markets in the next few months, than the ruble is set to weaken," said Vladimir Kolychev, chief economist at VTB Capital in Moscow.

The ruble was off 0.8% at 33.3 against the U.S. dollar Monday. ING Bank forecasts it will weaken further to 35.7 rubles a dollar by the end of the year, as Russia continues to grapple with slow economic growth and high capital outflows.

The ruble weakened 8% against the basket last year amid concerns that investors would pull back from emerging markets as the U.S. Federal Reserve began to taper its bond-buying program.

Russia has long used its large foreign currency reserves to defend the ruble against sharp depreciation. The central bank is shifting its monetary policy to focus on the stubbornly high level of inflation rather than the exchange rate by 2015, meaning it will manage liquidity in the economy through interest-rate policy only.

Government officials have said that a weaker ruble could help Russia's economy--buffeted by weaker prices and diminished demand for its commodities exports--which the government forecast would grow 1.4% last year. Growth slowed to 1.3% year-over-year in November, the most recent figures available,

A free-floating ruble could also help Russia to proceed with its ambitious plan to make the ruble a regional currency and possibly a reserve currency.

The central bank keeps the ruble within a floating range against a basket made up 55% of dollars and 45% of euros. It sells dollars and euros to ease downside pressure on the ruble when it hovers in the upper range of the band. In the lower range, it buys foreign currencies, and in the middle it carries out no interventions.

That range is from 38.2 rubles to 39.2 rubles, and the central bank sells $200 million a day to smooth out excessive volatility. When the total purchases or sales of foreign currencies exceed $350 million, the central bank moves the ruble band five kopecks either way.

MOSCOW, Dec 11 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble, which has officially acquired a new symbol to gain recognition on global markets, edged down on Wednesday, pressured by sluggish economic growth and year-end corporate selling.

The rouble was down 0.2 percent against the dollar at 32.77 , and 0.1 percent lower to 45.11 against the euro, leaving it 0.2 percent weaker at 38.32 against the dollar-euro basket.

"A weak macro environment is likely to keep rouble trading softly," Vladimir Osakovsky, an economist at BofAML said in a note, adding it was likely to remain dependent on year-end seasonal flows, such as debt payouts, and on the oil price.

Osakovsky sees the rouble at 33 per dollar by the end of this year and into next.

Russia's central bank approved the public's choice of a Cyrillic "P" with horizontal strokes as its official symbol, backing Kremlin efforts to enhance the international appeal of the currency.

The symbol was picked out of five proposed logos in a poll on the central bank website. In Russia's Cyrillic alphabet, the first letter of the word rouble resembles the Latin "P", a possible source of confusion for many foreigners.

"I don't see anything terrible (in the Cyrillic letter), investors will get used to it, as they did to balalaika or matryoshka," said Denis Davydov, an analyst at Nordea bank, referring to the instrument and the dolls.

The central bank is allowing the currency to float more freely as Russia opens up its markets to foreign investors.

On Tuesday Russia's central bank cut the amount of cumulative intervention it would make to maintain the rouble's floating exchange rate corridor to $350 million from $400 million.

The central bank has sold around $23 billion in currency market interventions in the year to date, so the rouble is trading 1.0-1.5 stronger against the dollar than it otherwise would be, Natalia Orlova, economist at Alfa bank said.

Reuters calculations suggest the central bank has sold around $24.5 billion to stem the rouble's slide this year.

Moscow stock indexes inched up, trimming earlier losses with uncertainty over whether the Federal Reserve will start scaling back its bond buying next week capping further gains.

At 1248 GMT the rouble-denominated MICEX index was up 0.3 percent at 1,468 points and dollar-denominated RTS index rose 0.1 percent to 1,411 points.

The Russian stock market is traditionally strong in the fourth quarter and some investors are still hoping for a rally ahead of the New Year.

The RTS index has performed positively in December since 1995 with an average 5.9 percent monthly return but is down 1.4 percent over the current quarter and up 0.6 percent so far this month.

"The retreat in November has created a 6 percent fundamental upside," Slava Smolyaninov, a strategist at Uralsib Capital said in a note.

MOSCOW--Russia's central bank said Friday it will fully switch to inflation targeting and float the ruble by 2015.

In its report on monetary policy for 2014-2016, which will be submitted to the government later this year, the Bank of Russia said it has set an inflation target of 4.5% for 2014 and 2015, and 4% for 2016, while setting the maximum deviation from the target at 150 basis points either way.

The central bank also said it would gradually reduce its foreign-exchange interventions in 2014, before floating the ruble by 2015.

title: Bank of Russia to Tolerate Quicker Ruble Weakening
text:
MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia has curtailed the amount of foreign exchange interventions needed to move the ruble's trading band, it said on its website late Monday, opening the door for a quicker weakening of the currency.

The central bank started selling dollars and euros in order to tame the ruble's weakening in April and since then it has sold more than $13 billion and around 850 million euros ($1.12 billion), with interventions increasing after the ruble fell to its 2013 low in August.

The central bank said on its website that it made the move "in order to further increase flexibility of the exchange rate".

Keeping the ruble within a floating range against the euro-dollar basket, the central bank will now move this corridor by five kopecks either way if the amount of its accumulated purchases or sales of foreign currencies exceeds $400 million.

Previously, the central bank had to buy or sell $450 million to move the band, which it did 14 times this year, bringing the band to RUB32.20-RUB39.20 versus the basket on Sept. 4 from RUB31.65-RUB38.65 as of late 2012.

In the upper range of the band the central bank sells dollars and euros to ease downside pressure on the ruble and starts buying foreign currencies when the ruble firms toward the lower boundary of the band. In the middle of the corridor the central bank carries out no interventions.

ING bank said in a research note that the central bank's decision will result in "a bit quicker" five-kopeck shifts in the corridor should the ruble remain under selling pressure.

Since the start of the year, the ruble has weakened by nearly 9% against the dollar, hit by expectations of tapering of quantitative easing in the U.S., Russia's slowing economic growth and the economy ministry's comment that a weaker currency would benefit growth.

Denis Korshilov, head of fixed income, currencies and commodities at Citi in Moscow, said the central bank's decision would be "neutral" for the market, but may also indicate that the central bank tolerates a further possible weakening in the ruble.

"The move fits the central bank's long-term strategy of cutting down its presense on the currency market as it switches to inflation targeting. I don't think it will result in a deep weakening of the ruble," Mr. Korshilov said.

The central bank also said in the statement that the current seven-ruble width of the trading corridor was adequate for the needed scale of the ruble's flexibility.

title: Russia Finance Minister Says Sharp Ruble Volatility To Stop
text:
ST. PETERSBURG--Sharp fluctuations in the Russian ruble will ease as the Bank of Russia moves to bolster the currency's stability, Russia's Finance Minister said Friday.

Anton Siluanov, speaking on the sidelines of the summit of the Group of 20 industrial and developing nations, said the ruble's recent weakening has not been caused by "systemic reasons."

"The ruble is not weakening, it's fluctuating," he said, adding that the central bank is focused on "maintaining the ruble's stability."

"There will be no sharp volatility of the ruble," he added.

The ruble has lost about 8.5% of its value against the U.S. dollar so far this year, as investors pull their assets from emerging markets. The Russian ruble has suffered much less than the currencies of other developing nations, notably India and Brazil, as it is being supported by high oil prices.

Russia's central bankintervenes in foreign exchange markets to smooth out daily volatility of the ruble, but by widening the currency's trading corridor and adjusting its boundaries in accordance with demand and supply it is moving it toward a freer-floating currency.

Mr. Siluanov said the Bank of Russia "keeps everything under control," adding that the ruble needs no support from a newly created reserve fund of the five largest developing nations, collectively known as BRICS.

text:
MOSCOW, Sept 3 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank raised its foreign currency sales to $6.1 billion in August to stem the rouble's slide, in its largest monthly intervention since September 2011, data showed on Tuesday.

The expected tapering of U.S. monetary stimulus as soon as this month and the crisis in Syria - both weighing particularly heavily on emerging markets - as well as a possible interest rate cut in Russia has dragged on the rouble in recent weeks.

By Alexander Kolyandr

MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia won't introduce quantitative easing to battle the slowing Russian economy because such a policy would result in higher inflation, the bank's new chairwoman said in an interview Tuesday.

Elvira Nabiullina told state news agency Tass that quantitative easing, whereby a central bank pumps cheap money into a stagnating economy, would jeopardize the central bank's low inflation policy goal.

"[Quantitative easing] will ease the pain only for some time and will have no long-term impact on economic growth, as it will cause risks of higher inflation and higher capital outflow" she said.

Russia's economic growth stood at 1.2% in the second quarter, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of slowing expansion. It comes against a background of low investment, high capital outflow and declining demand for oil and other commodities, which is Russia's main source of hard currency. The government has cut growth forecast twice this year to 1.8% from an earlier projection of 3.6%, a far cry from about 5% target President Vladimir Putin set for a medium term.

"The slowing growth is not cyclical, but structural," she said, adding that only institutional changes and lower inflation can boost investment and growth.

Russia's inflation stood at 6.5% in July remaining above the central bank's target of 6%. which prevents it to cut lending rates.

Mrs. Nabiullina said she still expects inflation to be at between 5% and 6% in 2013, and confirmed a target range of between 3% to 6% in 2014. She said such a target would only be possible if the government agrees to rise regulated utility tariffs below inflation.

As inflation remains the Bank of Russia's main policy goal, the ruble's exchange rate may face more volatility in the future, the head of the Central Bank admitted. Russia's Central Bank abstains from sizeable interventions on the foreign exchange market as part of its inflation-targetting policy. Without the Central Bank's support the ruble lost about 8.5% of its value against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of the year.

Mrs. Nabiullina said she agrees with the government's estimate of capital outflow in 2013 at between $70 billion and $75 billion.

title: Russian stocks, rouble edge up as Syria tension subsides
text:
MOSCOW, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Russian stocks rose on Thursday after a four-day losing streak, with metals and mining stocks outperforming as the market focused on core earnings rather than bottom-line losses in second quarter results.

Pressure on risky assets worldwide eased after British and U.S. lawmakers raised objections to possible Western military strikes against Syria over last week's suspected chemical weapons attacks in which hundreds of deaths were reported.

The dollar-traded RTS share index was up 0.3 percent at 1,303 points and the rouble-denominated MICEX rose by the same margin to 1,374 points.

The MICEX metals and mining index, heavily sensitive to risk sentiment, rose by 0.9 percent, on a busy day for company results.

Steelmaker Evraz posted a second-quarter loss but its shares rose by 5 percent in London after core earnings beat expectations. The company may pay an interim divided if it can complete asset disposals.

Severstal rallied by 2.4 percent in Moscow even as it swung to a worse-than-expected net loss due to forex losses. Earnings before interest, taxation, depreciation and amortisation posted a double-digit gain.

"Reports from Severstal and Evraz were better than the expected ... If we compare their earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) to market forecasts for this year, then Severstal has (already) fulfilled 48 percent, Evraz 52 percent," said Vladimir Dorogov, an analyst at Alfa-Bank.

Prices for oil - Russia's top export commodity - and central bank interventions on the currency market buoyed the rouble, which, however, remained close to four-year lows against the dollar-euro currency basked eyed by the central bank.

The rouble has escaped the heavy selling that has hit other emerging market assets, as the higher cost of oil implies a stronger current account surplus and budget revenues.

The rouble was flat against the dollar at 33.20 . The rouble lost 0.5 percent over the week so far despite a 0.4 percent rise in oil prices. The rouble rose 0.6 percent on Thursday versus the euro at 44.03.

The rouble was up 0.4 percent at 38.06 to the dollar-euro basket used by the central bank to guide its interventions, but still close to its lowest since September 2009.

A combination of a weaker rouble and high oil prices makes investors more cautious towards domestic sectors, such as banks and telecoms.

The Economy Ministry cut its 2013 growth forecast this week to 1.8 percent - the slowest pace since recession in 2009

Sberbank Investment Research upgraded the Russian oil sector "that outperforms at times of risk aversion thanks to low valuations with 12-month earnings expectations at 5.6".

"This environment does not favour the low-growth domestic sectors of banks and telecoms, as they do not enjoy fast enough growth rates to outpace the rouble's decline," the strategists said in a note.

"We stick with our long-standing 1,350 year-end RTS Index target, but note that we will upgrade this if the conflict in the Middle East continues to escalate".

Shares in Rosneft rose 1.1 percent, while oil prices hovered at $115 per barrel.

title: UPDATE 2-Kazakhstan pegs tenge to  fx  basket, dilutes dollar focus
text:
* Kazakhstan moves away from focus on dollar, to deter speculators

* New peg seen as a more predictable and flexible rate mechanism

By Mariya Gordeyeva

ALMATY, Aug 28 (Reuters) - Kazakhstan's central bank said on Wednesday it would peg the tenge currency to a basket of foreign currencies, a similar system to that used by its close trade partner Russia.

The new system will start on Sept. 2, replacing a managed float of the tenge that used the dollar as a reference currency.

National Bank Chairman Grigory Marchenko said the move aimed to move Central Asia's largest economy away from a pure dollar focus to an array of currencies that better reflects underlying trade flows, and to deter speculators.

The U.S. dollar will account for 70 percent of the currency basket, the euro for 20 percent and the Russian rouble 10 percent, the bank said.

The initial rate of the tenge to the basket of foreign currencies will be set at 113.7 tenge, Marchenko said.

"We do not rule out that hina's yuan can become part of the currency basket in the future," he told a news briefing.

"The main advantage of introducing a multi-currency basket will be a gradual reduction of the role of the U.S. dollar on the internal market and in foreign trade."

Kazakhstan's economy relies heavily on exports to the European Union, China and large northern neighbour Russia. Kazakhstan's imports are dominated by Russia and China, which neighbours Kazakhstan in the southeast.

The vast Central Asian nation, which is a major producer and exporter of oil, industrial metals, uranium and grain, is a member of a customs union with Russia and Belarus.

Russia's central bank runs a managed float of the rouble against a target currency basket made up of dollars and euros.

The policy allows Russia's central bank to use market interventions to smooth volatility, without having to defend levels that might encourage a speculative attack.

"I think they are following in Russia's footsteps ... and the Russian currency basket regime has worked quite well in recent years," said Tim Ash, analyst at Standard Bank.

"They (Kazakhstan) need to have a system which mirrors the rouble," said Barbara Nestor, emerging markets strategist at Commerzbank London.

MOVING TO A MORE FLEXIBLE RATE

The steppe nation of 17 million, the second-largest post-Soviet oil producer after Russia, had previously used a currency corridor which it dropped in 2011.

The new peg reflects Kazakhstan's "medium-term strategy of moving towards a flexible tenge", said one Moscow-based analyst who covers the former Soviet Union. "This is a first step on the road to a more flexible, floating corridor arrangement."

Marchenko said the peg to a currency basket was set "to lessen speculative moods on the market".

"It will soften negative consequences of inflows and outlows of speculative capital ... which cause volatility of the tenge against the dollar," he said.

The official rate of the tenge rose to 152.16 per dollar on Wednesday from 152.47 in the previous trading session, and Marchenko said it would not be allowed to strengthen further below 152.

He said the central bank had sold $1 billion in July and bought $800 million in August to help steady the currency.

Short-lived weakening of the tenge to nearly 154 per dollar in recent weeks triggered an avalanche of speculation in Kazakhstan's social networks about its imminent depreciation.

"When the central bank was letting the tenge weaken, locals were worried that they might need to dollarise savings, because it was an unpredictable policy - this is a more predictable policy framework," said Nestor of Commerzbank London.

The euro fell against the dollar Tuesday, despite signs emerging the long-running recession in the euro zone could be coming to an end.

"Generally there's a lack of activity and liquidity....there are still are lot of participants on the sidelines taking no active positions," said Aurelija Augulyte, a senior analyst at Nordea.

The Center for European Economic Research, or ZEW's, monthly indicator of expectations jumped to 42.0 in August, from 36.3 in July, beating expectations for an increase to 40.0 from economists surveyed by the Wall Street Journal ahead of the release. Economic expectations for the euro zone also jumped to their highest level since 2010.

"This is a good sign that the worst [of] the recession in the euro zone might be over," said Michael Schroeder, head of the international finance and financial management department at ZEW.

In a further positive sign, another data release showed industrial output in the 17 nations that use the euro rose at its fastest pace in more than two-and-a-half years during the three months to June.

Elsewhere, the dollar rose above Y98 against the yen, as the Nikkei Stock Average jumped 2.6% to 13,867.00, the sharpest percentage gain for the benchmark since Aug. 2.
