The focus now turns to Wednesday's unemployment release after the Bank of England said it will hold interest rates at record lows until the U.K.'s jobless rate falls 7%.

"Generally we expect that the pound will start to become a lot more sensitive to the labor market report, similar to what the dollar has started to do with payrolls ever since the Federal Reserve put their own explicit target in," said Chris Walker, a currency strategist at Barclays in London.

title: Dollar Gains; US Retail Sales Eyed
text:
--Euro gains briefly on German ZEW indicator

--Dollar rises above Y98 against yen

--U.S. retail sales data, Chile rate decision on the agenda

By Clare Connaghan

The euro fell against the dollar Tuesday, despite signs emerging the long-running recession in the euro zone could be coming to an end.

The euro rose to the day's high of $1.3317 against the dollar, after a key indicator showed economic sentiment in Europe's largest economy--Germany--increased to its highest level since March. But the move quickly subsided and by 1056 GMT the euro was trading down at $1.3297.

"Generally there's a lack of activity and liquidity....there are still are lot of participants on the sidelines taking no active positions," said Aurelija Augulyte, a senior analyst at Nordea.

The Center for European Economic Research, or ZEW's, monthly indicator of expectations jumped to 42.0 in August, from 36.3 in July, beating expectations for an increase to 40.0 from economists surveyed by the Wall Street Journal ahead of the release. Economic expectations for the euro zone also jumped to their highest level since 2010.

"This is a good sign that the worst [of] the recession in the euro zone might be over," said Michael Schroeder, head of the international finance and financial management department at ZEW.

In a further positive sign, another data release showed industrial output in the 17 nations that use the euro rose at its fastest pace in more than two-and-a-half years during the three months to June.

Elsewhere, the dollar rose above Y98 against the yen, as the Nikkei Stock Average jumped 2.6% to 13,867.00, the sharpest percentage gain for the benchmark since Aug. 2.

Meanwhile, the pound had a choppy session against the dollar in the aftermath of data showing the annual rate of inflation fell to 2.8% in July from 2.9% in June. The focus now turns to Wednesday's unemployment release after the Bank of England said it will hold interest rates at record lows until the U.K.'s jobless rate falls 7%.

"Generally we expect that the pound will start to become a lot more sensitive to the labor market report, similar to what the dollar has started to do with payrolls ever since the Federal Reserve put their own explicit target in," said Chris Walker, a currency strategist at Barclays in London.

In other news, the Norwegian krone rose to a three-week high against the euro after retail sales fell 0.2% in June, much less-than expected.

The krone's reaction to the data is fully justified, says Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, chief analyst at Danske Bank, "Together with the higher inflation last week it further removes the risk of a rate cut from Norges Bank," he said.

Looking ahead to later Tuesday, July's retail sales data in the U.S. due at 1230 GMT will in focus. Economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires see an increase in July of 0.3% from June.

In emerging markets, the Indian rupee strengthened against the U.S. dollar after the government raised import taxes on gold and silver, as part of its latest effort to curb an outflow of dollars and support the local currency which fell to a record low last week. The dollar fell to as low as 60.90 rupees following the measures, down from around 61.10 before they were announced.

Elsewhere, the Bank of Russia raised the ruble's trading band for the second time this month to reduce the amount of foreign-exchange interventions taking place amid a slide in Russia's currency.

The currency band was moved five kopecks higher Tuesday to RUB31.95-RUB38.95 against its reference basket of euros and dollars. The central bank keeps the ruble within a floating range against the basket and moves it by five kopecks either way if the amount of its purchases or selling of foreign currencies exceeds $450 million in a day.

Up ahead, Chile's central bank is expected to maintain the benchmark overnight lending rate at 5% later Tuesday, according to a poll of analysts.

At 1059 GMT, the euro was trading at $1.3298 against the dollar, up from $1.3300, late Monday in New York, according to trading system EBS.

The dollar was at Y98.07 against the yen, compared with Y96.90, while the euro was at Y130.41, compared with Y128.86. The pound was trading at $1.5450 against the dollar, compared with $1.5463 late Monday in New York.

The Wall Street Journal Dollar Index, which tracks the U.S. dollar against a basket of major currencies, was at 73.86 from 73.613.

title: Russian  central bank 's July  FX  sales highest in nearly 2 years
text:
MOSCOW, Aug 1 (Reuters) - The Russian central bank sold $4.2 billion and 377 million euros from its currency reserves in July, central bank data showed on Thursday, the biggest amount since October 2011.

The central bank has been stepping up interventions over recent months as the rouble comes under sustained selling pressure.

In June, the central bank had sold $2.7 billion and 246 million euros, while in May it sold just $237 million and 19 million euros.

Under the rouble's floating corridor regime, the central bank automatically intervenes to smooth volatility whenever the rouble approaches the top or bottom of its corridor.

Emerging market currencies such as the rouble have been weakening in recent weeks, as expectations that U.S. monetary stimulus will be wound down lift the dollar. The rouble has been skirting the bottom of the corridor, forcing central bank interventions.

On Thursday, the Russian central bank also announced that it had shifted the corridor downwards, another automatic response to sustained selling pressure.

The new corridor extends from 31.85-38.85 roubles to the basket, compared with 31.75-38.75 last announced by the central bank on July 8. (Reporting by Jason Bush; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: UPDATE 1-Rouble hits 13-month low, Uralkali shares slump
text:
(Updates prices, adds comments)

MOSCOW, July 30 (Reuters) - Shares in Russia's top potash producer Uralkali plunged as much as 24 percent on Tuesday after it announced it is quitting the top potash cartel BPC, while the Russian rouble extended losses to hit multi-month lows.

At 1228 GMT, the rouble-denominated MICEX share index was 0.3 percent lower at 1,394 points, weighed down by the chemicals sector. The dollar-denominated RTS fell 0.6 percent to 1,334 points.

Shares in Uralkali, the world's largest potash miner by output, nosedived after the company said it would leave the Belarusian Potash Corporation (BPC) due to a "deadlock" over sales, a move it expects will cause global prices to plunge by 25 percent.

As the market leader it hopes it can boost sales volumes to offset a decline in prices but investors were not convinced.

"This may very well mark the end of supply discipline in the potash market and is negative for the entire potash space," a trader at a Western bank said.

Uralkali shares were down 18.4 percent by 1400 GMT, after shedding 24 percent at one point. The news affected the rest of the sector.

The MICEX Chemicals index was down 10 percent. Shares in Acron , one of Europe's top 10 fertiliser producers, fell 9.8 percent, while stocks in Russia's Phosagro were down 11 percent on concerns about falling prices for the key fertiliser mineral.

Uralkali also announced it was freezing its share buy-back programme launched in 2011.

"Shares of Uralkali will remain under pressure in the market in any attempt to recover, as without the support of the buyback programme the shares should trade at a substantial discount to global peers," said Kirill Yankovsky, a trader at Uralsib Capital.

The rouble weakened 0.3 percent to 37.79 against the euro-dollar basket, a 13-month low, as the tax payment period ended. It was also 0.3 percent weaker against the dollar at 32.92 and down 0.4 percent against the euro at 43.75.

The rouble is being weakened by local demand for foreign currencies for dividend conversions and by expectations for a traditionally weaker current account surplus during summer months when imports of services rise.

The currency is supported by central bank interventions. The level of 37.8 against the currency basket is seen by traders as a major resistance level at which the bank increases selling of foreign currency to around $400 million per day from $200 million.

Demand for the central bank's debut one-year refinancing auction on Monday, the first auction under a scheme to cut the cost of long-term funding for banks, fell short of market expectations. That has fuelled speculation the central bank will soon cut policy rates to support the economy.

Interbank rouble overnight rates fell to 6.09 percent from 6.25 percent on Monday.

Some traders are now betting that the central bank could also widen the rouble's floating basket corridor to reduce interventions that drain rouble liquidity.

Russia last widened the corridor further to 7 roubles in July 2012.

"The widening of the corridor is the next logic step after such an auction," said Ivan Mikhailov, a dealer at Credit Suisse.

However, Sergei Fishgoit, a dealer at Otkritie bank said the central bank was unlikely to widen the corridor while the rouble was in the zone of central bank interventions.

title: Rouble erases gains vs basket, c.bank shifts floating band corridor
text:
MOSCOW, June 26 (Reuters) - Russia's rouble erased earlier gains of up to one percent versus the dollar-euro basket on Wednesday before the central bank said it moved the floating trading band up, selling more than $2 billion to ease the rouble's fall in June.

Russia's treasury bond yields extended gains, while the rouble and stocks edged up, buoyed by easing concerns about the health of the world's biggest economies.

Reassurance that the United States may be strong enough to cope if the Federal Reserve scales back its stimulus programme and the central bank of China's pledge to prevent any lasting credit crunch soothed emerging markets after a sell-off.

At 1038 GMT the rouble was 0.4 percent weaker against the dollar at 32.95 and 0.4 percent stronger versus the euro at 42.90. The Russian currency was flat percent at 37.43 against the dollar-euro basket, propped up by local tax payments and central bank interventions.

Russia's central bank said it shifted upwards the boundaries of the rouble trading corridor by five kopecks as of June 25.

Russia last widened the floating rouble corridor by 7 roubles in July 2012 - from 31.65 to 38.65 roubles - and decreased the amount of cumulative interventions necessary for the band to shift by 5 kopecks to $450 million.

"The market is only oriented to the weakening of the rouble and the tax payment period may only limit this," said Igor Akinshin, a trader at Alfa-bank.

Artyom Biryukov, an analyst at HSBC, had expected the boundaries to be shifted on Tuesday, taking into account cumulative interventions at around $50 million per day.

The central bank has sold $2.2 billion since the start of June to June 24 to ease the rouble's fall, according to Reuters calculations.

The rouble has depreciated by just over 5 percent against the dollar since Chairman Ben Bernanke first signalled on May 22 that the Fed may "taper" its bond buying programme, holding up better than the Brazilian real and Indian rupee, which have fallen by 8 and 9 percent

Russia's central bank manages a flexible exchange-rate corridor to smooth volatility in the exchange rate, but does not seek to defend specific levels. Its oil-fuelled economy runs large surpluses on the current account, and while net capital outflows continue, the central bank has an arsenal of half a trillion dollars in reserves at its disposal.

The rouble is seen undervalued by analysts at Sberbank Investment Research, as the long-term trend shows the rouble at 32.3 per dollar if oil prices are at $101 per barrel, suggesting some strengthening.

"On the other hand, we cannot exclude emerging markets investors adjusting their approach to evaluating risk, specifically moving to view the rouble as being in a 'devaluation' transition", Sberbank analysts said.

"If the winds blow in this direction, the current rate could instead be seen as part of the 'new normal'".

The rouble is weighed by concerns about an economic slowdown that has led the government to support a weakening of the rouble to restore export competitiveness.

The yield on Russia's treasury bond, maturing in February 2027, fell 13 basis points to 8.09 percent.

"The market is close to bottom, and the majority of non-residents have already withdrawn their funds. Current levels will be attractive to Russian players when global markets stabilise," Ekaterina Leonova, senior analyst at Alfa-bank, said in a note.

The dollar-traded RTS stock index was up 1.3 percent at 1,260 points. The rouble-denominated MICEX was up 1.5 percent at 1,317 points, led by gains in AFK Sistema, up 4.5 percent.

Uralsib raised its price target for Sistema's global depositary receipts to $34 from $33 per GDR, seeing an 82 percent upside potential after the oil-to-telecoms conglomerate announced it is selling a 49 percent stake in oil firm Russneft for $1.2 billion.

Preferred shares of Bashneft extended losses, falling 6.6 percent on concern prompted by a newspaper report that minority investors might lose out in any takeover by Rosneft.

"We will just address their demand (for cash) in our interventions. Nothing else is planned," Shvetsov told journalists on the sidelines of St Petersburg International Economic Forum.

title: Bank of Russia Defends Ruble for First Time in 5 Months in April
text:
MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia intervened in April in the local currency market for the first time in five months to ease downward pressure on the ruble, the central bank data showed Tuesday.

The central bank sold $663.1 million and 45.1 million euros ($59.1 million) from foreign exchanges reserves in April to smooth ruble volatility. The central bank didn't intervene in March, after buying $714.9 million and EUR72.6 million in the first two months of 2013.

The central bank, aiming to switch to a policy of inflation targeting over the next two years, is gradually paring its presence in currency markets.

Higher flexibility of the ruble exchange rate makes the currency an absorber of external shocks, related to commodity market volatility, which are crucial for balance of payments in one of the world's largest oil and gas producers.

Keeping the ruble within a corridor of RUB31.65-RUB38.65 against a euro-dollar basket, the central bank buys dollars and euros when the Russian currency trades in the lower half of the range to avoid excessive ruble appreciation, while it sells foreign currencies when the ruble hovers in the upper half of the band.

The bank is inactive if the ruble trades between RUB34.65 and RUB35.65 versus the basket of $0.55 and EUR0.45.

In early April, the ruble weakened beyond RUB35.65 following a fall in oil prices amid rising global risk aversion, but returned to the intervention-free zone April 25.

title: Falling Ruble Prompts  Central Bank Intervention
text:
MOSCOW--Russia's central bankintervened this week in the currency market to ease downside pressure on the ruble for the first time since November, the bank's data showed Friday.

The central bank sold 30 million rubles ($0.95 million) on the Moscow exchange Wednesday when the ruble dropped after the finance ministry said it will start buying foreign currencies on the open market in the second half of 2013 to boost liquidity.

The central bank's intention to cut lending rates as inflation slows also put pressure on the ruble. Lower lending rates mean the ruble and ruble-denominated assets become less attractive for using in carry trade where low yielding currencies are used to buy into higher-yielding assets.

"[The] ruble is under pressure which comes from everywhere," analysts at Nordea bank said in a note, pointing to a slump in oil prices, the ruble's key benchmark, and expectations of a rate cut.

The central bank keeps the ruble within a corridor against the euro-dollar basket of $0.55 and 0.45 euros. The central bank sells foreign currencies from its reserves when the ruble weakens, moving closer to the upper half of the corridor, and buys dollars and euros when the ruble firms towards the lower half of the band.

In the middle of the corridor between RUB34.65 and RUB35.65, where the ruble has traded since the middle of November, the central bank carries out no interventions.

The ruble is on track to stage its biggest weekly drop against the basket since August. In the five days to April 5 the ruble has already lost 2.1% versus the basket, hovering at around RUB35.72 as of 1020 GMT, its weakest since mid-September.

On Friday, the ruble gained 0.1% against the dollar to RUB31.55, after touching its lowest level since November at RUB31.75 earlier this week. Against the euro Friday, the ruble was steady at RUB40.82, close to its weakest point since January of RUB40.86 hit this week.

Analysts at Rosbank said in a note that the ruble could rebound from multi-month lows but given all risks it is better not to open long positions in the currency.

In the near term the ruble can stabilize at around RUB35.7-RUB36.0 versus the basket and in the range of RUB31.7-RUB32.0 against the dollar, said Nordea bank.

title: Russian finmin may convert windfall revenues via  fx  market
text:
* Sovereign funds now held at c.bank

* Transfers done off market

* Hold combined $174 billion in assets

By Katya Golubkova and Maya Dyakina

MOSCOW, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Russia's Finance Ministry said on Wednesday it was considering a central bank proposal for the ministry to convert windfall oil revenues on its own openly on the foreign exchange market.

Such a step would separate the government's management of its sovereign wealth funds from the currency market operations conducted by the central bank, which is gradually increasing the freedom with which it allows the rouble to float.

The Bank of Russia has scaled back its currency interventions, to the point where it was hardly present on the market in the final quarter of last year, as it turns its focus towards Western-style inflation-targeting.

Currently, Russia's central bank acts as the agent to convert rouble oil and gas proceeds into foreign currencies for the Finance Ministry in off-market transactions.

"The central bank has indeed addressed this proposal to us. It has its reasons, it is very interesting, we are considering it at the moment, there is no decision taken," Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Moiseyev told reporters. No reason was given for the central bank proposal.

The proposed move would potentially soften central bank interventions on the forex market, as the regulator struggles to focus on inflation.

"The transactions conducted by the finance ministry bypassing the market ... affect the money supply and may have inflationary consequences," said Alexander Morozov , chief economist for Russia and CIS at HSBC .

The Reserve Fund and the second outlet for Russia's windfall oil revenue, the National Welfare Fund (NWF), are kept 45 percent in euros, 45 percent in dollars and 10 percent in sterling and total 8.5 percent of GDP.

The two sovereign wealth funds hold a combined 5.3 trillion roubles ($176 billion), and are counted towards the central bank's gold and foreign exchange reserves, which totalled $534 billion at the last count.

The Reserve Fund was created as a safety net against external shocks such as falls in global oil prices, while the NWF is designed to cover deficits in the pension system and is mostly invested in the bonds of Western governments.

The finance ministry transfers oil and gas proceeds which come above budget target to the Reserve Fund once a year in February via off-market exchanges with the central bank.

"Extra demand for foreign currency, all things being equal, would contribute to weakening of the rouble when oil prices are high," Morozov said.

"But when Russia needs money from the Reserve Fund to patch holes in the budget, the finance minister would step in to sell foreign currency. It is quite reasonable and countercyclical."

($1 = 30.0560 Russian roubles)

text:
MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia warned Tuesday there could be a shortfall in ruble liquidity in the money market during the first quarter of 2013, which would prompt lenders to seek refinancing from the central bank.

title: Bank of  Russia  To Refrain From  FX Interventions  In Evening Trade
text:
MOSCOW--Russia's central bank won't carry out foreign exchange interventions at the Moscow exchange in the newly introduced evening trading session, the central bank said Wednesday.

The Moscow exchange, formerly known as the Micex-RTS exchange, extended the forex trading session by four hours and 50 minutesstarting from Jan. 8. The bourse now trades the ruble, the euro and the dollar from 0600 GMT to 1950 GMT.

The central bank said on its website it will "be present" at the currency trading session only from 0600 GMT to 1500 GMT, as before.

The central bank keeps the ruble within a band against the euro-dollar basket, comprised of 0.55 dollars and 0.45 euros, which market players say is now at RUB31.65-RUB38.65.

The bank buys foreign currencies at the lower end of the band to prevent the ruble from excessively firming, and sells dollars and euros when the ruble closes in on the upper end of the corridor to limit its depreciation. The central bank doesn't carry out interventions in the middle of the trading band.

The ruble traded at RUB34.60 versus the basket by 0730 GMT Wednesday, losing some 0.4% on the day.

title: Ruble at Six-Week High vs Dollar on Fiscal Cliff Hopes
text:
The Russian ruble rallied against the dollar to its strongest level in six weeks Thursday, boosted by last month-end tax payments and expectations that the U.S. will resolve its "fiscal cliff" issues.

The ruble gained 1.2% to RUB30.80 against the dollar, its strongest level since Oct. 19, before easing slightly to 30.83 by 1403 GMT. Against the euro, the ruble strengthened 0.36% to RUB40.04.

"The ruble's firming is driven by a spike in optimism about the U.S. It's obvious that neither the U.S. nor the global economy would allow a slump, and the ruble, as a risky currency, is gaining from that," said Dmitry Novoselov, head of derivative sales at Nordea in Moscow.

Earlier this week U.S. House of Representatives Speaker John Boehner said he is optimistic a deal over the so-called fiscal cliff could be reached, and U.S. President Barack Obama said he is hopeful the White House and Congress can reach a deal by Christmas.

Against the euro-dollar basket, the central bank's gauge of the currency market, the ruble strengthened 0.6% to RUB35.0, remaining in the range of RUB34.65-RUB35.65, in which the Bank of Russia doesn't carry out interventions.

Local month-end taxes also worked in the ruble's favor, as they prompted export-focused companies to convert dollars and euros to meet local liability.

The ruble could strengthen to RUB34.6 against the basket in the near term before easing gradually to around RUB35.0 by the end of December, analysts at Raiffeisen said.

"We are entering the last month of the year and people usually prefer piling up hard currencies on the eve of super-long holidays," Mr. Novoselov said, referring to Russia's annual New Year holidays. Russian markets will close Dec. 30 and won't open again until Jan. 9.

title: WSJ BLOG/Emerging Europe: Russia's Massive Capital Outflow Has Silver Lining
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's Emerging Europe blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/emergingeurope.)

By Andrey Ostroukh

Capital outflows are usually deemed to be a negative development for any economy, but in Russia's case they help avoid economic overheating and are natural considering the country's poor business climate, Russia's finance ministry and the International Monetary Fund say.

Before the crisis that began in 2008, Russia was benefiting from rallying oil prices and risk appetite, attracting net capital inflows of $41.1 billion in 2006 and $81.7 billion in 2007, according to the central bank. In the following four years, however, the world's largest oil producer saw nearly $305 billion leave and is on track to post around $60 billion in outflows this year.

"It is inevitable in the current state of the economy and, in some sense, it's not that bad as Russia's exports with current oil prices are generating more resources than it could be invested in Russia without creating bubbles," Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Moiseev told journalists on the sidelines of a banking conference in Moscow on Friday. "It's a big achievement that with a transition to the floating ruble the economy can balance itself. It digests exactly the same amount of money as it is able to do."

The IMF agrees that capital outflows from Russia are natural in the current global and domestic environment.

"With the switch towards a more flexible ruble exchange rate, the Bank of Russia's interventions in the foreign exchange market have been scaled back, and the capital outflows that we see are to a large extent the counterpart to Russia's current account surpluses," said Odd Per Brekk, IMF's representative in Russia.

Mr. Moiseev said that the government's target now is to improve the country's business climate. According to the World Bank, Russia was ranked 120th out of 183 countries in the organization's 'Doing Business' report.

Russian leaders have repeatedly called for structural changes to make the country more investment-friendly and diversify the economy, cutting its dependence on global commodity prices, although no major breakthroughs have been made yet.

"The government calls for diversification but is not in a rush to spend on investments. Households and business can't see reasons to behave differently," said Evgeniy Nadroshin, chief economist with Russia's conglomerate Sistema.

Without diversification of the economy and reforms to improve the investment climate, capital outflows keep the ruble under pressure, which supports Russia's production, "far from the world's most competitive," said Mr. Nadorshin.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian shares continue rally, rouble firms on oil
text:
* Rouble edge up vs dollar on oil

 * Stocks indexes creep higher

 * Worries about euro zone, China growth weigh 

(Adds quotes, detail, updates prices)

 MOSCOW, Oct 1 (Reuters) - Russian shares extended fragile gains on Monday, helped by a buoyant mood on global markets, while the rouble inched higher, catching up with an oil price recovery.

 At 1423 GMT, the rouble-denominated MICEX exchange rose 1.9 percent to 1,485.9 points. The dollar-denominated RTS index was up 2.4 percent to 1,511.1. 

 Russian stocks await a boost in fund flows from the U.S. Federal Reserve's stimulus plan, but the market is not yet positioned for a rally, having a larger proportion of long positions, said Ivan Samokhin at Aton brokerage.

 In a sign of lukewarm investor interest, market volatility and declining trading volumes in Central and Eastern Europe, including Russia, has forced Dutch bank ING to close its equity markets desk for the region.

 Russian stocks have underperformed the price of oil and languish at a 50 percent valuation discount to other emerging markets. 

 However, stocks were supported on Monday by Russia's PMI manufacturing data showing monthly growth. 

 "Importantly, output growth strengthened at the end of the third quarter, signalling a still solid pace of production expansion," Alexander Morozov, chief economist for Russia at HSBC, said in a note.

 The data provided an argument for Russia's central bank to continue monetary policy tightening, Morozov added. 

 The regulator surprised the market by raising all its key interest rates in mid-September, attracting carry trade and pushing the rouble higher.

 Economists, polled by Reuters last Friday, expected rates to stay on hold in October because of slowing economic growth in Russia.

 A recovery in the oil price - a key source of revenues for Russia - helped the rouble to firm. 

 The rouble was up 0.5 percent versus the dollar at 31.03. Overall, the rouble has gained 3.0 percent against the greenback this year, outperforming its BRIC peers.

 The Russian currency firmed 0.3 percent to 35.11 against the euro-dollar basket. It was flat versus the euro at 40.10.

 Better than expected U.S. manufacturing data eclipsed the signs of weakness in China and Brent crude futures rose 0.3 percent to $112.7 per barrel.

 "In general, hope for positive trends, for central banks' stimuli, are prevailing, but the euro zone economy remains weak," said Igor Akinshin, a dealer at Alfa Bank, adding that the rouble may get stuck in the range of 34.65-35.65 against the basket, where Russia's central bank does not intervene.

 Also overhanging markets is weak Chinese and euro zone manufacturing data, highlighting the frailty of the global economy and continuing uncertainty over a bail-out for Spain, whose credit rating is due for a review by Moody's Investors Service.

 A Reuters poll last week showed the rouble weakening to 31.71 against the greenback by the end of 2012. On Monday non-deliverable forwards showed the rouble at 31.7890 per dollar in three months' time.

 The Russian debt market was broadly flat on Monday. The yield on Russia's benchmark Eurobond maturing in 2030 fell to 2.96 percent from 2.98 percent on Friday.

title: Syria's Russian Connection
text:
Syria's embattled regime laid plans to use Russian banks as part of an emergency effort to sidestep American and European sanctions on oil and financial transactions, according to Syrian government documents and correspondence reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

The documents offer an inside look at how a shrinking group of regime loyalists is working to prop up Bashar al-Assad's government. Over the past several weeks, senior Syrian officials have held a series ofmeetings to discuss how to conduct business after being cut off from most Western banking institutions and trade, the documents indicate.

The documents, which span a period from March until early July, also underscore the difficulties facing Western governments in sustaining comprehensive sanctions against Syria, as long as Damascus keeps its strong diplomatic alliance with Moscow. Earlier this month, Russia received a delegation of top Syrian economic officials, including its oil and finance ministers, to discuss the possibility of government loans and long-term oil deals, Syrian Deputy Prime Minister Qadri Jamil said in a news conference.

The sanctions, which began last year and were strengthened this spring, are aimed at Syria's oil and financial sectors. The unilateral actions are coordinated by Western and Middle Eastern countries allied against Syria, but aren't legally binding on Russian and other companies that don't have operations in the U.S. or Europe. Russia and China have used their veto power at the United Nations Security Council to block the possibility of international sanctions.

A cache of documents reviewed by the Journal includes what appears to be authentic correspondence between Syrian government officials and certain foreign companies. In interviews with the Journal, some people who were parties to correspondence confirmed details. None of the people reached by the Journal questioned the authenticity of documents referenced in this article, although some denied conducting any business with Syrian entities.

Syria isn't a globally significant oil producer. The 360,000 barrels of crude it pumps daily represent less than 1% of the world's daily oil production. But Syria's oil sales are one of the last sources of foreign currency for President Assad.

The roughly 150,000 barrels per day Syria has available for export, after its domestic needs are met, are worth approximately $380 million per month at current prices. That is a key reason why the U.S. and the European Union targeted Syria's state oil companies, its central bank and financial sector. The sanctions have cut Syria off from its traditional buyers in Europe, including in Italy, Germany and Spain.

Last summer, the Syrian government announced it had approximately $17 billion in foreign-currency reserves, a figure that some Western diplomats believe has fallen by between one-third and one-half.

The U.S. imposed sanctions on Syria's central bank and oil sector in August 2011. The EU placed limited sanctions on the Syrian oil sector last September, then strengthened them this March. Both the EU and U.K. imposed sanctions on the Syrian central bank in February.

The Russian government has long been opposed to international sanctions, both in general and in the case of Syria, saying they hinder political solutions. Diplomats at the United Nations say Moscow's strong views have kept other countries from initiating debate on sanctioning Syria's oil or banking sectors. Although Russian companies don't have any legal obligation to follow U.S. and EU sanctions against Syria, such commerce has the potential to complicate diplomacy on other issues.

Syria's plan to work around Western sanctions took shape this summer in a series of meetings between four officials -- the central-bank governor, the ministers of oil and finance and the head of the state oil-marketing company in charge of selling Syrian oil, one government document shows.

After a July 1 meeting, the four officials drafted a letter to then-Prime Minister Riad Hijab saying that international sanctions had limited their ability to collect revenue by cutting off "conventional solutions [and] customary banking" practices, according to a copy of the letter reviewed by the Journal. A copy of the letter was included in correspondence between the Syrian central bank and Syria's oil-marketing company, known as Sytrol, whose head was one of the letter's four signatories. It isn't known if the prime minister received the letter. Mr. Hijab defected on Aug. 6.

So far this year, despite the sanctions, Sytrol has secured 11 contracts to sell oil, that letter said. In addition, the letter said, Sytrol had secured deals to import half the diesel fuel Syria is projected to need each year -- fuel it doesn't produce at home but needs for military and industrial uses.

In that letter, the officials recommended a change in Syrian laws that would allow them to set up offshore companies and conduct business through them in order to minimize the impact of sanctions.

"Offshore companies are being formed in Russia and Malaysia and bank accounts are being activated in Russia in euro and Russian-ruble [denominated accounts] and could be ready Thursday July 5, 2012... . [T]hen we would be able to pay for the value of the imports and receive the money for crude exports easily, while all concerned parties will take all the necessary actions to ensure the confidentiality of the proceedings in order not to open the way to the European Union and the United States to track the work of these companies and include them on the list of sanctions," according to the letter.

It isn't clear from the documents reviewed by the Journal whether the steps outlined in that letter were completed. The letter addressed to the prime minister didn't include any names of offshore companies or Russian banks.

Separate documents reviewed by the Journal indicate that as recently as June Syrian government entities on the U.S. and EU sanctions lists were considering commercial transactions that would involve Russian banks.

Those documents suggest that Syria was looking to do business with Gazprombank, the lending affiliate of Russia's natural-gas monopoly.

A sample contract form sent by Sytrol in February to prospective oil buyers, after both the U.S. and EU had imposed some sanctions, listed Gazprombank as the financial institution through which payments for crude could be made, according to documents reviewed by the Journal, suggesting that Syria intended to clear foreign-currency payments for oil via that bank. It isn't known whether Gazprombank ever cleared any such payments, or what companies were involved in the 11 contracts that the Syrian government letter says have been signed this year.

In March, officials from Syria's central bank traveled to Moscow and met with executives from Gazprombank, in part to try to strengthen business relationships, including exchanging information to facilitate electronic money transfers, according to a separate document.

Gazprombank didn't respond to the Journal's question about the authenticity of the documents that mention the bank. It said it had a "correspondent banking relationship" with the Syrian central bank before the U.S. and EU sanctions were in place, but it "is no longer engaged in business (including international settlements) with the central bank of Syria and other Syrian financial institutions."

Correspondence in June between Sytrol and a small, Dubai-based oil trader identified Moscow-based Novikombank as Sytrol's "nominated bank" through which the trader would send money to the Syrian government. A June 21 letter from the trading firm, called Intertrade, to the head of Sytrol strikes an apologetic tone for the delays in closing an oil contract due to what the writer refers to as "your banking issues." It isn't clear from this letter whether any such contracts were closed.

In a telephone interview, the head of Intertrade, whose name appears on the letter, denied having any commercial relationship with Sytrol or Syria. After he was shown the correspondence reviewed by the Journal, he responded in writing that "we were just preparing the road for future commercial relations once it is legal and feasible to do so."

Novikombank, whose chairman is a former officer of the Soviet-era secret service and a colleague of President Vladimir Putin, said in a statement it doesn't do business with Syrian entities. A spokesman said that the bank doesn't comment on "rumors," and he declined to answer other questions about the bank's clients, citing Russian bank-secrecy laws.

Other Sytrol and Syrian government documents describe efforts to find buyers for the nation's surplus oil.

In pitches to several prospective customers, Sytrol officials agreed to discount Syrian crude, pricing it between $10 and $15 a barrel less than the Brent and the Dubai averages from which Middle Eastern oil is sometimes set.

One logistical problem posed by the sanctions was how to ship oil to buyers. Documents reviewed by the Journal show that Russian buyers of Syrian crude made plans to load Syrian oil onto leased tankers from Singapore and Russian-owned tankers based in the Black Sea. Correspondence between potential Russian buyers and Sytrol indicate that the buyers planned to use Russian insurance companies to cover the shipments.

Other documents showed that Syrian oil officials had found suppliers for diesel fuel. Sytrol agreed to buy 200,000 metric tons of diesel per month for 12 months from Angola's state oil company, Sonangol, at a price of $855 per ton, according to a contract reviewed by the Journal.

A South African firm, Avon Oil Trading Ltd., negotiated the deal on behalf of Sytrol after Syria's ambassador to South Africa approached the firm, according to Avon Chief Executive May Kiefer, who said she had tried unsuccessfully to do business with Syria previously.

"At the beginning of the year, they came back to us and said, "Look, there's an opportunity if you guys are interested," and of course we were interested," Ms. Kiefer said.

South African officials said their government has generally remained neutral on the issue of sanctions against Syria. In July, South Africa, which currently holds a rotating seat on the U.N. Security Council, joined Pakistan in abstaining from a vote that could have laid the groundwork for international military intervention. Russia and China vetoed the measure.

The Angolan state oil company, Sonangol, didn't respond to written requests for comment. Ms. Kiefer said that when she was negotiating the deal, Angolan executives said they were aware of Western sanctions against Syria but that they and their government felt no obligation to follow them.

Ms. Kiefer confirmed the contract terms laid out in the document reviewed by the Journal. The contract says her firm would be paid a commission of $1 million per month for the diesel deliveries from Sonangol.

---

James Marson in Moscow, Patrick McGroarty in Johannesburg, Summer Said in Dubai and Joe Lauria at the United Nations contributed to this article.

title: Bank Of  Russia  Sold $1.12 Bln In July  Forex Interventions
text:
MOSCOW--The Bank Of Russia cut its forex interventions by almost 50% in July compared with the month before, selling $1.04 billion and 69.4 million euros ($86.15 million) to support the ruble, data from the bank's website showed Tuesday.

June interventions totalled $2.06 billion.

Russia's central bank manages the ruble in a trading corridor against a basket of dollars and euros, buying foreign currency when the ruble weakens toward the upper end of the corridor and selling dollars and euros when the ruble strengthens.

The regulator widened the corridor's boundaries by 100 kopecks to seven rubles last month as part of its shift to a free-floating currency. The boundaries now stand at RUB31.65 and RUB38.65 versus the basket.

title: Russia spends $1.12 bln to prop up rouble in July
text:
MOSCOW, Aug 7 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank nearly halved forex interventions in July compared to the previous month and sold $1.04 billion and 69.4 million euros ($86.15 million), to ease downside pressure on the rouble, the bank said on its web site on Tuesday.

 The central bank keeps the rouble within a floating band, where it buys foreign currencies closer to the lower boundary and starts selling dollars and euros when the rouble weakens towards the upper boundary.

 The bank widened the rouble's trading band by 100 kopecks to seven roubles in late July in a move aimed at boosting the rouble's flexibility and the efficiency of the bank's interest rate policy. 

The lower boundary stands at 31.65 roubles and the upper boundary at 38.65 roubles versus the euro-dollar basket , comprised of 0.55 dollars and 0.45 euros.

 The rouble had eased 0.15 percent to 35.08 versus the basket by 0614 GMT on Tuesday, sliding off its strongest levels since May hit overnight. ($1 = 0.8056 euros)

   By Alexander Kolyander 
 

MOSCOW--Russia's central bank widened the ruble's trading band versus a basket of dollars and euros to a corridor of seven rubles from six rubles Tuesday.

It's the second shift in seven months.

The bank also lowered the amount of interventions it will conduct before moving the corridor's boundaries, it said in a statement. It will now shift the corridor after buying or selling $450 million worth of foreign currency.

The previous amount for a trading band shift was $500 million.

The Bank of Russia manages the ruble in a trading band versus a basket of dollars and euros, buying foreign currency when the ruble strengthens, selling foreign currency to support the ruble when it weakens, and doing nothing when the ruble is in the middle of the band.

"Raising the potential flexibility of the currency exchange rate through these changes will help the effectiveness of the interest rate policy used by the Bank of Russia to maintain price stability," the central bank said.

The last time the bank acted was in December, widening the corridor by a ruble and lowering the intervention volume by $100 million.

title: Russian  Central Bank  Halts  Interventions  As Ruble Strengthens
text:
MOSCOW--The Bank of Russia did not carry out foreign currency interventions on June 8 to support the ruble, the first time it didn't act in more than two weeks, central bank data showed Wednesday.

Russia's central bank manages the ruble in a six-ruble-wide band against the basket, purchasing dollars and euros when the ruble appreciates to upper limit of the corridor, and selling foreign exchange as the ruble approaches the band's lower edge. The band currently ranges from 32.15 rubles ($0.98) to RUB38.15.

The central bank sold almost $1 billion to support the ruble between May 25 and June 7, as the currency weakened against the basket of euros and dollars the central bank uses as a broad gauge of the ruble's strength.

The volume of its interventions peaked June 4 t $207 million and tapered to $70 million June 7, the data showed.

The ruble fell by nearly 14% against the dollar in May on lower oil and euro zone woes to a low of RUB34.14, its weakest in more than three years, before rebounding with the help of central bank interventions.

title: Falling Oil Price Cuts Short Ruble Rally
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Falling oil prices and dashed hopes for stimulus from the U.S Federal Reserve slammed the Russian ruble Friday, reversing a four-day rally and sending the currency tumbling against the dollar.

At around 12:26 GMT, the ruble traded at RUB32.81 against the dollar, a loss of 1.4% from the previous day's close. Against a basket of dollars and euros used by the central bank as a broader gauge of the ruble's strength, Russia's currency was off by 1.1% to RUB36.39.

After hitting its lowest levels in more than three years Monday, the ruble reversed course as investors took profits amid growing intervention from the Bank of Russia.

Global markets dipped Friday, a day after Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke said the regulator should see serious signs of economic deterioration before expanding current stimulus measures or introducing new ones.

Oil prices--Russia's chief export--hovered around a 16-month low of $98 per barrel, far below the estimated $117 per barrel the country needs to balance its budget.

Investors were also closing out ruble positions ahead of a four-day holiday weekend in Russia which may bring negative news on global markets. Markets will be open on Saturday before closing until Wednesday.

"We're expecting the central bank to become active in the markets once again, but this will have little positive effect right now," ING said in a note to clients.

The Bank of Russia sold $70 million in the open market Thursday, cutting its support of the ruble by more than half from the $183 million sold on Wednesday, central bank data showed.

title: UPDATE: Ruble Hits Three-Year Low;  Central Bank  Downplays Drop
text:
--Ruble pares losses after central bankers comment on slide

--Bank of Russia Chairman Ignatyev says ruble not "doomed to fall"

--Depreciation stems from euro-zone crisis, chairman says

--Bank of Russia won't deviate from intervention policy, chairman says

(Updates with closing prices, additional comments.)

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Russia's ruble declined to a fresh-three year low Friday on falling oil prices and fears of slowing global growth, but recovered some of its decline near the close after Central Bank Chairman Sergei Ignatyev downplayed the depreciation as a by-product of the euro-zone crisis.

The ruble lost as much as 1.8% to RUB34.08 per dollar, its weakest level since April 2009, as prices for Brent crude oil fell below $100 per barrel for the first time in eight months on disappointing manufacturing data from China and Europe. Traders were later encouraged by Ignatyev's comment that central bankintervention to support the ruble had already been "quite intensive" and the currency's decline would slow. The ruble pared its loss to 0.6% on the day.

"The selling had to stop at some point," said Roman Pakhomenko, a trader at Lanta bank in Moscow. "We can't just keep falling day after day."

The ruble depreciated as much as 2.8% against the dollar Thursday, though it rallied slightly near the close of trading. Last month, it was one of the world's worst performing currencies, losing 12.2% against the greenback. Ignatyev blamed the ruble's weakness on one factor--the sovereign debt crisis in Europe.

"Unfortunately, the situation in Europe is worsening and so far, European politicians have not offered the market a program for combat ting these difficulties," Ignatyev said.

Ignatyev said the ruble is not "doomed to fall," and predicted the currency's slide will slow, even if oil prices keep sinking. But he also stated the Bank of Russia is unlikely to change its policy on market intervention because of "fleeting events."

The central bank is gradually reducing its presence in the market as it moves the ruble closer to a free float, a policy that is expected to shield the economy in times of economic crisis, but also makes for greater currency volatility. Investors have complained in recent days that the central bank wasn't doing enough to support the ruble, a criticism that another central banker, Deputy Chairman Sergei Shvetsov, tried to deflect.

"I don't see this as a collapse," Shvetsov told the Vedomosti newspaper. "If you look at the ruble's performance compared with that of many other emerging-market currencies... there is not that much of a difference."

Russia's central bank manages its currency in a six-ruble-wide band against a basket of dollars and euros, purchasing foreign currency when the ruble appreciates to upper limit of the corridor, and selling foreign exchange as the ruble approaches the band's lower edge. The band currently ranges from RUB32.15 to RUB38.15.

The ruble closed 0.6% weaker at RUB37.26 against the basket Friday, from RUB37.05 at the end of trading Thursday. The regulator typically shifts the borders of its floating corridor by five kopecks after it has exhausted a daily intervention allotment of $500 million at the borders of the trading band, a policy Shvetsov said is still in place.

The currency's recent volatility is "within the limits of our corridor," Shvetsov said. "It is pretty okay with us."

title: DJ UPDATE: Ruble Drops To 2009 Crisis Levels
text:
-- Ruble down as much as 2.8% vs US dollar

-- Analysts see further weakening

-- Central bank steps up support

(Rewrites throughout.)

By Ira Iosebashvili

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Russian ruble plummeted to its lowest level in more than three years against the dollar on Thursday, bruised by falling oil prices and a fresh round of European sovereign debt worries, with market watchers predicting further weakness ahead despite interventions from the central bank.

Russia's currency weakened by as much as 2.8% against the greenback to RUB33.69, its lowest level since April 2009, when Russia was still fighting the initial waves of the global financial crisis amid plummeting oil prices and a 35% ruble decline.

After a strong start to the year, the ruble is now one of the world's worst-performing currencies, having shed 11.7% against the dollar in May alone.

Prices for oil, Russia's chief export, hovered near a six-month low of $103 per barrel for Brent crude as fears of a Greek exit from the euro eroded risk appetite across markets. Traders and fund managers have said that ruble selling may intensify if prices for oil slip below $100 per barrel and stay there.

"There is a recognition that Russia is far more vulnerable than ever if commodity prices crack on the back of weaker Chinese or European growth," said Tim Ash, emerging-markets economist at RBS. "It will not take much in terms of lower oil prices to cause serious stress to the Russia story."

While Russia's sovereign debt--which stands at just over 11% of gross domestic product--is enviably low compared with most of its European neighbors, successive waves of government spending have boosted the oil price needed to keep the budget in the black to an estimated $117 per barrel, from as low as $50 per barrel in 2008.

Turbulence on global markets and a lack of solid investment opportunities within the country have caused both foreign and domestic capital to flee Russia, with some $42 billion in capital outflows recorded in the first four months of the year and a total of $80.5 billion in capital flight in 2011. With markets continuing to look shaky and investors unimpressed by their first glimpses of the economic policies of President Vladimir Putin, who was sworn in to a third Kremlin term on May 7, analysts said the outflow is likely to continue.

Because oil prices remain at historically high levels, the ruble may still have more weakness ahead, said Kingsmill Bond, chief strategist at Citi in Moscow.

"The ruble is still not cheap," Bond said, noting that the currency is only 5% off its all-time high when adjusted for inflation. "It is noteworthy that the ruble is today more expensive in real terms that at its 2008 pre-crisis valuation peak."

While both global and domestic factors seem to be against it at the moment, the ruble is about to get support from at least one source--the central bank. The regulator resumed interventions last Friday for the first time since Jan 17. While those interventions have so far been small--totaling almost $90 million so far this week--they will grow steadily as the ruble gets weaker.

Russia's central bank manages its currency in a six-ruble-wide band against a basket of dollars and euros, purchasing foreign currency when the ruble strengthens towards the lower edges of the band, and selling when it weakens. The borders of the ruble's corridor against the basket are RUB32.15 to RUB38.15. The ruble closed at RUB37.05 against the basket Thursday.

Analysts said the regulator is likely to stick with this policy of exchange-rate flexibility, rather than drawing a line in the sand beyond which it will defend the ruble--a move that cost it nearly a third of its reserves in 2008.

"The central bank has learned its lessons well," said Alexander Morozov, chief economist at HSBC in Moscow.

title: Russia cbank to buy $3 bln in April to curb rouble
text:
MOSCOW, April 24 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank has already bought $2 billion in April to limit the rouble's rise

and sees full-month forex interventions at around $3 billion, Interfax news agency cited the central bank's first deputy chairman on Tuesday.

"The central bank plans to buy around $3 billion at the domestic market in April, it has already purchased $2 billion," Alexei Ulyukayav was quoted as saying.

The central bank keeps the rouble in a floating band against a euro-dollar basket, comprised of 0.55 dollars and 0.45 euros, which last stood at 32.15-38.15 roubles per basket.

The bank buys foreign currencies when the rouble closes in on the lower boundary of the corridor, starts selling dollars and euros from reserves when the rouble is closer to the upper boundary, and does not intervene in the middle of the range.

title: UPDATE 2- Russia  to try to minimize  FX intervention  - official
text:
(Adds detail about conference)

NEW YORK, April 18 (Reuters) - Russia intends to minimize intervention in the foreign exchange market, a top central bank official said on We dnesday, though excess currency volatility remains a risk.

The country also has a "good chance" to decrease its budget shortfall this year and should achieve a balanced budget in coming years, said Alexei Ulyukayev, first deputy chairman of the Central Bank of Russia.

Speaking at the VTB Capital Investment conference in New York, Ulyukayev said that with interest rates pinned at or near zero in the United States, Europe and other advanced economies, "exchange rate volatility is a real challenge for us."

But he said the central bank is trying to spend less each month to limit excess ruble strength against the dollar and euro. The bank bought $4.3 billion last month, and Ulyukayev said this month's total so far was below $2 billion.

In the past, he said the central bank often bought between $10 billion and $15 billion a month in intervention.

The ruble last traded at 29.4750 per dollar and is up more than 8 percent so far this year.

Inflation is expected to rise this year as government spending increases. During his election campaign, President-elect Vladimir Putin promised to increase public sector pay and social benefits.

Ulyukayev said he expects inflation to be within the central banks' 5 percent to 6 percent target by year end, up from 3.7 percent in the year to March.

Economists say a modestly stronger ruble could help keep price pressures in check. But while a strong currency can ease inflation, it can also make a country's exports more expensive and hurt growth.

Despite the expected spending increases, Ulyukayev said Russia still had "a good chance to minimize the budget deficit."

Under its three-year fiscal plan, Russia forecasts a federal budget deficit this year of 1.5 percent of gross domestic product, rising to 1.6 percent in 2013 and falling to 0.7 percent of GDP in 2014.

He said the biggest risk to the Russian and global economies was slower growth in big emerging markets, led by China.

Risks Relating to the Russian Federation

Any material reduction in the price of crude oil or natural gas may materially adversely affect the revenues and financial condition of the Russian Federation



The Russian Federation's revenues are affected by international oil and natural
gas prices, which have fluctuated widely in recent years in response to global
supply and demand, general economic conditions, competition from other energy
sources and other factors. In 2008, for example, the peak price of Urals oil
was U.S.$140.80 per barrel and the average price per barrel was U.S.$94.37,
compared to a peak price of U.S.$78.15 and an average price of U.S.$60.89 in
2009. In 2010, the peak price of Urals oil was U.S.$92.05 per barrel and the
average price per barrel was U.S.$78.20, compared to a peak price of
U.S.$123.38 and an average price of U.S.$109.33 in 2011. Russia's 2012 Budget
Law assumes an average price per barrel of Urals oil of U.S.$100, U.S.$97 and
U.S.$101 for 2012, 2013 and 2014, respectively. See "Public Finance-2012
Federal Budget Law." Natural gas prices have likewise fluctuated significantly
in recent years, in part because crude oil prices often provide a benchmark for
natural gas prices. In 2008, the lowest monthly average export price of natural
gas was U.S.$294.80 per thousand m3, the highest monthly average export price
of natural gas was U.S.$417.10 per thousand m3 and the average export price of
natural gas was U.S.$359.10 per thousand m3, compared to the lowest monthly
average export price of U.S.$217.70 per thousand m3, a peak monthly average
export price of U.S.$332.90 per thousand m3 and an average export price of
U.S.$257.10 per thousand m3 in 2009. In 2010, the lowest monthly average export
price of natural gas was U.S.$254.40 per thousand m3, the highest monthly
average export price of natural gas was U.S.$287.60 per thousand m3 and the
average export price of natural gas was U.S.$273 per thousand m3 (excluding
trade with Kazakhstan from 1 July 2010), compared to the lowest monthly average
export price of U.S.$328.3 per thousand m3, the peak monthly average export
price of U.S.$436 per thousand m3 and the average export price of U.S.$381.48
per thousand m3 in 2011. Any material reduction in the price of crude oil or
natural gas will have a significant effect on Russia's budgetary revenues and
foreign reserves, and, if sustained, may materially adversely affect the
Russian Federation's financial condition.



The Russian Federation's economy, like many economies, is vulnerable to external shocks. A global economic crisis, significant future economic difficulties of the Russian Federation's major trading partners, and more general "contagion"effects all could have a material adverse effect on the Russian Federation's economic growth and the market for the Bonds



The Russian Federation's economy and finances were adversely affected in
2008-09 by the global financial crisis. Real gross domestic product ("GDP"),
for example, declined by 7.8% in 2009 compared to 2008, and the average
unemployment rate (using the definition of the International Labour
Organisation (the "ILO")) increased from 7.1% in the fourth quarter of 2008 to
8% in the fourth quarter of 2009. The value of the rouble against the dollar
also declined in 2009, by 12.2% in real terms, as did the value of the real
effective exchange rate, which fell by 5.6%.

The Russian Federation's economy remains vulnerable to further external shocks.
A significant decline in the economic growth of the EU or any of the Russian
Federation's other major trading partners could have a material adverse effect
on the Russian Federation's balance of trade and adversely affect the Russian
Federation's economic growth.

Events occurring in one geographic or financial market sometimes result in an
entire region or class of investments being disfavoured by international
investors-so-called "contagion effects." The Russian Federation has been
adversely affected by contagion effects in the past, and it is possible that
the market for Russian investments, including the Bonds, will be similarly
affected in the future by negative economic or financial developments in
countries whose economies or credit ratings are similar to those of the Russian
Federation.

There can be no assurance that a future external economic crisis will not have
a negative effect on investors' confidence in Russia's markets or on the
Russian Federation's economy or ability to raise capital in the international
debt markets, all of which could have a material adverse effect on the trading
price of the Bonds.



No waiver of immunity; enforcement of liabilities



The Russian Federation is a sovereign state and has not waived any rights to
sovereign immunity it may have in any jurisdiction. Accordingly, the Russian
Federation may be entitled to immunity from suit in any action or proceeding in
any jurisdiction arising out of the Bonds, and the Russian Federation and its
assets, properties and revenues may be entitled to immunity in any related
enforcement action. The Russian Federation has also not submitted to the
jurisdiction of any court, agreed that any disputes may be resolved in any
forum or appointed any agent for service of process in any jurisdiction, in
connection with any action or proceeding arising out of the Bonds. As a result
of the foregoing, it may be difficult or impossible for an investor to obtain a
judgment against the Russian Federation in a foreign court and/or have such
judgment recognised and/or enforced in any jurisdiction.

A final judgment rendered by a foreign court will generally be recognised and
enforced in the Russian Federation if there is an international treaty in
effect between the Russian Federation and the country where the judgment is
rendered providing for the mutual recognition and enforcement of judgments.
There are no international treaties in effect today providing for the mutual
recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments rendered by courts in the
Russian Federation and courts in most of the countries where Bond investors are
likely to reside, including the United States and the United Kingdom.

In the absence of an applicable treaty, enforcement of a final judgment
rendered by a foreign court may still be recognised by a Russian court on the
basis of reciprocity, if courts of the country where the foreign judgment is
rendered have previously enforced judgments issued by Russian courts. While
Russian courts have recently recognised and enforced English and Dutch court
judgments on these grounds, the existence of reciprocity must be established at
the time the recognition and enforcement of a foreign judgment is sought, and
it is not possible to predict whether a Russian court will in the future
recognise and enforce on the basis of reciprocity a judgment issued by a
foreign court, including an English or Dutch court.

Even if an applicable international treaty is in effect or a foreign judgment
might otherwise be recognised and enforced on the basis of reciprocity, the
recognition and enforcement of a foreign judgment will in all events be subject
to exceptions and limitations provided for in Russian law. For example, a
Russian court may refuse to recognise or enforce a foreign judgment if its
recognition or enforcement would contradict Russian public policy.



As a result, it may be difficult to obtain recognition or enforcement in the Russian Federation of a foreign judgment in respect of the Bonds.

authorised denomination upon the surrender of the Bond Certificate representing

denomination and a new Bond Certificate in respect of the balance not so
transferred will be issued to the transferor.

Each new Bond Certificate to be issued upon a transfer of any Bonds will,
within five business days of the request for transfer being duly made, be
delivered at the specified office of the Registrar or, as the case may be, any
Transfer Agent or (at the request and the risk of such transferee) be mailed by
uninsured post to such address as the transferee entitled to the Bonds

(b), "business day" means a day (other than a Saturday or Sunday) on which
commercial banks are open for business (including dealings in foreign
currencies) in the cities in which the Registrar and any such Transfer Agent

nature which may be levied or imposed in connection with such registration

or
transfer.

No Bondholder may require the transfer of a Bond to be registered during the

All transfers of Bonds and entries on the Register will be made subject to the

manner which is reasonably required by the Russian Federation (after

any other manner which is not prejudicial to the interests of the Bondholders.
A copy of the current regulations will be sent by the Registrar to any
Bondholder who so requests.



3 Status



The Bonds constitute direct, unconditional, unsecured and unsubordinated
obligations of the Russian Federation and the full faith and credit of the
Russian Federation is pledged for the due and punctual payment of principal of,
and interest on, the Bonds and for the performance of all other obligations of
the Russian Federation pursuant to the Bonds. The Bonds shall at all times rank
pari passu without any preference among themselves and pari passu in all
respects with all other present and future unsecured and unsubordinated
obligations of the Russian Federation.

So long as any of the Bonds remains outstanding (as defined in the Fiscal

So long as any Bond remains outstanding the Russian Federation shall obtain,
and do or cause to be done all things necessary to ensure the continuance of,
all consents, licences, approvals and authorisations, and make or cause to be

required to be obtained or made in the Russian Federation for the execution,
delivery or performance of the Bonds or for the validity or enforceability

thereof.

5 Interest



Each Bond bears interest on its outstanding principal amount from 4 April 2012
at 4.50 per cent. per annum, payable semi-annually in arrear on 4 April and
4 October in each year until maturity, commencing on 4 October 2012 (each, an "
Interest Payment Date"). Interest will be paid subject to and in accordance
with the provisions of Condition 7. The period beginning on and including
4 April 2012 and ending on but excluding the first Interest Payment Date and
each successive period beginning on and including an Interest Payment Date and
ending on but excluding the next successive Interest Payment Date is called an
"Interest Period".

Each Bond will cease to bear interest from the due date for redemption unless,
after surrender of such Bond, payment of principal is improperly withheld or
refused, in which case the outstanding principal amount of such Bond will
continue to bear interest at the rate specified above (after as well as before
judgment) until whichever is the earlier of (a) the day on which all sums due
in respect of such Bond up to that day are received by or on behalf of the
relevant Bondholder and (b) the day which is seven days after notice has been
given to the Bondholders that the Fiscal Agent has received all sums due in
respect of the Bonds up to such seventh day (except, in the case of payment to
the Fiscal Agent, to the extent that there is any subsequent default in payment
in accordance with these Conditions).



If interest is required to be calculated for a period of less than a complete Interest Period, it will be calculated on the basis of a year of 360 days consisting of 12 months of 30 days each and, in the case of an incomplete month, the actual number of days elapsed.

Unless previously redeemed, or purchased and cancelled, each Bond will be redeemed at its principal amount on 4 April 2022 (the "Maturity Date") subject as provided in Condition 7.

The Russian Federation and its affiliates may at any time purchase Bonds in the
open market or otherwise at any price. Any Bonds so purchased may be cancelled
or held and resold (provided that such resale is outside the United States, as
defined in Regulation S under the Securities Act). Any Bonds so cancelled will
not be reissued.

Bond

of

All payments of principal and interest in respect of the Bonds by the Russian
Federation shall be made free and clear of, and without withholding or
deduction for, any taxes, duties, assessments or governmental charges of
whatever nature imposed, levied, collected, withheld or assessed by the Russian
Federation or any political subdivision or any authority thereof or therein
having power to tax (together, "Taxes"), unless such withholding or deduction
is required by law. If at any time any Taxes are withheld or deducted, the

case may be, to such amount as will result in the receipt by the Bondholders of

deduction been required, except that no such increased amount shall be payable:



(a) to a holder, or to a third party on behalf of a holder, if such holder is liable to such Taxes by reason of having some connection with the Russian Federation other than the mere holding of a Bond or the receipt of payments thereunder;

for payment more than 30 days after the Relevant Date, except to the extent
that the holder would have been entitled to such additional amounts on
presentation and surrender of such Bond Certificate for payment on the last day

individual and is required to be made pursuant to European Council Directive
2003/48/EC or any other Directive implementing the conclusions of the ECOFIN

and no Bondholder shall incur any obligation with respect thereto (including,

therewith).

have no right to make any deduction or withholding in respect of (nor will it

9 Events of Default

If any of the following occurs and is continuing (each an "Event of Default") in respect of the Bonds, as applicable:

(a)Non-payment

The Russian Federation fails to pay any amount of principal or interest in respect of the Bonds, as the case may be, when due and such failure continues for a period of 30 calendar days; or

(b)Breach of other obligations or undertakings



The Russian Federation defaults in performance or observance of or compliance
with any of its other obligations or undertakings in respect of the Bonds, as
the case may be, which default (if capable of remedy) is not remedied within
60 days after written notice of such default shall have been given to the
Russian Federation by any holder of the Bonds, as the case may be, it being
understood that a default in respect of the undertaking set forth in
Condition 4(a) shall be deemed capable of remedy for purposes hereof; or



(c)Cross-acceleration

Any Public External Indebtedness shall become due and payable prior to the
stated maturity thereof otherwise than at the option of the debtor following a
default or the Russian Federation, the Government of the Russian Federation or
the Ministry of Finance shall fail to make the final payment of principal in
respect of any Public External Indebtedness on the date on which such final
payment is due and payable or at the expiration of any grace period originally
applicable thereto or, in the case of any guarantee which constitutes Public
External Indebtedness, the underlying obligation in respect of which such
guarantee has been given shall have become due and payable prior to the stated
maturity thereof otherwise than at the option of the debtor following a default
or the debtor shall have failed to make the final payment of principal in
respect of such underlying obligation on the date on which such final payment
is due and payable or at the expiration of any grace period originally
applicable thereto and the guarantee shall not be honoured when due and called
upon; provided that the aggregate amount of the relevant Public External
Indebtedness in respect of which one or more of the events mentioned in this
Condition 9(c) shall have occurred equals or exceeds U.S.$75,000,000 (or its
equivalent in any other currency or currencies); and provided, further, that
any secured Public External Indebtedness that by its terms is fully
non-recourse to the Russian Federation, the Government of the Russian
Federation or the Ministry of Finance shall not be counted as Public External
Indebtedness for purposes of this Condition 9(c); or



(d)Moratorium

A moratorium on the payment of principal of, or interest on, all or any part of Public External Indebtedness; or

(e)Unlawfulness or Invalidity



The validity of the Bonds is contested by the Russian Federation or any agency
or entity acting on behalf of the Russian Federation or the Russian Federation
or any agency or entity acting on behalf of the Russian Federation shall deny
any of the Russian Federation's obligations under the Bonds or it is or will
become unlawful for the Russian Federation to perform or comply with any of its
obligations under or in respect of the Bonds or under or in respect of the
Fiscal Agency Agreement or any of such obligations shall be or become

the Bonds or under the Fiscal Agency Agreement or for the validity or
enforceability thereof shall expire or be withheld, revoked or terminated or

holders of the Bonds, as the case may be,

then holders of 25 per cent. or more in aggregate outstanding principal amount
of the Bonds may declare the Bonds to be immediately due and payable whereupon

Bondholders to consider any matter affecting their interests, including the
modification by Extraordinary Resolution of these Conditions. The quorum at any
such meeting for passing an Extraordinary Resolution shall (subject as provided
in the Fiscal Agency Agreement in the event that all outstanding Bonds are held
by one person) be two or more persons holding or representing a clear majority
of the aggregate principal amount of the outstanding Bonds, or at any meeting
that is adjourned two or more persons being or representing Bondholders
(whatever the principal amount of the outstanding Bonds so held or
represented), and the majority for passing an Extraordinary Resolution at any
such meeting shall be at least 662/3 per cent. of the votes cast except that at

Reserved Matters, including, inter alia, (i) to modify the maturity of the

percentage required to pass any resolution, the necessary quorum for passing an

Agreement in the event that all outstanding Bonds are held by one person) be

the Bondholders, to any modification of any provision of the Fiscal Agency
Agreement or the Bonds which is of a formal, minor or technical nature or is

or

5 Interest



Each Bond bears interest on its outstanding principal amount from 4 April 2012
at 5.625 per cent. per annum, payable semi-annually in arrear on 4 April and
4 October in each year until maturity, commencing on 4 October 2012 (each, an "
Interest Payment Date"). Interest will be paid subject to and in accordance
with the provisions of Condition 7. The period beginning on and including
4 April 2012 and ending on but excluding the first Interest Payment Date and
each successive period beginning on and including an Interest Payment Date and
ending on but excluding the next successive Interest Payment Date is called an
"Interest Period".

Each Bond will cease to bear interest from the due date for redemption unless,
after surrender of such Bond, payment of principal is improperly withheld or
refused, in which case the outstanding principal amount of such Bond will
continue to bear interest at the rate specified above (after as well as before
judgment) until whichever is the earlier of (a) the day on which all sums due
in respect of such Bond up to that day are received by or on behalf of the
relevant Bondholder and (b) the day which is seven days after notice has been
given to the Bondholders that the Fiscal Agent has received all sums due in
respect of the Bonds up to such seventh day (except, in the case of payment to
the Fiscal Agent, to the extent that there is any subsequent default in payment
in accordance with these Conditions).



If interest is required to be calculated for a period of less than a complete Interest Period, it will be calculated on the basis of a year of 360 days consisting of 12 months of 30 days each and, in the case of an incomplete month, the actual number of days elapsed.
