text:
MOSCOW, May 14 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Wednesday it would begin regular interventions in the local forex market as part of transition to an inflation targeting regime.

To read the main story click on [ID:nL14841077]

SHAHIN VALLEE, EMERGING MARKETS STRATEGIST BNP PARIBAS

"There is no corridor at present, there is a spot reference level that the central bank is defending. The central bank allows the currency to move a bit against the spot reference level when it wants to create volatility."

"This announcement is quite a big deal, because there have been a lot of rumours about the rouble revaluation.

The central bank is creating some uncertainty, it could increase weakness in the short term and shake out positioning, then the central bank could potentially revalue later. I do not think the fundamentals have changed about the sources of appreciation in the rouble."

SERGEI ROMANCHUK, DEALER METALLINVESTBANK

"It means the bank will change more often its bid parameters to the basket, but to me it does not mean it is dropping the basket. Today and yesterday we saw some big volatility, which was difficult to explain, and now we can say that was the central bank which was buying (dollars). Now there will be days when it will lift the (rouble) to basket and days when it will drop it.

NIKOLAI PODGUZOV, ANALYST, RENAISSANCE CAPITAL

"The central bank's statement most likely means it wants to increase the rouble volatility to the basket.

It will not only bid at the corridor lower level of 29.6 but at higher levels as well to increase the rouble volatility, reduce predictability and reduce speculative mood on the market as far as the rouble level to the basket is concerned.

But it does not mean that it will not take a decision to let the rouble appreciate.

The central bank is currently trying to switch to interest rates from currency policies as a tool to control inflation. It may result in lower speculative capital inflows."

DEALER AT A MAJOR FOREIGN BANK

"The central bank wants to increase the rouble/basket volatility to reduce speculative pressure it is currently facing, when market players sell the currency and go long on the rouble against the basket on rouble appreciation expectations.

Should volatility increase, it will force investors to reduce their long positions. Dollar sales to the central bank will fall, it will have to print fewer roubles, which will in turn cut the rouble liquidity and inflation." title: UPDATE 2-Russia c.bank moves to fend off rouble speculators
text:
(Adds c.bank comments, dealers, analysts)

MOSCOW, May 14 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Wednesday it would begin daily interventions in the local forex market as of May 14 to discourage currency speculators and make the rouble's exchange rate more flexible.

The move followed weeks of intense rumours the central bank will allow the rouble to appreciate after the inauguration of President Dmitry Medvedev to curb inflation and protect popularity of the new leader and his predecessor and political mentor Vladimir Putin, who became prime minister.

"We believe this measure will demotivate speculative capital from entering the Russian money market, fixing the profit and leaving," First Deputy Chairman of the central bank Alexei Ulyukayev told Interfax news agency.

Ulyukayev said a more flexible exchange rate policy will make more difficult for speculators to calculate the exchange rate at a given date, decreasing the volatility of capital flows, which make Russia's balance of payments less predictable.

The rouble exchange rate is the central bank's main anti-inflation weapon and with annual inflation running at over 14 percent going long on the rouble has become a popular trade with major international players.

The bank said in a statement its intervention policy would now be guided by the situation in the local forex market, the country's trade balance and the federal budget. It said the move was also part of a transition to an inflation targeting regime.

The central bank had intervened to keep the rouble stable against a basket made of 0.55 dollars and 0.45 euros. Currency dealers say the central bank has bought about $30 billion since the start of the year.

"If earlier we saw that the exchange rate de facto hovered close to one of the ends of the corridor, most often the lower end, now we will see the exchange rate fluctuating inside the corridor," Ulyukayev said.

"EVIL CARRY-TRADERS"

The rouble surprisingly weakened to the basket in the last two days and dealers told Reuters they suspected there could have been a leak about the central bank's upcoming move.

The rouble closed at 29.73 against the dollar/euro basket on Wednesday, calculated on a daily weighted average basis versus 29.65 on Tuesday and 0.4 percent weaker than the 29.61 currently seen by the market as the central bank's bid level.

The central bank has never disclosed its corridor, but market players say it is set at 29.61-29.91 per basket.

Sources familiar with the policy told Reuters the move will also help the central bank plan better its currency purchases for two oil funds which collect windfall oil revenues. They also said the new policy will help smooth liquidity fluctuations.

Ulyukayev told Interfax the central bank carried out its first intervention on Wednesday buying several hundred million dollars and promised the regulator will intervene daily with volumes increasing during corporate tax payments.

The central bank earlier dismissed the appreciation talk as "irrational" while Putin told the parliament the country could live with double digit inflation for some years, dampening appreciation expectations. "The central bank is creating some uncertainty, it could increase weakness in the short term and shake out positioning, then the central bank could potentially revalue later," said Shahin Vallee, emerging markets strategist at BNP Paribas.

"The central bank's main task is to get carry-traders off the market, they see them as the main evil and want to cut their hands off," said Nikolai Kashcheyev, analyst at state-owned VTB. Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin and Ulyukayev said earlier this year Russia may move to an inflation targeting regime in the medium term once its huge trade surplus shrinks.

The regime will give the central bank more leverage over inflation with its interest rates policy but will require the regulator to abandon its managed float policy and allow the rouble to float freely.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian gold/ forex  reserves pass $0.5 trln threshold
text:
(Updates with analyst quotes, details)   

MOSCOW, March 20 (Reuters) - Russia's gold and foreign exchange reserves have passed the $0.5 trillion threshold, rising to $502.1 billion on March 14 from $494.5 billion on March 7, central bank data showed on Thursday.   

The figure suggested the central bank has resumed its purchases of petrodollars in the market in March as prices for oil, Russia's main export commodity, hit record highs on speculative demand and supply uncertainty.   

Analysts estimated the central bank has already bought about $10 billion in March after it only intervened three or four times in January-February, buying about $2 billion in these two months amid net capital outflows.   

The inflow of currency from energy exports in March has neutralised capital outflows, expected to net at about $9 billion, forcing the central bank to resume its currency interventions. Russia's reserves are the world's third largest.   

"The inflow of foreign currency is so big, the price for oil is so high, that it beats everything," said Yevgeny Nadorshin, analyst at Trust Bank, suggesting Russia has returned to its 'natural' state of reserve growth of the past few years.   

"It is positive for liquidity. It is positive for interest rates," Nadorshin said, adding renewed currency inflows would flood the money market with liquidity, badly needed by banks and corporations that have foreign debt.   

The central bank expects a liquidity shortage in the next few weeks, with the daily refinancing demand from banks hitting 400 billion roubles in April. Currently, money market rates <RUBOND=> are around 3.25-4.20 percent. (Reporting by Gleb Bryanski; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: UPDATE 3-Russia's RTS index down, rouble weakens
text:
(Releads, updates market data after close)   

MOSCOW, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Russian stocks and the rouble pared heavy intraday losses on Tuesday as blue chips outperformed other emerging markets, but traders said a sharp cut in U.S. interest rates did little to change a gloomy outlook.   

Analysts said they believe Russia is better positioned to weather the global storm than other emerging markets. The rouble also recovered in late trading in Moscow after dipping close to a level below which central bank intervention could be expected.   

"Do not panic, Russia is no Turkey. The rouble still makes Russia a relative safe haven," analysts at Troika Dialog brokerage wrote in a research note.   

"The key markets at risk from the current bout of panic over the U.S. growth are those with expensive currencies funded by foreign capital. With its strong macro backdrop, Russia is not subject to this risk," Troika analysts said.   

The RTS stock index <.IRTS> ended down 1.61 percent at 1967.7 points. It had earlier fallen briefly below 1,900 points for the first time since September 2007, before rebounding into positive territory above 2,000 points.   

The turnover on Russia's biggest bourse, MICEX's equity section, was a healthy 131.7 billion roubles ($5.29 billion).   

The U.S. Federal Reserve cut its interest rates by a dramatic 75 basis points, in a move usually reducing the flight to safer assets, such as government bonds in rich economies.   

"First there was euphoria (after the Fed decision). The market spiked up, but then started sliding again," said Pavel Vashchenko from trading company IK Region.   

"We see it could not impress the market, which will continue to be driven by the same negative factors," he said.   

Russian stocks outperformed other emerging markets for most of the day, but by 1608 GMT were marginally worse. The MSCI Russia index <.MIRU00000PUS> fell 2.9 percent versus a 2.5 percent slide in the MSCI Emerging Markets index <.MSCIEF>.   

Former electricity monopoly Unified Energy System led the fall with a 4.0 percent decline, while state oil major Rosneft fell by 3.4 percent.   

But not all stocks ended down. Gazprom , the world's largest gas producer and one of the world's 10 largest stocks, climbed 1.1 percent, and mining giant Norilsk Nickel was up 1.9 percent.   

Russia's 2008 budget is balanced at an average oil price of $53 per barrel, and analysts see no major external threats to macroeconomic stability if the oil price stays above this level. U.S. crude <CLc1> was trading at $88.19 a barrel by 1510 GMT.   

ROUBLE CLOSE TO MINIMUM LEVEL   

The rouble weakened about 0.4 percent to 29.82 against the central bank's dollar/euro currency basket made of 0.55 dollars and 0.45 euros as of 0800 GMT and dealers said the central bank was not seen on the market.   

The rouble <RUBUTSTN=MCX> weakened to 24.92 to the dollar, which accounts for the lion's share of currency trade on the Russian market, but then climbed back to 24.75.   

"We believe that the rouble is close to its minimum level and the central bank is unlikely to allow it to weaken further," said Stanislav Ponomarenko, head of research at ING in Moscow.   

The central bank, which runs the world's third-largest gold and forex reserves, does not comment on currency moves.   

OFFERINGS POSTPONED   

Analysts said the market turbulence would affect Russian companies' plans to float stocks and raise debt.   

"It is clear that all offerings scheduled for the next month will be postponed. The first quarter outlook is more blurred. A lot will depend on the situation in the United States," said Oleg Lukhton, head of investment banking at Uralsib.   

Russian Eurobonds remained stable with the 2030 bond <0#RU011428878=> trading with a spread of 184 basis points against the U.S. treasuries. (Reporting by Gleb Bryanski and Olga Popova; Editing by Jason Neely; Editing by Paul Bolding)

title: UPDATE 1-Russian c.bank seen buying dollars after CPI data
text:
(Releads on c.bank interventions)   

MOSCOW, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank was seen actively buying dollars on the foreign exchange market on Friday after the release of higher-than-expected inflation data, traders told Reuters.   

Russia's consumer price index (CPI) rose by 0.8 percent month-on-month in September, the Federal Statistics Service (FSS) said, significantly exceeding analysts' expectations.   

"Market players expect the central bank to appreciate the rouble against the dual currency basket in order to lower inflationary pressure. They have opened long positions in the rouble," a Moscow bank dealer told Reuters.   

The central bank controls inflation through the rouble exchange rate and uses a dual currency basket, made up of 0.55 dollars and 0.45 euros, to guide its forex interventions.   

A stronger rouble makes imported goods cheaper but impacts the inflation rate only with a time lag of several months. Analysts have said any exchange rate move by the central bank now is unlikely to influence the full-year inflation rate.   

Traders said they believed the central bank had bought between $2.5 and $3.0 billion by 1250 GMT. The rouble remained stable against the dollar/euro currency basket.   

HORRIBLE FIGURE   

The CPI rise follows massive liquidity injections into the banking sector by the central bank and suggests Russia may significantly overshoot its annual inflation target of 8.0 percent.   

"This is a horrible figure. I do not remember a time when expectations and reality were so different. It means it will even be difficult to have the same inflation as last year's 9 percent," said Natalya Orlova, economist at  Alfa Bank.

Some analysts said the current liquidity squeeze gives the central bank more leverage over inflation through its interest rates policy -- a major shift in Russia's monetary policy, which was aimed at tackling excess liquidity in recent years. "The central bank now has considerably greater latitude to use interest rate policy to address inflation, since it is supplying liquidity to the banking system," said Rory MacFarquhar, senior economist at  Goldman Sachs.

POLICY FAILURE   

The September rise brings price growth in the first nine months of the year to 7.5 percent, for the first time in 2007 exceeding last year's corresponding figure. The CPI grew by 7.2 percent in the same period of 2006.   

Officials as well as analysts polled by Reuters had expected the CPI index to rise 0.4 percent.   

"This is a very unpleasant surprise for the government. It puts it in a situation when measures aimed to support liquidity levels in the banking system contradict anti-inflation measures," said Yulia Tsepliaeva from  Merrill Lynch.

The central bank provided banks with billions of roubles of liquidity in August and September after a global credit crunch shut sources of cheap financing abroad.   

Russia had 9 percent inflation in 2006, after raising the annual target and introducing tough anti-inflation measures, including the rouble appreciation.   

Kremlin economic aide Arkady Dvorkovich told Reuters last month that an overshoot above last year's figure would represent policy failure.   

The FSS said core inflation, an indicator cleared of seasonal and volatile factors, rose 1.6 percent in September. The spike in core inflation suggests monetary factors were the main culprit behind the surprisingly high figure.   

Food prices jumped 1.0 percent due to increases in prices for milk, dairy products and sunoil. Russian dairy producers said last month prices for milk powder and raw milk spiked in Russia due to a soaring global demand for milk products. (Additional reporting by Yelena Fabrichnaya and Maria Kiselyova)

title: INSTANT VIEW 7-Putin nominates financial regulator as PM
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin has nominated Viktor Zubkov, head of the Federal Financial Monitoring Service, for the vacant post of prime minister, the speaker of the lower house of parliament said on Wednesday.   

COMMENTS   

JONATHAN EYAL, ROYAL UNITED SERVICES INSTITUTE, LONDON:   

"What Mr Zubkov is, is effectively a friend of Putin -- which confirms the little clique that runs Russia -- and another St Petersburger. But he is not presidential material.   

"It is an indication that Putin has not made up his mind whether he wants to go for a constitutional amendment and go for another term in office himself, or whether he wants to opt for one of the other two contenders."   

EARLIER COMMENTS   

ROLAND NASH, HEAD OF RESEARCH, RENAISSANCE CAPITAL:   

"The nomination of Viktor Zubkov to replace outgoing Prime Minister Mikhail Fradkov is at least in keeping with one well established Kremlin tradition -- it was entirely unexpected.   

"Nonetheless, our first reaction to this particular PM is that, while he is now among the front runners, we do not see him as the likely successor.   

"More likely, we see him as another means of cementing some stability during the period of power transfer, a Prime Minister who will serve under both the current and the next President.   

"The little we do know about Mr Zubkov suggests he is loyal to Putin, has proven successful in fighting some difficult political battles and holds a great deal of that precious Russian political commodity, information and kompromat -- in other words, somebody who can be relied upon to maintain stability in government during a potentially uncertain transition of power."   

CHRIS WEAFER, STRATEGIST, URALSIB:   

"Appointing someone with a successful background in fighting corruption can be seen as part of the Duma election campaign. We can expect to see a few high-profile arrests and prosecutions over the next few months.   

"It puts another name in the frame (on the Putin succession), but not into a leading position. It does highlight him as a strong candidate, but not the automatic choice -- it still needs to be someone popular and acceptable to the people.   

"He's in something of a probationary period. He needs now to prove he can be the people's choice. It's his job to lose.   

"This would be a de facto continuation of the Putin presidency, until Putin wants to take back the reins, and that won't be after four years, it will certainly be sooner. A safe pair of hands until Putin wants the job back."   

SERGEI MARKOV, HEAD OF INSTITUTE FOR POLITICAL STUDIES:   

"I think the candidacy of the prime minister will be a political appointment," Markov told the Vesti-24 TV news channel.   

"Sergei Ivanov is candidate No.1 and Dmitry Medevedev is candidate No.2. But there is always the possibility for something unexpected as Putin has shown before that he can surprise people.   

"Probably the (next prime minister) will become the (Kremlin's) candidate for the presidency but it could equally be that this person will work as the partner of the next president and will remain as prime minister under the new president in order to ensure continuity for Putin's policies."   

ALEXANDER KARPOV, CURRENCY DEALER, ZENIT BANK:   

"There was some short-term impact of this news on the currency market. Someone tried to buy dollars, weakening the rouble slightly. Everyone understands that there is no crisis in the economy and this news is not related to the economic situation."   

OLEG VYUGIN, MDM BANK CHAIRMAN, FORMER HEAD OF FINANCIAL MARKETS WATCHDOG:   

"I do not think this will have a big impact on the markets. Such a scenario has been discussed. It was not clear when it will happen. Obviously it is the preparation for the election. What is interesting is who will head the new government. That is what the markets will be waiting for."   

STANISLAV PONOMARENKO, ANALYST AT ING BANK, MOSCOW:   

"If everything with the new appointments resolves itself quickly, we do not expect it to have a major impact on the economy."   

MARKET REACTION:

"The market consensus is: Ivanov bad, (First Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry) Medvedev good, so the markets might take an Ivanov appointment badly.

title: UPDATE 3- Russia  c.bank  intervenes  to support rouble
text:
(Adds Gref on inflation, second repo auction)   

MOSCOW, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank intervened on Tuesday to support a weakening rouble and pumped fresh liquidity into the banking system as foreign investors cut their exposure to risky assets in a global credit crunch.   

Typically, the  Central Bank of Russia is seen bidding for dollars as it offsets upward pressure on the rouble stemming from the half a billion petrodollars a day earned by the world's No.2 oil exporter.   

But this time the central bank stepped in as a dollar seller when the rouble eased by over half a percent against the dollar/euro currency basket it targets under its managed float. Analysts said the investor pullback may actually help Russian policy makers in their fight against inflation. Economy Minister German Gref predicted that consumer price growth would hit the 8 percent official target this year.   

The rouble's fall wiped out last week's gains and pared back its advance against the currency basket, composed of 55 U.S. cents and 45 euro cents, to just 0.6 percent so far this year.   

Dealers said non-residents trading through several large banks were closing their short positions in the basket. Some market watchers expected the rouble weakness to be short-lived. "The rouble will come back within the coming days. The central bank will make sure of that," said Lars Rasmussen, analyst at  Danske Bank.

LIQUIDITY INJECTION   

Russian stocks fell by up to 2 percent and overnight money market rates remained high as the central bank injected a total of 87.8 billion roubles ($3.4 billion) into the banking system at rates of 6.05 and 6.1 percent via one-day repo auctions.   

Russia's authorities are having to walk a fine line between keeping the financial system liquid and containing money pressures that threaten this year's inflation target.   

Economists say the latest capital outflows weighing on the rouble, after record inflows early this year, could offset price pressures. "These outflows could be a blessing in disguise," said Yaroslav Lissovolik, chief economist at  Deutsche UFG in Moscow.   

Gref said consumer prices rose by 0.2 percent in the first two weeks of August but should then stabilise for the rest of the month.   

"I think we have every chance of meeting our forecast target (for 2007) of 8 percent," Gref told President Vladimir Putin at a meeting, according to Interfax news agency.   

Analysts said Russia's financial system was feeling some of the strain stemming from the crisis in the risky U.S. subprime mortgage sector, but is now much better able to cope than a few years ago.   

"This is a more normal market. It's getting more mature," said Evgeny Gavrilenkov, chief economist at Troika Dialog.   

Three years ago, the forced closure of two small banks was enough to trigger a run that forced the owners of  Alfa-Bank, Russia's largest private bank, to inject hundreds of millions of dollars in fresh capital to steady the ship.   

Now, Russia has a deposit insurance scheme, its central bank has $420 billion in reserves and it was quick last week to relaunch repo operations dormant since March to allow banks to pledge securities in return for ready cash.   

"The central bank has been pretty quick to act and so far we aren't seeing any signs of major strains being felt by any of the major banks," said Lissovolik.

title: UPDATE 2-Rouble slips, market suspects Rosneft dlr buying
text:
(Adds Rosneft statement, Ignatyev comments on reserves)   

MOSCOW, June 27 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble eased against its dollar/euro currency basket on Wednesday, giving back some gains from the day before, as a single buyer was spotted scooping up dollars.   

Dealers and analysts suggested the dollar buyer could have acted on behalf of state-controlled oil firm Rosneft which could be buying dollars so it could retire foreign debt.   

The basket, 55 percent of which is dollars and 45 percent euros, closed at 29.8478 roubles, up 0.16 percent.   

That followed a 0.5 percent rouble revaluation on Tuesday as the central bank, which runs a managed float, sought to combat inflation pressures.   

"There is active dollar buying going on at the moment," said Pyotr Milovanov, currency dealer at Metallinvestbank.   

Yevgeny Nadorshin, analyst at Trust Bank, added: "One can suggest that a single market player is collecting the cash for Rosneft."   

Rosneft said on Wednesday it had received 237 billion roubles ($9.2 billion) of debt owed to it by bankrupt oil company YUKOS and that would use the cash to pay off debt.   

Rosneft raised $22 billion in short-term loans from a consortium of international banks earlier this year to buy assets of bankrupt oil firm YUKOS at a series of auctions.   

The bankrupt firm's receiver announced on Wednesday he had started paying back 400 billion roubles ($15.52 billion) of YUKOS debt to creditors. YUKOS owes Rosneft about $10 billion.   

For a Reuters interview with Rosneft finance vice president Peter O'Brien on debt repayment, click on [ID:nL27878831].   

Dollar volumes at MICEX currency exchange stood at $4.2 billion, compared with about $3 billion for all of Tuesday. Dealers said they the central bank appeared to be staying out of the market.   

"Looks like the central bank is not present," Nadorshin said. "For some reasons the central bank does not want to sell its dollars to this single player."   

The central bank guided the rouble about 0.5 percent higher on Tuesday against the basket in a revaluation aimed at keeping inflation within its annual target. Wednesday's bounce left analysts wondering why the central bank had not yet intervened to keep the basket stable. The central bank runs a managed float of the rouble and buys foreign currency, mainly dollars, flowing into Russia as companies repatriate export revenues and raise funds in the international market.   

The Russian currency market largely follows international forex moves when the central bank does not intervene.   

Russia's central bank runs the world's third-largest gold and forex reserves and about half of its currency holdings are in dollars. The central bank's chairman, Sergei Ignatyev, told parliament on Wednesday he expected reserves growth to slow.   

"Imports are growing, exports are growing too but at a slower rate, therefore our forecast is for moderate growth of gold and forex reserves," Ignatyev said.

title: Swedbank OAO Subject To Public Authority  Intervention ,  Russia
text:
Edited Press Release   

STOCKHOLM (Dow Jones)--Swedbank (SWED-A.SK) said Thursday that Swedbank OAO is subject to public authority intervention. It said the Central Bank of Russia has issued an order to restrict certain operations of Swedbank OAO in Russia for a period of three months.   

It said the central bank quotes violations of the federal law and the normative acts of the Central Bank on prevention of illicitly acquired funds.   

The order is issued as a result of an audit performed during March to April this year, Swedbank said, and the following restrictions mainly concerns the area of correspondent banking, carrying out foreign exchange operations, attracting new business and interbank loans.   

"We are currently establishing the further circumstances and have also requested clarifications. The order was unexpected and we are of course ready to take necessary measures," said Swedbank CEO Jan Lidén. "Meanwhile we continue to serve clients with respect to operations not restricted by the order and to minimize the effects for our clients," Lidén said.   

Swedbank is requested to adjust its operations quoted in the order and to further enhance internal control systems, it said.   

Swedbank said Swedbank Russia has three branches and a portfolio of approximately SEK4B. The total number of employees is 238, it said. [ 07-06-07 0735GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Russia cbank mulls reserves diversification
text:
(Wraps central bank stories)  

TULA, Russia, Jan 24 (Reuters) - Russia may diversify further the currency structure of its $300 billion in gold and foreign exchange reserves, the world's third largest, a senior central banker said on Wednesday.  

"Diversification will happen. It makes sense. We are discussing it," Alexei Ulyukayev, first deputy chairman of the Central Bank of Russia, told a seminar for journalists.  

The central bank keeps its reserves in four currencies -- U.S. dollars, euros, sterling and yen. Their exact structure is a secret, but Chairman Sergei Ignatyev said last July they were composed of roughly 50 percent dollars and 40 percent euros.  

Ulyukayev said the bank may fully disclose the currency structure of its reserves this year. Officials have named the Canadian and Australian dollars and Swiss franc as possible candidates for diversification.  

Russia's gold and foreign exchange reserves, pumped up by windfall oil export revenues, grew by 74 percent last year to $303 billion. They have since dipped slightly to $301.7 billion as of Jan. 12.  

LESS INTERVENTION

Falling oil prices are likely to reduce Russia's current account surplus, which hit a record $95.6 billion last year, reducing pressure on the central bank to intervene on forex markets to curb excessive rouble appreciation, Ulyukayev said.  

"All other things being equal we may continue to use this instrument. It is very effective," said Ulyukayev, a liberal economist widely regarded as the central bank's top policy spokesman.  

"There are fewer reasons (than there were previously) for us to use the exchange rate mechanism to fight inflation, but we are free to use it."  

He said the central bank wants to move to pure inflation targeting but this cannot happen as long as it runs a managed float of the rouble using a currency basket, composed of 60 U.S. cents and 40 euro cents, as its policy guide.  

"Inflation targeting combined with a regulated exchange rate is impossible. Targeting requires a free float," Ulyukayev said, adding the bank would be ready for a free float in three years.  

Russia's central bank buys foreign currency that oil firms bring to Russia to pay salaries and taxes. The bank allowed the rouble to appreciate by 4.3 percent against the currency basket in 2006, helping get inflation into single digits.  

The central bank targets 8 percent inflation in 2007.  

Ulyukayev said that, with Russia's current account surplus shrinking due to lower oil prices, the liquidity wave may ebb with the central bank occasionally only intervening to smooth market movements.  

Lower liquidity levels should push up money market rates, forcing banks to turn to the central bank for funds and giving it more leverage over the economy through interest rates.  

Ulyukayev said the bank was prepared to lower its refinancing rate, currently at 11 percent, which is mainly used as a ceiling for official interest rates, by a half point.  

The bank's key interest rate is its repo rate, now just over 6 percent, at which banks can raise funds from the central bank through repurchase operations.  

CAPITAL INFLOWS SEEN STRONG  

Even as the current account surplus narrows, capital inflows this year may exceed the $15 billion forecast in the central bank's monetary policy guidelines, Ulyukayev forecast.  

Major equity raising by power companies and banks will suck billions of dollars into Russia, keeping the central bank under pressure to keep the exchange rate low enough for Russian firms to compete with their international rivals.  

"What we can predict is the IPO activity of Russian companies -- Unified Energy System , Sberbank and VTB," Ulyukayev said.  

"What we cannot estimate is the inflow of speculative capital caused by exchange rate fluctuations as well as other (political) risks," Ulyukayev said, referring to a parliamentary election in December and presidential polls in March 2008.

title: US Treasury:China Moving To Flexible Yuan But Too Slowly
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. Treasury Department on Tuesday again declined to designate China as guilty of currency manipulation in a report, noting the government in Beijing is moving steadily, though slowly, toward a flexible foreign exchange regime.  

"The Department of Treasury concluded that no major trading partner of the U.S. met the technical requirements for designation," according to the closely watched and overdue report to Congress on international exchange rate policies during the first half of 2006.  

Treasury outlined steps China is taking to loosen restrictions on capital moving in and out of the country and develop new financial instruments, such as currency futures, to prepare for a freely floating currency. In recent months, the government has allowed the value of the Chinese yuan to fluctuate more and the pace of appreciation has picked up. This progress made it difficult to say that China is managing its currency regime with the intent of gaining a trade advantage, a senior Treasury official told reporters on condition of anonymity.  

Nonetheless, China is moving too cautiously and the pace of reforms are too slow, Treasury said.  

"China's cautious approach to exchange rate reform continues to exacerbate distortions in the domestic economy and impede adjustment of international imbalances," Treasury said. "Clamping down on exchange rate fluctuations has increased pressures in other parts of the economy."  

Treasury's decision, originally due Oct. 15, was widely expected. The department has refused to call China a currency manipulator in recent reports. And since the last report, released in May, China has allowed the yuan to appreciate more rapidly. The yuan strengthened 0.5% against the U.S. dollar in the second half of 2005 and another 1.0% in the first half 2006. Since China abandoned the dollar peg in July 2005, the yuan has risen just under 6.0%.  

This is far too little, say U.S. manufacturers and their representatives in Congress, who argue the yuan is undervalued by as much as 40%. Indeed, China's central bank continues to accumulate massive foreign exchange reserves as a result of currency market intervention to prevent faster yuan appreciation.  

Treasury will be under fire from those critics, who say the Bush administration hasn't been tough enough on China, when Congress returns for a new session in January. They got a boost last week when Federal Reserve Board Chairman Ben Bernanke, in the prepared text of a speech, called the undervalued yuan an export "subsidy."  

Members from both the House and the Senate are working on legislation to overhaul the foreign exchange reporting requirement and develop new laws, mostly directed at China, to pressure countries that limit currency appreciation. A measure backed by Sens. Max Baucus, D-Mont., and Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, would target currency "misalignment" rather than "manipulation," taking the question of intent out of consideration of whether Treasury should call out a country for problematic currency policy.  

Treasury officials have said repeatedly that they believe diplomacy will be far more effective in getting China to reform than trade sanctions. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson led a delegation including almost half of President George W. Bush's cabinet for talks with senior Chinese officials on economic relations between the two countries.  

The meeting yielded some modest agreements, such as for sharing environmental and energy technology and pledges to work on an agreement protecting investment flows. At the close of the meeting, Paulson said the currency issue will remain "at the core" of U.S.-China engagement.  

In the report released Tuesday, Treasury noted China's average monthly accumulation of foreign exchange reserves was $20.4 billion in the first half this year. That measure fell to $15.6 billion in the third quarter, coinciding with a pick-up in the pace of yuan appreciation.  

The burden of intervention on the central bank has hindered its ability to control interest rates and inflation, Treasury said. It has also impeded rebalancing of Chinese growth away from investment and exports in favor of more consumption, a stated goal of the Chinese government.  

For its part, the U.S. should help reduce global trade imbalances, which economists warn could spark financial market instability, by encouraging its citizens to save more and by cutting budget deficits.  

Turning to other trading partners, Treasury said tepid economic growth in Europe and Japan has contributed to global trade imbalances.  

"Europe and Japan each need to achieve higher rates of growth of domestic demand on a sustained basis," Treasury said, noting that it is uncertain whether Europe's brighter economic outlook will last. Growth in Japan is already decelerating from last year's recovery, Treasury said.  

Most important U.S. trading partners have floating currency regimes in place. Japan, whose trade-weighted yen is at its weakest level in two decades, hasn't intervened in currency markets since March 2004.  

Malaysia - noted in previous Treasury reports for its large and growing current account surplus - like other oil-exporting countries would benefit from more currency flexibility, Treasury said.  

Trade surpluses among major oil exporters are now outpacing those of Southeast Asia's developing economies, inflated by higher oil prices. title: US Treasury:China Moving To Flexible Yuan But Too Slowly
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. Treasury Department on Tuesday again declined to designate China as guilty of currency manipulation in a report, noting the government in Beijing is moving steadily, though slowly, toward a flexible foreign exchange regime.  

"The Department of Treasury concluded that no major trading partner of the U.S. met the technical requirements for designation," according to the closely watched and overdue report to Congress on international exchange rate policies during the first half of 2006.  

Treasury outlined steps China is taking to loosen restrictions on capital moving in and out of the country and develop new financial instruments, such as currency futures, to prepare for a freely floating currency. In recent months, the government has allowed the value of the Chinese yuan to fluctuate more and the pace of appreciation has picked up. This progress made it difficult to say that China is managing its currency regime with the intent of gaining a trade advantage, a senior Treasury official told reporters on condition of anonymity.  

Nonetheless, China is moving too cautiously and the pace of reforms are too slow, Treasury said.  

"China's cautious approach to exchange rate reform continues to exacerbate distortions in the domestic economy and impede adjustment of international imbalances," Treasury said. "Clamping down on exchange rate fluctuations has increased pressures in other parts of the economy."  

Treasury's decision, originally due Oct. 15, was widely expected. The department has refused to call China a currency manipulator in recent reports. And since the last report, released in May, China has allowed the yuan to appreciate more rapidly. The yuan strengthened 0.5% against the U.S. dollar in the second half of 2005 and another 1.0% in the first half 2006. Since China abandoned the dollar peg in July 2005, the yuan has risen just under 6.0%.  

This is far too little, say U.S. manufacturers and their representatives in Congress, who argue the yuan is undervalued by as much as 40%. Indeed, China's central bank continues to accumulate massive foreign exchange reserves as a result of currency market intervention to prevent faster yuan appreciation.  

Treasury will be under fire from those critics, who say the Bush administration hasn't been tough enough on China, when Congress returns for a new session in January. They got a boost last week when Federal Reserve Board Chairman Ben Bernanke, in the prepared text of a speech, called the undervalued yuan an export "subsidy."  

Members from both the House and the Senate are working on legislation to overhaul the foreign exchange reporting requirement and develop new laws, mostly directed at China, to pressure countries that limit currency appreciation. A measure backed by Sens. Max Baucus, D-Mont., and Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, would target currency "misalignment" rather than "manipulation," taking the question of intent out of consideration of whether Treasury should call out a country for problematic currency policy.  

Treasury officials have said repeatedly that they believe diplomacy will be far more effective in getting China to reform than trade sanctions. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson led a delegation including almost half of President George W. Bush's cabinet for talks with senior Chinese officials on economic relations between the two countries.  

The meeting yielded some modest agreements, such as for sharing environmental and energy technology and pledges to work on an agreement protecting investment flows. At the close of the meeting, Paulson said the currency issue will remain "at the core" of U.S.-China engagement.  

In the report released Tuesday, Treasury noted China's average monthly accumulation of foreign exchange reserves was $20.4 billion in the first half this year. That measure fell to $15.6 billion in the third quarter, coinciding with a pick-up in the pace of yuan appreciation.  

The burden of intervention on the central bank has hindered its ability to control interest rates and inflation, Treasury said. It has also impeded rebalancing of Chinese growth away from investment and exports in favor of more consumption, a stated goal of the Chinese government.  

For its part, the U.S. should help reduce global trade imbalances, which economists warn could spark financial market instability, by encouraging its citizens to save more and by cutting budget deficits.  

Turning to other trading partners, Treasury said tepid economic growth in Europe and Japan has contributed to global trade imbalances.  

"Europe and Japan each need to achieve higher rates of growth of domestic demand on a sustained basis," Treasury said, noting that it is uncertain whether Europe's brighter economic outlook will last. Growth in Japan is already decelerating from last year's recovery, Treasury said.  

Most important U.S. trading partners have floating currency regimes in place. Japan, whose trade-weighted yen is at its weakest level in two decades, hasn't intervened in currency markets since March 2004.  

Malaysia - noted in previous Treasury reports for its large and growing current account surplus - like other oil-exporting countries would benefit from more currency flexibility, Treasury said.  

Trade surpluses among major oil exporters are now outpacing those of Southeast Asia's developing economies, inflated by higher oil prices. title: UPDATE:  Russia  Bought Total $4.6B In Feb  Forex Interventions
text:

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Russia increased its foreign currency purchases seven-fold in February from the previous month as it tried to slow a surging ruble, central bank data showed Wednesday.

The central bank bought a total of $3.5 billion and 796.42 million euros for the month--its highest volume of purchases since May 2010, the data showed. Purchases for January totaled around $646,000.

At a briefing earlier this month, first deputy central bank chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said the regulator purchased $4.5 billion for February.

The central bank carried out cumulative interventions--which it performs to smooth out volatility in the ruble--totalling $1.34 billion for the month, the data showed.

Russia's central bank manages volatility in the ruble by keeping it in a floating corridor against a basket of euros and dollars. Interventions are carried out when the currency touches the upper or lower borders of the corridor.

The regulator widened the corridor to five rubles from four on March 1.

The ruble strengthened by around 3% in February, as the central bank raised interest rates across the board amid accelerating inflation and increased oil-driven inflows.

title: Ruble Powers To 26-Month High Against Dollar
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Russian ruble powered to a new 26-month high against the dollar Friday, advancing for the third straight day after the central bank widened the currency's trading corridor earlier in the week.

Russia's currency has appreciated by 4% in the past two weeks and almost 9% since the start of the year against the dollar, buoyed by higher oil prices and the central bank's measures to cut inflation.

"We may see some stabilization here," said Nikolay Podguzov, an economist at VTB Capital. "There has been quite a rally and there will be some profit taking."

The ruble hit RUB28.11 against the dollar Friday, advancing 0.5% to its strongest level since December 2008. Against a basket of dollars and euros used by the central bank to manage fluctuations in the currency, the ruble was down less than 0.1% to RUB33.22.

Bank of Russia widened the ruble's trading band against the basket to five rubles earlier this week, with the aim of allowing the currency to strengthen in order to fight inflation while at the same time making the ruble's movements less predictable to speculators. The ruble's trading band now stands at 32.45-37.45.

"As we come near the lower edges of the band, we are likely to see more foreign currency buying from the central bank," Podguzov said, estimating the regulator may purchase up to $400 million in daily interventions below 33.10.

Russia's central bank raised rates across the board last week in a bid to control surging inflation, with further rate increases seen as likely.

The recent surge in oil prices may provide further support to the ruble in the near term, RBC said, adding that the ruble may hit RUB27.50 against the dollar by the second quarter before weakening slightly later in the year. Oil prices are currently close to two-and-a-half year highs as a result of political turmoil in the Middle East.

title: 2nd UPDATE:Russia Widens Ruble Trading Range Amid High Inflation
text:
(Adds quotes, context)

-- Bank of Russia widens ruble's trading corridor to five rubles from four

-- Move seen as measure to fight inflation, move towards ruble free float

-- Central bank expects ruble to strengthen in near term

By Ira Iosebashvili

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Russian central bank said Tuesday it would let the ruble trade in a wider range, a move market players said will allow the currency to strengthen and moderate a recent bout of steep inflation.

Starting Tuesday, the Bank of Russia will manage the ruble in a wider corridor of between RUB32.45 and RUB37.45 to its dollar-euro basket, First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev told reporters in Moscow. Previously the ruble was managed at levels of around RUB33 and RUB37 to the basket. It traded at RUB33.64 to the basket at the close of Micex exchange trade in Moscow.

"This measure will ensure more effective operation of our interest rate policy, with the aim of providing price stability and controlling inflation," Ulyukayev said.

Inflation -- a recurring economic headache in Russia -- has in recent months become a major concern for the government, which is slated to hold presidential elections in 2012. Russians see inflation as the biggest problem facing the country, according to a poll published by the state-run VTsIOM research center last week.

In an effort to combat rising prices, the Bank of Russia raised interest rates across the board last week for the first time since the financial crisis.

The central bank will also reduce the size of the interventions it performs at the edge of the ruble's trading corridor to $600 million from $650 million, Ulyukayev said.

Ulyukayev also said the ruble has a greater chance of strengthening in the short term, rather than weakening.

"Considering today's prices for oil and the state of Russia's current account, the trend will probably be towards strengthening," he added.

While higher interest rates typically draw speculative inflows, a wider trading band would "increase the risk for investors in the market," making the ruble less predictable and therefore less attractive to speculators, Ulyukayev said.

The ruble on Tuesday hit a new 15-month high against the dollar of RUB28.69, because of higher oil prices and the central bank's rate hikes. The currency has strengthened by nearly 10% since late November, when central bank chief Sergei Ignatyev warned that those betting on the weakness of the ruble would be "disappointed."

Analysts agreed the move would likely lead to more ruble appreciation in the near term.

"Widening of the ruble corridor while the ruble is strengthening big time is clearly a sign that the central bank will not stand on the way of further ruble strengthening," said Aurelija Augulyte, analyst at Nordea Denmark, in a note to investors.

The central bank is sticking to its annual inflation target of 7% for 2011, Ulyukayev said. Prices have already risen by 3.1% this year, while on-year inflation hit 9.7% as of Feb. 21, according to central bank data.

"We expect that inflation will begin to slacken in the second quarter, and we won't see double digit on-year inflation in 2011 after all," Ulyukayev said.

He added that the Bank of Russia purchased $4.5 billion in open market interventions during February.

Russia continued to see capital outflows in January, despite a stronger ruble and higher oil prices, Ulyukayev said, without giving the volume of outflows.

Capital outflows may continue in February as well, although final data wasn't yet available, he said. Russia saw some $30 billion in capital outflow in 2010, most of it coming in the second half of the year as domestic companies rushed to repay foreign debt.

The rouble gave up earlier gains in the interbank market after news of the blast -- which came after the end of the daily currency trading session on the MICEX exchange -- while stock markets extended losses. [ID:nLDE70N1SH]

Dealers said some market players preferred to minimise risks and sell the rouble and rouble assets after the attack, which central bank chairman Sergei Ignatyev said would likely have little impact on the exchange rate. [ID:nLDE70N1UU]

The negative reaction appeared to be short-lived, however, and the rouble added 2 kopecks to 34.64 against the euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX> from around 34.70 earlier and levels of 34.90 seen in the interbank market late on Monday <RUS=OTC>.

"The blast sparked a fall in the rouble as it has raised uncertainty but it has not changed the fundamentals. In the coming days, the rouble may rise to 34.50 versus the basket," said a dealer at a major Western bank in Moscow.

That level may serve as resistance for further gains in Russia's currency as the central bank is expected to intervene in the market by buying few hundred million dollars a day if the basket falls below 34.50 roubles, market players say.

Versus the dollar, the rouble added 3 kopecks to 29.80 <RUBUTSTN=MCX> and was flat at 40.53 against the euro after briefly touching its weakest mark so far in 2011 of 40.75 <EURRUBTN=MCX>.

"The rouble is moving in the right direction and has more room to improve", said David Karsbol, chief economist at Saxo bank.

The rouble retains support from strong oil prices [O/R] above $90 per barrel and expectations of capital inflows that may be spurred by the central bank, which is seen tightening monetary policy to contain inflation.

Higher interest rates should boost a demand for the rouble by increasing its yields.

"Further rouble support ought to also come from the central bank, we expect a 25-50 basis point hike when the bank meets on Monday, Jan. 31," analysts at Unicredit said in a note.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has revised its forecast for Russia's economy growth and now sees it expanding 4.5 percent in 2011 versus 4.3 percent predicted in Oct. 2010, which is expected to play into the rouble's hands. [ID:nLDE70O0VZ]

title: UPDATE 1-Russia cbank head eyes move toward rouble free float
text:
* Says could stop regular interventions within 2 years

* Oil prices, c/a surplus to support rouble

* Worried about inflation, but 2011 target "achievable"

* Does not rule out rate hikes in Q1

(Recasts, adds quotes, details, background)

By Toni Vorobyova and Yelena Fabrichnaya

MOSCOW, Dec 8 (Reuters) - Russia could be ready to stop regular interventions to prop up the rouble in the next two years as it moves ever closer to allowing the currency to float freely, central bank governor Sergei Ignatyev said on Wednesday.

In a rare press briefing, Ignatyev also forecast the time of chronic rouble weakness could be over, said he was concerned about inflation and did not rule out near-term rate hikes.

His comments boosted the rouble in late trade, pushing it towards Tuesday's one-week high versus the euro-dollar basket used by the central bank to track the exchange rate.

"Anything is possible," he said, when asked about the possibility of interest rate hikes starting late this year or in the first quarter of 2011.

Analysts see the refi rate hiked from 7.75 percent in the first quarter of 2011 -- expectations which were fuelled by the central bank dropping its wording in November on policy likely staying unchanged in comings months.

Rates at record lows, rising inflation, foreign debt repayments by corporates, acquisitions abroad, rising imports and global risk aversion all combined this autumn and prompted the rouble to shed all its 2010 gains in just a few weeks.

"Some people expect a further weakness of the rouble -- I think they may be disappointed," Ignatyev said.

"At the moment oil prices are very high... and against the backdrop of current account surplus it is very difficult to expect a further rouble weakness."

Russia remains committed to increasing exchange rate flexibility, further widening the rouble's floating corridor.

"My opinion is that in the next 2-3 years, the central bank cannot take on this obligation that it will not carry out interventions," Ignatyev said.

"But what I call an "almost free-float" -- we could arrive at that regime in the next two years -- where we go along the path of widening the corridor, and the rouble wobbles in its central part without any interventions."

UPBEAT ON GROWTH, WORRIED ON INFLATION

Ignatyev estimated November's capital outflows at $9 billion -- meaning some $29 billion has now left Russia since the start of the year -- but said an inflow was possible in December.

Russia's $32 billion privatisation plan could lead to more inflows in 2011-3, he said.

Echoing the central bank's recent tone, Ignatyev sounded upbeat on the economy, saying he sees no serious macroeconomic risks for Russia in 2011 and hopes for gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 5 percent -- higher than the official forecast.

Next year's target to cut inflation to 6-7 percent "is quite achievable", he said but sounded less sanguine on the near-term.

"Inflation is starting to worry us," he said, forecasting it could reach 8.4 percent this year -- the lowest in post Soviet history but far higher than had been expected before a severe summer drought wiped out a third of the harvest, pushing up food prices.

The rouble's weakness this autumn may also have played a part in fuelling price pressures, Ignatyev conceded.

RESERVES

Russia has recently started buying the Canadian dollar for its near-$500 billion gold and forex reserves, and Ignatyev said that currency's share of the portfolio could rise to 1-2 percent next year.

The central bank is also preparing to invest in the Australian dollar and, not least because of the addition of the new currencies, Ignatyev said the structure of reserves could change a little next year.

"I do not rule it out. But it is unlikely that something will change significantly," he said.

Prior to the addition of the loonie, the FX part of the reserves was held in 47 percent dollars, 41 percent euros, 10 percent sterling and 2 percent yen.

(Editing by John Stonestreet)

title: UPDATE 1- Russia FX interventions  to be smaller,less often-c.bank
text:
* Russia c.bank plans less frequent FX interventions

* Deputy c.bank head sees less Dec hard currency sales

* C.bank sees no Aussie dollars purchases for minimum 6 mths

LONDON, Dec 1 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank plans less frequent and lower-volume currency market interventions in future to let markets set the rouble's exchange rate as much as possible, First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said on Wednesday.

He stressed however it would not be possible to stop interventions altogether as the bank would need to prevent volatile swings in the currency. Speaking in Russian at the annual Adam Smith Russian banking forum, Ulyukayev said: "In the near term we will keep intervening to iron out volatility but we think they won't be frequent and not in big volumes."

The central bank sold around $5 billion in November as the rouble weakened but Ulyukayev said he expected lower sales in December.

"It seems to me it will be less in December, the task of repaying debt (by corporates) is over," he told reporters.

"My feeling is the market will require less volume in future, I think it should be in the region of $4 to $6 billion in future," he added.

The rouble's floating corridor was located at 33-37 roubles against the euro-dollar basket, Ulyukayev told Reuters, correcting earlier comments to reporters that put the basket at 35-39 roubles, differing from market estimates. [ID:nLDE6B00XG].

Ulyukayev reiterated that the widening of the rouble's floating trading band on Oct. 13 would be followed by further such moves, but gave no details on the possible timing.

"We will keep taking steps to keep widening this band in future," Ulyukayev earlier told the conference, noting that the $700 million intervention threshold at which the bank widened the band had been lowered recently to $650 million.

"We will keep reducing it so that the exchange rate is determined as far as possible by markets," he added.

The rouble has been hit in recent months by capital outflows mostly due to debt repayments. Estimates are for total outflows of around $22 billion this year and Deputy Economy Minister Andrey Klepach said this week outflows could be as high as $25 billion.

But Ulyukayev forecast a lower figure, noting the possibility of zero outflows in December. Outflows ran at around $21 billion in the first 10 months of 2010.

Russia has the world's third-largest central bank reserves, of around $490 billion and is diversifying the currency mix, recently starting purchases of the Canadian dollar.

But Ulyukayev said planned purchases of the Australian dollar would not start for another six months at least.

"It took us almost a year to start Canadian dollar <CAD=> purchases. At the last central bank meeting we decided to include the Australian dollar in the list of currencies for reserves," Ulyukayev said.

The Russian economy is recovering steadily from the worst recession in 15 years and Ulyukayev forecast banks' loan books to grow by 15-20 percent next year, a figure he said the central bank considered "desirable."

"A measured rise is good," he said.

(Reporting by Sujata Rao and Carolyn Cohn in London and Elena Fabrichnaya in Moscow; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

By Andrey Ostroukh

MOSCOW, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The rouble firmed on Thursday, boosted by the central bank's comments about smaller than expected capital outflows and a recovery in oil prices.

Russia's central bank first deputy chairman said he was "surprised" by the rouble's recent weakness, adding that debt-driven capital outflows in the fourth quarter may total $7 billion. [ID:nLDE6AH0WE]

Market players, however, were puzzled by the statement, saying that this amount of outflows might had been seen in October alone -- judging from Russia's current account balance and the central bank's interventions, which totalled $3.2 billion. [ID:nLDE6A713R]

"The rouble was supported by the external background and then by central bank as the announced $7 billion of capital outflows can be easily offset by the current account surplus," said Denis Korshilov, chief dealer at Citi in Moscow.

Russia's current account surplus rose in January-September 2010 to $60.9 billion from $52.2 billion in January-June 2010. [ID:nLDE6950GC]

"People who were holding long positions (in dollars and euros) suggested that the demand for foreign currencies may fade rapidly," said Viktor Kholoshnoy, a dealer at Gazprombank.

Citi's Korshilov said such figures imply that the current amount of the central bank's daily interventions of $300 million seems excessive, which may push the rouble higher, to the range where the central bank sells $150 million a day.

The central bank keeps the rouble rate within a floating range against the euro-dollar basket with presumed boundaries at 33.0-37.0 roubles <RUS=MCX>.

Dealers say the regulator sells some $300 million a day when the rouble trades at 36.0-36.5 versus the basket and halves interventions in the range of 35.5-36.0 roubles per basket.

The rouble inched up 24 kopecks to 36.07 against the basket on Thursday, hovering some 35 kopecks above its 2010 lows hit in early November.

Versus the dollar, the rouble gained 38 kopecks to 30.99 <RUBUTSTN=MCX>. It was up 2 kopecks at 42.31 versus the euro <EURRUBTN=MCX>.

Oil, Russia's chief exports, rebounded on Thursday toward $82 per barrel of U.S. crude oil futures [O/R], lending support for the Russian currency.

Closely watching developments in euro zone financials, Russia's market also received some relief as Ireland agreed to work with a European Union-IMF mission on steps to shore up its shattered banking sector. [ID:nLDE6AG004]

Russia's upcoming month-end taxes -- which may total at least 550 billion roubles ($17.63 billion) -- may support the rouble as well in coming days, said Dmitry Kharlampiyev, analyst at Petrocommerce bank.

He said the nearest target for the rouble's rise lies at 36.0 against the basket, the next target level is 35.70.

In the longer-run, the rouble is poised to firm further as Russia pushes on with planned sales of more stakes in major state-controlled companies.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Vladimir Putin approved a plan to sell 1 trillion roubles ($32 billion) in state assets over the next three years to help plug a gap in the budget and lure investors. [ID:nLDE6AG1F1]

title: UPDATE 1-Rouble ends week off 2010 lows, market puzzled by cbank
text:
* C.bank intervenes, says moves rouble floating band * Dealers confused by c.bank's changes

* Rouble bolstered by exporters preparing for tax payments

* No clear short-term trend seen

(Adds c.bank quotes, details, updates prices)

MOSCOW, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The rouble weathered a volatile week, managing to recover from 2010 lows due to local tax payments and the central bank's interventions, however dealers say it is too early to speak of a steady trend.

The market's main focus turned to the central bank which recently granted the rouble more freedom by widening the floating band, but made investors wary of new positions by raising uncertainty about its current forex exchange policy.

On Friday, central bank board member Sergei Shvetsov said the rouble's floating range against the basket was raised by 5 kopecks after its interventions in the last few days reached an accumulative amount of $650 million. [ID:nLDE69L0CM]

The presumed boundaries of the current corridor are at 32.85-36.85 and the central bank is expected to sell or buy $650 million at these frontiers before moving the band by 5 kopecks.

Market players said they were confused by the fact that the amount of interventions needed to move the floating band is being accumulated within the band but not only on its boundaries as was the case in the spring when the central bank would buy dollars and euros to tame the then rouble's rally.

"Everything is unclear, and again people don't understand why the central bank used to buy and sell foreign currencies at its boundaries and now it refers to accumulation of interventions," said Alexander Karpov, a dealer at Zenit bank.

Later on Friday Shvetsov said the accumulation of interventions is maintained over a period of several days.

"We have a counter that ticks and ticks, and once $650 millions are accumulated, we move the corridor," he said.

Right after saying this Shvetsov corrected himself, noting that the "floating corridor" is now called a "floating interval".

Shvetsov also reiterated that the central bank will gradually increase the rouble's flexibility by widening the floating interval and reducing the amount of accumulative interventions from current $650 million.

"...with the new band regime, reaching the fast moving boundaries would be possible only in a situation of extremely high and persistent imbalances between forex demand and supply," Alexander Morozov, chief economist at HSBC in Moscow, said in a note.

"By doing so, the central bank has made another step toward a quasi-floating forex regime".

ROUBLE

The Russian currency wiped off all its 2010 gains, hitting earlier year lows this week against the basket at 36.31 <RUS=MCX> and at 43.13 versus the euro <EURRUBTN=MCX>, according to Reuters data.

However, it trimmed losses due to the central bank's interventions and Russia's export-focused companies' conversion of their dollar and euro revenues to meet local quarter- and month-end tax payments.

"We have to thank the central bank for the rouble's rebound as its interventions satisfied the demand for foreign currencies," said Mikhail Anisimov, head of FX at VTB Capital.

Against the basket, the rouble ended the week little changed at 35.77. The rouble's weekly slide against the dollar totalled 0.5 percent <RUBUTSTN=MCX>, while it posted a weekly gain of 0.7 percent versus the euro <EURRUBTN=MCX>.

On Friday alone, the rouble rose 0.86 percent versus the greenback, gained 1.23 percent against the single currency, and firmed 1.06 percent versus the basket.

"Foreign currencies were overbought, so their Friday slide against the rouble was logical. But it's early to speak about a new real trend, we are likely to see volatile trade," said Anisimov at VTB Capital.

Artyom Roshin, a dealer at Alba Alliance bank, agreed with short-term uncertainty about the rouble's trend, adding that the first days of November after the end of month-end taxes will become a "trial for the currency".

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Russian ruble hit its lowest levels of the year against a basket of euros and dollars Wednesday, pressured by foreign debt payments, a lack of central bank intervention and Russia's increasingly cloudy macroeconomic picture.

"There is a significant demand for dollars and euros from importers right now, and not too many sellers," said Selim Agarzayev, a dealer at Metallinvest Bank.

The ruble fell 0.7% to as low as 36.09 against the basket, while also losing 1.1% against the dollar to 30.78.

Russian corporations must pay off some $36 billion in foreign debt by the end of the year, a factor which has been putting pressure on the ruble as companies sell the local currency and buy dollars and euros.

Market participants have also been knocked off balance by the central bank's changes to the floating trading band versus the dollar-euro basket. Last week, the regulator confirmed that it had widened the trading band's borders by one ruble, to 32.80-36.80, in order to allow for greater ruble flexibility.

"Now, there is much less certainty about where the central bank will step in to support the ruble. People are much less willing to make speculative bets," Agarzayev said.

Longer term, the ruble is being pressured by Russia's deteriorating current account surplus, as imports flood the market while the level of exports remains little changed. Imports into the country jumped by 13.3% in August while exports rose by only 0.5%.

"People have taken notice of this dynamic and are making their decisions accordingly," said Eugene Belin, head of fixed income and currency trading at Citi in Russia.

title: Russia CB: Widens Basket Corridor To RUB4 From RUB3 -Report
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Russia's central bank said it will intervene to a lesser degree in the foreign exchange market, Interfax reports Wednesday, citing Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev.

The bank buys and sells foreign currency on the Micex exchange to manage the ruble's exchange rate against a basket of dollars and euros and to smooth out its volatility.

In the past, the central bank moved its floating corridor for the exchange rate by 5 kopeks, or RUB0.05, after buying or selling $700 million to smooth out sudden movements in the currency. Starting today, it will adjust the corridor when only $650 million is bought or sold, Interfax reported. The width of the floating corridor will also be increased to 4 rubles from 3 rubles.

The new boundaries for the floating corridor are believed to be at RUB32.90 and RUB36.90 to the dollar-euro basket, Reuters reported Wednesday.

Concerns about a change in central bank policy, as well as recent data about a sliding trade balance, contributed to ruble weakness Wednesday, traders said.

title: =DJ UPDATE: Russia Loosens Ruble Policy; No Major Effects Seen
text:
(Adds central bank confirmation, market comments) 
 
  By William Mauldin 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Russia's central bank said it will start intervening to a somewhat lesser degree in the ruble exchange rate starting Wednesday, but traders and analysts said the new policy won't have an immediate effect on the currency.

The Bank of Russia buys and sells foreign currency on the Micex exchange to manage the ruble's exchange rate against a basket of dollars and euros, smoothing out volatility caused by sudden movements in the oil price or local demand for foreign currency.

In the past, the central bank moved its floating corridor for the exchange rate by 5 kopeks, or RUB0.05, after buying or selling $700 million to smooth out sudden movements in the currency. Starting today, it will adjust the corridor when only $650 million is bought or sold, the central bank said on its website.

More importantly, the width of the floating corridor will also be increased to 4 rubles rather than 3 rubles.

The new boundaries for the floating corridor are believed to be at either RUB32.80 or RUB32.90 to the dollar-euro basket on the one side, and RUB 36.80 or RUB36.90 on the other, Renaissance Capital analyst Anton Nikitin said Wednesday.

Brown Brothers Harriman analysts said that judging by the last official confirmation of the floating corridor, it may now reach from RUB33.40 to RUB37.40.

In either case, the closing level Wednesday of 35.4798 to the basket, recorded before the central bank's policy announcement, is well within estimates of the floating corridor.

Concerns about a change in central bank policy, as well as recent data pointing to a sliding trade balance, contributed to ruble weakness Wednesday, but the currency's tendency to strengthen or weaken Thursday won't be affected much by the announcement, traders said.

The ruble was little changed at 30.1205 against the dollar. The currency has been bucking general trends. It has tended to depreciate in recent weeks, even as oil holds steady and other emerging markets struggle to contain higher exchange rates.

title: FACTBOX-Russia's rouble policy
text:
MOSCOW, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank on Wednesday widened the rouble's floating corridor against the basket to 4 roubles from 3 -- its first shift in exchange rate policy since the spring.

Following are details of current central bank policy. For a story on Wednesday's move, please see [ID:nLDE69C0TW]

BASKET <RUS=MCX>

Russia introduced a basket for tracking the rouble's course on Feb. 1, 2005, initially made up of 0.1 euros and 0.9 dollars.

The euro's share was gradually increased to reach the current 0.45 euros and 0.55 dollars composition on Feb. 8, 2007.

WIDE FIXED TRADING BAND

In January 2009, the central bank defined the rouble's wide trading band as 26 to 41 roubles. This remains in force and the central bank says it has no plans to change it for now.

SMALLER FLOATING CORRIDOR WITHIN WIDE BAND

Within that set trading band, the central bank introduced a 3-rouble-wide floating corridor, whose boundaries are shifted up or down by 5 kopecks for each $700 million of central bank intervention at, respectively, the upper or lower boundary.

Between mid-February and mid-May 2010 the central bank made 32 such steps, bringing the corridor to 33.40-36.40 roubles against the basket.

On Wednesday it widened the corridor by 50 kopecks in each direction. The central bank did not give the new boundaries, but dealers said they were likely 32.90-36.90.

The floating corridor itself is split into three bands. When the rouble is at the weak end of the band, the central bank sells small volumes of dollars each day. In the middle of the band it does nothing and when the rouble is strong it buys foreign currency. The central bank did not disclose the exact boundaries of the three bands or the size of interventions.

OUTLOOK

The rouble has potential for gains from current levels but they are likely to be capped by demand for foreign currencies due to rising imports and redemption of foreign debt. More substantial gains now require stronger oil prices, analysts say.

A consensus forecast from analysts polled by Reuters late last month [ECILT/RU] shows the rouble at 28.50 per dollar and 33.23 versus the basket in 12 months from, respectively, 30.82 and 33.97 on April 19.

MOVE TOWARDS 'DIRTY' FREE FLOAT

Russia is gradually moving towards targeting inflation rather than exchange rates and the widening of the corridor is seen as the latest step in that direction.

However, the central bank says it is aiming for a managed -- or 'dirty' -- free float and will continue to reserve the right to intervene in the currency market if it deems necessary.

Some $500 billion in gold and forex reserves, the world's third largest, give Russia the power to intervene.

The regulator says it already does not target a particular exchange rate, and its interventions are merely aimed at smoothing out excessive market volatility.

Unlike other BRICs, Russia has no capital controls, having resisted calls to reintroduce them during the crisis.

(Compiled by Andrey Ostroukh and Toni Vorobyova; Editing by John Stonestreet)

title: UPDATE 1-Russia cbank calm on rouble, inflation, rates
text:
* Chances of rouble appreciation greater than depreciation

* Inflation mostly driven by food, cbank official says

* No plans to hike rates or reserve requirements for now

* Economists wary after rouble losses, Sept inflation spike

(Adds quotes, details, background, Kudrin)

MOSCOW, Oct 5 (Reuters) - Russian inflation is benign, the rouble may appreciate soon and there is no need to hike reserve requirements or rates for now, a senior central bank official said on Tuesday, moving to dispel concerns about the economy.

"(In) the short-term perspective, the chances of rouble appreciation are greater than of depreciation. In the medium term they are equal," the bank's first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev told reporters on the sidelines of a conference.

In September, the rouble tumbled more than 3.3 percent against its euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX>, losing almost all its 2010 gains in less than two weeks.

The move was caused by strong demand for foreign currencies which eclipsed a positive background of strong oil prices.

Inflation also surged as the impact of a severe summer drought filtered through to non-food prices, data showed on Monday, raising expectations of central bank action to keep price pressures in check. [ID:nLDE6931JS]

"The exchange rate is set by the balance between supply and demand," Ulyukayev earlier told VTB Capital's Russia Calling forum, adding that the central bank interventions played a marginal role, with sales of around $1.3 billion in the whole of September.

That compares to daily turnover of around $3-4 billion on the MICEX exchange.

'LOCALISED SHOCK'

Ulyukayev said the spike in inflation was largely driven by the impact of the drought on food costs and thus the long-term outlook on prices remains comfortable.

"It is not the result of fundamentals but of a localised shock on the food market due to weather conditions. This... should not last for more than six to nine months, especially as global prices are not rising," Ulyukayev said.

"For now we think the situation is under control."

Ulyukayev reiterated the central bank's mantra from its Sept. 28 meeting that interest rates would likely remain on hold at record lows in coming months.

Most analysts expect rate hikes from early 2011 but do not rule out other measures -- such as hikes in banks' reserve requirements -- before the end of this year.

"There is a danger of falling into a big macroeconomic trap, HSBC economist Alexander Morozov said recently.

"By not influencing inflationary expectations, the risk is growing that such expectations will start to rise and companies will increase prices rather than production, thus further suppressing demand in the economy."

But Ulyukayev also played down the possibility of other monetary tightening moves.

"Today we do not see the need for (reserve requirement hikes). We are not worried by capital inflows," he said.

"We expect that in the fourth quarter there will be a small capital inflow. For the year as a whole there will be (an outflow) of under $12 billion, even less than that. It will be an insignificant number."

Russia saw record outflows of $134 billion in 2008, followed by drain of $57 billion in 2009.

Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin, speaking at the same conference, forecast that inflows will soon resume, boosted by foreign direct investment. He sees FDI topping $40 billion this year after $36 billion in 2009 and reaching $50 billion annually in the next two years.
