title: UPDATE 1-Rouble hits 3-wk peak vs dlr on taxes, oil
text:
* Rouble rises to 3-week high after bout of weakness

* Buoyed by month-end tax payments, strong oil prices

* Market positioning, uncertainty may curb further gains

(Adds quotes, details, updates prices)

By Andrey Ostroukh

MOSCOW, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The rouble hit a three-week high versus the dollar on Monday, extending a recovery from multi-month lows thanks to buying amid ongoing local tax payments, though a sustained appreciation trend looks unlikely.

Against the dollar <.DXY>, which was under pressure from several major currencies, the rouble rose 27 kopecks, or 0.87 percent to 30.51 <RUBUTSTN=MCX>. This was its strongest level since September 6, heading away from a 10-week low of 31.39 touched two weeks ago.

"Today's trading day featured the absence of a dollar buyer that has been recently pulling the dollar/rouble pair towards 31.0. Generally, the balance of market powers was biased towards selling (foreign currencies)" said Alexander Panasenko, a dealer at Metallinvestbank.

Remaining relatively stable at around 31.0 against the dollar for the last few days, the rouble hit eight-month lows against the euro and the basket last week, bruised by lingering local demand for foreign currencies.

In the course of a correction that started late last week, the rouble inched up 19 kopecks, or 0.9 percent to 41.20 versus the euro <EURRUBTN=MCX> after reaching 41.66 on September 23, its lowest since February 2010.

Versus the euro-dollar basket, used by the central bank to track exchange rates, the rouble rose 24 kopecks, or 0.7 percent to 35.31 <RUS=MCX>, exiting the zone of the central bank's interventions and receding from last week's eight-month low of 35.84.

Dealers say the central bank does not carry out forex interventions in the range of 34.40-35.40 roubles against the basket and sells some $150-200 million a day when the rouble slides to the range of 35.40-36.40.

"Tax payments and high oil prices are the main factors that favour a stronger rouble," said Alexei Borichev, a dealer at ING bank in Moscow.

Russia's monthly corporate tax payments usually spur demand for roubles, prompting exporters to convert part of their dollar and euro revenues to meet local liabilities.

Natural resource taxes due by Sept. 27 and income taxes due by Sept. 28 could generate up to 360 billion roubles ($11.6 billion) in total, according to Trust bank estimates.

Oil prices also comforted the rouble [O/R], with futures for Brent crude rising to almost $79 per barrel <LCOc1>, high enough to generate inflows of dollars into Russia's export-focused economy.

CAUTIOUS GAINS AHEAD?

Russia's heatwave and drought -- the worst in decades -- hurt the country's harvest and spurred a rise in imports that boosted inflation and undermined growth to put downward pressure on the rouble in recent weeks.

On Tuesday, Russia's central bank is expected to shed light on the drought's implications in the accompanying statement for the board meeting while keeping interest rates unchanged at record lows. [ID:nLDE68N1FQ]

Dealers say the market reaction to keeping rates on hold will be negligible as such a decision is already priced in and the rouble is likely to remain volatile but still at a long distance from recent multi-month lows.

"The rouble has a chance to inch up but I think it is premature to speak of a new trend of appreciation", said Panasenko at Metallinvestbank.

Any further rise in the rouble against the basket will face resistance, especially at levels close to 35.20 per basket where players had been opening short positions in the basket and now may use any rouble rise as a chance to square these positions, said a dealer at a Russian bank in Moscow.

While the short-term outlook remains murky for the rouble, its longer run potential looks positive due to Russia's sound fundamentals, supported by strong oil prices.

Technical analysis points to more potential downside for the rouble, although analysts believe the central bank's intervention mechanism and Russia's current account surplus will keep this in check. [ID:nLDE68N09T] (Additional reporting by Dmitry Antonov; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: UPDATE 1-Rouble rises on firmer oil, more volatility seen
text:
* Rouble rises slightly, following recovery in oil prices

* Market eyes c.bank rate decision but reaction seem muted

* Activity is low, should pick up in September -- dealers

(Adds quotes, details, updates prices)

MOSCOW, Aug 30 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble firmed in calm trade on Monday thanks to a rise in oil prices and risk appetite, and dealers see volatility increasing as investors start to return from summer vacation.

"The basket went lower, pricing in higher stock indexes and oil prices. But summer hibernation is still in place though Moscow's weather is already autumnal," said Sergei Romanchuk, chief dealer at Metallinvestbank.

Against the euro-dollar basket, the rouble gained 5 kopecks, or 0.15 percent to 34.44 <RUS=MCX>, closing in on the range of 33.40-34.40 where the central bank maintains so-called "target" interventions, aimed at reducing upward pressure on the rouble.

The regulator sets the volume of interventions based on oil prices and Russia's current account, and usually buys some $150-200 million a day within that range, dealers say.

Prices of oil -- Russia's key export and contributor to its current account surplus -- recovered above $76 per barrel from last week's lows of around $72 per barrel [O/R].

Stock markets pointed to a pick-up in appetite towards riskier assets, with Russian benchmark RTS <.IRTS> and MICEX <.MCX> indexes adding some 0.7 percent.

But the rouble's recovery was subdued as London's foreign exchange market was closed for a public holiday and many investors were still on summer vacation.

"Mostly local players took part in trading today and they were pretty inactive", said Vladimir Demishev, a trader at Troika Dialog.

The volume of dollar/rouble transactions on the MICEX exchange for settlement tomorrow totalled $1.98 billion compared to average volumes of $2.5-3.5 billion.

Against the dollar, the rouble inched up 2 kopecks to 30.68 <RUBUTSTN=MCX>, well off its seven-week low of 30.97 touched last week. Versus the euro, it rose 8 kopecks to 39.00 <EURRUBTN=MCX>.

As Monday was the last day for month-end tax payments the rouble was set to loose support from export-focused companies converting their dollar and euro revenues to meet tax payments, analysts said.

The market is awaiting a central bank board meeting, which is expected to take place on Tuesday, with the regulator widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged. Market players say the decision is unlikely to affect the forex market as it has been already priced in. [ID:nLDE67T0O4]

Dealers said volatility in the rouble was likely to increase at the beginning of the new month as investors started returning back from holiday.

"The tax period is over so it will not support the rouble further. (In September) the rouble may break out of the recent narrow range," said Demishev at Troika.

At the same time, oil prices remain supportive for the rouble and there is no evidence of massive capital outflows from Russia, said Dmitry Kharlampiyev, analyst at Petrocommerce bank.

The rouble's movement against the basket may be limited by technical support at 34.65 and resistance at 34.00, said Kharlampiyev. [ID:nLDE67T1BT] (Reporting by Andrey Ostroukh, Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: UPDATE 2-Russian rouble rallies on strong oil, more gains seen
text:
* Rouble hits three-month high of 29.67 vs dollar

 * Touches two-month peak vs basket at 34.00

 * Underpinned by stronger oil, position squaring

 * More speculative gains possible

   (Adds quotes, details, updates prices)

 By Andrey Ostroukh

 MOSCOW, Aug 3 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble jumped to multi-month peaks on Tuesday, showing increased correlation with oil prices that soared above $81 per barrel, and dealers say further speculative gains look possible.

 Against the dollar, the rouble closed up 37 kopecks, or 1.24 percent at 29.73 <RUBUTSTN=MCX>, breaking through the psychologically key 30 mark for the first time since early May.

 Moving deeper into the central bank's interventions zone,  the rouble hit its highest since May 31 against the euro-dollar basket of 34.00 <RUS=MCX>. It closed up 24 kopecks or 0.7 percent at 34.05 versus the basket, used by the regulator to track exchange rates.

 The central bank maintains so-called "target" interventions, buying some $150 million a day in the range of 33.40-34.40 roubles per basket, to ease upward pressure on Russia's currency, dealers say.

 But on Tuesday such interventions had no evident impact on the rouble as they were fully offset by the effect of oil prices, which rallied above $81 per barrel [O/R] amid broader dollar weakness and expectations of falling U.S. inventories.

 According to Reuters data, the correlation between oil prices and the rouble has been increasing for the last few weeks and is the highest since early June. [ID:nLDE6720SF]

 "We saw a squaring of long positions (in foreign currencies) by foreigners and big local banks," said Sergei Fishgoit, a dealer at Otrkitiye bank.

 "Today we've passed an important level for non-residents of 34.10 (roubles per basket) and I don't exclude a further firming in the rouble as soon as tomorrow," he said. Non-residents tend to look at technical levels more than domestic investors.

  The rouble gains were also seen on the forward market, with the six-month dollar/rouble non-deliverable forward (NDF) implied yield falling to a one-month low of 3.3 percent.

 "Amid a weaker basket, non-residents and major domestic banks were selling the curve (NDFs for the dollar/rouble)," said Alexei Kulakov, a forward trader at Promsvyazbank.

 Currently, technical analysis points to rouble resistance at 34.00 per basket and a breakthrough would mean a further possible upside move to 33.75, Petrocommerce bank said. [ID:nLDE672158]  (Editing by Susan Fenton)

MOSCOW, July 5 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble showed modest gains versus the euro and its currency basket in light trade on Monday, supported by stable oil prices and with the market eyeing commodities for clues as to future moves.

Against the euro-dollar basket, the rouble was up 2 kopecks at 34.70 <RUS=MCX>, staying 12 kopecks off a five-week low hit last Friday.

On the global forex market, the euro <EUR=> was steady.

"Oil stands still, the euro stands still. So the rouble doesn't head anywhere," said Roman Pakhomenko, dealer at Lanta bank.

Investors were also reluctant to take new positions due to the Independence Day holiday in the U.S., dealers said.

Versus the dollar, the rouble shed 6 kopecks to 31.16 <RUBUTSTN=MCX> but it gained 10 kopecks against the euro to 39.05 <EURRUBTN=MCX>.

Further moves in the rouble will depend mainly on commodity prices, dealers said, noting that the last time the rouble had been trading at similar levels, oil prices were below $70 per barrel.

"If oil continues sliding, it will make sense betting on the stronger basket towards the area of 35.0 roubles," said Viktor Anisimov, a dealer at Alba Alliance.

Consolidation of crude oil prices at current levels, or an increase, will provide the rouble with the potential to recover back to levels of 34.40 against the basket pretty soon, said Pakhomenko at Lanta.

Dealers are eyeing 34.40 because Russia's central bank is entering the market with targeted interventions in the range of 33.40-34.40, buying several hundred millions of dollars a day to absorb capital inflows.

title: INTERVIEW- Russia  c.bank happy with  FX intervention  mechanism
text:
MOSCOW, June 25 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank is happy with its current currency intervention mechanism and pleased that its actions have become harder to predict for the market, first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev told Reuters in an interview.

"If our rules and logic is clear, that's good. And the fact that our actions have become hard to work out is also good. I think the result is quite satisfactory," Ulyukayev said.

The central bank refined its two-stage intervention mechanism in April, according to dealers, and in June formally announced that some operations are directly tied to oil prices -- a key driver for the economy and markets. [ID:nLDE6561OI]

"Our market presence is defined by two different conditions. One condition is the trade balance which is, above all, determined by the price of our exports, mainly oil. This imbalance is forecastable...we can make some predictions about balancing it in advance," Ulyukayev said.

"The second component is the capital account, which is much harder to predict."

The central bank tracks the rouble within a 3-rouble wide, floating corridor against the euro-dollar basket, currently located at 33.40-36.40 roubles <RUS=MCX>.

It then tries to forecast the oil price component of market imbalances and compensates with 'targeted' intervention.

"We presume a certain oil price level which is normal for our economy and we can calculate how much extra foreign currency will come into our country if the real oil price is higher than the normal one," Ulyukayev said.

"All that excess, it turns out, pressures the domestic currency market. We calculated the size of the excess over a year, divided by the number of working days in a year and came to the volume of targeted intervention which we do every day, but this does not affect the exchange rate."

Since the start of the month, the central bank has bought around $2 billion in interventions, he added.

Ulyukayev confirmed dealers' assumption that the corridor is divided into three one-rouble bands, currently located around 33.40-34.40, 34.40-35.40 and 35.40-36.40.

"In the lower one we buy (foreign currency), in the top one we sell, and in the middle one we do nothing," he said.

If the targeted intervention proves to be insufficient to hold the rouble within the corridor, the central bank puts such moves down to the less predictable capital account component.

In that case, as per previous statements, it intervenes at the corridor's boundary -- buying foreign currency at the bottom level or selling it at the top -- and allows the band to shift by 5 kopecks after $700 million of interventions.

"The parameters are the same -- $700 million, 5 kopecks," Ulyukayev said. (Writing by Toni Vorobyova; Editing by Kazunori Takada)

title: UPDATE 1- Russia  cbank seeks to cap oil volatility in rouble
text:
* "Planned interventions" renamed "target interventions"

* Target interventions within band linked to oil price

* C.bank confirms mechanism of boundary interventions

(Adds quotes from central bank, analyst, dealer)

MOSCOW, June 7 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Monday it would tweak currency interventions to further discourage one-way oil-fuelled bets and dealers said the opaque statement was likely to cap volatility in the short-term.

The regulator said it would look more closely at oil prices -- a key driver for the rouble -- to determine the size of its daily currency market interventions. Russia is the world's largest oil producer and energy revenues cover 60 percent of its budget needs.

The regulator said it had bought $3.4 billion and 699 million euros ($835 million) in May in 'target' interventions, which were previously known as 'planned' interventions.

Such interventions are "directed mainly at neutralising the firm expectations of forex market participants related to the changes in the rouble's exchange rate, which are formed under the influence of the external economic situation," it said.

"The volumes of the target interventions are determined taking into account the dynamics of energy prices."

Thus higher oil prices -- which would normally encourage investors to bet more actively on the rouble -- would lead to higher interventions against the trend from the central bank.

That is in line with comments from central bank's first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev, who said last week that a lower trade balance -- potentially caused by lower prices for oil and commodity exports -- is a reason to consider lower interventions, and vice versa [ID:nLDE6531FG].

The statement chimes with the central bank's aim for more transparency as part of its long-term plan to move to inflation targeting but dealers called for more clarity.

"In the coming days, the players may behave cautiously on the market, because the central bank has announced a change in the interventions mechanism and until the details are clear, significant speculations in either directions should not be expected," said Sergei Romanchuk, dealer at Metallinvestbank.

In addition to target interventions, the central bank intervenes more heavily at the boundaries of the floating corridor, which, dealers say, are currently located at 33.40-36.40 roubles against the euro-dollar basket <RUS-MCX>.

"The operations of the Bank of Russia on purchases/sales of foreign currency undertaken in excess of the set target volumes are directed at smoothing out the movements in the rouble's exchange rate which are not determined by the influence of fundamental economic factors," the central bank said.

It reiterated that under the current parameters after $700 million worth of interventions at the boundary of the rouble's floating band the corridor is shifted by 5 kopecks.

Including the boundary interventions, the central bank bought $4.3 billion and 1.1 billion euros in May. (Reporting by Yelena Fabrichnaya, Toni Vorobyova and Vladimir Abramov; editing by Jason Webb)

title: UPDATE 1-Russian rouble ends down on risk aversion
text:
* Rouble volatile, ends week down

* Hit by risk aversion and U.S. payrolls

* Some recovery possible, volatility to remain

(Adds comments, recasts with weekly results)

By Andrey Ostroukh

MOSCOW, June 4 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble fell on Friday to finish lower on the week as it was pressured by rising risk aversion and was not helped by a pull-back in oil prices after disappointing U.S. employment data.

Talk of a "Greek-style" debt crisis in Hungary [ID:LDE65306M] raised risk aversion in global markets on Friday, helping pressure the rouble which lost 12 kopecks, or 0.3 percent to 34.32 versus the euro-dollar basket and fell 38 kopecks, or 1.2 percent against the dollar.

Meanwhile oil prices, the rouble's main driver, pulled back after a weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs report [ID:nOAT004640]. However, analysts said oil prices remain generally supportive for the currency at current levels still above $70 a barrel.

On the week, which saw Russia cut interest rates on Monday, the rouble lost 37 kopecks, or 1.1 percent to 34.31 against the euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX> -- used by the central bank to track currency moves -- heading away from a 17-month high of 33.40 hit in mid-May.

Against the broadly stronger dollar <RUBUTSTN=MCX>, the rouble lost 75 kopecks, or 2.3 percent on the week, sliding to 31.42 which is 27 kopecks above its 2010 low of 31.68 touched last week.

Although persistent worries about the fiscal health of countries in Europe bruised the rouble, they also helped it to a slight 0.2 percent gain on the week versus the euro to 37.85 <EURRUBTN=MCX>.

VOLATILE TRADE

On Friday, Russia's currency hit a session low of 34.35 versus the basket from a peak of 34.03 on the MICEX exchange. However, dealers said it was premature to speak of a rapid depreciation. "We don't see distinct flows, the rouble becomes more volatile. I don't think one should be afraid of devaluation moves but the dollar may rise higher," said Mikhail Anisimov, chief dealer at VTB Capital.

The central bank also continued to add pressure by maintaining its so-called "planned" interventions, purchasing around $300 million a day to absorb inflows of foreign currencies given the current account surplus, dealers say.

After the market close on Friday, the central bank's first deputy chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said the regulator may consider reducing the size of planned interventions following a fall in Russia's trade surplus. [ID:nLDE6531FG]

The currency could recover next week as bad news this week has been priced in and as oil prices are expected to stay above $70 a barrel, dealers said.

In the weeks ahead, domestic factors are likely to come into play, they said.

"The first important thing is whether the central bank will reduce its purchases (interventions). Apparently, it will. The second important thing is how RUSAL will set its debts", said Viktor Kholoshnoy, dealer at Gazprombank.

The world's top aluminium producer RUSAL > faces a loan redemption to the amount of $4.5 billion, with Russian banks VEB and Sberbank most likely to refinance the loan. [ID:nLDE6530OX]

"If RUSAL or banks buy foreign currencies in the market to repay the debt, it may bury the rouble's correlation with oil prices," Kholoshnoy said. (Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Russia bought gold for reserves in conservative '09
text:
MOSCOW, May 17 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank stuck to a conservative investment policy for its reserves in 2009, buying gold and reducing holdings of non-sovereign bonds, according to its annual report submitted to parliament on Monday.

The report also appeared to show that Russia had increased the share of dollars in its reserves at the expense of euros as of end-2009, but the data excludes conversion transactions, which have yet to be calculated, and the regulator has said that the nominal currency structure remains unchanged.

Excluding the not-yet accounted conversion transactions, Russia's reserve assets were held 44.5 percent in dollars, 43.8 percent in euros, 10.4 percent in sterling and 1.3 percent in yen. That compared to 41.5 percent dollars, 47.5 percent euros, 9.7 percent sterling and 1.3 percent yen at end-2008.

The figures include Russia's gold and forex reserves as well as assets against which the central bank has obligation. Russia regularly intervenes in the currency market, mostly in the dollar/rouble pair, and does not rebalance its reserves on a daily basis, meaning the reading for any particular day does not necessarily reflect the true structure of reserves.

Last year's annual report had prompted speculation that Russia was trying to limit its exposure to the dollar, but this was later disproved by central bank officials. [ID:nLK576828]

Officials have said the nominal structure of the foreign currency part of Russia's reserves remains unchanged at 47 percent U.S. dollars, 41 percent euros and 10 percent sterling -- the same as it was a year ago.

The report also showed the central bank bought 142.87 tonnes of gold, increasing its holdings of the metal by 30 percent during 2009. The non-gold part of reserves was spread between deposits and accounts at foreign banks' accounting for 5.4 percent, repo transaction with foreign counterparties at 1.4 percent and foreign bonds at 93.2 percent.

Russia's reserves, the world's third largest, were worth $440.6 billion at end-2009. (Reporting by Yelena Fabrichnaya; Writing by Toni Vorobyova; editing by Jason Webb)

title: UPDATE 1-Russia cbank buys $11.3 bln, 412 mln euros in April
text:
* Buys $11.34 billion and 412 million euros in April

* "Planned" purchases at $4.17 billion and 170 million euros

* Suggests rise in daily planned interventions, as expected

(Adds background)

MOSCOW, May 7 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Friday it had bought $11.34 billion and 412 million euros ($552.8 million) in April in currency market interventions aimed at slowing down the rouble's oil-fuelled appreciation.

The data confirmed that the regulator slightly increased so-called daily planned purchases last month. But it stuck by its policy of keeping the rouble within a floating band against a euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX> and shifting the corridor by 5 kopecks for each $700 million of interventions at its boundary.

It made 10 such shifts in April, implying $7 billion of boundary interventions, dealers have estimated -- a figure in line with the official central bank data released on Friday.

In addition, the central bank carries out so-called "planned" interventions within the band. The planned purchases totalled $4.17 billion and 170 million euros in April -- up from $3.06 billion and 174 million euros the previous month.

That translates into around $200 million of planned interventions per day in April and backs dealers' theory that the size of such purchases had been increased. In March, planned interventions averaged around $150 million a day.

For the fourth month in a row there were no foreign currency sales by the central bank in April, reflecting a broad appreciation trend in the rouble fanned by high oil prices, a domestic economic recovery and relatively high yields.

In March, the central bank had bought $14.48 billion and 443 million euros, with the higher volume of total interventions reflecting the bigger rally in the rouble seen that month. (Writing by Toni Vorobyova; Editing by Susan Fenton)

Risks Relating to the Russian Federation

Any material reduction in the price of crude oil or natural gas may materially adversely affect the revenues and financial condition of the Russian Federation



The Russian Federation's revenues are affected by international oil
and natural gas prices, which have fluctuated widely in recent years in
response to global supply and demand, general economic conditions, competition
from other energy sources and other factors. In 2008, for example, the peak
price of Urals oil was U.S.$137.40 per barrel and the average monthly price
per barrel was U.S.$94.40, compared to a peak price of U.S.$78.10 and an
average monthly price of U.S.$61.00 in 2009. The average price per barrel of
Urals oil in the first two months of 2010 was U.S.$74.30, and the spot price
of Urals oil was U.S.$81.03 on 1 April 2010. Russia's 2010 Budget Law assumes
an average price per barrel of Urals oil of U.S.$58, increasing to U.S.$59 in
2011 and to U.S.$60 in 2012. See "Public Finance--2010 Federal Budget Law."
Natural gas prices have likewise fluctuated significantly in recent years, in
part because crude oil prices often provide a benchmark for natural gas
prices. In 2008, the peak price of natural gas was U.S.$13.31 per mmbtu and
the average monthly price was U.S.$8.85 per mmbtu, compared to a peak price of
U.S.$6.14 and an average monthly price of U.S.$3.96 in 2009. While the
existing price for Urals oil is substantially above the price assumed in the
2010 Budget Law for 2010, 2011 and 2012, any material reduction in the price
of crude oil or natural gas will have a significant effect on Russia's
budgetary revenues and foreign reserves, and may materially adversely affect
the Russian Federation's financial condition, including its ability to make
payments on the Bonds.

The Russian Federation's economy, like many economies, is
vulnerable to external shocks. The current global economic crisis, significant
future economic difficulties of the Russian Federation's major trading
partners, and more general "contagion" effects all could have a material
adverse effect on the Russian Federation's economic growth and the market for
the Bonds

The Russian Federation's economy and finances have been adversely
affected by the current global economic crisis. Real GDP, for example,
declined by 7.9% in 2009 compared to 2008, and the average unemployment rate
(using the definition of the International Labour Organisation (the "ILO"))
increased from 7.1% in the fourth quarter of 2008 to 8.0% in the fourth
quarter of 2009. The value of the rouble against the dollar also declined in
2009, by 12.2% in real terms, as did the value of the real effective exchange
rate, which fell by 5.6%.



The Russian Federation's economy remains vulnerable to further external shocks, including the ongoing global economic crisis. A significant decline in the economic growth of the EU or any of the Russian Federation's other major trading partners could have a material adverse effect on the Russian Federation's balance of trade and adversely affect the Russian Federation's economic growth.



Events occurring in one geographic or financial market sometimes
result in an entire region or class of investments being disfavoured by
international investors--so-called "contagion effects." The Russian Federation
has been adversely affected by contagion effects in the past, and it is
possible that the market for Russian investments, including the Bonds, will be
similarly affected in the future by negative economic or financial
developments in countries whose economies or credit ratings are similar to
those of the Russian Federation.

There can be no assurance that the current economic crisis, or a
future external economic crisis, will not have a negative effect on investors'
confidence in Russia's markets or on the Russian Federation's economy or
ability to raise capital in the international debt markets, all of which could
have a material adverse effect on the trading price of the Bonds.



No waiver of immunity; Enforcement of liabilities



The Russian Federation is a sovereign state and has not waived any
rights to sovereign immunity it may have in any jurisdiction. Accordingly, the

proceeding in any jurisdiction arising out of the Bonds, and the Russian
Federation and its assets, properties and revenues may be entitled to immunity

court and/or have such judgment recognised and/or enforced in any
jurisdiction.

A final judgment rendered by a foreign court will generally be
recognised and enforced in the Russian Federation if there is an international
treaty in effect between the Russian Federation and the country where the
judgment is rendered providing for the mutual recognition and enforcement of
judgments. There are no international treaties in effect today providing for
the mutual recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments rendered by courts
in the Russian Federation and courts in most of the countries where Bond
investors are likely to reside, including the United States and the United
Kingdom.

In the absence of an applicable treaty, enforcement of a final
judgment rendered by a foreign court may still be recognized by a Russian
court on the basis of reciprocity, if courts of the country where the foreign
judgment is rendered have previously enforced judgments issued by Russian
courts. While Russian courts have recently recognized and enforced English and
Dutch court judgments on these grounds, the existence of reciprocity must be
established at the time the recognition and enforcement of a foreign judgment
is sought, and it is not possible to predict whether a Russian court will in
the future recognize and enforce on the basis of reciprocity a judgment issued
by a foreign court, including an English or Dutch court.

Even if an applicable international treaty is in effect or a
foreign judgment might otherwise be recognised and enforced on the basis of
reciprocity, the recognition and enforcement of a foreign judgment will in all
events be subject to exceptions and limitations provided for in Russian law.
For example, a Russian court may refuse to recognise or enforce a foreign
judgment if its recognition or enforcement would contradict Russian public
policy.



As a result, it may be difficult to obtain recognition or enforcement in the Russian Federation of a foreign judgment in respect of the Bonds.
