for any pre-settlement occurring within Euroclear or Clearstream. Under this
approach, the purchasing accountholder may take on credit exposure to
Euroclear or Clearstream until the beneficial interest in the Unrestricted
Global Bonds is credited to its account one day later. As an alternative, if
Euroclear or Clearstream has extended a line of credit to the purchasing
accountholder, it can elect not to pre-position funds and allow that credit
line to be drawn upon to finance settlement. Under this procedure, the
Euroclear or Clearstream accountholder purchasing the beneficial interest in
the Unrestricted Global Bonds would incur overdraft charges for one day,
assuming it cleared the overdraft when the beneficial interest was credited to
its account. However, interest on the Unrestricted Global Bonds would accrue
from the value date. Therefore, in many cases, the investment income on the
Unrestricted Global Bonds earned during that one-day period may substantially
reduce or offset the amount of such overdraft charges, although this result
will depend on each accountholder's particular cost of funds.



Because the settlement is taking place during New York business hours, the DTC participant can use its usual procedures for transferring a beneficial interest in the Global Bonds to the common depositary for the benefit of the Euroclear or Clearstream accountholder. The sale proceeds will be available to the DTC seller on the settlement date. Thus, to the DTC participant, a cross-market transaction will settle no differently than a trade between two DTC participants.



Day traders that use Clearstream or Euroclear to purchase interests
in the Bonds from DTC participants for delivery to Clearstream participants or
Euroclear participants should note that these trades will automatically fail
on the sale side unless affirmative action is taken. At least three techniques
should be readily available to eliminate this potential problem:



- Borrowing through Clearstream or Euroclear for one day, until the purchase side of the day trade is reflected in their Clearstream or Euroclear accounts, in accordance with the clearing system's customary procedures; or

- Borrowing the interests in the United States from a DTC participant no later than one day prior to settlement, which will give the interests sufficient time to be reflected in their Clearstream or Euroclear account in order to settle the sale side of the trade; or



- Staggering the value date for the buy and sell sides of the trade
so that the value date for the purchase from the DTC participant is at least
one day prior to the value date for the sale to the Clearstream participant or
Euroclear participant.



Trading between Euroclear/Clearstream Seller and DTC Purchaser



Due to time zone differences in its favour, a Euroclear or
Clearstream accountholder may employ customary transfer procedures when
transferring a book-entry interest in the Unrestricted Global Bonds to the
account of a DTC participant wishing to purchase a beneficial interest in
Restricted Global Bonds (subject to such certification procedures as are
provided in the Fiscal Agency Agreements). The seller must send instructions
to Euroclear or Clearstream at least one business day prior to the settlement
date. Euroclear or Clearstream will instruct the common depositary to credit
the beneficial interest in the Global Bonds to the DTC participant's account
and receive payment. Payment will include interest accrued on the beneficial
interest in the Bonds from and including the last interest payment date to and
excluding the settlement date. Payment will be reflected in the account of the
Euroclear or Clearstream accountholder the following day. Receipt of cash
proceeds in the Euroclear or Clearstream accountholder's account will be
back-valued to the value date, which will be the preceding day, when
settlement occurs in New York. If the Euroclear or Clearstream accountholder
has a line of credit with its clearing system and elects to draw on such line
of credit in anticipation of receipt of sale proceeds in its account, the
back-valuation may substantially reduce or offset any overdraft charges
incurred over that one-day period. If settlement is not completed on the
intended value date, that is, if the trade fails, receipt of the cash proceeds
in the Euroclear or Clearstream accountholder's account will instead be valued
as of the actual settlement date, whenever that may be.



For a further description of restrictions on the transfer of Bonds, see "Transfer Restrictions" below.

title: UPDATE 2-Russian rouble at 16-mo highs on oil, more to come
text:
* Rouble rallies to 16-month highs vs basket and euro

* Central bank moves floating boundaries 29th time in 2 mos

* Gradual rouble gains are likely to continue

(Adds quotes, detail, updates prices)

By Andrey Ostroukh

MOSCOW, April 21 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble scaled to new 16-month highs versus the basket and the euro on Wednesday, prompting the central bank to move its floating band, and dealers said the modest appreciation was likely to continue.

Strong oil prices, attractive carry trade and Russia's current account surplus favour gains in the rouble, which are, however, limited by the central bank interventions.

The central bank tracks the rouble moves inside a floating corridor and shifts the band by 5 kopecks after $700 million of interventions at each boundary.

On Wednesday, the rouble's oil-driven rally prompted the regulator to take the 29th such step in just over two months, bringing the band to 33.55-36.55 roubles versus the euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX>, dealers said.

The rouble closed up 9 kopecks on the day, at 33.57 against the basket, trimming gains slightly from after touching a 16-month high of 33.54.

"The day started with the sale of foreign currencies but the upward rouble's trend went under some pressure amid the lower euros and negative dynamics in Russia's stock market," said Mikhail Spolokhov, dealer at MDM bank.

The euro's weakness on the global market pushed it down to its lowest since December 2008 versus the rouble at 38.94 <EURRUBTN=MCX>. The dollar was slightly up at 29.13 roubles <RUBUTSTN=MCX>.

The rouble retained its main support from oil prices [O/R] that returned back above $85 per barrel, ensuring money flows into Russia's export-oriented economy. ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ For a graphic comparing rouble rate and oil prices click http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/10/04/RU_RROIL0410.gif("http://graphics.thomsonreuters.com/10/04/RU_RROIL0410.gif") ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Russian exporters and their banks also bolster the rouble by selling part of dollar and euro revenues for roubles to meet local tax payments, and that will continue next week.

Petrocommerce bank estimates tax liabilities will amount to around 250 billion roubles ($8.6 billion) until the month-end..

Economic data also favours the rouble. On Wednesday, Economy Minister Elvira Nabiullina said Russia's economy grew 4.9 percent year-on-year in March and expansion is likely to continue. [ID:nLDE63K0II]

The central bank's request for commercial banks to close their foreign currency correspondent accounts brought further proof of positive developments in Russia's financial system. [ID:nLDE63K1N4]

HIGHER INTERVENTIONS

Along with interventions at the floating boundaries the regulator maintains so-called "planned" interventions within the floating boundaries, which are thought to have increased last week to $250 million to 300 million a day from the previously presumed $150 million.

"An increase in planned interventions will naturally slow down the pace of the rouble's appreciation and will contribute more volatility to the main rouble currency pairs," said Dmitry Kharlampiev, analyst at Petrocommerce bank.

The rouble may reach a key technical level of 33.50 per basket this week if oil stays strong and there is a positive progress in bailout for Greece [ID:nLDE63K0CE], he said.

"We see the gradual strengthening continuing this year," said analysts at Nomura in a research note, adding near-term volatility is always possible due to changes in risk sentiment and speculations.

The volume of Russsian exporters' revenues, being converted into roubles, is likely to offset the impact of external negative newsflow, and short positions in dollar and euro seem to be overwhelming for now, dealers say.

Many players have been seen using occassion downside rouble moves to re-enter short positions in foreign currencies, Spolokhov at MDM said.

title: Russia  c.bank:  interventions  size not set in stone
text:
MOSCOW, April 8 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank will stick to its current mechanism of forex interventions for the foreseeable future but reserves the right to change the size of each step, a senior official said on Thursday.

 The central bank currently shifts the rouble's floating trading band versus a euro-dollar basket by 5 kopecks <RUS=MCX> for each $700 million of interventions. 

 The policy is designed to smooth out excessive volatility without stifling market trends.

 "In the foreseeable future, the mechanism which existed will remain. But the numbers which were aired are not a dogma. Of course, the numbers can change, but there are no plans to change the mechanism for now," Kirill Vergunov, head of domestic market operations at the central bank, told a MICEX conference.  (Reporting by Andrey Ostroukh; Writing by Toni Vorobyova)

title: Russia cbank bought net $14.5 bln, 443 mln euro March
text:
MOSCOW, April 7 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank bought a net $14.5 billion and 443 million euros ($592 million) in interventions in March as part of its policy to smooth out excessive rouble volatility, data showed on Wednesday.

 Of that, $3.1 billion and 174 million euros were purchased within the rouble's floating corridor in so-called "planned" interventions, while the rest was bought on the band's boundary.

 The data confirmed that the central bank has stuck by its policy of shifting the rouble's floating band by 5 kopecks for each $700 million of interventions at its boundary.

 It shifted the boundary 16 times in this way during March, dealers have said, as high oil prices powered the rouble to 15-month highs versus the euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX>.

 There were no foreign currency sales last month, according to the central bank's data.  (Writing by Toni Vorobyova)

title: Russian rouble's rally stalls near recent highs
text:
* Rouble's rally pauses near 14-mth highs vs basket

* External factors remain supportive, market eyes oil

MOSCOW, March 22 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble's rally stalled on Monday as oil and other high-yielding currencies turned lower, but the currency should still be supported by tax payments this week and relatively strong fundamentals.

In early trade, the rouble was down 3 kopecks against the euro-dollar basket at 33.97 <RUS=MCX>, still in sight of a 14-month high of 33.93 hit last Friday, according to Reuters data.

Downside pressure on the rouble reflects the oversold state of the local market, that has been already betting on the rouble's rise for almost two months.

"The appreciation has not paused yet, only excessive firming is on pause. Short positions (in foreign currency) are preferred and are very big now. The weather is grey so the market is grey as well," said a dealer at a Russian bank.

The rouble showed rapid rises in the last seven weeks, supported by strong oil prices, exporters converting part of their revenues in foreign currencies into roubles, and the appeal of carry trade operations, given the relatively big spread in interest rates compared to the U.S. or euro zone.

The central bank has gradually cut rates since April 2009, bringing them to record lows, but with the benchmark refinancing rate at 8.50 percent -- higher than in all the other G8 states -- Russian assets retain their high-yielding status.

This appeal is set to remain even if the regulator slashes rates again this month, expectations for which were supported by lacklustre economic data last Friday [ID:nLDE62I1AZ].

The rouble may gain some support this week from tax payments in Russia -- value added tax payments are due on Monday and the tax on natural resources by March 25. The total tax payments will be close to 200-250 billion roubles ($6.8-$8.5 billion), according to Trust bank estimates.

Russia's central bank has been intervening in the currency market, shifting the rouble's floating corridor by 5 kopecks for each $700 million of purchases at its boundary.

It has taken 22 such steps since mid-February, bringing the band to 33.90-36.90 against the basket on Friday, dealers said. The new presumed boundary has yet to be tested.

The rouble's performance will heavily depend on oil prices but, generally, the upward trend remains intact.

"The rouble's exchange rate is still 17 percent lower than pre-crisis levels, so the possibility of further appreciation is pretty high. Our view on the Russian currency remains positive," analysts at Uralsib bank said in a note to clients.

By 0825 GMT, the rouble was down around 5 kopecks against the dollar at 29.33 <RUBUTSTN=MCX>. Versus the euro <EURRUBTN=MCX>, the rouble climbed to a fresh 15-month maximum of 39.5945, as the single currency came under broad pressure on ongoing concerns over aid to debt-burdened Greece [FRX/]. title: EMERGING MARKETS-Greek woes weigh; Russia rouble rises
text:
* Emerging markets dip Greece overshadows Bernanke comments

* Turkish shares snap losing streak but lira weaker

* Rouble hits 14-month high; Serb dinar to test new low

By Sebastian Tong

LONDON, Feb 25 (Reuters) - Mounting concerns over Greece's financial health weighed on emerging markets on Thursday though the U.S. Federal Reserve's pledge to keep interest rates exceptionally low for an extended period provided investors some comfort. Turkish shares <.XU100> broke a three-day losing streak sparked off by a probe into an alleged coup plot that heightened tensions between its secularist military and Islamist-rooted government while Russia rouble hit 14-month highs against its euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX>.

Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke's Wednesday affirmation that he would maintain loose monetary conditions sparked a rally that fizzled after stark warnings from rating agencies Moody's and Standard & Poor's that Greek sovereign ratings were jeopardised by its inability to curb spending. [ID:nLDE61N2KL] [ID:nTOE61O07C]

Emerging shares <.MSCIEF>, which have underperformed world stocks <.MIWD00000PUS> since the start of the year, were 0.8 percent lower by 1145 GMT, while emerging sovereign debt spreads <11EMJ> widened two basis points to trade at 302 bps over U.S. Treasuries.

"Greece has overshadowed Bernanke's testimony to Congress and risk is on the back foot. The market is seeking some clarity on Greece - it's waiting for the sovereign bond issue and to see what the European Union will do about the situation," said Manik Narain, economist at Standard Chartered.

The sombre note sounded by the Fed chief on the U.S. economy also provided a sobering reminder of the fragility of the global recovery, Narain added.

"It's not just sovereign credit worthiness that is a worry but the state of the global economy."

Hungarian shares <.BUX> recovered 0.6 percent after sinking to a two-week low earlier in the day while Turkish shares rose over one percent after dropping some three percent to plumb 12-week lows in the previous session.

TURKEY; SERBIA

The lira pared losses against the dollar <TRY=> but languished near seven-month lows with investors continuing a close eye on developments on the unfolding investigation into an alleged plot by some Turkey's military officers to overthrow the government. [ID:nIST006632]

Five-year credit default swaps to insure Turkish sovereign debt were quoted unchanged at 197.5 bps from the previous day's close, according to CMA DataVision.

Emerging European currencies were broadly weaker with the Polish zloty backing further off from the 13-month highs reached on Tuesday <EURPLN=>.

Serbia's dinar <EURRSD=>, however, looked set to test the historic lows reached on Wednesday after its central bank said interest rates are likely to be cut rather than left unchanged. [ID:nLDE61O0WB]

The central bank moved to slow the unit's slide on Wednesday, blamed by local dealers on demand for euros from importers. [ID:nLDE61N23V]

However, analysts also say Greek fiscal woes could be a factor for Balkan economies such as Serbia.

"Bulgaria is the most exposed as Greece is one of the top-three export destinations (almost 10 percent of exports)... Greek foreign direct investments in Serbia are notable as well," said UniCredit in a client note.

Russia's central bank also intervened in the market but its move was sparked off by the strength of the rouble.

The rouble hit multi-month highs against its dual currency basket reinforced by healthy tax receipts and buoyant crude prices. [ID:nLDE61O0O4] (Reporting by Sebastian Tong; )

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Russia's current low inflation leaves room for further interest rate cuts, First Deputy Central Bank Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said Thursday, Interfax reported.

"I think that that as long as the situation doesn't carry inflationary risks, it allows us to consider lowering the refinancing rate," Ulyukayev said.

The central bank had cut interest rates by 425 basis points last year, bringing the refinancing rate to a record low of 8.75% in an effort to stimulate lending and turn away speculative capital.

Russian consumer prices are up 2.1% since the start of the year, compared with 3.2% in the same period last year.

Last week, First Deputy Central Bank Chairman Gennady Melikyan said the authorities would "wait a bit and see what is going on with inflation" before cutting rates further.

The Central Bank has already purchased a net $2 billion in the currency market through interventions so far this month, Ulyukayev said.

Russia saw $13 billion in capital outflow in January but was unlikely to see any outflows this month, he said.

title: Russia rouble hits 2010 high, eyes c.bank boundary
text:
MOSCOW, Feb 16 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble hit its strongest level of the year on Tuesday, closing in on the current boundary of the central bank's floating trading band thanks to higher oil prices and upcoming domestic tax payments.

The rouble firmed as far as 35.05 versus the euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX> -- just 5 kopecks away from the boundary of the central bank's current floating corridor of 35-38.

The rouble also firmed as far as 30.09 per dollar, its strongest in nearly two weeks <RUBUTSTN=MCX>. "Slowly but surely we are moving lower (in the basket/rouble rate)," said Mikhail Kulyk, dealer at Alfa Bank, forecasting that the central bank's boundary could be reached "tomorrow if not today". As per its policy of smoothing out excessive exchange rate volatility, the central bank steps in with interventions at the band's boundary before allowing the corridor to shift slightly.

In the past, the central bank allowed the band to shift by 5 kopecks for each $700 million of interventions. This last happened in November 2009, but Kulyk said the parameters of the interventions have likely remained unchanged since then.

Urals oil -- Russia's key export -- jumped over 2 percent to above $72 a barrel, or some $14 more than the average price for 2010 factored into the government budget <URL-E>.

"Some recovery in euro/dollar, as well as upward pressure on commodity prices could keep the rouble supported in the coming days," analysts at BNP Paribas said in a research note.

Also positive for the rouble are month-end domestic tax payments due next week, which analysts at Zenit estimated at around 370 billion roubles ($12.28 billion).

"Exporters are selling foreign currency, there will be a lot of payments coming up," said Kulyk, adding that companies were getting ready for the payments earlier than usual due to two days of public holidays at the start of next week. Nonetheless, not everyone expects the rouble's appreciation trend to prove long-lasting, with BNP Paribas recommending shorting the Russian currency versus the basket with a target of 36.50 "in anticipation of disappointing growth".

Markets have also turned slightly more negative on the rouble in the long term, with non-deliverable forwards showing it at 31.75 per dollar in a year's time -- over 50 kopecks weaker than at the end of last week, but still implying a fairly modest depreciation of around 5 percent <RUB1YNDFOR=>. (Writing by Toni Vorobyova; editing by Stephen Nisbet)

title: Investors flock to Russia in 1st working week of 2010
text:
* Flows into Russia funds at 12-week highs

* Rouble firm, interventions cap gains

* MICEX index posts biggest weekly gain in 3 months

By Toni Vorobyova

MOSCOW, Jan 15 (Reuters) - Investors have flocked to Russia in its first working week of 2010, boosting the rouble, snapping up bonds, and sending stocks to 1-1/2-year highs on expectations of a continued economic recovery and high oil prices.

Flows into Russian equity funds hit a 12-week high of $244 million, outperforming emerging market peers China, India and Brazil, according to fund tracker EPFR Global. [ID:nTOE60E038] "As 2010 gets underway, the mood amongst international investors is increasing Russiaphilia," said Chris Weafer, analyst at UralSib.

The MICEX stocks index <.MCX> on Friday hits its highest intra-day level since August 2008 and was on track for its biggest weekly gain in 3 months -- 6.5 percent -- as investors rushed to make up for lost time once Russia returned to work on Monday, Jan. 11 after over a week of public and market holidays.

The dollar-denominated RTS performed similarly well <.IRTS>.

Russian bonds were also in demand, with prices rising and yields falling. The yield on benchmark sovereign 2030 Eurobond hovered near record lows <RU011428878=>, while yields on rouble bonds fell to multi-month lows <0#RUTSY=MM>.

The rouble started the year with its biggest ever one-day jump versus a euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX>, reflecting 15-month highs in the price of Russia's Ural oil blend <URL-E>. It later stabilised to end the week 2.6 percent higher at 35.36.

Dealers said the central bank had likely stepped into the market during the week, buying dollars as part of its policy to limit excessive volatility in the rouble in either direction.

CAUTION AHEAD

In a sign of returned confidence in the rouble, Russia's biggest lender Sberbank from Friday resumed giving out mortgages in foreign currency. It has halted the practice in December 2008 -- during a phase of crisis-time rouble devaluation -- due to high currency risks.

"Most foreign investors now have neutral positions or are overweight Russia, but 2009 performance and strong commodities may attract new money in 2010," Unicredit analysts said in a research note. "So far the data supports our view."

Data released this week showed consumer confidence [ID:nLDE60D0FR] and exports [ID:nLDE60D20O] at one-year highs, rail freight picking up [ID:nLDE60B1I5], the slowdown in car sales moderating [ID:nLDE60D0XM] and the budget deficit coming in smaller than expected [ID:nLDE60D0FP].

Nonetheless, the economic recovery is expected to be slow, with Russia unlikely to return to pre-crisis health before 2012.

As such, the central bank is expected to continue cutting interest rates, which may limit the future rally potential for the rouble in the longer term by slashing its yield advantage.

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs), a barometer of market sentiment, show the rouble <RUB=> holding broadly steady against the dollar over the next 3 months and then weakening gradually in the second half of the year <RUBNDFOR=>.

Some are also questioning how much further stocks can rally after Moscow's bourses more than doubled in value last year.

"I think this is already the final wave of the rally which started in the spring of last year. At most, the indexes will add another 15 percent, and already from March the correction will start," said Sergei Ryndin at Zurich Capital Management. (Additional reporting by Olga Popova and Oksana Kobzeva; Editing by Toby Chopra)

title: Russia c.bank bought net $602 mln in December
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank bought a net $602 million in December, intervening within the rouble's trading band as part of a policy to smooth out excessive currency volatility in either direction, data showed on Monday.

The net figure balances out sales of $412 million, as well as purchases of $1.014 billion.

That reflects the rouble's volatile performance in the final month of 2009, when year-end profit-taking and rising risk aversion caused periods of weakness in the Russian currency, followed by sharp rebounds sparked by recoveries in oil price and by domestic tax payments.

In December the rouble stayed within the central bank's 35-38 floating trading band versus a euro-dollar basket <RUS=MCX>. Thus all the interventions were in the so-called "planned" format, meaning they took place within the band rather than at its boundaries.

The central bank also bought 241 million euros ($345 million) in December, the data showed.

The official data was broadly in line with expectations, after central bank chairman Sergei Ignatyev said the regulator had both bought and sold foreign currency in December, resulting in net purchases of around $400 million in the first 15 days of the month. [ID:nLDE5BF0CI]

In November, the central bank bought a net $7.317 billion and 745 million euros. (Writing by Toni Vorobyova; Editing by Andy Bruce)

title: UPDATE 1-Russia rouble retrieves bulk of early week losses
text:
* Rouble regains 63 kopecks of early week losses

 * Still remains 3.8 pct below mid-November highs

 * Seen stable, slightly strengthening next week

 By Lidia Kelly and Andrei Ostroukh

 MOSCOW, Dec 11 (Reuters) -- Russia's rouble retrieved a big chunk of its early week losses by Friday-end, as crude prices started rising again and further signs of rebound in the global economy reinstated investors interest in riskier assets. The rouble closed at 36.45 against the dollar-euro basket <RUS=MCX> Russia's central bank uses for guiding the currency's nominal exchange rate -- some 63 kopecks stronger than Wednesday's three-month low.

 The currency still traded weaker than last week's close of 35.98 and was 3.8 percent down from mid-November highs. But analysts said the improving sentiment across international markets should support the rouble in coming days.

 "We expect the rouble to continue to appreciate slowly, heading toward the middle of the central bank of Russia's floating currency band (currently at 35-38 roubles against the basket0," Nikolai Podguzov, the head of fixed income strategy at Renaissance Capital in Moscow, said in a research note.

 Oil prices reversed their week-long falling trend on Friday, [O/R] and Chinese data showed solid industrial growth, renewing confidence in emerging markets and their riskier, but higher-yielding currencies.

 "Next week might be a bit more optimistic than the beginning of this week," Artyom Arkhipov, chief market and macroeconomic analyst at Gazprombank, said.

 "At the same time activity will be lower ahead of the New Year. We expect volatility to decrease and rouble could stabilize or strengthen modestly if oil prices don't fall below $70 (per barrel)."

 Russia's central bank has been allowing much greater flexibility in the currency rate than previously, but it still guards carefully against high volatility, stepping in when it deems necessary to prevent excessive rouble fluctuations in either direction.

 Some analysts suggest shorting the rouble at and above current levels around 30.00 per dollar, targeting a 27-28 roubles per dollar in the first quarter of next year <RUB=>, it is still a laggard versus other emerging market currencies.

 "While the central bank of Russia is likely to continue to intervene to slow pace of forex appreciation, it does not appear outright hostile to a stronger currency and hard capital controls are unlikely," said RBC Capital Markets analysts.

 The market at large believes the rouble should stay fairly stable in the next 12 months. Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs), which mirror investors' attitude towards currencies, showed the rouble only slightly weaker in a year's time  at 31.85 per dollar --  compared to expectations for a 20 percent decline this time last year <RUB1YNDFOR=>.

title: =DJ UPDATE:  Russia  To Step Up  Currency Interventions

(Adds details, context.) 
 
   By Ira Iosebashvili 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The central bank plans to increase its use of foreign currency transactions to combat a tide of speculative capital flowing into Russia, Central Bank First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said Wednesday.

Russia will be "more active" in using currency interventions to keep the ruble within the floating corridor of RUB35-RUB38 against a basket of dollars and euros, Ulyukayev said.

Like other emerging-market economies, Russia is grappling with a deluge of hot money attracted by its comparatively high interest rates, which are significantly above those found in developed nations.

Although the central bank has cut the refinancing rate by 400 basis points since April to a record low 9.0% and bought $16 billion in foreign currency in October and the first half of November, the ruble has kept on rising, appreciating by around 10% against the dollar since September.

Ulyukayev's comments failed to budge the currency, which closed down four kopecks against the dollar at RUB28.79.

Russia will continue cutting interest rates into next year, as there are no inflationary risks on the horizon, Ulyukayev said. Russian consumer prices edged up 0.1% in the week to Nov. 23, bringing inflation to 8.4% since January, data released by the Federal Statistics Service showed Wednesday.

Inflation for next year will be "much lower" than 9%, Ulyukayev said.

title: UPDATE 2-Russia eyes new measures to cap rouble rally
text:
* Rouble hits highest since Jan vs currency basket

* Russia may consider soft measures to stem inflows

* C.bank chief reiterates he is against capital controls

(Recasts with Ignatyev comments)

By Yelena Fabrichnaya and Andrei Ostroukh

MOSCOW, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Russia allowed the rouble to scale fresh, oil-fuelled highs versus a euro-dollar basket on Wednesday, but the central bank said it would consider "soft" measures to limit future speculative inflows into the country.

The rouble has firmed 9 percent versus the basket since September to 35.03, its strongest since January <RUS=MCX> as investors regain confidence in emerging markets, the domestic economy starts to recover from recession and oil prices hold near one-year highs <URL-E>.

The central bank has so far intervened only to slow down the appreciation rather than stop it, but there are some signs officials are getting concerned about the inflow of hot money.

"I am against resuming capital control measures. At the same time, there are other measures, softer ones, which could slow down the inflow of speculative capital...It is being discussed," central bank chairman Sergei Ignatyev told reporters.

Such measures could include monitoring external borrowing of state-controlled companies, as well as re-introducing differentiated minimum reserve requirements for banks' liabilities in foreign currency versus those in the rouble, he added.

Currently the central bank allows the rouble's floating corridor to shift by 5 kopecks for each $700 million of interventions at either of the band's boundaries. Dealers say the latest intervention level is at 35.00 against the basket.

Ignatyev said earlier on Wednesday the central bank had bought $6 billion in currency market interventions between Nov. 1 and Nov. 17, after purchases of over $15 billion last month.

"The order of interventions may change ... It is possible that the floating (rouble) corridor could be altered not just automatically," Ignatyev told reporters later.

However he reiterated Russia's long-term goal remains to move to a floating exchange rate and inflation targeting.

"By my estimates it will take 1-1/2 years, possibly 2. And possibly it will not be an absolutely clean float," he said.

Officials have previously said Russia intends to reserve the right to intervene in the currency market if it deems necessary even after the free float.

Another factor that could discourage capital inflows and cap the rouble's rally would be further interest rate cuts.

Ignatyev reiterated the likelihood of more monetary easing to come, saying the benchmark refinancing rate could be cut to under annualised 9.00 percent next year from 9.50 percent currently.

The minimum one-day repo rate, now at 6.75 percent, will be reduced more slowly than the refi, he added. The daily repo auctions have been the central bank's chief tool for providing short-term liquidity to the banking sector.

Russia saw a net capital outflow of $53 billion in the first 10 months of 2009, Ignatyev told parliament earlier. Based on previously reported data, that implies capital inflows of over $9 billion in October, in line with previous estimates. (Writing by Toni Vorobyova; Editing by Victoria Main)

title: WRAPUP 1-Russia, Kazakhstan eye  forex  action to stem rallies
text:
* Russian, Kazakh currencies pushed up by strong oil

* Russia considering soft measures to limit inflows

* Kazakhstan warns foreigners betting on tenge rally

(Adds details, background, quotes)

By Yelena Fabrichnaya and Olzhas Auyezov

MOSCOW/ALMATY, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Russia and Kazakhstan on Wednesday stepped up rhetoric against speculative bets on their currencies, with Moscow eyeing new measures against capital inflows and Astana ready to crack down on foreign players.

Investors keen to cash in on the rally in oil prices [O/R] have rushed into the two energy-exporting neighbours, sending their currencies higher and causing some concern that fragile economic recoveries could be compromised.

Russia has to date allowed the rouble to appreciate gradually to 35.03 versus a euro-dollar basket, its strongest since January and up 9 percent since September <RUS=MCX>.

But there are some signs officials are getting concerned about the inflow of hot money.

"I am against resuming capital control measures. At the same time, there are other measures, softer ones, which could slow down the inflow of speculative capital ... It is being discussed," Russian central bank chairman Sergei Ignatyev told reporters.

Measures could include monitoring external borrowing of state-controlled companies and re-introducing differentiated minimum reserve requirements for banks' liabilities in foreign currency versus those in the rouble, he added. [ID:nLI559680]

Analysts say Russia could also step up its currency interventions and press on with interest rate cuts in a bid to further restrain the rouble's rally. [ID:nLH521118]

FOREIGNERS

Kazakhstan has kept the tenge in a fairly narrow 145-155 range versus the dollar since February <KZT=>, but the rise in oil prices as well as the rally in the rouble are putting more appreciation pressure on the currency.

"We ... had to buy over $2 billion to stop the tenge from appreciating too fast," Kazakh central bank chief Grigory Marchenko said on Wednesday, adding that about a quarter of that sum had come from foreign players.

"They (foreign players) will be able to earn some money," he said. "But we won't allow them to gain a lot." [ID:nLI22425]

Marchenko pledged to intervene more if the tenge goes beyond 147.50 per dollar compared to 149.14 now and 150.69 a week ago.

In other emerging markets, the weak dollar has prompted countries to look for new ways to cushion their economies, with Brazil introducing a tax on foreign investment in its fixed income and stock markets. [ID:nN19264977]

Analysts have said Moscow is unlikely to follow in Brazil's footsteps, but could implement less radical measures.

Moscow has repeatedly pledged not to re-introduce capital controls -- scrapped in 2006 -- and resisted pressure to do so during the height of crisis-time capital flight.

Prime Minister Vladimir Putin has said that a lack of capital controls is key to attracting foreign investment into Russia, which is looking for fresh cash to help the economy recover from its first recession in a decade. [ID:nLI729685]

Russia hopes to raise $3 billion from privatisations next year and cut state share in the economy to 30 percent from 50 percent in the next few years. Analysts and investors say the country needs to improve its investment climate and the rule of law if it wants to attract long-term, strategic capital.

Kazakhstan has introduced legislation allowing it to enforce capital controls if deemed necessary [ID:nLA336688] but so far the authorities have not used the option. (Writing by Toni Vorobyova and Maria Golovnina; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: RPT-INTERVIEW-IMF: Russia  shd shift spending, limit  intervention
text:
(Repeats, without changes, story first published on Monday)

* IMF: Russia to have 'fairly good' recovery in Q4 '09

* Stimulus should focus on social, infrastructure spending * Urges decisive moves to address bank capitalisation

* Rouble interventions only to avoid short-term swings

By Lidia Kelly

MOSCOW, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Russia needs to make its economic recovery more self-sustaining by shifting stimulus spending towards infrastructure and social needs and ensuring banks have enough capital, the IMF's senior representative in Moscow told Reuters.

Odd Per Brekk also said the central bank was right to aspire to a policy of inflation targeting and should confine its intervention in the currency market to smoothing out excessive short-term swings in the exchange rate.

"The economy has turned a corner," Brekk said in an interview. "It's driven by the recovery in the world economy, it's driven by the large budget stimulus and it is driven by a rebound in inventories ... Now, looking ahead, there is a question how sustained these factors will be."

Russia's gross domestic product grew by 0.6 percent during the third quarter, seasonally adjusted, ending a recession that wiped out more than tenth of its economy in year-on-year terms. [ID:nLO623617].

The IMF expects Russia's economy to shrink by 7.5 percent this year, milder than the government's 8.5 percent estimate.

"We're seeing a fairly good recovery continued also in the fourth quarter of 2009, but then as these factors (budget stimulus) become less potent, the economy will grow at a slower pace during 2010," Brekk said, estimating growth at around 1.5 percent next year.

This is more conservative than the consensus in a recent Reuters poll of economists for 3.1 percent growth next year. [ID:nLU728233].

SOCIAL SPENDING

Brekk reiterated the IMF's earlier praise for the government's overall response to the global economic crisis but said spending should have focused on social and infrastructure needs rather than on injecting liquidity into companies.

"You would get more boost to domestic demand and therefore more positive effect on growth," he said.

The IMF has previously recommended scaling back the fiscal stimulus to 2.5 percent of GDP from 5.5 percent.

Social and infrastructure spending "will have a relatively larger effect on domestic demand in the short term and then they will self-correct, self-reverse once the economy starts gaining momentum on its own," he added.

The government should also "deal decisively" with the banking system to ensure it extends credit to companies and households, Brekk said.

"The main point is to make sure there is a clear picture of capitalisation needs first," he said. "The second step is to ensure that the necessary capital is actually injected."

ROUBLE SWINGS

Brekk said the IMF supports the central bank's current managed appreciation of the rouble -- relatively high prices for Russia's oil exports [O/R] and increased optimism in global economic recovery have been pushing the currency up <RUB=>.

But he added the central bank should intervene only to avoid excessive short-term swings in the exchange rate.

"If there are long-term fundamental changes in the underlying economy they should not try to resist that," he said. "If there are permanent changes in oil prices it may not be possible to resist changes in the real exchange rate."

He said it was more "productive" to think of the central bank's goal of moving towards inflation targeting as a gradual process. However, "if you want to move to a formal inflation targeting framework ... that is not compatible with also trying to target the exchange rate," Brekk added.

(Reporting and writing by Lidia Kelly; Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

7 Aug 2009 09:00 EDT =DJ  IMF: Russia Must Be Proactive On Banks, Redirect Stimulus


 
   By Andrew Langley and Will Bland 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--Russia should take a more hands-on approach to tackling problems in its banking sector and redirect its stimulus package towards more temporary spending in order to build on early signs of an economic recovery, the International Monetary Fund said Friday.

The IMF - which sees the Russian economy shrinking 6.5% in 2009 - also welcomed recent interest rate cuts by the central bank but warned against being too aggressive in easing monetary policy further amid volatility in the ruble exchange rate.

"Banks' financial situation and loan portfolios are now deteriorating at a notably faster pace. The key immediate challenge facing the authorities at this time is how to deal with these mounting problems," the IMF's executive board wrote in an annual report.

It said Russia should be more "proactive" in addressing the issues affecting the sector to avoid a prolonged credit freeze, advising the authorities to recapitalize struggling lenders, stress-test the largest institutions and beef up the central bank's supervisory powers, in part to better understand thus-far opaque asset quality.

Reductions in lending rates, which have been cut five times since April, will eventually filter through to the real economy, although banks remain inclined to strengthen their balance sheets rather than lend at present, the IMF said.

"Absent a more determined policy intervention, there is a risk that banks will continue to struggle to adjust balance sheets, stifling credit expansion and impeding a recovery."

Battered by lower commodity prices and scant access to credit, Russia's economy shrank by more than 10% on the year between January and June. Gross domestic product will fall by 8.5% for the whole 2009, according to the latest government forecasts.

But recent reports on manufacturing and rail cargo suggest that the worst of Russia's first recession in a decade has now passed and that the second half of the year will be better.

"The latest data...provide tentative signs that the economy may have recently reached a turning point," the IMF said.

But it warned that growth in 2010 will be slow, while the focus of the government's current stimulus program could endanger future economic expansion.

"A better-targeted yet smaller stimulus could have a similar impact on economic activity...but would reduce the risk of causing a permanent change in the tax and expenditure structure."

"[The IMF] recommends reorienting the stimulus toward a temporary increase in social transfers targeted on credit-constrained households, and suggests a front-loading of infrastructure projects for which preparations are advanced alongside a strengthening of procurement procedures."

On the ruble, the IMF said Russia should intervene in foreign exchange markets on a temporary basis if rates become unsettled.

It said that the rates should be flexible but that the current exchange rate "remains broadly in equilibrium."

title: RPT-UPDATE 2-Russian c.banker sees rouble free float in 2 years
text:
(Repeats, without changes, to additional subscribers)

* Russia central bank head sees rouble free float in 2 years

* Ignatyev expected to be re-appointed this week

* World Bank cuts Russian forecast for 2009

(Adds analyst quote, World Bank report, background)

By Dmitry Sergeyev and Gleb Bryanski

MOSCOW, June 22 (Reuters) - Russia may float the rouble in two years but should continue currency market interventions during the transition period, the central bank head said on Monday, outlining his policy vision for the next term.

Sergei Ignatyev, who steered the central bank since 2002, overseeing accumulation of the world's third largest foreign currency reserves and managing both appreciation and depreciation of the rouble, is expected to be re-appointed for a third term on Wednesday.

A free float would enable the central bank to steer the economy through interest rates and may even make the rouble attractive as an international reserve currency -- a cherished dream of the Russian leadership.

"Our main goal is a transition to an inflation targeting regime and (the rouble's) free float. I believe we can approach these decisions in the next two years," Ignatyev told parliament members during a committee hearing.

"I think we should not take any strict obligations in terms of stopping currency interventions in the next two years," Ignatyev said, adding that Russia was already half way towards a free float.

Analysts and policy makers have said the rouble decision will depend on Russia's current account balance and economic growth -- both heavily dependent on its oil and other commodity exports.

On Monday the World Bank cut its Russian forecast for this year to predict 7.5 percent contraction this year, down from an earlier forecast of 4.5 percent shrinkage. However, it revised up next year's forecast to 2.5 percent growth from stagnation.

POLITICAL SUPPORT

After devaluing the rouble by a third earlier this year, Russia's central bank has set a wide trading band of between 26 and 41 roubles to a dollar/euro basket, intervening in the market to iron out what it sees as excessive exchange rate volatility.

Ignatyev, a 61-year old technocrat and a former deputy to Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin, often faces criticism in parliament but with the firm backing of President Dmitry Medvedev his re-appointment is seen as a done deal.

Analysts see the re-appointment as a sign of gratitude from the country's leadership for the crisis management during the toughest weeks in September-October 2008 when the country's banking system was on the verge of collapse.

"The Chairman of the central bank will work as long as he has support from the political leadership, it is not like in the Bank of England or the Fed," said Troika analyst Anton Tabakh. The central bank is by law independent from the government.

A move to free float would be Russia's most significant economic decision since lifting capital movement restrictions in 2006, allowing the rouble to join the Brazilian real and South African rand among freely floating emerging currencies.

NO CONSENSUS

The move would require a legal change to formally charge the central bank with controlling inflation as opposed to its current task of ensuring exchange rate stability.

There is no consensus between policy makers on the free float, with Ignatyev's own deputy Alexei Ulyukayev saying a free float is possible next year and Kremlin economic aide Arkady Dvorkovich saying a decision would be premature.

Russia's Prime Minister Vladimir Putin, seen as an ultimate decision-maker in Russia, has not yet spoken on the issue but has repeatedly said that the rouble should eventually become an international reserve currency.

The World Bank expects Russia's current account to remain in surplus equal to 3 percent of gross domestic product in 2010 after 2.4 percent in 2009, which should provide fundamental support for the currency.

However, "possible oil price declines, the Russian banks' problems maturing into an acute form, or an emerging markets sell-off would be sufficient to weaken the rouble," said Alexander Morozov, HSBC's chief economist on Russia. (Writing by Gleb Bryanski, Editing by Ruth Pitchford)

title: US Treasury:China Moving To Flexible Yuan But Too Slowly
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The U.S. Treasury Department on Tuesday again declined to designate China as guilty of currency manipulation in a report, noting the government in Beijing is moving steadily, though slowly, toward a flexible foreign exchange regime.  

"The Department of Treasury concluded that no major trading partner of the U.S. met the technical requirements for designation," according to the closely watched and overdue report to Congress on international exchange rate policies during the first half of 2006.  

Treasury outlined steps China is taking to loosen restrictions on capital moving in and out of the country and develop new financial instruments, such as currency futures, to prepare for a freely floating currency. In recent months, the government has allowed the value of the Chinese yuan to fluctuate more and the pace of appreciation has picked up. This progress made it difficult to say that China is managing its currency regime with the intent of gaining a trade advantage, a senior Treasury official told reporters on condition of anonymity.  

Nonetheless, China is moving too cautiously and the pace of reforms are too slow, Treasury said.

title: Russia's dollar buying risks inflation-Greenspan
text:
NEW YORK, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Russia should be wary about the inflationary impact of buying U.S. dollars to insulate its economy from an influx of foreign earnings from oil exports, former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said on Thursday.  

Russia, the world's second largest oil exporter, has been earning about $600 million a day from its oil and gas exports, pushing its rouble currency higher and threatening to cause "Dutch Disease".  

Dutch Disease refers to the potential negative long-term impact of one explosive sector -- oil, in the case of Russia -- which boosts the value of the currency, making locally produced goods less competitive compared to foreign goods.  

Greenspan warned that the standard cure for Dutch Disease -- central bank buying of foreign currencies -- could increase the monetary base without the necessary infrastructure to neutralize the move's impact on inflation.  

"Unless you're able to sterilize these (foreign) assets, it's going to be a struggle," Greenspan told the Fifth Annual Investor Conference on Russia.  

The Russian central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market by buying U.S. dollars to slow the rouble's rise. The move, however, fuelled money supply growth of about 45 percent and inflation of around 10.9 percent in 2005.  

The term Dutch Disease was coined to describe the decline of the manufacturing sector in the Netherlands after the discovery of natural gas in the 1960s.  

Russia has about $268 billion in reserves, the third highest after Japan and China. The country's reserves have grown 54 percent this year due to record high oil prices.  

The rouble has risen 4.3 percent to the dollar/euro basket this year.  

Greenspan said the creation of Russia's stabilization fund has helped the country "combat Dutch Disease" because the fund is "insulated from the political system."  

When the price of oil exceeds $27 per barrel, the extra revenues from oil and gas are channeled to a budget stabilization fund aimed at financing social welfare programs and helping during emergencies.  

Greenspan also discussed the prospects of the rouble as a reserve currency similar to the dollar and euro.  

The rouble is "still far from being a reserve currency. A reserve currency like the dollar and euro should be extremely liquid," he said.  

Greenspan added that for the rouble to be an "external currency" it is important that the "rule of law" prevails.  

"People would want to invest in a country where they feel their money would be safe. In the United States, we have worked on that for over 200 years. It doesn't happen overnight," Greenspan said.

title: Eyeing Georgia, Russia mulls money transfer ban
text:
MOSCOW, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Russia's parliament said on Monday it will debate a draft law that would allow officials to ban cross-border money transfers, a measure clearly directed at ex-Soviet neighbour Georgia.  

The decision followed the arrest last week by Georgia of four Russian army officers on spying charges, triggering the worst crisis in years between the ex-Soviet neighbours.  

The four officers were allowed to fly back to Russia on Monday after intervention by international mediators.  

"This was a provocation and the State Duma deputies must respond to it," Boris Gryzlov, speaker of the lower house of parliament, told reporters. "I think we will prepare and submit this draft law on Wednesday."  

Any measure that would make it harder for Georgian workers in Russia to send money home could be a huge blow for their country's economy.  

About one million Georgians work in Russia. They sent home $219 million in the first half of 2006, or 14.6 percent of gross domestic product, according to estimates by Georgia's central bank.  

Vladislav Reznik, head of the Duma's banking committee, said the draft law would give the government powers to limit or ban cross-border money transfers.  

"We believe the government must have this right but whether it uses it or not, the government can decide for itself," Reznik told Reuters.  

The Duma is controlled by the pro-government United Russia faction and normally rubber stamps legislation supported by President Vladimir Putin.  

Russia last changed its currency laws in July this year, lifting controls on capital currency movements in a move to make the rouble a convertible currency.  

CHASING OIL WEALTH  

Millions of workers from ex-Soviet states work in Russia, where windfall oil revenues have been driving a rise in incomes. Many do jobs Russians are not prepared to do, such as cleaning streets, repairing apartments and manning market stands.  

The Russian central bank estimates migrant workers from ex-Soviet states sent $3.2 billion to their home countries in 2005 and the amount is expected to grow further.  

Money transfers have also become a booming business and dozens of newcomers, including state-owned giant Sberbank and Russian Post as well as many smaller firms, compete with industry veterans like Western Union.  

Russian Post said on Monday it would temporarily freeze all money transfers to Georgia from Russia by mail. It cited unsatisfactory work by their Georgian counterparts. Tbilisi said any ban on money transfers would have little effect on Georgia's economy.  

"We can use the banks of other countries," said Nika Rurua, deputy head of the security and defence committee in the Georgian parliament. Moscow slapped a ban on imports of Georgian wines and bottled water in early 2006 while on Monday, Russia's transport ministry ordered air, rail, land and sea links to Georgia to be suspended. title: UPDATE 4-Russian rouble jumps after bad inflation number
text:
(Adds Putin's aide comment in para 5-6)  

MOSCOW, Sept 5 (Reuters) - Russia's consumer price index rose by a worse-than-expected 0.2 percent in August, data showed on Tuesday, leading the central bank to allow the rouble to rise as it seeks to curb persistent price pressures.  

The rouble traded at 29.68 to the central bank's dollar/euro currency basket -- made up of $0.6 and 0.4 euros -- up 0.4 percent from Monday's close. The rouble <RUBUTSTN=MCX> also reached its highest against the dollar since Dec. 1999.  

Analysts and traders said the rise in prices in August -- a month when they traditionally fall -- led the central bank to step back from the exchange rate level it had defended since mid-July.  

"Obviously, the bad inflation data pushed the central bank into doing this. There were no other reasons for the rouble to go up," said Ruslan Tongiyev, head of forex operations at Petrokommerts Bank in Moscow.  

President Vladimir Putin's aide Igor Shuvalov said the central bank's method of tying up money supply was not helping prices and acknowledged that annual inflation may overshoot the government's 9 percent target.  

"The rouble is firming so much, but inflation is not coming down -- everything testifies to the fact that with such strengthening (of the rouble) we will not meet the set parameters and inflation will be a little higher," Shuvalov told reporters.  

No comment was available from the central bank but Economy Minister German Gref stood by the government's annual inflation forecast for 2006 of 9.0 percent despite the August uptick.  

"We are sticking to our forecast, 0.2 percent is higher than we expected but it is not critical," Gref told reporters.  

The central bank intervenes to take out some of Russia's $600 million a day in oil and gas export revenues but, concerned by the runaway growth in the money supply that results, has let the rouble rise in several small steps this year.  

In allowing the rouble to appreciate, the central bank is attracting speculative bets on further gains, analysts say.  

"I do not think it is a good idea to let the rouble rise now. The central bank is using the tool it is familiar with, but this move is likely to provoke speculators into buying roubles," said Yevgeny Nadorshin, economist at Trust Bank.  

OPPOSITION TO STRONG ROUBLE  

The central bank last let the rouble rise on July 17, by 0.3 percent against the basket. The latest move follows record dollar purchases in August by the central bank, whose $259 billion hoard of gold and forex is the world's third largest.  

However, opposition to further rouble strengthening among Russian exporters is rising, especially among metal and mining firms whose margins are squeezed by a strong national currency, creating a policy dilemma the government has yet to solve.  

President Vladimir Putin told Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin last month to curb rouble appreciation because it hurts domestic industry.  

The rouble has now risen by 4.3 percent to the basket since the start of the year. It is up by 8 percent against the dollar and virtually unchanged against the euro.  

Russia's money supply, which economists see as the key factor behind high inflation, rose by 45 percent in year-on-year terms as of Aug. 1. Excess liquidity drives up retail prices as well as prices for real estate and stocks.  

Economists polled by Reuters had expected prices to rise by a median 0.1 percent in August, while the government and the central bank had predicted a modest fall in prices.  

The food component of the CPI basket fell by 0.5 percent because abundant fruit and vegetables became cheaper while prices for non-food items and services climbed by 0.8 percent.  

Analysts said petrol price hikes, a poor grain harvest and botched reforms to alcohol sales licences were behind the bad number. Prices rose by 7.1 percent in the year to date, closing in on the government's 2006 target.  

"It's very difficult to see them hitting 9 percent by the end of the year, it would be good if they get under 10 percent," said Yevgeni Gavrilenkov, chief economist at Troika Dialog.  

Gref said the cabinet would continue consultations with oil firms on capping retail gasoline prices, which, he said, were the culprit behind the bad number in August.  

"There is nowhere for them (gasoline prices) to grow further, we will appeal to our previous agreements," Gref said, referring to a moratorium on rising gasoline prices reached with oil firms last year. (Additional reporting by Artyom Danielyan, James Kilner and Christian Lowe)

title: UPDATE 2-Russia ready to raise rates, reserve requirements
text:
(Writes through with full news conference)  

MOSCOW, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Friday it was ready to raise interest rates and tighten banking reserve requirements to curb inflation, but was still confident of meeting its 2006 price and exchange rate targets.  

First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev also told reporters the central bank had submitted for parliamentary review its monetary policy guidelines for 2007 -- which foresee a reduction in inflation -- without significant changes.  

"We are sticking to our inflation target for this year -- the figure of 8.5 percent remains unchanged," Ulyukayev told a news conference.  

Inflation was 9.3 percent in the 12 months to July, but Ulyukayev forecast a fall of 0.1 percent in consumer prices in the month of August. The central bank's full-year inflation goal is below the government's own 9.0 percent forecast.  

He said the central bank was also keeping its 9.0 percent target for the rouble's real effective appreciation -- a measure of competitiveness which accounts for differences in inflation with Russia's trading partners.  

The twin policy targets, criticised by many economists as contradictory, have come under pressure this year as Russia, now the world's largest petroleum producer, harvests a massive windfall from near-record oil prices.  

The central bank regularly intervenes on the currency market to take out some of Russia's half a billion dollars a day in oil export revenues, seeking to prevent a sharp rise in the rouble which would hurt the competitiveness of domestic businesses.  

But the dollar-buying intervention floods the local money market with rouble liquidity and, with the banking system still unable to channel all that cash into investment, much of it is going into pumping up the prices of goods, services and assets.  

LESSER EVIL  

Next year's monetary policy guidelines, which see inflation at between 6.0 and 8.5 percent and allow for real effective rouble appreciation of zero to 10 percent, give the central bank more wiggle room on the exchange rate.  

"Growth in the nominal effective exchange rate is a lesser evil than high inflation," said Ulyukayev, adding the central bank considered fighting inflation its primary task.  

The rouble has risen by about four percent in nominal terms this year against a currency basket comprising $0.6 and 0.4 euros, an operational guide used by the central bank which irons out some of the volatility in the dollar-euro currency pair.  

Ulyukayev said there were no plans for now to alter the composition of the basket. "We are examining the theoretical possibility of changing the basket, but in general we are happy with the current composition," he told reporters.  

POLICY OPTIONS  

The central bank has come under fire from politicians -- most recently President Vladimir Putin -- for allowing the rouble to rise. That has forced it to experiment with other measures to contend with inflation.  

It has raised its short-term deposit rates three times this year to 2.0-2.5 percent, although they remain negative in real terms and have failed to put a floor under the money market.  

Also this week, the central bank raised the minimum reserve requirements on liabilities of banks towards non-resident banks, in a step aimed at curbing rapid growth in foreign borrowing by the banks and corporates.  

Analysts say that a wide current account surplus, external borrowing by the private sector, foreign direct investment and speculative inflows after Russia's recent abolition of capital controls are all putting upward pressure on the rouble.  

"We don't rule out making use of minimum reserve requirements, but we don't have any concrete plans," Ulyukayev said. "The same applies to deposit rates. We don't rule out raising them in the future."

title: ANALYSIS-Rouble to rise but market guessing how much
text:
MOSCOW, March 7 (Reuters) - The rouble is set to rise as Russian policy makers have made it clear they are ready to use the exchange rate to rein in inflation, but analysts remain divided over how much appreciation they will tolerate.  

The rouble <RUBUTSTN=MCX> has appreciated by 2.5 percent this year in nominal terms against the currency basket, comprised of dollars and euros, used by the central bank to guide its daily interventions on the currency market.  

Trading volumes have hit record levels, peaking on Feb. 8 amid market speculation that the authorities would allow the rouble to make a big move higher.  

But the central bank took out all dollar offers in that session, and expects to keep piling up foreign reserves -- up by 12 percent this year to $196 billion -- as it tries to stop the rouble from turning into an overvalued petro-currency.  

"The big question is whether this is just another trading opportunity on the back of the dollar-euro trade, or whether this is the start of the long awaited next step-up in the rouble," said Chris Weafer, chief strategist at Alfa-Bank.  

The central bank prints roubles to buy excess dollars flowing into Russia as a result of massive oil revenues. Its open market operations create a liquidity wave which is driving up prices for goods and assets like stocks and property.  

Prices in Russia grew by 10.9 percent in 2005. Big hikes in household utility charges and food prices mean that, just two months into the year, the consumer price index has risen by almost half the government's full-year target of 8.5 percent.  

President Vladimir Putin berated ministers on Monday for letting prices get out of control and a row has broken out between the government and the central bank over what remedial action to take.  

A senior Economy Ministry official told Reuters last week that the only way to curb prices would be to allow the rouble to rise in nominal terms. The central bank responded by hiking its deposit rates, although analysts said that would achieve little.  

"The trend is clearly towards more strengthening," said Zsolt Papp, emerging markets economist at ABN Amro, suggesting the rouble could test the level of 27 to the dollar towards the end of the year. It traded at around 28 on Tuesday.  

NEUTRAL EXPECTATIONS  

Economists polled by Reuters this month saw the rouble at 28.05 to the dollar by the end of March, 28.75 by mid-year and 27.75 by year's end.  

Central bankers say they have succeeded in creating neutral expectations on the exchange rate, as a result keeping market interest rates high enough to have a dampening effect on prices.  

The central bank's currency basket, which is 'reset' every morning and operates from 10 a.m. (0700 GMT) to 5 p.m. (1400 GMT), has succeeded in reducing market volatility, but has not removed the need for sustained intervention.  

The central bank estimates that with oil prices at around $60 per barrel, it must buy $7 billion a month, but analysts say the bank's presence in the market may decrease as it tries to prepare markets for convertibility of the rouble.  

"As the central bank is moving towards full convertibility of the rouble and trying to prepare markets for that, I think it will intervene less and less," said Papp.  

CONVERTIBILITY  

Russia wants to lift capital controls, which include deposit requirements of up to 20 percent on capital account transactions, later this year.  

The move will pave the way for full rouble convertibility but at the same time may expose Russia to the risk of speculative capital inflows.  

"It is a positive signal and should support the rouble going forward. The fact that money will be able to circulate more freely should also boost investment," said Elisabeth Gruie, emerging markets strategist at BNP Paribas in London.  

Analysts also said that if the central bank succeeds in reining in inflation it might be instructed to reverse the rising trend around mid-year to protect domestic producers.  

"I would not be surprised if the central bank is instructed by policy makers to reverse the current trend of rouble appreciation," Papp said. (Additional reporting by Sujata Rao in London)

 "The central bank might take part in the session soon but I do not think it will start selling dollars to stop it from rising," said Artyom Roshchin at Alba Alliance.  

 "The rouble is weakening in line with the euro-dollar market, we just have a mirror image of this trend here. There is no conspiracy behind it."  

 The dollar was buoyed on international markets by its widening yield advantage against overseas markets, repatriation of funds by U.S. companies to take advantage of a tax break and continuing urban riots in France.  

 The rouble has shed over 3 percent in value against the dollar so far this year, but has rallied by 11 percent against the ailing euro.  

 That has made it easier for the central bank to mitigate the inflationary impact of high prices for oil while keeping the rouble's exchange rate against the greenback -- closely watched by ordinary Russians -- relatively stable.

title: UPDATE 2-Putin picks Ignatyev for second Russia c.bank term
text:
(Updates with lawmaker, paras 5-6, adds background)  

MOSCOW, Nov 3 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin has nominated Sergei Ignatyev for a second four-year term as chairman of the Bank of Russia, the presidential press service said on Thursday.  

Ignatyev, a low-profile technocrat who has also held senior finance ministry posts, has steered the central bank through an oil-fuelled boom during which inflation has gradually fallen but stayed stubbornly above single-digit rates.  

He is widely seen as a steadying hand and a welcome contrast to his predecessor Viktor Gerashchenko, who headed the bank for two turbulent spells before his final dismissal in 2002.  

"It is clear from this appointment that Ignatyev has successfully carried out what the Kremlin wanted him to do. Monetary policy under Ignatyev was fairly balanced," said Peter Westin, chief economist at MDM Bank in Moscow.  

A lawmaker said Ignatyev's candidacy should quickly win parliamentary confirmation, although some members of the central bank's board may be replaced in spring 2006.  

"Ignatyev is an exceptionally professional central bank chairman. Any banking system would be proud of him," Vladislav Reznik, head of the State Duma's finance committee, was quoted by Prime-Tass news agency as saying.  

Analysts said, however, that Ignatyev has had to work within political constraints that have complicated his task of defending price stability.  

"We haven't seen him being somebody who can stand up and protect the central bank's opinion against political influence," said Alexei Moisseev, head of fixed income research at Renaissance Capital.  

Soon after winning re-election last year, Putin instructed Ignatyev to keep the rouble exchange rate low to protect Russia's economic competitiveness. The central bank obliged, intervening on forex markets, and inflation rose as a result.  

The central bank eventually yielded to speculators betting on a stronger rouble, but inflation has since failed to respond and the authorities will struggle this year to improve on the final 2004 figure of 11.7 percent.  

"The central bank has to say, 'Inflation is a problem and we're going to fight it and we don't care if that hurts this or that producer ... We are independent,'" said Moisseev.  

STABILITY RESTORED  

Under Ignatyev's stewardship, Russia recovered from the aftermath of its 1998 devaluation and default on $40 billion in domestic debts.  

The central bank has accumulated the largest foreign currency reserves of any country outside Asia, now a record $164 billion, as oil export revenues flood into the country.  

While its dollar-buying intervention has prevented the rouble <RUB=> from turning into an overvalued petro-currency, there have been economic side-effects.  

Money supply is expanding at an annual rate of over 40 percent. Interest rates are far below inflation, hurting savers and sending mixed signals to investors.  

And, in real terms, Russia has lost the competitive edge it won in the 1998 crash, putting pressure on Ignatyev to focus more on beating inflation and less on the exchange rate.  

"The problem now is how to deal with the dual target -- inflation and rouble exchange rate. Towards the end of this year or at the beginning of next year we should see the central bank leaning towards targeting inflation," said Westin.  

The central bank has won praise for strengthening Russia's banking system, introducing a deposit insurance scheme and killing off non-viable "pocket" banks.  

But the banking system remains vulnerable to shocks, as a run on secondary lenders in summer 2004 showed. And Russia still has over 1,200 banks, a number that must fall for the financial sector to become a a motor of economic development.  

"Ignatyev should also show initiative and speed up the banking sector reform," said Westin. (Additional reporting by Gleb Bryanski and Meg Clothier)

title: POLL-Slower growth, faster inflation to trouble Russia
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Russia's goals for economic growth and inflation this year and next remain excessively optimistic, a Reuters poll of 15 economists showed on Thursday, while its fiscal position is top-notch.  

The future of the Russian currency is harder to call. Analysts' forecasts diverge sharply, with most seeing the rouble rising against the dollar while a significant minority expect it to weaken. The survey predicts Russia will have managed to nail consumer price growth flat in August, a glimmer of improvement for a data series that has disappointed for most of the year.  

Economists forecast gross domestic product growth slipping to a median 5.7 percent this year and 5.3 percent next year after two years of expansion above 7 percent. The 2005 forecast is markedly weaker than last month's 6.0 percent.  

Full-year inflation is seen at 12 percent in 2005 and 10 percent in 2006, well above government targets. For a full table of poll results, please click on [ID:nL30724029].  

Analysts did, however, say there was a marked improvement in the business climate, after the pursuit of oil firm YUKOS and other companies for back tax bills proved such a menace to investors' faith in Russia.  

"It's impossible to say economic policy has acquired a liberal bias," said Anton Stroutchenevski at Troika Dialog. "But it has to be acknowledged that there are fewer of the aggressive attacks that have been disturbing the business community."  

SHOULDER THE BURDEN  

Although retail sales growth has been strong this year, underpinned by Russians' rising salaries, the industrial sector is flagging -- full year growth is expected to be 4.8 percent this year after 7.3 percent last year.  

And Russia's key natural resources sector is growing at a fraction of the pace of manufacturing.  

"Real appreciation of the rouble and a high tax burden on the oil sector remain some of the main obstacles to growth in industrial production," Raiffeisenbank noted.  

Only three economists thought Russia could drag 2005 inflation below last year's 11.7 percent -- the government is still officially hoping for 11 percent. Nor did anybody set any store by a target of 8.5 percent that is in place for next year.  

"Summer deflation, which the central bank has been hoping for, will barely be achieved this year, largely because of a new upturn in petrol prices and the continuing effect of earlier tariff price rises," said Uralsib's Vladimir Tikhomirov.  

As for the rouble, which at the moment takes its cue from swings in the euro/dollar rate globally, the poll shows it at a median 28.20 to the dollar at the close of 2005, firming to 27.25 at the end of 2006.  

However, by then the predictions range from 25 to 29.1 to the dollar, evidence of split views firstly about the direction Russian central bank policy is likely to take and secondly about investor sentiment towards the U.S currency longer term.  

Massive oil receipts and hard-currency purchases during market interventions should nudge Russia's gold and foreign exchange reserves well past the $200 billion mark by the end of next year and up to $175 billion this year.  

And, despite a move to ease fiscal policy and spend a chunk of oil money in the run-up to presidential elections in 2008, analysts expect healthy budget surpluses this year and next.  

(Additional reporting by Maria Kiselyova)
