title: UPDATE 2-Russian c.bank begins rouble/euro  operations
text:
(Updates with background, analysts)   

MOSCOW, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Friday it had begun intervention operations on the rouble/euro market as it continues a drive to wean the market off its fixation with the dollar.   

The move, signalled well in advance, comes as the Bank of Russia seeks to broaden the local forex market to better reflect burgeoning trade flows with Europe and prepare for the removal of capital controls by 2007.   

But it does not herald an immediate increase in the share of euros in Russia's big foreign exchange reserves, which at nearly $150 billion are the largest of any country outside Asia, a top central banker said.   

There is "absolutely no connection", central bank Deputy Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko told Reuters.   

Korishchenko added that if the central bank wanted to buy euros, it could now do so by selling roubles, whereas previously it had to buy and then sell dollars as an intermediary currency.   

The central bank runs a 'dirty' rouble float, typically buying dollars to stem upward pressures on the rouble arising from high prices for oil, Russia's main export, and defend the competitiveness of domestic industry.   

The rouble has fallen by around 2 percent against the resurgent dollar year-to-date, but is up by 8 percent against the euro.   

VOLUMES UP   

The Bank of Russia said in a statement it had begun rouble/euro operations on Aug. 25, in support of the currency basket comprising 0.35 euros and $0.65 it uses to guide its day-to-day exchange rate policy.   

Trade in euros for 'tomorrow' delivery jumped to 23 million euros on Thursday and 18 million euros on Friday, well above typical volumes, figures from the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) showed.   

But, the central bank added, the dollar would remain the core of the local forex market, "where the situation determines the official exchange rate of the rouble and the scale of possible intervention operations by the Bank of Russia."   

Russia's economy remains heavily dollarised, with the greenback a safe haven for many Russians who suffered painful losses in the hyperinflation and financial crashes of the 1990s.   

Euros account for 30-35 percent of central bank reserves, and despite Korishchenko's assurances to the contrary, analysts expect that share to rise gradually over time.   

"This is the experience of the countries that do have in place these currency basket regimes," said Yaroslav Lissovolik, an economist at United Financial Group in Moscow.   

Analysts agree that broadening the market reduces pressure on the central bank to intervene in defence of a target exchange rate.   

They also say that a well diversified market should make it easier for policymakers to fight inflation running at around 13 percent -- above the government's year-end target of 11 percent.   

"It has taken very long to get here but it's very welcome," said Lars Christensen, economist at Danske Bank in Copenhagen. "Now we need to see an appreciation of the rouble, which is a politically hard process to handle ... to reduce inflation."   

The central bank introduced its operational currency basket early this year and has increased the share of euros in small steps. Analysts expect the euro to end up with a weighting of at least half of the basket.   

The operational basket should not be confused with the trade-weighted basket used to calculate the real effective exchange rate, a measure used by the central bank alongside inflation to guide its policy.

title: FX  basket allows  Russia  cbank to cut  intervention
text:
MOSCOW, June 14 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank reduced its foreign exchange interventions by nearly a third month-on-month in May, it said on Tuesday, aided by its dual currency basket.  

Russia launched the basket earlier this year to guide the rouble day-to-day, providing the market with a good idea of where the central bank wants the currency to trade at any given euro/dollar rate <EUR=>.  

"The Bank of Russia's use of a dual currency basket ... has contributed to a lowering in the volume of Bank of Russia interventions on the domestic currency market by 30 percent compared to the previous month to $4.27 billion," it said in a monthly report.  

The basket is currently made up of $0.7 and 0.3 euros.  

It also confirmed that the main factor driving the Russian currency last month had been "the strengthening of the U.S. dollar on world currency markets".  

The rouble has tracked moves on global markets doggedly so far this year, meaning that Monday's nine-month low for the single currency against the dollar sent the Russian currency <RUBUTSTN=MCX> to its weakest since mid-November on Tuesday.  

Monday was a market holiday in Russia.  

When the central bank intervenes to buy dollars it pumps roubles into the economy, which has played a role in frustrating Russia's attempts to cut inflation, which a Reuters poll sees dipping to 11.5 percent this year from 2004's 11.7 percent.  

Although printing fewer roubles may have a positive impact on inflation, the report said banking sector liquidity declined in May.  

"The main factor ... was that the rate funds were accumulated on budget accounts in the Bank of Russia, including the stabilisation fund, outstripped the volume of intervention by the Bank of Russia on the domestic market," it said.  

Overnight rates on the interbank market <RUBOND=>, which were hovering around 1-2 percent at the start of this year, are now around 5 percent.  

That is still well below levels of over 20 percent that short-term rates hit last summer, when the closure of two small banks triggered a run on deposits.

title: UPDATE 2- Russia  could start rouble/euro  intervention  -cbank
text:
(Adds analysts' comments, edits)  

MOSCOW, May 12 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank said on Thursday it may begin intervening on the rouble/euro market later this year as the euro becomes increasingly important to the country's economy and trade.  

Rouble/euro trade <EURRUBON=MCX> accounts for as little as 1 percent of forex volumes on Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) with dollar/rouble dominant.  

But the Bank of Russia is raising the euro's profile -- over half of Russia's foreign trade is with Europe -- increasing the single currency's share in the basket it uses to manage the rouble rate day-to-day.  

The central bank intervenes regularly on the rouble/dollar market -- as dealers said it did on Thursday -- to smooth out exchange rate fluctuations. But it plans to scale back its presence in the run-up to lifting capital controls in 2007.  

"In some ways this will be a substitute for rouble/dollar intervention," Deputy Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko told a panel discussion. He said a decision was in the offing but there was no precise timeframe as yet.  

SECOND FIDDLE  

There are plans to support euro liquidity, with a new rouble/euro contract for "tomorrow" settlement planned for early June, as well as a longer trading session of at least 3-1/2 hours, said MICEX General Director Alexander Potyomkin.  

However, as long as Russia's commodity exports continue to be priced in dollars, the euro will play second fiddle.  

"Not only are most of the current account flows dollarised, but also the man on the street thinks in dollars which is why I don't think we'll see euro unseat the economic importance of the dollar," said Jens Nystedt, a Deutsche Bank economist in London.  

"I still see the rouble/euro as a derivative of the main rouble/U.S. dollar cross but they are heading in the right direction," he added, saying the share of euro trade might hit 20 percent in five or six years.  

DUAL BASKET  

Russia uses a dual currency basket to guide the rouble's nominal exchange rate intraday. This is different from the basket with which it measures its real effective exchange rate.  

At the moment the proportions are 0.2 euros and $0.8, but Korishchenko reiterated that the bank will change this to 0.3 euros soon. Analysts expect the amount of euros and dollars to become roughly even over time.  

The key result of the dual currency basket has been for the rouble/dollar to shoulder more of the volatility stemming from moves on global currency markets.  

"Last year the central bank would try to maintain the rouble/dollar rate unchanged for a week or two at a time. Then if there was clearly a new trend in the euro/dollar it would change its (dollar) bid by 10 kopecks," said Troika Dialog chief economist Yevgeny Gavrilenkov.  

"Now it does this on an everyday basis. It has become more adaptable to global fluctuations."  

If the central bank did not dip in and out of the market, Russia's booming oil export receipts would drive the rouble higher, killing domestic producers' competitiveness.  

Despite intervention and the funnelling of windfall oil revenues into a budget stabilisation fund, the rouble is still appreciating fast -- by 6.6 percent in real, trade-weighted terms in the first four months of this year.  

"We would like to try to reduce the level of our involvement in the market, which is hard at the moment, but that is the direction we are trying to move in," Korishchenko added.  

Potyomkin also said the share of euros in Russia's gold and foreign reserves was around 25-30 percent, in line with recent comments by officials.  

Any suggestion Russia is preparing to raise the euro share can boost the single currency on global markets. Russia's reserves, the largest outside Asia, have hit a new record high of $144.7 billion, weekly data showed on Thursday.

title: Russia rouble hits month-highs, cbank cuts dlr bid.
text:
MOSCOW, Feb 18 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble hit month-highs against the dollar on Friday, forcing the central bank to step in and support the U.S. currency at 27.93 roubles, dealers said.    

 The Russian currency was riding high on its two favourite bull signals - gloomy inflation data at home and a lacklustre dollar abroad.    

 "It's hard to say exactly why the bank lowered its dollar bid - but its either high inflation or a firm euro (against the dollar)," one dealer said.    

 By 1110 GMT roubles for "tomorrow" delivery  were up 0.2 percent at 27.9405, having been fixed at 27.9998 the previous session. They peaked at 27.9200.    

 The central bank had bought dollars at 28.00 roubles the previous session, dealers said.    

 On global markets the dollar hovered near a recent two-week low against the euro, with investors torn between strong U.S. economic data and worries about long-term damage to the dollar from the U.S. current account deficit.    

 Late on Thursday Russian presidential advisor Andrei Illarionov told Reuters consumer price growth in the first two weeks of February was 0.7 percent, after 2.6 percent in the whole of January.    

 This could mean 4 percent price growth in the first two months of the year was not out of the question, making the government's target of 8.5 percent for 2005 look "interesting", he said.    

 In Russia, a country where a tighter monetary policy means a stronger currency, analysts say the best way to combat stubborn inflation would be a stronger rouble.    

 "Anticipation that the central bank will let the rouble appreciate faster as a response to fast CPI is growing," Vneshtorgbank head of treasury research, Nikolai Kascheev, said in a note.    

 Standard & Poor's, the last of the Big Three ratings agencies to award Russia investment grade status, has also added its voice to calls to for rouble appreciation, saying it would combat Russia's case of "Dutch disease".    

 Heavy intervention in the forex market was unsustainable, it said, and a stronger currency would force domestic industry to reform by undermining the competitive advantage an undervalued rouble had given them.

title: UPDATE 1-IMF urges Russian reforms to restore growth.
text:
WASHINGTON, Feb 16 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund on Wednesday said investors' doubts about Russia's commitment to market-orientated reforms and a perception of increased state intervention had slowed investment growth.   

In a statement issued at the end of annual economic talks in Moscow, the IMF said the drop in investment growth and lower oil export volumes had slowed Russian growth since mid-2004, despite high oil prices.   

"In the mission's view, boldly launching long-delayed structural reforms - not least administrative and civil service reforms - and ensuring the tax administration and other state agencies act in a transparent and even-handed manner are crucial for reassuring investors and restoring growth momentum," the IMF said.   

It also urged Russia not to spend more of its oil revenue windfall, which had added to inflation.   

The IMF said planned increases in pension benefits and other expenditures of more than 0.75 percent of GDP will add to budget pressures.   

Therefore it was becoming "a matter of urgency" to resist spending more oil revenue profits, while no further amendments to the 2005 budget should be considered, the fund added.   

"In line with this, the floor on the amount of resources in the (oil) stabilization fund that cannot be spent should be lifted to facilitate saving in full the oil windfall, except for that part that is allocated to the prepayment of external debt," the IMF said.   

Russia should also increase exchange rate flexibility, the fund said.   

It said unless Russia's central bank was prepared to reduce foreign exchange interventions and allow faster ruble appreciation if inflation deviates from the target, inflation was unlikely to fall in 2005.   

"The trade-off between reducing inflation and resisting ruble appreciation is likely to sharpen this year as the balance of payments is set to improve further, provided there is no repeat of the negative jolts to confidence that caused a sharp rise in capital flows in 2004," it said.

title: Russian rouble firms unimpeded by c.bank.
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 25 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble climbed for a third session against the dollar on Tuesday, recovering from near two-month lows hit last week, with no sign of the central bank intervening, dealers said.  

The previous session the rouble ran into some central bank dollar-buying intervention at 28.0050 roubles, halting its rise.  

"With no central bank there has been pressure on the dollar and it has sunk," one dealer said.  

The month-end is traditionally a bullish period for the Russian currency as exporters switch their hard currency earnings into roubles to pay taxes.  

By 1015 GMT roubles for "tomorrow" delivery had firmed 0.3 percent to 27.9425 to the dollar, having been fixed at 28.0157 the previous session.  

Dealers said the outlook would depend on how the dollar behaved against the euro on global markets and whether Russia's central bank decided to intervene.  

So far this year it has not stuck to any level for long - and has been seen both buying and selling dollars. It says it does not comment on the specifics of its intervention policy.

title: Russia  cbank  intervenes  as dollar breaks 28 rbls.
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 18 (Reuters) - The dollar strengthened to more than 28 roubles for the first time in a month on Tuesday but traders said the central bank stepped in at 28.1250 to halt any further decline by the Russian currency. Roubles slipped to a weighted average for tomorrow settlement of 28.1150 at 1120 GMT from 27.9668 the previous session.   

Dealers said the U.S. unit's strength against major international currencies had pulled it higher against the rouble, but its next step would depend on intervention.

title: Russian rouble slips to month-lows, no c.bank seen.
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 17 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble slipped on Monday to trade at its weakest against the dollar since early December, with dealers pinning the fall on short-covering and expectations the central bank could raise its dollar bid.  

Russia's central bank intervened on the local currency market on Thursday buying dollars at 27.8450 roubles, but traders said the bank was probably not intervening this session.  

"Dollar buying started this morning with major banks covering short positions. There are also rumours that the central bank could raise the level of its dollar bid," said Raiffeisenbank dealer Dmitry Akulov.  

By 1045 GMT roubles for "tomorrow" delivery were down 0.2 percent at 28.0075 to the dollar, having been fixed at 27.9469 the previous session. They hit their weakest in over a month at 28.0200 in relatively light trade.  

Akulov added that dollar sales for tax payments later in month could trigger a correction and the rouble might rise again.  

The Russian currency had been trading around four-year highs at the end of 2004 but fell sharply after the long holiday break, adjusting to a dollar rally on global markets at the start of January.  

Alfa Bank dealer Alexei Bukleyev said the central bank could appear on the market selling the U.S. currency if the rouble retreated as far as 28.05 to dollar.

title: Russia's gold/ forex  reserves hit new record high.
text:
MOSCOW, Dec 9 (Reuters) - Russia's gold and foreign exchange reserves jumped $4.5 billion in the week to Dec 3. to hit a new record high of $121.6 billion, data showed on Thursday.   

 High prices for Russia's chief export oil and dollar-buying intervention by the central bank to dampen rouble appreciation have driven reserves growth.   

 Russia's reserves, up by half since the start of this year, are the largest outside Asia. They now outstrip Russia's public foreign debt and already exceed Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin's latest year-end forecast of $120 billion.   

 Russia's fast-growing reserves have made foreign exchange markets sensitive to any hint it might increase the proportion of euros it holds - at the expense of the weak dollar.   

 On Wednesday, the head of the central bank said it was "thinking about" changing its reserves mix but said no decision had been taken yet.

title: Russia rouble at 4-year high vs dlr, cbank steps in.
text:
MOSCOW, Dec 6 (Reuters) - The rouble rose to new four-year highs against a globally weak dollar on Monday, prompting the Russian central bank to step into the foreign exchange market to buy dollars and check the Russian currency's climb.   

The rouble's peak came at 27.8250 to the dollar, its strongest since November 2000, before it slipped back by 1020 GMT to trade at 27.8650 - still firmer than its fixing at 27.9271 the previous session.   

Dealers said they saw the central bank (CBR), which intervenes periodically to stem rouble appreciation, buying dollars at around 27.8250 to 27.8300.   

With the greenback under pressure and Russia needing to combat inflation, analysts say the rouble's rise looks set to continue. It has already gained nearly 5 percent against the dollar in less than two months.   

"The central bank shows continued focus on the euro/dollar exchange rate," said Metallinvestbank dealer Sergei Romanchuk.   

The greenback fetched $1.3449 against the euro , having fallen to around $1.3460 on Friday in the wake of a disappointing U.S. payrolls report.   

"The downslide of the dollar goes on forever. Sporadic interventions by the CBR are probably the only ... unpredictable market factor," Vneshtorgbank said in a note.   

Dealers say it is always difficult to predict the central bank's moves - and the bank itself says it never comments on the specifics of its intervention policy.   

For much of this year, Russia kept the rouble artificially depressed to spur competitiveness, which economists warned would fuel inflation. The authorities say prices could rise as much as 11.5 percent this year, above an original 10 percent target.   

Consumer price data for November is due to be released at 1200 GMT. Analysts polled by Reuters predict price growth of 1.1 percent month-on-month, the same as the previous month and the fastest since January.

title: UPDATE 2-Russia takes steps to curb rouble demand.
text:
MOSCOW, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank acted on Friday to reduce upward pressure on the rouble , trading near four-year highs to the dollar, by cutting the amount of roubles exporters are required to purchase.  

Russia will lower the percentage of revenues exporters must switch from hard currency to roubles to 10 percent from 25 percent, Deputy Central Bank Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko said.  

The decision, which will mean exporters are committed to buying fewer roubles with their dollars, will come into force when published in the central bank's official bulletin, normally issued on Thursdays, Korishchenko told a financial conference.  

Exports topped $16 billion in both September and August, according to central bank data. The rouble has surged on receipts from booming oil exports.  

Analysts said the move was also aimed at trumpeting confidence that there was no danger of another rouble collapse like one in 1998 which destroyed Russians' savings.  

"It demonstrates that they do not see any problems with dollar supply and no risks for rouble weakness," said ING analyst Julia Tsepliaeva.  

Tsepliaeva estimated, however, that firms repatriate as much as 60 percent of their export earnings, suggesting the central bank move may be "psychological than practical".  

Roubles for "tomorrow" delivery last traded down on the previous session's fix at 28.3375 to the dollar on the MICEX exchange, giving up earlier near four-year highs, shadowing moves on international currency markets.  

The rouble has become highly sensitive to moves in the euro-dollar as sophisticated speculative money is playing a bigger role in the market.  

Moscow's currency exchange said it plans to create a new rouble/euro contract in early 2005 to make it easier to trade euros, lending more depth to Russia's dollar-driven foreign exchange market.  

KEEP COMPETING  

Russia must counteract upward pressure on the rouble if its fledgling non-energy sector is to stay competitive, as it aims to have a free-floating currency in 2007.  

At the moment the central bank dampens rouble appreciation by periodically buying dollars - $11 billion in October - at artificially high prices, but economists warn this exacerbates inflation, one of Russia's most enduring economic problems.  

On Thursday First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said if the bank did not intervene the rouble could surge to 20 to the dollar, which would damage the economy, so the bank would continue to play a major role in the market during 2005.  

Korishchenko said the rouble would become more volatile next year as the central bank completes a shift in its exchange rate policy from targeting the dollar to focusing on a basket of currencies.  

The central bank now uses a currency basket weighted at least 60 percent in euros and at least 30 percent in dollars to guide its exchange rate policy.  

"What we are seeing on the market will disappear, and the market will behave more flexibly," he said. "This will allow the central bank to intervene less."  

Russia also hopes that its plans to convert a budget stabilisation fund of surplus oil revenues into foreign currency would also reduce pressure on the rouble, analysts say.  

At the moment the fund - set to top 500 billion roubles ($17.5 billion) this year - is held in interest-bearing rouble accounts, but the government will move the cash into top-rated investments in dollars, euros and sterling in early 2005.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian rouble at highest since Jan 01 on weak dlr.
text:
MOSCOW, Nov 26 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble jumped 0.2 percent on Friday to hit its highest against the dollar since early January 2001, with no sign of the central bank intervening to stem its rise, dealers said.    

 This is third session where the rouble has scored sharp gains after the central bank, which runs a "dirty float" of the Russian currency, made it clear on Tuesday that it would not resist moves on global currency markets.    

 On Friday the dollar fell to a record low against the euro as traders seized on a report that China has pared its U.S. Treasury bond holdings.    

 "(The rise in the rouble) is connected to the rise in the euro against the dollar. Recently the central bank has reacted quickly to euro-dollar moves," one dealer said.    

 By 0810 GMT roubles for "tomorrow" delivery  had peaked at 28.2500 to the dollar on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange having been fixed at 28.3205 the previous session.    

 First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said on Thursday that the central bank would not withdraw entirely from the market for some time, however, as it needs to smooth out the rouble's moves to preserve Russia's economic competitiveness.    

 "In the end we mean to move to a regime with a free-floating national currency - to leave the market, not to acquire a mass of hard currency - but maybe we cannot do that, let us say at least not for the next year," Ulyukayev told a parliamentary committee.    

 Data on Thursday showed that the central bank's gold and foreign exchange reserves rose to a record $113.9 billion - equalling Russia's public foreign debt.    

 The central bank is taking out much of the country's petrodollar inflows with intervention, but analysts note that the need to do that may abate over time as Russia switches an oil-funded budget stabilisation fund into hard currencies.    

 At the moment, the fund - set to top 500 billion roubles ($17.5 billion) this year - is held in interest-bearing rouble accounts, but the government will move the cash into top-rated investments in dollars, euros and sterling in early 2005.    

 That, in turn, could reduce the pressure on the central bank to accumulate foreign exchange reserves and enable it to reduce its operations on the forex market as it focuses on debt reduction, said Rory MacFarquhar of Goldman Sachs in a note.    

 "Once the fund has been moved offshore, its purchases of currency will be more or less automatic, the central bank of Russia's discretionary interventions will be much lower and more balanced," MacFarquhar said.

title: Russia  rouble gropes for cbank  intervention  level.
text:
MOSCOW, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble retreated from Thursday's 7-month highs against the dollar on Friday, trading cautiously as dealers said they had tried and failed to discover where the central bank would next cap Russia's buoyant currency.   

A falling dollar on global markets has added to rouble appreciation pressure stemming from high prices for Russia's major export, oil, driving the rouble within sight of multi-year highs.   

"We tried to grope for the central bank's (dollar) bid, but it is not there yet," said Viktor Anisimov, an Aljba Alliance dealer.   

By 1230 GMT the rouble for "tomorrow" settlement was little changed in official trade at 28.5375 to the dollar, having been fixed at 28.5387 the previous session. On Thursday, it hit 28.5101, the highest since early April, which was when the central bank moved to a weaker rouble policy to help exporters.   

Dealers said that if the dollar wilted further against the euro next week, the rouble could challenge year-highs around 28.45. "A battle will start at 28.45, that's a level we won't go through quickly," Anisimov added.   

On Thursday, Central Bank Deputy Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko told Reuters that Russia could not keep the rouble stable if the dollar was falling on global markets, which dealers saw as bullish for the Russian currency.   

The central bank targets real rouble apprecation against a basket of currencies, giving the bank leeway to allow the rouble to rise against the dollar if the greenback weakens against other currencies.   

But analysts say appreciation against the dollar is proving unpopular. "We ... understand that there has been significant political lobbying on the part of the domestic manufacturing and mining sectors to keep the rouble nominally weak," Alexei Moisseev, a Renaissance Capital analyst, said in a note.

title: ANALYSIS-Russia  currency  policy seen helping euro one day.
text:
LONDON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Russia signalled on Thursday a greater role for the euro in its foreign exchange policy, lending support to the belief that Europe's single currency is gaining credibility and demand from world central banks.  

This spells out potentially greater support for the euro in the long term as monetary authorities, including Russia's central bank, buy euros to replace some of the dollars in their foreign exchange reserves.  

Analysts said it was not clear how soon or to what extent Russia would boost the proportion of euros in its coffers, after Deputy Central Bank Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko said the proportion of the euro in the current basket that helps guide the value of the rouble was bigger than many analysts expected.  

But many believed a continued rise in the euro part of the reserves was inevitable.  

"The fact that they are telling us that the currency basket will have a much higher proportion of the euro means that their reserves will have a higher proportion of the euro," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, chief currency strategist at UBS in London.  

"This is a likely scenario. And it is supportive of the euro."  

The proportion of euros in Russia's foreign exchange reserves of more than $100 billion is 25-30 percent, up from 10 percent two years ago, Korishchenko told Reuters in an interview.  

JOINING THE BANDWAGON  

Russia's reserve breakdown compares with data from the International Monetary Fund's annual report which shows that global central banks hold about two thirds of their foreign currency reserves in U.S. dollars and 19.7 percent in euros.  

In 1999, the euro's first year, the currency took up 13.5 percent of official foreign exchange reserves.   


Other central banks are also expected to beef up their euro holdings as
the dollar remains mired in a multi-year downtrend. On Thursday, the
dollar hit a record low at $1.3074 per euro  and a nine-year low versus
a basket of currencies       .
  

But little information is available about the extent of their plans for future euro purchases. And analysts said Russia's comments were also too difficult to interpret.  

At 60 plus percent, the euro's share in the basket used by the central bank to guide the value of the rouble is much bigger than the bank's euro reserves.  

But analysts said it was not clear if Russia would seek to bring the level of reserves up to match the currency basket, even though Korishchenko said this heavy weighting was derived from the high proportion of Russia's trade with countries linked in some way to the euro.  

At current rates, Russia would have to buy roughly $30 billion worth of euros in order to bring its euro portion of reserves up to 60 percent.  

But many analysts believed Russia's heavy debt servicing costs denominated in dollars were an argument to keep the euro reserves lower.  

"In terms of external debt structure, that is roughly 1/3 in euros and the rest in dollars, but they confused everyone by saying reserve composition would also reflect trade weightings, which would mean a higher proportion of euros," said Dwyfor Evans, strategist at Bank of America in London.  

"They haven't been particularly clear, in fact they've probably been deliberately ambiguous. They're not going to tell the market what they're going to do on reserves.  

"The only thing we can say is there is likely to be more euro buying from the central bank."  

Korishchenko's comments appeared to back this view, many analysts said. "Our decisions are based on several factors including foreign debt structure, the structure of our foreign trade and so on," the central banker said.  

PSYCHOLOGICAL WORK  

Another issue is currency intervention. Russia's central bank has been coming to the currency market recently to buy dollars and depress the appreciating rouble in order to protect its export competitiveness.  

Analysts said this was unlikely to change.  

But rhetoric such as Thursday's comments from Korishchenko was likely aimed at increasing the euro's role as a transaction currency in Russia which is struggling to make its economy less dollarised.  

"It's mainly psychological - they're making it more explicit that they're targeting the basket and maybe hope that people will start trading against the basket rather than just the dollar," said Giancarlo Perasso, head of emerging markets research at WestLB. "It's a buffer against dollar weakness."

title: Russian rouble slips, cbanker comments weigh.
text:
MOSCOW, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The Russian rouble softened against the dollar on Wednesday, retreating after a top central banker said the rouble would end the year flat-to-weaker if the euro/dollar rate stayed the same, dealers said.  

"Current trends in the nominal (rouble/dollar) rate strongly depend on the euro/dollar rate, and if that relationship remains unchanged then the exchange rate at the end of the year will be between 28.6 and 29 roubles to the dollar," First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev said.  

Effective rouble appreciation against a basket of currencies should be 6 percent or a little more this year, he added, well inside a government target of no more than 7 percent.  

"Ulyukayev of course gave hope to dollar bulls," said one dealer. "But he did not say where the exchange rate would be if the euro is at $1.20 or $1.35."  

By 1300 GMT roubles for 'tomorrow' delivery slipped to 28.6775 to the dollar in official trade, having been fixed at 28.6502 the previous session.  

The dollar was down on the day at around $1.2970 per euro, struggling above record lows hit earlier this week.  

However, dealers thought the rouble would perk up quickly.  

"The market will steady at current levels with export revenues arriving. Then it will seek out the central bank('s dollar support level)," said Zenit bank dealer Alexander Karpov.  

The central bank intervenes periodically to stop oil-driven forex exchange inflows driving the rouble sharply higher, which would undermine Russia's economic competitiveness.  

It last intervened with a dollar bid of 28.6450 roubles on Tuesday, but with the rouble weakening it was absent from the market this session, dealers said.  

The central bank has allowed the rouble to rise nearly 2 percent against the dollar in the last month in what it calls an adjustment to account for broad dollar weakness, but analysts say it is trying to dampen inflation.  

Ulyukayev said he saw inflation at 10.5 percent to 11 percent this year, above a now largely discredited government target of 10 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-Russian cbank seen on lower dlr bid at 28.6450 rbls.
text:
MOSCOW, Nov 9 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank was seen intervening with a lower dollar bid of 28.6450 roubles to the dollar, dealers said on Tuesday, down from 28.7650 seen last week.   

On Friday "tomorrow" roubles jumped to 6-1/2 month highs in official trade after there was no sign of the central bank intervening to cap their gains. Monday was a market holiday in Russia.   

"The central bank placed a (dollar) bid at 28.6450. Then the market stabilised," Aljba Alliance dealer Artyom Roshchin said.   

Since mid-October the central bank, which runs a heavily managed "dirty float" of the Russian currency, has periodically allowed the rouble to rise in what is seen as a bid to tackle inflation and adjust to a weaker dollar on global markets.   

By 1030 GMT, roubles for "tomorrow" delivery were trading at 28.6675, below the bank's dollar bid and little changed from Friday's official fix of 28.6680.   

The central bank has said it does not comment on the specifics of its intervention policy.

title: Emerging  FX -Central European  currencies  await US vote.
text:
LONDON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Central European currencies held their breath on Tuesday with few domestic factors available to offset the uncertainty gripping global markets over U.S. presidential elections.  

A repeat of the drawn-out courtroom wranglings for the White House between Republicans and Democrats of four years ago would leave the United States without a decisive leader and could weaken the dollar and unsettle global markets, analysts and traders said.  

"It was pretty unseemly then and for it to happen twice in four years to the world super-power would be the worst result possible (for the dollar)," a London-based rand trader said.  

If the dollar lost ground against the euro it would also knock back many of the central European currencies which are traded mainly against the single currency.  

At 1340 GMT the Polish zloty traded slightly stronger against the euro at week highs of 4.3011 , while the Hungarian forint was steady at 245.55 per euro .  

Graham Stock, emerging markets strategist at JP Morgan, said the best result for central European currencies would be a clear victory. He also said they were not as vulnerable as southeast Asian currencies to volatility in currency markets that an indecisive U.S. election result would cause.  

"Central European currencies are slightly more immune because their performance is linked in with euro convergence and ERM-2. They are becoming more and more divorced from the emerging markets world," he said.  

Many European Union newcomers want to join the euro by the end of this decade and some have already entered the single currency ante-chamber, the ERM-2.  

FREE THE ROUBLE  

Russia's finance minister Alexei Kudrin told Reuters in an interview that the country's central bank should free up the rouble to curb inflationary pressures.  

Russia's central bank regularly intervenes by buying dollars, but in recent weeks has allowed the rouble to appreciate by around 1.5 percent against the greenback.  

However, Kudrin's comments had little impact in the closely-controlled rouble which softened slightly against the dollar to 28.7845 , compared to Monday's 28.7651 close. It remained close to a recent six-month high.  

Analysts said pressure on the central bank was likely to increase in the future.  

"In the past few weeks we have seen increasing number of comments from Russian officials talking about increasing the rouble's value against the dollar," Wike Groenenberg, emerging markets strategist at Citibank, said.  

"The actual rouble decisions are made by the central bank but Kudrin is definitely somebody they would talk to and listen to," she said.

title: UPDATE 1-Russia cbank reserves jump to new record high.
text:
MOSCOW, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Russia's gold and foreign exchange reserves jumped $3 billion in one week to hit a new all-time high on the back of record global oil prices, central bank figures showed on Thursday.  

Reserves rose to $98.3 billion on Oct. 8 from $95.3 billion on Oct. 1, the biggest one-week gain since February.  

"The trade surplus Russia is running is absolutely enormous. Oil prices are going off the scale," said Renaissance Capital economist Alexei Moisseev.  

Russia posted its highest monthly trade surplus in August in official data going back to 1998. Exports reached $16.2 billion - as much as Russia exported during an entire quarter while it climbed out of that year's economic slump.  

Russia's "rain-day" oil fund sterilises some of these inflows, helping combat inflationary pressure, Moisseev added. Russia's monetary base - although trending upwards - has not been rising at the same pace as foreign exchange reserves.  

But Russia's bulging current account puts upward pressure on the rouble which the central bank combats by buying up dollars.  

"Clearly under these oil prices pressure on the rouble has increased. During this period the central bank was active in the market buying dollars," said Aton brokerage chief economist Peter Westin.  

Analysts are warning that continued intervention threatens Russia's ability to control price growth, which they forecast will overshoot the government's 10 percent target this year.

title: UPDATE 1-Russia c.bank warns rouble speculators of losses.
text:
(repeats to make clear Korishchenko's title)   

MOSCOW, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank, defending its policy of stabilising the rouble, warned foreign exchange market players on Tuesday against trying to speculate on moves in the currency.   

"Any speculation, on either a rise or fall in the dollar or rouble ... may have highly painful consequences for those who take part in these operations," central bank Deputy Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko told Reuters.   

Korishchenko was speaking after the rouble rose to 3-month highs on Monday after dealers said the central bank retreated from a dollar intervention bid, fuelling market talk that the rouble may appreciate further.   

"It is one thing to study the broad economic picture, and to try and forecast the behaviour of the government and the central bank. It is another matter to try and open major positions on one side (of the market) or the other," he said.   

The central bank runs a heavily-managed "dirty" float of the rouble, intervening to buy up foreign exchange earnings on Russia's record oil exports, in a policy analysts say may lead it to miss its 10 percent inflation target this year.   

Korishchenko declined to comment on intervention policy after dealers said the central bank had re-entered the market on Tuesday with a dollar bid of 29.1150 roubles, down from its long-held earlier bid of 29.2150.

title: POLL-Russia to hit '04 growth target, overshoot on CPI.
text:
MOSCOW, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Russia will hit government growth targets this year but overshoot its inflation goal, spurred by high oil prices and soaring factory-gate costs, a Reuters survey of 16 economists showed on Monday.  

For a table of survey findings, click here.  

The rouble will finish the year marginally weaker at 29.34 to the dollar, with further softening seen next year, according to a mean average of forecasts.  

"We think that under the conditions of high oil prices, the central bank will continue the policy of capping the rouble's real exchange rate, whereas the task of lowering inflation will remain secondary," CSFB analyst Sergei Voloboev said.  

The twin - and contradictory - planks of Russia's monetary policy are to cap inflation at 10 percent and real effective rouble appreciation at 7 percent this year.  

The analysts polled saw inflation at 10.9 percent this year, with consumer prices set to grow 0.3 percent month-on-month in September.  

Latest monthly CPI figures are due on Tuesday.  

"There are price pressures across the board," said Julia Ovanessian, an economist at JP Morgan.  

With no parliamentary and presidential elections due anytime soon, the government may ease back on curbing service prices, she said. High oil costs and a lower-than-usual seasonal drop in fruit and vegetable prices also played a role.  

Producer price inflation would hit 24.7 percent this year, nearly double the 2003 figure, the poll showed.  

However, the government is likely to meet its growth target, with economists predicting 7 percent growth this year.  

Central bank gold and forex reserves will top $100 billion by the end of this year, climbing to nearly $120 billion by the end of 2005, the survey showed.  

Driving the increase is central bank dollar-buying intervention to curb rouble strength and keep Russia's economy competitive, as well as heavy borrowing by corporates looking to invest and refinance existing debt on better terms.  

"Central bank gold and forex reserves continue to grow at a fast pace because of high global oil and metal prices and because Russian banks and companies are acquiring loans in foreign currencies," Trust analyst Michael Workman said.

title: Russia  c.bank aims for less  forex intervention .
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank hopes new monetary instruments could allow it to scale down its frequent interventions on the foreign exchange market, a top bank official said on Thursday.  

The central bank frequently steps in to buy back dollars and cap the rouble, which it wants to keep at competitive levels. But pumping roubles into the economy causes inflationary pressures.  

"We are determined that central bank intervention on the currency market will be the exception rather than the rule in situations where there is a danger of some volatility," First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev told a parliamentary budget committee.  

Yields on government securities are below inflation, meaning Russian banks prefer to park excess money in dollars, prompting a flood of dollar-selling when banks need roubles to pay taxes at the end of each month.  

"We want banks to raise money more through our refinancing instruments," Ulyukayev added.  

A refusal by big banks to lend to small banks on the interbank market was one of the reasons behind a mini-banking crisis this summer.  

The bank wants to add corporate and regional debt to the range of instruments banks can use as collateral for short-term refinancing deals with the central bank. Banks can already exchange government debt when they need cash.  

The central bank has also revived its own OBR bonds after nearly three years, with an issue slated for Oct. 6. Earlier this week Ulyukayev said he expected the issue to yield a little over 6 percent to a July 15, 2005 put option.  

The central bank sees inflation in 2005 of 6.5 to 8.5 percent, down from this year's 10 percent target.

title: Russia sees Sept capital inflow, $12 bln 04 outflow.
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank on Thursday forecast the country's first capital inflow in many months for September but forecast net outflow of $12 billion for 2004, almost six times 2003's figure.  

"In September, we are expecting not an outflow but an inflow of capital of between $500 million and $1 billion and this tells us that a $12 billion figure, which we and the government have lately given, is realistic for 2004," Central Bank First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev told the parliamentary budget committee.  

Ulyukayev also revised the first half capital outflow forecast upwards to $7.5 billion from an earlier forecast for $5.5 billion but did not give any reason.  

Last year $2.3 billion of investment capital left Russia, the lowest since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.  

On Tuesday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zhukov said high prices for oil, the country's key export, were behind this year's increase in capital outflows which he forecast at between $10 billion and $15 billion.  

Russian oil companies tend to keep their earnings in dollars rather than repatriate them, meaning earnings from high oil prices do not appear as capital inflows.  

Zhukov also said expectations of rising U.S. interest rates and falling yields on different Russian instruments were prompting more capital to leave the country.  

Many economists blame a recent crisis of confidence in the banking sector and the troubles besetting oil major YUKOS (YUKO.RTS) for the rise in net capital outflows.  

Russia's central bank manages the exchange rate, using intervention to stop the rouble turning into a petro-currency.  

But the rouble liquidity resulting from the intervention forces down interest rates, with the U.S. Fed funds rate acting as a floor.

title: UPDATE 2-Russia to hit  forex , inflation targets-c.bank.
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The Russian central bank said on Monday it was on course to meet its twin policy targets for inflation and the rouble this year, despite market expectations that price growth will overshoot its 10 percent goal.  

The central bank also signalled it may cut its refinancing rate to 12 percent from 13 percent this year, although this would be a largely symbolic move because its management of the exchange rate blunts interest rates as a policy tool.  

First Deputy Chairman Alexei Ulyukayev forecast the rouble would end 2004 barely changed in nominal terms at between 29.22 and 29.50 roubles to the U.S. dollar . Monday's day-ahead rouble fix was 29.2164.  

Ulyukayev said the real effective exchange rate - which strips out differences in inflation - would rise by just below the central bank's target of 7 percent this year.  

He also forecast that monthly inflation would be zero in September, down from a rise of 0.4 percent in August which led some analysts to say the full-year target of 10 percent was no longer realistic.  

"We count on fulfilling these two fundamental tasks," Ulyukayev told a Brunswick UBS investment conference.  

INTERVENTION

Russia's monetary authorities run a dual policy regime, intervening with dollar buying to neutralise appreciation pressure stemming from record oil export earnings.  

At the same time, the central bank is trying to bring down inflation gradually - although that goal has come under threat from the rouble liquidity generated by its intervention policy.  

The authorities have taken some action to keep liquidity from flooding into the economy - including channelling oil windfall gains into a government stabilisation fund and issuing central bank bonds to soak up roubles.  

Dollar intervention and recent Eurobond issues by Russian corporates are boosting Russia's gold and foreign currency reserves, which Ulyukayev forecast would reach "a little more than" $100 billion by the end of this year.  

Reserves rose to a new all-time high of $92.6 billion on Sept. 17 from $90.0 billion on Sept. 10, the bank said last week. They were $77 billion at the start of the year.  

Commenting on interest rates, Ulyukayev said the central bank may cut its 13 percent refinancing rate by up to one point by the end of the year.  

"It is possible, although we promise nothing, that we will lower it before the end of the year. I think it will not be less than 12 percent," Ulyukayev said.  

Commercial banks do not usually borrow from the central bank at this rate but it is commonly used as a reference rate for overdue payments by banks and companies.  

Short-term interbank rates are now 3-5 percent - negative in real terms.  

The central bank last lowered the refinancing rate during a mini-banking crisis in June of this year, by one percent from 14 percent, in a bid to shore up confidence.

title: INTERVIEW-Higher rouble rates to hurt short-sellers - cbank.
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 6 (Reuters) - Russian money market rates will take their lead from abroad and hold above recent near-zero levels, making it harder to short-sell the rouble, central bank Deputy Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko said on Monday.  

Korishchenko told Reuters in an interview that, with short-term rates rising, it will not be easy for foreign exchange traders to turn a profit by borrowing roubles to fund long dollar positions.  

The central bank manages the rouble's float, limiting its control over short-term domestic interest rates. The money market is therefore driven by foreign interest rates and liquidity created by central bank intervention to buy dollars, which is aimed at neutralising Russia's massive inflows of the U.S. currency due to the high value of its energy exports.  

Overnight rates were near zero from last December through to March, but rose during a recent financial crisis which forced eight Russian banks to close, and have been underpinned by recent tightening by the U.S. Federal Reserve.  

"All this speculation as to whether the central bank will raise its (dollar) bid by 3-5 kopecks or not is only all right for those who have no liquidity problems," Korishchenko said.  

"I do not think it is a very sensible strategy to try to establish long dollar positions to the detriment of the goal of managing liquidity."  

Korishchenko's comments appeared aimed at sowing uncertainty to compensate for flaws in Russia's policy of targeting both inflation and the exchange rate which create ample opportunities for forex traders to turn a profit.  

The central bank, which has set a target for the real effective appreciation of the rouble this year of seven percent, has been regularly seen bidding on the dollar to weaken the rouble.  

And, with Russian inflation likely to top an official target of 10 percent this year, analysts say the central bank will have to push the rouble's nominal value down further if it is to hit its exchange rate goal.  

The rouble has fallen by 2.5 percent to the dollar since March and traded at 29.2140 on Monday.  

END-MONTH SPIKE  

Higher Russian money market rates have been underpinned by two U.S. interest rate hikes this year, with analysts expecting a third quarter-percentage point hike to 1.75 percent at the next Fed meeting on Sept. 21.  

The overnight rate ended last month as high as 8-10 percent, as liquidity was drained by companies paying their monthly tax bills, and has eased in September only to 4-6 percent.  

"We are entering a phase when, it appears, rates will be significantly different from zero," Korishchenko said.  

"Since the situation has changed with rates starting to rise abroad, careful steering of liquidity is now on the agenda ... It is a general macro-economic process, beyond the scope of Russia. We must recognise it and carefully follow the trend that it sets," he said.

title: UPDATE 2-Russia not ready for rouble free float-cbank paper.
text:
MOSCOW, Aug 17 (Reuters) - Russia will continue to target both the exchange rate and inflation next year because its economy is not ready for a free-floating rouble, according to a central bank strategy paper obtained by Reuters on Tuesday.  

In its draft monetary policy guidelines for 2005, the Bank of Russia targets real effective appreciation of the rouble of 8 percent, up from 7 percent this year. It sees inflation at 6.5-8.5 percent, down from 10 percent in 2004.  

That implies a broadly stable nominal exchange rate for the rouble , which is widely seen as undervalued but whose appreciation the central bank has curbed through intervention aimed at maintaining Russia's economic competitiveness.  

"Russia, with an open and insufficiently diversified economy highly dependent on the external financial and economic climate, is not yet able to move to a freely-floating rouble regime," the document said.  

The rouble has made good only a fraction of the losses it sustained in the 1998 financial collapse, enabling the economy to maintain rapid rates of growth led by a revival of oil and industrial production.  

But the twin-track policy of targeting both the exchange rate and inflation has risks, and the central bank said it would continue to prepare the ground for the rouble to float freely, enabling monetary policy to focus on taming inflation.  

Other planks of the strategy include tighter banking supervision in the wake of a mini-crisis which has forced eight lenders to close since May, and increased use of existing money market tools to fine-tune banking sector liquidity.  

SCENARIO PLANNING  

The strategy contains three scenarios: The first assumes an average price of $22.50 per barrel for Russia's Urals crude oil export blend, the second a price of $26 a barrel and the third a price of $31.  

Those scenarios do not tally, however, with the latest three-year outlook released on Monday by the Economy Ministry, which forecast oil at $28 a barrel and hiked its 2005 inflation outlook to 8-9 percent from 6.5-8.5 percent previously.  

Urals crude was was trading at $41.54 on Tuesday, as world prices hover near record highs. That spells a huge revenue windfall for Russia, the world's number two oil exporter, but also creates policy headaches as the authorities print money in their bid to stop the rouble turning into a petro-currency.  

A source said the central bank had not received the revised Economy Ministry forecast - to be used in finalising the 2005 budget draft - when it was working on its projections.  

Depending on the scenario used by the central bank, Russia's oil-fuelled balance of payments surplus is seen at $19.7-$40.6 billion in 2005, after a projected $39.1 billion this year.  

It also forecasts an increase in foreign exchange and gold reserves of $6-$24.9 billion, compared with a forecast $23 billion gain in 2004.  

Foreign exchange reserves have risen due to dollar-buying intervention by the central bank, which has in turn boosted the money supply. The central bank raised its forecast for money supply growth to 34-38 percent this year from 25 percent.  

It forecast growth of demand for money of 20-35 percent next year but, with a reassurance that this would not translate into faster inflation, said the rate of circulation of money should slow.  

Net capital outflows are forecast at $4-$6 billion next year, compared with $6.7 billion this year, the central bank said.  

Again, that appears out of date after the Economy Ministry recently raised its forecast of capital outflows this year to $8-$12 billion this year, driven largely by bank withdrawals by savers shaken by the recent banking turmoil.

title: DJ. UPDATE: Russian  Central Bank Intervenes  To Ease Crisis
text:
MOSCOW, Jul 07, 2004 (ODC via COMTEX) --  

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES  

Russia's Central Bank intervened Wednesday to ease Russia's worsening banking crisis, pumping liquidity into the system and arranging a bailout for the biggest bank to have run into trouble. Also, one of Russia's biggest private banks, Alfa Bank (ALFA.YY), moved to reassure the market that it has sufficient funds to meet its obligations after lines of depositors formed outside its branches. Alfa said it will meet all its obligations "in full and without delay." The Central Bank has halved the amount it requires retail and commercial banks to place on deposit with it in statutory reserve accounts, only three weeks after a smaller move failed to stop the spread of the country's most serious loss of confidence in its banks since 1998. The reserve requirement for all ruble deposits, and foreign-currency deposits held by corporate clients, will fall to 3.5% from 7% as of July 8. Cuts in the reserve requirement are one of the scarce tools effectively available to the Central Bank, since few of the banks in trouble hold enough government-quality collateral to pledge against Central Bank credit. The only other way for the Central Bank to inject liquidity would be to sell more rubles at its daily foreign-exchange auctions, but that would threaten to expand the money supply and increase inflation rip, analysts say. Separately, the Central Bank confirmed it is brokering a deal for state-owned Vneshtorgbank, Russia's second-largest lender, to acquire ZAO Guta Bank, Russia's 22nd biggest bank by assets. Guta Bank closed its doors and stopped making payments Tuesday. It's the largest victim to date of a wholesale loss of confidence by Russia's small and medium-sized banks in each other. A more modest cut of 2 percentage points on reserve requirements two weeks ago freed over $1 billion for the interbank market, according to Central Bank estimates. But that wasn't enough to solve the problems faced by banks such as Guta. Central Bank chairman Sergei Ignatyev said VTB's buy-out of Guta would be financed by a Central Bank loan secured against VTB's portfolio of government bonds. Guta's shareholders said later they have accepted the proposal, while VTB said it expects talks over the details to continue until the weekend. The "rescue" of Guta comes at the price of nationalizing a bank which was technically solvent, inasmuch as its assets exceeded its liabilities. As such, the incident has spurred painful memories of Russia's ruthlessly aggressive corporate wars of the 1990s - all the more since it coincides with an intensification of what many believe to be the politically motivated assault on oil company OAO Yukos (YUKO.RS). It isn't clear from either bank's statements, or Ignatyev's, whether the solution to Guta's problems is intended as a temporary or a permanent one. The panic in the banking sector has evoked alarming memories of Russia's 1998 financial crash, when some of its biggest banks collapsed. Compared with six years ago, Russia's economy is much healthier and experts say there is no underlying cause for alarm. Ignatyev said the problems currently facing the industry are "psychological." "There is no crisis," he told reporters. The trouble started in May when the Central Bank revoked the license of OOO Sodbusinessbank for alleged money-laundering. Another smaller bank, CreditTrust, went into voluntary liquidation three weeks later after a run by depositors. Rumors then surfaced of a "blacklist" of other banks facing closure, leading to a crisis of confidence throughout the system. Interest rates surged on the interbank market, as banks effectively stopped lending to each other. Ignatyev said there was no blacklist, and that the country's biggest privately owned banks - Alfa Bank, MDM Bank and Rosbank - had no problems. The issue has so far not affected the country's larger banks, especially VTB and state-owned OAO Sberbank (SBER.RS). Ignatyev also said that a Russian commercial bank, which he didn't name, had identified itself as a possible buyer for AKB Dialog-Optim, a smaller bank that is also experiencing liquidity problems. Dialog-Optim declined to comment Wednesday but its sole shareholder, Alexander Polyakov, told journalists last Friday that he didn't want to sell.  

-By Geoffrey T. Smith, Dow Jones Newswires (+7 095) 974 8055; geoffrey.smith@dowjones.com

title: ANALYSIS-Momentum building for G7 expansion.
text:
LONDON, June 17 (Reuters) - Momentum seems to be building at last for the Group of Seven economic powers - the closest the global economy has to a governing council - to be expanded.  

Although economic experts and commentators have for years called for a reform of the Group's membership to better reflect shifts in world economic geography and power over the past decade, G7 members are now acknowledging the need for change.  

The issue of expanding the informal club, first started almost 30 years ago, was a key topic at last week's annual summit of the Group of Eight (G7 plus Russia).  

"It's about time there was some movement on this issue and we think it rather urgent now," said Jim O'Neill, Chief Global Economist at Goldman Sachs. "There are just two many pressing world economic issues that cannot be adequately addressed or resolved by such a narrow western dominated grouping."  

G7 has its roots in the mid-1970s, when economic crises resulting from the breakdown of the post-war Bretton Woods currency system and soaring oil prices led to regular gatherings of political and financial leaders from the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada.  

Genuinely representing the biggest economic powers back then, it rocked financial markets in the 1980s by sanctioning several successful bouts of coordinated central bank intervention to control volatile currency markets. Russia was added to the annual summits in the 1990s to make it G8, but the finance teams which focus on the pressing economic issues remain just the G7 and meet four times a year.  

On many measures, G7 is now a lopsided world grouping.  

Measuring 2003 economic output by adjusting for currency's purchasing power puts the top seven powers more along of the lines of the U.S., China, the European Union, India, Russia Brazil and Japan. Last week, German Chancellor Gerhard Schroeder confirmed Brazil, China and India had been mentioned as candidates for G7/G8. And Brazil's Foreign Minister Celso Amorim claimed France supported inviting the three to the table too.  

Canadian Prime Minister Paul Martin and Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berluconi, leaders of two countries who could have most to lose from a rebalancing of the Group to reflect global economic weight, talked openly of expanding the group.  

And only last month, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Snow said China was likely to be invited to the next meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bankers in Washington in October.  

REFORM TO WHAT?  

Goldman's O'Neill and its Vice Chairman Robert Hormats, a U.S. G7 Deputy for the first eight G7 meetings, jointly penned an paper this month suggesting a number of expanded formats.  

O'Neill said the first and simplest step would be to add China. But he said a longer term proposal was for the creation of what Goldman called "F8" - this would be the U.S., Japan, China, Britain, Canada and three pan-European representatives for the euro zone.  

The European Central Bank chief, chairman of the euro group and European Monetary Commissioner already attend G7 meetings but not as full members. Germany, France and Italy retain the top seats at the table.  

"Getting the Europeans to consolidate representation may be a harder job than adding China," O'Neill said.  

But a suggestion that is gaining support from several quarters is elevating the role and scope of the wide and inclusive G20 grouping, which currently meets once at year at finance ministry level, and convening a summit of the group too.  

Canada advocates a bigger role for the G20 and premier Martin held out the possibility of a summit next year.  

"Canada's idea is gaining a lot of support. Is it for today? No. Could it be done at the beginning of next year? I think so. The possibility is improving," Martin said  

In a paper for Washington-based think-tank The Brookings Institution, former World Bank Vice President Johannes Linn said the G20 bloc, which includes developing giants such as China, India, Russia and Brazil as well as the G7, was the only appropriate bloc to represent a global economic council.  

"In a world where the G7/G8 economies still appear so dominant, it may be difficult to grasp the degree to which the global economy is today already multipolar," wrote Linn and co-author Colin Bradford, a former chief economist at the United States Agency for International Development (USAID).  

The G20 as a whole represents two thirds of the world's population, 90 percent of the world's gross national product and accounts for 80 percent of world trade.  

G20, chaired by Germany this year, consists of the G7, including European Union representatives, and Australia - alongside China, India, South Korea, Indonesia, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Russia, Turkey, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. Heads of the IMF and World Bank also take part.  

With China taking up the presidency of the group next year, it may well be the ideal opportunity to make the switch.  

Set up in Berlin in 1999 to deal with flawed market and institutional mechanisms that led to the Asian financial turmoil of 1997 and 1998, the G20's remit has widened since.  

O'Neill at Goldman said convening G20 summits on single issues would be a way forward and with its membership is ideal, for example, to restart the stalled Doha trade round next year. There is no reason why the G7 or F8 could not continue to meet more regularly around this event, he said.  

Others feel G7 and G8 may just have to wither away.  

"G7 is a relic of an old order that no longer exists," said Avinash Persaud, investment director at GAM London. "It can try to prolong its life by reforming, but ultimately it will be abolished in its current form."

title: ANALYSIS-Euro gains firmer footing in  FX  reserves contest.
text:
LONDON, April 28 (Reuters) - The euro is gaining ground as a credible rival to the dollar and moves by emerging market central banks to diversify their currency reserves are likely to give the single currency long-term support.  

Central banks around the world have slowly been buying euros since its birth in 1999 to diversify dollar-dominated currency reserves, minimise risks and enhance returns.  

Now Russia, which keeps a tight grip on the rouble, is planning to replace dollar-based monitoring of its currency with a dollar/euro basket, which could entail buying euros to curb rouble strength.  

China's FX chief said last week the country is diversifying its vast reserves out of dollars to include more European and Asian bonds. Libya also said it planned to change the peg for its dinar to give the euro a bigger weighting.  

"Diversification has been going on and it has played a big part in the euro's rally, when a growth gap between the United States and the euro zone is so wide. Given the size of global currency reserves, even a 10 percent rise in a euro weighting means massive euro buying," said Jim McCormick, head of FX research at Lehman Brothers.  

"Reserve management comes down to liquidity and trade flows. For return and confidence reasons the euro's share can go up to a 50-50 status with the dollar over the very long term."  

The euro hit a record high of $1.2927 in February. Since then, it has fallen 10 cents as financial market focus shifted to strength in the U.S. economy and expectations of higher interest rates. It stood at $1.19 on Wednesday.  

Data from the International Monetary Fund showed the euro's share in official FX reserves rose to 18.7 percent in 2002 from 12.7 in 1999. Demand for the dollar stood at 64.5 percent in 2002 compared with 67.9. 2003 data is due later this year.  

Global currency reserves exceeded $3.2 trillion at the end of March, according to BNP Paribas using IMF data.  

"Part of the substantial euro buying last year was related to the rebalancing of reserves by central banks. It is clearly euro positive in the long term," said Mary Davis, currency strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.  

GRADUAL PROCESS  

Russia's central bank intervenes regularly to prevent the rouble from strengthening due to a rising current account surplus and capital inflows.  

Russia's current account surplus stood at $35.9 billion at the end of 2003, up from $29.1 in 2002. Russia's currency and gold reserves rose to $83.2 billion in April from $57.7 billion a year ago, reflecting increased dollar-buying intervention by the central bank.  

CSFB estimates Russia's net currency reserves will reach $90 billion by the end of 2004.  

The central bank said under the new basket scheme, the euro would represent 10 to 20 percent of the basket and its weight would gradually rise to 50 percent.  

Analysts say such a basket composition is more consistent with Russia's trade relationships. Mostly commodity-based exports are priced in dollars and imports are mainly invoiced in euros.  

Using a trade-weighted currency link and Russia's current account surplus, BNP Paribas estimates the introduction of the basket will create additional euro demand of around 10-15 billion euros each year, supporting the euro in the long term.  

In China, chief FX regulator Guo Shuqing said in a newspaper interview last week the country wants to move towards a floating currency system that would link the yuan to a basket of currencies rather than just to the dollar as at present.  

China holds the majority of its $440 billion reserves, the world's second largest, in dollars.  

In India, the central bank has already been diversifying its reserves out of dollars into the euro. The Indian rupee is linked to a basket of four currencies - the dollar, euro, sterling and yen - and the government is considering reforms of its FX regime towards eventual full flotation.  

"Diversification means central banks would sell U.S. assets to buy other assets and, as an adequate reserve currency, the euro is in a prominent position," said Hans Redeker, chief foreign exchange strategist at BNP Paribas.

title: Russia cbank to target rouble against dlr/euro basket.
text:
MOSCOW, April 13 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank will overhaul its managed float of the rouble by replacing its exclusively dollar-based monitoring with a dollar/euro currency basket, Deputy Chairman Konstantin Korishchenko said on Tuesday.   

The euro would represent 10 to 20 percent of the basket, Korishchenko told reporters at an investment conference, but its weight would gradually rise to 50 percent.   

The central bank is currently the main player on Russia's forex exchanges, intervening when it thinks the market is too volatile or to guide rouble/dollar rates towards annual targets.   

"Currently the central bank sets its goals in 'dollar to rouble' terms," Korishchenko said.   

The central bank uses a basket of currencies for statistical purposes, but has until now preferred to base its actions on the rouble's rate against the U.S. currency alone.   

Korishchenko said the new basket would be introduced after the merger in May of the interbank market and a joint trading session of eight exchanges.   

The rate that emerges from the exchanges' joint trading session currently serves as the central bank's official rouble/dollar exchange rate for the following day.   

The introduction of the basket would make it more difficult for dealers to see the rate at which the central bank intervenes, Korishchenko said, and could lead to a higher market volatility.   

"The steps we are going to take mean less central bank influence on the foreign exchange market and make it easier for the market to find the balance itself," he told the conference.   

The bank was considering whether it would carry out interventions in euros as well as dollars after introducing the basket, Korishchenko added.

title: Russia  cbank ups  FX intervention  rate to curb rouble.
text:
MOSCOW, April 12 (Reuters) - Russia's central bank raised its rouble intervention rate on Monday for the first time in three months after its chairman promised President Vladimir Putin he would curb the strengthening currency which is hurting local producers.  

The rouble, which has gained almost five percent against the euro-dollar basket since the start of the year, fell almost five kopecks against the dollar and dealers said they expected a further nominal weakening.  

Its strength has been caused by a heavy inflow of dollars from the country's oil exports, the backbone of Russia's economy, heavy corporate borrowing abroad and Russians switching their savings from dollars into roubles.  

The rouble fell in early official trade on Monday to a weighted average for tomorrow settlement of 28.5535 per dollar compared with 28.5065 the previous session.  

Dealers said the central bank offered to buy $200 million at 28.5250 a dollar, or four kopecks more than before.  

"As soon as banks saw the bid, everything became clear," said Alfa bank dealer Alexei Bukleyev.  

Dealers said the central bank had changed its bid after Friday's meeting between Central Bank Chairman Sergei Ignatyev and Putin. Ignatyev promised to curb the rouble's gains against the dollar to seven percent this year, a level which he said would not hurt local companies.  

A firmer rouble erodes the competitiveness of local goods and may threaten Putin's target of doubling the size of the economy within a decade.  

Nikolai Kashcheyev, an analyst at Trust investment bank, said the central bank seemed to have changed its priorities to containing the rouble's strength from controlling inflation.  

The rouble has firmed 4.7 percent against a basket of the dollar and euro since the start of 2004 compared with a 4.1 percent gain in the whole of 2003.  

Consumer price inflation stood at 3.5 percent in the first quarter. Russia targets a 10 percent annual inflation rate and with prices usually weaker in summer months the central bank is in a position to achieve the goal easily.  

ROUBLE SEEN DOWN  

Bukleyev said that given current inflation the central bank would have to make sure the rouble was traded at around 29 per dollar by the end of the year if it wants to prevent it from firming by more than seven percent.
