title: FOCUS - Primakov seeks unity to fight Russia's chaos.
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Prime Minister Yevgeny Primakov struggled on Monday to forge a broad-based government to tackle Russia's economic mayhem and suffered an early setback when several key political forces said they would not join his team. 

 As both Communists and liberals distanced themselves from him, Primakov confirmed a shift of policy from strict monetarism towards social welfare and industrial growth in comments likely to worry Western lenders meeting in London to discuss Russia. 

 President Boris Yeltsin, severely weakened by the financial crisis, remained at his country residence. Primakov was due to brief him on Tuesday in the Kremlin on his cabinet plans. 

 "This is a national government, a patriotic government, which must concern itself with the interests of Russia and her people," Primakov told the cabinet, still largely composed of acting ministers from the outgoing administration. 

 The former foreign minister, approved by parliament on Friday, faces a tough task to try to restore order to Russia's chaotic finances and to regain the trust of international investors dismayed by its default on some foreign debt. 

 He has vowed to push on with reforms but wants to cushion their impact on the most vulnerable parts of society. 

 "We cannot conduct reforms which reflect badly among the people," Primakov said as he chaired his first cabinet meeting. 

 But despite his pitch, the Communists and their parliamentary allies, who all supported his candidacy, said they would not propose new candidates to join the government. 

 Their statement also called for stepping up preparations for a nationwide protest on October 7 that would call for Yeltsin's resignation and an early presidential election. 

 Grigory Yavlinsky, leader of the pro-reform Yabloko party which also voted for Primakov, similarly refused to join the cabinet, saying his economic views differed too sharply from those of First Deputy Prime Minister Yuri Maslyukov. 

 Maslyukov, a moderate Communist, is now in broad charge of economic policy and has said Russia will pursue a more interventionist strategy aimed at reviving domestic industry. 

 "It would be wrong to turn the government into a debating club," Yavlinsky told reporters after meeting Primakov. 

 This means that of the eight parties or groupings in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, all but three have ruled out taking part in what Primakov has said should be a non-partisan government reflecting a wide spectrum of opinions. 

 On Monday Maslyukov said his top priority would be paying off wage and pension arrears - a chronic problem affecting millions of Russians including soldiers, doctors and teachers. 

 Interfax news agency quoted Primakov, 68, as saying he could not rule out "extraordinary measures" to clear the wage backlog. 

 It was unclear what measures he had in mind but Western economists and Russian liberals fear he might start printing money - a move which could spark hyperinflation. 

 Acting Finance Minister Mikhail Zadornov, a liberal, said he hoped Russia would avoid printing its way out of the crisis. 

 "We would prefer not to rush towards central bank credits," Interfax quoted Zadornov as saying. "Hopefully it will be possible to get by without an emission." 

 Maslyukov, who once headed the Soviet state planning organisation Gosplan, has said he will have an economic programme ready by the end of the week. 

 His proposals are sure to be carefully scrutinised by Western countries and global lenders like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which have told Moscow it can only expect further financial help if it sticks to tough market reforms. 

 U.S. President Bill Clinton said Russia must reaffirm its commitment to democracy and free markets. 

 "If Russia is willing to take these steps, we must do everything we can to provide support," he said. 

 Senior foreign and finance ministry officials from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations met in London on Monday to discuss Russia and reached similar conclusions to Clinton. 

 Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Mamedov told reporters after briefing the G7 officials that a team of IMF experts was likely to visit Moscow later this week. 

 Russia is keen to get its hands on another tranche of the $22.6 billion rescue package agreed with the IMF in July. 

 In some sorely needed good news for the beleaguered government, Russian markets appeared calmer on Monday. 

 The central bank, now headed by Soviet-era banker Viktor Gerashchenko, set its official rouble rate for Tuesday at 8.6707 to the dollar, up from Monday's level of 11.4281. The battered currency briefly hit around 20 roubles to the dollar last week. However, analysts said the rouble rebound may be short-lived. 

 The central bank's first deputy chairman, Sergei Aleksashenko, followed former chairman Sergei Dubinin by resigning and said he had a different approach to Gerashchenko. 

 After Monday's cabinet meeting, Primakov consulted former premier Viktor Chernomyrdin. Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's favoured candidate for prime minister, stepped aside last week to clear the way for Primakov after being rejected twice by the Duma. 

 Chernomyrdin, who served as premier from 1992 until his sacking in March this year, also reiterated his intention to run for the presidency in the next election due in mid-2000. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Is the bull market over?
text:
NEW YORK, Aug 30 (Reuters) - The world's woes have washed ashore for U.S. investors, ruining summer vacations and casting into doubt the health, if not the life, of the bull market. 

 The global tumult, climaxed by Russia's near meltdown last week, has produced widespread wreckage on Wall Street. Last week, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 481.97 points, its largest weekly point loss in history. 

 While leading Russian politicians, led by acting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, reached a compromise Sunday aimed at halting Russia's crisis, that development may have litte impact on Wall Street. 

 Most major U.S. stock indexes are now well into double-digit loss territory since peaking in July. The Dow and Standard & Poor's 500 index have each skidded more than 13 percent and the Nasdaq Composite more than 18 percent. 

 Another grim statistic: Nearly four out of five stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange are trading below their 10-week and 30-week moving averages. 

 Those numbers put the market well into correction territory and have many on Wall Street talking bluntly about the prospects of a market other than the bull variety. 

 "The odds are increasing we are going to have a serious bear market," Morgan Stanley Dean Witter global strategist Barton Biggs said during a Friday interview on CNBC television. 

 While definitions of a bear market vary, most use 20 percent as the threshhold, meaning Nasdaq is already in the ballpark. But that simple definition falls short for some. 

 "There are plenty of people who are using that phrase," said Charlie Crane, chief market strategist at Key Asset Management. "I don't think we're in one. The thing for me that distinguishes a true bear market from a nasty correction is duration." 

 Which is not to say Crane is bullish. Rather, he said, he "prematurely" called the end of the bull market last year and now views a 20 percent correction - such as the market experienced in 1987, just a bit slower - as a possibility. 

 The bears have more company than at any point in the past three years. Recent sentiment surveys are extremely bleak, with just 22 percent of respondents expressing a bullish outlook in the last weekly survey by the American Association of Individual Investors. Bears claimed a 32 percent share of the investor market. 

 And yet, even with fear apparently trouncing greed in the sentiment market, some bulls are holding fast, Goldman Sachs U.S. strategist Abby Joseph Cohen, for example. 

 On Friday, Cohen again stated her view that stocks were undervalued and predicted the Dow, which ended the week a quiet day's decline from 8,000, would finish 1998 well above 9,300. 

 "We conclude that problems of great consequence to other nations have been largely responsible for recent declines in U.S. stock prices, and that these declines are notably out of proportion with the likely impact on the U.S. economy," Cohen said in a note to clients. 

 Cohen is not alone in her view. Brown Brothers Harriman market analyst Charles Blood also said recent events had not convinced him to alter his expectations for an upturn, albeit a somewhat delayed one. 

 "Nothing has changed about our outlook," he said. "We've done a lot of damage here but I think the background is still okay." 

 One reason the domestic story is taking a back seat to international events is a lack of fresh U.S. news. Wall Street is between earnings seasons and last week offered a dearth of domestic economic news to digest. 

 This Friday, the market is slated to receive the one report that in the past has proven capable of unilaterlly turning markets - the monthly payrolls report. 

 For the first time in years, analysts will scrutinise the data not for its inflationary impact - inflation has been all but disregarded as a threat by many - but for any weakness that may free the hand of the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates. 

 Few on Wall Street expect such an easing anytime soon, however, as the Fed has given little sign it would consider such a move. 

 The most recent Fed comments on rates were offered on Friday by St. Louis Fed President William Poole, who would go only so far as to say the central bank would take a "wait-and-see" approach on rates. 

 The recent conclusion of the General Motors strike will also cloud the jobs numbers, making it difficult to pin any policy hopes on the report. 

 In the absence of news at home, investors have fixed on the dismal news from abroad. 

 A stream of bad news that started with last summer's economic woes in Southeast Asia has swelled to flood levels, sweeping through the economies in Russia and Latin America. 

 The global malaise has sent commodity prices slumping, which in turn has hit some developed economies like Canada and Australia, both of which have felt the effects in slumping currencies. 

 Canada resorted to raising interest rates to protect its currency, Hong Kong directly intervened in equity markets as a defensive measure and Russia all but blocked rouble trading, all efforts analysts generally argued were doomed to failure. 

 "Authorities around the world are bungling," Morgan Stanley's Biggs said. "These aren't catastrophes but Canada, Hong Kong and Russia are all negatives." 

 ((-Wall Street desk, 212-859-1730)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Aug 27.
text:
NEW YORK, August 27 (Reuters) - The Wall Street Journal reported the following business stories in its electronic edition Thursday: 

 * Russia's Central Bank said it would stop intervening to support the rouble, allowing the currency to plunge. The central bank also cancelled dollar trading on the Moscow currency exchange. Credit Suisse and its First Boston unit said profits were hit by Russia's economic woes. Moscow's moves roiled world markets, and U.S. stocks fell 79.30 points to 8523.35. 

 * Some on Wall Street believe the Fed could be forced to cut interest rates in the coming months to address the global crisis, though the prospects of an imminent rate cut seem slim. 

 * Northwest Airlines  cancelled hundreds of weekend flights because of a threatened walkout by pilots if agreement on a new labour contract isn't reached by midnight tomorrow. 

 * A former lawyer for Liggett  plans to testify the company believed rivals would retaliate if it continued work on a safer cigarette. Meanwhile, R.J. Reynolds  and Brown & Williamson  said they are dropping out of settlement talks with a group of states. 

 * Durable-goods orders shot up 2.4 percent last month, marking the biggest rise in eight months, mainly driven by businesses investing in new technology. 

 * An FTC judge ordered the Trans Union credit-reporting agency to stop selling marketing lists with consumer credit data, citing privacy protection. 

 * Quark's CEO said his company's move on Adobe  was earnest, though he offered few details on how Quark would fund the offer for the much larger firm. Adobe shares rose 13 percent.

title: FOCUS-World urges Moscow to finally take charge.
text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The world's top economic powers told Russia on Wednesday it alone held the key to rescuing its ravaged economy and rouble currency, urging Moscow to finally get a grip on its staggering financial problems. 

 "There are no shortcuts in restoring market confidence, and the next steps are up to the Russians," White House deputy spokesman Barry Toiv told reporters in Edgartown, Mass., where U.S. President Bill Clinton was on vacation. 

 "Now more than ever it's critical that they get their fiscal house in order and establish policies on the rouble, on government debt and the banking system that will lead Russia back to financial stability," he said. 

 Toiv was speaking as fears were growing in world markets over Russia's economic fate. The rouble dropped more than 40 percent against the German mark on Wednesday, prompting the Russian central bank to declare it could no longer afford to intervene to boost its ailing currency. 

 Washington's harsh line was echoed by its key partners in Europe, which put the responsibility for pulling Russia back from the financial abyss squarely on Moscow's shoulders. 

 "Russia must do it by itself," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said in Germany. 

 In Paris, French President Jacques Chirac urged Moscow to push through economic reforms, saying international support would only work if reforms were implemented decisively by the new government of acting prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. 

 The British Treasury said it was closely monitoring the Russia crisis and was in contact with other members of the Group of Seven (G7) top industrial nations. 

 But there appeared to be no plans for a meeting by G7 leaders to discuss the crisis. "There's no plan that I'm aware of for any such meeting," Toiv said. 

 European sources said the four European members of the G7 - Germany, France, Britain and Italy - were in close contact but it was premature to speculate on any joint initiative. 

 Clinton is scheduled to travel to Moscow next week. He is expected to be joined by Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, the administration's top trouble-shooter when it comes to problems on the international financial scene. 

 Russia in July clinched a $22.6 billion rescue package with the International Monetary Fund and other international lenders aimed at resolving a deep economic crisis that jolted financial markets across the globe. 

 But conditions deteriorated dramatically since that agreement was reached. The rouble plunged to new lows against major currencies and a sense of panic spread among ordinary Russians, many of whom stood in long lines to withdraw their savings. 

 "If Russia can take the significant steps that they need to take, they can experience a recovery," Toiv said. "But it's not going to be easy and nobody ever suggested it would be." 

 Even as the United States and top European nations all but ruled out providing fresh funds for Russia, the IMF's top official, managing director Michel Camdessus, rushed off for a set of emergency talks with Russian and Ukrainian leaders. 

 An IMF spokesman said Camdessus would meet Chernomyrdin and Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma in the Ukraine to discuss "recent developments" in Russia and the fallout on the region. 

 The German government ruled out granting any more international financial aid to Russia, on top of the bailout package put together in July, until Moscow moves to implement agreed tax and budget reforms. Germany is Russia's biggest foreign lender and investor. 

 Russia stunned world markets a week ago by effectively devaluing the rouble and declaring a 90-day moratorium on some of its foreign debt repayments. President Boris Yeltsin then fired the entire government of Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko and named Chernomyrdin, whom he had fired from that very job in March, as acting prime minister. 

 Waigel said Germany had good relations with Chernomyrdin, and would "make use of these relations to help Russia." 

 France's Chirac said the international community should back Camdessus's efforts to ease the crisis. But he said, "His intervention today in Russia, with the full support of the G7, will only succeed if the essential domestic reforms sought by President Yeltsin are implemented resolutely by the new government of Chernomyrdin."

title: Russia  c.bank to halt wide-scale  forex intervention .
text:
MOSCOW, Aug 26 (Reuters) - The Russian central bank on Wednesday said it would refrain from major interventions in the currency markets because it was virtually the only seller of foreign currency for roubles. 

 "The Central Bank of the Russian Federation does not consider it reasonable to continue to undertake large-scale foreign currency interventions as it is pratically the only seller of foreign currency on the domestic market, which would inevitably lead to a reduction in Russia's reserves," the central bank said. 

 The central bank said it had spent $8.8 billion in currency markets from July to August, while it needed the remaining reserves to meet the urgent needs of the government and to support a minimal level of critical imports. 

 Commercial banks had bought $1.8 billion from the central bank since August 17, when Russia announced the suspension of the domestic debt market pending restructuring of short-term debt and a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt, the bank said. 

 Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin sharply criticised central bank chief Sergei Dubinin for his failure to protect the rouble, which fell five percent against its previous dollar fix on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) earlier in the day, and later fell by a third against the mark.

title: Europe says Russia must go it alone.
text:
BONN, Aug 26 (Reuters) - Major European powers told Russia on Wednesday it would have to go it alone in salvaging its battered economy and currency. 

 "Russia must do it by itself," said German Finance Theo Waigel. 

 He said neither the Group of Seven industrialised nations, the International Monetary Fund nor the European Union could fix Russia's problems. 

 French President Jacques Chirac urged Moscow to push through economic reforms, saying international support would only work if reforms were implemented decisively by the new government of acting prime minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. 

 A Berlin newspaper reported that German and French finance ministers planned to write to Russia urging "fundamental and possibly painful" reforms to fight Moscow's currency and debt crisis. 

 The Berliner Tagesspiegel said in an unsourced report to appear on Thursday that Waigel had spoken by telephone with his French counterpart Dominique Strauss-Kahn on Monday and agreed to draft a joint letter. 

 Details are expected to be finalised by the end of the week, and the two will probably address the letter to Chernomyrdin, the paper said. 

 German finance officials were not immediately available to comment on the report. 

 The British Treasury said it was closely monitoring the Russia crisis and was in contact with other Group of Seven members. 

 European sources said the four European members of the G7 - Germany, France, Britain and Italy-were in close contact but it was premature to speculate on a joint initiative or letter. 

 Waigel told reporters in Cologne it was up to the Russian government and Duma lower house of parliament to take action to restore confidence in the rouble. 

 He was speaking as the rouble plunged more than 40 percent against the German mark and a bewildered Russian central bank said it could no longer afford to defend its currency. 

 The German government has ruled out granting any more international financial aid to Russia, on top of a $22.6 billion package put together by the IMF last month, until Russia implements agreed tax and budget reforms. 

 Germany is Russia's biggest foreign lender and investor. Russia's sovereign and commercial debt to Germany totals 75.8 billion marks. 

 The financial crisis led to declines in European shares. Frankfurt was hardest hit among major European bourses, with the Xetra-DAX plunging more than three percent in a reflection of German banks' estimated $30 billion exposure to Russian debt. 

 Waigel said Germany had good relations with Chernomyrdin, who was unexpectedly re-appointed by President Boris Yeltsin last weekend. 

 "We will make use of these relations to help Russia," Waigel added. 

 Chirac also offered moral support to Russia but insisted on reform. 

 In an annual speech to French ambassadors in Paris, Chirac said the international community should back efforts by IMF chief Michel Camdessus to ease the crisis. 

 But he added: "His intervention today in Russia, with the full support of the G7, will only succeeed if the essential domestic reforms sought by President Yeltsin are implemented resolutely by the new government of Chernomyrdin." 

 Chernomyrdin flew off to Ukraine suddenly on Wednesday to meet Camdessus. 

 Chirac renewed a call for a strengthening of the IMF, in particular by giving its policy-making interim committee decision-making powers.

title: WRAP:Russia Seen Close Imposing Ruble Exchange Controls
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Russian government appeared close to imposing foreign exchange controls Wednesday as the ruble tumbled and long lines appeared at exchange booths throughout Moscow. 

 The central bank canceled trading at the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICE) when it was overwhelmed by demand for dollars. Investors responded by snatching up other foreign currencies, including Deutsche marks. At the MICE, the ruble plummeted to RUR7.6 per mark from RUR4.4995 Tuesday. That implied the ruble had fallen to RUR13 per dollar, compared to RUR7.6 on Tuesday. 

 The Central Bank of Russia later announced that it would avoid massive interventions on behalf of the currency to conserve foreign exchange reserves. Those queuing at exchange booths had a hard time finding dollars to buy at any price. 

 "There are essentially no dollars available," said Eric Jayaweera, analyst at MFK Renaissance investment bank. "People can't even buy (the dollars) at exchange booths on the street and the black market is developing very quickly." 

 He estimated the running black market rate could be around RUR15 per dollar. 

 A Deutsche Bank economist estimated ruble cash and bank deposits total an equivalent of $50 billion. If even a portion of that were to be converted into dollars, the central bank's reserves could be wiped out. 

 "The central bank doesn't have the means to meet even 20% (of the outflow) if it were to go," said Marcel Cassard, chief economist at Deutsche Bank in London. "If locals continue to worry, there are going to be outflows. The only way to stop it is to impose controls."

title: Copy Of Statement From Russia Govt,  Central Bank
text:
MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The following is the joint text released Monday by the Russian government and central bank announcing a ruble devaluation and debt restructuring: 

 The Russian Government and the Central Bank of Russia on Monday issued a statement,the text of which was relayed to Itar-Tass by the Government Information Agency. Follows the full text of the statement. 

 Statement 

 of the Government of the Russian Federation 

 and the Central Bank of Russia 

 August 17, 1998 

 A crisis broke out on world financial markets when the Russian economy was at the start of a recovery. From October 1997 the Government and the Bank of Russia have been protecting the main achievements of the economic policy of the recent years -- stable prices and a fixed rouble and, hence, the living standards of the people. 

 The problem of servicing the national debt aggravated sharply with the worsening of the foreign economic situation and because of the unsatisfactory state of affairs with revenues of the budget. Expenditures for the redemption of the earlier issued state securities and the payment of interest on them have become a heavy burden on the state budget with tax collection being low. The Russian Government has to reduce the domestic state debt, cutting expenditures under the federal budget and making external borrowings. The Government's economic programme was backed in July by international financial organisations and leading countries of the world. 

 However, the crisis aggravating in Asia and a new fall of world prices of oil have not permitted the restoration of the confidence in Russian securities and, hence, the improvement of the situation with the budget. The country's foreign currency reserves continue to shrink and the banking system experience difficulties. 

 In this situation the Government and the Bank of Russia deem it necessary to take a set of measures aimed at the normalisation of the financial and budget policy. 

 1. As of August 17, 1998, the Bank of Russia is moving to a new policy of setting the ruble a new "currency corridor" fixed at the level of from 6 to 9.5 rubles to the US dollar. Interventions by the Bank of Russia will be made to lessen sharp fluctuations in the ruble rate. The Bank of Russia will be using the interest policy for the same purpose. 

 2. State securities (treasury bills and federal loans bonds) that are to be cancelled up to December 31, 1999, inclusively, will be exchanged for new securities. The technical parameters of the exchange will be announced on Wednesday, August 19, 1998. Biddings in the market of treasury bills -- federal loan bonds are suspended till the securities' exchange is completed. 

 3. Under the provisions of the regulations of the International Monetary Fund, the Government and the Bank of Russia are introducing temporary restrictions for Russian residents on large-scale foreign currency operations. A 90-day moratorium is imposed as of August 17, 1998 on the repayment of credits received from non-residents in the Russian Federation, on the payment of insurance on credits insured by the mortgage of securities, on the payments under fixed-term contracts in foreign currency. Non-residents in the Russian Federation are prohibited to invest funds into rouble assets with the time for repayment of up to one year. 

 4. The Government and the Bank of Russia regard a stable functioning of the banking system and the system of settlements and payments in the Russian Federation as one of important priorities. In this connection, the Government and the Bank of Russia favour the setting up of a payments' pool by the biggest Russian banks to maintain stability of interbank settlements. At the same time the Bank of Russia will make efforts to consolidate the Russian banking system, and draw into this stable Russian Banks and leading foreign banks. 

 5. To restore the financial market, the Russian Government will shortly begin placing short-term treasury bills (for a term of one or two weeks). A broader range of securities will be issued for the population. 

 6. The Government and the Bank of Russia address to the Federal Assembly a legislative initiative to tighten control over the flow of currency abroad. At the same time the Government and the Bank of Russia are going to take urgent actions in the area within the bounds of their powers. 

 7. The Russian Government repeatedly suggests to the State Duma to hold an extraordinary session before the end of August to pass key draft laws to help to insure the timely payment of pensions and wages to workers in the state sector, to create legislative procedures for banks' stabilisation and to strengthen the system of currency regulation and currency control. 

 Prime Minister of President

 S.V.Kiriyenko S.K.Dubinin

title: Intervention  Concerns For Dlr/Yen On Back Burner For Now
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Heightened concerns about intervention in the dollar/yen aren't being given much credence yet, even as the Japanese currency began the week by staging a slight comeback Monday. 

 While much of the spotlight Monday focused on Russia and the fallout of its de facto ruble devaluation, the yen won't be overshadowed for long, as market participants eye dollar/yen levels on the top and bottom that could compel a central bank to intervene. 

 Monday, Russia stole the show when it cut the lower limit for the ruble by 34% to RUR9.50, from RUR6.30, spurring discussions of what's next for the gravely ill Russian economy and what the devaluation means for other emerging markets. 

 "That's all we've been talking about this morning," said Bob Johnson, vice president of foreign exchange at ABN-AMRO Bank in Chicago. 

 However, the market managed to absorb the news in an orderly fashion after the dollar initially spiked higher against the yen and Deutsche mark early in Monday trading before retreating gradually for the rest of the session.

title: Russia's Prime Minister Pledges To Stand By Ruble, Austerity Plan
text:
MOSCOW -(Dow Jones)- The recent turmoil in Russian financial markets has not caused the government to alter its plans to defend the ruble, or shore up finances with austerity measures, Russia's prime minister told the Itar-Tass news agency Wednesday. 

 Russian markets have been falling sharply in recent weeks on fears that the government will be forced to devalue the ruble. However, the Russian stock market appeared to steady somewhat Wednesday, with the RTS index losing about 1.6% after falling 9% on both Monday and Tuesday. 

 Still, the ruble sank against the dollar Wednesday, after Russia's central bank moved to limit its intervention on behalf of the currency. The central bank cut the maximum quotas of dollars it will sell to commercial banks. The banks are desperate to raise the U.S. currency amid this week's mass exodus from Russian financial markets. The dollar for next-day delivery closed at 6.3150 rubles, up from 6.31 at Tuesday's close. 

 The government has repeatedly said it will defend the currency, despite the toll on central bank reserves. The government is also redoubling efforts to bolster budget revenues through higher tax collections and privatizations. 

 "No kinds of changes in the policy of the central bank and government will happen," said Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko. "The worse the financial situation becomes, the harder we must work to fulfill the program." 

 Russian Finance Minister Mikhail Zadornov echoed Kiriyenko's words, and said Wednesday the government would service Russian debt on schedule, and continue to support the ruble. 

 Zadornov said that redemptions in the treasury market would not be that substantial in August, thanks in part to the government's recent efforts to restructure the market and swap the obligations into dollar-denominated paper. 

 The central bank and state-controlled savings bank Sberbank have promised to roll over maturities and even increase holdings. 

 In August, redemptions on maturing government bonds total 15 billion rubles, without the central bank's and Sberbank's debt rollovers. 

 "Through the debt conversions we managed to substantially reduce the redemption payments (in August), therefore we look at the debt payments calmly," he said. 

 He said that tax collections continued to improve in early August, and were higher in the first 11 days of the month than in the corresponding period in July.  "Therefore we can expect that revenues in August will be bigger than in July," he said. 

 He said the government would double monthly tax collections to 23-25 billion rubles by the end of the year. 

 "If we thought that devaluation was unavoidable, we would not be taking the measures we are taking now," Zadornov said. 

 Zadornov confirmed that the government expects in all around $4.27 billion of loan disbursements from the International Monetary Fund in September, rejecting rumors that the fund has reduced the amount. 

 The expected total consists of $2.8 billion of the fund's additional loans pledged in July, a $670 million tranche of the previously-agreed loan, as well as the $800 million the fund suspended in July after Russia's Parliament rejected a number of bills aimed at increasing budget revenue. 

 "Naturally this (disbursement) depends on the adoption of the stabilization program," Zadornov said. 

 Amid the recent sharp losses on Russia's external debt, the government doesn't plan any new conversions of ruble-denominated debt into longer-term dollar borrowing. 

 "There isn't any demand, so it would be senseless," Zadornov said. 

 Amid talk that the $22.7 billion loan package already pledged to Russia by international lenders may not be enough to reassure investors, Zadornov said Russia won't use U.S. President Bill Clinton's upcoming visit to Moscow to request direct aid from Washington. 

 "We aren't attaching any issues of additional aid to this visit, because it wouldn't be decided during the visit," Zadornov said. "It isn't a simple procedure - and on the whole, we aren't counting on direct, bilateral aid from the G-7," the finance minister added. 

 Clinton is due to arrive in Moscow Sept. 1. for a three-day visit. 

 At his briefing Wednesday, Zadornov announced plans to streamline the Finance Ministry and tighten spending controls, a move that will involve cutting the ministry's staff by 20%.

title: Russia  Ruble Ends Lower After Panic On  Intervention  Limits

MOSCOW (Dow Jones)--The Russian ruble sank against the dollar Wednesday, after the central bank's move to limit its intervention on behalf of the currency caused a panic on the interbank market. 

 After the banks' initial rush to buy whatever amount of dollars they could, activity nearly halted, traders said. 

 Government bonds recovered a touch after Tuesday's massive losses. However, traders were not convinced there would be a turnaround. 

 The dollar for next-day delivery closed at RUR6.3100-6.3200, up from RUR6.3000-6.3200 at the Tuesday close. 

 Practically the whole trading session, the Russian currency remained below the daily lower limit set by the central bank at RUR6.2960 against the dollar.

 "It caused a panic on the market because commercial banks count on being able to buy a certain amount (of dollars) at a fixed rate," said Dmitri Panteta, trader at International Moscow Bank.

title: Russian shares end stronger after yen gains.
text:
MOSCOW, Aug 4 (Reuters) - Russian shares surged higher in thin trade on Tuesday as local traders turned bullish following an afternoon strengthening in the yen, dealers said. 

 Reuters composite index rose 2.33 percent to 99.86 from 97.59 on Monday, when the index lost 4.79 percent against a background of troubled Asian markets. 

 "Russian players are traditionally more oriented toward buying," said Regent European Securities trader Nikolai Gusev. "Since there is no news about Russia that one could play on, everyone has started to look to Asia." 

 The yen, which had earlier slipped to 146 to the dollar, rebounded to 144.89 in early New York trading on Tuesday after Japan's new government warned currency markets to beware of central bank intervention to support the yen. 

 In Russia, national power grid UES advanced to $0.1290 from $0.1230 on Monday, LUKoil bounced up to $8.15 from $8.00 and Rostelekom was at $2.235 from $2.280. 

 But dealers said thin volumes had boosted levels, too, and said the absence of Western clients would leave the rise shortlived. 

 "Activity is very low and when there are low volumes the market makes fairly sharp twists," said one trader at a Western investment company. "These levels don't attract either big buyers or big sellers." 

 And Regent's Gusev added: "At these levels it's dangerous to short and it's also frightening to buy." ((Olga Popova, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941-8520 moscow.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Zloty hits all-time high on Russia despite c.bank.
text:
WARSAW, July 14 (Reuters) - The zloty flew to a new all-time high despite central bank interventions against it as foreigners rushed for Polish treasuries after Russia secured a huge aid deal which may help it overcome financial problems. 

 The zloty ended at 8.41/8.34 percent firmer than the parity rate on Tuesday against Monday's 8.33/8.27 percent close as an estimated $200 million worth of interventions pushed it down from intraday highs of more than 8.60 percent. 

 Analysts said the wave of optimism spilling out from Russia was coupled by expectations that Polish interest rates and the zloty's crawling devaluation could be cut on Thursday, when the Monetary Policy Council (RPP) meets. 

 "The market is generally expecting cuts in interest rates, by about 100 basis points, and zloty crawling peg by 0.1 point, which should be roughly neutral to the zloty," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Barings in Warsaw. 

 "Apart from that, there is this pressure from foreigners who again perceive Poland as a very attractive emerging market after Russia stabilised. The situation is likely to continue, prompting more central bank interventions," Rybinski added. 

 On Tuesday central bank bought dollars on the local market, its first intervention since May 11, when the currency traded between 8.63 and 8.28 percent stronger than the parity rate. 

 "They (the interventions) add to the pressure for a cut in interest rates, with the zloty so strong and the situation in Russia looking to improve a little bit," said Ehsun Khan, analyst at Morgan Stanley & Co International in London. 

 "The central bank already has many reasons to cut interest rates, but the strength of the currency and the likelihood that the strength of the currency would remain in the absence of cuts just adds to the logic for a cut," Khan added. 

 Polish debt yields continued their steady slide on Tuesday. 

 Two-year notes were on Tuesday at 17.6/17.4 percent against the 18.49 percent average yield at the last auction on July 1. Five-year paper traded at 15.5/15.4 against 15.72 percent. 

 The benchmark 52-week bill yield fell to 17.8/17.6 percent on Tuesday against an average of 18.2 percent at this Monday's primary auction.

title: Polish Zloty/Russia -2: Polish Fundamentals Improved
text:
Concerns about Poland's current-account deficit have eased as export performance has been stronger than expected. A number of economists have reduced their forecast for the deficit at the end of the year to 3.5% of gross domestic product from 4% or more. 

 And the year-on-year inflation rate in May fell to 13.3% from 13.7% in April. 

 But a stronger zloty also increases the likelihood of central bankintervention as the zloty approaches the limit of its 20-point trading band against a basket of western currencies, analysts said. 

 "They will definitely have to intervene if the zloty gets stronger," said Krzysztof Rybinski, chief economist at ING Barings in Warsaw. 

 Before the latest crisis in Russia, the central bank was forced to intervene heavily in the foreign exchange market to keep the zloty within its trading band. 

Central bank officials privately have said they were relieved that the Russian crisis had taken the pressure off the Polish currency. Now, the central bank must once again deal with the strong zloty. 

 Even before Monday's accord between the international lenders and Russia was announced, analysts had predicted that the Polish monetary policy council, which meets on Thursday, would reduce key interest rates and lower the monthly devaluation rate of the zloty. 

 Many economists are forecasting that interest rates will likely be cut by one percentage point. Currently, the Lombard rate stands at 26%, and the rediscount rate is at 23.5%. Many also predict that the monthly devaluation rate will be reduced to 0.6% from 0.8%.

title: Stalled aid for Russia may be discussed by G7.
text:
TOKYO, June 19 (Reuters) - Financial aid to Russia is likely be among the issues discussed by deputy finance ministers of the Group of Seven (G7) nations when they meet in Tokyo on Saturday, analysts and officials said on Friday. 

 "Russia will be among the issues for the G7, particularly after Moscow made a plea for emergency financing," Kosuke Nakahira, a former Japanese vice finance minister for international affairs, told Reuters. 

 Russia said on Thursday that it needed at least $10 billion from the IMF to help stabilise its turbulent markets. 

 But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Thursday decided to put off the disbursement of a $670 million tranche of an existing $9.2 billion IMF loan, saying that Moscow had not fulfilled its promises on economic reform. 

 IMF payments to Russia have been delayed because the IMF is worried about dismal tax revenues and the degree of Moscow's commitment to its structural reform efforts. 

 Last week, the G7 nations backed further support for Russia through the IMF, but failed to announce a concrete aid package after a meeting of deputy finance ministers in Paris. 

 Asked if Japan, at the meeting, would be asked by the United States to put up fresh aid for Russia if Russia implemented substantial reform,Nakahira said: "It is possible, as they have asked many different things at one time during these sorts of occasions." 

 He added: "But under the prevailing rules of global society, aid to fix damage caused by short-term capital flows is centrally organised by the IMF, rather than bilaterally." 

 Apart from Moscow's problem, there is a problem with donors - they do not necessarily have ample funds, he said. 

 The United States has made clear it supported new loans, if needed, from both the IMF and the World Bank to Moscow, but has steered clear of offering bilateral aid on its own. 

 The U.S. administration has been asking Congress to approve $18 billion in funding for the IMF, but so far its efforts have failed. 

 The IMF said last month that it needed cash from its members because without further funding its usable resources would be just $10 billion to $12 billion. 

 Analysts said they expected to see the G7 call for Japan to buy more products made in Southeast Asia to help put the region's economies back on growth tracks, and to give new money to Moscow when it is judged eligible to receive it. 

 The financial stability of Russia is also important for European members of the G7, particularly for Germany, whose banking sector has Russian loan exposure of more than $30 billion, they said. 

 "The United States is likely to ask for future Japanese aid for Russia, either explicitly or implicitly, now that Japan owes them after Wednesday's currency market intervention," said Yasushi Okada, chief economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Securities (Japan). 

 The Bank of Japan and the U.S. Federal Reserve sold an estimated $6 billion in Wednesday's joint effort to rein in the galloping dollar against the yen, traders said. The United States was estimated to have spent some $2 billion of the total, they said. 

 The surprise move pushed down the dollar by more than seven yen to around 136 yen in New York on Wednesday. 

 "The two things (currency market intervention and Japanese aid to Russia) are utterly unrelated," said an official at the Ministry of Finance. The official added, however, that aid to Moscow could well be on the G7 agenda. 

 Okada said in reference to the intervention: "Nothing is free." 

 A spokesman for the Export-Import Bank of Japan said there had been no request for fresh aid from Moscow prior to the G7 deputies meeting on Saturday. 

 He said the bank intended to smoothly disburse $1.2 billion worth of aid and export credit earlier earmarked for Russia. ((Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3 3432 1396 tokyo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging debt prices bolstered by yen  intervention .
text:
NEW YORK, June 17 (Reuters) - Emerging debt was up for the second straight day Wednesday as investors took heart, at least temporarily, from news that help is on the way for the troubled yen. 

 "The real catalyst for the rally was the intervention on the dollar/yen," one emerging debt trader said. 

 The United States rode to the rescue of the battered Japanese currency Wednesday in a dramatic shift from its recent hands-off approach on mounting concern about Japan's slumping economy. 

 Joining forces with Japan's central bank, the Treasury Department instructed the New York Federal Reserve to spend an estimated $2 billion to boost the value of the yen against the dollar - the first U.S. intervention on behalf of the yen in more than six years. 

Intervention happens when central banks buy or sell a currency on the open market to affect its value. 

 The value of the yen immediately surged to 137 to the dollar, compared with 142 yen just before the intervention. 

 The Japanese currency had fallen to its lowest level in eight years recently on fears the ailing Japanese economy would spark another round of Asian financial shocks. 

 The emerging debt market was bolstered also by rumours that an aid package from the Group of Seven Industrialised Nations (G-7) is on the way. 

 Moscow cancelled two of three government debt auctions that had been expected Wednesday. 

 "This brought a feeling that Russia may have money very soon from other sources," an emerging debt trader said. 

 "I'd say 75 percent of the gains in Brady bond prices today came from the dollar/yen intervention and 25 percent came from Russia." 

 A top Russian finance official said Wednesday the country was considering launching at least one dollar-denominated Eurobond by the end of June. 

 And rumours circulated on Wall Street that Russia was seeking a 30-year, $1 billion issue, with a spread of around 775 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. 


The benchmark Brazil C bond		  was up 1-1/4 to bid 76-7/8, Argentine PARs		 were up 1/8 to bid 74-7/8 and Russian PRIN bonds		  were up 1/8 to bid 55-1/4.



Elsewhere, on a more sober note, a senior Chinese official on Wednesday issued Beijing's first explicit warning that a sliding Japanese yen could force China to devalue its currency.



Sun Zhenyu, the vice-minister for foreign trade, said a devaluation may be necessary if the tumbling yen hit Chinese exports too hard.



Although Washington's intervention on the yen will help the Chinese currency, Devi aurora, Asia analyst at Standard & Poor's DRI, said she expects a devaluation early next year.



"The worsening outlook for Chinese exports will put great pressure on the yuan," Aurora said.



The markets for Chinese goods has declined over the last year due to recessions throughout Asia.

title: Yeltsin, in Germany, hopes to win Kohl's support.
text:
BONN, June 9 (Reuters) - President Boris Yeltsin hoped to wrap up a high-profile visit to Germany on Tuesday by securing support from his closest ally in the West, Chancellor Helmut Kohl, to help stem Russia's financial crisis. 

 Kohl and Yeltsin, who met for talks over dinner late on Monday at the Bonn chancellery, discussed Russia's financial crisis "in a friendly, relaxed atmosphere", German government spokesman Otto Hauser said. 

 "They discussed the current state of the Russian economy and prospects for economic reforms," he said. Details of the type of help Russia might receive from its biggest trading partner Germany were still unclear. 

 They were due to announce the results of the two-day visit at a news conference at 0915 GMT. It was Yeltsin's first foreign appointment since the crisis was sparked two weeks ago by mass selling on Russian stock and bond markets. 

 Yeltsin and members of his government delegation dismissed suggestions on Monday that the Russian economy was on the verge of collapse and that they had come to beg for more loans to prop it up. 

 A senior economic adviser to Yeltsin said the president had no intention of asking Kohl for direct financial aid, but left open the question of whether he might seek Yeltsin's backing for further aid from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 "We don't expect any help apart from political support," Yeltsin aide Alexander Livshits said. 

 Yeltsin said Moscow had no plans to devalue the rouble currency because the Russian government had taken sufficient measures to stabilise the currency and it had ample reserves to support it if necessary. 

 Foreign policy experts say Yeltsin is likely ask Kohl, with whom he has a warm friendship, to help him cope with the crisis. 

 The Central Bank tripled interest rates to 150 percent at the height of the financial crisis on May 27 to support the rouble, bringing them down again to 60 percent only when market pressure had eased. The rouble was steady at around 6.18 to the dollar on Monday. 

 Russian debt to Germany, Russia's chief Western trading partner, is 75.2 billion marks ($42.4 billion). 

 Although Germany has ruled out bilateral help, it is a key player in the IMF's continuing involvement in Russia. The Fund is expected to release a $670 million tranche of a $9.2 billion lending facility this month. 

 Yeltsin suggested in an interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel that Russia had learned from past mistakes and would not use any additional credits for "stop-gap" measures, such as paying off wage arrears. 

 Any future credits would be pinned to specific projects to help structural reform, Yeltsin was quoted as saying on Monday. 

 Kohl and Yeltsin also discussed bilateral cooperation in combating organised crime - an area of growing concern to Bonn since the collapse of Communism in the east. 

 It is also one of the few areas where Yeltsin can offer Kohl something in return for political backing, foreign policy experts say. 

 Kohl and Yeltsin also spoke about the conflict in the Serbian province of Kosovo and the recent series of nuclear tests by India and Pakistan, Hauser said. 

 Russian Defence Minister Igor Sergeyev, accompanying Yeltsin, said Russia would not in principle oppose NATO intervention in the Kosovo crisis if it was conducted with the approval of the U.N. Security Council. 

 The possibility of NATO intervention to contain the conflict has been mooted in recent days following new reports of Serb police action against Kosovo Albanian separatists. The action has prompted a flow of refugees from the region. 

 German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and his Russian counterpart Yevgeny Primakov also met on Monday night, ahead of a big powers Contact Group meeting in London on Friday to discuss how to prevent the conflict from developing into war. 

 In the first agreements to concluded on the trip, Kinkel and the Russian Atomic Energy Minister Yevgeny Adamov signed two agreements on trade in nuclear materials. 

 The first and more controversial allows Russia to ship weapons-grade, highly enriched uranium to a research reactor in Germany. The second limits German firms' liability in the event of a nuclear accident at Russian plants they serve.

title: Confidence in Russia still elusive - U.S. analysts.
text:
NEW YORK, May 28 (Reuters) - Investors riding on the roller-coaster Russian financial market were bracing for more bumps on the downward course unless outside help came quickly, U.S. analysts and fund managers said. 

 While the battered ruble got a respite on Thursday - stabilising at 6.1490 per dollar - the clock was ticking as no economy could sustain Russia's 150 percent interest rates for long, they said. 

 The ruble's fate was now tied to the expectation for outside help, even though the currency, on the flow of fund basis, was fundamentally sound, said Gretchen Rodkey, analyst at Bear Stearns and Co. 

 Russia is awaiting the release of a $670 billion tranche of the $9.2 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund. 

 "The market is expecting an additional aid package," she said. "With the expectation out, it becomes self-fulfilling." 

 With dwindling foreign reserves, foreign investors needed assurance that the demand for dollars would be met. "The reserves were one of the weak spots," Rodkey said. 

 Russia had official reserves of just over $14.5 billion, down from 15.5 billion last week after heavy intervention to defend the ruble. 

 Excluding gold, however, Russia's reserves amounted to only $10.5 billion, Rodkey said. 

 Halliwell, Chief Executive Officer of River Capital International, said Russia needed only "a few billion dollars" in addition to the IMF loan disbursement to tide it over the crisis. 

 The aid could come in the form of bridge loans, short of tapping the currency stabilisation fund at the IMF, he said. 

 A fund manager noted that the stampede to get out of the ruble assets was triggered by fears of that Russian banks might not honour the dollar forward contracts. 

 "The problem of Tokobank last week highlighted the counterparty risk for foreign inventors in the GKO (Russian T-bill) market," he said. 

 Tokobank, one of Russia's 20 largest banks, was put under "temporary administration" by the central bank pending debt rescheduling and a new share issue. 

 As the yield of the three-month Russian treasury bills zoomed to 80 percent, the exceedingly high return induced some foreign investors to stay in the ruble debt market. 

 "The choice is between the counterparty risk and the currency risk," he said. 

 But high interest rates and an emergency aid package would not get Russia out of the woods, unless they were followed immediately by other measures to rebuild investors' confidence, analysts said. 

 Foreign investors confidence had been eroding for some time as the Russian government chronically failed to bridge the fiscal gap by its attempt to raise revenues, said Keith Crane, an economist at consultancy PlanEcon Inc. 

 Unlike Brazil, which weathered the storm last October by raising interest rates to defend the currency, Russia needed to build the basic framework to ensure a minimal level of tax collection, he said.

title: Analysts' comments on Russian interest rate moves.
text:
MOSCOW, May 15 (Reuters) - The Russian Central Bank said on Friday it would leave its key refinancing raise unchanged at 30 percent but would raise the 3-14 day Lombard rate to 36 from 30 percent and the 15-30 day Lombard rate to 40 from 30 percent effective from May 18. 

 Analysts gave the following comments to Reuters and to Reuters television after the central bank announcement: 

 STEPHEN LEWIS, MONUMENT DERIVATIVES, LONDON: "This is a good strategy as long as it works. If it starts falling apart the risk will be that the economy itself will begin to suffer from inflationary pressures through a weakening in the currency and that will probably force some increase in the refinancing rate as well as in some of the other rates. 

 "International investors, speculators, call them what you will, I think that they do look at risky situations where they suspect that official reserves are not large enough to cover potential outflow on short term capital account and that is one dimension where Russia could be said to bear some similarities to nations that have got themselves into trouble in Asia." 

 "Russian authorities have shown some skill in warding off pressures...They do seem to be getting more expert in dealing with the markets." 

 RICHARD GRAY, BANK OF AMERICA, LONDON: "I think it is a fairly notional move on the Lombard rate. Longer term, though, it might become a bit more interesting in terms of a change of direction in how Russian authorities manage money market instruments in Russia. 

 Just recently they've been using interventions in the GKO (t-bill) auctions as a primary tool of monetary policy. If they are coming back onto these headline rates, then that's a change of gear, but it could be constructive long term." 

 INNA FRANCIS, UNITED FINANCIAL GROUP, MOSCOW: "The refinancing rate is a key benchmark, and its being kept at the same level is just a sign that they want to show there is nothing really disturbing about the situation in the economy and that the pressures everyone is talking about on the rouble are not that substantial. 

 "But at the same time raising the long-term Lombard rate means that they are trying to prevent arbitrage opportunities... for Russian banks between the rate at which banks borrow money and rate at which the government places GKOs (t-bills) at auction. 

 "There was no outflow of capital so I don't know whether by raising the rate they will attract new money...They are trying to ease pressure on GKO yields but I don't think (just because of the rate raise) the GKO levels will slam down to 22 percent, which is the desirable level according to central bank officials. Something major has to happen before that happens...like passing the tax code or a rise in oil prices." ((Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941-8520 moscow.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Chicago/Ruble Futures -2: Liquidity Seen Low At First
text:
But there are myriad risks associated with trading in any new contract, let alone one that is tied directly to a wobbly emerging market. Liquidity in the ruble futures - which will be non-deliverable, cash-settled contracts sized at 500,000 rubles - will initially be low, meaning investors who decide to own them may find it difficult to locate a buyer. Furthermore, if the future's price plummets, as some analysts predict, the investor could suffer huge losses. 

 Russia's troubled financial sector may not have seen its worst bout of investor fright. The country is plagued with problems, from its ineffective tax system to its massive wage arrears to the likelihood that the slowdown in exports could result in its first trade deficit. Those factors in part precipitated a flight from the Russian bond and stock markets and, in turn, led to the Russian central bank's move last Friday to hike interest rates 14 percentage points to 42%. 

 And that's not all, said Max Tessier, an analyst at Bank Credit Analyst Research Group who has closely followed Russia's markets. Russia has a central bank that doesn't have a strong mandate from the government, leading to weak central bank intervention efforts and an anemic banking system, he added. 'Russia's market is driven by insider trading, there's a big underground economy, and it's a well-known fact that 'gray' money moves around. All these things add up to much greater risk,' concluded Tessier. 

Currency futures are commonly used by financial institutions to hedge foreign currency risk. But speculators and large hedge funds can also employ the instruments to depress the currency. Market watchers say further market instability in Russia could prompt corporations to dump rubles for a safe-harbor currency, opening the ruble to speculative attacks. title: Dubinin says Russia has reserves to defend rouble.
text:
MOSCOW, Sept 11 (Reuter) - Central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin said on Wednesday that Russia has sufficient reserves to keep the rouble within its exchange rate corridor against the dollar. 

 Dubinin told a news conference Russia had, in spite of significant intervention to support the rouble in August, managed to keep its foreign reserves within levels agreed with the International Monetary Fund. 

 "Despite the quite large volume of intervention, by buying gold and other similar operations, we are managing to support the necessary level of net international reserves and not to allowing a fall either in gross or net reserves," he said. 

 Dubinin earlier said the bank had spent $1.6 billion on intervention in August, when a faster than usual decline in the rouble made short-term T-bills unattractive. 

 Under Russia's crawling peg exchange rate policy, which runs until the end of this year, the rouble should be trading in a 5,500-6,100 per dollar corridor on December 31 this year. 

 The rouble was fixed at 5,373 per dollar on Wednesday on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX). 

 "We have sufficient reserves to keep the rouble exchange rate within the framework of the corridor as we consider necessary," said Dubinin, adding they were approximately the same as at the beginning of July. 

 He said in late July that gross central bank reserves in mid-July were $14.9 billion. 

 Net reserves are one of the economic indicators for which the IMF has set targets under its $10 billion, three-year loan agreement with Russia. 

 First deputy chairman Alexander Khandruyev said the current situation was calm, but that there was some pressure on the rouble. 

 He said the bank's board had on Wednesday discussed various options for exchange rate policy after the expiry of the corridor. It was not yet clear which would be adopted.

title: Russia central banker says rouble in managed float.
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 31 (Reuter) - The rouble is already effectively floating but it is too soon to say what currency regime will be introduced when the current fluctuation limits expire at the end of June, a top central banker said on Wednesday. 

 "It is clear that we have entered a period of dirty float," first deputy chairman Alexander Khandruyev told Reuters. 

 A dirty float, also known as a managed float, is a system in which no official parities for currencies are declared but the monetary authorities intervene in foreign exchange markets. 

Russia stabilised the rouble last summer, introducing a currency "corridor" with upper and lower limits in July. The current 4,550-5,150 per dollar corridor runs until July 1. 

 Khandruyev said the central bank would start discussions on a new currency regime after the bank and government have agreed an economic policy declaration in February. 

 It was possible that the corridor could be continued. 

Central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin has said the authorities could find some other way of regulating the rouble in the second half of the year. 

 The rouble has stayed well within the corridor, although in recent weeks the central bank has allowed it to fall. 

 The rouble fell to 4,734 per dollar on Wednesday on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) from 4,640 at the start of the year and around 4,500 in early November. 

 But Khandruyev said the corridor may be preserved, adding that the central bank had not yet discussed the matter.

 'We're forced to buy foreign currency from companies and individuals and as a result release more and more new money, which supports the inflationary process,' Tass quoted her as telling reporters at a banking congress in St. Petersburg. 

 The ruble has gained 4% against the dollar since the beginning of May and the central bank has intervened heavily to stem the rise. In Moscow Wednesday, the dollar rebounded slightly, gaining 6 points to 4906 rubles. 

 Paramonova said that if it weren't for the intervention, monthly inflation would be below the current 7%-8% rate. In May, consumer prices rose 7.9%, above government targets of 5%-6%. 

 In the past, the central banker has noted that money-supply growth caused by intervention isn't as inflationary as central bank lending to finance the budget deficit, the main source of inflation in Russia in recent years.

title: Russia ready to offer higher yields on T-bills.
text:
VIENNA, March 14 (Reuter) - Russia plans to finance nearly half of this year's budget deficit with state securities issues and is prepared to offer higher yields to meet this target, the finance ministry's head of securities, Bella Zlatkis, said. 

 In a clear signal to Russia's inflation-hit financial markets that Moscow will stick to its stabilisation promises, Zlatkis said domestic debt would be a major policy tool this year to support the rouble and to soak up liquidity. 

 She said the government would issue state securities -- mainly short-term Treasury bills -- worth 30 trillion roubles in 1995 to help finance a 72 trillion rouble budget deficit. 

 "We see the domestic debt market as the most important instrument for financial stabilisation now," Zladkis told an international conference on capital markets in the former Soviet Union. 

 "We are also looking for ways to influence money markets to stabilise the rouble jointly with the central bank because interventions on Russia's foreign exchange market are not enough," she said. 

 "We are not panicking about our domestic debt sitiuation, it must be under control. If the only solution is to issue domestic debt at high yields, we are going to do that." 

 Yields on Russian Treasury bills, which were first issued in May 1993, are running at annualised rates of around 300 percent. Inflation was 11 percent a month in February. 

 --Elif Kaban, Vienna Newsroom, 43-1-53112-258

title: Russian Ruble Continues Lower Vs. Dlr, But Shortage Seen
text:
MOSCOW (AP-DJ)--The ruble continued lower against the dollar Friday, but traders said the Russian currency was in short supply and attributed the slide to central bank intervention. 

 At the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICE), Russia's largest, the dollar was fixed at 4191.0 rubles Friday, up from 4170.0 rubles Thursday. 

 Off the exchange, the dollar was quoted about 25 points below the MICE fixing level, reflecting slack demand, traders said. 

 But on the exchange, the central bank took advantage of the situation and bought dollars to keep the market on track. The bank has committed itself to keeping the ruble sliding roughly in line with inflation. 

 Investors, meanwhile, were shifting money back and forth from the exchange to the interbank market to capitalize on the spread, traders said, with no longer-term trends to latch onto. 

 Volume on the exchange was light at 79 million dlrs Friday, down from 102 million dlrs Thursday. 

 Participants said the ruble shortage is likely to continue early next week ahead of Wednesday's record 2.8-trillion-ruble treasury bill offering. T-bills are among the highest-yielding instruments in the money market at the moment, and demand at recent auctions has been strong. 

 Nonetheless, traders said the central bank is likely to keep the dollar steady if not rising against the ruble next week, building its reserves. 

 This week, the dollar gained 1.8% against the Russian currency.

title: Russian Ruble Steadies Vs. Dlr;  Central Bank  Buys Dlrs
text:
MOSCOW (AP-DJ)--The ruble held steady against the dollar Wednesday, but only thanks to huge intervention by the Central Bank of Russia, soaking up huge dollar sales by commercial banks, traders said. 

 At the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICE), Russia's largest, the dollar was fixed at 3988.0 rubles Wednesday, unchanged from Tuesday. 

 'Everyone's out of rubles,' said Alexander Afonin, chief dealer at Credo Bank. 

 Off the MICE, where the central bank's influence isn't as strong, the dollar fell below 3900 rubles Wednesday, trading as much as 100 points below the MICE level. 

 Afonin noted that Russian companies need rubles this week for tax payments, leaving the market undersupplied. Rising ruble interest rates - overnight quotes have surged above 400% a year - also are drawing funds out of the dollar, traders said. 

 New central bank regulations imposed last week to sap demand for the dollar also have thinned demand this week, leaving the central bank the main buyer at the MICE. 

 Wednesday, traders said, the bank bought about 140 million dlrs of the 214 million dlrs traded. 

 'They won't let the dollar fall,' said Afonin. Instead, traders said, the bank has taken the opportunity to build up its reserves. 

 The market is expected to stabilize slightly by the end of this week, traders said, with rubles flowing in. 

 Thursday, however, the dollar is likely to remain steady or gain only slightly, traders said.
